DDB_G0281385.summary:
''rasC'' encodes a G protein of the Ras family of small GTPases. G proteins are key components of signal transduction networks in which they function as molecular signaling switches, binding to GDP in the off state while binding GTP in the on state. Guanine nucleotide-exchange factors (GEF, rasGEF) promote the exchange of GDP for GTP on Ras GTPases thus activating them, while GTPase-activating proteins (GAP, rasGAP) inactivate Ras GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP. RasC activation is abolished in a ''gefA'' null mutant ([/gene/DDB_G0284329 gefA]), indicating that ''gefA'' is the GEF which activates RasC ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11500376 Lim et al. 2001]), ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17380187 Kae et al. 2007]).
''rasC'' is expressed throughout the life cycle with peak expression during development at 20 hours, and with expression enriched in prestalk cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11500376 Lim et al. 2001]). ''rasC'' null cells are incapable of aggregation, but this defect is rescued by exogenous cAMP pulses. ''rasC'' null cells do not produce cAMP in response to 2'-deoxy-cAMP, indicating that G-protein-coupled cAMP receptor activation of adenylate cyclase is regulated by RasC. ''rasC'' null cells also exhibit decreased chemotaxis to cAMP during development and reduced phosphorylation of protein kinase B (AKT/PKB) ([/gene/DDB_G0268620 pkbA]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11500376 Lim et al. 2001]), ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16885420 Bolourani et al. 2006]). Prior to development, vegetative ''rasC'' null cells exhibit reduced random motility, are less polarized and have an altered F-actin distribution. They also have an increased number of lateral pseudopods and an increased rate of endocytosis. ''rasC'' null cells chemotax poorly to folate and exhibit reduced F-actin accumulation, reduced ERK2 ([/gene/DDB_G0283903 erkB]) phosphorylation and reduced PKB phosphorylation in response to folate, indicating that RasC is also involved in transducing chemotactic signals in vegetative cells. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15878331 Lim et al. 2005]).
RasC is a crucial mediator of the chemotactic response to cAMP. Activated RasC binds to the catalytic domain of tor ([/gene/DDB_G0281569 tor]) and stimulates TORC2 to phosphorylate downstream protein kinases, PKB and PKBR1 ([/gene/DDB_G0290157 pkgB]), as well as to activate adenylyl cyclase ([/gene/DDB_G0281545 acaA]) [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/27172998 (Khanna et al. 2016)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18635356 (Kamimura et al. 2008)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20660630 (Cai et al. 2010)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19763972 (Kamimura et al. 2009)]. Rap1 ([/gene/DDB_G0291237 rapA]) positively regulates the RasC-mediated activation of TORC2, suggesting that dual Ras/Rap1 regulation of TORC2 may allow for integration of Ras and Rap1 signaling pathways in directed cell migration. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/27172998 Khanna et al. 2016)]. The Sca1 Ras signaling complex, which includes the RasGEFs GefA and GefH ([/gene/DDB_G0276963 gefH]), and the scaffold protein Sca1 ([/gene/DDB_G0277843 scaA]), is recruited to the plasma membrane of the leading edge of chemotaxing cells during cAMP stimulation where it regulates F-actin dynamics and signal relay by controlling the activation of RasC and the downstream TORC2-PKB pathway. PKB and PKBR1 phosphorylate Sca1 and regulate the membrane localization of the Sca1 complex, and thereby RasC activity, in a negative feedback fashion ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20493808 Charest et al. 2010]). In ''pkaC'' ([/gene/DDB_G0283907 pkaC]) null cells stimulated with cAMP, RasC activation is decreased and Sca1 fails to localize to the plasma membrane, indicating that PKA ([/gene/DDB_G0283907 pkaC], [/gene/DDB_G0279413 pkaR]) is also needed for optimal RasC activation ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28302905 Scavello et al. 2017)]. RasC phosphorylation of AKT/PKB is also dependent on the small GTPase RacE ([/gene/DDB_G0280975 racE]). In contrast to the prevailing view that the GDP-bound forms of G proteins are inactive, RacE-GDP promotes AKT/PKB phosphorylation by assembling a super-complex with RasC-GTP and mTORC2. This super-complex formation is controlled by the cAMP-induced phosphorylation of RacE-GDP by glycogen synthase kinase GSK-3. ([/gene/DDB_G0272110 gskA]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31263268 Senoo et al. 2019)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 22-JAN-2020 RD

DDB_G0269138.summary:
14-3-3 proteins are a group of well-conserved adaptor proteins that form dimers and bind to phosphorylated serine/threonine residues on target proteins. 14-3-3 proteins are involved in the regulation of signaling pathways. ''fttB'' is the sole 14-3-3 related gene in the ''Dictyostelium'' genome. Highest levels of ''fttB'' expression are observed in vegetative cells with decreased expression during development; however FttB protein levels remain constant during development ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9223628 Knetsch et al. 1997]). FttB is found in the cytosol ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/32818671 Li et al. 2020]), is enriched at the cell cortex ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20951045 Zhou et al. 2010]), and is localized to the centrosome during cytokinesis ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25298405 Plak et al. 2014]). FttB interacts with numerous proteins, including the ankyrin repeat-containing protein kinase A ([/gene/DDB_G0289555 arkA]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14597204 Aubry et al. 2003]) the TOR complex 2 protein PiaA ([/gene/DDB_G0277399 piaA]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16079174 Lee et al. 2005]) and the SH2 domain protein LrrB ([/gene/DDB_G0287823 lrrB]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20457612 Sugden et al. 2010]).
In ''Dictyostelium'' FttB coordinates three major cytoskeletal elements: microtubules, actin, and myosin II-to control two critical processes, cytokinesis and cortical mechanics ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20951045 Zhou et al. 2010]). In addition, FttB plays a role in cAMP signaling during development and contributes to the regulation of chemotaxis to cAMP and tip formation ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/32818671 Li et al. 2020]). Down-regulated FttB cells have a slower growth rate and are multi-nucleated and have an altered cleavage furrow morphology, indicating a cytokinesis defect. The cells also have a defect in cytoskeleton organization with shorter microtubules and decreased cortical tension ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20951045 Zhou et al. 2010]). Down-regulated FttB cells also have defects in chemotaxis to cAMP and form mounds with multiple tips ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/32818671 Li et al. 2020]). FttB fails to localize to the cell cortex in ''racE'' null cells ([/gene/DDB_G0280975 racE]) and over-expression of FttB partially rescues the mechanical defect in ''racE'' null cells, suggesting that FttB functions downstream of RacE to regulate the cell cortex and cytokinesis. FttB also interacts with the myosin II heavy chain ([/gene/DDB_G0286355 mhcA]) to regulate its distribution and assembly ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20951045 Zhou et al. 2010]). Large scale immunoprecipitation identified 100 proteins that potentially interact with FttB, including the protein kinases PakA ([/gene/DDB_G0269166 pakA]) and Fray1 ([/gene/DDB_G0278863 fray1]), and the Ras guanine nucleotide exchange factors (RasGEFs) GefM ([/gene/DDB_G0274607 gefM]) and GefQ ([/gene/DDB_G0289665 gefQ]). FttB binding to GefQ regulates tip formation through the Ras GTPase RasB ([/gene/DDB_G0292998 rasB]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/32818671 Li et al. 2020]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 16-DEC-2020 RD

DDB_G0272112.summary: Besides ''mhcA'' ([/gene/DDB_G0286355 mhcA]) that encodes the classical myosin heavy chain, ''Dictyostelium'' carries genes for 12 unconventional myosins. The first 5 unconventional myosins ([/gene/DDB_G0280039 myoA]), ([/gene/DDB_G0289117 myoB]), ([/gene/DDB_G0276617 myoC]), ([/gene/DDB_G0275447 myoD]), ([/gene/DDB_G0288679 myoE]), were isolated from whole genome plasmid clones by low stringency probing with portions of the head region of ''mhcA''. The next 6 unconventional myosins ([/gene/DDB_G0289177 myoF]), ([/gene/DDB_G0276363 myoG]), ([/gene/DDB_G0289447 myoH]), ([/gene/DDB_G0274455 myoI]), ''myoJ'', ([/gene/DDB_G0274575 myoK]) were recognized in large YAC clones that represent the whole genome [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7937787  (Titus et al. 1994)]. MyoJ is a large protein with a myosin motor domain at the N-terminus and a coiled-coil structure in the tail that is predicted to lead to dimerization [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8636147  (Hammer and Jung, 1996)]. MyoJ has the domain structure of class-V unconventional myosins but its sequence is not closely related [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8884597  (Peterson et al. 1996)]. MyoJ is a processive motor that can move long distances along actin filaments without dissociating [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18650439  (Taft et al. 2008)]. MyoJ localizes to contractile vacuole membranes, moves them along the actin cortex, and is required for efficient osmoregulation and the normal accumulation of contractile vacuole membranes in the cortex. [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19687255  (Jung et al. 2009)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 04-SEP-2019 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0291117.summary: NoxA ([/gene/DDB_G0289653 noxA]), NoxB ([/gene/DDB_G0287101 noxB]) and NoxC are homologs of the heme-containing subunit of NADPH oxidase flavocytochromes that generate superoxide for defense and signaling. Each of them has 6 predicted transmembrane regions and uses 4 histidine moieties to bind 2 heme groups. Mutations that inactivate the ''nox'' genes in the genetic background of strain JH10 result in a developmental block at the tipped mound stage, but have no effect on growth in association with bacteria. [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15950752  (Lardy et al. 2005)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16367873  (Benghezal et al. 2006)]. A triple mutant in which ''noxA'', ''noxB'', and ''noxC'' are disrupted in the genetic background of strain AX2 develops normally, but has defects in the defense response to bacteria. The Sentinel cells that normally provide innate immunity in slugs are unable to generate superoxide when all 3 of the ''nox'' genes are deleted. Reactive oxygen species (ROS) stimulate S cells to take up bacteria by phagocytosis and to release mitochondrial DNA nets that trap extracellular bacteria. ''noxA''/''noxB''/''noxC'' triple null mutants release very few DNA nets and fail to clear bacteria from the slugs. [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26927887  (Zhang et al. 2016)]. ''noxA'' is expressed at high levels in vegetative cells and at lower levels during development. ''noxB'' and ''noxC'' are only expressed after 6 hrs of development [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15950752  (Lardy et al. 2005)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 21-DEC-2018 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis
DDB_G0291117.note: There is a 5 nt difference between the sequence from the Sequencing Center and the sequence in GenBank record AY224390, resulting in 2 amino acid exchanges at positions 224 and 225.

DDB_G0273875.summary:
Developing ''Dictyostelium'' cells aggregate to form fruiting bodies containing typically 2 x 10(4) cells. To prevent the formation of an excessively large fruiting body, streams of aggregating cells break up into groups if there are too many cells. The breakup is regulated by a secreted complex of polypeptides called counting factor (CF). CF is composed of 4 polypeptides, including Countin (encoded by the [/gene/DDB_G0274597 ctnA] gene), cf50, [/gene/DDB_G0269248 cf45-1] and [/gene/DDB_G0284363 cf60]. CF50 is 30% identical to lysozymes (but has very little lysozyme activity) and contains distinctive serine-glycine motifs. Transformants with a disrupted cf50 gene, like ''ctnA-'' cells, form abnormally large groups, exhibit increased levels of cytosolic glucose, increased cell-cell adhesion and decreased cell motility. CF50 is present in the same conditioned medium sieve column fraction as the 450 kDa CF complex. In the absence of CF50, secreted countin is degraded, suggesting that one function of CF50 may be to protect countin from degradation. However, unlike''ctnA-'' cells, ''cf50-'' cells differentiate into an abnormally high percentage of cells expressing [/gene/DDB_G0276761 cotB] (a marker expressed in a subset of prespore cells). Also unlike countin, addition of recombinant CF50 decreases the cAMP pulse following stimulation with cAMP. Countin and CF50 require each other's presence to affect group size, but the presence of countin is not necessary for CF50 to bind to cells, and CF50 is not necessary for countin to bind to cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12117815 Brock et al.2002], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12912898 Brock et al. 2003]). CF and group size have also been mathematically modeled [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16371424 (Dallon et al. 2006)], which together with experimental evidence has been reviewed in [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18426773 Jang and Gomer 2008].
Recent studies classified all lysozymes in ''Dictyostelium''. CF50 and CF45-1 have been assigned to belong to the Entamoeba-type lysozyme family that contain a GH25 domain. Like the other family members ([/gene/DDB_G0274181 lyEh1], [/gene/DDB_G0293492 lyEh2], [/gene/DDB_G0293566 lyEh3], [/gene/DDB_G0276439 lyEh4]), CF50 and CF45-1 have the three conserved Asp and Glu residues, though these counting factor proteins have shown only little, if any lysozyme activity [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/32061941 (Lamrabet et al. 2020)]Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 13-APR-2020 PF

DDB_G0288257.summary:
DNA-dependent RNA polymerase catalyzes the transcription of DNA into RNA using the four ribonucleoside triphosphates as substrates ([/ontology/go/0003899/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase activity]). Three distinct zinc-containing RNA polymerases are found in eukaryotic nuclei: [/gene/DDB_G0275759 rpa1] for the ribosomal RNA precursor ([/ontology/go/0006360/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase I promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005736/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase I complex]), [/gene/DDB_G0279193 rpb1] for the mRNA precursor ([/ontology/go/0006366/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase II promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005665/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase II, core complex]), and [/gene/DDB_G0277199 rpc1] for 5S and tRNA genes ([/ontology/go/0006383/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase III promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005666/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase III complex]).
RNA polymerase II is composed of 12 subunits: [/gene/DDB_G0279193 rpb1], [/gene/DDB_G0288257 rpb2], [/gene/DDB_G0292244 rpb3], [/gene/DDB_G0282739 rpb4], [/gene/DDB_G0291636 rpb5], [/gene/DDB_G0291037 rpb6], [/gene/DDB_G0284891 rpb7], [/gene/DDB_G0278039 rpb8], [/gene/DDB_G0268306 rpb9], [/gene/DDB_G0272036 rpb10], [/gene/DDB_G0277677 rpb11], and[/gene/DDB_G0283365 rpb12]. Subunits 5, 6, 8, 10, and 12 are common to all threeRNA polymerases (reviewed by [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9618449 Hampsey] in 1998).
Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 09-APR-2004 PG

DDB_G0268198.summary:
DNA-dependent RNA polymerase catalyzes the transcription of DNA into RNA using the four ribonucleoside triphosphates as substrates ([/ontology/go/0003899/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase activity]). Three distinct zinc-containing RNA polymerases are found in eukaryotic nuclei: [/gene/DDB_G0275759 rpa1] for the ribosomal RNA precursor ([/ontology/go/0006360/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase I promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005736/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase I complex]), [/gene/DDB_G0279193 rpb1] for the mRNA precursor ([/ontology/go/0006366/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase II promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005665/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase II, core complex]), and [/gene/DDB_G0277199 rpc1] for 5S and tRNA genes ([/ontology/go/0006383/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase III promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005666/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase III complex]).
RNA polymerase I is a multisubunit complex. The subunits encoded by [/gene/DDB_G0275759 rpa1] (ortholog of ''S. cerevisiae RPA190''), [/gene/DDB_G0288449 rpc2] (''RPA135''), [/gene/DDB_G0268198 rpa43] (''RPA43''), [/gene/DDB_G0290909 rpa49] (''RPA49''), and [/gene/DDB_G0278263 rpa12] (''RPA12'') are unique to RNA polymerase I. Two subunits, [/gene/DDB_G0291362 rpc19] and [/gene/DDB_G0282339 rpa5] (''RPC19'' and ''RPC40'' in ''S. cerevisiae''), are common to RNA polymerase I and RNA polymerase III and correspond to subunits 3 and 11 of RNA polymerase II. Subunits [/gene/DDB_G0291636 rpb5], [/gene/DDB_G0291037 rpb6], [/gene/DDB_G0278039 rpb8], [/gene/DDB_G0272036 rpb10], and [/gene/DDB_G0283365 rpb12] are common to all three RNA polymerases. Yeast has two additional subunits, ''RPA34'' and ''RPA14'', that do not have clear orthologs in other species, including in ''Dictyostelium'' ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12407181 Peyroche et al. 2002], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12381659 Schramm and Hernandez 2001]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 13-APR-2004 PG

DDB_G0274595.summary: ''catA'' encodes the catalase that converts methanol to the toxic compounds formaldehyde and formic acid such that cells cannot grow in the presence of 2% methanol [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11004503  (Garcia et al. 2000)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11782526  (Garcia et al. 2002)]. Mutations in ''catA'' that inactivate the enzyme make the cells methanol resistant (metR). The metR phenotype is a useful recessive marker in parasexual genetics of ''Dictyostelium'' that can be easily selected. Mutants with little or no catalase activity in vegetative cells grow and develop normally but are hypersensitive to oxidative stress from hydrogen peroxide which is normally converted to harmless oxygen and water by catalase [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2921242  (Madigan and Katz 2002)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11004503  (Garcia et al. 2000)]. Curcumin reduces catalase A enzyme levels and negatively regulates ''catA'' mRNA levels, an effect that is mediated by PKA ([/gene/DDB_G0283907 pkaC], [/gene/DDB_G0279413 pkaR]) [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29135990  (Swatson et al. 2017)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 27-SEP-2018 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0269124.summary: ''dcsA'' encodes cellulose synthetase which adds beta-1,4 glucosyl units from UDP-glucose to cellulose polymers [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10681463  (Blanton et al. 2000)]. Cellulose is found in the extracellular matrix that surrounds ''Dictyostelium'' slugs as well as in the cell walls of spores and stalk cells. The ''dcsA'' gene was isolated from a REMI mutant that fails to accumulate cellulose at any stage of development. DcsA has a transmembrane domain with 3 hydrophobic regions that is essential for proper function [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25208883  (Kuwayama et al. 2014)]. mRNA starts to accumulate from ''dcsA'' after aggregation is complete (T=11 hrs) and reaches a peak during culmination at T=20 hrs [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25887420  (Rosengarten et al. 2015)]. This pattern is consistent with the flux-balance model of carbohydrate metabolism during development [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/988019  (Loomis and Thomas, 1976)]. Cells in which ''dcsA'' is disrupted can form migrating slugs that initiate culmination, but cannot form fruiting bodies because they collapse due to the lack of cellulose in the stalk as they try to stand up [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10681463  (Blanton et al. 2000)]. After some time, they make small, round spore-like cells, but these do not have the spore coats like those observed on the outside of wild type spores because their spore coat proteins are not organized around a central layer of cellulose [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11428129  (Zhang et al. 2001)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 15-MAR-2017 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0274081.summary: ''gstA2'' encodes the enzyme glutathione S-transferase. Glutathione S-transferase plays an important role in cellular metabolism and detoxification by catalyzing the conjugation of glutathione to electrophilic endobiotic and xenobiotic substrates to reduce their interaction with cellular macromolecules. The plant polyphenol curcumin induces a significant increase in ''gstA2'' expression ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26449461 Garige et al. 2015]). ''gstA2'' is expressed in vegetatively growing cells. ''gstA2'' expression decreases during early development, but increases during slug and fruiting body formation. RNAi-mediated knockdown of ''gstA2'' results in decreased cell proliferation. In addition, ''gstA2'' knockdown cells have developmental abnormalities starting at the slug stage, including abnormally thick slugs which failed to form mature fruiting bodies at 24 hours of development. These results demonstrate that ''gstA2'' plays a role in proliferation and late stage development (Garige, et al 2021, PMID:33909675). Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 22-JUL-2021 RD

DDB_G0277503.summary:
Ammonia signaling is essential to the developmental program of ''Dictyostelium''. It is involved in regulatingchemotaxis, the choice between slug migration and culmination, and cell-type specification via differential geneexpression. Ammonia concentrations are regulated in part by environmental factors, however, cellular processes such astransport ([/ontology/go/0008519/annotation/page/1 ammonium transmembrane transporter activity]) and metabolism can alter intracellular concentrations. In the ''Dictyostelium'' proteome, three putative ammonium transporters exist: [/gene/DDB_G0277503 amtA], [/gene/DDB_G0277889 amtB], and [/gene/DDB_G0267424 amtC]. The transcript levels of the three ''amt'' genes are constant throughout development, as determined by RT-PCR ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14686953 Follstaedt et al. 2003]); however, by Northern blot, another group has found the ''amtA'' gene to be strongly expressed until after the post-aggregation stage ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17951519 Yoshino et al.2007]). Discrepancies were also found in the spatial expression pattern: Follstaedt ''et al.'' localized ''amtA'' to the prestalk cells using ''in situ'' hybridization; while cell separation followed by Northern blotting showed an enrichment in prespore cells (Yoshino ''et al.''). The ''amtB'' transcript is observed primarily in prepore regions and in the spore region of the sorus, but is absent from the upper and lower cups. Expression of ''amtC'' is similar to that of '' amtB'', however, it appears transiently in the anterior tip during the first finger stage. Disruption of the '' amtC'' gene results in larger multicelluar structures and developmental arrest at the slug stage, although a small percentage of slugs are able to fruit after 40+ hours of starvation ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14686953 Follstaedt et al.2003]).
The ''amtA'' null mutant forms small aggregates and small fruiting bodies ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14686953 Follstaedt et al.2003], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17951519 Yoshino et al.2007]). In addition, the mutant has increased intracellular ammonium levels and reduced extracellular ammonium levels, indicating a role for AmtA in ammonium export. This defect in ammonium homeostasis is also associated with decreased spore viability ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17951519 Yoshino et al. 2007]). Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 18-AUG-2008 PG

DDB_G0282739.summary:
DNA-dependent RNA polymerase catalyzes the transcription of DNA into RNA using the four ribonucleoside triphosphates as substrates ([/ontology/go/0003899/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase activity]). Three distinct zinc-containing RNA polymerases are found in eukaryotic nuclei: [/gene/DDB0216292 DDB0216292] for the ribosomal RNA precursor ([/ontology/go/0006360/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase I promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005736/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase I complex]), [/gene/DDB0215406 DDB0215406] for the mRNA precursor ([/ontology/go/0006366/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase II promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005665/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase II, core complex]), and [/gene/DDB0215406 DDB0215406] for 5S and tRNA genes ([/ontology/go/0006383/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase III promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005666/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase III complex]).
RNA polymerase II is composed of 12 subunits: [/gene/DDB0215406 DDB0215406], [/gene/DDB0187850 DDB0187850], [/gene/DDB0216289 DDB0216289], [/gene/DDB0204958 DDB0204958], [/gene/DDB0215452 DDB0215452], [/gene/DDB0219633 DDB0219633], [/gene/DDB0216295 DDB0216295], [/gene/DDB0204381 DDB0204381], [/gene/DDB0202109 DDB0202109], [/gene/DDB0216949 DDB0216949], [/gene/DDB0218015 DDB0218015], and[/gene/DDB0216300 DDB0216300]. Subunits 5, 6, 8, 10, and 12 are common to all threeRNA polymerases (reviewed by [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9618449 Hampsey] in 1998).
Expression of ''rbp4'' in ''Dictyostelium'' is developmentally regulated, with highest expression at the loose aggregate stage. In vegetative cells and early developing cells, two transcripts are detected, while only the largest form of the transcript is found at later stages. In late development, the ''rbp4'' transcript is found in prespore cells. The Rpb4 protein is found both in the cytoplasm and in the nucleus. DDB_G0292268.summary:
''rab2A'' encodes a guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G protein) of the Rab family of small GTPases. G proteins are key components of signal transduction networks in which they function as molecular signaling switches, binding to GDP in the off state while binding GTP in the on state. Guanine nucleotide-exchange factors (GEFs) promote the exchange of GDP for GTP on Rab GTPases thus activating them, while GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) inactivate Rab GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP. Rab2A is highly similar to human RAB2B. Rab2A is associated with both the Golgi membrane and the contractile vacuole system [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/27240981 (Maringer et al. 2016)]. In addition, proteomic analysis revealed that Rab2A is localized to lipid droplets ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24036346 Du, et al. 2013]) and also to the Legionella-containing vacuole [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28183814 (Schmolders et al. 2017)].
''rab2A'' is involved in signaling networks that regulate vesicle trafficking, contractile vacuole function and response to osmotic stress. Rab2A over-expressing cells and dominant-negative (DN) Rab2A cells display a significant decrease in the rate of phagocytosis, while the rate of phagocytosis is significantly increased in constitutively active (CA) Rab2A cells. Both CA and DN Rab2A mutants also had defects in development, growth, and cell-cell adhesion [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25157910 (Maringer et al. 2014)]. Both Rab2A and Rab GTPase RabS ([/gene/DDB_G0282537 rabS]) localize to both the Golgi membrane and the contractile vacuole system. ''rab2A'' and ''rabS'' over-expressing and mutant cell lines show defects in osmoregulation under osmotically stressed conditions, indicating that both genes are involved in the regulation of the response to osmotic stress. In both Rab2 overexpressing cells and CA Rab2 mutant cells in hypo-osmotic conditions, the contractile vacuoles appeared to have fused into one large contractile vacuole, indicating that these cells were not able to expel water and these cells eventually lysed. DN Rab2 mutant cells were swollen and lacked contractile vacuoles [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/27240981 (Maringer et al. 2016)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 22-SEP-2020 RD

DDB_G0287689.summary: Microtubules are cytoskeletal components found in all eukaryotes where they buttress cellular extensions and connect chromosomes to centrosomes. These hollow filaments are polymers of alpha-tubulin and beta-tubulin that are encoded by ''tubA'' and ([/gene/DDB_G0269196 tubB]), respectively, in Dictyostelium [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8227212  (Trivinos-Lagos et al. 1993)]. Polymerization of alpha/beta heterodimers is initiated at the MicroTubule Organizing Center (MTOC) and extends in the plus end direction to the periphery of the cell where the microtubules can couple to the actin cortex and make rapid sweeping movements across the whole cell [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15527790  (Fischer et al. 2004)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16942924  (Heinrich and Sackmann 2006)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20658257  (Samereier et al. 2010)]. The molecular motors dynein ([/gene/DDB_G0276355 dhcA]), ([/gene/DDB_G0280849 dicA]) and the kinesin genes organize the microtubule network and use it to move cargo to specific destinations [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8816999  (Koonce and Samso, 1996)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10545495  (Pollock et al. 1999)]. The sequence of the gene encoding alpha-tubulin has been highly conserved during evolution making it useful for phylogenetic analyses of the dictyostelids [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17068267  (Schaap et al. 2006)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 06-NOV-2017 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

LSM10 and LSM11 associate with the U7snRNA, whereas LSM12 is hypothesized to be involved in RNA methylation ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11574479 Pillai et al. 2001], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15225602 Albrecht and Lengauer 2004]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 13-MAR-2006 KP

DDB_G0269212.summary: The ABC superfamily of genes is one of the largest in the genomes of both bacteria and eukaryotes. The proteins encoded by these genes all carry a characteristic 200- to 250-amino-acid ATP-binding cassette that gives them their family name ([/ontology/go/0042626/annotation/page/1 ATPase activity, coupled to transmembrane movement of substances]). In bacteria they are mostly involved in nutrient import, while in eukaryotes many are involved in export ([/ontology/go/0006810/annotation/page/1 transport]). Seven different families have been defined in eukaryotes based on sequence homology, domain topology, and function. Sequences from the well-advanced ''Dictyostelium'' genome project have allowed to recognize 71 members of this superfamily (including one on the chromosome 2 duplication). The ABCG family is characterized by the ABC domain preceding the transmembrane domain ([/ontology/go/0016021/annotation/page/1 integral to membrane]). All of the members of this family in animals are half-transporters while all of the fungal members are full transporters with two ABC-transmembrane units. No members of this family are found in bacteria. ''Dictyostelium'' and ''Arabidopsis'' have members of both types ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12456012 Anjard and Loomis 2002]). Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 18-OCT-2004 PG

DDB_G0288511.summary:
The ''sadA'' gene has been identified by its disruption in a substrate adhesion-deficient REMI mutant. SadA- cells grow in plastic dishes without attaching to the substrate. The sadA- mutant also shows slightly impaired cytokinesis, aberrant actin filament organization, and a phagocytosis defect. Deletion of the sadA gene by homologous recombination recreated the original mutant phenotype. Expression of sadA-GFP in sadA-null cells restored the wild-type phenotype. SadA-GFP localized to the cell surface, appropriate for an adhesion molecule. SadA contains nine putative transmembrane domains and three conserved EGF-like repeats in a predicted extracellular domain. EGF repeats are found in proteins known to be involved in adhesion, such as tenascins and integrins, suggesting that sadA is the first substrate adhesion receptor to be identified in Dictyostelium [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12499361 (Fey et al. 2002)].
Kowal and Chisholm showed that the cytoplasmic tail of the SadA protein has an important function in cell-substrate adhesion. A SadA tailless mutant was unable to rescue the sadA adhesion deficiency and overexpression of the SadA tail domain reduced adhesion in wild-type cells. Mutation analysis revealed that the phosphorylation status of serine residues in the tail region plays a role in adhesion. In fractionation assays SadA was found in the insoluble fraction and was also identified to interact with the actin bundling protein Cortexillin I ([/gene/DDB_G0289483 ctxA]). This might suggest that phosphorylation/dephosphorylation regulates adhesion through the binding of SadA to Cortexillin I [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21441344 (Kowal and Chisholm 2011)].
SadA also plays a role in cell adhesion by controlling the levels of [/gene/DDB_G0287363 sibA] adhesion molecules at the cell surface by stabilizing the intracellular SibA protein and possibly by assisting intracellular transport to the surface[http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22219373 (Froquet et al. 2012)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 27-SEP-2012 PF; annotation contributions: PMID 22219373 Pierre Cosson.

Two additional PLDs, [/gene/DDB_G0287649 pldY] and[/gene/DDB_G0282579 pldZ], are related to mammalian PLD3 which is related to the PLD family but its function is unclear.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 26-OCT-2004 KP

DDB_G0283903.summary: ''erkB'' encodes a MAP kinase that is essential for aggregation and cAMP relay ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7844154 Segall et al. 1995)]. The protein kinase activity is stimulated by cAMP binding to CAR1 ([/gene/DDB_G0273397 carA-1]), ([/gene/DDB_G0273533 carA-2]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8631932 Maeda et al. 1996)]. ERK2 associates with and reversibly inhibits RegA ([/gene/DDB_G0284331 regA]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31730032 Adhikari et al. 2019)] which reduces the turnover of internal cAMP such that it can accumulate and activate PKA ([/gene/DDB_G0283907 pkaC]), ([/gene/DDB_G0279413 pkaR]). A feedback loop in which PKA activity inhibits ERK2 inhibition of RegA leads to an increase in cAMP phosphodiesterase activity that reduces the concentration of cAMP. As a result of this circuit and the activation of adenylyl cyclase when cAMP binds to CAR1, cAMP oscillates with a period of about 6 minutes during early aggregation ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9843585 Laub and Loomis et al. 1998)] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15131307 Maeda et al. 2004)]. Stochastic noise and synchronization make these oscillations robust ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17997595 Kim et al. 2007)]. ERK2 was also found to associate with Galpha4 ([/gene/DDB_G0285425 gpaD]) which is generated in response to folate. Activated ERK2 also appears to have a function in morphogenesis during culmination ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19765570 Nguyen and Hadwiger et al. 2009)]. A phosphoproteomics analysis revealed a core set of around 80 proteins that are phosphorylated by ''erkB'' in response to different chemoattractants. Many of the phosphorylated proteins are themselves other signaling proteins, revealing a central role for ''erkB'' in regulating chemotaxis ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30612939 Nichols et al. 2018)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 11-DEC-2015 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0291293.summary: ''rabU'' encodes a guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G protein) of the Rab family of small GTPases. G proteins are key components of signal transduction networks in which they function as molecular signaling switches, binding to GDP in the off state while binding GTP in the on state. Guanine nucleotide-exchange factors (GEFs) promote the exchange of GDP for GTP on Rab GTPases thus activating them, while GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) inactivate Rab GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP.Basic annotations have been added to this gene, 10-FEB-2021 RD

DDB_G0271514.summary:
DNA-dependent RNA polymerase catalyzes the transcription of DNA into RNA using the four ribonucleoside triphosphates as substrates ([/ontology/go/0003899/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase activity]). Three distinct zinc-containing RNA polymerases are found in eukaryotic nuclei: [/gene/DDB_G0275759 rpa1] for the ribosomal RNA precursor ([/ontology/go/0006360/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase I promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005736/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase I complex]), [/gene/DDB_G0279193 rpb1] for the mRNA precursor ([/ontology/go/0006366/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase II promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005665/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase II, core complex]), and [/gene/DDB_G0277199 rpc1] for 5S and tRNA genes ([/ontology/go/0006383/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase III promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005666/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase III complex]).
RNA polymerase III is a multisubunit complex. The subunits encoded by [/gene/DDB_G0277199 rpc1] (ortholog of ''S. cerevisiae RPO31''), [/gene/DDB_G0293560 rpa2] (''RPC2''), [/gene/DDB_G0268080 rpc3] (''RPC82''),[/gene/DDB_G0277671 rpc4] (''RPC53''), [/gene/DDB_G0271514 rpc5] (''RPC37''), [/gene/DDB_G0286521 rpc9] (''RPC17''), [/gene/DDB_G0272022 rpc34] (''RPC34''), [/gene/DDB_G0273425 rpc25-1] (''RPC25''), and [/gene/DDB_G0287707 rpc11] (''RPC11'') are unique to RNA polymerase III. Orthologs of ''RPC31'' and ''RPC17'' have not been identified in the ''Dictyostelium'' genome. Two subunits, [/gene/DDB_G0291362 rpc19] and [/gene/DDB_G0282339 rpa5] (''RPC19'' and ''RPC40'' in ''S. cerevisiae''), are common to RNA polymerase I and RNA polymerase III and correspond to subunits 3 and 11 of RNA polymerase II. Subunits [/gene/DDB_G0291636 rpb5], [/gene/DDB_G0291037 rpb6], [/gene/DDB_G0278039 rpb8], [/gene/DDB_G0272036 rpb10], and [/gene/DDB_G0283365 rpb12] are common to all three RNA polymerases ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12407181 Peyroche et al. 2002], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12381659 Schramm and Hernandez 2001]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 11-JUN-2009 PG

DDB_G0275123.summary:
The AlyA protein has been purified from ''Dictyostelium'' cells as a major protein with lysozyme activity. The protein sequence of this lysozyme was backtranslated and used to search the cDNA database, resulting in retrieval of the full ''alyA'' coding sequence. AlyA-GFP localized to numerous small vesicles devoid of other known lysozymal enzymes, distributed throughout the cytoplasm.
Deletion of the alyA gene by homologues recombination resulted in a mutant that had only 40% of the wild-type lysozyme activity. When mutant cells were grown on bacteria, they initially made plaques that were only half the size measured in wild-type. However, repeated plating showed that the plaque size for mutants recovered over time, even surpassing that of wild-type. The larger plaque size occurred despite the constant lower level of enzyme activity. Uptake of fluorescently labeled yeast showed that the larger plaque size was due to increased phagocytosis. Thus, the mutant seems to compensates a defect in digestion with an increase in food uptake.
A search of ''alyA''-similar ''Dictyostelium'' sequences resulted in the identification of two almost identical adjacent genes, [/gene/DDB_G0275119 alyB] and [/gene/DDB_G0275121 alyC], and two more distantly related genes: ''alyD'', (present in two copies on chromosome 2: [/gene/DDB_G0273197 alyD-1], [/gene/DDB_G0273731 alyD-2]) and [/gene/DDB_G0286229 alyL]. These enzymes are not similar to any other known lysozymes. Thus, it has been suggested that these proteins represent a new class of lysozymes [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15640146 (Mueller et al., 2005)].
A comprehensive study classified all lysozymes in ''Dictyostelium''. In addition to the 5 known amoeba like lysozymes ([/gene/DDB_G0275123 alyA], [/gene/DDB_G0275119 alyB], [/gene/DDB_G0275121 alyC], [/gene/DDB_G0273197 alyD-1] and [/gene/DDB_G0286229 alyL] ), two new related lysozymes in this family have been identified, [/gene/DDB_G0282905 alyE] and [/gene/DDB_G0282893 alyF]. Because in the past, gene models for these two new lysozymes gave rise to proteins with transmembrane domains, one or two respectively, they first have been named alyTM1 and alyTM2. However, new sequence analyses resulted in updated gene models coding for proteins containing signal peptides like the other 5 members of the aly family. Alignment of the 7 proteins allowed the identification of one conserved Asp and one Glu residue in the C- terminal portion [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/32061941 (Lamrabet et al. 2020)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 20-APR-2020 PF

DDB_G0293362.summary: SRCP1, a novel molecular chaperone unique to ''Dictyostelium'', suppresses aggregation of proteins with long polyglutamine (polyQ) tracts. PolyQ-expanded proteins misfold and lead to formation of protein aggregates, causing neurodegenerative diseases in human. SRCP1 is necessary for the resistance of ''Dictyostelium'' to polyglutamine aggregation, and is sufficient to convey resistance to polyglutamine aggregation in human and zebrafish. In the presence of SRCP1, aggregation-prone polyQ proteins are degraded via the proteasome. SRCP1 lacks any identifiable chaperone domains but rather utilizes a C-terminal domain that resembles amyloid to suppress aggregation of polyQ-expanded proteins. [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30029002  (Santarriaga et al. 2018)]. Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 26-JUL-2018 RD

DDB_G0267404.summary: The motor domain in the kinesin encoded by ''kif6'' belongs to the MCAK subfamily of minus-end directed mitotic motors that are also able to catalyze the depolymerization of microtubules that occurs as chromosomes move towards the poles during anaphase [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9693369  (de Hostos et al. 1998)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14641909  (Kollmar and Glockner 2003)]. There is a SAM domain at the N-terminus that can associate with SAM domains in other proteins. The motor domain is central in Kif6. Reduction of ''kif6'' expression by regulated RNAi indicated that this kinesin plays a vital role in ''Dictyostelium''. As the level of Kif6 went down, many of the spindle assemblies became abnormal and the chromosomes were seen to lag during anaphase [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19286984  (Tikhonenko et al. 2009)]. Based on the sequences of the motor domains six of the 13 kinesins ([/gene/DDB_G0267396 kif2], [/gene/DDB_G0285101 kif4], ''kif6'', [/gene/DDB_G0291039 kif11], [/gene/DDB_G0268258 kif12], and [/gene/DDB_G0288361 kif13]) are members of mitotic motor families. Like each of the other mitotic kinesins, ''kif6'' mRNA levels are low in growing cells and increase to relatively high levels between 12 and 18 hrs of development before returning to very low levels [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9693369  (de Hostos et al. 1998)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25887420  (Rosengarten et al. 2015)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 13-JUN-2017 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0281563.summary:
Members of the Myb family of transcription factors are typically composed of two or three imperfect repeats each of about 50 amino acids. These repeats fold into a variant of the helix-turn-helix motif have DNA binding activity. The Myb motif has been well conserved during evolution (see [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10331990 Guo et al. 1999] and references therein).
''mybC'' was isolated as a REMI mutant that is unable to culminate. This defect is non-cell autonomous and can be rescued by overexpression of [/gene/DDB_G0283907 pkaC]. However even when their defect is bypassed, ''mybC'' null slugs and culminants produce little if any of the intercellular signalling peptides SDF-1 and SDF-2 that are believed to be released by prestalk cells at culmination. In ''mybC'' null cells, several culmination genes are expressed at reduced levels: [/gene/DDB_G0269132 ecmB], [/gene/DDB_G0289075 spiA], [/gene/DDB_G0276941 cotA], and [/gene/DDB_G0276761 cotB]. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10331990 Guo et al. 1999]). ''mybC'' is downregulated in a STATa ([/gene/DDB_G0281381 dstA]) null mutant. In addition, the transcription factor CudA ([/gene/DDB_G0284465 cudA]), as well as additional prestalk genes, such as ([/gene/DDB_G0291291 ecmF]) are downregulated in ''mybC'' null mutants, suggesting that ''mybC'' may work in conjunction with STATa to regulate the expression of prestalk-specific genes. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/27125566 (Saga et al. 2016)]).
MybC was found in the nucleus of prestalk cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10331990 Guo et al. 1999]) using a beta-galactosidase gene driven by 1.85 kb of upstream sequence and the first 16 amino acids of mybC. [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11553701 Iranfar et al. (2001)] found this gene overexpressed in prespore cells by Northern blot. Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 18-OCT-2016 RD
DDB_G0281563.note: There is a 1 nt difference between the sequence from the Sequencing Center and the sequence in GenBank record AF098507, resulting in 1 amino acid substitution at position 29.

DDB_G0277143.summary: Signal transduction from surface receptors is often mediated by heterotrimeric G proteins that dissociate into alpha and beta/gamma subunits when GTP replaces bound GDP on the Galpha subunit. ''gpbA'' encodes the evolutionarily conserved beta subunit which dimerizes with the gamma subunit in the presence of the phosducin-like protein PhLP1 ([/gene/DDB_G0292850 phlp1]) [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3151181  (Pupillo et al. 1988)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16135826  (Knol et al. 2005)]. Mutant cells lacking Gbeta grow well axenically but are defective in phagocytosis of bacteria [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8099335  (Lilly et al. 1993)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9647646  (Peracino et al. 1998)]. ''gpbA'' mutant cells have reduced levels of the cAMP receptor CAR1 ([/gene/DDB_G0273397 carA-1], [/gene/DDB_G0273533 carA-2]) and so do not respond to the chemoattractant cAMP. Consequently, neither adenylyl cyclase nor guanylyl cyclase are stimulated by cAMP and the cells fail to develop [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7790362  (Wu et al. 1995)]. The Cytosolic Regulator of Adenylyl Cyclase (CRAC) ([/gene/DDB_G0285161 dagA]) appears to serve as an adaptor linking beta/gamma subunits to activation of adenylyl cyclase ([/gene/DDB_G0281545 acaA]) [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8089184  (Insall et al. 1994)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7790361  (Lilly and Devreotes, 1995)]. The cAMP generated when adenylyl cyclase is activated acts as a feedback inhibitor by stimulating PKA ([/gene/DDB_G0283907 pkaC], [/gene/DDB_G0279413 pkaR]) activity that inhibits ACA activation by beta/gamma/CRAC [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9843585  (Laub and Loomis, 1994)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18783170  (Loomis et al. 2008)]. Galpha2 ([/gene/DDB_G0276267 gpaB]) and Gbeta/Ggamma remain dissociated as long as cAMP is bound to CAR1 which indicates that adaptation of the cAMP response is achieved downstream of the G protein response [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11264536  (Janetopoulos et al. 2001)]. The rate of dissociation of Gbeta/Ggamma from the membrane increases when cAMP is bound to CAR1 which may facilitate activation of cytosolic components such as RasGAPs [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19584094  (Elzie et al. 2009)]. Using an acute ''gpbA'' gene inhibition approach, Hoeller and colleagues suggest that G-beta regulates the strength of coupling between actin oscillators for efficient polarity and directional migration [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26890004  (Hoeller et al. 2016)]. ElmoE ([/gene/DDB_G0279657 elmoE]) associates with the Gbeta/Ggamma subunits and interacts with Dock-like proteins DocC ([/gene/DDB_G0292004 docC]) and possibly ZizA ([/gene/DDB_G0275035 zizA]) to activate the small GTPase RacB ([/gene/DDB_G0279605 racB]) and promote actin polymerization in the leading edge of migrating cells [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22264729  (Yan et al. 2012)]. In addition to its role in cAMP signaling, ''gpbA'' is also involved in folate-mediated calcium signaling-the calcium responses of vegetative cells to folate are dramatically impaired in gpbA and gpaD ([/gene/DDB_G0285425 gpaD]) null mutants [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12952083  (Nebl et al. 2002)]. Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 04-APR-2019 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis
phenotypes: decreased protein localization to plasma membrane
decreased positive regulation of GTPase activity

DDB_G0277825.summary: ''arcA'' encodes the 41 kDa subunit of the Arp2/3 complex [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11807934  (Insall et al. 2001)]. The seven subunits of this 200 kDa complex are encoded by ''arcA'', ([/gene/DDB_G0282813 arcB]), ([/gene/DDB_G0292804 arcC]), ([/gene/DDB_G0269102 arcD]), ([/gene/DDB_G0288319 arcE]), ([/gene/DDB_G0272106 arpB]) and ([/gene/DDB_G0283755 arpC]). The subunits of mammalian Arp2/3 are very similar to ''Dictyostelium'' homologs. Arp2/3 binds to the side of F-actin filaments and initiates polymerization of a new F-actin chain at an angle of 70 degrees leading to a branched actin network that can alter the shape of cells. The ability to nucleate new actin filaments is greatly stimulated by direct interactions with members of the WASP/SCAR family [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11807934  (Insall et al. 2001)]. The Arp2/3 complex largely mediates the actin polymerization response to chemotactic stimulation and contributes to cell motility, pseudopod extension and adhesion in Dictyostelium chemotaxis. The complete Arp2/3 complex is essential for growth; partial loss of activity of either ArcB or ArpB impairs growth and chemotaxis [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17553489  (Langridge and Kay, 2007)]. mRNA from each of the genes encoding Arp2/3 subunits accumulates coordinately to reach a peak at 3 hours of development and gradually decreases thereafter [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25887420  (Rosengarten et al. 2015)]. The Arp2/3 complex interacts with the protein CARMIL, which serves as a scaffold for the assembly of a larger complex of proteins involved in the nucleation and termination of actin filament assembly. The complex consists of CARMIL ([/gene/DDB_G0292386 carmil]), AcpA, ([/gene/DDB_G0267374 acpA]) AcpB, ([/gene/DDB_G0272104 acpB]) the Arp2/3 complex, and type I myosins MyoB ([/gene/DDB_G0289117 myoB]) and MyoC ([/gene/DDB_G0276617 myoC]) [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11425877  (Jung et al. 2001)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 17-MAY-2019 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0274387.summary: ''Dictyostelium'' development is sensitive to Li+ treatment. Mutants that lack the ''dpoA'' gene, encoding a prolyl oligopeptidase, are able to develop in the presence of Li+. Prolyl oligopeptidases [EC 3.4.21.26] are endopeptidases that cleave Pro-X amino acid bonds on small polypeptides ([/ontology/go/0006508/annotation/page/1 proteolysis]), ([/ontology/go/0004287/annotation/page/1 prolyl oligopeptidase activity]). Inositol (1,4,5) trisphosphate (IP3) levels, known to be affected by Li+, are increased in the ''dpoA'' mutant ([/ontology/go/0009966/annotation/page/1 regulation of signal transduction]). IP3 concentrations increase via an unconventional mechanism that involves enhanced dephosphorylation of inositol (1,3,4,5,6) pentakisphosphate. Loss of DpoA activity therefore counteracts the reduction in IP3 concentration caused by Li+ treatment. No genetic interaction was observed with [/gene/DDB_G0272110 gskA], another major cellular target of Li+ ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10329620 Williams et al. 1999]). Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 19-SEP-2003 PG

DDB_G0288147.summary: ''pkcA'' encodes a protein kinase C ortholog that is expressed throughout development, but expression switches from pre stalk cells in the mound to prespore cells in slugs. ''pkcA'' null cells form multiple small mounds and display multiple cAMP wave generating centers. In addition, ''pkcA'' null cells have defects in chemotaxis and cell-cell adhesion. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26183108 Mohamed et al. 2015)]. ''pkcA'' regulates the initiation of development through the quorum sensing pathway, serving as a negative regulator of aggregation. ''pkcA'' and phospholipase D ([/gene/DDB_G0279483 pldB]) functionally interact to regulate a number of developmentally critical processes, such as adhesion, cell sorting and differentiation. PkcA positively regulates phospholipase D activity, suggesting that PkcA acts through regulating PldB ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28257811 Singh et al. 2017)]. ''pkcA'' is involved in the signal transduction pathway responsible for AprA-dependent ([/gene/DDB_G0281663 aprA]) chemorepulsion. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30462573 Rijal et al. 2018]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 11-DEC-2018 RD

DDB_G0292850.summary:
In mammalian cells, phosducin binds to G proteins and modulate their activity. Phylogenetic analyses revealed that there are three groups of phodsucin proteins. ''Dictyostelium'', like mammalian cells and ''Drosophila'', has one member from each group: [/gene/DDB_G0292850 phlp1], [/gene/DDB_G0285433 phlp2], and [/gene/DDB_G0293848 phlp3]. Phosducins consist of an N-terminal domain containing three helices which binds the alpha subunit of G proteins, and a C-terminal domain which bears similarity to thioredoxin and binds to the beta/gamma subunit of G proteins.
Phlp1 contains all the conserved residues necessary for Galpha and Gbeta/gamma binding. Disruption of the ''phlp1'' gene causes numerous defects. The mutant grows slowly both on bacteria and in axenic medium. The mutant fails to aggregate ([/ontology/go/0031152/annotation/page/1 aggregation involved in sorocarp development]), and that defect is not rescued with mixing with wild-type cells or with exogenous cAMP. The mutant also has defects in [/ontology/go/0043327/annotation/page/1 chemotaxis to cAMP] and [/ontology/go/0043326/annotation/page/1 chemotaxis to folate]. The mutant has several defects in cAMP signaling: the number of high affinity cAMP binding sites on the cell membranes is significantly reduced, and the mutant fails to produce cAMP or cGMP following cAMP stimulus ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14517243 Blaauw et al. 2003]).
The phenotype of ''phlp1'' null cells is very similar to that of Gbeta ([/gene/DDB_G0277143 gpbA]) null cells. In support of a link between G proteins and Phlp1, Gbeta and Ggamma are mislocalized in ''phlp1''- cells: there are found in the cytosol rather than on the cell surface. Also, Gbeta and Ggamma are present as monomers rather than associated together. Finally, Ggamma is not prenylated, neither in ''phlp1''- nor in ''gpaB''- cells. This data, together with evidence obtained in other systems, is consistent with a model where Phlp1 plays a role in the heterodimerization of Gbeta and Ggamma, which is presumed to be necessary for prenylation of Ggamma and its association with plasma membranes ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16135826 Knol et al. 2005]). Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 27-SEP-2005 PG

DDB_G0283267.summary:
The protein encoded by [/gene/DDB_G0283267 shkA] contains a C-terminal SH2 (Src homology 2) domain that shares sequencesimilarity with the mammalian PI3K adaptor protein p55 and has been shown to possess [/ontology/go/0004713/annotation/page/1 protein-tyrosine kinase activity] in addition to [/ontology/go/0004674/annotation/page/1 protein serine/threonine kinase activity]. Cells carrying a null mutation for''shkA'' exhibit severe developmental phenotypes and have defective [/ontology/go/0030036/annotation/page/1 actin cytoskeleton organization and biogenesis],[/ontology/go/0006935/annotation/page/1 chemotaxis], and [/ontology/go/0006909/annotation/page/1 phagocytosis]. Biochemical analysis shows that protein kinase B([/gene/DDB_G0268620 pkbA]) activation is significantly higher than wild-type. In addition, the rate of translocationof PH (pleckstrin homology) domain-containing proteins [/gene/DDB_G0285161 dagA], [/gene/DDB_G0268620 pkbA], and [/gene/DDB_G0285845 phdA] is reduced. The ShkA protein localizes to the [/ontology/go/0005938/annotation/page/1 cell cortex]; this localization isdependent upon its SH2 domain ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11274054 Moniakis 2001]).
Four additional uncharacterized genes exist in the ''Dictyostelium'' genome that are highly similar to shkA in domainarchitecture: [/gene/DDB_G0288617 shkB], [/gene/DDB_G0290451 shkE], [/gene/DDB_G0278409 shkC], and [/gene/DDB_G0281343 shkD].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 06-JAN-2005 KP

DDB_G0291241.summary: Mutations in ''modB'' (''gnt2'') were isolated by screening cells for loss of a post-translational modification on the cell-cell adhesion molecule gp80 ([/gene/DDB_G0289073 csaA]) that is recognized by a monoclonal antibody [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6717432  (Murray et al. 1984)]. Multiple glycoproteins were found to be affected in ''modB''- mutants indicating that the gene is responsible for a common post-translational modification [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3902823  (West and Loomis, 1985)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2580746  (Loomis et al. 1985)]. Spores of ''modB''- null strains are more permeable to ricin which binds internal carbohydrates, indicating that the structure of their spore coats is abnormal [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1692841  (Aparicio et al. 1990)]. Based on genetic complementation studies, a clone carrying the ''modB'' locus was recognized among those that affected cisplatin resistance. The clone was found to encode a protein closely related to a previously recognized GlcNAc transferase, ''gnt1'' ([/gene/DDB_G0275699 gnt1]), and shown to generate O-linked GlcNAc modifications on SP29 ([/gene/DDB_G0267412 pspA]) and SP85 ([/gene/DDB_G0276939 pspB]) by transfer of GlcNAc from UDPGlcNAc to serine or threonine [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14551185  (Wang et al. 2003)]. Consequently, the locus name was changed to ''gnt2''. The gene product is a transmembrane protein that is localized to the Golgi apparatus where it generates mucin-type O-glycosylation [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15616122  (Ercan and West, 2005)]. The original nitrosoguanidine induced mutation in ''modB'' resulted in a stop codon upstream of the catalytic domain.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 25-JAN-2019 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0286127.summary:
''roco8'' encodes a large, multi-domain protein of the Roco family. Roco8 contains two N-terminal DEP domains, a leucine-rich repeat (LRR) region, a Roc small GTPase domain, a COR (C-terminal of Roc) domain, and a protein kinase domain. Eleven ''Dictyostelium'' proteins belong to the Roco family: ([/gene/DDB_G0291079 gbpC]), ([/gene/DDB_G0273259 qkgA-1]), ([/gene/DDB_G0269250 pats1]), ([/gene/DDB_G0288251 roco4]), ([/gene/DDB_G0294533 roco5]), ([/gene/DDB_G0279417 roco6]), ([/gene/DDB_G0267472 roco7]), Roco8, ([/gene/DDB_G0288183 roco9]), ([/gene/DDB_G0291710 roco10]) and ([/gene/DDB_G0268636 roco11]).
Roco8 is localized to the cytosol and ''roco8'' expression is relatively constant throughout growth and development. Disruption of the ''roco8'' gene did not result in any significant developmental defects ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20348387 van Egmond and van Haastert 2010]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 18-OCT-2021 RD

DDB_G0290853.summary: The 'steely' protein StlB catalyzes the first step in the biosynthesis of differentiation-inducing factor 1 (DIF-1), the prestalk and basal disc inducer [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11163223  (Thompson and Kay, 2000)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16906151  (Austin et al. 2006)]. StlB is a large protein (330 kDa) with six catalytic domains similar to type I fatty acid synthases followed by a type III polyketide synthase domain which catalyzes both iterative polyketide extension and cyclization. This polyketide synthase generates the C12 phlorocaprophenone intermediate that is subsequently modified by the products of ''chlA'' ([/gene/DDB_G0290825 chlA]) and ''dmtA'' ([/gene/DDB_G0289329 dmtA]) to give rise to the chlorinated alkyl phenone DIF-1. ''stlB'' mRNA accumulates only after 7 hrs of development and is found preferentially in prespore cells at the slug stage. Cells in which ''stlB'' is disrupted fail to synthesize any DIF-1 or its unmethylated precursor dM-DIF-1. ''stlB''- mutant strains form long thin slugs with somewhat fewer prestalk cells. Most of the mutant slugs break up leaving a mass of prespore cells that initiates culmination along the substratum. Basal disc cells are missing from the fruiting body and few lower cup cells differentiate to keep the spore mass from slipping down the stalk [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16906151  (Austin et al. 2006)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18402932  (Saito et al. 2008)]. Adding DIF-1 to the environment restores normal development. Most of the phenotypes observed in ''stlB''- null cells are also observed in mutants lacking DmtA, however, defects in expression of prestalk O specific genes are more pronounced in the methyl transferase ''dmtA''- mutants [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12796308  (Maeda et al. 2008)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18402932  (Saito et al. 2003)]. The precursor dM-DIF-1 builds up in cells lacking DmtA and inhibits PstO cell differentiation in slugs.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 29-JAN-2019 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0285101.summary: The motor domain in the kinesin encoded by ''kif4'' is at the N-terminus and belongs to the CENP-E family of domains of kinetochore associated proteins that align chromosomes during mitosis [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14641909  (Kollmar and Glockner 2003)]. A nuclear localization signal is found following the motor domain. Based on the sequences of the motor domains six of the 13 kinesins ([/gene/DDB_G0267396 kif2]), ''kif4'', ([/gene/DDB_G0267404 kif6]), ([/gene/DDB_G0291039 kif11]), ([/gene/DDB_G0268258 kif12]), and ([/gene/DDB_G0288361 kif13]) are members of mitotic motor families. ''kif4'' null cells grow considerably more slowly than wild type cells but develop normally [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18430243  (Nag et al. 2008)]. When ''kif4'' null cells were transformed with a plasmid expressing the 380-kDa truncated version of dynein heavy chain, ([/gene/DDB_G0276355 dhcA]), transformants were able to grow on a solid surface but did not grow in suspension and displayed aberrant spindle formation [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18430243  (Nag et al. 2008)]. It appears that Kif4 and dynein cooperate in mitotic spindle assembly. Like each of the other mitotic kinesins, ''kif4'' mRNA levels are low in growing cells and increase to relatively high levels between 12 and 18 hrs of development before returning to very low levels [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9693369  (de Hostos et al. 1998)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25887420  (Rosengarten et al. 2015)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 02-JUN-2017 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0282893.summary: A comprehensive study classified all lysozymes in ''Dictyostelium''. In addition to the 5 known amoeba type lysozymes ([/gene/DDB_G0275123 alyA], [/gene/DDB_G0275119 alyB], [/gene/DDB_G0275121 alyC], [/gene/DDB_G0273197 alyD-1] and [/gene/DDB_G0286229 alyL] ), two new related lysozymes in this family have been identified, [/gene/DDB_G0282905 alyE] and [/gene/DDB_G0282893 alyF]. These genes are next to each other and almost identical, thus possibly a more recent gene duplication. In the past, gene models for these two new lysozymes gave rise to proteins with one or two transmembrane domains. Thus they first have been named alyTM1 and alyTM2, respectively. However, new sequence analyses resulted in updated gene models coding for proteins containing a signal peptide like the other 5 aly family members. Alignment of the 7 proteins allowed the identification of one conserved Asp and one Glu residue in the C- terminal portion of each protein, which might represent the amoeba lysozyme active site [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/32061941 (Lamrabet et al. 2020)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 22-APR-2020 PF

DDB_G0281167.summary: DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) can be repaired by either non-homologous end-joining (NHEJ) or homologous recombination (HR). In vertebrates, NHEJ is initated when Ku70/Ku80 heterodimers bind to DNA ends and recruit the catalytic subunit of DNA-dependent protein kinase (DNA-PKcs). Homologs of these components in Dictyostelium are encoded by ''ku70'' ([/gene/DDB_G0286069 ku70]), ''ku80'' ([/gene/DDB_G0286303 ku80]),and ''dnapkcs'' ([/gene/DDB_G0281167 dnapkcs]) [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16243037  (Hudson et al. 2005)]. Both Ku70 and Ku80 are members of the family of ATP-dependent DNA helicases and are coordinately expressed during growth and early development [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16112620  (Block and Lees-Miller, 2005)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25887420  (Rosengarten et al. 2015)]. Poly ADP-ribose is generated by the polymerase Adprt1a ([/gene/DDB_G0278741 adprt1A]) at sites of DNA DSBs. Poly ADP-ribose polymers promote NHEJ by binding Ku70 at DSBs and attaching Ku80 [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21807880  (Couto et al. 2011)]. Ku80 has a C-terminal domain that binds DNA-PKcs together with the homolog of the DNA repair endonuclease Artemis, Dclre1 ([/gene/DDB_G0277755 dclre1]), that is essential for NHEJ [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16112620  (Block and Lees-Miller, 2005)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16582628  (Hsu et al. 2006)]. Null mutations in either ''ku80'' or ''dnapkcs'' render recently germinated cells unusually sensitive to the DSB-inducing agent bleomycin. The ''dnapkcs'' null mutation renders H2AX ([/gene/DDB_G0279667 H2AX]) phosphorylation defective in response to this DNA damage. However, these mutations have no effect on bleomycin sensitivity in populations of growing cells, because DSBs can be repaired by the HR pathway in these cells with often two copies of each gene. Haploid cells emerge from spores in the G1 phase of the cell cycle where HR is inoperable; however, growing cells are in G2 where HR can compensate for loss of NHEJ [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16243037  (Hudson et al. 2005)]. The DNA joining events that result in integration of plasmid sequences at random sites of double-strand cleavage during REMI mutagenesis appear to depend on the NHEJ pathway, since ''ku70'', ''ku80'', ''adprt1a'' and ''dclre1'' null mutants do not show the increase in plasmid integration seen in wild type cells transformed together with restriction enzymes [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21807880  (Couto et al. 2011)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21536833  (Hsu et al. 2011)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 05-JAN-2019 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis
phenotypes: decreased double-strand break repair via nonhomologous end joining

DDB_G0272568.summary:
''Dictyostelium'' cofilin-2 (''cofC'') was identified as a cofilin-related protein from the ''Dictyostelium'' cDNA project. It has significant homology to conventional cofilin [/gene/DDB_G0277833 cofA] and contains residues responsible for actin binding ([/ontology/go/0003779/annotation/page/1 actin binding]). Cofilin-2 was shown to depolimerize actin filaments ([/ontology/go/0030042/annotation/page/1 actin filament depolymerization]) in a dose- and pH-dependent manner and to decrease the viscosity of an actin solution, but it did not co-sediment with actin filaments. In contrast to ''cofA'', the cofilin-2 protein is not expressed in vegetative cells but predominantely during aggregation. Immunohistochemistry showed that cofilin-2 colocalized with actin at substrate adhesion sites. However, disruption of the ''cofC'' gene did not result in any adhesion defect, mutants appeared to be normal. Cofilin-2 did not rescue a yeast mutant deficient in conventional cofilin, suggesting ''cofC'' has different function(s) than ''cofA''. Aggregation-specific expression suggests ''cofC'' plays a role in destabilizing the actin cytoskeleton ([/ontology/go/0015629/annotation/page/1 actin cytoskeleton]) during development [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11683919 (Aizawa et al., 2001) ].
Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 24-MAY-2004 PF

DDB_G0277901.summary: The AP-3 adaptor complex (AP-3 complex) is comprised of 4 subunits: beta ([/gene/DDB_G0272578 ap3b-1], [/gene/DDB_G0274003 ap3b-2]), delta ([/gene/DDB_G0279537 ap3d1]), mu, and sigma ([/gene/DDB_G0275405 ap3s1]). ''apm3'' encodes the medium chain (mu subunit) of the AP-3 complex. The AP-3 complex is associated with the trans-Golgi network and endosomal membranes, and mediates delivery of membrane proteins to lysosomes. The ''apm3'' protein (mu3) shares 51% identity with the human mu3A. Expression levels of ''apm3'' remain constant throughout development [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11179674  (de Chassey et al., 2001)]. ''apm3'' plays an essential role in the establishment of a compartmentalized endocytic system. In ''apm3'' null cells, post-lysosomes are generated more slowly than in wild-type cells, and the fusion of post-lysosomes with the cell surface is also defective, possibly because of defects in actin polymerization ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17010123 Charette et al. 2006]), ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18194410 Charette et al. 2008]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 30-JUL-2020 RD

DDB_G0287583.summary: A family of nearly identical small proteins, GerA, GerB, and GerC, ([/gene/DDB_G0287293 gerA]), ([/gene/DDB_G0287687 gerB]) are coordinately synthesized during late culmination and again following the initiation of germination of spores [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2926809  (Giorda et al. 1989)]. Each of the proteins is 127 amino acids long and has a cannonical signal sequence at the N-terminus that could direct co-translational transport across membranes. No conserved domains are present that could give an indication of possible functions. The nucleotide sequences of the respective genes, ''gerA'', ''gerB'', and ''gerC'', are all very similar and are free of introns. These genes may result from recent duplications.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 10-OCT-2018 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0272520.summary:
There are 29 genes encoding actin in ''Dictyostelium'' with amino acid identity greater than 83%, ''act1''-''act29''. Seventeen of these genes encode identical proteins: [/gene/DDB_G0289553 act1], [/gene/DDB_G0274133 act2], [/gene/DDB_G0289005 act4], [/gene/DDB_G0289663 act5], [/gene/DDB_G0274135 act6], [/gene/DDB_G0280545 act7], [/gene/DDB_G0269234 act8], [/gene/DDB_G0274601 act9], [/gene/DDB_G0288879 act11], [/gene/DDB_G0274129 act12], [/gene/DDB_G0274599 act13], [/gene/DDB_G0274137 act14], [/gene/DDB_G0272520 act15], [/gene/DDB_G0272248 act16], [/gene/DDB_G0274727 act19], [/gene/DDB_G0274285 act20], and [/gene/DDB_G0274561 act21], while [/gene/DDB_G0289811 act10], [/gene/DDB_G0275023 act22], and [/gene/DDB_G0289487 act3] respectively have 1, 4 and 11 amino acid differences compared to the 17 identical genes. The proteins encoded by [/gene/DDB_G0274131 act17], [/gene/DDB_G0289489 act18], [/gene/DDB_G0268744 act23] and [/gene/DDB_G0289505 act24]are more divergent.
Actin is a major [/ontology/go/0005200/annotation/page/1 structural constituent of cytoskeleton]. Actin is one of the most abundant proteins in ''Dictyostelium'', constituting approximately 8% of the total protein in vegetative cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/561722 Alton and Lodish et al. 1977]).Actin synthesis is developmentally regulated, peaking shortly after starvation (reviewed by [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6894564 Firtel] in 1981). The different actin genes differ in their levels of expression, with [/gene/DDB_G0274135 act6], [/gene/DDB_G0269234 act8] and [/gene/DDB_G0274129 act12] being highly expressed both during growth and development compared to [/gene/DDB_G0289005 act4], [/gene/DDB_G0289663 act5], [/gene/DDB_G0280545 act7] and [/gene/DDB_G0272248 act16] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6286214 McKeown and Firtel 1981]). Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 19-SEP-2003 PG

DDB_G0288975.summary:
The homeodomain is a sequence-specific DNA binding motif that consists of a helix-turn-helix. Homeobox-containing proteins have transcription factor activity. They have beenidentified in most if not all phyla of eukaryotes. Inmetazoans, homeobox-containing proteins are known to be involvedin regulating the anterior-posterior body plan and in thespecification of certain cell types and anterior-posteriorcompartments (see [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9486804 Han and Firtel 1998] and references therein). There are 14 predicted proteins that contain homeobox domains in ''Dictyostelium'':[/gene/DDB_G0275173 hbx2], [/gene/DDB_G0291075 warA], [/gene/DDB_G0291197 hbx3], [/gene/DDB_G0272967 hbx4], [/gene/DDB_G0273127 hbx5-1] (on the chromosome 2 duplication: [/gene/DDB_G0273645 hbx5-2]), [/gene/DDB_G0277505 hbx6], [/gene/DDB_G0278225 hbx7], [/gene/DDB_G0279257 hbx8], [/gene/DDB_G0280473 hbx9], [/gene/DDB_G0284293 hbx10], [/gene/DDB_G0295787 hbx11], [/gene/DDB_G0286733 hbx12], [/gene/DDB_G0288975 hbx13], and [/gene/DDB_G0289677 hbx14].
[http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25963254 Mishra and Saran 2015] performed a genome-wide classification and comparative genomic analysis of the 14 homeobox genes present in D. discoideum, and found that they could be classified into 3 groups: TALE, OTHER and NOVEL classes, ''hbx13'' belonging to the OTHER class.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 07-JUL-2015 RD

DDB_G0278495.summary:
One of the first enzyme activities seen to increase specifically during ''Dictyostelium'' development was alkaline phosphatase [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/13563787 (Krivanek and Krivanek, 1956 ]; [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14329960 Gezelius and Wright, 1965 ]; [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/5344104 Loomis, 1969) ]. Both a 5' nucleotidase and a classical alkaline phosphatase contribute to the activity assayed with the chromogenic substrate p-nitrophenyl phosphate. Mutant strains carrying deletions of ''alp'' lack the classical alkaline phosphatase but retain the 5' nucleotidase; they develop just as well as wild type strains in the laboratory [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12717731 (Rutherford et al. 2003)]. In vegetative cells, alkaline phosphatase is found in vesicles associated with the plasma membrane rather than with cisternae of the contractile vacuole complex [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15511086 (Clarke and Maddera, 2004)].
The specific activity of alkaline phosphatase increases first in early development and is highest during culmination. It is expressed in prestalk regions during development and in the lower and upper cup of the fruiting body [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12204284 (Ubeidat et al. 2002)]. Synthesis of mRNA can be inhibited as early as 10 hrs after development onset without affecting the increase in alkaline phosphatase during culmination [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/5344104 (Loomis, 1969)]. Direct measurement by RNA-seq showed that ''alp'' mRNA had accumulated to near maximal levels by 10 hrs of development [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25887420 (Rosengarten et al. 2015)]. Since the enzyme does not accumulate significantly until culmination, translation or enzyme stability appears to be subject to developmental regulation. Basic annotations have been added for this gene, 25-JUN-2015 PF; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0272522.summary: Sphingosine kinase phosphorylates sphingosine to form sphingosine 1-phosphate (S1P), a lipid signaling molecule involved in many varied cellular and physiological processes ([/ontology/go/0017050/annotation/page/1 D-erythro-sphingosine kinase activity], [/ontology/go/0006648/annotation/page/1 dihydrosphingosine-1-P pathway]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15059942 Saba and Hla, 2004]). Biochemical properties of the SgkA and SgkB proteins demonstrate that they correspond to the human Sphk1 and Sphk2, respectively. SgkA is localized to the [/ontology/go/0005829/annotation/page/1 cytosol], the [/ontology/go/0005634/annotation/page/1 nucleus], and in some pseudopodia ([/ontology/go/0031143/annotation/page/1 pseudopodium]). Single and double knock outs showed that sphingosine kinase is involved in [/ontology/go/0008284/annotation/page/1 positive regulation of cell proliferation] and in resistance to the chemotherapeutic drug cisplatin ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15643073 Min et al., 2004]). DDB_G0281827.summary: The ''dwwA'' gene is required for [/ontology/go/0000910/annotation/page/1 cytokinesis] of ''Dictyostelium'' cells on solid surfaces. Its product, DwwA, contains two WW domains, an IQ motif, a C2 domain and a proline-rich region. DwwA is localized to the [/ontology/go/0005938/annotation/page/1 cell cortex] and the [/ontology/go/0005634/annotation/page/1 nucleus]; the N-terminal half of the protein, which contains the C2 domain, is required for the cortical localization of DWWA. ''dwwA''-null cells have higher levels of F-actin around the periphery of the ventral surface of the cell ([/ontology/go/0007015/annotation/page/1 actin filament organization]). The IQ motif of DwwA binds [/gene/DDB_G0279407 calA] ''in vitro'' ([/ontology/go/0005516/annotation/page/1 calmodulin binding]). DwwA has been proposed to function as an adaptor protein, participating in cytokinesis by mediating the interaction of Ca(2+)/calmodulin with the actin cytoskeleton ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14595117 Nagasaki and Uyeda 2003]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 21-NOV-2003 PG
