DDB_G0267976.summary: ''Dictyostelium'' contains orthologs of the core components of the presenilin/gamma-secretase complex: presenilin A ([/gene/DDB_G0291352 psenA]), presenilin B ([/gene/DDB_G0292310 psenB]), Aph-1 ([/gene/DDB_G0267976 aph1]) and nicastrin ([/gene/DDB_G0287801 ncstn]) which are capable of amyloidogenic processing of ectopically expressed human amyloid precursor protein (APP) to generate amyloid-beta peptides. Gamma-secretase activity is required for phagocytosis in Dictyostelium, and gamma-secretase mutants have primary defects in pre-spore/spore differentiation [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20699477  (McMains et al. 2010)]. ''Dictyostelium'' orthologs of the gamma-secretase complex PsenA, PsenB, Aph-1, and Nicastrin are necessary for macropinocytosis, phagocytosis, and autophagy, indicating roles in a general defect in lysosomal trafficking and degradation. In addition, loss of psenA/psenB and Aph-1 leads to an accumulation of ubiquitinated proteins, suggesting impaired protein degradation in these mutants. All of the endocytic defects in PSEN ortholog mutants can be fully restored by proteolytically inactive ''Dictyostelium'' PsenB and human PSEN1, demonstrating an evolutionarily conserved non-proteolytic role for presenilin in lysosomal trafficking and autophagy. [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30806144  (Sharma et al. 2019)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 23-JUL-2019 RD

DDB_G0269140.summary:
''gapA'' (''iqgB'') was identified in a REMI screen for cytokinesis mutants ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7811269 Adachi et al. 1994]). The GapA (IQGAP2) protein contains a central Ras GTPase-activating domain followed by a C-terminal RasGAP domain, but RasGAP activity has not been demonstrated for GapA. GapA is present in the cytosol and cell cortex, and during cytokinesis translocates to the cleavage furrow. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21085675 Mondal et al. 2010]). GapA interacts with a number of Rac small GTPases, including Rho GTPase Rac1A ([/gene/DDB_G0277869 rac1A]) and Rac1B ([/gene/DDB_G0268622 rac1B]) and interacts specifically with activated Rac1A. GapA forms oligomers and also interacts with a number of additional proteins, including the actin-binding protein filamin ([/gene/DDB_G0269100 abpC]) and the actin-bundling protein cortexillin ctxA ([/gene/DDB_G0289483 ctxA]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20375144 Lee et al. 2010]), ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21085675 Mondal et al. 2010]).
''gapA'' null mutants have multiple phenotypes. ''gapA'' null mutant cells have a cytokinesis defect in which daughter cells fail to separate, remaining linked by a thin cytoplasmic bridge and resulting in multinucleate cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7811269 Adachi et al. 1994]), ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9151691 Adachi et al. 1997]). ''gapA'' null cells also display a decreased ability to suppress lateral pseudopodia, and thus reduced directionality during chemotaxis to cAMP, aberrant F-actin organization, increased myosin II assembly, and have multiple, F-actin-enriched small projections, which may be filopodia. A double mutant of ''gapA''/''rgaA'' (IQGAP1) ([/gene/DDB_G0287585 rgaA]) has a more severe chemotaxis defect ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20375144 Lee et al. 2010]) and a more severe cytokinesis defect ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11447112 Faix et al. 2001]) than either single mutant. In addition, ''gapA'' null cells have a defect in response to mechanical stress that is not observed in ''gapA''/''rgaA'' double null mutants, indicating that GapA maintains myosin II ([/gene/DDB_G0286355 mhcA]) and cortexillin I mechanosensing by suppressing IQGAP1 ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22379107 Kee et al. 2012]). ''gapA'' null cells have a lower F-actin content than wt cells. Overexpression of filamin partially rescues the ''gapA'' null cytokinesis defect ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21085675 Mondal et al. 2010]). Taken together, these results reveal that GapA plays a role in cytokinesis, chemotaxis and mechanical stress sensing. Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 11-MAR-2022 RD

DDB_G0290491.summary: Generation of single and double knockout mutants of ''atg8b'' and ''atg8a'' ([/gene/DDB_G0286191 atg8a]) revealed unique roles for each protein in autophagy. Knockout of ''atg8b'' displayed only a mild develpmental phenotype, while ''atg8a'' mutants displayed a complex phenotype with delayed development, reduced growth, phagocytosis and cell viability, and an increase in ubiquitinylated proteins and a concomitant decrease in proteasomal activity. However knockout mutants of both genes displayed more severe phenotypes than the single ''atg8a'' mutant, indicating that both proteins function in parallel. Immunofluorescence analysis of knock-out strains suggests a crucial function for ATG8b in autophagosome-lysosome fusion. Atg8b localized around ATG8a and was presumably mainly present on the outer membrane of the autophagosome while Atg8a appears to be mainly associated with the inner membrane. These results suggest that Atg8b predominantly acts as adapter for the autophagy machinery at the outer and Atg8a as cargo receptor at the inner membrane of the autophagosome. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28413119 Messling et al. 2017])Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 14-JAN-2019 RD

DDB_G0277897.summary: ''racI'' encodes a guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G protein) of the Rho family of small GTPases. G proteins are key components of signal transduction networks in which they function as molecular signaling switches, binding to GDP in the off state while binding GTP in the on state. Guanine nucleotide-exchange factors (GEFs) promote the exchange of GDP for GTP on Ras GTPases thus activating them, while GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) inactivate Ras GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP. Possible GEFs for RacI include GxcC ([/gene/DDB_G0284845 gxcC]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23363311 Plak et al. 2013]) and gxcDD ([/gene/DDB_G0279733 gxcDD]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17584488 Mondal et al. 2007]). ''racI'' is weakly expressed at all stages with maximum expression levels after 12 h of starvation, corresponding to the first finger stage ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11201251 Okuwa et al. 2001]), ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11222756 Rivero et al. 2001]). mRNA levels of ''racI'' increase during sexual development, suggesting that ''racI'' may function in sexual development ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16573737 Muramoto et al. 2006]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 29-MAY-2020 RD

DDB_G0285849.summary: Spc97 and Spc98 ([/gene/DDB_G0283909 spc98]), form a complex with gamma-tubulin ([/gene/DDB_G0271738 tubC]) that initiates microtubule polymerization in the spindle pole body of yeast. The ''Dictyostelium'' homologs are encoded by ''spc97'' and ''spc98'', respectively. Throughout the cell cycle they are found in the centrosome which functions as the main microtubule-organizing center (MTOC) [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12018385  (Daunderer and Graf, 2002)]. Under high salt conditions Spc98 co-immunoprecipitates with gamma-tubulin but Spc97 fails to co-immunoprecipitate. In other organisms all 3 proteins are strongly held in a complex. In contrast to mammalian cells, there is no dramatic increase in microtubule nucleation during mitosis of ''Dictyostelium''. At prometaphase the gamma-tubulin/Spc98 complex rapidly redistributes from the centrosomal corona to the inner surfaces of the two outer layers of the centrosome allowing the microtubule spindle to drive the two spindle poles apart [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9880333  (Ueda et al. 1999)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12018385  (Daunderer and Graf, 2002)]. Functional microtubule-nucleating units may be formed when Spc97 associates with the gamma-tubulin/Spc98 complex. About 100 different proteins contribute to centrosomal functions including the products of ''tubC'', ''spc97'', ([/gene/DDB_G0283909 spc98]), ([/gene/DDB_G0288427 cenA]), ([/gene/DDB_G0288375 lis1]), ([/gene/DDB_G0270814 nek2]), ([/gene/DDB_G0283607 eb1]), ([/gene/DDB_G0268616 cepJ]) and ([/gene/DDB_G0278809 cepG]). [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15548420  (Graf et al. 2004)]. Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 23-NOV-2017 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0279409.summary: CbfA is a nuclear DNA binding protein that represses genes during growth including ([/gene/DDB_G0271870 agnC]) and induces genes during developement including ([/gene/DDB_G0281545 acaA]) [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8898890  (Geier et al. 1996)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15470262  (Winckler et al. 2004)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23355006  (Schmith et al. 2013)]. ''agnC'' encodes an Argonaute type protein that is a subunit of the RNA-induced silencing complex RISC. Cells transformed with a construct in which ''agnC'' is driven by act15 have high levels of Argonaute C that block accumulation of RNA from members of the TRE5-A family of repetitive elements [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26339297  (Schmith et al. 2015)]. Likewise, cells with only 5% of wild type CbfA activity as the result of a partially suppressed mutation in cbfA do not efficiently transpose TRE5-A because the high levels of Argonaute C reduce RNA of the repetitive element. These cells fail to develop as the result of lack of induction of ''acaA'', the gene encoding the adenylyl cyclase activity necessary for the generation of the chemoattractant cAMP [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15470262  (Winckler et al. 2004)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16607013  (Siol et al. 2006)]. This developmental block can be bypassed by pulses of cAMP that advance the mutant cells to the aggregation stage where they can sustain expression of ''acaA'' and other genes necesssary for cAMP relay by positive feedback. CbfA (C-Binding Factor) was discovered among proteins that bind to the C-module at the 3' end of TRE5-A which controls synthesis of minus-strand (antisense) RNA [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8898890  (Geier et al. 1996)]. The C-terminal domain of CbfA binds to high dA/dT stretches in the C-module ''in vitro'' but does not regulate C-module promoter activity ''in vivo'' [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10491202  (Horn et al. 1999)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19343174  (Lucas et al. 2009)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21076008  (Bilzer et al. 2010)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 06-MAR-2018 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis; annotation contributions PMID:23355006 Thomas Winckler

DDB_G0274597.summary:
Developing ''Dictyostelium'' cells aggregate to form fruiting bodies. The group size of aggregates is largely regulated by a secreted complex of 4 polypeptides called counting factor (CF). CF is composed of countin (encoded by the [/gene/DDB_G0274597 ctnA] gene), [/gene/DDB_G0273175 cf50-1], [/gene/DDB_G0269248 cf45-1] and [/gene/DDB_G0284363 cf60]. In transformants with a disrupted ''ctnA'' gene, aggregation streams do not break up, resulting in large fruiting bodies ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10444594 Brock and Gomer 1999]). The presence of caffeine rescued the ''ctnA'' null increased aggregate size phenotype and induced formation of smaller aggregates ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22269093 Jaiswal et al. 2012)]. CF regulates group size by negative regulation of cell adhesion ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11090633 Roisin-Bouffay et al. 2001]), cell motility ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11818526 Tang et al. 2002]), down-regulating the cAMP-induced cGMP pulse through inhibition of guanylyl cyclase activity, and decreasing the cAMP-stimulated cAMP pulse ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11371560 Tang et al. 2001]). In contrast, recombinant countin potentiates the cAMP pulse ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14557265 Brock et al. 2003]). The presence of countin enhances the cAMP-stimulated transient translocation of [/gene/DDB_G0268620 pkbA] and [/gene/DDB_G0285161 dagA] from the cytosol to membranes ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15470246 Gao et al. 2004]).
CF increases actin filament polymerization and myosin phosphorylation and redistribution ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11818526 Tang et al. 2002]). The specific roles of countin have been investigated by comparing the effect of addition of recombinant countin to cells compared to addition of semi-purified CF. The responses to recombinant countin and CF are similar with respect to cAMP signal transduction, and cell motility. However, countin does not decrease cell-cell adhesion or group size to the extent that semi-purified CF does ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12070154 Gao et al. 2002]). Cells lacking bioactive CF have high glucose levels, whereas transformants over-secreting CF have low glucose levels. Adding exogenous glucose negates the effect of high levels of extracellular CF on group size and mimics the effect of depleting CF on glucose levels, cell-cell adhesion, cAMP pulse size, actin polymerization, myosin assembly, and motility. These results suggest that glucose is a downstream component in part of the CF signaling pathway ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12161440 Jang et al. 2002]). In support, it has been shown that CF decreases the activity of the gluconeogenic enzyme glucose-6-phosphatase ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15643062 Jang and Gomer 2005]).
Countin represents a new family within the amoebapore superfamily of proteins based on the presence of three predicted disulfide bridges and a tertiary structure similar to that of other members of the superfamily. Amoebapore superfamily proteins bind membranes and are extremely stable ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10998571 Zhai and Saier 2000]). CF is over-secreted in [/gene/DDB_G0287587 smlA] mutants ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10444594 Brock and Gomer 1999]). Secreted countin appears to be protected from degradation by CF50 [/gene/DDB_G0273175 cf50-1] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12117815 Brock et al.2002]). The eIF2alpha kinase [/gene/DDB_G0272837 ifkA] can stabilize and enhance the translational efficiency of countin mRNA ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12697064 Fang et al.2003]). CF and group size have also been mathematically modeled [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16371424 (Dallon et al. 2006)], which together with experimental evidence has been reviewed in [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18426773 Jang and Gomer 2008].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 03-APR-2020 PF

DDB_G0268616.summary: The ''Dictyostelium'' XMAP215 family member DdCP224 encoded by the ''cepJ'' gene is involved in centrosome duplication and cytokinesis and is concentrated at the centrosome and microtubule tips. The functions of the N- and C-terminal halves of DdCP224 were investigated using GFP-fusion proteins. The N-terminal construct shows only cytosolic localization, whereas the C-terminal construct localizes exclusively to the centrosome. Both ends of the protein are required for microtubule binding ''in vitro'' ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10769206 Graf et al. 2000], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12134070 Rehberg and Graf 2002]). Overexpression of the ''cepJ'' gene leads to supernumerary microtubule-organizing centers and, independently, an increase of the number of multinuclear cells. In contrast, underexpression of ''mtaA'' inhibits cell growth, reduces the number and length of astral microtubules, and causes nocodazole hypersensitivity ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14517319 Graf et al. 2003]).Basic annotations have been added to this gene, 26-SEP-2012 RD

DDB_G0292986.summary: The ABC superfamily of genes is one of the largest in the genomes of both bacteria and eukaryotes. The proteins encoded by these genes all carry a characteristic 200- to 250-amino-acid ATP-binding cassette that gives them their family name ([/ontology/go/0042626/annotation/page/1 ATPase activity, coupled to transmembrane movement of substances]). In bacteria they are mostly involved in nutrient import, while in eukaryotes many are involved in export ([/ontology/go/0006810/annotation/page/1 transport]). Seven different families have been defined in eukaryotes based on sequence homology, domain topology, and function. Sequences from the well-advanced ''Dictyostelium'' genome project have allowed to recognize 71 members of this superfamily (including one on the chromosome 2 duplication). The ABCG family is characterized by the ABC domain preceding the transmembrane domain ([/ontology/go/0016021/annotation/page/1 integral to membrane]). All of the members of this family in animals are half-transporters while all of the fungal members are full transporters with two ABC-transmembrane units. No members of this family are found in bacteria. ''Dictyostelium'' and ''Arabidopsis'' have members of both types ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12456012 Anjard and Loomis 2002]). Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 18-OCT-2004 PG

DDB_G0290157.summary:
The sequence and structure of the protein encoded by ''pkgB'', PkbR1, is closely related to that of PKB ([/gene/DDB_G0268620 pkbA]), and these protein kinases have partially overlapping functions during aggregation ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10873800 Meili et al. 2000)]. mRNA from ''pkgB'' starts to accumulates only after several hours of development while mRNA from ''pkbA'' is present in growing cells and decreases during early development. Unlike PKB, PkbR1 does not have a PH-domain but, as the result of N-terminal myristoylation, is permanently tethered to membranes where it can be activated in response to cAMP binding to the G protein coupled receptor, Car1 ([/gene/DDB_G0273397 carA-1], [/gene/DDB_G0273533 carA-2]). Stimulation of the RasC-GEF, AleA ([/gene/DDB_G0284329 gefA]), by Gbeta/gamma ([/gene/DDB_G0277143 gpbA]), ([/gene/DDB_G0274125 gpgA]), leads to RasC-GTP ([/gene/DDB_G0281385 rasC]), which activates the protein kinase complex TORC2 ([/gene/DDB_G0281569 tor]). Both PkbR1 and PKB are phosphorylated by TORC2 in a hydrophobic motif and activated when PDK1 ([/gene/DDB_G0281471 pdkA]) phosphorylates the activation loop ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16079174 Lee et al. 2005)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18635356 Kamimura et al. 2008)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20200230 Kimmel et al. 2010)].
The adaptor protein, Daydreamer (dydA), ([/gene/DDB_G0287875 dydA]) is responsible for deactivating PkbR1 ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23135995 Kolsch et al. 2013)]. One of the substrates of PkbR1 is the phosphoinositol 5-kinase, PikI ([/gene/DDB_G0267588 pikI]) which generates PI(4,5)P2 from PI(4)P. Activation of PikI by PkbR1 initiates a positive feedback loop in which PI(4,5)P2 plays an essential role in further activation of PkbR1 ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24485835 Fets et al. 2014)]. PKB functions predominantly during aggregation to control cell polarity, whereas PKBR-1 is required for morphogenesis during multicellular development. ''pkgB'' null mutants arrest at the mound stage but this block can be suppressed by over expression of PKB ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10873800 Meili et al. 2000)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21335531 Ochiai et al. 2011)]. PkbR1 plays a role in the signal transduction pathway by which GABA induces release of the SDF-2 precursor AcbA ([/gene/DDB_G0270658 acbA]) during culmination ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16672332 Anjard and Loomis, 2006)]. Fluid uptake is almost abolished in ''pkbA'' ([/gene/DDB_G0268620 pkbA]) ''pkgB'' double mutants due to the signifcantly reduced size of macropinosomes in these mutant cells. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30617109 Williams et al. 2019)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 19-JUN-2019 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0277869.summary:
''rac1A'' encodes a guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G protein) of the Rho family of small GTPases. G proteins are key components of signal transduction networks in which they function as molecular signaling switches, binding to GDP in the off state while binding GTP in the on state. Guanine nucleotide-exchange factors (GEFs) promote the exchange of GDP for GTP on Ras GTPases thus activating them, while GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) inactivate Ras GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP. RacGEFs for Rac1A include ''docD'' ([/gene/DDB_G0284725 docD]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19037099 Para et al. 2009]), zizB ([/gene/DDB_G0293084 zizB]), ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22366457 Pakes et al. 2012]), ''gflB'' ([/gene/DDB_G0286773 gflB]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/27009206 Senoo et al. 2016]), Myosin M ([/gene/DDB_G0292262 myoM]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11208126 Geissler et al. 2000]) and possibly gxcDD ([/gene/DDB_G0279733 gxcDD]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17584488 Mondal et al. 2007]). DRG ([/gene/DDB_G0291978 xacA]) contains both GAP and GEF domains and displays GEF activity and weak GAP activity for Rac1A ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11285226 Manstein et al. 2001]), ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9188459 Ludbrook et al. 1997]). Although the IQGAP-related protein DGAP1 ([/gene/DDB_G0287585 rgaA]) binds to Rac1A, it does not affect its GTPase activity ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9739079 Faix et al. 1998]), ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10825297 Dumontier et al. 2000]). Filamin ([/gene/DDB_G0269100 abpC]) and activated Rac1A associate with the rasGAP GAPA ([/gene/DDB_G0269140 gapA]) to regulate actin re-modelling. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21085675 Mondal et al. 2010]).
Rac1A has multiple binding partners that may function as downstream effectors. These include: the protein kinase PakA ([/gene/DDB_G0269166 pakA]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12952073 Mueller-Taubenberger et al. 2002]), PakC ([/gene/DDB_G0267450 pakC]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15470506 Park et al. 2004]), Lissencephaly-related protein LIS1 ([/gene/DDB_G0288375 lis1]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15800059 Rehberg et al. 2005]), diaphanous-related formin H ([/gene/DDB_G0285589 forH]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15908944 Schirenbeck et al. 2005]), the myosin heavy chain kinase PakB ''pakB'' ([/gene/DDB_G0276459 pakB]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15509655 de la Roche et al. 2005]), coronin A ([/gene/DDB_G0267382 corA]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24347642 Swaminathan et al. 2013]) and WASP ([/gene/DDB_G0293834 wasA]) [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31786060 (Amato et al. 2019)]. Rac1A also binds to the Rho GDP-dissociation inhibitor 1 RhoGDI1 ([/gene/DDB_G0291077 rdiA]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12163018 Imai et al. 2002]).
''rac1A'' is highly similar to two additional ''Dictyostelium'' rho GTPases: ''rac1B'' ([/gene/DDB_G0268622 rac1B]) and ''rac1C'' ([/gene/DDB_G0282365 rac1C]). Expression of the three ''rac1'' genes is low during growth but increases 3-fold during aggregation before again declining to growth-stage levels during the slug stage ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8294042 Bush et al. 1993]). Expression levels for ''rac1A'' are 2.5 fold higher than for either ''rac1B'' or ''rac1C''. Overexpression of ''rac1'' genes results in increased filopodium formation, while constitutively active Rac1A and Rac1C mutants are severely impaired in growth, motility and endocytosis. In addition, these mutants were delayed in development and displayed defects in cytokinesis and F-actin organization ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10825297 Dumontier et al. 2000]). These results indicate that the Rac1 GTPases mediate processes such as cell motility, endocytosis and cytokinesis in ''Dictyostelium'' that depend on the reorganization of the actin cytoskeleton. Activated Rac1A recruits either DGAP1 or GAPA into a protein complex with cortexillin I ([/gene/DDB_G0289483 ctxA]) and cortexillin II ([/gene/DDB_G0276893 ctxB]). Assembly of this complex is necessary for the recruitment of cortexillin to the midzone of a dividing cell and for the formation of a cleavage furrow during cytokinesis ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11447112 Faix et al. 2001]). cAMP stimulation activates ''rac1A'' and it then plays a role in signaling networks that lead to both protrusion at the front and retraction at the back of ''Dictyostelium'' cells. One population of activated Rac1A accumulates at the leading edge while a distinct population accumulates at the rear. At the leading edge of migrating cells activated Rac1A participates in Scar/WAVE ([/gene/DDB_G0285253 scrA])-mediated actin polymerization and pseudopod extension. At the trailing edge activated Rac1A forms a complex with DGAP1 and the actin-binding proteins cortexillin I and cortexillin II enabling proper cell retraction ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22302991 Filic et al. 2012]), ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22891261 Veltman et al. 2012]), ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23503127 Faix et al. 2013]), ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26940518 Rivero et al. 2016]). Activated Rac1A and RacC ([/gene/DDB_G0293526 racC]) both regulate, and are regulated by, WASP. WASP interacts with activated Rac genes via its CRIB motif, and this interaction is required for WASP to generate pseudopods in the absence of SCAR/WAVE. However, this interaction also provides a means for WASP to remove activated Racs from the membrane via endocytosis. Thus, WASP contributes to front-rear cell polarity by controlling localization and cellular levels of activated Rac. [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31786060 (Amato et al. 2019)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 08-APR-2020 RD

DDB_G0293530.summary:
The [/gene/DDB_G0291081 pefA] and [/gene/DDB_G0293530 pefB] genes were identified as homologs of mammalian ALG-2 (apoptosis-linked gene 2), which is involved in programmed cell death, as its name suggests. The PefA and PefB proteins eachcontain five calcium-binding ([/ontology/go/0005509/annotation/page/1 calcium ion binding]) EF hand motifs ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11481037 Ohkouchi et al.2001], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11927596 Aubry et al. 2002]).
Expression of ''pefB'' mRNA is developmentally regulated; the message peaks at 4-8 hours, followed by a rapid decline([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11481037 Ohkouchi et al. 2001], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11927596 Aubry et al. 2002]). PefBhas been shown to localize intracellularly to the cytoplasm ([/ontology/go/0005737/annotation/page/1 cytoplasm]), the nucleus ([/ontology/go/0005634/annotation/page/1 nucleus]) and, in the presenceof calcium, to the membrane fraction ([/ontology/go/0005624/annotation/page/1 membrane fraction]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11481037 Ohkouchi et al. 2001],[http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11927596 Aubry et al. 2002]). In situ hybridization analysis of '' pefB'' shows expression inthe anterior tip of the prestalk region ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11481037 Ohkouchi et al. 2001]).
In surface plasmon resonance experiments, [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11927596 Aubry and colleagues (2002)] demonstrate thatPefA is capable of dimerizing with itself ([/ontology/go/0042803/annotation/page/1 protein homodimerization activity]), PefB ([/ontology/go/0046982/annotation/page/1 protein heterodimerization activity]), and with murine Alix (ALG-2 interacting protein X, homolog of ''Dictyostelium'' [/gene/DDB_G0275451 alxA]). PefB, on the other hand, heterodimerizes ([/ontology/go/0046982/annotation/page/1 protein heterodimerization activity]) with PefA but fails to dimerize with murineAlix. Additionally, they show that null mutants of both '' pefA'' and ''pefB'' and double mutants ''pefA-''/''pefB-'' have no detectable developmental phenotype.
[http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15950752 Lardy et al. 2005] recently found that pefB acts as a supressor in mutant strains of the NADPH oxidase large subunits [/gene/DDB_G0289653 noxA] and [/gene/DDB_G0287101 noxB], and the small subunit [/gene/DDB_G0267460 cybA].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 08-SEP-2004 KP

DDB_G0287291.summary: The ''abpD'' gene was identified in a search for novel members of the alpha-actinin superfamily. The interaptin protein has an approximate molecular weight of 200 kD and consists of three distinct domains: the N-terminal actin binding domain ([/ontology/go/0003779/annotation/page/1 actin binding]), a central coiled-coil rod domain, and a C-terminal membrane binding domain. It has been shown that interaptin associates with the nuclear envelope and the ER ([/ontology/go/0042175/annotation/page/1 nuclear envelope-endoplasmic reticulum network]) via the membrane binding domain. The ''abpD'' transcript and protein are developmentally and cAMP-regulated. In the abpD- mutant development ([/ontology/go/0007275/annotation/page/1 multicellular organismal development]) is delayed and cell agglutination ([/ontology/go/0016337/annotation/page/1 cell-cell adhesion]) is slighly impaired [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9700162  (Rivero et al., 1998)]. When abpD-null cells were investigated on soil substrate (under conditions closer to natural ones), more severe developmental defects were found. The fruiting body size and shape is heterogenious and slugs have enlargements all over the slug body and release a high amount of slime sheath. Spore viability ([/ontology/go/0009847/annotation/page/1 spore germination]) was also shown to be severely reduced [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10704840  (Ponte et al., 2000)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 19-SEP-2003 PF

DDB_G0280043.summary:
''rab8A'' encodes a guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G protein) of the Rab family of small GTPases. G proteins are key components of signal transduction networks in which they function as molecular signaling switches, binding to GDP in the off state while binding GTP in the on state. Guanine nucleotide-exchange factors (GEFs) promote the exchange of GDP for GTP on Rab GTPases thus activating them, while GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) inactivate Rab GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP. Rab8A binds to disgorgin ([/gene/DDB_G0280955 dsgg]) which exhibits strong GAP activity towards Rab8A ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18636095 Du et al. 2008]). Rab8A interacts with the exocyst complex subunit protein Exoc6 (Sec15) ([/gene/DDB_G0293936 exoc6]) [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22323285 (Essid et al. 2012)]. ''rab8A'' is expressed during growth and throughout development with maximum expression at 15 hours ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2109188 Saxe et al. 1990]). Rab8A localizes to the contractile vacuole membrane ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18636095 Du et al. 2008]), [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22323285 (Essid et al. 2012)], and proteomic analysis reveals that Rab8A also localizes to the Legionella-containing vacuole ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18980612 Urwyler et al. 2009]), ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24373249 Hoffmann et al. 2013]), [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28183814 (Schmolders et al. 2017)].
Rab8a regulates the exocyst-mediated discharge of the contractile vacuole. Constitutively active ''rab8A'' contains smaller contractile vacuoles compared with wt, while dominant-negative ''rab8A'' cells contain an increased number of larger contractile vacuoles. Rab8A interacts with the exocyst complex subunit protein Exoc6, and in dominant-negative ''rab8A'' cells, the localization of Exoc6 to the contractile vacuole (CV) bladder is abolished. Rab8A is recruited to the CV by drainin ([/gene/DDB_G0269130 phgA]), and CV-associated Rab8a is activated by a GEF activity associated with the exocyst complex that acts at the time of its recruitment onto the CV bladder. Rab8A regulates contractile vacuole to plasma membrane tethering via the exocyst complex which is then followed by the discharge of water out of the cell. The RabGAP activity of disgorgin then inactivates rab8A, leading to dissociation of the Rab8a-GDP exocyst complex from the CV bladder membrane ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18636095 Du, et al. 2008]), [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22323285 (Essid et al. 2012)]. In addition, constitutively active and dominant-negative ''rab8A'' mutants have defects in actin cytoskeleton organization, development, secretion and cell-cell adhesion ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15289548 Powell et al. 2004]). Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 10-DEC-2020 RD

DDB_G0282135.summary: The gene product encoded by [/gene/DDB_G0281663 aprA] is a secreted protein that exists in a 150 kDa protein complex. The AprA protein contains the PhoPQ-activated pathogenicity-related protein domain, which is thought to play a role in virulence of Salmonella. From its mutant phenotype,AprA functions in negative regulation of cell proliferation and is also clearly important for sporulation. Although it plays a role in cellproliferation, AprA does not have an effect on cell growth, as evidenced by an unchanged mass per number of cells in comparison to wild-type. Four proteins in the ''Dictyostelium'' genome are highly similar to AprA: [/gene/DDB_G0286625 DDB_G0286625], [/gene/DDB_G0277031 DDB_G0277031], [/gene/DDB_G0276897 DDB_G0276897], [/gene/DDB_G0282135 DDB_G0282135]([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16176950 Brock and Gomer 2005]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 06-FEB-2006 KP

DDB_G0269108.summary: ''catB'' encodes a catalase that is 42% identical to the product of ''catA'' ([/gene/DDB_G0274595 catA]) [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11004503  (Garcia et al. 2000)]. However, unlike ''catA'' that is expressed in all cells throughout development, ''catB'' is only expressed in prespore cells after 12 hrs of development. Transcription is regulated by the MADS-box transcription factor SrfA ([/gene/DDB_G0281387 srfA]) [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15075287  (Escalante et al. 2004)]. Disruption of ''catB'' results in asynchronous fruiting body formation and spores that are hypersensitive to hydrogen peroxide revealing a role for ''catB'' in the regulation of levels of reactive oxygen species and protection of mature spores [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12788229  (Garcia et al. 2003)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 28-SEP-2018 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0288319.summary: ''arcE'' encodes the 16 kDa subunit of the Arp2/3 complex [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11807934  (Insall et al. 2001)]. The seven subunits of this 200 kDa complex are encoded by ([/gene/DDB_G0277825 arcA]), ([/gene/DDB_G0282813 arcB]), ([/gene/DDB_G0292804 arcC]), ([/gene/DDB_G0269102 arcD]) ''arcE'', ([/gene/DDB_G0272106 arpB]) and ([/gene/DDB_G0283755 arpC]). The subunits of mammalian Arp2/3 are very similar to ''Dictyostelium'' homologs. Arp2/3 binds to the side of F-actin filaments and initiates polymerization of a new F-actin chain at an angle of 70 degrees leading to a branched actin network that can alter the shape of cells. The ability to nucleate new actin filaments is greatly stimulated by direct interactions with members of the WASP/SCAR family [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11807934  (Insall et al. 2001)]. The Arp2/3 complex largely mediates the actin polymerization response to chemotactic stimulation and contributes to cell motility, pseudopod extension and adhesion in Dictyostelium chemotaxis. The complete Arp2/3 complex is essential for growth; partial loss of activity of either ArcB or ArpB impairs growth and chemotaxis [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17553489  (Langridge and Kay, 2007)]. mRNA from each of the genes encoding Arp2/3 subunits accumulates coordinately to reach a peak at 3 hours of development and gradually decreases thereafter [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25887420  (Rosengarten et al. 2015)]. The Arp2/3 complex interacts with the protein CARMIL, which serves as a scaffold for the assembly of a larger complex of proteins involved in the nucleation and termination of actin filament assembly. The complex consists of CARMIL ([/gene/DDB_G0292386 carmil]), AcpA, ([/gene/DDB_G0267374 acpA]) AcpB, ([/gene/DDB_G0272104 acpB]) the Arp2/3 complex, and type I myosins MyoB ([/gene/DDB_G0289117 myoB]) and MyoC ([/gene/DDB_G0276617 myoC]) [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11425877  (Jung et al. 2001)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 30-MAY-2019 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0283615.summary:
''rpkA'' is a member of a characterized class of G protein-coupled receptors found in ''Dictyostelium'' and in the plant pathogen ''Phytophthora'' and that contain a phosphatidylinositol-4-phosphate 5-kinase (PIP5K) domain at the carboxyl terminus of the protein ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16876997 Bakthavatsalam et al. 2006]). In ''Dictyostelium'', ''rpkA'' is constitutively expressed and localizes to the endosome.
Null mutants in ''rpkA'' fail to aggregate at low cell density due to their inability to respond to cAMP and CMF (conditioned medium factor). The G protein domain of the protein is sufficient to rescue the developmental defects of ''rpkA''-. No role for the PIP5K domain in development has been found, but this domain is required for proper localization of the protein. Double mutants in ''rpkA'' and [/gene/DDB_G0283349 gpaA] (G alpha 1) can bypass the developmental defect of ''rpkA'' nulls, indicating that RpkA is an effector of G-protein coupled receptor protein signaling pathway ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17481898 Bakthavatsalam et al. 2007]).
RpkA is also involved in phagocytosis and in the response to infectious bacteria. The protein localizes to late phagosomes, and colocalizes with and binds [/gene/DDB_G0287127 vatA] and [/gene/DDB_G0291858 vatM]. The PIPK domain binds predominantly monophosphorylated phosphoinositides and also phosphatidylserine and loss of RpkA leads to reduced levels of phosphoinositides ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22073313 Riyahi et al. 2011]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 01-NOV-2012 PF

DDB_G0292188.summary: ''DDB_G0292188'' is a member of a conserved family of ''Dictyostelium'' proteins containing a von Willebrand factor A-like domain and a P-loop containing nucleoside triphosphate hydrolase domain. An RNA-sequencing approach was used to identify mTORC1/AMPK-regulated transcriptional networks and associated signaling pathways that are essential for early developmental induction. A combination of starvation and treatment with rapamycin was used to identify a set of ~500 transcripts upregulated during the transition from growth to development, among which is ''DDB_G0292188''. A ''DDB_G0292188'' null mutant is unable to aggregate and displays reduced expression of CAR1 ([/gene/DDB_G0273397 carA-1]),([/gene/DDB_G0273533 carA-2]), supporting a role for ''DDB_G0292188'' in the induction of early development [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31319820  (Jaiswal and Kimmel, 2019)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 05-APR-2022 RD

DDB_G0268258.summary: The motor domain in the kinesin encoded by ''kif12'' belongs to the MKLP1 family of mitotic kinesins and is found near the N-terminus but preceeded by a 120 aa extension [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14641909  (Kollmar and Glockner 2003)]. Kif12 has two nuclear localization signals that localize it to the nucleus during interphase. As cells enter metaphase, Kif12 leaves for the cytoplasm and localizes along spindle fibers [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15546981  (Lakshmikanth et al. 2004)]. Cells in which ''kif12'' is deleted are unable to grow in suspension but can multiply by traction-mediated cytofission when attached to a surface submerged by medium. Under these conditions, the large, multinucleated mutant cells divide asymmetrically, forming smaller cells that survive as long as they capture at least one nucleus. Very little myosin II ([/gene/DDB_G0286355 mhcA]), accumulates in the cleavage furrow and the rate of separation of the nuclei during karyokinesis is reduced. It was suggested that Kif12 might transport vesicles containing myosin II along mitotic extranuclear microtubules towards the center of the cell to be inserted into the cleavage furrow membrane [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15546981  (Lakshmikanth et al. 2004)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22379107  (Kee et al. 2012)]. Like each of the other mitotic kinesins, ''kif12'' mRNA levels are low in growing cells and increase to relatively high levels between 12 and 18 hrs of development before returning to very low levels [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25887420  (Rosengarten et al. 2015)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 02-OCT-2017 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0280975.summary:
''racE'' encodes a guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G protein) of the Rho family of small GTPases. G proteins are key components of signal transduction networks in which they function as molecular signaling switches, binding to GDP in the off state while binding GTP in the on state. Guanine nucleotide-exchange factors (GEFs) promote the exchange of GDP for GTP on Ras GTPases thus activating them, while GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) inactivate Ras GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP. GxcC ([/gene/DDB_G0284845 gxcC]) is a likely GEF for RacE ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23363311 Plak et al. 2013]). GxcT ([/gene/DDB_G0269610 gxcT]) binds to and may also activate RacE ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24248334 Wang et al. 2013]). The armadillo-like protein Darlin ([/gene/DDB_G0288771 darA]) binds RacE, but a GEF activity has not been demonstrated ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9802899 Vithalani et al. 1998]). Other possible GEFs for RacE include GxcDD ([/gene/DDB_G0279733 gxcDD]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17584488 Mondal et al. 2007]) and DockD ([/gene/DDB_G0284725 docD]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/27009206 Senoo et al. 2016]). DRG ([/gene/DDB_G0291978 xacA]) is a GAP for RacE ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11285226 Manstein et al. 2001]). GflB ([/gene/DDB_G0286773 gflB]) has both ras GEF and rho GAP domains, and it functions as a GAP for RacE ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/27009206 Senoo et al. 2016]). DGAP1 ''rgaA'' ([/gene/DDB_G0287585 rgaA]) is also a possible GAP for RacE ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9739079 Faix et al. 1998]).
RacE has multiple binding partners that function as downstream effectors. RacE interacts with formin A ([/gene/DDB_G0279607 forA]), formin E ([/gene/DDB_G0269626 forE]), and formin H ([/gene/DDB_G0285589 forH]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30808751 Litschko et al. 2019]). GDP-bound RacE binds to the tor complex components tor ([/gene/DDB_G0281569 tor]) and pia ([/gene/DDB_G0277399 piaA]), and GDP-bound RacE binds to activated, GTP-bound ''rasC'' ([/gene/DDB_G0281385 rasC]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31263268 Senoo et al. 2019]). RacE also binds to PakB ([/gene/DDB_G0276459 pakB]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15509655 de la Roche et al. 2005]) and the Rho GDP-dissociation inhibitor RhoGDI1 ([/gene/DDB_G0291077 rdiA]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12163018 Imai et al. 2002]).
''racE'' plays an important role in signaling networks that regulate cytokinesis, chemotaxis, and organization of the cortical cytoskeleton to maintain proper cortical integrity ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26940518 Rivero et al. 2016)]. ''racE'' null cells are multi-nucleate and unable to divide when grown in suspension, however cytokinesis is normal in ''racE'' null cells grown on a substrate ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8682867 Larochelle et al. 1996]), ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9368749 Chisholm 1997]). Abnormal F-actin aggregates form in ''racE'' null mutants and the cells display decreased cortical tension, which is the likely cause of ''racE'' cytokinesis defects ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9548725 Gerald et al. 1998]). RacE is required for the localization of several proteins to the cell cortex. In ''racE'' null cells, three cytoskeletal components essential for cytokinesis: dynacortin ([/gene/DDB_G0283767 dct]), coronin A ([/gene/DDB_G0267382 corA]), and 14-3-3 ([/gene/DDB_G0269138 fttB]) all fail to localize to the cell cortex ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10953006 Robinson et al. 2000]), ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20951045 Zhou et al. 2010]). In addition, formin A ([/gene/DDB_G0279607 forA]) fails to localize to the cortex in ''racE'' nulls. Activated RacE localizes to the rear cortex of cells as do the RacE effectors formin A, formin E ([/gene/DDB_G0269626 forE]), and formin H ([/gene/DDB_G0285589 forH]). A ''forA''/''forE''/''forH'' triple null mutant displays nearly identical phenotypes as the ''racE'' null mutant ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30808751 Litschko et al. 2019]). ''racE'' null cells also have a defect in chemotaxis to cAMP, impaired growth on bacterial lawns, and fail to aggregate normally during development. In cells lacking RacE or the RacGEF GxcT ([/gene/DDB_G0269610 gxcT]), the accuracy of directional sensing is reduced, and pseudopods are abnormally extended from the lateral sides of migrating cells resulting in impaired chemotaxis ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24248334 Wang et al. 2013]). GflB is required for both chemotaxis to cAMP and cytokinesis, and GflB activates RasG ([/gene/DDB_G0293434 rasG]) and also inactivates RacE. As RacE and RasG ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10725225 Khosla et al. 2000]) also function in cytokinesis, GflB may coordinate signal transduction of RacE and RasG for both chemotaxis and cytokinesis ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/27009206 Senoo et al. 2016]).
RacE occupies a unique position as a signaling molecule in cell migration by connecting GPCR activation to mTORC2-AKT signaling. Chemoattractant-induced phosphorylation of GDP-RacE by glycogen synthase kinase GSK-3 ([/gene/DDB_G0272110 gskA]) promotes its hetero-oligomerization with GTP-RasC. At the front of migrating cells, GDP-RacE-GTP-RasC hetero-oligomers directly activate mTORC2 signaling and AKT/PKB ([/gene/DDB_G0268620 pkbA]) phosphorylation to then regulate the actin cytoskeleton and cell migration. GTP-bound RacE localizes to the rear of migrating cells where it antagonizes mTORC2-AKT signaling by inhibiting the oligomerization of GDP-RacE with GTP-RasC. Thus RacE plays two opposite roles at two different intracellular locations to polarize the actin cytoskeleton in migrating cells: GDP-RacE activates mTORC2-AKT signaling at the front of migrating cells while GTP-RacE inhibits signaling at the rear of migrating cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31263268 Senoo et al. 2019)], Senoo ''et al.'' 2020, PMID: 33238110.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 11-MAR-2021 RD

phenotypes: abolished protein localization to cell cortex

DDB_G0279919.summary: The ABC superfamily of genes is one of the largest in the genomes of both bacteria and eukaryotes. The proteins encoded by these genes all carry a characteristic 200- to 250-amino-acid ATP-binding cassette that gives them their family name ([/ontology/go/0042626/annotation/page/1 ATPase activity, coupled to transmembrane movement of substances]). In bacteria they are mostly involved in nutrient import, while in eukaryotes many are involved in export([/ontology/go/0006810/annotation/page/1 transport]), ([/ontology/go/0016021/annotation/page/1 integral to membrane]). Seven different families (A to G) have been defined in eukaryotes based on sequence homology, domain topology, and function. ''Dictyostelium'' has 71 ABC transporters (including one on the chromosome 2 duplication) and 3 ABCD family members: [/gene/DDB_G0279917 abcD1], [/gene/DDB_G0293194 abcD2] and [/gene/DDB_G0279919 abcD3]. The ABCD family contains only half-transporters. Those that have been studied are all targeted to the peroxisome ([/ontology/go/0005779/annotation/page/1 integral to peroxisomal membrane]), where they regulate the transport of long-chain fatty acids [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12456012 (Anjard and Loomis 2002)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 16-JUN-2003 PG

DDB_G0291239.summary: In a screen of REMI transformants, ''ubpA'' was isolated as mutant with defective aggregation. ''ubpA'' encodes a protein with similarity to ubiquitin-specific processing proteases, which are involved in the regulation of protein degradation. UbpA was demonstrated to have deubiquitinase activity and to be a functional ortholog of ''Saccharomyces cerevisiae'' ubiquitin carboxyl terminal hydrolase UBP14. ''ubpA'' is expressed in both vegetative and development stage cells. Expression increases in early development reaching a maximum at 7.5 hours with continued expression throughout the remainder of development. UbpA is localized in both the nucleus and cytoplasm throughout growth and development. ''ubpA'' mutant cells grow normally, but have several developmental defects, including impaired aggregation, chemotaxis, and cell-cell adhesion, as well as a decreased ability to relay a cAMP pulse. In addition, in ''ubpA'' mutant cells, the expression of aggregation-specific genes CarA ([/gene/DDB_G0273397 carA-1]) ([/gene/DDB_G0273533 carA-2]), PDE ([/gene/DDB_G0285995 pdsA]) and gp80 ([/gene/DDB_G0289073 csaA]) is decreased. These results suggest that developmental transitions in ''Dictyostelium'' require the degradation of specific proteins which in turn requires the disassembly of polyubiquitin chains by UbpA [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9786928  (Lindsey et al. 1998)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 23-SEP-2021 RD
DDB_G0291239.note: Note that the coding sequence in the curated model does not start with an ATG and that there are several sequence differences, especially at the 5' end, to GenBank record U48271. This and overall sequence similarity suggest problems in the genomic sequence.

DDB_G0273729.summary: ''mkpB'' is one of 14 genes in Dictyostelium with similarity to the human dual-specificity protein phosphatase DUSP1. [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21300429  (Moncho-Amor et al. 2011)] found that ''mkpB'' is expressed in all the cells of developmental structures, but its mRNA is enriched in cells with a distribution typical of anterior-like cells. Cells that express a catalytically inactive mutant of MkpB grow and aggregate like wild-type cells, but show a greatly impaired post-aggregative development. In addition, the expression of cell-type specific genes is significantly delayed, indicating that this protein plays an important role in cell differentiation and development.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 26-MAR-2014 RD

DDB_G0269130.summary:
''phgA'' encodes a Drainin, a member of the Rab-GTPase-TBC domain superfamily. Drainin lacks the conserved catalytic Arg and Gln residues required for Rab GTPase-activating protein (RabGAP) activity (Bos, et al 2007, PMID: 17540168) and does not exhibit rabGAP activity on any tested Rab GTPase: ([/gene/DDB_G0280043 rab8A]), ([/gene/DDB_G0269238 rab11A]), ([/gene/DDB_G0277101 rab11C]) and rab14 ([/gene/DDB_G0281337 rab14]) suggesting that Drainin is not a functional RabGAP ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18636095 Du et al. 2008]). ''phgA'' null cells are sensitive to hypo-osmotic stress and have enlarged contractile vacuoles which fail to discharge water because the vacuoles do not fuse with the plasma membrane ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10369671 Becker et al. 1999]).
Drainin, along with Disgorgin ([/gene/DDB_G0280955 dsgg]), Rab8A and Rab11A, functions in a signaling pathway to regulate CV fusion with the plasma membrane (PM) and subsequent CV discharge. Drainin binds strongly to constitutively active Rab GTPase Rab11A, and in response to hypo-osmotic stress, Rab11A is activated and recruits Drainin to the contractile vacuole membrane. Rab8a, the exocyst complex, and disgorgin then are sequentially recruited to the CV bladder, and the exocyst complex tethers the CV to the PM. Drainin also interacts ''in vivo'' with the exocyst complex subunit 6 (Sec15) ([/gene/DDB_G0293936 exoc6]). Drainin is enriched at the back of the CV bladder away from the bladder-PM contact site while Sec15 is localized to small patches at the bladder-PM contact site. In ''phgA'' null cells, Sec15 instead localized to a large area between the CV bladder and the PM, suggesting that the absence of Drainin leads to uncontrolled accumulation of the exocyst tethers and a block in CV discharge. These results suggest that Drainin is essential for correct localization of the exocyst complex and Rab8a for CV discharge. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18636095 Du et al. 2008]), ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22323285 Essid et al. 2012]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 01-DEC-2021 RD
DDB_G0269130.note: The Curated Model is based on GenBank record U81500, which predicts 2 exons, whereas the Sequencing Center Gene Prediction has only 1 exon.  There is a discrepancy between the sequence from the Sequencing Center and the sequence in GenBank record U81500, however, the sequence from the Sequencing Center has been verified.
phenotypes: aberrant protein localization to contractile vacuole

DDB_G0284337.summary: ''cynA'' was identified in a screen to identify novel regulators based on the spatial distributions of GFP-tagged proteins in migrating cells. CynA (Callipygian) localizes to the rear of randomly migrating cells and the lagging edge membrane of cells migrating in a cAMP gradient, and it also accumulates at the cleavage furrow during cytokinesis. CynA is a member of the myotubularin phosphatase family and contains an N-terminal pleckstrin homology (PH) domain followed by a WD40 domain. ''cynA'' is expressed at low levels in growing cells and transcription is up-regulated during development, reaching a peak at 8 hr. of starvation. [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26130809  (Swaney et al. 2015)]. CynA binds phosphatidylinositol-3,4-bisphosphate (PI(3,4)P2), and specifically to surface-tethered lipid vesicles containing PI(3,4)P2 [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30194235  (Li et al. 2018)]. Aggregation is delayed in ''cynA'' null cells and the cells also have an aberrant morphology, being elongated and with protrusions around the lateral edges. Motile ''cynA'' null cells display decreased directional persistence and an irregular trajectory, and an increase in lateral pseudopodia during chemotaxis compared with wild type cells. ''cynA'' null cells appear to have a slightly prolonged and elevated actin response suggesting that the presence of CynA locally inhibits actin polymerization. These results indicate that CynA increases migration efficiency and plays a role in the establishment of cell polarity by regulating the localization of actin polymerization [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26130809  (Swaney et al. 2015)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 18-MAR-2022 RD

DDB_G0275931.summary: NCS-1/frequenin proteins regulate a variety of cellular processes, including neurotrasmitter release, cyclic nucleotide metabolism, polyphosphoinositide synthesis, gene expression, and protein secretion. A member of this family, ''ncsA'' has been identified in ''Dictyostelium''. NcsA exhibits [/ontology/go/0005509/annotation/page/1 calcium ion binding] activity. The ''ncsA'' transcript is maximally expressed during late aggregation and the slug stage. ''ncsA''-null cells grow normally in axenic culture but grows slowly on bacterial lawns. Development of ''ncsA''-null cells is accelerated by 3-4 h compared to wild type cells. Unlike the ''S. cerevisiae'' and mammalian NCS1, NcsA does not appear to interact with PI4K ([/gene/DDB_G0288485 pikD]) and therefore its mode of action has yet to be elucidated ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15606490 Coukell et al. 2004]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 04-JAN-2005 PG

DDB_G0292878.summary:
The Dictyostelium WASP family was first described by [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20573979 Veltman and Insall 2010]. All WASH complex subunits have been identified, wshA, fam21, cdc53, strumpellin, and swip. [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21606208 Carnell et al. 2011] found that WASH is responsible for V-ATPase retrieval and vesicle reneutralization before exocytosis. In wsh- knockout cells, neutralization of lysosomes to form post-lysosomes is blocked similar to when latrunculin inhibits F-actin polymerization. Furthermore, indigestible material such as dextran is not exocytosed. The actin mediated The V-ATPase recycling was the first shown lysosomal recycling function of WASH.
The role of WASH in lysosomal function was further assessed by [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23885127 King et al. 2013]. They demonstrate that WASH is required for the lysosomal digestion of both phagocytic and autophagic cargo. wshA null cells are unable to grow on many bacteria, or to digest their own cytoplasm to survive starvation. Proteomic analysis of the wshA phagosome revealed a reduced delivery of lysosomal hydrolases, including both proteases and lipases, resulting in both reduced phagosomal proteolysis and lipid catabolism. Starvation-induced macroautophagy lead to phospholipid accumulation within WASH-null lysosomes, causing the formation of multilamellar bodies typical of many lysosomal storage diseases. In addition, cathepsin D becomes trapped in a late endosomal compartment, unable to be recycled to nascent phagosomes and autophagosomes, demonstrating that WASH is required for the maturation of lysosomes to a stage at which hydrolases can be retrieved and reused.
[http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24119059 Kolonko et al. 2013] showed that after phagocytosis of mycobacteria, F-actin accumulates on the mycobacterial vacuole, and WASH is associated as F-actin nucleating factor. However, disruption of WASH or depolymerization of F-actin prevented F-actin coating the vesicle and thus the proton pumping V-ATPase gains access. The resulting acidification reduces the replication of mycobacteria. This demonstrates an evolutionarily conserved mechanism by which pathogenic mycobacteria subvert the actin-polymerization activity of WASH to prevent phagosome acidification and maturation, as a prerequisite to generate and maintain a replicative niche.
During phagocytosis and macropinocytosis bulk plasma membrane is internalized with its integrating proteins. [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/27647881 Buckley et al. 2016] addressed how WASH drives sorting and recycling from endosomes and is thus maintaining surface receptor levels and sustain phagocytosis. They report that WASH is recruited to both early and late phagosomes during maturation. By co-expression and mutant studies, the authors show that surface proteins such as p25 (''dynE'') or the integrins ''sibA'' and ''sibC'', are recycled via WASH early during phagocytosis, before acidification. In addition they demonstrate that WASH recycles the retromer complex, during both early and late stages of the endocytic cycle.
In ''wshA'' null cells, ''Legionella pneumophila'' replicates more efficiently than in wt cells, and the deletion of WASH strongly impairs the recruitment of Rab1 ([/gene/DDB_G0283757 rab1A]) and Rab8 ([/gene/DDB_G0280043 rab8A]) to Legionella-containing vacuoles (LCVs) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29602783 Welin et al. 2018]). Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 16-FEB-2017 PF; annotation contributions: PMID:24119059, Margot Kolonko

DDB_G0283365.summary:
DNA-dependent RNA polymerase catalyzes the transcription of DNA into RNA using the four ribonucleoside triphosphates as substrates ([/ontology/go/0003899/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase activity]). Three distinct zinc-containing RNA polymerases are found in eukaryotic nuclei: [/gene/DDB_G0275759 rpa1] for the ribosomal RNA precursor ([/ontology/go/0006360/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase I promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005736/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase I complex]), [/gene/DDB_G0279193 rpb1] for the mRNA precursor ([/ontology/go/0006366/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase II promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005665/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase II, core complex]), and [/gene/DDB_G0277199 rpc1] for 5S and tRNA genes ([/ontology/go/0006383/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase III promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005666/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase III complex]).
RNA polymerase II is composed of 12 subunits: [/gene/DDB_G0279193 rpb1], [/gene/DDB_G0288257 rpb2], [/gene/DDB_G0292244 rpb3], [/gene/DDB_G0282739 rpb4], [/gene/DDB_G0291636 rpb5], [/gene/DDB_G0291037 rpb6], [/gene/DDB_G0284891 rpb7], [/gene/DDB_G0278039 rpb8], [/gene/DDB_G0268306 rpb9], [/gene/DDB_G0272036 rpb10], [/gene/DDB_G0277677 rpb11], and[/gene/DDB_G0283365 rpb12]. Subunits 5, 6, 8, 10, and 12 are common to all threeRNA polymerases (reviewed by [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9618449 Hampsey] in 1998).
Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 09-APR-2004 PG

DDB_G0284499.summary: Members of the structural maintentance of chromosomes (SMC) family are involved in manybiological processes, including sister chromatid cohesion ([/ontology/go/0007064/annotation/page/1 mitotic sister chromatid cohesion]), chromosome condensation([/ontology/go/0007076/annotation/page/1 mitotic chromosome condensation]), and DNA repair ([/ontology/go/0006281/annotation/page/1 DNA repair]). DDB_G0280849.summary: ''dicA'' encodes the highly conserved dynein intermediate chain that associates with dynein heavy chains ([/gene/DDB_G0276355 dhcA]) to make the motor complexes which function in retrograd transport of cargos along microtubules [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1469051  (Koonce et al. 1992)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7866389  (Koonce et al. 1994)]. An N-terminal region of DicA binds the dynactin complex that allows dynein to move organelles long distances along microtubules. A C-terminal region of DicA binds dynein heavy chain. Expression of truncated versions of ''dicA'' missing either the N-terminal region or the C-terminal region results in mislocalization of the Golgi, collapse of microtubules into large bundles, and alterations in centrosome separation resulting in defective mitosis. It appears that dynactin-mediated dynein function is required for organization of interphase microtubule network as well as centrosome replication and separation. As expected, dynein intermediate chain is essential for viability of ''Dictyostelium'' [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10601339  (Ma et al. 1999)]. Dynein motors cluster into microdomains on phagosomal membranes, resulting in rapid directed transport of the phagosome toward microtubule minus ends, likely promoting phagolysosome fusion and pathogen degradation. [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26853472  (Rai et al. 2016)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 23-MAY-2017 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0269416.summary: ''rab32B'' encodes a guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G protein) of the Rab family of small GTPases. G proteins are key components of signal transduction networks in which they function as molecular signaling switches, binding to GDP in the off state while binding GTP in the on state. Guanine nucleotide-exchange factors (GEFs) promote the exchange of GDP for GTP on Rab GTPases thus activating them, while GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) inactivate Rab GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP. Rab32B is similar to human RAB32 and human RAB38 which are involved in the regulation of phagosome maturation. Rab32B is also similar to ([/gene/DDB_G0283603 rab32A]) and ([/gene/DDB_G0275675 rab32C]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 08-OCT-2020 RD

DDB_G0276887.summary:
FbxA belongs to a family of proteins that contain an F-box and WD40 repeats and that target specific proteins for degradation via proteasomes ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10898960 Nelson et al. 2001]). The F-box is a protein motif of approximately 50 amino acids that functions as a site of protein-protein interaction ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11178263 Kipreos and Pagano 2000]). This class of protein usually forms part of a Skp1, Cullin, F-box [/ontology/go/0019005/annotation/page/1 SCF ubiquitin ligase complex] that targets specific protein substrates for ubiquitination and degradation ([/ontology/go/0006511/annotation/page/1 ubiquitin-dependent protein catabolic process]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10725352 Ennis et al. 2000]).One of the targets of FbxA is the cAMP phosphodiesterase [/gene/DDB_G0284331 regA] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12796307 Tekinay et al. 2003]).
In fruiting bodies formed from ''fbxA'' null cells, most structures arrest at the mound stage, and in those that progress further the spore mass fails to fully ascend the stalk. The development of ''fbxA'' null cells is hypersensitive to ammonia, the signaling molecule that regulates [/ontology/go/0031154/annotation/page/1 culmination during sorocarp development]. In ''fbxA'' null slugs the pstO region is reduced in size and the prespore region is proportionately expanded ([/ontology/go/0045595/annotation/page/1 regulation of cell differentiation]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10898960 Nelson et al. 2001]). ''fbxA'' (Cheater A) was independently isolated as a ''Dictyostelium'' mutant that preferentially form spores in chimeras with isogenic wild-type cells. The mutant causes wild-type cells that have begun to express spore-specific genes to accumulate in the prestalk compartment of the developing organism ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10725352 Ennis et al. 2000]).
The ''fbxA'' transcript is absent in growing cells and appears early in development ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10725352 Ennis et al. 2000]) and is highly enriched in the prestalk cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10898960 Nelson et al. 2001]).
Overexpression of the PKA catalytic subunit, [/gene/DDB_G0283907 pkaC], rescues many of the defects of ''fbxA'' null cells, suggesting a regulatory role for FbxA proteins in PKA function. FbxA is believed to regulate multicellular development together with [/gene/DDB_G0291972 culA] by targeting [/gene/DDB_G0284331 regA] for degradation via a pathway that requires [/gene/DDB_G0283903 erkB] function, leading to an increase in cAMP and PKA activity ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11390363 Mohanty et al. 2001]).Null mutations in [/gene/DDB_G0284331 regA] or [/gene/DDB_G0280961 dhkA] partially restores the developmental defects observed in ''fbxA'' null cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12796307 Tekinay et al. 2003]).
Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 16-JUN-2003 PG

DDB_G0278781.summary:
''D. discoideum'' Pah is the only aromatic amino acid hydroxylase in this organism and has phenylalanine 4-monooxygenase activity. Gel filtration showed this enzyme to form a tetramer. As the most efficient cofactor this enzyme requires DH4 (''D-threo''-BH4), and with lower efficiency BH4, which is the major cofactor of metazoan PAH enzymes tetrahydrobiopterin binding. However, ''Dictyostelium'' Pah cannot be activated by L-Phe like its metazoan counterparts. The low affinity for the substrate and the overall lower activity than human PAH may provide a constitutive level of activity in ''D. discoideum'', pointing to an anabolic function of Pah in lower eukaryotes and bacteria. A more strict allosteric regulation of the enzyme by L-Phe seems to be needed in higher eurkaryotes. By determining the structure of ''D. discoideum'' Pah, high similarity to human PAH in the catalytic domain was found. However, differing residues could be identified in the regulatory domain that might be important for cofactor selection and L-Phe binding ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18835579 Siltberg-Liberles et. al 2008)].
In vivo studies to clarify the roles of L-erythro-tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) and its stereoisomer D-threo-BH4 (DH4) in ''D. discoideum'' suggested that BH4 is the preferred cofactor for Pah, and that DH4 functions mainly as an antioxidant ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21871890 Kim et. al 2011)]. In a subsequent publication, [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23017206 Kim et. al 2012] studied the regulatory function of Pah by characterizing the oligomeric status and kinetic parameters of both full-length and partial Pah constructs consisting of the regulatory, tetramerization, or both domains. Their results suggest that phenylalanine activates Pah, which is functional in vivo as a tetramer. In addition, kinetic studies suggest that the regulatory domain of dicPAH may play a role different from that of the domain in mammalian PAH.Gene has been comprehensively annotated 19-FEB-2013 RD

DDB_G0274191.summary: The histidine kinase ''dhkC'' regulates the choice between migrating slugs and culmination. ''dhkC'' encodes a histidine kinase similar to DhkA ([/gene/DDB_G0280961 dhkA]) and DhkB ([/gene/DDB_G0277845 dhkB]) but lacking transmembrane domains. High levels of ammonia result in prolonged slug migration in wild type strains but not in ''dhkC'' null mutants. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9808785 Singleton et al. 1998)]. Cells lacking ''dhkC'' develop to the finger stage more rapidly than wild type cells and skip the slug stage to culminate directly, a phenotype shared by mutant strains in which PKA ([/gene/DDB_G0283907 pkaC]), ([/gene/DDB_G0279413 pkaR]) is abnormally active for a variety of genetic reasons. Mutant strains expressing the central kinase domain of DhkC without the flanking control regions resulted in constitutive gain-of-function that blocked culmination. This slugger phenotype was suppressed in these cells by mutations in the cAMP phosphodiesterase gene, RegA ([/gene/DDB_G0284331 regA]); [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9808785  Singleton et al. 1998)]. In addition, it has been demonstrated that the ammonium transporter genes, amtA ([/gene/DDB_G0277503 amtA]) and amtC ([/gene/DDB_G0267424 amtC]) regulate the dhkC phosphorelay ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16835443 Singleton et al. 2006)] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16188250 Kirsten et al. 2005)]. In response to ammonia, it appears that DhkC activates RegA by phosphorelay to its response regulatory region. ''regA'' is expressed in both prespore and prestalk cells in the slug, while ''dhkC'' expression is prestalk specific at this stage ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25887420 Rosengarten et al. 2015)]. The histidine kinase keeps the phosphodiesterase activity high in prestalk cells until the levels of ammonia drop. Thereafter, cAMP and PKA activity can increase and trigger stalk formation. The signaling molecule differentiation-inducing factor 2 (DIF-2) modulates chemotaxis to cAMP via the DhkC-RegA-RdeA ([/gene/DDB_G0282923 rdeA]) signaling pathway ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26919666 Kuwayama and Kubohara 2016)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 24-JAN-2017 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0274605.summary: ''gefR'' encodes a Ras guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF, RasGEF). rasGEFs are key components of signaling networks in which they activate Ras family small GTPases by promoting the exchange of GDP for GTP. GefR is dephosphosphorylated in response to activated RasG ([/gene/DDB_G0293434 rasG]) expression; however a ''gefR'' null mutant displayed no discernible phenotypes in either growth, development or motility ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15352238 Secko et al. 2004)]. A large-scale proteomic analysis revealed that GefR is also dephosphorylated in response to the prestalk inducer Differentiation Inducing Factor-1 (DIF-1) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25518940 Sugden et al. 2014)]. ''gefR'' is expressed weakly during growth but with increased expression levels during development ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16086850 Wilkins et al. 2005)]. In response to cAMP, RasG activation was greatly reduced in a ''gefR'' null mutant, indicating that GefR has GEF activity towards RasG ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17380187 Kae et al. 2007)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 07-MAY-2021 RD

DDB_G0293758.summary:
Histones form the nucleosomal core ([/ontology/go/0000786/annotation/page/1 nucleosome]) ([/ontology/go/0006334/annotation/page/1 nucleosome assembly]) that is fundamental to chromatin structure (). The histone octamer is composed of an H3-H4 tetramer (two H3-H4 dimers) coupled with an H2A-H2Btetramer (two H2A-H2B dimers). The histone H1 linker protein plays a role in packaging nucleosomes into the 30 nmfiber found in chromatin ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9177486 Bukenberger et al. 1992]).
In ''Dictyostelium discoideum'' and ''Saccharomyces cerevisiae'', only one copy of histone [/gene/DDB_G0285319 H1] appears to be present, in comparison to other eukaryotes which have multiple copies and subtypes([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7867938 Hauser et al. 1995], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9046096 Ushinsky et al.1997]). Two putative H2A family members, [/gene/DDB_G0279667 H2AX] and [/gene/DDB_G0286747 H2AZ], and three H2Adomain-containing proteins, [/gene/DDB_G0289187 H2Av1], [/gene/DDB_G0289193 H2Av2], [/gene/DDB_G0289197 H2Av3], are present in ''Dictyostelium''. Two H2B domain-containing proteins also exist inthe ''Dicty'' genome: [/gene/DDB_G0293758 H2Bv1] and [/gene/DDB_G0276273 H2Bv2]. There are three histone H3proteins, [/gene/DDB_G0267402 H3a] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9177486 Bukenberger et al. 1992]), [/gene/DDB_G0270838 H3b], and [/gene/DDB_G0271092 H3c], and two H3 domain-containing proteins, [/gene/DDB_G0291185 H3v1] and [/gene/DDB_G0277979 H3v2]. We have also identified two histone H4proteins, [/gene/DDB_G0277183 H4a] and [/gene/DDB_G0276863 H4b], which have identical protein sequences but non-identical nucleotide sequences.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 13-APR-2004 KP

DDB_G0270306.summary: A comparative phylogenetics analysis of ''cudA''-like genes ([/gene/DDB_G0284465 cudA]) in Dictyostelia revealed that two paralogous genes: ([/gene/DDB_G0286351 cdl1A]) and ''cdl1B'' result from duplication of an ancestral ''cdl1'' gene. Expression of ''cdl1A'' and ''cdl1B'' is upregulated at 16 hours when migrating slugs have formed, with highest expression of both genes in pre-stalk cells. ''cdl1A''/''cdl1B'' double null mutants develop normally until culmination, but then show severe defects in stalk formation. The cellulose stalk tube formed but with a disorganized arrangement of stalk cells inside the tubes, indicating that Cdl1a and Cdl1b are both required for proper stalk morphogenesis. Deletion of ''cdl1'' in an outgroup species, ''Polysphondylium violaceum'' also caused defects in stalk morphogenesis, suggesting that the ancestral function of ''cdl1'' in the Dictyostelia was stalk formation (Kin, et al. 2021, PMID:34883046).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 20-DEC-2021 RD

DDB_G0285161.summary: The ''dagA'' gene product CRAC is required for positive regulation of adenylate cyclase activity ([/gene/DDB_G0281545 acaA]). The null mutant exhibits defects in chemotaxis and is unable to complete development ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8089184 Insall et al. 1994]). Upon stimulation with cAMP, CRAC is translocated from the cytosolic to the membrane fraction. This translocation requires the G-protein beta subunit ([/gene/DDB_G0277143 gpbA]) [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7790361  (Lilly and Devreotes 1995)]. CRAC associates with the plasma membrane at the leading edge of the membrane through its pleckstrin homology (PH) domain. This localized activation transmitted by the recruitment of cytosolic proteins leads to a localized response allowing the cells to move in the direction of the chemoattractant ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9778249 Parent et al. 1998]). DagA is involved in the signal transduction pathway responsible for AprA-dependent ([/gene/DDB_G0281663 aprA]) chemorepulsion. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30462573 Rijal et al. 2018]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 16-JUN-2003 PG

DDB_G0286359.summary:
Severin kinase was identified by screening DEAE column fractions of a soluble cell homogenate for kinase activity by adding severin [/gene/DDB_G0289327 sevA], actin, or a severin-actin complex. Kinase activity was detected that phosphorylated severin alone, or in complex with actin. A 62 kDa polypeptide co-eluted with the protein kinase activity. Subsequently the ''svkA'' cDNA was cloned and sequenced. The ''svkA'' gene was found to encode a protein kinase that is, over it's entire length, 51 % identical and 64% similar to human SOK1, a STE20-like kinase that is induced by oxidative stress. Similarity is even higher when the N-terminal catalyic domains are compared (75% / 84%, respectively) [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9582328 (Eichinger et al., 1998)].
The substrate specificity of severin kinase has been tested with several other actin binding proteins and different domains of severin. Only severin residues 1-151 and 152-362 turned out to be substrates, suggesting that the kinase phosphorylates severin at at least two sites. Severin kinase is activated by autophosphorylation, and severin phosphorylation was shown to be reduced in the presence of Ca2+. The presence of a STE20-like severin kinase in ''Dictyostelium'' suggests a direct signal transduction induced by stress, from the plasma membrane to the actin cytoskeleton by phosphorylation of the actin-binding protein severin [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9582328 (Eichinger et al., 1998)].
When the svkA gene was deleted, the cells showed a strong cytokinesis phenotype leading to multinucleated cells sometimes with more than 30 nuclei. The defect stems from the frequent inability of svkA-knockout cells to maintain symmetry during formation of the cleavage furrow and to sever the last cytosolic connection. GFP-SvkA is enriched at the centrosome and localizes to the midzone during the final stage of cell division. This suggests that SvkA is part of a regulatory pathway from the centrosome to the midzone, thus regulating the completion of cell division [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18042625 (Rohlfs et al., 2007)].
Detailed sequence analysis of the severin kinase revealed it to be a member of the hippo related kinases, while it has been identified as an interaction partner of CEP161 (gene [/gene/DDB_G0282851 cepL]). Furthermore, SvkA has been shown to co-localize with CEP161, which in turn inhibits autophosphorylation of the enzyme and it's kinase activity [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25607232 (Sukumaran et al., 2015)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 04-MAY-2015 PF
