DDB_G0280531.summary:
The mutated gene in one of the first REMI mutants was named ''lagC'' because morphogenesis stopped at the loose aggregate stage [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7926779 (Dynes et al. 1994)]. The gene encodes a secreted protein with a carboxy-terminal transmembrane domain that acts as an intercellular signal essential for post-aggregative gene expression [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7926779 (Dynes et al. 1994]; [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14651934 Kibler et al. 2003]; [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16386729 Iranfar et al. 2006)]. ''lagC'' was later found to be a member of a large family of highly similar genes and was renamed ''tgrC1'' (for Transmembrane, IPT, IG, E-set, Repeat protein); [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19285397 (Benabentos et al. 2009)].
Antibodies to TgrC1 protein were found to recognize gp150, a characterized surface glycoprotein responsible for late EDTA-resistant cell-cell adhesion [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11071787 (Wang et al. 2000)]. Strains in which [/gene/DDB_G0289073 csaA], encoding the adhesion protein gp80, has been deleted, express TgrC1 precociously and retain EDTA-resistant adhesion; however, ''csaA-''/''tgrC1-'' double mutants do not develop EDTA-resistant cell adhesion demonstrating that TgrC1 is an adhesion protein. TgrC1 mediates cell-cell adhesion by heterophilic interaction with the related protein TgrB1 ([/gene/DDB_G0280689 tgrB1]); [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21700835 (Hirose et al. 2011]; [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23477311 Chen et al. 2013]; [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24490801 Chen et al. 2014)]. Signal transduction from TgrB1/TgrC1 regulates expression of post-aggregative genes and thereby synchronizes temporal aspects of differentiation [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16386729 (Iranfar et al. 2006]; [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21700835 Hirose et al. 2011)].
Independent isolates from nature show a high degree of polymorphism of TrgB1 and TgrC1. Cells with compatible TgrB1 / TgrC1 pairs form common aggregates but distant kin that express variants are excluded. This mechanism of kin recognition protects from potential cheaters that fail to make their fair share of stalk cells [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23910661 (Ho et al. 2013]; [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26018043 Ho and Shaulsky 2015)]. ''tgrB1'' and ''tgrC1'' are coordinately transcribed between 2 and 8 hours of development [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25887420 (Rosengarten et al. 2015)]. Transcriptome analysis of several ''tgrB1'' / ''tgrC1'' gene replacement strains revealed 68 differentially expressed genes at 8 hours and 85 genes at 12 hours development (only one gene differentially expressed at both time points). This underlines the necessity of allorecognition facilitating the transition to multicellularity during development [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26395484 (Hirose et al. 2015)]. TgrB1/TgrC1 mediated development but not allorecognition is regulated by N-glycosylation through Alg9 ([/gene/DDB_G0279349 alg9]), a putative mannosyl transferase [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26359303 (Li et al. 2015)]. Cells lacking all three adenylate cyclase genes ([/gene/DDB_G0281545 acaA], [/gene/DDB_G0267376 acrA], [/gene/DDB_G0274569 acgA]) and overexpressing PKA ([/gene/DDB_G0283907 pkaC], [/gene/DDB_G0279413 pkaR]) exhibited cell polarization, tissue formation and cooperation when mixed with allotype-compatible wild-type cells, but not with incompatible ''tgrB1''-/''tgrC1''-/QS31 cells, indicating that TgrB1/TgrC1-mediated allorecognition and tissue formation do not require cAMP production as long as PKA is active (Hirose, et al 2021, PMID: 34169317).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 10-June-2016 PF; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0288183.summary:
''roco9'' encodes a large, multi-domain protein of the Roco family. Roco9 contains an N-terminal RhoGAP domain, a leucine-rich repeat (LRR) region, a Roc small GTPase domain, a COR (C-terminal of Roc) domain, and a protein kinase domain. Eleven ''Dictyostelium'' proteins belong to the Roco family: ([/gene/DDB_G0291079 gbpC]), ([/gene/DDB_G0273259 qkgA-1]), ([/gene/DDB_G0269250 pats1]), ([/gene/DDB_G0288251 roco4]), ([/gene/DDB_G0294533 roco5]), ([/gene/DDB_G0279417 roco6]), ([/gene/DDB_G0267472 roco7]), ([/gene/DDB_G0286127 roco8]), Roco9, ([/gene/DDB_G0291710 roco10]) and ([/gene/DDB_G0268636 roco11]).
Roco9 is localized to the cytosol and ''roco9'' is expressed during both growth and development with the highest level of expression during aggregation. Disruption of the ''roco9'' gene did not result in any significant developmental defects ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20348387 van Egmond and van Haastert 2010]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 18-OCT-2021 RD

DDB_G0292734.summary:
Initiation of protein translation in eukaryotes is regulated by phosphorylation of the alpha subunit of eukaryotictranslation initiation factor 2 (eIF2alpha). During periods of amino acid starvation, eIF2alpha is inactivated viaphosphorylation by the serine/threonine kinase ([/ontology/go/0004674/annotation/page/1 protein serine/threonine kinase activity]) GCN2 (general control nonderepressible), also known asPEK (pancreatic eukaryotic translation initiation factor kinase). The PEK family of protein kinases is highly conservedfrom yeast to humans, however, the effect on translation in metazoans is global whereas GCN2 in yeast acts to inhibittranslation of specific species of mRNA ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7855893 reviewed in Wek 1994]).
In ''Dictyostelium'', two members of the PEK family of protein kinases have been identified: [/gene/DDB_G0272837 ifkA] and[/gene/DDB_G0276829 ifkB]. Putative proteins belonging to the PEK family are: [/gene/DDB_G0276043 ifkC], [/gene/DDB_G0283065 DDB_G0283065], [/gene/DDB_G0268642 DDB_G0268642], [/gene/DDB_G0292734 DDB_G0292734], and [/gene/DDB_G0292734 DDB_G0292734].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 17-SEP-2004 KP

DDB_G0271092.summary:
Histones form the nucleosomal core ([/ontology/go/0000786/annotation/page/1 nucleosome]) ([/ontology/go/0006334/annotation/page/1 nucleosome assembly]) that is fundamental to chromatin structure (). The histone octamer is composed of an H3-H4 tetramer (two H3-H4 dimers) coupled with an H2A-H2Btetramer (two H2A-H2B dimers). The histone H1 linker protein plays a role in packaging nucleosomes into the 30 nmfiber found in chromatin ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9177486 Bukenberger et al. 1992]).
In ''Dictyostelium discoideum'' and ''Saccharomyces cerevisiae'', only one copy of histone [/gene/DDB_G0285319 H1] appears to be present, in comparison to other eukaryotes which have multiple copies and subtypes([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7867938 Hauser et al. 1995], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9046096 Ushinsky et al.1997]). Two putative H2A family members, [/gene/DDB_G0279667 H2AX] and [/gene/DDB_G0286747 H2AZ], and three H2Adomain-containing proteins, [/gene/DDB_G0289187 H2Av1], [/gene/DDB_G0289193 H2Av2], [/gene/DDB_G0289197 H2Av3], are present in ''Dictyostelium''. Two H2B domain-containing proteins also exist inthe ''Dicty'' genome: [/gene/DDB_G0293758 H2Bv1] and [/gene/DDB_G0276273 H2Bv2]. There are three histone H3proteins, [/gene/DDB_G0267402 H3a] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9177486 Bukenberger et al. 1992]), [/gene/DDB_G0270838 H3b], and [/gene/DDB_G0271092 H3c], and two H3 domain-containing proteins, [/gene/DDB_G0291185 H3v1] and [/gene/DDB_G0277979 H3v2]. We have also identified two histone H4proteins, [/gene/DDB_G0277183 H4a] and [/gene/DDB_G0276863 H4b], which have identical protein sequences but non-identical nucleotide sequences.
The three H3 histones present in the ''Dictyostelium'' genome are highly similar to H3 histones in othereukaryotes, including mammalian sequences. [/gene/DDB_G0270838 H3b] and [/gene/DDB_G0271092 H3c] encode proteins 136 amino acids in length, theconserved length for H3, whereas [/gene/DDB_G0267402 H3a] has a 3 amino acid insert compared to other sequences ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9177486 Bukenberger et al. 1992]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 13-APR-2004 KP

DDB_G0272022.summary:
DNA-dependent RNA polymerase catalyzes the transcription of DNA into RNA using the four ribonucleoside triphosphates as substrates ([/ontology/go/0003899/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase activity]). Three distinct zinc-containing RNA polymerases are found in eukaryotic nuclei: [/gene/DDB_G0275759 rpa1] for the ribosomal RNA precursor ([/ontology/go/0006360/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase I promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005736/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase I complex]), [/gene/DDB_G0279193 rpb1] for the mRNA precursor ([/ontology/go/0006366/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase II promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005665/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase II, core complex]), and [/gene/DDB_G0277199 rpc1] for 5S and tRNA genes ([/ontology/go/0006383/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase III promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005666/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase III complex]).
RNA polymerase III is a multisubunit complex. The subunits encoded by [/gene/DDB_G0277199 rpc1] (ortholog of ''S. cerevisiae RPO31''), [/gene/DDB_G0293560 rpa2] (''RPC2''), [/gene/DDB_G0268080 rpc3] (''RPC82''),[/gene/DDB_G0277671 rpc4] (''RPC53''), [/gene/DDB_G0271514 rpc5] (''RPC37''), [/gene/DDB_G0286521 rpc9] (''RPC17''), [/gene/DDB_G0272022 rpc34] (''RPC34''), [/gene/DDB_G0273425 rpc25-1] (''RPC25''), and [/gene/DDB_G0287707 rpc11] (''RPC11'') are unique to RNA polymerase III. Orthologs of ''RPC31'' and ''RPC17'' have not been identified in the ''Dictyostelium'' genome. Two subunits, [/gene/DDB_G0291362 rpc19] and [/gene/DDB_G0282339 rpa5] (''RPC19'' and ''RPC40'' in ''S. cerevisiae''), are common to RNA polymerase I and RNA polymerase III and correspond to subunits 3 and 11 of RNA polymerase II. Subunits [/gene/DDB_G0291636 rpb5], [/gene/DDB_G0291037 rpb6], [/gene/DDB_G0278039 rpb8], [/gene/DDB_G0272036 rpb10], and [/gene/DDB_G0283365 rpb12] are common to all three RNA polymerases ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12407181 Peyroche et al. 2002], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12381659 Schramm and Hernandez 2001]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 11-JUN-2009 PG

DDB_G0269262.summary: ''rabT2'' encodes a guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G protein) of the Rab family of small GTPases. G proteins are key components of signal transduction networks in which they function as molecular signaling switches, binding to GDP in the off state while binding GTP in the on state. Guanine nucleotide-exchange factors (GEFs) promote the exchange of GDP for GTP on Rab GTPases thus activating them, while GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) inactivate Rab GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP. Basic annotations have been added to this gene, 04-FEB-2021 RD

DDB_G0269610.summary: ''gxcT'' encodes a Rac guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF, RacGEF). RacGEFs are key components of signaling networks in which they activate Rho family GTPases by promoting the exchange of GDP for GTP. GxcT localizes to the cytosol, both in the presence and absence of cAMP stimulation. ''gxcT'' null mutants have defects in both growth and cytokinesis. The mutants also have a developmental defect, failing to aggregate normally and forming smaller fruiting bodies. ''gxcT'' null mutants also have defects in chemotaxis to cAMP, with a reduced speed of chemotaxis and decreased directional accuracy of movement toward the cAMP source. The mutant cells are less polarized than wild type cells, and pseudopods often extended from the lateral sides of the cells. In response to cAMP gradients, PIP3 production and Ras activation are not well oriented toward the cAMP gradient in ''gxcT'' null cells suggesting that ''gxcT'' orients the position of PIP3 production and Ras activation in a chemoattractant gradient. ''racE'' ([/gene/DDB_G0280975 racE]) null cells display many of the same phenotypes as ''gxcT'' null mutants, and GxcT binds to RacE in a GST pull down assay. In addition, GxcT binds to Rac1C ([/gene/DDB_G0282365 rac1C]), RacC ([/gene/DDB_G0293526 racC]), and RacF1 ([/gene/DDB_G0269176 racF1]). These results suggest that GxcT has GEF activity toward ''racE'', and possibly toward ''rac1C'', ''racC'' and ''racF1'', and that GxcT and RacE are involved in a signaling pathway regulating the stability and orientation of spatial sensing during chemotaxis ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24248334 Wang et al. 2013]), ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26940518 Rivero et al. 2016]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 12-JUL-2021 RD; annotation contributions: PMID:24248334, Miho Iijima

DDB_G0283453.summary:
Cyclic di-(3':5')-guanosine monophosphate (c-di-GMP), a major prokaryote signalling intermediate, has been identified in the eukaryote ''Dictyostelium''. the DgcA protein synthesizes c-di-GMP in a GTP-dependent manner and is expressed at the slug tip, the site of stalk cell differentiation. Disruption of the DgcA gene blocks fruiting body development at the stage of slug migration. Culmination and stalk formation are restored by exposing DgcA-null slugs to wild type secretion products or to c-di-GMP. Moreover, c-di-GMP specifically induces stalk gene expression in cell monolayers.
Like the bacterial proteins, Dictyostelium DgcA contains a C-terminal GGDEF domain, which is essential for DgcA function. DgcA has been identified in all four clades of Dictyostelia, and the ''P. pallidum'' DgcA (PPA_G1423310) expressed in the ''D. discoideum'' DgcA null mutant restores stalk formation and culmination. This research identifies the long-elusive stalk-inducing morphogen and a role for c-di-GMP in eukaryotes [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22864416 (Chen and Schaap, 2012)].
[http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28057864 (Chen et al. 2017)] further investigated the c-di-GMP signal transduction pathway and demonstrated that the stalk-inducing signal cyclic diguanylate (c-di-cGMP) activates cAMP synthesis by adenylate cyclase A ([/gene/DDB_G0281545 acaA]) which is specifically expressed at the apical tip. cAMP then activates cAMP-dependent protein kinase A (PKA) ([/gene/DDB_G0283907 pkaC], [/gene/DDB_G0279413 pkaR]), which then triggers stalk differentiation. Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 11-SEP-2012 PF; annotation contribution: PMID 22864416 Zhi-Hui Chen.

DDB_G0277861.summary:
PAT1 is a calcium-translocating P-type ATPase ([/ontology/go/0005388/annotation/page/1 calcium-transporting ATPase activity]), the type IIB ATPase which is responsible for translocating calcium ions across the plasma membrane ([/ontology/go/0006816/annotation/page/1 calcium ion transport]). ''Dictyostelium'' PAT1 is very similar to other Ca2+ ATPases of the plasma membrane, and ''patA'' gene expression is upregulated when cells are grown in Ca2+-rich medium. The rate of intracellular P-type Ca2+ uptake is also increased ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7499325 Moniakis et al., 1995]). Upregulation of ''patA'' expression is strongly reduced when the serine/threonine phosphatase calcineurin ([/gene/DDB_G0276883 canA], [/gene/DDB_G0267446 cnbA]) was inhibited, suggesting the regulation of PAT1 by calcineurin ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9885293 Moniakis et al., 1999]).
PAT1-deficient cells, due to antisense expression of ''patA'' RNA or to the presence of calcineurin inhibitors, grow normally in low Ca2+ medium but poorly in high Ca2+ medium. PAT1 colocalizes with calmodulin ([/gene/DDB_G0279407 calA]) to the [/ontology/go/0031164/annotation/page/1 contractile vacuolar membrane] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7499325 Moniakis et al., 1995]), and also localizes to the [/ontology/go/0005886/annotation/page/1 plasma membrane]. These findings suggest that the contractile vacuole fuses with the plasma membrane to eliminate excess intracellular Ca2+ and maintain Ca2+ homeostasis ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9885293 Moniakis et al., 1999]). Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 04-FEB-2005 PF

DDB_G0282581.summary: Wdr45l belongs to a conserved group of proteins termed PROPPINs (beta-propeller that binds phosphoinositides) which are phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate (PtdIns3P)-binding proteins required for autophagosome biogenesis. ''wdr45l'' is similar to human WDR45, mutations in which cause Beta-Propeller Protein-Associated Neurodegeneration (BPAN). Wdr45l localizes to the autophagosome. ''wdr45l'' null mutants are unable to aggregate, have a severe growth defect and display a block in autophagy. In addition, ''wdr45l'' null mutants have phenotypes that are remarkably similar to those of ''vmp1'' ([/gene/DDB_G0285175 vmp1]) null mutant cells, including the abnormal enrichment of PtdIns3P at the autophagosome formation site, and a chronically activated endoplasmic reticulum stress response, suggesting that both proteins are involved in the regulation of autophagosome formation (Tornero-Ecija, et al 2021, PMID: 34328055).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 06-AUG-2021 RD

DDB_G0280539.summary: The ABC superfamily of genes is one of the largest in the genomes of both bacteria and eukaryotes. The proteins encoded by these genes all carry a characteristic 200- to 250-amino-acid ATP-binding cassette that gives them their family name ([/ontology/go/0042626/annotation/page/1 ATPase activity, coupled to transmembrane movement of substances]). In bacteria they are mostly involved in nutrient import, while in eukaryotes many are involved in export([/ontology/go/0006810/annotation/page/1 transport]), ([/ontology/go/0016021/annotation/page/1 integral to membrane]). Seven different families (A to G) have been defined in eukaryotes based on sequence homology, domain topology, and function. ''Dictyostelium'' has 71 ABC transporters (including one on the chromosome 2 duplication) and 13 ABCC family members: [/gene/DDB_G0280541 abcC1], [/gene/DDB_G0280055 abcC2], [/gene/DDB_G0287691 abcC3], [/gene/DDB_G0286559 abcC5], [/gene/DDB_G0287593 abcC6], [/gene/DDB_G0291243 abcC7], [/gene/DDB_G0284867 abcC8], [/gene/DDB_G0285165 abcC9], [/gene/DDB_G0280977 abcC10], [/gene/DDB_G0280973 abcC12], [/gene/DDB_G0280539 abcC13], [/gene/DDB_G0287589 abcC14], and [/gene/DDB_G0280459 abcC15]. Transporters of the C family have been shown to transport glutathione conjugants as well as to export cadmium ions. They are always found as full transporters with two copies of the transmembrane-ABC unit. Many of the genes of this family in humans and other animals have an additional transmembrane domain at the N terminus [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12456012 (Anjard and Loomis 2002)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 16-JUN-2003 PG

DDB_G0272837.summary:
''ifkA'' and [/gene/DDB_G0276829 ifkB] encode homologs of a kinase that phosphorylate the translation initiation factor eIF2alpha ([/ontology/go/0004686/annotation/page/1 elongation factor-2 kinase activity]), ([/ontology/go/0006445/annotation/page/1 regulation of translation]). The two Ifk proteins possess all of the hallmarks of typical GCN2 proteins, including the characteristic kinase domain and the HisRS domain. ''ifkA'' is expressed during growth and drops dramatically soon after the onset of development.
Disruption of the ''ifkA'' gene causes defects in early development. ''ifkA'' null cells aggregate earlier than parental cells due to a more rapid establishment of the cAMP pulsing system. Cells lacking a functional IfkA protein form larger mounds and subsequent developmental structures ([/ontology/go/0007275/annotation/page/1 multicellular organismal development]), ([/ontology/go/0009653/annotation/page/1 anatomical structure morphogenesis]). This defect was linked to a reduced extracellular level of Countin ([/gene/DDB_G0274597 ctnA]). Efficient translation of ''ctnA'' mRNA requires increased phosphorylation of eIF2a by IfkA [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12697064 (Fang et al. 2003)].
In ''Dictyostelium'', two members of the GCN2 (also known as PEK, pancreatic eukaryotic translation initiation factor kinase) family of protein kinases have been identified: [/gene/DDB_G0272837 ifkA] and[/gene/DDB_G0276829 ifkB]. Putative proteins belonging to the GCN2 family are: [/gene/DDB_G0276043 ifkC], [/gene/DDB_G0283065 DDB_G0283065], [/gene/DDB_G0268642 DDB_G0268642], [/gene/DDB_G0292734 DDB_G0292734], and [/gene/DDB_G0292734 DDB_G0292734].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 14-NOV-2003 PG

DDB_G0277107.summary: The LSM (like-Sm) proteins are a conserved group known to function in mRNA splicing and mRNA degradation.Complexes containing Lsm2-8 function in [/ontology/go/0000398/annotation/page/1 nuclear mRNA splicing, via spliceosome] in association with [/ontology/go/0005688/annotation/page/1 snRNP U6]. Complexes consistingof Lsm1-7, on the other hand, are believed to function in [/ontology/go/0006402/annotation/page/1 mRNA catabolic process] (reviewed in [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15916535 Beggs 2005]). In ''Dictyostelium'', clear orthologs of the Lsm proteins exist:[/gene/DDB_G0279837 lsm1], [/gene/DDB_G0281779 lsm2], [/gene/DDB_G0277107 lsm3], [/gene/DDB_G0287053 lsm4], [/gene/DDB_G0268716 lsm5],[/gene/DDB_G0275719 lsm6], [/gene/DDB_G0289499 lsm7], and [/gene/DDB_G0288479 lsm8]. Additionally, the ''Dictyostelium''genome contains putative orthologs of human LSM10 ([/gene/DDB_G0291015 DDB_G0291015]), LSM11 ([/gene/DDB_G0289453 DDB_G0289453]), and LSM12 ([/gene/DDB_G0270402 DDB_G0270402]). LSM10 and LSM11 associate with the U7snRNA, whereas LSM12 is hypothesized to be involved in RNA methylation ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11574479 Pillai et al. 2001], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15225602 Albrecht and Lengauer 2004]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 13-MAR-2006 KP

DDB_G0276455.summary: G proteins are evolutionarily conserved heterotrimeric GTP binding proteins that can act as molecular switches. ''gpaG'' encodes G-alpha 7 that, together with the G-beta and G-gamma subunits ([/gene/DDB_G0277143 gpbA], [/gene/DDB_G0274125 gpgA]) associates with the gamma aminobutyric acid (GABA) receptor GrlE ([/gene/DDB_G0291356 grlE]). Overexpression of G-alpha 7 results in abnormal morphogenesis starting at the slug stage and spore differentiation factor 2 (SDF-2) production is abolished in ''gpaG'' null mutants [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1930158  (Wu and Devreotes 1991)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7949425  (Wu et al. 1994)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16672332  (Anjard and Loomis 2006)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19176583  (Anjard et al. 2009)]. Exogenous GABA induces release of AcbA ([/gene/DDB_G0270658 acbA]) so that it can be processed into the signal peptide SDF-2 that induces rapid sporulation. This signal transduction pathway depends on ''grlE'', ''gpaG'', ''pikA'', ([/gene/DDB_G0278727 pikA]) and ''pkgB'' ([/gene/DDB_G0290157 pkgB]) [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16672332  (Anjard and Loomis 2006)]. Cells carrying mutations in these genes do not form SDF-2.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 02-MAY-2019 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0289677.summary:
The homeodomain is a sequence-specific DNA binding motif that consists of a helix-turn-helix. Homeobox-containing proteins have transcription factor activity. They have beenidentified in most if not all phyla of eukaryotes. Inmetazoans, homeobox-containing proteins are known to be involvedin regulating the anterior-posterior body plan and in thespecification of certain cell types and anterior-posteriorcompartments (see [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9486804 Han and Firtel 1998] and references therein). There are 14 predicted proteins that contain homeobox domains in ''Dictyostelium'':[/gene/DDB_G0275173 hbx2], [/gene/DDB_G0291075 warA], [/gene/DDB_G0291197 hbx3], [/gene/DDB_G0272967 hbx4], [/gene/DDB_G0273127 hbx5-1] (on the chromosome 2 duplication: [/gene/DDB_G0273645 hbx5-2]), [/gene/DDB_G0277505 hbx6], [/gene/DDB_G0278225 hbx7], [/gene/DDB_G0279257 hbx8], [/gene/DDB_G0280473 hbx9], [/gene/DDB_G0284293 hbx10], [/gene/DDB_G0295787 hbx11], [/gene/DDB_G0286733 hbx12], [/gene/DDB_G0288975 hbx13], and [/gene/DDB_G0289677 hbx14].
[http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25963254 Mishra and Saran 2015] performed a genome-wide classification and comparative genomic analysis of the 14 homeobox genes present in D. discoideum, and found that they could be classified into 3 groups: TALE, OTHER and NOVEL classes, ''hbx14'' belonging to the NOVEL class.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 07-JUL-2015 RD

DDB_G0273069.summary:
''ndkC'' encodes the cytosolic form of nucleoside diphosphate (NDP) kinase (EC 2.7.4.6). The related [/gene/DDB_G0279911 ndkM] gene encodes a mitochondrial NDP kinase ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8244981 Troll et al. 1993]). This enzyme is responsible for the phosphorylation of nucleoside or deoxynucleoside diphosphates into the corresponding triphosphates at the expense of ATP ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8931563 Deville-Bonne et al. 1996]). NDP kinase is transiently phosphorylated on an active site histidine as part of the catalytic process (see [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9786875 Schneider et al. 1998 and references therein]).
This enzyme plays a crucial role in equilibrating the cellular nucleotide pools (see [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9786875 Schneider et al. 1998 and references therein]). Besides this role in intermediate nucleotide metabolism, NDP kinase has been implicated in a large number of cellular functions. Part of the cellular NDP kinase is associated with the plasma membrane and stimulated by cell surface cAMP receptors. The GTP produced by the action of NDP kinase is capable of activating G-proteins as monitored by altered G-protein-receptor interaction and the activation of the effector enzyme phospholipase C ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8389692 Bominaar et al. 1993]). Nucleoside diphosphate kinase is also associated with the cytoskeleton where it channels ATP to the myosin molecule ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8816286 Aguado-Velasco et al. 1996]). Yet another role for NDP kinase is to feed GTP into the translation machinery, as inferred by its association with active ribosomes ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7733916 Sonnemann and Mutzel 1995]). Knock down of NDP kinase expression suppressed the phenotypic defects that are caused by AMPK ([/gene/DDB_G0277905 snfA]), hyperactivity resulting either from overexpression of AMP alpha T or from mitochondrial dysfunction. These included rescue of defects in slug phototaxis, fruiting body morphology and growth in a liquid medium. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21374069 Annesley et al. 2011]).
The X-ray structure of nucleoside diphosphate kinase (NDP kinase) from ''Dictyostelium discoideum'' has been determined ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1846924 Dumas et al. 1991], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7966307 Morera et al. 1994]). The protein is a hexamer with D3 symmetry. The X-ray structure of wild type and several mutants nucleoside diphosphate kinase bound to substrates, co-factors and inhibitors has also been determined (see [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12171931 Gallois-Montbrun et al. 2002], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11277918 Schneider et al. 2001], and references therein).
Nucleoside analogs are currently used in antiretrovirus therapies. The best known example is AZT, one of the first drugs to be used for the treatment of AIDS. However, only the triphosphate derivatives of these compounds act as substrates of the viral reverse transcriptase. Since these compounds cannot enter cells, nucleoside analogs are administered and phosphorylated by cellular kinases, including nucleoside diphosphate (NDP) kinase. Studies of the enzymatic mechanism of this enzyme provide essential information for the design of new nucleoside analogs with increased efficiency in antiretroviral therapies ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11768316 Schneider et al. 2000]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 16-JUN-2003 PG

DDB_G0271096.summary: The ''atg7'' gene was isolated among several members of the autophagy family of genes, conserved from yeast to man. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12626495 Otto et al. 2003)]. Macroautophagy is used by eukaryotic cells to recycle non-essential cellular components during starvation and development. ''atg7'' null mutants grow normally, but survival during nitrogen starvation is reduced and development of the mutant is severely impaired. On bacterial lawns ''atg7'' mutant cells do not aggregate, but form multi-tipped aggregates on filters ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12626495 Otto et al. 2003)]. The multi-tipped phenotype of ''atg7'' mutants is similar to that of mutants in other autophagy genes atg6, ([/gene/DDB_G0269244 atg6A]) atg101, ([/gene/DDB_G0288287 atg101]) tipC, ([/gene/DDB_G0267422 tipC]) and tipD ([/gene/DDB_G0275323 tipD]). In yeast, the E1-like ATG7 protein has been shown to activate ATG12 in an ubiquitination-like reaction before conjugation with ATG5. This interaction was confirmed in ''Dictyostelium'' when the ATG5-ATG12 ([/gene/DDB_G0282929 atg12]) was found to be absent in ''atg7'' null mutants [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12626495  (Otto et al. 2003)] and further confirmed with the finding that ''Dictyostelium'' ATG12 recognizes ATG7 in 2-hybrid assays which suggests the formation of an E1-like complex ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26246495 Mesquita et al. 2015)]. Axenically grown ''atg7'' null cells plated on filters form aberrant fruiting bodies which do not produce viable, detergent-resistent spores. Wild-type cells in a chimaera do not rescue the developmental defects, showing that the ''atg7'' mutation is autonomous ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12626495 Otto et al. 2003)]. A screen for mutants defective in spore differentiation identified ''atg7'' as being essential for this process, and further analysis revealed that an ''atg7'' null mutant was specifically impaired in cAMP induction of prespore gene expression. Mutants lacking ''atg5'' ([/gene/DDB_G0289881 atg5]) and ''atg9'' ([/gene/DDB_G0285323 atg9]) have the same defect, indicating that autophagy is required for cAMP induction of prespore gene expression ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31051160 Yamada et al. 2019)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 09-DEC-2019 RD

DDB_G0275711.summary:
The [/gene/DDB_G0275711 nhe1] gene, predicted to have sodium-hydrogen antiporter activity, is expressed in chemotactically competent cells but not in vegetative cells. Immunostaining for Nhe1 shows that the protein is localized at the membrane, cytoplasm, and in the leading edge membrane of chemotaxing cells. Null ''nhe1-'' cells have a reduced level of intracellular pH (regulation of intracellular pH), a reduced chemotaxis rate, and mislocalized F-actin. Additionally, ''nhe1-'' cells do not have a polarized cell morphology, however, they retain the ability to sense a gradient, as indicated by asymmetric localization of GFP-CRAC ([/gene/DDB_G0285161 dagA]) in response to a PI3-kinase inhibitor ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15851518 Patel and Barber 2005]).
Barber and colleagues showed that expression of the [/gene/DDB_G0278733 aip1] gene suppresses the ''nhe-'' chemotaxis and F-actin assembly phenotype, while expressing just a C-terminal fragment enhances these phenotypes. Since the Aip1 C-terminal fragment binds cofilin they suggest a cooperative role of Aip1 and cofilin in pH-dependent cell migration, and that the defective chemotaxis in ,''nhe1-'' cells is determined primarily by loss of cofilin-dependent actin dynamics ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20668166 Patel and Barber 2010]).
Extracellular Ca2+ and K+ have long been known to affect cell motility. Nhe1 plays no role in Ca2+ facilitation or the Ca2+ requirement for chemotactic orientation. However, Nhe1 has been shown to be involved in both K+ facilitation for motility (at a minimum of 15 mM) and a K+/ Na+ requirement for chemotactic orientation. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21239624 Lusche et al.2011]).
Wessels and colleagues found that nhe1, like [/gene/DDB_G0272344 htt], is required for calcium chemotaxis and for potassium-facilitated chemotaxis. Localizes to leading edge, however is mislocalized in the ''htt-'' mutant ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25149514 Wessels et al.2014]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 14-APR-2015 PF

DDB_G0288771.summary: ''darA'' encodes the protein darlin, an atypical guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) of the Rap1 GTPase-GDP dissociation stimulator 1 family. ''darA'' is an ortholog of the human RAP1GDS gene, which encodes Rap1 GTPase-GDP dissociation stimulator 1 and which acts as a guanine exchange factor (GEFs) through a distinct exchange mechanism compared with canonical GEFs. Darlin was identified as protein that binds to the Rho small GTPases RacE ([/gene/DDB_G0280975 racE]) and RacC ([/gene/DDB_G0293526 racC]). Darlin preferentially binds to the GDP-bound form of RacE. ''darA'' is expressed throughout growth and development. ''darA'' null cells lack defects in growth or cytokinesis. When plated on agar plates with bacteria as a food source, ''darA'' null mutants are able to ingest bacteria and form colonies at the same rate as wild type cells, and when bacteria are depleted the mutant cells develop normally. However, under a layer of starvation buffer, ''darA'' null cells are unable to initiate aggregation, and when grown on non-nutrient agar, ''darA'' null cells form very small aggregating centers leading to smaller sized slugs and fruiting bodies. Taken together, these results suggest that darlin is a non-canonical GEF which plays a role in the efficient streaming of cells in early development ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9802899 Vithalani et al. 1998]), ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26940518 Rivero et al. 2016]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 13-JUL-2021 RD

DDB_G0275687.summary:
[/gene/DDB_G0275689 abcG2] and ''abcG18'' are present in the ''Dictyostelium'' genome as a tandem. In insertional mutant that disrupts both [/gene/DDB_G0275689 abcG2] and ''abcG18'' (''mdrA1/mdrA2'') results in release from the developmental block and the suppression of the defect in initial cell type choice caused by loss of the [/gene/DDB_G0271916 rtoA] gene. AbcG2 is localized to the endosome. ''abcG2-/abcG18-'' cells have an endocytosis rate roughly 70% that of wild-type ([/ontology/go/0006897/annotation/page/1 endocytosis]). The triple null ''abcG2-/abcG18-/rtoA-'' has even lower endocytosis rates, about 20% that of wild type cells. The exocytosis rates of ''abcG2-/abcG18-''and ''abcG2-/abcG18-/rtoA-'' are roughly that of wild-type. ''abcG2-/[/gene/DDB_G0275687 abcG18]-'' endosomes have an unusually high pH ([/ontology/go/0030641/annotation/page/1 regulation of cellular pH]), whereas ''abcG2-/abcG18-/rtoA-'' endosomes have an almost normal pH [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11719559 (Brazill et al. 2000)].
The ABC superfamily of genes is one of the largest in the genomes of both bacteria and eukaryotes. The proteins encoded by these genes all carry a characteristic 200- to 250-amino-acid ATP-binding cassette that gives them their family name ([/ontology/go/0042626/annotation/page/1 ATPase activity, coupled to transmembrane movement of substances]). In bacteria they are mostly involved in nutrient import, while in eukaryotes many are involved in export([/ontology/go/0006810/annotation/page/1 transport]). Seven different families have been defined in eukaryotes based on sequence homology, domain topology, and function. Sequences from the well-advanced ''Dictyostelium'' genome project have allowed to recognize 71 ABC transporters (including one on the chromosome 2 duplication) of this superfamily. The ABCG family is characterized by the ABC domain preceding the transmembrane domain([/ontology/go/0016021/annotation/page/1 integral to membrane]). All of the members of this family in animals are half-transporters while all of the fungal members are full transporters with two ABC-transmembrane units. No members of this family are found in bacteria. ''Dictyostelium'' and ''Arabidopsis'' have members of both types[http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12456012 (Anjard and Loomis 2002)]. Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 18-OCT-2004 PG
DDB_G0275687.note: The sequences from the Sequencing Center and GenBank record AF482381 are identical.

DDB_G0292384.summary: The ABC superfamily of genes is one of the largest in the genomes of both bacteria and eukaryotes. In bacteria they are mostly involved in nutrient import, while in eukaryotes many are involved in export([/ontology/go/0006810/annotation/page/1 transport]). Seven different families (A to G) have been defined in eukaryotes based on sequence homology, domain topology, and function. ''Dictyostelium'' has 71 ABC transporters (including one on the chromosome 2 duplication). The ABCH family includes members that do not fit into the seven eukaryotic families and are not necessarily related to each other. ''Dictyostelium'' has five genes that compose this group: [/gene/DDB_G0292384 abcH1], [/gene/DDB_G0267428 abcH2], [/gene/DDB_G0275697 abcH3], [/gene/DDB_G0283479 abcH4], and[/gene/DDB_G0293528 arsA]. The ''Dictyostelium'' [/gene/DDB_G0292384 abcH1] and [/gene/DDB_G0267428 abcH2] genes have a single ABC domain and no TM domain. They cluster with ABC transporters involved in the uptake of polar amino acids[http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12456012  (Anjard and Loomis 2002)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 16-JUN-2003 PG

DDB_G0289811.summary:
There are 29 genes encoding actin in ''Dictyostelium'' with amino acid identity greater than 83%, ''act1''-''act29''. Seventeen of these genes encode identical proteins: [/gene/DDB_G0289553 act1], [/gene/DDB_G0274133 act2], [/gene/DDB_G0289005 act4], [/gene/DDB_G0289663 act5], [/gene/DDB_G0274135 act6], [/gene/DDB_G0280545 act7], [/gene/DDB_G0269234 act8], [/gene/DDB_G0274601 act9], [/gene/DDB_G0288879 act11], [/gene/DDB_G0274129 act12], [/gene/DDB_G0274599 act13], [/gene/DDB_G0274137 act14], [/gene/DDB_G0272520 act15], [/gene/DDB_G0272248 act16], [/gene/DDB_G0274727 act19], [/gene/DDB_G0274285 act20], and [/gene/DDB_G0274561 act21], while [/gene/DDB_G0289811 act10], [/gene/DDB_G0275023 act22], and [/gene/DDB_G0289487 act3] respectively have 1, 4 and 11 amino acid differences compared to the 17 identical genes. The proteins encoded by [/gene/DDB_G0274131 act17], [/gene/DDB_G0289489 act18], [/gene/DDB_G0268744 act23] and [/gene/DDB_G0289505 act24]are more divergent.
Actin is a major [/ontology/go/0005200/annotation/page/1 structural constituent of cytoskeleton]. Actin is one of the most abundant proteins in ''Dictyostelium'', constituting approximately 8% of the total protein in vegetative cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/561722 Alton and Lodish et al. 1977]).Actin synthesis is developmentally regulated, peaking shortly after starvation (reviewed by [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6894564 Firtel] in 1981). The different actin genes differ in their levels of expression, with [/gene/DDB_G0274135 act6], [/gene/DDB_G0269234 act8] and [/gene/DDB_G0274129 act12] being highly expressed both during growth and development compared to [/gene/DDB_G0289005 act4], [/gene/DDB_G0289663 act5], [/gene/DDB_G0280545 act7] and [/gene/DDB_G0272248 act16] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6286214 McKeown and Firtel 1981]). Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 19-SEP-2003 PG
DDB_G0289811.note: This gene is called actR in PMID 8643615 (Loomis, pers. comm.) PG 5-23-2003

DDB_G0283419.summary: G proteins are evolutionarily conserved heterotrimeric GTP binding proteins that can act as molecular switches within G protein-coupled receptor signaling pathways. ''gpaI'' encodes the Galpha9 subunit that functions in signal transduction pathways that inhbit both growth and development [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12176329  (Brzostowski et al. 2002)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19635129  (Bakthavatsalam et al. 2009)]. ''gpaI'' null mutants grow more rapidly and complete mound formation more quickly than wild type strains. Galpha9-dependent processes appear to limit the time of accumulation of PIP3, cAMP and cGMP following cAMP receptor stimulation during early development. Thus ''gpaI'' negatively regulates the PI3K/PTEN, adenylyl cyclase, and guanylyl cyclase signaling pathways and thereby regulates chemotaxis to cAMP [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15059962  (Brzostowski et al. 2004)]. During culmination, cells secrete high levels of glutamate that inhibit release of the SDF-2 precursor AcbA ([/gene/DDB_G0270658 acbA]). This inhibition is dependent on the Gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) receptor GrlE ([/gene/DDB_G0291356 grlE]) and the Galpha9 subunit [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16672332  (Anjard and Loomis 2006)]. GrlE also binds GABA but does so only when it is bound to G protein containing the Galpha7 ([/gene/DDB_G0276455 gpaG]) subunit [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19176583  (Anjard et al. 2009)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 24-DEC-2018 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis
phenotypes: aberrant activation of adenylate cyclase activity
aberrant protein localization to plasma membrane

DDB_G0282595.summary: ''gmfA'' encodes a protein of the ADF-H/Gelsolin-like domain superfamily. GmfA is widely conserved and is an ortholog of human Glia maturation factor gamma and yeast AIM7. GmfA isolated from ''Dictyostelium'' suppresses the activation of actin assembly by Arp2/3 complex (Nakano, et al. 2010, PMID:20517925). ''gmfA'' null cells have defects in growth, cytokinesis, and increased cell-substrate adhesion. Migrating ''gmfA'' null cells have a fan-like shape, and extend a single broad pseudopod that is almost three times as large as pseudopods of wild type (wt) cells. In addition, ''gmfA'' null cells form broken, disconnected aggregation streams and migrate with a higher persistency than wt cells. These results suggest that GmfA plays a role in the regulation of actin assembly and cell migration (Fujimoto, et al. 2021, PMID:34855306).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 09-DEC-2021 RD

DDB_G0268618.summary: The ''pinA'' gene encodes a parvulin-type peptidyl prolyl cis-trans isomerase. ''pinA'' was shown to be a functional homolog of ''Saccharomyces cerevisiae'' ESS1. ''pinA'' null mutants have a decreased growth rate, reduced spore formation and display abnormal prespore-prestalk patterning suggesting that ''pinA'' is important for growth, cell patterning, and cell differentiation. [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/27836548  (Haokipp et al. 2016)]Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 17-NOV-2016 RD

DDB_G0293528.summary: The ArsA family of bacterial genes are involved in the transport of arsenate, selenate, and other anionic compounds. These proteins possess an ABC (ATP-binding cassette) domain but do not have transmembrane domains, rather they associate with another protein, [/gene/DDB_G0289879 arsB], that has two potential transmembrane domains. There are homologs of ArsA in plants, animals, and fungi. ''Dictyostelium'' has a single ArsA gene with more than 55% identity with its eukaryotic counterparts ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6420574 Anjard and Loomis 2002]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 16-JUN-2003 PG

DDB_G0281969.summary: MybE is responsible for expression of prestalk genes in PstO cells at the slug stage and stalk genes in lower cup cells during culminants [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16571632  (Fukuzawa et al. 2006)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17237363  (Tsujioka et al. 2007)]. MybE was purified from nuclear extracts of slug cells by affinity chromotography to a 30 bp region from the regulatory region of ecmA ([/gene/DDB_G0277853 ecmA]) that is essential for expression in PstO cells. The carboxy terminal portion of MybE has a region of regularly spaced tryptophan residues that is found in the Myb family of DNA binding proteins followed by a conserved motif that occurs predominantly in Myb proteins of plants but is also found in those of fish and reptiles. There are 6 other genes in Dictyostelium encoding additional members of this family. MybE binds preferentially to the dyad AACTGTT followed by a C-rich region found in the regulatory regions of both ''ecmA'' and ecmB ([/gene/DDB_G0269132 ecmB]). Mutants in which mybE is knocked out grow and aggregate normally but form long, thin slugs that often fragment [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16571632  (Fukuzawa et al. 2006)]. The proportion of prestalk cells appears to be reduced in these slugs.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 02-MAR-2018 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0284611.summary: RipA is a component of the TORC2 complex, which consists of ([/gene/DDB_G0281569 tor]), ([/gene/DDB_G0292592 lst8]), ([/gene/DDB_G0277399 piaA]) and ''ripA''. The TORC2 complex plays a central and critical role in chemotaxis and relay of the cAMP signal [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10473630  (Lee et al. 1999)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16079174  (Lee et al. 2005)]. RipA was isolated as a Ras-interacting protein and later found to be orthologous to the SinA component of human TORC2. Activated RasC ([/gene/DDB_G0281385 rasC]) stimulates TORC2 to phosphorylate downstream protein kinases, PKB ([/gene/DDB_G0268620 pkbA]) and PKBR1 ([/gene/DDB_G0290157 pkgB]), as well as to activate adenylyl cyclase ([/gene/DDB_G0281545 acaA]) [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18635356  (Kamimura et al. 2008)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20660630  (Cai et al. 2010)]. The small GTPase RapA ([/gene/DDB_G0291237 rapA]) binds to RipA, and also regulates TORC2 activity along with RasC [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/27172998  (Khanna et al. 2016)]. ''ripA'' null cells are unable to aggregate or polarize in a cAMP gradient but express early developmental genes in response to cAMP pulses [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10473630  (Lee et al. 1999)]. Treating ''ripA'' null cells with artificial pulses of cAMP rescues development, indicating that ligand binding to CAR1 ([/gene/DDB_G0273397 carA-1]), ([/gene/DDB_G0273533 carA-2]) can stimulate TOR activity in the absence of RipA [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10473630  (Lee et al. 1999)]. Cells lacking ''ripA'', ''piaA'' and ''lst8'' have significantly elevated rates of phagocytosis, revealing that the TORC2 complex is also a negative regulator of phagocytosis [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22266904  (Rosel et al. 2012)]. Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 03-JUL-2019 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

Tumor necrosis factor (TNF) receptor-assocated protein 1 (TRAP1) plays a role in many cellular processes, suchas cell cycle regulation, differentiation, and apoptosis, however, its exact molecular function is unknown.First identified by [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12372338 Morita and colleagues (2002)], the ''Dictyostelium'' Trap1 protein localizes to the [/ontology/go/0030864/annotation/page/1 cortical actin cytoskeleton]. During theprestarvation response, Trap1 translocates to the [/ontology/go/0005739/annotation/page/1 mitochondrion], a process that is induced byhigh cell density and by conditioned medium, indicating that an extracellular factor regulates this process. Trap1 has also been observed in the [/ontology/go/0005730/annotation/page/1 nucleolus] and [/ontology/go/0031160/annotation/page/1 spore wall] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15652353 Yamaguchi et al. 2005]).
Inantisense RNA experiments, the reduction of Trap1 protein results in reduced growth rate and delayed development([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15507488 Morita et al. 2004]). Cells overexpressing Trap1 exhibitprecocious aggregation, however, development arrests before the tight mound stage. Changes in Trap1 expressionaffect the expression of [/gene/DDB_G0280531 lagC], [/gene/DDB_G0289073 csaA], and the prestarvation genes [/gene/DDB_G0285431 dia1] and ''dia3'', but not [/gene/DDB_G0273063 dscA-1] or [/gene/DDB_G0273397 carA-1]. Additionally, thetranslocation of Trap1 to the mitochondria is not altered in [/gene/DDB_G0277143 gpbA] or in [/gene/DDB_G0283907 pkaC]mutant cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15507488 Morita et al. 2004]). Further analysis of trap1-RNAi cells shows defects in [/ontology/go/0030435/annotation/page/1 sporulation] and in resistance to heat shock, an indication that Trap1 does in fact function as a chaperone, as its membership in the HSP90 family suggests.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 04-NOV-2004 KP

DDB_G0287101.summary: NoxA ([/gene/DDB_G0289653 noxA]), NoxB and NoxC ([/gene/DDB_G0291117 noxC]) are homologs of the heme-containing subunit of NADPH oxidase flavocytochromes that generate superoxide for defense and signaling. Each of them has 6 predicted transmembrane regions and uses 4 histidine moieties to bind 2 heme groups. Mutations that inactivate the ''nox'' genes in the genetic background of strain JH10 result in a developmental block at the tipped mound stage, but have no effect on growth in association with bacteria. [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15950752  (Lardy et al. 2005)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16367873  (Benghezal et al. 2006)]. A triple mutant in which ''noxA'', ''noxB'', and ''noxC'' are disrupted in the genetic background of strain AX2 develops normally, but has defects in the defense response to bacteria. The Sentinel cells that normally provide innate immunity in slugs are unable to generate superoxide when all 3 of the ''nox'' genes are deleted. Reactive oxygen species (ROS) stimulate S cells to take up bacteria by phagocytosis and to release mitochondrial DNA nets that trap extracellular bacteria. ''noxA''/''noxB''/''noxC'' triple null mutants release very few DNA nets and fail to clear bacteria from the slugs. [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26927887  (Zhang et al. 2016)]. ''noxA'' is expressed at high levels in vegetative cells and at lower levels during development. ''noxB'' and ''noxC'' are only expressed after 6 hrs of development [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15950752  (Lardy et al. 2005)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 21-DEC-2018 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0272210.summary: Isocitrate dehydrogenases are important enzymes of carbohydrate metabolism, which catalyze the oxidative decarboxylation of isocitrate into alpha-ketoglutarate (). IdhC and IdhM are very similar to the corresponding proteins in mammals, which are thought to form homodimers.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 08-FEB-2005 PF

DDB_G0268634.summary: ''pde3'' encodes a type I phosphodiesterase which participates along with PdeD ([/gene/DDB_G0274383 pdeD]) in breaking down intracellular cGMP. Pde3 is activated by bivalent cations, mainly by manganese and to a lesser degree by magnesium; the protein sequence contains two metal binding sites [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11171061  (Kuwayama et al. 2001)]. Pde3 has a higher affinity for cGMP than PdeD but has lower activity [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17040207  (Bader et al. 2007)]. Pde3 accounts for about 20% of the intracellular cGMP hydrolysis. Cells lacking Pde3 have increased basal cGMP levels. Overexpression of the catalytic domain of ''pde3'' results in only a slight decrease in internal cGMP levels and fails to give an overt morphological phenotype [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11171061  (Kuwayama et al. 2001)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 03-NOV-2021 PF; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0291237.summary: ''rapA'' (rap1) is a key regulator of cell adhesion and cell motility in ''Dictyostelium.'' ''rapA'' is a vital gene that encodes a small G protein of the Ras family of molecular switches. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7507418 Rebstein et al. 1993)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12186953 Kang et al. 2002)]. RapA plays a role in the progression through cytokinesis. During cell division, activated Rap1 (RapGTP) is found at the furrow where the contractile ring of myosin forms ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25298405 Plak et al. 2014)]. When the daughter cells separate, RapGTP is localized to the poles. RapGTP interacts with Rac guanine nucleotide exchange factor 1 (RacGEF1) ([/gene/DDB_G0277987 gxcA]) and coordinates microtubules, actin and myosin organization in the cytoskeleton ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22644079 Mun and Jeon 2012)]. cAMP signaling activates Rap1 through the RasG ([/gene/DDB_G0293434 rasG]) pathway by stimulating the RapGEF (guanine nucleotide exchange factor) activity of GbpD ([/gene/DDB_G0282373 gbpD]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16769729 Kortholt et al. 2006)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18180289 Bolourani et al. 2008)]. RapGTP accumulates at the front of cells migrating chemotactically and activates myosin heavy chain kinase ([/gene/DDB_G0291231 mhkA]) leading to the disassembly of myosin II at the front ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18039932 Jeon et al. 2007)]. RapGTP also activates guanylyl cyclase and the protein kinase Phg2 ([/gene/DDB_G0283699 phg2]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12186953 Kang et al. 2002)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16769729 Kortholt et al. 2006)]. There are several GAP activities that return RapGTP to the inactive GDP form, including RapGAP1 ([/gene/DDB_G0271734 rapgap1]) and RapGAP3 ([/gene/DDB_G0271806 rapgap3]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18039932 Jeon et al. 2007)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19284976 Jeon et al. 2009)]. RapA induces cell-cell adhesion through direct binding to TalB ([/gene/DDB_G0287505 talB]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26744136 Plak et al. 2016)]. In addition, RapA binds the TORC2 component Sin1/Rip3 ([/gene/DDB_G0284611 ripA]) and positively regulates the RasC-mediated ([/gene/DDB_G0281385 rasC]) activation of TORC2. RasC also activates TORC2 through directly binding the tor kinase ([/gene/DDB_G0281569 tor]), suggesting that dual Ras/Rap1 regulation of TORC2 may allow for integration of Ras and Rap1 signaling pathways in directed cell migration. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/27172998 Khanna et al. 2016)]. GflB ([/gene/DDB_G0286773 gflB]) was identified as a G-alpha-stimulated, Rap1-specific GEF required to balance Ras and Rap signaling at the leading edge of chemotaxing cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/27237792 Liu et al. 2016)]. PKA ([/gene/DDB_G0283907 pkaC], [/gene/DDB_G0279413 pkaR]) plays a role in gradient sensing and chemotaxis to cAMP by regulating the Ras ([/gene/DDB_G0281385 rasC], [/gene/DDB_G0293434 rasG]), Rap1 and TORC2 signaling pathways in response to cAMP ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28302905 Scavello et al. 2017)]. Fusion of the C-terminal domain of RapC ([/gene/DDB_G0270340 rapC]) onto RapA reverses the normal function of RapA, suggesting that the C-terminal residues of RapC may function as a suppressor of Ras signaling (Kim et al. 2021, PMID:34449058). RapA and RapC have opposite roles: RapC is a negative regulator of cell spreading and cell-substrate adhesion, thus increasing cell migration speed; however RapA positively regulates cell spreading and cell-substrate adhesion, thus decreasing cell migration speed (Jeon, et al. 2021, PMID: 34413965).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 21-SEP-2021 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0293536.summary:
In a search for genes up-regulated by intracellular calcium ([/ontology/go/0043157/annotation/page/1 response to cation stress]), [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14871937 Coukellet al. (2004)] identified [/gene/DDB_G0277861 patA], a homolog of the yeast vacuolar ATPase PMC1, andseven ''cup'' genes, which encode highly conserved proteins that contain ricin B lectin domains involved incarbohydrate binding. During the developmental program, ''cup transcripts'' are detected at low levels at earlyand late stages and at higher levels during the slug stage. Immunoflourescent staining shows Cup proteinsthroughout the cell in vegetative cells ([/ontology/go/0005737/annotation/page/1 cytoplasm] and [/ontology/go/0005634/annotation/page/1 nucleus]), however, aggregating cells and cellsstressed with 50 mM calcium chloride show increased staining in the [/ontology/go/0005938/annotation/page/1 cell cortex]. Overexpression of [/gene/DDB_G0289815 cupB] antisense mRNA abolishes multicellular development; cells fail to aggregate completely. The sevencalcium up-regulated ''cup'' genes identified are: [/gene/DDB_G0267466 cupA], [/gene/DDB_G0289815 cupB], [/gene/DDB_G0289283 cupC], [/gene/DDB_G0293536 cupD], [/gene/DDB_G0294531 cupE], [/gene/DDB_G0289813 cupF], and [/gene/DDB_G0289883 cupG]([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14871937 Coukell et al. 2004]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 14-FEB-2005 KP

DDB_G0280983.summary:
In a search for novel receptors similar to the cAR (cAMP receptor) proteins [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14732403 Raisley et al. (2004)] identified three crl (cAMP receptor-like) genes: ''crlA'', [/gene/DDB_G0289395 crlB], and [/gene/DDB_G0283619 crlC]. All three of the Crl proteins are predicted to contain a seven transmembrane domain characteristic of G-protein coupled receptors. The ''crlA'' transcript is expressed at low levels throughout growth and development, whereas the ''crlB'' and ''crlC'' transcripts are developmentally regulated. A ''crlA-'' mutant developed in the KAX3 background has an increased growth rate, implying a role for ''crlA'' in negative regulation of growth. The ''crlA-'' mutant also exhibits a delayed tip formation phenotype. ''crlA'' overexpression fails to rescue the [/gene/DDB_G0283605 yakA] null mutant phenotype, which is similar to that of ''crlA-''. Additionally, chimeric aggregates with a 1:20 ratio of GFP labeled ''crlA-'' cells to wild-type cells show that ''crlA-'' cells preferentially sort to the prespore region [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14732403 (Raisley et al. 2004)].
The ''crlA-''/KAX3 mutant is deficient in spore formation and is insensitive to the polyketide MPBD (4-methyl-5-pentylbenzene-1,3-diol) a component of the SDF-1 (spore differentiation factor-1) signalling cascade, suggesting that CrlA is the MPBD receptor [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21602484 (Anjard et al. 2011)]. However, a ''crlA-'' mutant developed in the AX2 background displays none of the phenotypes associated with the ''crlA-''/KAX3 mutant, demonstrating that CrlA does not act as the sole receptor for MPBD in Ax2 cells [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28158557 (Narita et al. 2017)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 13-FEB-2017 RD

DDB_G0274117.summary: The ABC superfamily of genes is one of the largest in the genomes of both bacteria and eukaryotes. The proteins encoded by these genes all carry a characteristic 200- to 250-amino-acid ATP-binding cassette that gives them their family name ([/ontology/go/0042626/annotation/page/1 ATPase activity, coupled to transmembrane movement of substances]). In bacteria they are mostly involved in nutrient import, while in eukaryotes many are involved in export ([/ontology/go/0006810/annotation/page/1 transport]). Seven different families have been defined in eukaryotes based on sequence homology, domain topology, and function. Sequences from the well-advanced ''Dictyostelium'' genome project have allowed to recognize 71 members of this superfamily (including one on the chromosome 2 duplication). The ABCG family is characterized by the ABC domain preceding the transmembrane domain ([/ontology/go/0016021/annotation/page/1 integral to membrane]). All of the members of this family in animals are half-transporters while all of the fungal members are full transporters with two ABC-transmembrane units. No members of this family are found in bacteria. ''Dictyostelium'' and ''Arabidopsis'' have members of both types ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12456012 Anjard and Loomis 2002]). Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 18-OCT-2004 PG

DDB_G0276617.summary:
Besides ''mhcA'' ([/gene/DDB_G0286355 mhcA]) that encodes the classical myosin heavy chain, ''Dictyostelium'' carries genes for 12 unconventional myosins. ''myoC'' encodes myosin IC which has a 45 kDa globular head and a carboxy terminal domain that is rich in glycine, proline and alanine and can bind actin [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2519618 (Titus et al. 1989)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8143877 (Jung and Hammer, 1994)]. MyoC associates with a 8 kDa light chain encoded by ''mlcC'' ([/gene/DDB_G0289563 mlcC]) which has two EF-hands but does not bind calcium [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21671662 (Crawley et al. 2011)]. ''myoC'' mRNA is abundant during the first two hours of development, decreases to a minimum at T=8 hrs and then reaccumulates to a peak at T=11 hrs. ''mlcC'' is coordinately expressed. [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25887420 (Rosengarten et al. 2015)].
Disruption of ''myoC'' had no obvious consequences to growth or development [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7622596 (Peterson et al. 1995)]. Fluid phase dextran uptake by pinocytosis is normal in cells lacking MyoA, ([/gene/DDB_G0280039 myoA]) MyoB, ([/gene/DDB_G0289117 myoB]) or MyoC but is impaired in cells lacking both MyoA and MyoB or both MyoB and MyoC suggesting that myosin I isoforms function cooperatively [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8522584 (Novak et al. 1995)]. The double null mutants ''myoA''/''myoB'' and ''myoB''/''myoC'' are covered in spikey filopodia suggesting that these myosin Is may have a role in limiting the extension of processes. MyoC has also been shown to bind to microtubules through its tail domain such that it can mediate F-actin-microtubule interactions at the mitotic spindle [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21712373 (Rump et al. 2011)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 23-AUG-2019 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0267376.summary: The ''acrA'' gene encodes the late developmental stage adenyl cyclase which is essential for spore encapsulation ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10556070 Soderbom et al. 1999)]. This multi-domain protein contains a histidine kinase domain, two receiver domains, transmembrane helices and an adenyl cyclase domain. Mutation of ATP-binding residues in the histidine kinase domain does not affect adenyl cyclase activity, however, the dimerizing phosphoacceptor subdomain is essential for adenyl cyclase activity ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20966074 Chen et al. 2010)]. Low levels of adenyl cyclase activity independent of the aggregation stage adenyl cyclase ACA ([/gene/DDB_G0281545 acaA]) or germination stage adenyl cyclase ACG ([/gene/DDB_G0274569 acgA]), were observed in vegetative cells and referred to as ACB ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9812977 Kim et al. 1998)]. This activity was found to reach a maximum during early fruiting body formation just when ''acrA'' is maximally active ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10419694 Meima and Schaap, 1999)]. ''acrA'' was isolated from a REMI mutant that develops well up to the slug stage but makes fruiting bodies with long, thin stalks and very few viable spores ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10556070 Soderbom et al. 1999)]. During culmination cells synthesize and release the cytokinin, discadenine, that stimulates the accumulation of cAMP in a manner dependent on ''acrA'' and ''dhkB'' ([/gene/DDB_G0277845 dhkB]) but independent of ''rdeA'' ([/gene/DDB_G0282923 rdeA]) that encodes the small phosphorelay protein of two component systems ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18216168 Anjard and Loomis, 2008)]. It appears that cytokinins trigger autophosphorylation of the histidine kinase DhkB so that it can dimerize with AcrA and stimulate its activity. The resulting increase in cAMP and PKA ([/gene/DDB_G0283907 pkaC]), ([/gene/DDB_G0279413 pkaR]) activity induces the MADS-box transcription factor SrfA, ([/gene/DDB_G0281387 srfA]) essential for spore differentiation ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12204259 Escalante and Sastre, 2002)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 28-APR-2016 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0273073.summary: The ABC superfamily of genes is one of the largest in the genomes of both bacteria and eukaryotes. The proteins encoded by these genes all carry a characteristic 200- to 250-amino-acid ATP-binding cassette that gives them their family name ([/ontology/go/0042626/annotation/page/1 ATPase activity, coupled to transmembrane movement of substances]). In bacteria they are mostly involved in nutrient import, while in eukaryotes many are involved in export ([/ontology/go/0006810/annotation/page/1 transport]). Seven different families have been defined in eukaryotes based on sequence homology, domain topology, and function. Sequences from the well-advanced ''Dictyostelium'' genome project have allowed to recognize 71 members of this superfamily (including one on the chromosome 2 duplication). The ABCG family is characterized by the ABC domain preceding the transmembrane domain ([/ontology/go/0016021/annotation/page/1 integral to membrane]). All of the members of this family in animals are half-transporters while all of the fungal members are full transporters with two ABC-transmembrane units. No members of this family are found in bacteria. ''Dictyostelium'' and ''Arabidopsis'' have members of both types ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12456012 Anjard and Loomis 2002]). Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 18-OCT-2004 PG

DDB_G0291039.summary: The motor domain in the kinesin encoded by ''kif11'' is at the N-terminus and belongs to the CENP-E family of domains of kinetochore-associated proteins that align chromosomes during mitosis [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14641909  (Kollmar and Glockner 2003)]. Disruption of the ''kif11'' showed that Kif11 is not required for mitotic spindle assembly, cell growth or development. [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18430243  (Nag et al. 2008)]. Microtubule distributions appear normal in ''kif11'' null cells but the effects of expression of the truncated 380-kDa form of dynein were less pronounced in ''kif11'' cells than in wild type cells suggesting that dynein and Kif11 cooperate to some extent in organizing the radial interphase microtubule distribution. Imaging of GFP-labeled Kif11 expressing cells indicates that Kif11 is a plus-end directed motor that accumulates at microtubule plus ends. [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23333327  (Kosem et al. 2013)]. Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 02-OCT-2017 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis; annotation contributions PMID:23333327 Annette Mueller-Taubenberger

DDB_G0273885.summary:
Papers from the early '80's suggested that there are two genes, ''dscB'' and ''dscC'', with identical protein sequence but on a different chromosomal location. ''dscC'' is situated next to ''dscD''; the gene corresponding to ''dscB'' cannot be found in AX4.
The lectin Discoidin I binds N-acetylgalactosamine and galactose [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/4517669 (Rosen et al. 1973)]. Discoidin I subunits associate to form a tetramer [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/4858710 (Simpson et al. 1974)] and are expressed from a family of 3 different genes: ''dscA'' ([/gene/DDB_G0273063 dscA-1]) ([/gene/DDB_G0273919 dscA-2]), ''dscC'' and ''dscD'' ([/gene/DDB_G0273067 dscD-1]) ([/gene/DDB_G0273887 dscD-2]). [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6279874 (Poole et al. 1981)]. Monomeric discoidin I is located mainly in the cytosol, while the tetrameric form of discoidin I is detected in multilamellar bodies and is externalized during aggregation [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2581974 (Barondes et al. 1985)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8416797 (Fukuzawa et al. 1993)]. Discoidin I gene expression is induced by prestarvation factor (PSF) and conditioned medium factor, ([/gene/DDB_G0275007 cmfA]) but is down-regulated by cAMP [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7641976 (Blusch et al. 1995)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2049883 (Rathi et al. 1991)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1663029 (Gomer et al. 1991)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2196444 (Vauti et al. 1990)]. Mutants defective in discoidin I fail to stream during aggregation, implicating discoidin I in cell-substrate adhesion [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6509552 (Springer et al. 1984)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/4075402 (Crowley et al. 1985)]. In addition, discoidin I is thought to play an intracellular role, as mutants in which discoidin genes are not expressed also have an abnormally centered microtubule organizing center and more rounded cell morphology, suggesting a role for discoidins in cytoskeleton organization during aggregation [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1334012 (Alexander et al. 1992)].
''Dictyostelium discoideum'' strains that carry bacteria secrete approx. 80 times higher levels of DscA and DscC than non-carriers. Secreted DscA binds to ''Klebsiella pneumoniae''. DscA binding protects bacteria from extracellular killing, promotes their internalization and prolongs their retention in both ''Dictyostelium discoideum'' and mammalian cells. Plant lectins induce the same response, suggesting that modified uptake and persistence of lectin-coated bacteria in eukaryotic cells is a general phenomenon, termed lectin-induced modified bacterial internalization [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30049880 (Dinh et al. 2018)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 23-AUG-2018 RD

DDB_G0281557.summary: ''lrrkA'' encodes a protein with a C-terminal kinase domain and an N-terminal domain consisting of 7 leucine-rich repeats. ''lrrkA'' was isolated from a collection of random insertion mutants as a mutant defective in growth on bacteria. ''lrrkA'' null cells grow poorly on a lawn of Gram-positive bacteria. In ''lrrkA'' null cells, intracellular killing of ''Klebsiella pneumoniae'' was significantly slower than in wild type cells; however, intracellular killing of ''Bacillus subtilis'' was just as efficient as in wild type cells. In addition, intracellular killng of ''Klebsiella pneumoniae'' was also significantly slower in ''lrrkA''/''kil2'' ([/gene/DDB_G0279183 kil2]) double null cells; however, no slower than in ''lrrkA'' null cells, suggesting that LrrkA and Kil2 play partially redundant roles in intracellular bacterial killing. Phagosomal proteolysis was less efficient in both ''lrrkA'' and ''kil2'' null cells. Intracellular killing of bacteria was not stimulated in ''lrrkA'' null cells upon exposure to folate. These results reveal a signaling pathway where folate is recognized at the cell surface by the folic acid receptor Far1 ([/gene/DDB_G0281211 far1]), leading to the sequential activation of LrrkA and Kil2 and increased intracellular killing of bacteria within phagosomes ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31652367 Bodinier et al. 2019]). ''lrrkA'' null cells also display an increase in cell motility and an increase in the efficiency of phagocytosis, indicating that LrrkA is a negative regulator of cell motility and phagocytosis. In addition, folate increases motility in wt cells, but not in ''lrrkA'' null cells, further suggesting that LrrkA plays a role in the cellular response to folate. Taken together, these results suggest that LrrkA functions in two modes: in the absence of folate, LrrkA inhibits motility and phagocytosis, but does not stimulate killing of intracellular bacteria; however, in the presence of a high concentration of folate, Far1 activates LrrkA which in turn stimulates intracellular killing via activation of Kil2 (Bodinier et al. 2021, PMID:33763419).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 26-JUL-2021 RD

DDB_G0274607.summary: ''gefM'' encodes a Ras guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF, RasGEF). rasGEFs are key components of signaling networks in which they activate Ras family small GTPases by promoting the exchange of GDP for GTP. ''gefM'' is differentially expressed throughout growth and development ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16086850 Wilkins et al. 2005)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16336640 Arigoni et al. 2005)]. ''gefM'' null mutant cells have multiple phenotypes. ''gefM'' null mutants are defective in development, forming small, flat aggregates that fail to develop further. Chemotaxis towards cAMP is also strongly impaired in the mutant cells, due to inability to inhibit lateral pseudopods. Both of these phenotypes are at least partially rescued by pulsing the cells with cAMP. The expression of genes involved in cAMP signaling and aggregation: adenylate cyclase A ([/gene/DDB_G0281545 acaA]), cAMP receptor 1 ([/gene/DDB_G0273397 carA-1], [/gene/DDB_G0273533 carA-2]) and contact site A protein ([/gene/DDB_G0289073 csaA]) is delayed in ''gefM'' null mutants. In addition, in ''gefM'' null mutants endogenous cAMP accumulates during early development to a much lower extent than in wild type. Adenylyl cyclase activation in response to cAMP pulses is strongly reduced, but guanylyl cyclase is stimulated to higher levels than in wild type. GefM is not an activator of either RasC ([/gene/DDB_G0281385 rasC]) or RasG ([/gene/DDB_G0293434 rasG]), and the target of its GEF activity remains unknown. These results indicate that ''gefM'' is involved in the establishment of the cAMP relay system, acting as positive regulator for adenylyl cyclase and negative regulator for guanylyl cyclase ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16336640 Arigoni et al. 2005)]. A genome-wide DNA microarray analysis revealed that ''gefM'' expression is down-regulated during phagocytosis ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18559084 Sillo et al. 2008]). A co-immunoprecipitation assay revealed that GefM interacts with the adaptor protein FttB ([/gene/DDB_G0269138 fttB]), which is also involved in the regulation of cAMP signaling ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/32818671 Li et al. 2020)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 22-APR-2021 RD

DDB_G0289329.summary:
Differentiation-inducing factor (DIF)-1 is a chlorinated alkyl phenone released by developing ''Dictyostelium'' cells and that can induce stalk cell differentiation [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/183142 (Town et al. 1976)]. The last step in DIF-1 synthesis, the methylation of des-methyl-DIF-1 to form DIF-1, is catalyzed by the product of the ''dmtA'' gene, des-methyl-DIF-1 methyltransferase ([/ontology/go/0008171/annotation/page/1 O-methyltransferase activity]), ([/ontology/go/0008757/annotation/page/1 S-adenosylmethionine-dependent methyltransferase activity]). The ''dmtA'' mRNA is developmentally regulated, peaking at the first-finger/slug stage in parallel with DIF-1 and methyltransferase enzyme activity ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11163223 Thompson and Kay 2000], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9446571 Kay 1998]).
''dmtA'' null mutants can form slugs that are able to produce one prestalk cell type, the pstA cells, and can form mature stalk cells. However, the other major prestalk cell type, the pstO cells, is missing ([/ontology/go/0030154/annotation/page/1 cell differentiation]). Differentiation defects are restored by development on a uniform concentration of DIF-1. It therefore appears that pstO and pstA cells are induced by separate signals and that DIF-1 is the pstO inducer [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11163223 (Thompson and Kay 2000)]. DIF-1 biosynthesis occurs mostly in prespore cells. These results support a model in which prespore cells cross-induce the differentiation of pstO cells by making DIF-1, and that this is one of the regulatory loops that sets the proportion of prespore-to-prestalk cells in the aggregate [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11748133 (Kay and Thompson 2001)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 19-SEP-2003 PG

DDB_G0279193.summary:
DNA-dependent RNA polymerase catalyzes the transcription of DNA into RNA using the four ribonucleoside triphosphates as substrates ([/ontology/go/0003899/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase activity]). Three distinct zinc-containing RNA polymerases are found in eukaryotic nuclei: [/gene/DDB_G0275759 rpa1] for the ribosomal RNA precursor ([/ontology/go/0006360/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase I promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005736/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase I complex]), [/gene/DDB_G0279193 rpb1] for the mRNA precursor ([/ontology/go/0006366/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase II promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005665/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase II, core complex]), and [/gene/DDB_G0277199 rpc1] for 5S and tRNA genes ([/ontology/go/0006383/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase III promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005666/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase III complex]).
RNA polymerase II is composed of 12 subunits: [/gene/DDB_G0279193 rpb1], [/gene/DDB_G0288257 rpb2], [/gene/DDB_G0292244 rpb3], [/gene/DDB_G0282739 rpb4], [/gene/DDB_G0291636 rpb5], [/gene/DDB_G0291037 rpb6], [/gene/DDB_G0284891 rpb7], [/gene/DDB_G0278039 rpb8], [/gene/DDB_G0268306 rpb9], [/gene/DDB_G0272036 rpb10], [/gene/DDB_G0277677 rpb11], and[/gene/DDB_G0283365 rpb12]. Subunits 5, 6, 8, 10, and 12 are common to all threeRNA polymerases.
A unique feature of the largest RNA polymerase II subunit is thepresence of tandem repeats of a heptapeptide sequence at its carboxy-terminus. This carboxy-terminal repeat domain(CTD) has the consensus sequence Tyr-Ser-Pro-Thr-Ser-Pro-Ser is highly conserved among eukaryotic organisms. Althoughthe CTD is a ubiquitous feature of RNA pol II, the repeat length varies.It probably projects out of the globular catalytic domain and may interact with the acidic activator domains of transcriptional regulatory proteins. It is also known to bind by intercalation to DNA. RNA polymerase II is activated by phosphorylation at the serine and threonine residues in the CTD (reviewed by [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9618449 Hampsey] in 1998). Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 09-APR-2004 PG
