DDB_G0280977.summary: The ABC superfamily of genes is one of the largest in the genomes of both bacteria and eukaryotes. The proteins encoded by these genes all carry a characteristic 200- to 250-amino-acid ATP-binding cassette that gives them their family name ([/ontology/go/0042626/annotation/page/1 ATPase activity, coupled to transmembrane movement of substances]). In bacteria they are mostly involved in nutrient import, while in eukaryotes many are involved in export([/ontology/go/0006810/annotation/page/1 transport]), ([/ontology/go/0016021/annotation/page/1 integral to membrane]). Seven different families (A to G) have been defined in eukaryotes based on sequence homology, domain topology, and function. ''Dictyostelium'' has 71 ABC transporters (including one on the chromosome 2 duplication) and 13 ABCC family members: [/gene/DDB_G0280541 abcC1], [/gene/DDB_G0280055 abcC2], [/gene/DDB_G0287691 abcC3], [/gene/DDB_G0286559 abcC5], [/gene/DDB_G0287593 abcC6], [/gene/DDB_G0291243 abcC7], [/gene/DDB_G0284867 abcC8], [/gene/DDB_G0285165 abcC9], [/gene/DDB_G0280977 abcC10], [/gene/DDB_G0280973 abcC12], [/gene/DDB_G0280539 abcC13], [/gene/DDB_G0287589 abcC14], and [/gene/DDB_G0280459 abcC15]. Transporters of the C family have been shown to transport glutathione conjugants as well as to export cadmium ions. They are always found as full transporters with two copies of the transmembrane-ABC unit. Many of the genes of this family in humans and other animals have an additional transmembrane domain at the N terminus [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12456012 (Anjard and Loomis 2002)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 16-JUN-2003 PG

DDB_G0288361.summary: The motor domain in the kinesin encoded by ''kif13'' belongs to the BimC/Eg5 family of mitotic kinesins that drive spindle pole separation during mitosis [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14641909  (Kollmar and Glockner 2003)]. Kif13 was found to co-purify along with more than 80 other proteins in samples enriched in centrosomes [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16512674  (Reinders et al. 2006)]. ''kif13'' null cells grow at rates indistinguishable from wild type suggesting that other kinesins can substitute for any vital roles of Kif13. However, the spindle halves separate prematurely in ''kif13'' null cells, indicating that Kif13 may play a specialized role in maintaining spindle integrity at the terminal stages of division [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18712789  (Tikhonenko et al. 2008)]. Like each of the other mitotic kinesins, kif13 mRNA levels are low in growing cells and increase to relatively high levels between 12 and 18 hrs of development before returning to very low levels [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25887420  (Rosengarten et al. 2015)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 03-OCT-2017 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0288287.summary: ''atg101'' encodes a homolog of human ATG101, a small protein that associates with ATG13 in the ATG1 complex ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20603609 Calvo-Garrido et al. 2010)]. The interaction of Dictyostelium ATG101 and ATG13 ([/gene/DDB_G0269162 atg13]) was confirmed in 2-hybrid assays. Autophagy was strongly reduced in mutant cells lacking ATG101. Strains carrying null mutations in ''atg101'' form multi-tipped aggregates that fail to make normal fruiting ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26246495 Mesquita et al. 2015)]. The multi-tipped phenotype of mutants in ''atg101'' is similar to that of mutants in other autophagy genes ''atg6'' ([/gene/DDB_G0269244 atg6A]), ''atg7'' ([/gene/DDB_G0271096 atg7]), ''atg9'' ([/gene/DDB_G0285323 atg9]), ''tipC'' ([/gene/DDB_G0267422 tipC]), and ''tipD'' ([/gene/DDB_G0275323 tipD]). mRNA from atg101 accumulates throughout development ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25887420 Rosengarten et al. 2015)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 09-MAR-2017 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis and Ricardo Escalante

DDB_G0277987.summary: ''gxcA'' encodes a Rac guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF, RacGEF). RacGEFs are key components of signaling networks in which they activate Rho family GTPases by promoting the exchange of GDP for GTP. GxcA (RacGEF1) is localized to the cell cortex in response to cAMP stimulation. In chemotaxing cells, GxcA is associated with the leading edge, and to a lesser extent with the trailing edge. GxcA has GEF activity toward the Rho GTPase RacB ''racB'' ([/gene/DDB_G0279605 racB]) and also has weak GEF activity towards Rac1B ([/gene/DDB_G0268622 rac1B]). ''gxcA'' null cells have a significant decrease in the activation of RacB, and also have an approximately 30% reduction in cAMP-mediated F-actin assembly. In ''gxcA'' null cells, development is delayed and cells overexpressing ''gxcA'' have more severe defects in development, indicating that ''gxcA'' also plays a role in development. These results indicate that GxcA directly activates RacB activity, and thereby regulates F-actin polymerization, and downstream chemotaxis and morphogenesis ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15470506 Park et al. 2004]). GxcA interacts ''in vitro'' with the Ras GTPase RapA ([/gene/DDB_G0291237 rapA]) suggesting that GxcA may be a RapA effector and that RapA mediates F-actin polymerization through GxcA and RacB ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22644079 Mun et al. 2012]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 24-JUN-2021 RD

DDB_G0286557.summary: The concentration of membrane phospholipid, phosphatidylinositol (3,4,5)-trisphosphate (PIP3), is higher at the front of cells in a chemotactic gradient than at the back ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12802064 Huang et al. 2003)]. Not only is PIP3 synthesized more rapidly at the front, it is also converted to PIP2 less rapidly at the front of cells than at the back. The conversion of PIP3 to PIP2 is catalyzed by the PIP3 3' phosphatase encoded by ''pten'' ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12062103 Ijima and Devreotes 2002)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12062104 Funamoto et al. 2002)]. PTEN binds to PIP2 in the membrane to position itself near its substrate ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25448479 Yang et al. 2014)]. Exposing cells to a gradient of cAMP results in rapid release of PTEN from the membrane followed by return of PTEN to the membrane at the rear and the sides. Cells lacking PTEN migrate poorly because they extend multiple spiky pseudopods in all directions and fail to suppress lateral pseudopods ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12062103 Ijima and Devreotes 2002)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17623773 Wessels et al. 2007)]. Disruption of the protein kinase PKB ([/gene/DDB_G0268620 pkbA]) restores polarity to cells lacking PTEN ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21169559 Tang et al. 2010)] indicating that high PIP3 levels affect the cytoskeleton largely by excessive stimulation of PKB activity and phosphorylation of its substrates. Cells that are unable to generate gradients in PIP3 because of knock-out mutations in the genes for all 5 type-1 PI3 kinases ([/gene/DDB_G0278727 pikA]), ([/gene/DDB_G0283081 pikB]), ([/gene/DDB_G0275011 pikC]), ([/gene/DDB_G0268548 pikF]), ([/gene/DDB_G0282625 pikG]), as well as in pten, move more slowly than wild type cells but are still able to navigate up a strong gradient of chemoattractant ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17462897 Hoeller and Kay 2007)]. PIP3 negatively regulates Pten membrane localization, with mutual inhibition between PIP3 and PTEN leading to a a clear spatial separation between PIP3 and Pten on the membrane ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30367048 Matsuoka et al. 2018]). Pten is involved in the signal transduction pathway responsible for AprA-dependent ([/gene/DDB_G0281663 aprA]) chemorepulsion. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30462573 Rijal et al. 2018]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 10-DEC-2018 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0281211.summary: The orphan GPCR receptor, ''far1'' has been identified as the ''D. discoideum'' folic acid receptor. fAR1 localizes to the cell surface and binds folic acid. Folic acid stimulation fails to trigger a phosphatidylinositol 3,4,5 trisphosphate (PIP3) response and actin polymerization in ''far1'' null mutants. fAR1 controls both chemotaxis toward folic acid and phagocytosis of bacterial particles. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26906738 Pan et al. 2016)] In addition, ''far1'' null cells result in decreased intracellular killing of ingested K. pneumoniae, revealing the critical role of folate sensing in stimulating intracellular killing of bacteria ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28076662 Leiba et al. 2017)]. A different ''far1'' null mutant showed identical rates of phagocytosis to pHrodo-labelled live Bacillus subtilis as wt cells, but impaired chemotaxis, indicating that phagocytosis is not dependent on chemo-receptor sensing ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28541182 Meena et al. 2017)]. fAR1 was subsequently shown to detect bacterial secreted folate, for chasing bacteria, and to simultaneously detect the bacterial coat lipopolysaccharide (LPS) for engulfing and consuming them. ''far1'' null and gbeta null ([/gene/DDB_G0277143 gpbA]) cells displayed a significant decrease in bacterial internalization, and ERK2 ([/gene/DDB_G0283903 erkB]) signaling triggered by LPS is also impaired in ''far1'' and gbeta null cells. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29799847 Pan et al. 2018)] fAR1 has also been shown to mediate the inhibitory effect of folate on macropinocytosis upregulation. DDB_G0273615.summary:
The [/gene/DDB_G0269230 fpaA] and [/gene/DDB_G0273251 fpaB-1]/[/gene/DDB_G0273615 fpaB-2] genes encode nearly identical proteins, differing by one intron, 33 nucleotides, and one amino acid ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9373134 West et al. 1997]). The ''fpa'' genes encode the Skp1 protein, which in ''Dictyostelium'' and other protists forms the SCF ubiquitin ligase complex (reviewed in [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15238247 West et al. 2004]) Both FpaA and FpaB proteins are found in the cytoplasm and enriched in the nucleus in immunocytochemistry experiments.During development, expression persists in the nucleus but also increases at the cell cortex. Glycosylation is required for nuclear enrichment ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11358877 Sassi et al. 2001]).
Glycosylation of Skp1 has been extensively studied in ''Dictyostelium''. The initial step in Skp1 glycosylation involves the hydroxylation of Pro143 by a proline hydroxylase ([/gene/DDB_G0277759 phyA], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9660787 Teng-umnuay et al. 1998]). HyPro143 is then modified by the glycosyltransferase [/gene/DDB_G0275699 gnt1], which transfers a GlcNAc (N-acetylglucosamine) to the Skp1 protein ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10593934 Teng-umnuay et al. 1999]). The Skp1-GlcNAc is extended by a bifunctional diglycosyltransferase, [/gene/DDB_G0283761 pgtA], which processively adds galactose and fucose ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11423539 van der Wel et al. 2001], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12244067 van der Wel et al. 2002]). Subsequently two additional galactose residues are added by [/gene/DDB_G0283005 agtA] to yield the Skp1 pentasaccharide (GGFGGnOSkp1; [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16495217 Ercan et al. 2006], reviewed in [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31128470 West and Kim 2019]).
West and colleagues reported that the proline hydroxylase ([/gene/DDB_G0277759 phyA]) performing the first SKP1 modification mediates oxygen signaling during ''Dictyostelium'' development. ''phyA''-null cells need strongly elevated oxygen levels to culminate ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17699611 West et al. 2007]). Mutant analyses showed not only is Skp1 a substrate for PhyA it is also a functional mediator of PhyA activity in cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20969846 Wang et al. 2011]). Further investigations showed that full SKP1 glycosylation is required for optimal oxygen sensing during development, for example [/gene/DDB_G0283005 agtA] knockout and overexpression mutants require elevated oxygen levels to culminate ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19687007 Wang et al. 2009], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22128189 Zhang et al. 2011], reviewed in [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25988702 West and Blader 2015]).
The ''Dictyostelium'' unmodified Skp1 seems to form a dimer. The SCF ubiquitin ligase complex has been investigated and binding to F-box protein seems to dissociate the dimer. Free Skp1 forms a complex with a CullinA homolog ([/gene/DDB_G0278991 culE]), and the F-box protein ([/gene/DDB_G0292312 fbxD]; [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24550398 Shafer et al. 2014], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25341530 Sheik et al. 2015]). Co-immunoprecipitation and proteomic analysis also showed the F-box protein [/gene/DDB_G0276887 fbxA] binding to Skp1. CulE binds proteins such as the RING box protein [/gene/DDB_G0287629 rbx1] and the cullin-associated neddylation-disassociated protein [/gene/DDB_G0274167 cand1]. F-box proteins preferentially associate with fully glycosylated Skp1 compared to unmodified Skp1. Thus low oxygen levels are rate limiting for the hydroxylation of nascent Skp1 in cells, and demonstrates that full Skp1 hydroxylation/glycosylation is to alter the repertoire of the F-box proteins with which it associates ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24506136 Sheik et al. 2014], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25341530 Sheikh et al. 2015]). Furthermore NMR and mass spec analyses showed that Skp1 complete glycolysation modifies the originally disordered protein conformation resulting in enhanced F-box protein binding ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28928219 Sheikh et al. 2017]; [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29251491 Xu et al. 2018], reviewed in [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31128470 West and Kim 2019]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 06-MAR-2020 PF

DDB_G0273995.summary: The ''icmA'' gene encodes the conserved isoprenylcysteine carboxyl methyltransferase in ''Dictyostelium''. The protein was shown to have [/ontology/go/0004671/annotation/page/1 protein-S-isoprenylcysteine O-methyltransferase activity]. The ''icmA''-null mutant shows defects in early development, such as no cell polarization ([/ontology/go/0030010/annotation/page/1 establishment of cell polarity]) or streaming, aberrant cAMP wave formation, and in some cases loose mound formation that may proceed to form aberrant fruiting bodies ([/ontology/go/0060176/annotation/page/1 regulation of aggregation involved in sorocarp development]). In the mutant, the starvation-induced expression of the cAMP receptor [/gene/DDB_G0273397 carA-1] is delayed, also reflected in the fact that mutant membranes bind only 34% of the CAMP that wild-type membranes bind. However, in pulsed mutant cells the cAMP relay response is 3 times larger than in wild type. In addition, Ras GTPase ([/gene/DDB_G0293434 rasG]) has been shown to be methylated and in the ''icmA''-null mutant RasG, as well as CRAC ([/gene/DDB_G0285161 dagA]) are mislocalized in cAMP-pulsed cells. In sum, these data show that isoprenylcysteine methylation is required for signalling in response to cAMP ([/ontology/go/0008277/annotation/page/1 regulation of G-protein coupled receptor protein signaling pathway]) and development ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17699599 Chen et al. 2007)]. Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 23-JAN-2008 PF

DDB_G0292956.summary:
Initiation of protein translation in eukaryotes is regulated by phosphorylation of the alpha subunit of eukaryotictranslation initiation factor 2 (eIF2alpha). During periods of amino acid starvation, eIF2alpha is inactivated viaphosphorylation by the serine/threonine kinase ([/ontology/go/0004674/annotation/page/1 protein serine/threonine kinase activity]) GCN2 (general control nonderepressible), also known asPEK (pancreatic eukaryotic translation initiation factor kinase). The PEK family of protein kinases is highly conservedfrom yeast to humans, however, the effect on translation in metazoans is global whereas GCN2 in yeast acts to inhibittranslation of specific species of mRNA ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7855893 reviewed in Wek 1994]).
In ''Dictyostelium'', two members of the PEK family of protein kinases have been identified: [/gene/DDB_G0272837 ifkA] and[/gene/DDB_G0276829 ifkB]. Putative proteins belonging to the PEK family are: [/gene/DDB_G0276043 ifkC], [/gene/DDB_G0283065 DDB_G0283065], [/gene/DDB_G0268642 DDB_G0268642], [/gene/DDB_G0292734 DDB_G0292734], and [/gene/DDB_G0292734 DDB_G0292734].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 17-SEP-2004 KP

DDB_G0290407.summary: ''rabO'' encodes a guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G protein) of the Rab family of small GTPases. G proteins are key components of signal transduction networks in which they function as molecular signaling switches, binding to GDP in the off state while binding GTP in the on state. Guanine nucleotide-exchange factors (GEFs) promote the exchange of GDP for GTP on Rab GTPases thus activating them, while GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) inactivate Rab GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP. Basic annotations have been added to this gene, 22-JAN-2021 RD

DDB_G0291498.summary: ''Dictyostelium cpnF'' belongs to the highly conserved copines, a family of ubiquitious Ca(2+)-dependent phospholipid-binding ([/ontology/go/0005544/annotation/page/1 calcium-dependent phospholipid binding]) proteins. In their N-terminal half, copines contain two Ca(2+)- and phospholipid-binding domains (C2 domains) present in such proteins as phospholipase C and protein kinase C. Much of the C-terminal half consists of a von Willebrand Factor type A domain (VWFA) typically found in the extracellular portions of membrane proteins like integrins. Thus copines represent a fusion of intracellular (C2) and extracellular (VWFA) domains. However, there are no signal sequence or hydrophobic transmembrane sequences in the predicted proteins suggesting copines are intracellular proteins. Copines are thought to be involved in membrane trafficking. It is of particular interest that copines, first found in the highly phagocytic protozoan ''Paramecium'' and then isolated from mammalian spleen and liver, seem to be abundant in cells and organs that are, or contain, phagocytes. In this context it comes as no surprise that phagocytic ''Dictyostelium'' has a total of six copine genes[http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16343335  (Damer et al. 2005)]. The widespread distribution of copines from protozoans to mammals and their high similarity suggest they play important role(s) in eukaryotic biology. Reviewed in [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12440769  (Tomsig and Creutz, 2001)]Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 19-JAN-2006 PF

Expression of ecmF is dependent on the transcription factor STATa ([/gene/DDB_G0281381 dstA]). Results published by [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/27125566  (Saga et al. 2016)] suggest that STATa regulation of ''ecmF'' is mediated by the transcription factor MybC ([/gene/DDB_G0281563 mybC]). Null mutations in ''ecmF'' have no observable consequences to development, most likely because of redundancy among members of the family ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15309638 Shimada et al. 2004)]. Since the slug sheath is made for several hours before ''ecmF'' is expressed, it is unlikely that EcmF is an essential sheath component, and more likely that it is involved in culmination.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 19-OCT-2016 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0274059.summary:
''Dictyostelium'' cofilin-2 (''cofC'') was identified as a cofilin-related protein from the ''Dictyostelium'' cDNA project. It has significant homology to conventional cofilin [/gene/DDB_G0277833 cofA] and contains residues responsible for actin binding ([/ontology/go/0003779/annotation/page/1 actin binding]). Cofilin-2 was shown to depolimerize actin filaments ([/ontology/go/0030042/annotation/page/1 actin filament depolymerization]) in a dose- and pH-dependent manner and to decrease the viscosity of an actin solution, but it did not co-sediment with actin filaments. In contrast to ''cofA'', the cofilin-2 protein is not expressed in vegetative cells but predominantely during aggregation. Immunohistochemistry showed that cofilin-2 colocalized with actin at substrate adhesion sites. However, disruption of the ''cofC'' gene did not result in any adhesion defect, mutants appeared to be normal. Cofilin-2 did not rescue a yeast mutant deficient in conventional cofilin, suggesting ''cofC'' has different function(s) than ''cofA''. Aggregation-specific expression suggests ''cofC'' plays a role in destabilizing the actin cytoskeleton ([/ontology/go/0015629/annotation/page/1 actin cytoskeleton]) during development [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11683919 (Aizawa et al., 2001) ].

DDB_G0286303.summary: DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) can be repaired by either non-homologous end-joining (NHEJ) or homologous recombination (HR). In vertebrates, NHEJ is initated when Ku70/Ku80 heterodimers bind to DNA ends and recruit the catalytic subunit of DNA-dependent protein kinase (DNA-PKcs). Homologs of these components in Dictyostelium are encoded by ''ku70'' ([/gene/DDB_G0286069 ku70]), ''ku80'' and ''dnapkcs'' ([/gene/DDB_G0281167 dnapkcs]) [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16243037  (Hudson et al. 2005)]. Both Ku70 and Ku80 are members of the family of ATP-dependent DNA helicases and are coordinately expressed during growth and early development [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16112620  (Block and Lees-Miller, 2005)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25887420  (Rosengarten et al. 2015)]. Poly ADP-ribose is generated by the polymerase Adprt1a ([/gene/DDB_G0278741 adprt1A]) at sites of DNA DSBs. Poly ADP-ribose polymers promote NHEJ by binding Ku70 at DSBs and attaching Ku80 [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21807880  (Couto et al. 2011)]. Ku80 has a C-terminal domain that binds DNA-PKcs together with the homolog of the DNA repair endonuclease Artemis, Dclre1 ([/gene/DDB_G0277755 dclre1]), that is essential for NHEJ [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16112620  (Block and Lees-Miller, 2005)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16582628  (Hsu et al. 2006)]. Null mutations in either ''ku70'' or ''dnapkcs'' render recently germinated cells unusually sensitive to the DSB-inducing agent bleomycin. However, these mutations have no effect on bleomycin sensitivity of populations of growing cells, probably because DSBs can be repaired by the HR pathway in cells with two copies of each gene. Haploid cells emerge from spores in the G1 phase of the cell cycle where HR is inoperable; however, growing cells are in G2 where HR can compensate for loss of NHEJ [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16243037  (Hudson et al. 2005)]. The DNA joining events that result in integration of plasmid sequences at random sites of double-strand cleavage during REMI mutagenesis appear to depend on the NHEJ pathway, since ''ku70'', ''ku80'', ''adprt1a'' and ''dclre1'' null mutants do not show the increase in plasmid integration seen in wild type cells transformed together with restriction enzymes [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21807880  (Couto et al. 2011)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21536833  (Hsu et al. 2011)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 05-JAN-2019 RD

DDB_G0269112.summary: ''celB'' is expressed coordinately with ''celA'' ([/gene/DDB_G0271134 celA]) in prespore cells as they start to encapsulate during culmination and later during germination [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1976383  (Giorda et al. 1990)]. ''celB'' encodes a 55 kDa protein with tandem copies of the unusual tetrapeptide repeat (TETP) and a cellulose binding domain like CelA but no measurable cellulase activity [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9334183  (Ramalingam and Ennis, 1997)]. About 600 bp upstream of the translation start sites of both ''celA'' and ''celB'' there is an 81 bp region sufficient for control of spore-specific transcription that includes the binding site (TAACTG) recognized by Myb transcription factors of ''Dictyostelium'' [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9334183  (Ramalingam and Ennis, 1997)]. It is likely that both celA and celB are repressed by a Myb factor. Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 04-OCT-2018 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0275299.summary: ''Dictyostelium'' ''cln5'' is the ortholog of human CLN5, mutations in which cause neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (NCL), also referred to as Batten disease. ''cln5'' is expressed during growth with expression increasing during early development and reaching peak levels at 4 hours after starvation. From 4 to 8 hours, ''cln5'' expression decreases sharply and then remains constant during the remainder of development. Cln5 has glycoside hydrolase activity and localizes to the endoplasmic reticulum, punctate regions in the cytoplasm, and the cell cortex. Numerous potential Cln5 interacting proteins were identified by LC-MS-MS, including: NagA ([/gene/DDB_G0287033 nagA]), Tpp1 ([/gene/DDB_G0269914 tpp1]) and CtsD ([/gene/DDB_G0279411 ctsD]) [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29128403  (Huber et al. 2017)]. Glycosylated Cln5 is secreted during early development, with secretion occurring via an unconventional pathway linked to autophagy. Cln5 secretion is increased in ''cln3'' ([/gene/DDB_G0291157 cln3]) and ''mfsd8'' (''cln7'') ([/gene/DDB_G0272192 mfsd8]) null mutants. ''cln5'' null mutants have decreased cell-cell and cell-substrate adhesion as well as decreased chemotaxis to cAMP [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30048658  (Huber et al. 2018)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/32087303  (Huber et al. 2020)]. ''cln5'' null mutants display numerous defects during growth, including decreased proliferation, aberrant cytokinesis and decreased chemotaxis to folate. In addition, growth-phase ''cln5'' null cells display an increased number of autophagosomes, increased autophagic flux, and an increased number of ubiquitinated proteins. Development-stage ''cln5'' null cell defects include delayed aggregation, precocious late-stage development, aberrant spore morphology and decreased spore germination. Several of these growth and developmental defects are associated with aberrant autophagy, supporting evidence in other systems linking NCL to the autophagy pathway. (McLaren, et al 2021, PMID: 34291044).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 03-AUG-2021 RD

DDB_G0270826.summary: The ABC superfamily of genes is one of the largest in the genomes of both bacteria and eukaryotes. The proteins encoded by these genes all carry a characteristic 200- to 250-amino-acid ATP-binding cassette that gives them their family name ([/ontology/go/0042626/annotation/page/1 ATPase activity, coupled to transmembrane movement of substances]). In bacteria they are mostly involved in nutrient import, while in eukaryotes many are involved in export ([/ontology/go/0006810/annotation/page/1 transport]). Seven different families have been defined in eukaryotes based on sequence homology, domain topology, and function. Sequences from the well-advanced ''Dictyostelium'' genome project have allowed to recognize 71 members of this superfamily (including one on the chromosome 2 duplication). The ABCG family is characterized by the ABC domain preceding the transmembrane domain ([/ontology/go/0016021/annotation/page/1 integral to membrane]). All of the members of this family in animals are half-transporters while all of the fungal members are full transporters with two ABC-transmembrane units. No members of this family are found in bacteria. ''Dictyostelium'' and ''Arabidopsis'' have members of both types ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12456012 Anjard and Loomis 2002]). Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 18-OCT-2004 PG

DDB_G0274133.summary:
There are 29 genes encoding actin in ''Dictyostelium'' with amino acid identity greater than 83%, ''act1''-''act29''. Seventeen of these genes encode identical proteins: [/gene/DDB_G0289553 act1], [/gene/DDB_G0274133 act2], [/gene/DDB_G0289005 act4], [/gene/DDB_G0289663 act5], [/gene/DDB_G0274135 act6], [/gene/DDB_G0280545 act7], [/gene/DDB_G0269234 act8], [/gene/DDB_G0274601 act9], [/gene/DDB_G0288879 act11], [/gene/DDB_G0274129 act12], [/gene/DDB_G0274599 act13], [/gene/DDB_G0274137 act14], [/gene/DDB_G0272520 act15], [/gene/DDB_G0272248 act16], [/gene/DDB_G0274727 act19], [/gene/DDB_G0274285 act20], and [/gene/DDB_G0274561 act21], while [/gene/DDB_G0289811 act10], [/gene/DDB_G0275023 act22], and [/gene/DDB_G0289487 act3] respectively have 1, 4 and 11 amino acid differences compared to the 17 identical genes. The proteins encoded by [/gene/DDB_G0274131 act17], [/gene/DDB_G0289489 act18], [/gene/DDB_G0268744 act23] and [/gene/DDB_G0289505 act24]are more divergent.
Actin is a major [/ontology/go/0005200/annotation/page/1 structural constituent of cytoskeleton]. Actin is one of the most abundant proteins in ''Dictyostelium'', constituting approximately 8% of the total protein in vegetative cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/561722 Alton and Lodish et al. 1977]).Actin synthesis is developmentally regulated, peaking shortly after starvation (reviewed by [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6894564 Firtel] in 1981). The different actin genes differ in their levels of expression, with [/gene/DDB_G0274135 act6], [/gene/DDB_G0269234 act8] and [/gene/DDB_G0274129 act12] being highly expressed both during growth and development compared to [/gene/DDB_G0289005 act4], [/gene/DDB_G0289663 act5], [/gene/DDB_G0280545 act7] and [/gene/DDB_G0272248 act16] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6286214 McKeown and Firtel 1981]). Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 19-SEP-2003 PG

DDB_G0285969.summary:
''deeJ'' encodes DJ-1, an ortholog of human PARK7 which is associated with Parkinsons disease and which plays a role in cell protection against oxidative stress and cell death. DJ-1 belongs to the Class I glutamine amidotransferase-like superfamily, but its exact cellular function is unclear. ''Dictyostelium'' DJ-1 is localized in the cytoplasm. ''deeJ'' antisense mutants display decreased phagocytosis, decreased pinocytosis, and aberrant fruiting body morphology, with fruiting bodies that have larger sori and shorter, thicker stalks. In contrast, ''deeJ'' overexpression mutants have increased phagocytosis, increased pinocytosis, and an increased growth rate. Knockdown of DJ-1 also causes a small but significant activation of mitochondrial respiratory function, while overexpression inhibits mitochondrial activity, revealing that reduced levels of ''deeJ'' do not phenocopy mitochondrial dysfunction [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28819044 (Chen et al. 2017)].
Additional studies reveal that the combination of oxidative stress and knockdown of DJ-1 causes more severe phenotypic outcomes than either alone, and that the additional effects of oxidative stress in DJ-1 knockdown cells are dependent on AMPK ([/gene/DDB_G0277905 snfA]). In the absence of oxidative stress, ''deeJ'' antisense cells lack a phototaxis defect. [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28819044 (Chen et al. 2017)]. However, during oxidative stress the accuracy of phototaxis is reduced in ''deeJ'' antisense cells and this phenotype is rescued in co-transformants in which expression of both DJ-1 and AMPK have been antisense-inhibited. In addition, AMPK knockdown in ''deeJ'' antisense cells rescued the cells from the additional effect of oxidative stress on phagocytosis rates, and substantially, but incompletely, rescued their growth defect. These results suggest that DJ-1 protects cells from the AMPK-mediated consequences of mitochondrial dysfunction arising from oxidative stress, and support a model in which, in the absence of oxidative stress, DJ-1 activates phagocytosis and pinocytosis and inhibits mitochondrial respiration, but under oxidative stress conditions DJ-1 also inhibits AMPK (Chen, et al 2021, PMID:34440642).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 18-FEB-2022 RD

Additionally, the ''Dictyostelium''genome contains putative orthologs of human LSM10 ([/gene/DDB_G0291015 DDB_G0291015]), LSM11 ([/gene/DDB_G0289453 DDB_G0289453]), and LSM12 ([/gene/DDB_G0270402 DDB_G0270402]). DDB_G0275115.summary: Succinate dehydrogenase, also known as complex II ([/ontology/go/5749/annotation/page/1 mitochondrial respiratory chain complex II]), catalyzes the oxidation of succinate to fumarate while FAD is reduced to FADH<sub>2</sub>. The enzyme contains 4 subunits: a flavoprotein (FP) ([/gene/DDB_G0280535 sdhA]), an iron-sulfur protein (IP) ([/gene/DDB_G0270120 sdhB]), and a cytochrome b composed of two integral membrane proteins ([/ontology/go/16021/annotation/page/1 integral to membrane]) ([/gene/DDB_G0275115 sdhC] and [/gene/DDB_G0278157 sdhD]). The 4 subunit complex is bound in the [/ontology/go/5740/annotation/page/1 mitochondrial envelope] and provides a link between the the [/ontology/go/6099/annotation/page/1 tricarboxylic acid cycle] and the membrane-bound [/ontology/go/6118/annotation/page/1 electron transport] system. It is part of the respiratory chain and repressed in anaerobic respiration.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 31-JAN-2005 PF

DDB_G0292592.summary: Lst8, along with RipA ([/gene/DDB_G0284611 ripA]), PiaA ([/gene/DDB_G0277399 piaA]), and TOR ([/gene/DDB_G0281569 tor]), make up the TORC2 complex that plays a critical role in chemotaxis and relay of the cAMP signal [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16079174  (Lee et al. 2005)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22081140  (Kortholt et al. 2011)]. Lst8 is a highly conserved homolog of yeast LST8 (lethal with sec thirteen). ''lst8'' null cells show reduced cell polarity, chemotactic speed and directionality, phosphorylation of PKB ([/gene/DDB_G0268620 pkbA]) and PKBR1 ([/gene/DDB_G0290157 pkgB]) and activation of adenylyl cyclase ([/gene/DDB_G0281545 acaA]) [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16079174  (Lee et al. 2005)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31263268  (Senoo et al. 2019)]. They also show elevated rates of phagocytosis of both yeast and latex beads [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22266904  (Rosel et al. 2012)]. Treating ''lst8'' null or piaA null mutant cells with artificial pulses of cAMP does not rescue development indicating that these components of TORC2 are essential for Ras stimulation or activity of the complex [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10473630  (Lee et al. 1999)]. During chemotaxis to cAMP, RacE ([/gene/DDB_G0280975 racE]) promotes phosphorylation of PkbA and PkgB by assembling a supercomplex with RasC-GTP ([/gene/DDB_G0281385 rasC]) and the TORC2 components tor, piaA and lst8. This supercomplex formation is controlled by the chemoattractant-induced phosphorylation of racE at S192 by the glycogen synthase kinase gskA ([/gene/DDB_G0272110 gskA]) [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31263268  (Senoo et al. 2019)]. Lst8 is also a subunit of the TORC1 complex that is involved in nutrient sensing [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22266904  (Rosel et al. 2012)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 16-JUL-2019 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0281899.summary: The ''drkC'' gene encodes the receptor-like tyrosine kinase VSK3 ([/ontology/go/0004713/annotation/page/1 protein-tyrosine kinase activity]) that is involved in [/ontology/go/0006909/annotation/page/1 phagocytosis]. It has been shown that the N-terminus of the protein is located inside the vesicle, whereas the C-terminal kinase domain resides in the cytoplasm where ATP is abundant for [/ontology/go/0005524/annotation/page/1 ATP binding]. ''Dictyostelium'' contains two more genes ([/gene/DDB_G0289791 drkA], [/gene/DDB_G0289709 drkB]) that encode putative receptor kinases with an N-terminal signal peptide, a transmembrane domain, and a C-terminal kinase domain [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17664333  (Fang et al. 2007)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 27-AUG-2007 PF

DDB_G0269178.summary:
''racG'' encodes a guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G protein) of the Rho family of small GTPases. G proteins are key components of signal transduction networks in which they function as molecular signaling switches, binding to GDP in the off state while binding GTP in the on state. Guanine nucleotide-exchange factors (GEFs) promote the exchange of GDP for GTP on Ras GTPases thus activating them, while GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) inactivate Ras GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP. Possible GEFs for RacG include RGBARG ([/gene/DDB_G0269934 rgbA]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/32531280 Buckley et al. 2020]), GxcC ([/gene/DDB_G0284845 gxcC]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23363311 Plak et al. 2013]) and ZizB ([/gene/DDB_G0293084 zizB]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22366457 Pakes et al. 2012]).
''racG'' mRNA is expressed at almost the same level from the vegetative to the slug stage, but expression gradually decreases after culmination ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11201251 Okuwa et al. 2001]). ''racG'' is also induced during sexual maturation but expression is reduced immediately after cell fusion, suggesting that RacG may be involved in cell/cell interactions during the sexual cycle ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16573737 Muramoto et al. 2006]). RacG participates in signaling pathways that regulate processes dependent on rearrangement of the cytoskeleton such as cell morphology, phagocytosis, and chemotaxis. RacG is targeted to the plasma membrane and localizes in the cell cortex, filipodia, and transiently to phagocytic cups. Overexpression of RacG stimulates phagocytosis and promotes formation of excess filipodia, resulting in a spiky morphology. ''racG'' null mutants have a mild defect in chemotaxis to cAMP, but growth, pinocytosis, exocytosis, development and cytokinesis were unaffected in the absence of ''racG''. In a cell-free system, RacG stimulates actin polymerization through the Arp2/3 complex. Cells overexpressing RacG have decreased levels of activated Rac1 ([/gene/DDB_G0277869 rac1A], [/gene/DDB_G0268622 rac1B], [/gene/DDB_G0282365 rac1C]), suggesting that the defects observed in this strain may be due to impaired Rac1 activation and interference with signaling through other Rho GTPases such as RacB ([/gene/DDB_G0279605 racB]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16950926 Somesh et al. 2006]), ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26940518 Rivero et al. 2016]). ''racG'' null mutants also display a decrease in the recruitment of RGBARG to the phagocytic cup ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/32531280 Buckley et al. 2020]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 17-JUN-2020 RD

DDB_G0269934.summary: ''rgbA'' encodes the large, multiple-domain protein RGBARG which contains RCC1, Rho GEF, BAR, and Ras GAP domains. RGBARB interacts with the Rho family small GTPases RacG ([/gene/DDB_G0269178 racG]) and RacH ([/gene/DDB_G0269240 racH]) suggesting that it may serve as a Rho GEF for these GTPases. In addition, the RGBARG RasGAP domain is active against numerous Ras family small GTPases. ''rgbA'' null cells display defects in macropinosome formation and phagocytosis, with a specific defect in phagocytosis of rod-shaped bacteria such as ''E. coli'' and ''M. smegmatis''. In ''rgbA'' null cells, Rac activity is not localized to the protrusive edge of macropinocytic cups as in wt cells. These results reveal that RGBARG integrates Ras and Rac signaling to allow efficient macropinosome formation and the engulfment of diverse bacteria of different geometry ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/32531280 Buckley et al. 2020]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 18-JUN-2020 RD

DDB_G0276355.summary: ''dhcA'' encodes the highly conserved dynein heavy chain that together with the dynein intermediate chain ([/gene/DDB_G0280849 dicA]) makes motor complexes that move cargo along microtubules [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1469051  (Koonce et al. 1992)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7866389  (Koonce et al. 1994)]. The heavy chain has a stem at the N-terminal that binds cargo, followed by the motor domain, 4 ATP binding sites and a long stalk ending in a microtubule binding site [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22398446  (Kon et al. 2012)]. Dimers walk along microtubules towards the minus-ends by coupling large structural changes to ATP [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17548361  (Mogami et al. 2007)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19203583  (Roberts et al. 2009)]. Endosomes are transported along microtubules with frequent reversals in direction due to a tug-of-war between dynein pulling to the minus-end and kinesin ([/gene/DDB_G0290963 kif1]) pulling to the plus-end [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19864630  (Soppina et al. 2009)]. Dynein heavy chains are essential for viability of ''Dictyostelium'' [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9453714  (Koonce and Knecht, 1998)]. ''In vitro'' assays of mutant forms of dynein heavy chain showed that the first ATP-binding/hydrolysis site is essential for the motor activities. Mutations in the second and fourth binding sites reduced microtubule-activated ATPase activity but had no effect on binding affinity. Mutations in the third binding site resulted in 20-fold slower sliding velocity on microtubules [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15366936  (Kon et al. 2004)]. Overexpression of a truncated 380 kDa form lacking the amino terminal region involved in dimerization results in collapse of the interphase radial microtubule array [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8816999  (Koonce and Samso, 1996)]. Dynein is also found associated with centrosomes [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15186508  (Hestermann et al. 2004)]. Dynein motors cluster into microdomains on phagosomal membranes, resulting in rapid directed transport of the phagosome toward microtubule minus ends, likely promoting phagolysosome fusion and pathogen degradation. [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26853472  (Rai et al. 2016)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 22-MAY-2017 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0277321.summary: The Plasmodium falciparum chloroquine resistance transporter (PfCRT) carries a point mutation (K76T)that is found in chloroquine-resistant strains of malaria, posing a major health risk. Threehomologs of PfCRT exist in ''Dictyostelium discoideum'': [/gene/DDB_G0276943 crtp1], [/gene/DDB_G0277321 crtp2], and [/gene/DDB_G0270204 crtp3] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11343215 Nomura et al.2001], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15883156 Naude et al. 2005]), all of whichcontain ten predicted transmembrane domains ([/ontology/go/0016021/annotation/page/1 integral to membrane]). The CRTp1 protein is localized to the[/ontology/go/0012506/annotation/page/1 vesicle membrane], and a fusion of the N-terminus of ''Dictyostelium'' CRTp1 with PfCRT localizes tothe endosomes. Transformation of ''Dictyostelium'' cells with mutant PfCRT allows the cells toexpel chloroquine, making it an ideal system in which to study malaria drug resistance ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15883156 Naude et al. 2005]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 20-OCT-2005 KP

DDB_G0281239.summary: ''impa1'' encodes inositol monophosphatase (IMPase), an enzyme of broad specificity which is inhibited by lithium and is involved in myo-inositol biosynthesis. IMPase dephosphorylates inositol phosphate to generate inositol, which may then be recycled into inositol lipids. ''impa1'' also plays a role in intracellular phosphatidylinositol (3,4,5) trisphosphate (PIP3) signaling. Lithium suppresses PIP3 signaling in both ''Dictyostelium'' and cultured human neutrophil cells, by suppressing synthesis of the phosphoinositide precursors of PIP3. Increased expression of IMPase reverses the effects of lithium, suggesting that lithium acts through inositol depletion. In the absence of lithium, elevated IMPase leads to elevated PIP3 signaling [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19383941  (King et al. 2009)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 09-OCT-2020 RD

DDB_G0269424.summary: ''gxcB'' encodes a Rac guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF, RacGEF). RacGEFs are key components of signaling networks in which they activate Rho family GTPases by promoting the exchange of GDP for GTP. GxcB contains a domain organization of three calponin homology (CH) domains in its N-terminus and a typical GEF domain composed of a diffuse B-cell lymphoma homology (DH)/pleckstrin homology (PH) tandem domain at its C-terminus. ''gxcB'' is maximally expressed from the vegetative growth phase to early stages of development, with expression declining sharply after about 12 hr. of development. GxcB is localized to the cortical region and late endosomes. GxcB both binds to and bundles F-actin filaments. ''gxcB'' null mutants display slight irregularities in the organization of the actin cytoskeleton and a slight delay in development; however there is a 30% reduction in the rate of exocytosis in the mutant cells. These results suggest that ''gxcB'' is involved in a signaling pathway that is required for regulation of the actin cytoskeleton during exocytosis ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16781009 Strehle et al. 2006]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 25-JUN-2021 RD

DDB_G0289479.summary:
In eukaryotic cells, asparagine-linked glycolysation is one of the most common protein modification reactions, protein amino acid N-linked glycosylation, in the endoplasmic lumen. The protein complex responsible for these processes is the oligosaccharyltransferase complex (OST). The OST is an integral membrane complex that mediates the transfer of a preassembled high mannose oligosaccharide onto asparagine residues of nascent polypeptides. In yeast and vetebrates, the hetero-oligomeric proteins have 7 to 9 different subunits. The ''Dictyostelium'' complex contains 7 conserved subunits: [/gene/DDB_G0293224 ost1], [/gene/DDB_G0291049 ost2], [/gene/DDB_G0285537 ost3], [/gene/DDB_G0280609 ost4], [/gene/DDB_G0285159 stt3], [/gene/DDB_G0289479 swp1], and [/gene/DDB_G0291780 wbp1], all of which are putative integral membrane proteins of the ER; reviewed in [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16317064 Kelleher and Gilmore, 2005]. Another conserved OST subunit has been identified when improving a gene model, [/gene/DDB_G0306378 ostc].
A phenotypic readout, ''swp1'' has been identified to control growth on Gram-positive bacteria. ''swp1'' mutant cells grew poorly on all tested Gram-positive bacterial species such as ''Bacillus subtitles'' or ''Staphylococcus aureus'', but grew well on Gram-negative bacteria such as ''Klebsiella pneumoniae''. The ''swp1'' gene encodes a subunit of the oligosaccharyl transferase protein complex that catalyzes asparagine (N-linked) glycosylation of proteins. Tests blocking glycosylation in wild-type and comparing expression profiles with mutants suggest N-linked glycolsylation is required for growth on Gram-positive bacteria, but is dispensable for growth on Gram-negative bacteria. [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23664307 (Nasser et al. 2013)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 29-APR-2020 PF

DDB_G0283617.summary: Cdc25 has [/ontology/go/0004725/annotation/page/1 protein tyrosine phosphatase activity] ([/ontology/go/0006470/annotation/page/1 protein amino acid dephosphorylation]) and regulates [/ontology/go/0007049/annotation/page/1 cell cycle] progression by controlling the phosphorylation state of [/gene/DDB_G0272813 cdk1]. The ''Dictyostelium'' Cdc25 has a predicted mass of 117 kDa, the largest compared to the cdc25 from other species. The proteins contains four long asparagine repeats, however, Western blot analysis demonstrated that the protein exists as a short form (56 kDa), which has the C-terminal active site of phosphatase. The protein appears to be phosphorylated in vegetative cells, and dephosphorylated in development ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15351882 Mayanagi et al. 2004]). Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 21-DEC-2004 PG

DDB_G0268144.summary: The ''vwkA'' gene has been demonstrated to play a role in contractile vacuole dynamics and in hypo-osmotic shock survival [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19843280  (Betapudi et al. 2009)]. ''vwkA'' null cells display large numbers of engorged contractile vacuoles that fail to undergo proper fusion with the plasma membrane. The authors further show that vwkA- cells have an aberrant cortical myosin II organization, and that perturbation of myosin II abundance or activity also results in defective contractile vacuole dynamics. Their results suggest a role for myosin II-based cytosolic tension in contractile function and for a role for VwkA in the regulation of these events.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 31-JAN-2014 RD

DDB_G0269150.summary:
''lvsA'' was isolated as a mutant that has a large volume sphere phenotype. ''lvsA''- cells have a [/ontology/go/0000910/annotation/page/1 cytokinesis] defect similar to that of ''Dictyostelium'' clathrin heavy-chain mutants ([/gene/DDB_G0277221 chcA]) but less pronounced defects in[/ontology/go/0006907/annotation/page/1 pinocytosis] and [/ontology/go/0006909/annotation/page/1 phagocytosis].In addition, ''lvsA'' null mutant has defects in [/ontology/go/0007032/annotation/page/1 endosome organization], as does [/gene/DDB_G0271504 lvsB] null mutant ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10588668 Kwak et al. 1999], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11865029 Cornillon et al. 2002]). Localization studies have shown that GFP-LvsA is primarily associated with the membranes of the contractile vacuole system and that it has a punctate distribution in the cytoplasm. In ''lvsA'' mutants the contractile vacuole becomes disorganized and calmodulin ([/gene/DDB_G0279407 calA]) dissociates from the contractile vacuole membranes. Consequently, ''lvsA-'' mutants have an aberrant [/ontology/go/0006971/annotation/page/1 hypotonic response] [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11872142 (Gerald et al. 2002)]. A truncated version of LvsA missing the 689 N-terminal amino acids rescues cytokinesis defects and partially rescues defects in osmoregulation of ''lvsA''- mutant. Further deletions resulted in the complete loss of LvsA function. The association of LvsA with the contractile vacuole is perturbed by the loss of [/gene/DDB_G0269130 phgA], a protein important for vacuole function. The exact function of LvsA is not known, but it has been shown to bind membranes ([/ontology/go/0005543/annotation/page/1 phospholipid binding])in a GTP-independent manner ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15086784 Wu et al. 2004]).
A double mutant in [/gene/DDB_G0280955 DDB_G0280955] and ''lvsA'' suppresses the large contractile vacuole phenotype of disgorgin-, while overexpression of GFP-lvsA enhances it, suggesting ''lvsA'' is involved in the organization of the contractile vacuole ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18636095 Du et al. 2008]).
Seven BEACH domain-containing proteins have been identified in the ''Dictyostelium'' genome: [/gene/DDB_G0269150 lvsA], [/gene/DDB_G0271504 lvsB], [/gene/DDB_G0280971 lvsC], [/gene/DDB_G0271502 lvsD], [/gene/DDB_G0282925 lvsE], [/gene/DDB_G0284333 lvsF], and [/gene/DDB_G0268088 lvsG]. Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 21-NOV-2008 PG

DDB_G0291356.summary: ''grlE'' encodes a member of the evolutionarily conserved family of seven transmembrane receptors that are coupled to G-proteins ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16735079 Prabhu and Eichinger, 2006)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16527814 Taniura et al. 2006)]. GrlE is most similar to metazoan GABA<sub>B</sub> receptors. GrlE is the major GABA receptor during late development ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23548898 Wu et al. 2013)], and spore differentiaton factor 2 (SDF-2) production is abolished in ''grlE'' null cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16672332 Anjard and Loomis, 2006)]. When GABA binds GrlE coupled to Galpha 7 ([/gene/DDB_G0276455 gpaG]) during culmination, PI3 kinases are activated leading to activation of the protein kinase PKB R1 ([/gene/DDB_G0290157 pkgB]) which then triggers release of the SDF-2 precursor AcbA ([/gene/DDB_G0270658 acbA]) from prespore cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16672332 Anjard and Loomis, 2006)]. Before GABA is synthesized in prespore cells, glutamate is bound to GrlE which inhibits release of AcbA. The glutamate-bound form of GrlE is coupled to Galpha 9 ([/gene/DDB_G0283419 gpaI]). When GABA displaces glutamate bound to GrlE on prestalk cells, it induces exposure of the protease domain of TagC ([/gene/DDB_G0286121 tagC]) such that it can convert AcbA to SDF-2 ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16672332 Anjard and Loomis, 2006)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 15-DEC-2016 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis; annotation contributions PMID:23548898 Chris Janetopoulos

DDB_G0284791.summary: ''Dictyostelium cpnC'' belongs to the highly conserved copines, a family of ubiquitious Ca(2+)-dependent phospholipid-binding ([/ontology/go/0005544/annotation/page/1 calcium-dependent phospholipid binding]) proteins. In their N-terminal half, copines contain two Ca(2+)- and phospholipid-binding domains (C2 domains) present in such proteins as phospholipase C and protein kinase C. Much of the C-terminal half consists of a von Willebrand Factor type A domain (VWFA) typically found in the extracellular portions of membrane proteins like integrins. Thus copines represent a fusion of intracellular (C2) and extracellular (VWFA) domains. However, there are no signal sequence or hydrophobic transmembrane sequences in the predicted proteins suggesting copines are intracellular proteins. Copines are thought to be involved in membrane trafficking. It is of particular interest that copines, first found in the highly phagocytic protozoan ''Paramecium'' and then isolated from mammalian spleen and liver, seem to be abundant in cells and organs that are, or contain, phagocytes. In this context it comes as no surprise that phagocytic ''Dictyostelium'' has a total of six copine genes[http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16343335  (Damer et al. 2005)]. The widespread distribution of copines from protozoans to mammals and their high similarity suggest they play important role(s) in eukaryotic biology. Reviewed in [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12440769  (Tomsig and Creutz, 2001)]Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 05-APR-2004 PF

DDB_G0277041.summary:
''rheb'' encodes a guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G protein) of the Ras superfamily of small GTPases. G proteins are key components of signal transduction networks in which they function as molecular signaling switches, binding to GDP in the off state while binding GTP in the on state. Guanine nucleotide-exchange factors (GEFs, rasGEFs) promote the exchange of GDP for GTP on Ras GTPases thus activating them, while GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs, rasGAPs) inactivate Ras GTPases. Rheb is inactivated by the RasGAP ([/gene/DDB_G0280527 tsc2]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22266904 Rosel et al. 2012)].
''rheb'' is expressed at all stages of development with expression localized largely in the prestalk/stalk region and also in the anterior-most prespore cells [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24499792 (Swer et al. 2014)]. ''rheb'' null cells exhibit an increased rate of phagocytosis. Expression of activated Rheb suppresses phagocytosis in wild-type and AKT null ([/gene/DDB_G0268620 pkbA]) cells, but it is unable to do so in either lst8 ([/gene/DDB_G0292592 lst8]) or rip3 null ([/gene/DDB_G0284611 ripA]) cells. Thus ''rheb'' GTPase regulates phagocytosis in a pathway that is independent of AKT, but integrated with TORC2. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22266904 Rosel et al. 2012)]. Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 22-MAY-2019 RD

DDB_G0273065.summary:
Papers from the early '80's suggested that there are two genes, ''dscB'' and ''dscC'', with identical protein sequence but on a different chromosomal location. ''dscC'' is situated next to ''dscD''; the gene corresponding to ''dscB'' cannot be found in AX4.
The lectin Discoidin I binds N-acetylgalactosamine and galactose [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/4517669 (Rosen et al. 1973)]. Discoidin I subunits associate to form a tetramer [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/4858710 (Simpson et al. 1974)] and are expressed from a family of 3 different genes: ''dscA'' ([/gene/DDB_G0273063 dscA-1]) ([/gene/DDB_G0273919 dscA-2]), ''dscC'' and ''dscD'' ([/gene/DDB_G0273067 dscD-1]) ([/gene/DDB_G0273887 dscD-2]). [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6279874 (Poole et al. 1981)]. Monomeric discoidin I is located mainly in the cytosol, while the tetrameric form of discoidin I is detected in multilamellar bodies and is externalized during aggregation [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2581974 (Barondes et al. 1985)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8416797 (Fukuzawa et al. 1993)]. Discoidin I gene expression is induced by prestarvation factor (PSF) and conditioned medium factor, ([/gene/DDB_G0275007 cmfA]) but is down-regulated by cAMP [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7641976 (Blusch et al. 1995)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2049883 (Rathi et al. 1991)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1663029 (Gomer et al. 1991)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2196444 (Vauti et al. 1990)]. Mutants defective in discoidin I fail to stream during aggregation, implicating discoidin I in cell-substrate adhesion [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6509552 (Springer et al. 1984)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/4075402 (Crowley et al. 1985)]. In addition, discoidin I is thought to play an intracellular role, as mutants in which discoidin genes are not expressed also have an abnormally centered microtubule organizing center and more rounded cell morphology, suggesting a role for discoidins in cytoskeleton organization during aggregation [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1334012 (Alexander et al. 1992)].
''Dictyostelium discoideum'' strains that carry bacteria secrete approx. 80 times higher levels of DscA and DscC than non-carriers. Secreted DscA binds to ''Klebsiella pneumoniae''. DscA binding protects bacteria from extracellular killing, promotes their internalization and prolongs their retention in both ''Dictyostelium discoideum'' and mammalian cells. Plant lectins induce the same response, suggesting that modified uptake and persistence of lectin-coated bacteria in eukaryotic cells is a general phenomenon, termed lectin-induced modified bacterial internalization [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30049880 (Dinh et al. 2018)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 23-AUG-2018 RD

DDB_G0283755.summary: ''arpC'' encodes the 47 kDa actin-related subunit of the Arp2/3 complex [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11807934  (Insall et al. 2001)]. The seven subunits of this 200 kDa complex are encoded by ([/gene/DDB_G0277825 arcA]), ([/gene/DDB_G0282813 arcB]), ([/gene/DDB_G0292804 arcC]), ([/gene/DDB_G0269102 arcD]), ([/gene/DDB_G0288319 arcE]), ([/gene/DDB_G0272106 arpB]) and ''arpC''. The subunits of mammalian Arp2/3 are very similar to their ''Dictyostelium'' homologs. Arp2/3 binds to the side of F-actin filaments and initiates polymerization of a new F-actin chain at an angle of 70 degrees leading to a branched actin network that can alter the shape of cells. The ability to nucleate new actin filaments is greatly stimulated by direct interactions with members of the WASP/SCAR family [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11807934  (Insall et al. 2001)]. The Arp2/3 complex largely mediates the actin polymerization response to chemotactic stimulation and contributes to cell motility, pseudopod extension and adhesion in Dictyostelium chemotaxis. The complete Arp2/3 complex is essential for growth; partial loss of activity of either ArcB or ArpB impairs growth and chemotaxis [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17553489  (Langridge and Kay, 2007)]. mRNA from each of the genes encoding Arp2/3 subunits accumulates coordinately to reach a peak at 3 hours of development and gradually decreases thereafter [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25887420  (Rosengarten et al. 2015)]. The Arp2/3 complex interacts with the protein CARMIL, which serves as a scaffold for the assembly of a larger complex of proteins involved in the nucleation and termination of actin filament assembly. The complex consists of CARMIL ([/gene/DDB_G0292386 carmil]), AcpA, ([/gene/DDB_G0267374 acpA]) AcpB, ([/gene/DDB_G0272104 acpB]) the Arp2/3 complex, and type I myosins MyoB ([/gene/DDB_G0289117 myoB]) and MyoC ([/gene/DDB_G0276617 myoC]) [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11425877  (Jung et al. 2001)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 10-JUN-2019 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

GATA transcription factors specifically bind the DNA sequence (A/T)GATA(A/G) in the regulatory regions of genes [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2249770 (Yamamoto et al. 1990)]. In ''Dictyostelium'', there are 24 predicted proteins that contain GATA-type zinc fingers: [/gene/DDB_G0277147 stkA], [/gene/DDB_G0280547 comH], [/gene/DDB_G0277589 gtaC], [/gene/DDB_G0286855 gtaD],[/gene/DDB_G0267640 gtaE],[/gene/DDB_G0268792 gtaF],[/gene/DDB_G0270756 gtaG],[/gene/DDB_G0277591 gtaH],[/gene/DDB_G0281661 gtaI],[/gene/DDB_G0281829 gtaJ],[/gene/DDB_G0282811 gtaK],[/gene/DDB_G0285139 gtaL],[/gene/DDB_G0286837 gtaM],[/gene/DDB_G0287057 gtaN],[/gene/DDB_G0289651 gtaO],[/gene/DDB_G0295707 gtaP],[/gene/DDB_G0286843 gtaQ],[/gene/DDB_G0279331 gtaR],[/gene/DDB_G0280627 gtaS],[/gene/DDB_G0280639 gtaT],[/gene/DDB_G0280853 gtaU],[/gene/DDB_G0281087 gtaV],[/gene/DDB_G0286839 gtaW], [/gene/DDB_G0290665 gtaX], as well as [/gene/DDB_G0279239 gtaY], which is missing a cysteine residue.
''gtaG'' is expressed in prestalk cells. Knockout mutants fails to progress beyond the finger stage of development and fruiting body formation is greatly compromised, revealing that ''gtaG'' is essential for terminal differentiation in ''Dictostelium''. Transcriptome anaylsis reveals that GtaG regulates prestalk gene expression, and that its activity overlaps with that of the well characterized transcription factor, Dd-STATa ([/gene/DDB_G0281381 dstA]). GtaG activity appears to be mediated by regulation of cyclic di-GMP and Spore Differentiation Factor-1 production [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26962009 (Katoh-Kurasawa et al. 2016)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 22-JAN-2018 RD

DDB_G0288375.summary: The 47 kDa protein encoded by ''lis1'' is a close homolog of mammalian LIS1 which is associated with lissencephaly. ''lis1'' consists of an N-terminal LIS1-homology domain and seven WD40 repreats. Like LIS1, it is found at the tips of microtubules where it asssociates with the XMAP215 family member DdCP224 ([/gene/DDB_G0268616 cepJ]) and dynein ([/gene/DDB_G0276355 dhcA]) to form cortical attachments. Partial loss of Lis1 function resulting from a hypomorphic point mutation leads to collapse of radial interphase microtubule arrays into bundles that whorl around the nucleus. Lis1 is also found directly assocated with the centrosome which it helps localize near the nucleus. [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15800059  (Rehberg et al. 2005)]. LIS1 may also affect actin dynamics through interactions with Rac1A ([/gene/DDB_G0277869 rac1A]) and doublecortin ([/gene/DDB_G0277115 dcx]) [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21034843  (Meyer et al. 2010)]. LIS1 over-expression mutants have a defect in the formation of the phagocytic cup and a reduced migration velocity, further suggesting that LIS1 is involved in the regulation of actin dynamics [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/32524725  (Chhatre et al. 2020)]. About 100 different proteins contribute to centrosomal functions including the products of ([/gene/DDB_G0271738 tubC]), ([/gene/DDB_G0285849 spc97]), ([/gene/DDB_G0283909 spc98]), ([/gene/DDB_G0288427 cenA]), ''lis1'', ([/gene/DDB_G0270814 nek2]), ([/gene/DDB_G0283607 eb1]), ([/gene/DDB_G0268616 cepJ]) and ([/gene/DDB_G0278809 cepG]) [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15548420  (Graf et al. 2004)]. DDB_G0291133.summary:
The wee1 family of tyrosine kinases ([/ontology/go/0004713/annotation/page/1 protein-tyrosine kinase activity]) were originally identified in a screen formutants that undergo mitosis at a reduced cell size in the fission yeast ''Schizosaccharomycespombe'' ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7262540 Nurse and Thuriaux 1980]). Since then, members ofthe wee1 family have been shown to play an essential role in cell cycle regulation ([/ontology/go/0000074/annotation/page/1 regulation of progression through cell cycle]) in several other organisms, including thebudding yeast ''Saccharomyces cerevisiae'', the African clawed frog ''Xenopus laevis'', andseveral metazoans ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14625382 reviewed in Kellogg 2003]).
Wee1 phosphorylates a specific tyrosine residue on the mitosis promoting protein Cdk1/Cdc2/Cdc28 ([/gene/DDB_G0272813 cdk1] in ''Dictyostelium''). Phosphorylation of this residue by Wee1 inhibits Cdk1/Cdc2/Cdc28,thereby delaying entry into mitosis from G2. Cdk1/Cdc2/Cdc28 is inactivated by dephosphorylation of thetyrosine residue by the phosphatase Cdc25/Mih1 ([/gene/DDB_G0283617 cdc25] in ''Dictyostelium''), allowingentry into mitosis ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14625382 reviewed in Kellogg 2003]).
Three uncharacterized putative wee1 family members exist in the ''Dictyostelium'' genome: [/gene/DDB_G0291842 DDB_G0291842], [/gene/DDB_G0277539 DDB_G0277539], and [/gene/DDB_G0291133 DDB_G0291133]. Interestingly, ''Schizosaccharomyces pombe'' and animals also have three wee1 family kinases: wee1, mik1, and myt1.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 21-MAY-2004 KP

DDB_G0268622.summary:
''rac1B'' encodes a guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G protein) of the Rho family of small GTPases. G proteins are key components of signal transduction networks in which they function as molecular signaling switches, binding to GDP in the off state while binding GTP in the on state. Guanine nucleotide-exchange factors (GEFs) promote the exchange of GDP for GTP on Ras GTPases thus activating them, while GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) inactivate Ras GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP. Myosin M ([/gene/DDB_G0292262 myoM]) has GEF activity towards Rac1B ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11208126 Geissler et al. 2000]) and RacGEF1 ([/gene/DDB_G0277987 gxcA]) also has weak GEF activity for Rac1B ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15470506 Park et al. 2004]). DGAP1 ([/gene/DDB_G0287585 rgaA]) and GAPA ([/gene/DDB_G0269140 gapA]) are possible GAPs for Rac1B ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10825297 Dumontier et al. 2000]), ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20375144 Lee et al. 2010]). Rac1B has multiple binding partners that may function as downstream effectors. These include: protein kinase PakA ([/gene/DDB_G0269166 pakA]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10545500 Chung et al. 1999]), myosin heavy chain kinase PakB ([/gene/DDB_G0276459 pakB]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15509655 de la Roche et al. 2005]), protein kinase PakC ([/gene/DDB_G0267450 pakC]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15470506 Park et al. 2004]), WASP ([/gene/DDB_G0293834 wasA]), WASP-B ([/gene/DDB_G0272811 wasB]) [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23791739 (Chung et al. 2013)] and coronin A ([/gene/DDB_G0267382 corA]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24347642 Swaminathan et al. 2013]). Rac1B also binds to the Rho GDP-dissociation inhibitor 1 RhoGDI1 ([/gene/DDB_G0291077 rdiA]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12163018 Imai et al. 2002]). ''rac1B'' is induced during sexual maturation but expression is reduced immediately after cell fusion, suggesting that Rac1B may be involved in cell/cell interactions during the sexual cycle ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16573737 Muramoto et al. 2005]). Expression of ''rac1B'' is upregulated in response to intracellular ''Mycobacterium marinum'' and ''Legionella pneumophila'' infection ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31823727 Kjellin et al. 2019]).
''rac1B'' is highly similar to two additional ''Dictyostelium'' rho GTPases: ''rac1A'' ([/gene/DDB_G0277869 rac1A]) and ''rac1C'' ([/gene/DDB_G0282365 rac1C]). Expression of the three ''rac1'' genes is low during growth but increases 3-fold during aggregation before again declining to growth-stage levels during the slug stage ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8294042 Bush et al. 1993]). Overexpression of ''rac1'' genes results in increased filopodium formation, while constitutively active Rac1 mutants are severely impaired in growth, motility and endocytosis. In addition, these mutants are delayed in development and display defects in cytokinesis and F-actin organization. These results indicate that the Rac1 GTPases mediate signaling cascades regulating processes such as cell motility, endocytosis and cytokinesis that depend on the reorganization of the actin cytoskeleton in ''Dictyostelium'' ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10545500 Chung et al. 1999]), ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10825297 Dumontier et al. 2000]), ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10962483 Palmieri et al. 2000]). At the leading edge of migrating cells activated Rac1 participates in Scar/WAVE ([/gene/DDB_G0285253 scrA])-mediated actin polymerization and pseudopod extension. At the trailing edge activated Rac1 forms a complex with DGAP1 and the actin-binding proteins cortexillin I ([/gene/DDB_G0289483 ctxA]) and cortexillin II ([/gene/DDB_G0276893 ctxB]) enabling proper cell retraction ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20375144 Lee et al. 2010]), ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22302991 Filic et al. 2012]), ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22891261 Veltman et al. 2012]), ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23503127 Faix et al. 2013]), ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26940518 Rivero et al. 2016]). DDB_G0285313.summary: ''cepH'' encodes the centrosomal protein Cep192. Despite low sequence similarity, Cep192 is an ortholog of human CEP192, which is involved in mitotic centrosome maturation and bipolar spindle assembly. Cep192 is an essential part of the outer layers of the centrosomal core and is present at mitotic spindle poles. Cep192 interacts with CDK5RAP2 ([/gene/DDB_G0282851 cepL]) and likely directly interacts with both CDK5RAP2 and CP91 ([/gene/DDB_G0275495 cepE]) in the centrosomal core. Both ''cepH'' over-expression mutants and ''cepH'' knockdown mutants displayed supernumerary cytosolic microtubule organizing centers, and ''cepH'' knockdown mutants also displayed an increased average DNA content. These results reveal Cep192 to be a major structural component of the outer core layers of the ''Dictyostelium'' centrosome and suggest that Cep192 is required for centrosome biogenesis and for the functional integrity of the corona [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19466752  (Schultz et al., 2009)], (Pitzen, et al. 2021, PMID: 34572033).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 06-OCT-2021 RD

The mammalian (rabbit) GSK3β was found to be tyrosine phosphorylated by ZAK1 [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10571182 (Kim et al. 1999)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 29-MAY-2007 PF

G proteins are key components of signal transduction networks in which they function as molecular signaling switches, binding to GDP in the off state while binding GTP in the on state. Guanine nucleotide-exchange factors (GEFs) promote the exchange of GDP for GTP on Rab GTPases thus activating them, while GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) inactivate Rab GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDPBasic annotations have been added to this gene, 21-JAN-2021 RD

DDB_G0289505.summary:
There are 29 genes encoding actin in ''Dictyostelium'' with amino acid identity greater than 83%, ''act1''-''act29''. Seventeen of these genes encode identical proteins: [/gene/DDB_G0289553 act1], [/gene/DDB_G0274133 act2], [/gene/DDB_G0289005 act4], [/gene/DDB_G0289663 act5], [/gene/DDB_G0274135 act6], [/gene/DDB_G0280545 act7], [/gene/DDB_G0269234 act8], [/gene/DDB_G0274601 act9], [/gene/DDB_G0288879 act11], [/gene/DDB_G0274129 act12], [/gene/DDB_G0274599 act13], [/gene/DDB_G0274137 act14], [/gene/DDB_G0272520 act15], [/gene/DDB_G0272248 act16], [/gene/DDB_G0274727 act19], [/gene/DDB_G0274285 act20], and [/gene/DDB_G0274561 act21], while [/gene/DDB_G0289811 act10], [/gene/DDB_G0275023 act22], and [/gene/DDB_G0289487 act3] respectively have 1, 4 and 11 amino acid differences compared to the 17 identical genes. The proteins encoded by [/gene/DDB_G0274131 act17], [/gene/DDB_G0289489 act18], [/gene/DDB_G0268744 act23] and [/gene/DDB_G0289505 act24]are more divergent.
Actin is a major [/ontology/go/0005200/annotation/page/1 structural constituent of cytoskeleton]. Actin is one of the most abundant proteins in ''Dictyostelium'', constituting approximately 8% of the total protein in vegetative cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/561722 Alton and Lodish et al. 1977]).Actin synthesis is developmentally regulated, peaking shortly after starvation (reviewed by [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6894564 Firtel] in 1981). The different actin genes differ in their levels of expression, with [/gene/DDB_G0274135 act6], [/gene/DDB_G0269234 act8] and [/gene/DDB_G0274129 act12] being highly expressed both during growth and development compared to [/gene/DDB_G0289005 act4], [/gene/DDB_G0289663 act5], [/gene/DDB_G0280545 act7] and [/gene/DDB_G0272248 act16] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6286214 McKeown and Firtel 1981]). DDB_G0284863.summary: The ''limB'' gene was isolated from a REMI mutant picked for being unable to form a tip on mounds ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10749929 Chien et al. 2000)]. The gene encodes a protein with 5 repeats of the conserved zinc-finger LIM domain and is expressed during early development. The protein is found in the plasma membrane where it may regulate the rearrangement of the actin cytoskeleton ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10749929 Chien et al. 2000)]. ''limB'' null cells exhibit an aberrant actin cytoskeleton, poor adhesion to a substratum and do not form tight cell-cell agglomerates in suspension. ''limB'' null cells are also unable to properly polarize in chemoattractant gradients and have a decreased chemotaxis rate. The mound arrest phenotype can be overcome by expression of ''limB'' under the control of the regulatory region of a prestalk specific gene, but not when it is under the control of the regulatory region of a prespore specific gene, indicating that tip formation may be driven by prestalk cells alone.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 03-FEB-2017 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0295787.summary:
The homeodomain is a sequence-specific DNA binding motif that consists of a helix-turn-helix. Homeobox-containing proteins have transcription factor activity. They have beenidentified in most if not all phyla of eukaryotes. Inmetazoans, homeobox-containing proteins are known to be involvedin regulating the anterior-posterior body plan and in thespecification of certain cell types and anterior-posteriorcompartments (see [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9486804 Han and Firtel 1998] and references therein). There are 14 predicted proteins that contain homeobox domains in ''Dictyostelium'':[/gene/DDB_G0275173 hbx2], [/gene/DDB_G0291075 warA], [/gene/DDB_G0291197 hbx3], [/gene/DDB_G0272967 hbx4], [/gene/DDB_G0273127 hbx5-1] (on the chromosome 2 duplication: [/gene/DDB_G0273645 hbx5-2]), [/gene/DDB_G0277505 hbx6], [/gene/DDB_G0278225 hbx7], [/gene/DDB_G0279257 hbx8], [/gene/DDB_G0280473 hbx9], [/gene/DDB_G0284293 hbx10], [/gene/DDB_G0295787 hbx11], [/gene/DDB_G0286733 hbx12], [/gene/DDB_G0288975 hbx13], and [/gene/DDB_G0289677 hbx14].
[http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25963254 Mishra and Saran 2015] performed a genome-wide classification and comparative genomic analysis of the 14 homeobox genes present in D. discoideum, and found that they could be classified into 3 groups: TALE, OTHER and NOVEL classes, ''hbx11'' belonging to the TALE class.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 07-JUL-2015 RD

DDB_G0291972.summary:
CulA is a member of the cullin family of proteins that function as scaffolds that, along with F-box/WD40-repeat-containing proteins, mediate the ubiquitination of proteins to target them for degradation by the proteasome ([/ontology/go/0004842/annotation/page/1 ubiquitin-protein ligase activity]). ''culA'' null cells are defective in inducing cell-type-specific gene expression and exhibit defects during aggregation, including reduced chemotaxis ([/ontology/go/0030154/annotation/page/1 cell differentiation]), ([/ontology/go/0006935/annotation/page/1 chemotaxis]).
Overexpression of the PKA catalytic subunit ([/gene/DDB_G0283907 pkaC]) rescues many of the ''culA'' null defects, as well as those of cells lacking [/gene/DDB_G0276887 fbxA], a F-box/WD40-repeat-containing protein, Whereas [/gene/DDB_G0284331 regA] protein levels drop as the multicellular organism forms in the wild-type strain, they remain high in ''culA'' null and ''fbxA'' null cells. CulA, FbxA, and RegA are found in a complex ''in vivo'' ([/ontology/go/0019005/annotation/page/1 SCF ubiquitin ligase complex]), and formation of this complex is dependent on the MAP kinase ERK2 ([/gene/DDB_G0283903 erkB]), which is also required for PKA function. This data suggest a model in which CulA and FbxA regulate multicellular development by targeting RegA for degradation via a pathway that requires ERK2 function, leading to an increase in cAMP and PKA activity [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11390363 (Mohanty et al. 2001)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 3-JUN-2008 PF
