DDB_G0279733.summary: ''gxcDD'' encodes a multidomain protein containing a CH domain, two IQ motifs, three PH domains, a RhoGEF domain and an ArfGAP domain. GxcDD is a putative Rac guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF, RacGEF). RacGEFs are key components of signaling networks in which they activate Rho family GTPases by promoting the exchange of GDP for GTP. ''gxcDD'' is expressed throughout development. The full-length GxcDD protein is present throughout the cytosol, membrane and cytoskeleton. However, the localization and roles of different GxcDD protein domains have been examined separately. The amino-terminal CH domain functions as a membrane anchor for the protein, while the C-terminal ArfGAP domain of GxcDD associates with the cell cortex and phagosomes. The RhoGEF domain of GxcDD interacts in vivo with several Rac GTPases: Rac1a ([/gene/DDB_G0277869 rac1A]), RacA ([/gene/DDB_G0286555 racA]), RacC ([/gene/DDB_G0293526 racC]), RacE ([/gene/DDB_G0280975 racE]), RacH ([/gene/DDB_G0269240 racH]), and RacI ([/gene/DDB_G0277897 racI]); however, the GEF activity of GxcDD has not been investigated. The C-terminal PH domain of GxcDD binds to phosphatidylinositol-3,4,5-trisphosphate (PIP3). ''gxcDD'' null cells lack defects in growth, phagocytosis, cytokinesis or actin cytoskeleton organization. However, ''gxcDD'' null cells display defects in development, with abnormal aggregation and streaming and delayed culmination. These results indicate that GxcDD is involved in Rac signaling pathways regulating streaming and development ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17584488 Mondal et al. 2007]), ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26940518 Rivero et al. 2016]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 08-JUL-2021 RD

AbiA is a member of the Scar/WAVE complex, consisting of (Scar) ([/gene/DDB_G0285253 scrA]), ''abiA'', ([/gene/DDB_G0279175 hspc300]), (PIR121) ([/gene/DDB_G0287855 pirA]), and ([/gene/DDB_G0274519 napA]). In migrating cells, the Scar/WAVE complex regulates the production of lamellipods and pseudopods through Arp2/3 complex activation. The Scar/WAVE complex localizes to the front of pseudopods and the tips of filopods, cell-cell contact zones, and the cell leading edge. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22891261 Veltman et al. 2012]). AbiA interacts directly with Scar ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17314411 Caracino et al. 2007]), Hspc300 ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21701600 Linkner et al. 2011]) and also with VASP family protein ([/gene/DDB_G0289541 vasP]). ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28889942 Litschko et al. 2017]).
In ''abiA'' null mutants, ScrA levels are reduced by approximately 5-fold, and both ScrA and PIR121 fail to localize to the leading edge of pseudopods. During chemotaxis to folate, ''abiA'' null mutants move more slowly, are more rounded, and extend smaller protrusions than do wild-type cells. ''abiA'' null mutants exhibit a reduced growth rate and 2-fold increase in the number of multinucleated cells due to a defect in cytokinesis. An ''abiA''/''scrA'' double null mutant has defects similar to a ''scrA'' single null mutant-a smaller cell size and reduced cell motility ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18261908 Pollitt and Insall 2008]). A series of ''abiA'' deletion mutants identified a minimal Abi fragment that stabilized the Scar/WAVE complex, demonstrating that Abi is not required for recruitment or activation of the Scar/WAVE complex and instead likely functions to modulate its activity. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24036345 Davidson et al. 2013]). Deletion of ''abiA'' in an AX2 background (''abiA''/AX2 null) had a negligible effect on levels of additional SCAR complex subunits and revealed additional phenotypes. ''abiA''/AX2 null cells have an increased number of crowns and aberrant pseudopodia, filopodia, and macropinocytic cups. ''abiA''/AX2 null cells have a reduced cell speed, but normal directionality. When grown in shaken suspension, they did not display a cytokinesis effect, although other SCAR complex subunits did so. Development of ''abiA''/AX2 null on SM agar plates was impaired, with cells only forming small slugs and fruiting bodies; however, a less severe phenotype was observed on non-nutrient plates. In ''abiA''/AX2 null cells, VasP did not translocate to newly formed pseudopods as in wt cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28889942 Litschko et al. 2017]).
AbiA is constitutively phosphorylated in unstimulated ''Dictyostelium'' cells, and both folate and cAMP chemoattractant signaling enhance Abi phosphorylation. Cell-substrate adhesion induces Abi phosphorylation while osmotic shock inhibits it, revealing that Abi phosphorylation is responsive to extracellular signals. Abi phosphorylation is decreased in pirA null cells expressing pirA with point mutations to eliminate Rac GTPase binding. As Scar/WAVE activation depends on Rac1 GTPAse ([/gene/DDB_G0277869 rac1A]), ([/gene/DDB_G0268622 rac1B]), ([/gene/DDB_G0282365 rac1C]) interacting with PirA, this confirms that Abi phosphorylation is a result of Scar/WAVE complex activation. Co-expression of unphosphorylatable and phosphomimetic Abi and Scar mutants in ''scrA''/''abiA'' double null cells suggests that neither Scar nor Abi phosphorylation is required for Scar/WAVE complex activation. Dictyostelium cells in which Scar and Abi are both unphosphorylatable can still form pseudopods, but migrate substantially faster. These results suggest that phosphorylation of both Scar and Abi enable the regulation of pseudopodia after they are formed, and that extracellular signals and environmental responses modulate cell migration by fine tuning Scar/WAVE complex behaviour after it has been activated. (Singh, et al. 2021, PMID:34943993).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 10-JAN-2022 RD

DDB_G0289665.summary:
''gefQ'' encodes a Ras guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF, RasGEF). rasGEFs are key components of signaling networks in which they activate Ras family small GTPases by promoting the exchange of GDP for GTP. ''gefQ'' is strongly expressed during both growth and development, with highest levels of expression at 8 and 12 hours of development ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16086850 Wilkins et al. 2005)]. GefQ has GEF activity toward two small GTPases: RasB ([/gene/DDB_G0292998 rasB]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18504297 Mondal et al. 2008)] and Rap1 ([/gene/DDB_G0291237 rapA]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25298405 Plak et al. 2014)]. GefQ has multiple binding partners: RasB, myosin heavy chain kinase A (MHCKA) ([/gene/DDB_G0291231 mhkA]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18504297 Mondal et al. 2008)], and 14-3-3 protein ([/gene/DDB_G0269138 fttB]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/32818671 Li et al. 2020)]. >). GefQ associates with F-actin, and is localized throughout the cytosol, enriched in the cell cortex and is also present in the nucleus ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18504297 Mondal et al. 2008)].
GefQ is involved in the regulation of processes requiring myosin II, such as cytokinesis, cell motility, and suppression of lateral pseudopods. ''gefQ'' null mutants lack GEF activity towards RasB. In addition, ''gefQ'' null mutants have a decreased growth rate and developmental defects, including defects in cell sorting and slug migration during later stages of development. ''gefQ'' null mutants also have increased levels of unphosphorylated myosin II, resulting in myosin II over-assembly and the production of many random pseudopodia. ''gefQ'' overexpression activates RasB, causes enhanced recruitment of MHCKA to the cortex, and leads to cytokinesis defects in suspension. GefQ and constitutively active RasB directly interact with the myosin heavy chain kinase MHCKA to regulate myosin II assembly ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18504297 Mondal et al. 2008)]. ''gefQ'' null cells show reduced Rap1 activation at the poles of dividing cells, suggesting that GefQ is important for regulating Rap1 during cytokinesis ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25298405 Plak et al. 2014)]. cAMP stimulates 14-3-3 protein binding to GefQ. Recombinant GefQ interacts with 14-3-3 after in vitro phosphorylation by PKA ([/gene/DDB_G0283907 pkaC], [/gene/DDB_G0279413 pkaR]) suggesting that PKA phosphorylates GefQ and promotes its interaction with 14-3-3 proteins in response to cAMP. ''gefQ'' mutant cells with an S431A point mutation are no longer able to bind 14-3-3, display a delay in development, and substantially lower ''rasB'' activation, suggesting that 14-3-3 binding to GefQ regulates development of ''Dictyostelium'' through RasB ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/32818671 Li et al. 2020)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 06-MAY-2021 RD

Two-hybrid assays reveal that PakB interacts with the Rho family GTPases ([/gene/DDB_G0286555 racA]), ([/gene/DDB_G0279605 racB]) , ([/gene/DDB_G0293526 racC]), ([/gene/DDB_G0269176 racF1]), ([/gene/DDB_G0277869 rac1A]) , ([/gene/DDB_G0268622 rac1B]) and ([/gene/DDB_G0282365 rac1C]). ''pakB'' null cells displayed no significant behavioral defects, but cells expressing activated PakB were unable to complete cytokinesis when grown in suspension and exhibited increased rates of phagocytosis and pinocytosis [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15509655  (de la Roche et al. 2005)]. ([/gene/DDB_G0273447 abpE-1]), ([/gene/DDB_G0273517 abpE-2]) and significantly enhances the binding of AbpE to actin filaments. When overexpressed in PakB- null cells, AbpE completely blocks early development at the aggregation stage, prevents cell polarization, and significantly reduces chemotaxis rates. While prestalk and prespore cell differentiation occurred with normal timing, proper patterning did not occur. The pollywog phenotype was dependent on a functional RegA, suggesting that DhkD functions to ensure the proper cAMP distribution within mounds. DDB_G0291157.summary: ''Dictyostelium'' ''cln3'' is the ortholog of human CLN3, which is linked to a juvenile form of neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (NCL), also referred to as Batten disease. Cln3 localizes primarily to the contractile vacuole system and to a smaller extent, compartments of the endocytic pathway and the Golgi complex. ''cln3'' null mutants display reduced adhesion during the early stages of development, which delays streaming and aggregation. Mid-to-late stage development of ''cln3'' null cells is precocious. Extracellular levels of the autocrine proliferation repressor AprA ([/gene/DDB_G0281663 aprA]) and the calcium-dependent cell-cell adhesion protein CadA ([/gene/DDB_G0285793 cadA]) are also altered in ''cln3'' mutants [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25330233  (Huber et al. 2014)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/27669405  (Huber et al. 2016)]. LC-MS/MS analysis revealed differences in the protein content of conditioned media (CM) from cln3 null cells compared to wt, which establishes a role for Cln3 in protein secretion. [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28365442  (Huber 2017)]. The absence or significant reduction of cell adhesion-related protein CsbA ([/gene/DDB_G0272833 csbA]), cell motility-related protein PsiM ([/gene/DDB_G0284759 psiM]) and density sensing factor CMF ([/gene/DDB_G0275007 cmfA]) in ''cln3'' null CM may help explain the adhesion and aggregation phenotypes. Other proteins involved in endocytosis, vesicle-mediated transport and proteolysis were either increased or found exclusively in the CM from ''cln3'' null cells. [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28365442  (Huber 2017)]. Cln3 also plays a role in osmoregulation. Cln3 localizes to the contractile vacuole system during mitosis, and ''cln3'' null cells display defects in cytokinesis. The recovery of ''cln3'' null cells from hypotonic stress is delayed, and during hypertonic stress, ''cln3'' null cells have reduced cell viability and inhibited development. In addition, Cln3-deficiency during osmotic stress upregulates the expression of tpp1 ([/gene/DDB_G0269914 tpp1]), the ''Dictyostelium'' ortholog of TPP1/CLN2, which has been implicated in Neuronal Ceroid Lipofuscinosis. [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30251676  (Mathavarajah et al. 2018)]. During starvation, a comparative transcriptomics RNA-seq analysis revealed 1153 genes differentially expressed in ''cln3'' null cells compared to wild type. In addition to supporting previous findings regarding the roles of ''cln3'', results also show that loss of ''cln3'' affects the expression and activity of lysosomal enzymes, increases endo-lysosomal pH, and alters nitric oxide homeostasis. During starvation, ''cln3'' null cells also accumulate autofluorescent storage bodies, which is the hallmark of Batten disease [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30771446  (Huber et al. 2019)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 24-MAY-2019 RD; annotation contributions: PMID:25330233, Robert Huber

DDB_G0277441.summary: ''rabJ'' encodes a guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G protein) of the Rab family of small GTPases. G proteins are key components of signal transduction networks in which they function as molecular signaling switches, binding to GDP in the off state while binding GTP in the on state. Guanine nucleotide-exchange factors (GEFs) promote the exchange of GDP for GTP on Rab GTPases thus activating them, while GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) inactivate Rab GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP. Rab GAP TbcrA ([/gene/DDB_G0282575 tbcrA]) binds to and is a possible RabGAP for RabJ (Tu, et al 2022, PMID:35379834).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 20-APR-2022 RD

DDB_G0272632.summary: ''gstA2'' encodes the enzyme glutathione S-transferase. Glutathione S-transferase plays an important role in cellular metabolism and detoxification by catalyzing the conjugation of glutathione to electrophilic endobiotic and xenobiotic substrates to reduce their interaction with cellular macromolecules. The plant polyphenol curcumin induces a significant increase in ''gstA2'' expression ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26449461 Garige et al. 2015]). ''gstA2'' is expressed in vegetatively growing cells. ''gstA2'' expression decreases during early development, but increases during slug and fruiting body formation. RNAi-mediated knockdown of ''gstA2'' results in decreased cell proliferation. In addition, ''gstA2'' knockdown cells have developmental abnormalities starting at the slug stage, including abnormally thick slugs which failed to form mature fruiting bodies at 24 hours of development. These results demonstrate that ''gstA2'' plays a role in proliferation and late stage development (Garige, et al 2021, PMID:33909675). Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 22-JUL-2021 RD

DDB_G0277831.summary:
A family of four highly related cell-surface receptors is responsible for the responses to cAMP at different stages of development in ''Dictyostelium''. The members are all 7 transmembrane G protein-coupled proteins but show different affinities to cAMP as well as different cell type specificities [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2049880 (Saxe et al., 1991]; [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7496377 Ginsburg et al., 1995)]. ''carD'' is expressed from late aggregation to culmination and encodes the low affinity CAR4 receptor that is enriched in prestalk cells and controls cytodifferentiation during late stages of development [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1537842 (Johnson et al., 1992]; [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7958880 Louis et al., 1994)].
CAR4 plays an essential role in regulating expression of certain prestalk specific genes by inactivating the protein kinase GSK3 (gene ''[/gene/DDB_G0272110 gskA]''). Furthermore, CAR4 stimulates a protein tyrosine phosphatase that removes the phosphate from GSK3, reducing its activity [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12408804 (Kim et al., 2002]; [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9284050 Ginsburg and Kimmel, 1997)]. CAR3 on the other hand, has a higher affinity for cAMP and activates GSK3 by stimulating the protein tyrosine kinase ZAK1 (gene ''[/gene/DDB_G0276025 zakA]''; [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15380246 Kimmel and Firtel, 2004)]. Thus, CAR3 and CAR4 antagonistically regulate GSK3 to establish cell fate choice. CAR3 signaling favors prespore differentiation and CAR4 signaling favors prestalk differentiation [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12408804 (Kim et al., 2002)]. It has been suggested that cell-type specific expression of receptors with different affinities for cAMP directs pattern formation in response to regional differences in cAMP concentration ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7958880 Louis et al., 1994)]. Further studies indicated that the switching of cAMP receptor subtypes during development enables the organism to respond to changing concentrations of the chemoattractant and thus program morphogenesis appropriately [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9578623 (Kim et al., 1998)]. Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 10-DEC-2015 PF; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0284725.summary:
''docD'' encodes a putative Rho guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF, RhoGEF). RhoGEFs are key components of signaling networks in which they activate Rho family GTPases by promoting the exchange of GDP for GTP. ''docD'' is expressed at all stages of development through early culmination (unpublished observations, cited in Para, 2009). In response to cAMP, DocD rapidly translocates to the cell cortex, and in chemotaxing cells, DockD preferentially localizes to the leading edge. Translocation is impaired in (PI3K) ([/gene/DDB_G0278727 pikA], [/gene/DDB_G0283081 pikB]) double null mutants, indicating that localization is dependent on localized production of phosphatidylinositol-3,4,5-trisphosphate. DocD forms a stable complex with the adaptor protein Elmo1 ([/gene/DDB_G0278051 elmoA]) in both vegetative and aggregation-competent ''Dictyostelium'' cells, either before or after chemoattractant stimulation. In addition, the DocD-ElmoA complex associates with the Rho small GTPases: Rac1A ([/gene/DDB_G0277869 rac1A]) and RacC ([/gene/DDB_G0293526 racC]) suggesting that DocD is a GEF for Rac1A and RacC.
''docD'' null mutant cells exhibit no growth or developmental defects. However, developmentally competent ''docD'' null mutants chemotax with moderately reduced speed and polarity in a cAMP gradient. The chemotaxis defect is more pronounced in ''docA''/''docD'' ([/gene/DDB_G0291974 docA]) double null mutant cells which have a further reduction in speed and polarity. Vegetative stage ''docD'' null mutants show a significant decrease in random motility, and the cell motility defect is no worse in the ''docA''/''docD'' double null mutant. However, expression of either DocA or DocD in the double null mutant rescues the phenotype, suggesting that DocA and DocD may function redundantly. Loss of DocA and DocD also affects the distribution of F-actin polymerization, as the vegetative double null cells appeared incapable of localizing F-actin accumulation at restricted regions of the cortex to create effective membrane protrusions. Vegetative stage cells over-expressing DocD have opposing phenotypes; they have increased cell motility, an increase in pseudopod formation and increased levels of F-actin polymerization compared with wild-type cells. Taken together, these results indicate that DocA and DocD regulate the actin cytoskeleton and cell motility ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19037099 Para et al. 2009]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 04-JUN-2021 RD

DDB_G0292406.summary: ''rab4'' encodes a guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G protein) of the Rab family of small GTPases. G proteins are key components of signal transduction networks in which they function as molecular signaling switches, binding to GDP in the off state while binding GTP in the on state. Rab subfamily small GTPases in many organisms are key regulators of intracellular membrane trafficking. DDB_G0283081.summary:
Disruption of ''pikB'' had no effect on growth or development; however strains in which both ''pikB'' and ([/gene/DDB_G0278727 pikA]) were disrupted showed both growth and developmental defects. [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7565716 (Zhou et al. 1995)]
To investigate the minimal requirements for chemotaxis, [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22081140 Kortholt et al. 2011] obtained quantitative data on Ras activation and chemotaxis in cAMP and folic acid gradients using a variety of Dictyostelium mutant cell lines from the four signaling pathways that contribute to chemotaxis: PI3K, TorC2, PLA2, and sGC. Their results demonstrate that Ras is activated at the leading edge, through a pathway consisting of G-alpha/beta/gamma, which does not depend on either of the four pathways. The authors measured chemotaxis of mutant cells exposed to cAMP gradients with different steepness and found that many mutants will chemotax in shallow gradients, despite a reduced sensitivity. Expression of multiple pathways increases sensitivity, with some combinations of pathways exhibiting weak amplification while others produce good chemotaxis with strong signal amplification. The results of cluster analysis revealed that one cluster of signaling pathways, including PI3K + TorC2 + sGC, is involved in inducing orientation of the cell towards the gradient, while a second cluster consists of cGMP + PLA2 and functions as a memory of current direction. Thus one individual pathway does not contribute strongly to chemotaxis, but it can synergize with other pathways, which together increases the sensitivity about 150-fold. These results suggest a conceptual model of chemotaxis in which a basal signaling module consisting of heterotrimeric and monomeric G proteins provides activation of Ras at the leading edge, which is sufficient for chemotaxis.Basic annotations have been added to this gene, 22-DEC-2014 RD

DDB_G0267436.summary: The ABC superfamily of genes is one of the largest in the genomes of both bacteria and eukaryotes. The proteins encoded by these genes all carry a characteristic 200- to 250-amino-acid ATP-binding cassette that gives them their family name. In bacteria they are mostly involved in nutrient import, while in eukaryotes many are involved in export. Seven different families (A to G) have been defined in eukaryotes based on sequence homology, domain topology, and function. ''Dictyostelium'' has 71 ABC transporters (including one on the chromosome 2 duplication) and 4 ABCF family members: [/gene/DDB_G0285997 abcF1], [/gene/DDB_G0284047 abcF2], [/gene/DDB_G0275637 abcF3] and [/gene/DDB_G0267436 abcF4]. The ABCF family is characterized by two ABC domains and no transmembrane domains. [/gene/DDB_G0285997 abcF1] and [/gene/DDB_G0267436 abcF4] are the most closely related to GCN20 from yeast and so are candidates for translational regulators [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6420574 (Anjard and Loomis 2002)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 16-JUN-2003 PG

DDB_G0277183.summary:
Histones form the nucleosomal core ([/ontology/go/0000786/annotation/page/1 nucleosome]) ([/ontology/go/0006334/annotation/page/1 nucleosome assembly]) that is fundamental to chromatin structure (). The histone octamer is composed of an H3-H4 tetramer (two H3-H4 dimers) coupled with an H2A-H2Btetramer (two H2A-H2B dimers). The histone H1 linker protein plays a role in packaging nucleosomes into the 30 nmfiber found in chromatin ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9177486 Bukenberger et al. 1992]).
In ''Dictyostelium discoideum'' and ''Saccharomyces cerevisiae'', only one copy of histone [/gene/DDB_G0285319 H1] appears to be present, in comparison to other eukaryotes which have multiple copies and subtypes([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7867938 Hauser et al. 1995], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9046096 Ushinsky et al.1997]). Two putative H2A family members, [/gene/DDB_G0279667 H2AX] and [/gene/DDB_G0286747 H2AZ], and three H2Adomain-containing proteins, [/gene/DDB_G0289187 H2Av1], [/gene/DDB_G0289193 H2Av2], [/gene/DDB_G0289197 H2Av3], are present in ''Dictyostelium''. Two H2B domain-containing proteins also exist inthe ''Dicty'' genome: [/gene/DDB_G0293758 H2Bv1] and [/gene/DDB_G0276273 H2Bv2]. There are three histone H3proteins, [/gene/DDB_G0267402 H3a] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9177486 Bukenberger et al. 1992]), [/gene/DDB_G0270838 H3b], and [/gene/DDB_G0271092 H3c], and two H3 domain-containing proteins, [/gene/DDB_G0291185 H3v1] and [/gene/DDB_G0277979 H3v2]. We have also identified two histone H4proteins, [/gene/DDB_G0277183 H4a] and [/gene/DDB_G0276863 H4b], which have identical protein sequences but non-identical nucleotide sequences.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 13-APR-2004 KP

DDB_G0280961.summary: The first member of a two-component system, the histidine kinase DhkA, functions in a signal transduction pathway regulating the terminal differentiation of prespore cells. DhkA was shown to be a transmembrane receptor for the signaling peptide SDF-2 ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8670894  Wang et al. 1996)] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10373524  Wang et al. 1999)]. DhkA autophosphorylates a histidine residue, and then transfers the phosphate to an aspartate in the carboxy terminal region from where it is relayed to a histidine in the small H2 protein RdeA ([/gene/DDB_G0282923 rdeA]; [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9582274  Chang et al. 1998)]. The phosphate on RdeA is in equilibrium with phosphate on an aspartate in the response regulator region of the cAMP phosphodiesterase RegA ([/gene/DDB_G0284331 regA]; [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10488068  Thomason et al. 1999)]. Phosphorylation of RegA increases its activity which reduces the internal level of cAMP. When SDF-2 binds to the external CHASE domain of DhkA, it converts the protein kinase to a protein phosphatase which reduces the activity of RegA and allows cAMP levels to increase ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15897458  Anjard et al. 2005)]. High levels of cAMP activate PKA ([/gene/DDB_G0283907 pkaC], [/gene/DDB_G0279413 pkaR]) which induces rapid sporulation in culminants.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 16-OCT-2015 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0276465.summary:
The ''sepA'' gene was identified during a REMI screen for proteins involved in regulating cytokinesis. A ''sepA'' null mutant displayed defects in both cytokinesis and multicellular development. ''sepA'' null cells are multinucleate and distinctly larger than wild-type cells. Mitosis is normal in ''sepA'' null cells, but organization of cortical actin is disturbed and proper formation of cleavage furrows is impaired. Cytokinesis in ''sepA'' null cells is highly variable from almost normal to completely missing. ''sepA'' null cells also have delayed aggregation with smaller than normal fruiting bodies. These results suggest that ''sepA'' acts as a master regulator of other elements in the signal transduction network controlling cleavage furrow formation and constriction ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19479821 Muller-Taubenberger et al. 2009]).
The sepA kinase interacts with the Scar complex and phosphorylates ScaR ([/gene/DDB_G0285253 scrA]). Similar to a ''scrA'' phosphorylation defective mutant, ''sepA'' null cells formed long-lived, exaggeratedly long pseudopods ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/32745097 Singh et al. 2020]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 25-FEB-2021 RD

DDB_G0284465.summary:
The ''cudA'' gene was identified in a random mutagenesis screen as being essential for correct culmination[http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9226443 (Fukuzawa et al. 1997)]. ''cudA'' was found to localize to the nucleus, and to be expressed both in a cone of cells at the extreme slug tip and in prespore cells. cudA- cells exhibit several phenotypes: they are defective in the expression of certain prespore genes, including [/gene/DDB_G0277141 cotC]; both stalk and spore formation are impaired; and cudA- slugs continue to migrate under conditions in which normal slugs culminate. The latter defect is corrected if the ''cudA'' gene is expressed in cudA- cells under the control of a promoter that selectively directs expression to the anterior of the prestalk region. CudA directly regulates ''cotC'' prespore gene expression by binding to a site in the ''cotC'' promoter. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18701541 Yamada et al. 2008]).
[http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10821768 (Fukuzawa and Williams 2000)] demonstrated that STATa ([/gene/DDB_G0281381 dstA]), activates ''cudA'' expression in tip-organizer cells of the migrating slug. CudA directly activates [/gene/DDB_G0288331 expl7] gene expression there, suggesting that ''cudA'' plays a transcriptional role in tip-organizer cell differentiation. [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19757394 (Wang et al. 2010)]. For pstA-specific genes, [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/27125566 (Saga et al. 2016)] demonstrate two distinct signaling pathways downstream of STATa: CudA-dependent and CudA-independent. In addition to ''expl7'', cudA also activates ''aslA'' ([/gene/DDB_G0273213 aslA-1], [/gene/DDB_G0273713 aslA-2]) and ''7E'' ([/gene/DDB_G0275437 7E]) gene expression.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 19-OCT-2016 RD

DDB_G0284329.summary:
''gefA'' (''aimless'') encodes a Ras guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF, RasGEF). rasGEFs are key components of signaling networks in which they activate Ras family small GTPases by promoting the exchange of GDP for GTP. ''gefA'' is expressed during both vegetative growth and development ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16086850 Wilkins et al. 2005]), and is preferentially expressed in the anterior prestalk (tip) region of slugs ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11422293 Tsujioka et al. 2001]). The ''gefA'' gene was isolated during a screen for aggregation-defective mutants. ''gefA'' null mutants grow at a normal rate, but have impaired chemotaxis to cAMP and adenylate cyclase ([/gene/DDB_G0281545 acaA]) activation, both of which are critical for aggregation involved in sorocarp development. The motility of mutant cells appears normal, suggesting a defect in gradient sensing ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8793298 Insall et al. 1996]). ''gefA'' null cells also exhibit a defect in cAMP-mediated activation of guanylyl cyclase ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10473630 Lee et al. 1999]). Cells lacking GefA exhibit defects similar to those of ([/gene/DDB_G0281385 rasC]) null cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11500376 Lim et al. 2001]). GefA has been shown to specifically exchange GDP for GTP on RasC, but not on other ras proteins, including RasB, ([/gene/DDB_G0292998 rasB]) RasD, ([/gene/DDB_G0292996 rasD]) RasG ([/gene/DDB_G0293434 rasG]) or Rap1 ([/gene/DDB_G0291237 rapA]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17380187 Kae et al. 2007]), ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11500376 Lim et al. 2001]). Disruption of ''gefA'' results in a more rapid, higher, and extended activation of the kinase Erk2 ([/gene/DDB_G0283903 erkB]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9020088 Aubry et al. 1997]).
''gefA'' is included within a Ras signaling complex, termed the Sca1 complex, which also includes an additional RasGEF GefH ([/gene/DDB_G0276963 gefH]), the protein phosphatase ([/gene/DDB_G0283601 pppA]), and a scaffold protein ([/gene/DDB_G0277843 scaA]). The Sca1 complex is recruited to the leading edge of chemotaxing cells where it regulates F-actin dynamics and signal relay by controlling the activation of RasC and the downstream target of rapamycin complex 2 (TORC2)-Akt/protein kinase B (PKB) pathway, and undergoes TORC2 and Akt/PKB-dependent negative feedback regulation ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20493808 Charest et al. 2010]). Both cAMP and folate use the same GefA-RasC axis to mediate AKT and PKBR1 phosphorylation by TORC2 ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23657816 Liao et al. 2013]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 18-MAR-2021 RD

DDB_G0274125.summary: The gamma subunit of heterotrimeric G proteins is a small evolutionarily conserved protein that carries a lipid tail for membrane association. In ''Dictyostelium'' ''gpgA'' encodes a G gamma protein of 69 amino acids that requires the phosducin-like protein PhLP1 ([/gene/DDB_G0292850 phlp1]) for addition of a lipid tail to the carboxy terminal amino acid motif CSVL [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11598203  (Zhang et al. 2001)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16135826  (Knol et al. 2005)]. G gamma forms a stable dimer with G-beta ([/gene/DDB_G0277143 gpbA]) and is involved in multiple signal transduction pathways. Both subunits are required for these functions. G-beta/G-gamma reassociates with G-alpha subunits to form a heterotrimeric G protein that can associate with surface receptors of the GPCR family. The subunits remain as receptor bound heterotrimers until GDP is displaced by GTP on G-alpha subunits. Amplification of the external chemoattractant signal appears to occur downstream of the G protein response since G-beta/G-gamma is distributed on the surface membrane in direct proportion to the concentration of external cAMP in a gradient [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10669414  (Jin et al. 2000)]. G-beta/G-gamma associates with an ELMO/DOCK complex that may act as a Rho guanine nucleotide exchange factor (RhoGEF) [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22754623  (Yan and Tin, 2012)]. RacB ([/gene/DDB_G0279605 racB]) and the Arp2/3 complex are also found together with G-beta/G-Gamma and this complex may mediate signaling from GPCR to the actin cytoskeleton during chemotaxis [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22647486  (Xu and Jin, 2012)]. The rate of dissociation of G-beta/G-gamma from the membrane increases when cAMP is bound to CAR1 ([/gene/DDB_G0273397 carA-1], [/gene/DDB_G0273533 carA-2]) which may facilitate activation of cytosolic components such as RasGAPs [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19584094  (Elzie et al. 2009)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 24-APR-2019 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0273259.summary:
QkgA (Roco2) contains an N-terminal leucine-rich repeat (LRR) motif similar to that of human LRRK2, in addition to the Roc (Ras-like), COR, and kinase domains present in eukaryotic Roco proteins. Eleven ''Dictyostelium'' proteins belong to the Roco family: [/gene/DDB_G0291079 gbpC], [/gene/DDB_G0273259 qkgA-1], [/gene/DDB_G0269250 pats1], [/gene/DDB_G0288251 roco4], [/gene/DDB_G0294533 roco5], [/gene/DDB_G0279417 roco6], [/gene/DDB_G0267472 roco7], [/gene/DDB_G0286127 roco8], [/gene/DDB_G0288183 roco9], [/gene/DDB_G0291710 roco10], and [/gene/DDB_G0268636 roco11]. Disruption of ''qkgA'' causes a marked increase in growth rate, indicating a role in the negative regulation of cell proliferation, and aggregation occurs relatively slowly resulting in abnormally large multicellular structures ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12954783 Abe et al. 2003]). QkgA is involved in a signal transduction network through the autocrine proliferation repressor AprA ([/gene/DDB_G0281663 aprA]). Similar to ''aprA'' and counting factor associated protein CfaD ([/gene/DDB_G0281605 cfaD]) null mutants, ''qkgA'' null cells proliferate to a higher cell density than wild type cells and tend to be multinucleate. In addition, ''qkgA'' null cells are insensitive to exogenous AprA and CfaD, indicating that QkgA is required for AprA and CfaD-mediated inhibition of proliferation ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20709790 Phillips and Gomer, 2010]). Wild-type cells adjacent to a source of recombinant AprA (rAprA) showed a significant bias in displacement away from rApA, whereas G protein alpha 8 ([/gene/DDB_G0284469 gpaH]), ''qkgA'', and ''cfaD'' null cells did not. These results indicate that AprA also functions as a chemorepellent, and that that Galpha8, QkgA, and CfaD are necessary for the chemorepellant effect of AprA ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22711818 Phillips and Gomer, 2012]).
''qkgA'' is a key regulator of the actin cytoskeleton during chemotaxis. QkgA is activated in response to chemoattractant stimulation, localizes to the pseudopodium, and binds to both the rab family GTPase ([/gene/DDB_G0283757 rab1A]) and filamin ([/gene/DDB_G0269100 abpC]). Constitutively active Rab1A pulls down 5 x more Roco2 than wild type Rab1A while dominant-negative Rab1A fails to interact with it, suggesting that activated Rab1A positively regulates Roco2 activity. ''qkgA'' null cells have defects in cell motility and chemotaxis to cAMP, aggregation and cytokinesis. ''qkgA'' null cells also display decreased chemoattractant-mediated F-actin polymerization. These results reveal a signal transduction pathway in which Rab1A activates Roco2 kinase which in turn mediates cell polarization and chemotaxis by regulating cortical F-actin polymerization and pseudopod extension. A major function of Roco2 is to stabilize the nascent pseudopod and enhance F-actin polymerization, in part through its downstream effector filamin ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21551065 Kicka et al. 2011]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 19-OCT-2020 RD

DDB_G0269244.summary: The ''atg6'' gene was isolated among several members of the autophagy family of genes, conserved from yeast to man [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12626495  (Otto et al., 2003)]. Macroautophagy ([/ontology/go/0016236/annotation/page/1 macroautophagy]) is used by eukaryotic cells to recycle non-essential cellular components during starvation and development. In ''atg6''-null cells, survival during nitrogen starvation ([/ontology/go/0006995/annotation/page/1 cellular response to nitrogen starvation]) is reduced.. Upon starvation mutant cells show little turnover of cellular components. Development ([/ontology/go/0007275/annotation/page/1 multicellular organismal development]) of the mutant is slightly impaired. On bacterial lawns cells aggregate mainly in the center of plaques and not in the periphery, and multi-tipped aggregates form very small fruiting bodies ([/ontology/go/0009653/annotation/page/1 anatomical structure morphogenesis]). Axenically grown cells plated on filters form multi-tipped aggregates that develop into small fruiting bodies with truncated stalks. These fruiting bodies produce few viable, detergent-resistent spores ([/ontology/go/0030435/annotation/page/1 sporulation]). Wild-type cells in a chimaera do not rescue the developmental defects, showing that the atg6 mutation is autonomous. The phenotype of the ''atg6''-null mutant is almost identical to that of the [/gene/DDB_G0286191 atg8]-null mutant. Both mutants have the mildest defects when compared to [/gene/DDB_G0292390 atg1], [/gene/DDB_G0289881 atg5], and [/gene/DDB_G0271096 atg7] mutants [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14736886  (Otto et al., 2004)]Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 27-SEP-2004 PF

DDB_G0281871.summary: TSET is the latest addition to trafficking proteins, which is ancient but frequently lost or reduced in evolution. The TSET complex is a heterohexamer and was named for the protein subunits in the complex, TSPOON (sigma-like), TPLATE (beta-like), TCUP (mu-like), TSAUCER (alpha, beta, gamma, delta, epsilon, zeta-like), TTRAY1, and TTRAY2. This ancient adaptor complex (AP) was identified in organisms such as Dictyostelids and land plants, such as ''Arabidopsis''. Only the TCUP subunit has been retained in fungi and animals, in mammals it has evolved into the cargo adaptor muniscin. A TSPOON-GFP fusion (gene tstD) has been shown to physically bind the 5 other TSET subunits. The TTRAY subunits form the scaffold for the TSPOON, TPLATE, TCUP, TSAUCER, heterotetramer. TIRF microscopy showed a punctate temporary localization of the complex to the plasma membran [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24867644  (Hirst et al. 2014)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated,, 07-DEC-2018 PF

DDB_G0287211.summary: ''rab11B'' encodes a guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G protein) of the Rab family of small GTPases. G proteins are key components of signal transduction networks in which they function as molecular signaling switches, binding to GDP in the off state while binding GTP in the on state. Guanine nucleotide-exchange factors (GEFs) promote the exchange of GDP for GTP on Rab GTPases thus activating them, while GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) inactivate Rab GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP. Rab subfamily small GTPases in many organisms are key regulators of intracellular membrane trafficking. Rab11B is similar to human RAB11A, which regulates endocytic recycling. The ''rab11B'' gene is expressed at a uniform, but low level throughout growth and development. ''rab11B'' null mutants showed no defects in growth, endocytosis or development, suggesting that the function of ''rab11B'' may be redundant with other ''rab'' genes in ''Dictyostelium'' ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9632105 Dragoi et al. 1998]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 07-SEP-2020 RD

DDB_G0267418.summary:
S-Adenosyl-L-homocysteine hydrolase (SAHH) catalyzes the reaction S-adenosyl-L-homocysteine + H2O =L-homocysteine + adenosine. S-[/ontology/go/0004013/annotation/page/1 adenosylhomocysteinase activity] was first characterized in ''Dictyostelium'' in a [/ontology/go/0030552/annotation/page/1 cAMP binding] protein with a molecular weight of 47 kilodaltons that likely exists as a 190 kilodaltontetramer ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6299402 Gunzburg et al. 1983]). The ''sahA'' gene was later identifiedand cloned, and its amino acid sequence is highly conserved with mammalian SAHH ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3288206 Kasir etal. 1988], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3139100 Guitton et al. 1988]). The biochemistry of SahAhas been extensively studied and has been shown to be activated by bound NAD+ and reversibly inactivated by cAMP andthe adenosine analog 2'-deoxyadenosine ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6319183 Hohman and Veron 1984], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6091559 Hohman et al. 1984]). Inactivation of the SahA protein by cAMP occurs via dissociationof SahA from NAD+, however, inactivation by 2'-deoxyadenosine is through the reduction of bound NAD+ to NADH ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2991881 Hohman et al. 1985]).
Cellular localization of SahA has been observed in the [/ontology/go/0005737/annotation/page/1 cytoplasm], in the [/ontology/go/0005634/annotation/page/1 nucleus], and in the [/ontology/go/0005938/annotation/page/1 cell cortex] of vegetative amoeba ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15358428 Yamada and Sameshima 2004]) and in the [/ontology/go/0031252/annotation/page/1 leading edge] of chemotaxing cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17172447 Shu et al. 2006]). SahA isalso a component of [/ontology/go/0031002/annotation/page/1 actin rod]s, which are large structures made of hexagonally arranged actin tubulesfound in the nuclei and cytoplasm of germinating spores ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11728467 Kishi et al.2001]). Additionally, the translocation of the SahA protein between the cytoplasm and the cell cortex isregulated in response to hypertonicity ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15358428 Yamada and Sameshima 2004]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 23-SEP-2004 KP

DDB_G0281343.summary:
The protein encoded by [/gene/DDB_G0283267 shkA] contains a C-terminal SH2 (Src homology 2) domain that shares sequencesimilarity with the mammalian PI3K adaptor protein p55 and has been shown to possess [/ontology/go/0004713/annotation/page/1 protein-tyrosine kinase activity] in addition to [/ontology/go/0004674/annotation/page/1 protein serine/threonine kinase activity]. Cells carrying a null mutation for''shkA'' exhibit severe developmental phenotypes and have defective [/ontology/go/0030036/annotation/page/1 actin cytoskeleton organization and biogenesis],[/ontology/go/0006935/annotation/page/1 chemotaxis], and [/ontology/go/0006909/annotation/page/1 phagocytosis]. Biochemical analysis shows that protein kinase B([/gene/DDB_G0268620 pkbA]) activation is significantly higher than wild-type. In addition, the rate of translocationof PH (pleckstrin homology) domain-containing proteins [/gene/DDB_G0285161 dagA], [/gene/DDB_G0268620 pkbA], and [/gene/DDB_G0285845 phdA] is reduced. The ShkA protein localizes to the [/ontology/go/0005938/annotation/page/1 cell cortex]; this localization isdependent upon its SH2 domain ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11274054 Moniakis 2001]).
Four additional uncharacterized genes exist in the ''Dictyostelium'' genome that are highly similar to shkA in domainarchitecture: [/gene/DDB_G0288617 shkB], [/gene/DDB_G0290451 shkE], [/gene/DDB_G0278409 shkC], and [/gene/DDB_G0281343 shkD].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 06-JAN-2005 KP

DDB_G0288179.summary: A small family of highly related cell-surface receptors is responsible for the responses to cAMP at different stages of development in ''Dictyostelium''. The members are all 7 transmembrane G protein-coupled proteins but show different affinities to cAMP as well as different cell type specificities. ''carB'' encodes the CAR2 receptor that is expressed briefly in prestalk cells following aggregation [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2049880  (Saxe et al., 1991]; [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8436297  Saxe et al., 1993)]. Null mutations in ''carB'' result in the inability of mound cells to form a tip or progress further in morphogenesis. It appears that CAR2 is required for sorting of prestalk cells in mounds. While prestalk specific genes are expressed normally in null mutants, the prespore gene pspB that encodes SP85 is expressed at >10 fold higher levels in carB- mutants than in wild type cells [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8436297  (Saxe et al., 1993)]. Mutations in ''[/gene/DDB_G0285253 scrA]'', which encodes SCAR, were selected that suppress the block to morphogenesis resulting from loss of CAR2 [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9732292  (Bear et al., 1998)]. It appears that CAR2 signaling normally inhibits SCAR to help regulate cell movement. CAR2 has also been implicated in the regulation of the prestalk pathway by facilitating the DIF induction of prestalk genes [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9742091  (Verkerke-Van Wijk et al., 1998)]. Comprehensive annotations have been added to this gene, 19-OCT-2015 PF; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0273397.summary:
A family of four highly related G-protein coupled receptors, CAR1, CAR2, CAR3, and CAR4 (genes ''[/gene/DDB_G0273397 carA-1]'' ''[/gene/DDB_G0288179 carB]'', ''[/gene/DDB_G0277829 carC]'', ''[/gene/DDB_G0277831 carD]'', respectively), mediate developmental responses to cAMP [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2049880 (Saxe et al., 1991]; [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7496377 Ginsburg et al., 1995)]. CAR1 and CAR3 have 56% amino acid identity and show approximately equal affinity to cAMP in vitro [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1537842 (Johnson et al., 1992)]. Both are coupled to trimeric G proteins with the Galpha2 subunit (gene ''[/gene/DDB_G0276267 gpaB]''). CAR1 is expressed immediately after the initiation of development. Single-molecule imaging using TIRF microscopy showed that CAR1 is uniformly distributed and diffuses rapidly in the plane of the membrane. The rate constant for dissociation of cAMP from CAR1 was found to be about 1 second [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11679673 (Ueda et al., 2001)]. CAR1 is phosphorylated upon persistent stimulation with cAMP resulting in internalization on a timescale of 5 min followed by degradation after 13 min [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21541374 (Serge et al. 2013)]. cAMP induces the cAR1-mediated dissociation of G protein subunits to a similar extent in both undifferentiated and differentiated cells. Dissociation is stimulated by caffeine and requires the microtubule network [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29698704 (Islam et al. 2018)].
Cells lacking CAR1 fail to aggregate or express developmentally regulated genes that are induced by pulses of cAMP [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1692327 (Sun et al., 1990)]. Stimulation of cAMP and cGMP accumulation in response to addition of cAMP is lost in these cells. However, they can still respond to high concentrations of cAMP by using the CAR3 receptor [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9578623 (Kim et al., 1998)]. A double ''carA/carC'' mutant lacking both receptors shows no response to cAMP and an abolished synthesis of cGMP [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7949426 (Insall et al., 1994)]. Using a non-phosphorylatable carA mutant, Brzostowski and colleagues demonstrated that receptor phosphorylation is required to regulate adenylyl cyclase adaptation, long-range oscillatory cAMP wave production and cytoskeletal actin responses [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23902692 (Brzostowski et al. 2013) ]. Sites critical for cAMP binding, coupling to G proteins and regulated phosphorylation were delineated by PCR-mediated random mutagenesis [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8999903 (Kim et al., 1997]; [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8999904 Milne et al., 1997)].
Binding of cAMP to CAR1 results in the transient activation of TorC2 and the adenylyl cyclase ACA through a Ras pathway [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20660630 (Cai et al., 2010]; [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23657816 Liao et al., 2013)]. An incoherent feedforward loop in which ligand bound CAR1 activates both a Ras-GEF and a Ras-GAP can result in perfect adaptation of activated Ras about 20 seconds after addition of cAMP in a spatially uniform manner [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22215733 (Takeda et al., 2012)]. The LEGI model points out that membrane localization of the activator (GEF) and free diffusion of the inhibitor (GAP) can generate a spatial gradient of activated Ras within the cells in response to an external gradient of cAMP [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10221901 (Parent and Devreotes, 1999)]. Ultrasensitivity resulting from the opposing activities of GEF and GAP can dramatically amplify the signal and ensure that cells only respond to constant or rising concentrations of cAMP and that they do not respond to the decreasing concentrations of cAMP in the back of a wave [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25249632 (Skoge et al., 2014)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated 08-DEC-2015 PF; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0290909.summary:
DNA-dependent RNA polymerase catalyzes the transcription of DNA into RNA using the four ribonucleoside triphosphates as substrates ([/ontology/go/0003899/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase activity]). Three distinct zinc-containing RNA polymerases are found in eukaryotic nuclei: [/gene/DDB_G0275759 rpa1] for the ribosomal RNA precursor ([/ontology/go/0006360/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase I promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005736/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase I complex]), [/gene/DDB_G0279193 rpb1] for the mRNA precursor ([/ontology/go/0006366/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase II promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005665/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase II, core complex]), and [/gene/DDB_G0277199 rpc1] for 5S and tRNA genes ([/ontology/go/0006383/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase III promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005666/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase III complex]).
RNA polymerase I is a multisubunit complex. The subunits encoded by [/gene/DDB_G0275759 rpa1] (ortholog of ''S. cerevisiae RPA190''), [/gene/DDB_G0288449 rpc2] (''RPA135''), [/gene/DDB_G0268198 rpa43] (''RPA43''), [/gene/DDB_G0290909 rpa49] (''RPA49''), and [/gene/DDB_G0278263 rpa12] (''RPA12'') are unique to RNA polymerase I. Two subunits, [/gene/DDB_G0291362 rpc19] and [/gene/DDB_G0282339 rpa5] (''RPC19'' and ''RPC40'' in ''S. cerevisiae''), are common to RNA polymerase I and RNA polymerase III and correspond to subunits 3 and 11 of RNA polymerase II. Subunits [/gene/DDB_G0291636 rpb5], [/gene/DDB_G0291037 rpb6], [/gene/DDB_G0278039 rpb8], [/gene/DDB_G0272036 rpb10], and [/gene/DDB_G0283365 rpb12] are common to all three RNA polymerases. Yeast has two additional subunits, ''RPA34'' and ''RPA14'', that do not have clear orthologs in other species, including in ''Dictyostelium'' ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12407181 Peyroche et al. 2002], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12381659 Schramm and Hernandez 2001]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 13-APR-2004 PG

DDB_G0275567.summary: The ''Dictyostelium'' adenosylmethionine decarboxylase is very similar to the ''H. sapiens'' AMD1, which is is a proenzyme that undergoes autocatalytic cleavage generating alpha and beta subunits and forming a pyruvate prosthetic group. The bond between glutamic acid 67 and serine 68 were shown to be the site of cleavage . These residues, located at position 96 and 97 in the ''Dictyostelium'' protein, are highly conserved. Spermine, formed from spermidine, is a polyamine involved in cellular metabolism found in all eukaryotic cells. [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2687270  (Stanley et al. 1989)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12600205  (Tolbert et al. 2003)]. Mutants overexpressing ''amd1'' display slower cell growth, delayed development and arrested cells in the S-phase of the cell cycle. Spermidine levels remained high throughout development in ''amd1'' overexpressing cells, revealing a role for ''amd1'' in polyamine biosynthesis [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30378390  (Sharma et al. 2018)]Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 05-NOV-2018 RD

DDB_G0280047.summary: The ''yelA'' gene was isolated from REMI mutant DG1014. This developmental gene has been found to play an essential role in regulating terminal differentiation in ''Dictyostelium''. The yelA- mutant aggregates and develops normally until the mound stage, but does not proceed to form fingers or migrating slugs. Over the following 10 to 20 hours the mounds accumulate a bright yellow pigment typical for the sorus at the top of the fruiting body ([/ontology/go/0009653/annotation/page/1 anatomical structure morphogenesis]). Detergent resistant spores are formed ([/ontology/go/0030435/annotation/page/1 sporulation]) after only 16 hours of development, at least 4 hours earlier than in wild-type populations.The N-terminal sequence of the predicted yelA protein shows significant similarity to domains found in the eIF-4G subunits of the translational initiation complex eIF-4F. In wild-type development the ''yelA'' mRNA acccumulates after 8 hours and is maintained in both prespore and prestalk cells until culmination, after which it is found in stalk cells only. YelA mutations can partially supress the block to sporulation in the prestalk gene mutants [/gene/DDB_G0293002 tagA] and [/gene/DDB_G0286119 tagB]. These experiments suggest that yelA inhibits premature encapsulation until a signal from prestalk cells is received. [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9254905  (Osherov et al. 1997)]Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 19-SEP-2003 PF

DDB_G0280353.summary:
The 2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenase complex catalyzes the overall conversion of 2-oxoglutarate to succinyl-CoA and CO2. It contains multiple copies of 3 enzymatic components: E1, E2, and E3. E1 ([/gene/DDB_G0280353 odhA]) has 2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenase activity (). Multiple copies of E1 are bound to a core of dihydrolipoamide succinyltransferase (E2), which also binds multiple copies of lipoamide dehydrogenase (E3). The lipoyl group of E2 ([/gene/DDB_G0275029 odhB]) is reductively succinylated by E1, and then passes this succinyl group to coenzyme A ([/ontology/go/4149/annotation/page/1 dihydrolipoyllysine-residue succinyltransferase activity]).
The E3 enzyme ([/gene/DDB_G0291648 lpd]) is adihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase ([/ontology/go/4148/annotation/page/1 dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase activity]) that is shared by three 2-oxo acid dehydrogenase multienzyme complexes. These include the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, the 2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenase complex, the glycine cleavage system, and the branched-chain 2-oxo acid dehydrogenase complex.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 03-DEC-2004 PF

DDB_G0293416.summary: The ABC superfamily of genes is one of the largest in the genomes of both bacteria and eukaryotes. The proteins encoded by these genes all carry a characteristic 200- to 250-amino-acid ATP-binding cassette that gives them their family name ([/ontology/go/0042626/annotation/page/1 ATPase activity, coupled to transmembrane movement of substances]). In bacteria they are mostly involved in nutrient import, while in eukaryotes many are involved in export([/ontology/go/0006810/annotation/page/1 transport]), ([/ontology/go/0016021/annotation/page/1 integral to membrane]). Seven different families (A to G) have been defined in eukaryotes based on sequence homology, domain topology, and function. ''Dictyostelium'' has 71 ABC transporters (including one on the chromosome 2 duplication) and 11 ABCB family members: [/gene/DDB_G0293416 abcB1], [/gene/DDB_G0293438 abcB2], [/gene/DDB_G0291714 abcB3], [/gene/DDB_G0279915 abcB4],[/gene/DDB_G0292554 abcB5], [/gene/DDB_G0282931 abcB6], [/gene/DDB_G0269720 abcB7], [/gene/DDB_G0293002 tagA], [/gene/DDB_G0286119 tagB], [/gene/DDB_G0286121 tagC], and [/gene/DDB_G0286123 tagD]. The B family includes three main subtypes: full transporters involved in multiple drug resistance (MDR), half-transporters targeted to mitochondria, and half-transporters involved in peptide transport [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12456012 (Anjard and Loomis 2002)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 16-JUN-2003 PG

DDB_G0276767.summary: Phospholipase B (PLB) catalyzes the degradation of phosphatidylcholine to glycerophosphocholine. [/ontology/go/0004622/annotation/page/1 lysophospholipase activity] has been detected in ''Dictyostelium'' in 1970 by [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/5528230 Ferber and colleagues]. The gene encoding this activity was described in 2004 by [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15193148 Morgan et al.] PLB does not share any similarity with other known phospholipase B proteins. Remarkably, proteins with significant similarity to ''Dictyostelium'' PLB are found in mammals, ''C. elegans'', and ''Drosophila''. This gene therefore appear to make up a new gene family that have phospholipase B activity. In addition to phosphatidylcholine, PLB also hydrolyses phosphatidylethanolamine and phosphatidylinositol, indicating that it plays roles in [/ontology/go/0009395/annotation/page/1 phospholipid catabolic process], [/ontology/go/0046338/annotation/page/1 phosphatidylethanolamine catabolic process], and [/ontology/go/0046488/annotation/page/1 phosphatidylinositol metabolic process]. Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 27-JAN-2005 PG

DDB_G0278971.summary:
''dimA'' encodes a bZIP/bRLZ transcription factor. The ''dimA'' null mutant shows similar developmental defects to the [/gene/DDB_G0289329 dmtA] null mutant, which is defective in DIF-1 synthesis. The mutants exhibit abnormal [/ontology/go/0009653/annotation/page/1 anatomical structure morphogenesis], producing fruiting bodies with long, thin stalks, have defective prestalkO cell differentiation, and increased number of prespore cells, indicating that DimA and DmtA are involved in [/ontology/go/0045595/annotation/page/1 regulation of cell differentiation]. ''dimA'' has been proposed to be a transcriptional regulator required to integrate DIF-1 signaling and subsequent patterning during ''Dictyostelium'' development ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14729573 Thompson et al. 2004]). Interestingly, although ''dimA'' mutants make more prespore cells, in chimeras with wild type cells they actually produce fewer spores. Therefore, loss of ''dimA'' is deleterious for [/ontology/go/0030435/annotation/page/1 sporulation] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15470429 Foster et al. 2004]).
The eukaryotic basic-leucine zipper (bZIP) transcription factors ([/ontology/go/0006355/annotation/page/1 regulation of transcription, DNA-dependent]) are proteins that dimerize through their leucine repeats to form a coiled coil with two flanking alpha-helices that constitute the basic region that binds DNA ([/ontology/go/0003677/annotation/page/1 DNA binding])[http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11017199 (Fujii et al. 2000)]. There are 19 putative bZIP transcription factors in the ''Dictyostelium'' genome: [/gene/DDB_G0278971 dimA], [/gene/DDB_G0284023 bzpL], [/gene/DDB_G0290173 bzpI], [/gene/DDB_G0282749 bzpG], [/gene/DDB_G0290169 bzpO], [/gene/DDB_G0274993 bzpJ], [/gene/DDB_G0291372 dimB], [/gene/DDB_G0286411 bzpN], [/gene/DDB_G0288705 bzpQ], [/gene/DDB_G0290171 bzpS], [/gene/DDB_G0290303 bzpP], [/gene/DDB_G0269338 bzpE], [/gene/DDB_G0278379 bzpD], [/gene/DDB_G0279529 bzpF], [/gene/DDB_G0290165 bzpR], [/gene/DDB_G0282047 bzpM], [/gene/DDB_G0282049 bzpK], [/gene/DDB_G0277681 bzpH], and [/gene/DDB_G0279439 bzpC].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 02-APR-2004 PG

DDB_G0287773.summary:
The glycine cleavage system complex consists of four proteins that function to catalyze the net reaction glycine + THFA <=> NH3 + CO2 + 5,10-methylene THFA. The glycine cleavage complex contains a P-protein ([/gene/DDB_G0287255 gcvP]), a glycine dehydrogenase, and an aminomethyltransferase T-protein ([/gene/DDB_G0292326 gcvT]). Interestingly, the ''Dicytostelium'' proteome includes five putative methylamine carrier H-proteins ''gcvH1'', ([/gene/DDB_G0290845 gcvH2], [/gene/DDB_G0287791 gcvH3], [/gene/DDB_G0287795 gcvH4] and [/gene/DDB_G0287861 gcvH5]) whereas other species contain only one H-protein. The final component of the glycine cleavage system is ([/gene/DDB_G0291648 lpd]) a dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase that is a member of several other dehydrogenase complexes, including the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1993704 Kume et al. 1991]).
A genetic screen of an insertional mutant library identified ''gcvH1'' as having reduced sensitivity to cannabidiol (CBD). The protein GCVH1 localizes to the mitochondrion. A ''gcvH1'' null mutant showed elevated glycine levels and increased tetrahydrofolate levels, supporting a role for ''gcvH1'' in the glycine cleavage system. Treatment of wild-type cells with CBD significantly lowered methionine levels, but this effect was lost in ''gcvH1'' null cells, suggesting a mechanism of CBD action through inhibition of methionine production and regulation of one carbon metabolism. A form of cannabidiol (CBD) has demonstrated seizure control activity in patients with Dravet syndrome. Induction of seizure-like activity also elevates rat neuronal methionine levels, and acute CBD treatment attenuates this effect. Thus these combined results from ''Dictyostelium'' and mammalian cells suggest a novel mechanism for CBD in regulating methionine levels, and identify altered one-carbon metabolism in Dravet syndrome and seizure activity. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31693171 Perry et al. 2019]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 13-NOV-2019 RD

DDB_G0285253.summary:
''scrA'' was isolated as a suppressor of the [/gene/DDB_G0288179 carB] phenotype, developmental arrest at the mound stage. SCAR orthologs exist in mammals, flies, fish, but not in yeasts, plants, or in bacteria. Scar is part of the SCAR complex consisting of [/gene/DDB_G0285253 scrA], [/gene/DDB_G0267956 abiA], [/gene/DDB_G0279175 hspc300], [/gene/DDB_G0287855 pirA], and [/gene/DDB_G0274519 napA] and involved in positive regulation of actin filament polymerization. The first 96 amino acids of ScrA are necessary for interaction with [/gene/DDB_G0267956 abiA] and [/gene/DDB_G0279175 hspc300]. This interaction is essential for SCAR complex function as the deletion of the amino terminus in ''scrA'' causes defects in chemotaxis to cAMP and cytokinesis ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17314411 Caracino et al. 2007]).
''scrA'' null mutants grow at normal rates but are smaller in size than normal wild type. The cytoskeleton is aberrant in ''scrA''- cells: there is decreased levels of filamentous actin, suggesting a role for SCAR in positive regulation of actin filament polymerization. Moreover, these cells are less polarized during aggregation and have an increased tendency to for lateral pseudopods. ''scrA'' null develops approximately 3 hours faster than wild type cells and form multiple tips. Each tip forms an individual slug and a relatively normal fruiting body ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9732292 Bear et al. 1998]).
[http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11683394 Seastone et al. 2001] demonstrated that rates of fluid phase macropinocytosis and phagocytosis are significantly reduced in ''scrA'' null cells. In addition, fluid phase exocytosis is delayed and movement of the fluid phase from lysosomes to post-lysosomes is also delayed. Furthermore, deletion of ''scrA'' in the profilin null background resulted in a further decrease in endocytosis and fluid phase release compared to either mutant alone, suggesting that profilin and SCAR both functionally contribute to regulate fluid phase endocytosis and endosomal membrane trafficking.
SCAR/WAVE is activated during mitosis and localizes to the cell poles, driving the separation of daughter cells. SCAR activity was shown to be essential for myosin-independent cytokinesis, stabilizing the cleavage furrow and thus ensuring symmetrical cell division. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20530573 King et al. 2010]).
Results from unphosphorylatable and phosphomimetic ''scrA'' mutants revealed that dephosphorylation of SCAR controls normal pseudopod dynamics ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22386315 Ura et al. 2012]).
In wild type cells, SCAR recruitment occurs in patches of activated Rac. This causes Arp2/3 recruitment and pseudopod formation but also (directly or indirectly) results in Rac1 inactivation. When SCAR function is lost, by deletion of the ''scrA'' gene or any regulatory members of the SCAR complex, this Rac inactivation no longer occurs, and the level of activated Rac increases. When the level of activated Rac becomes high enough, WASP ([/gene/DDB_G0293834 wasA]) is recruited through its CRIB domain and thus effectively replaces the functions of SCAR ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22891261 Veltman et al. 2012]).
''scrA'' is involved in the signal transduction pathway responsible for AprA-dependent ([/gene/DDB_G0281663 aprA]) chemorepulsion. AprA requires ScrA to activate Ras at the cell cortex ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30462573 Rijal et al. 2018]).
The sepA kinase ([/gene/DDB_G0276465 sepA]) interacts with the Scar complex and phosphorylates Scar's proline-rich domain after the complex is activated. Phosphorylation-deficient or phosphomimetic Scar/WAVE mutants are both normally functional and rescue the phenotype of ''scrA'' null cells, demonstrating that phosphorylation is dispensable for Scar activation. Cell-substrate adhesion induces Scar phosphorylation. Normal Scar activation in talA/talB ([/gene/DDB_G0290481 talA]), ([/gene/DDB_G0287505 talB]) double mutant cells forced into adhesion suggest that pseudopod engagement with the substratum is more important than extracellular signals at regulating Scar activity and that phosphorylation acts as a pseudopod timer by promoting Scar turnover ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/32745097 Singh et al. 2020])
''scrA'' mRNA is expressed maximally at the aggregation stage. Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 02-OCT-2012 PF; annotation contributions: PMID 22891261 Robert Insall.

DDB_G0274601.summary:
There are 29 genes encoding actin in ''Dictyostelium'' with amino acid identity greater than 83%, ''act1''-''act29''. Seventeen of these genes encode identical proteins: [/gene/DDB_G0289553 act1], [/gene/DDB_G0274133 act2], [/gene/DDB_G0289005 act4], [/gene/DDB_G0289663 act5], [/gene/DDB_G0274135 act6], [/gene/DDB_G0280545 act7], [/gene/DDB_G0269234 act8], [/gene/DDB_G0274601 act9], [/gene/DDB_G0288879 act11], [/gene/DDB_G0274129 act12], [/gene/DDB_G0274599 act13], [/gene/DDB_G0274137 act14], [/gene/DDB_G0272520 act15], [/gene/DDB_G0272248 act16], [/gene/DDB_G0274727 act19], [/gene/DDB_G0274285 act20], and [/gene/DDB_G0274561 act21], while [/gene/DDB_G0289811 act10], [/gene/DDB_G0275023 act22], and [/gene/DDB_G0289487 act3] respectively have 1, 4 and 11 amino acid differences compared to the 17 identical genes. The proteins encoded by [/gene/DDB_G0274131 act17], [/gene/DDB_G0289489 act18], [/gene/DDB_G0268744 act23] and [/gene/DDB_G0289505 act24]are more divergent.
Actin is a major [/ontology/go/0005200/annotation/page/1 structural constituent of cytoskeleton]. Actin is one of the most abundant proteins in ''Dictyostelium'', constituting approximately 8% of the total protein in vegetative cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/561722 Alton and Lodish et al. 1977]).Actin synthesis is developmentally regulated, peaking shortly after starvation (reviewed by [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6894564 Firtel] in 1981). The different actin genes differ in their levels of expression, with [/gene/DDB_G0274135 act6], [/gene/DDB_G0269234 act8] and [/gene/DDB_G0274129 act12] being highly expressed both during growth and development compared to [/gene/DDB_G0289005 act4], [/gene/DDB_G0289663 act5], [/gene/DDB_G0280545 act7] and [/gene/DDB_G0272248 act16] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6286214 McKeown and Firtel 1981]). Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 19-SEP-2003 PG

DDB_G0269206.summary: The ABC superfamily of genes is one of the largest in the genomes of both bacteria and eukaryotes. The proteins encoded by these genes all carry a characteristic 200- to 250-amino-acid ATP-binding cassette that gives them their family name ([/ontology/go/0042626/annotation/page/1 ATPase activity, coupled to transmembrane movement of substances]). In bacteria they are mostly involved in nutrient import, while in eukaryotes many are involved in export ([/ontology/go/0006810/annotation/page/1 transport]). Seven different families have been defined in eukaryotes based on sequence homology, domain topology, and function. Sequences from the well-advanced ''Dictyostelium'' genome project have allowed to recognize 71 members of this superfamily (including one on the chromosome 2 duplication). The ABCG family is characterized by the ABC domain preceding the transmembrane domain ([/ontology/go/0016021/annotation/page/1 integral to membrane]). All of the members of this family in animals are half-transporters while all of the fungal members are full transporters with two ABC-transmembrane units. No members of this family are found in bacteria. ''Dictyostelium'' and ''Arabidopsis'' have members of both types ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12456012 Anjard and Loomis 2002]). Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 18-OCT-2004 PG

DDB_G0350235.summary: TSET is the latest addition to trafficking proteins, which is ancient but frequently lost or reduced in evolution. The TSET complex is a heterohexamer and was named for the protein subunits in the complex, TSPOON (sigma-like), TPLATE (beta-like), TCUP (mu-like), TSAUCER (alpha, beta, gamma, delta, epsilon, zeta-like), TTRAY1, and TTRAY2. This ancient adaptor complex (AP) was identified in organisms such as Dictyostelids and land plants, such as ''Arabidopsis''. Only the TCUP subunit has been retained in fungi and animals, in mammals it has evolved into the cargo adaptor muniscin. A TSPOON-GFP fusion (gene tstD) has been shown to physically bind the 5 other TSET subunits. The TTRAY subunits form the scaffold for the TSPOON, TPLATE, TCUP, TSAUCER, heterotetramer. TIRF microscopy showed a punctate temporary localization of the complex to the plasma membran. The ''tstD'' knockout has a slightly faster growth rate in HL5, but place size on a bacterial lawn is slightly decreased. Plasma membrane turnover is also slower than in will type. In sum, the phenotype of the deletion of TSPOON, the central small subunit, has only subtle phenotypes in ''Dictyostelium'' [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24867644  (Hirst et al. 2014)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated,, 06-DEC-2018 PF

DDB_G0280967.summary: The motor domain and microtubule binding sites in the kinesin encoded by ''kif3'' are at the N-terminus as is seen in other members of the kinesin KHC subfamily that includes products of the Dictyostelium genes kif5 ([/gene/DDB_G0276369 kif5]) and kif7 ([/gene/DDB_G0281555 kif7]) [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12952062  (Klopfenstein et al. 2002)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14641909  (Kollmar and Glockner 2003)]. These conventional kinesins are involved in transport of diverse organelles to the plus ends of microtubules. Kif3 is a dimer that acts as a processive motor along microtubules and is found in the cytoplasm, and is enriched in vesicular structures that in part stain positive for the Golgi. It may transport cargo from the Golgi through the endosomal pathway. Kif3 is transcribed in both growing and developing cells and may be essential for survival since no knockout mutants could be isolated [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18160177  (Rohlk et al. 2008)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 01-JUN-2017 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0289429.summary:
NE81 (gene ''lmnB'') has been named for its nuclear envelope localization and has been shown to localize to the inner nuclear membrane during the entire cell cycle. The ''lmnB'' knockout and overexpression mutants revealed an important role in nuclear integrity, chromatin organization, and mechanical stability during shear stress. While GFP-NE81 does not exhibit considerable mobility at the nuclear envelope during interphase, as was expected for a structural component of a putative nuclear lamina, it is highly mobile between the onset of mitosis and early telophase. NE81 requires the prenylation signal as shown by deletion of the C-terminal CaaX box. In those cells, GFP-NE81 abolished localization of the protein to the nuclear envelope; instead, it resulted in clustering of the fusion protein inside the nucleus. During mitosis these clusters dissolve and become cellular. The protein has a conserved putative CDK1 ([/gene/DDB_G0272813 cdk1] phosphorylation site (S122). When this is mutated to alanine in the CaaX mutant, GFP-NE81 clusters do not dissolve during mitosis. This suggests regulation of lamin disassembly by CDK1 during mitosis. Also, GFP-NE81 and lamin B1 co-localize at the nuclear envelope in HeLa cells. These results are in agreement with the role a lamin plays in this organism and make NE81 the single lamin-like protein in Dictyostelium [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22090348 (Krueger et al. 2012]; [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22572958 Batsios et al., 2012)].
Src1 ([/gene/DDB_G0293138 src1]) has been identified as a protein of the nuclear inner membrane and shown to bind directly to the lamin NE81 [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26999214 (Batsios et al. 2016)]. Furthermore, lamin has been expressed lacking both the nuclear localization signal (NLS) and the CaaX box, resulting in a cytosolic protein that assembled in interphase and disassembled during mitosis mimicking the nuclear process. Expressing an additional phosphomimetic mutation (S122E) the same behavior was expected. However, image analysis showed that blue light induced cluster assembly, whereas green light and nearly ultra violet light did not induce assembly. Cell flattening under agarose also induced clustering. Both, blue light and cell flattening cause a lower pH, and when a lower pH was specifically tested, this also induced increased lamin assembly. While the effects were shown in a phosphomimetic mutant, these stress-induced assemblies likely also play a role in wild type lamin [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/32759812 (Grafe et al. 2020)].
