DDB_G0268620.summary:
''pkbA'' encodes the homolog of the protein kinase B made by the oncogene Akt ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10205164 Meili et al. 1999)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10192918 Tanaka et al. 1999)]. PKB is essential for aggregation at low cell densities but is dispensible in confluent monolayers. This protein kinase is transiently activated in response to cAMP binding to the G protein coupled receptor, Car1 ([/gene/DDB_G0273397 carA-1], [/gene/DDB_G0273533 carA-2]). Stimulation of PI3 kinase by Galpha2 ([/gene/DDB_G0276267 gpaB]) acting through RasG ([/gene/DDB_G0293434 rasG]), leads to rapid accumulation of phosphoinositids at the leading edge of chemotactically migrating cells. PKB can bind to PIP2 and PIP3 through its N-terminal PH-domain and become localized to the membrane at the front of migrating cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10192918 Tanaka et al. 1999)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11553719 Rupper et al. 2001)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15534002 Sasaki et al. 2004)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15352238 Secko et al. 2004)]. cAMP induced phosphorylation of PKB is blocked by loss of RasC ([/gene/DDB_G0281385 rasC]), or inhibition of PI3Ks ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11500376 Lim et al. 2001)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20660630 Cai et al. 2010)]. The protein kinase TORC2 ([/gene/DDB_G0281569 tor]) is responsible for phosphorylation of a hydrophobic motif in the C-terminal region of PKB ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16079174 Lee et al. 2005)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18635356 Kamimura et al. 2008)]. PKB can then be activated by the protein kinase PDK1 ([/gene/DDB_G0281471 pdkA]) which phosphorylates the activation loop ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20200230 Kimmel et al. 2010)]. The adaptor protein, Daydreamer ([/gene/DDB_G0287875 dydA]), is responsible for deactivating PKB ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23135995 Kolsch et al. 2013)]. The defects in chemotaxis that result from constitutive high levels of PIP3 in cells lacking PTEN ([/gene/DDB_G0286557 pten]) can be suppressed by knocking out ''pkbA'', suggesting that the localization of PKB to the front of cells is essential for polarization ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21169559 Tang et al. 2010)]. PKB localizes persistantly at the front when cell-cell contacts are formed ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10205164 Meili et al. 1999)]. Secreted Counting Factor (CF) increases cell motility by potentiating the cAMP-stimulated translocation and activation of PKB ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15470246 Gao et al. 2004)].
PKB phosphorylates serines and threonines in many different proteins including PakA, ([/gene/DDB_G0269166 pakA]), PikI, ([/gene/DDB_G0267588 pikI]), talinB, ([/gene/DDB_G0287505 talB]), GefN, ([/gene/DDB_G0275703 gefN]), GacG ([/gene/DDB_G0283955 gacG]) and triggers polymerization of dendritic actin at the leading edge ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11389841 Chung et al. 2001)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18635356 Kamimura et al. 2008)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18452713 Janetopoulos and Firtel, 2008)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20192768 Swaney et al. 2010)]. Phosphorylation of PikI activates its phosphoinositol 5-kinase activity leading to the production of PI(4,5)P2 which is essential for chemotaxis and activation of PKB ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24485835 Fets et al. 2014)]. PKB also phosphorylates a Ras signaling complex that controls activation of RasC and its downstream target TORC2 in a negative feedback loop ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20493808 Charest et al. 2010)]. Mutants lacking PKB show chemotactic defects including failure to suppress lateral pseudopods ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10205164 Meili et al. 1999)]. Fluid uptake by macropinocytosis is reduced about 3 fold and phagosomes remain more acidic in ''pkbA''- null cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11553719 Rupper et al. 2001)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11256995 Rupper et al. 2001)]. Fluid uptake is almost abolished in ''pkbA''/''pkgB'' ([/gene/DDB_G0290157 pkgB]) double mutants due to the signifcantly reduced size of macropinosomes in these mutant cells. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30617109 Williams et al. 2019)].The activity of PKB can be inhibited by AKT inhibitors IV and VIII ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16672332 (Anjard and Loomis, 2006)]. DIF-1 leads to rapid dephosphorylation of PKB and its substrates ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25518940 Sugden et al. 2014)]. PkbA and PkgB are also involved in polyphosphate signal transduction ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28584190 Seus et al. 2017)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 19-JUN-2019 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0282851.summary:
CEP161, encoded by the ''cepL'' gene, is a novel component of the centrosome which has been identified as a binding partner of the pericentriolar component CP250 (gene [/gene/DDB_G0293544 cepK]). Over-expression of truncated and full length CEP161 proteins revealed defects in growth, development, adhesion and centrosomal organization. The hippo related severin kinase ([/gene/DDB_G0289327 sevA]) was also found to bind CEP161 and both proteins co-localize at the centrosome. In in vitro kinase assays the N-terminal domain of CEP161 (residues 1-763) inhibited the kinase activity [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25607232 (Sukumaran et al., 2015)].
RNAi depletion of ''cepL'' results in complete disorganization of centrosomes and microtubules, while CepL overexpressing strains displayed supernumerary cytosolic microtubule organizing centers. In addition, CepL was shown to interact with several centrosomal proteins: CP75 ([/gene/DDB_G0283111 cepD]), CP91 ([/gene/DDB_G0275495 cepE]), CP148 ([/gene/DDB_G0278809 cepG]), Cep192 ([/gene/DDB_G0285313 cepH]) and gamma-tubulin ([/gene/DDB_G0271738 tubC]). Protein localization studies in ''cepL'' and ''cepG'' depletion strains reveal that both are scaffolding proteins cooperating in the organization of the centrosomal corona [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29690637 (Pitzen et al., 2018)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 02-FEB-2019 RD

DDB_G0289187.summary:
Histones form the nucleosomal core ([/ontology/go/0000786/annotation/page/1 nucleosome]) ([/ontology/go/0006334/annotation/page/1 nucleosome assembly]) that is fundamental to chromatin structure (). The histone octamer is composed of an H3-H4 tetramer (two H3-H4 dimers) coupled with an H2A-H2Btetramer (two H2A-H2B dimers). The histone H1 linker protein plays a role in packaging nucleosomes into the 30 nmfiber found in chromatin ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9177486 Bukenberger et al. 1992]).
In ''Dictyostelium discoideum'' and ''Saccharomyces cerevisiae'', only one copy of histone [/gene/DDB_G0285319 H1] appears to be present, in comparison to other eukaryotes which have multiple copies and subtypes([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7867938 Hauser et al. 1995], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9046096 Ushinsky et al.1997]). Two putative H2A family members, [/gene/DDB_G0279667 H2AX] and [/gene/DDB_G0286747 H2AZ], and three H2Adomain-containing proteins, [/gene/DDB_G0289187 H2Av1], [/gene/DDB_G0289193 H2Av2], [/gene/DDB_G0289197 H2Av3], are present in ''Dictyostelium''. Two H2B domain-containing proteins also exist inthe ''Dicty'' genome: [/gene/DDB_G0293758 H2Bv1] and [/gene/DDB_G0276273 H2Bv2]. There are three histone H3proteins, [/gene/DDB_G0267402 H3a] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9177486 Bukenberger et al. 1992]), [/gene/DDB_G0270838 H3b], and [/gene/DDB_G0271092 H3c], and two H3 domain-containing proteins, [/gene/DDB_G0291185 H3v1] and [/gene/DDB_G0277979 H3v2]. We have also identified two histone H4proteins, [/gene/DDB_G0277183 H4a] and [/gene/DDB_G0276863 H4b], which have identical protein sequences but non-identical nucleotide sequences.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 13-APR-2004 KP

DDB_G0279407.summary: Calmodulin is one of the most conserved proteins because it has to form complexes with a large number of diverse proteins in all eukaryotes. The calmodulin encoded by ''calA'' is a small protein in which 133 out of 152 amino acids are identical with the amino acids in human calmodulin [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3785182  (Goldhagen and Clark, 1986)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1493336  (Liu et al. 1992)]. However, the lysine at position 115 is not modified by trimethylation as it is in mammals but is conjugated to ubiquitin [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6087882  (Marshak et al. 1984)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2985583  (Gregori et al. 1985)]. Like all other calmodulins, as well as the regulatory subunit of calcineurin ([/gene/DDB_G0267446 cnbA]) it has two EF hand domains that bind calcium. The kinetic constants for binding and release of calcium are higher for calmodulin than for other EF hand proteins, making it well suited for mediating calcium signaling. Calmodulin purified from Dictyostelium interacts with bovine phosphodiesterase, calcium ATPase and troponin [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6259174  (Bazari and Clarke, 1981)]. Ca++/calmodulin binds to many Dictyostelium proteins including a ribosomal protein L19 ([/gene/DDB_G0281565 rpl19]), cyclin-dependent kinase ([/gene/DDB_G0288677 cdk5]) and nucleomorphin ([/gene/DDB_G0269114 numA]) among others [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6313344  (Maruta et al. 1983)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3409979  (Lydan and O'Day, 1988)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1719589  (Winckler et al. 1991)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1744106  (Sonnemann et al. 1991)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11919178  (Myre and O'Day, 2002)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17897809  (Catalano and O'Day, 2008)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23063531  (Huber et al. 2012)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23974243  (Huber, 2013)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25518940  (Sugden et al. 2014)]. Calmodulin also serves as the light chain for the unconventional myosins MyoA ([/gene/DDB_G0280039 myoA]), and MyoE ([/gene/DDB_G0288679 myoE]) where it provides calcium control [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21671662  (Crawley et al. 2011)]. Cells in which the levels of calmodulin mRNA and protein are reduced about two fold as the result of expression of calA antisense RNA are unable to complete cytokinesis and so become highly multinucleated before dying [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1493336  (Liu et al. 1992)]. Calmodulin is also associated with an unconventional myosin on the membranes of contractile vacuoles [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1629238  (Zhu and Clarke, 1992)]. Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 11-SEP-2018 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis; annotation contribution: PMID 23063531 Robert Huber

DDB_G0286895.summary:
''grlD'' encodes a G-protein coupled receptor containing 7 transmembrane domains. ''grlD'' is expressed throughout growth and development, with peak expression between 12 and 14 hours of development [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17501984 (Prabhu et al. 2007)]. Compared with wild type (wt) cells, ''grlD'' null cells have a decreased growth rate and a higher percentage have multiple nuclei, suggesting a cytokinesis defect in ''grlD'' null mutants. Cells lacking ''grlD'' were also insensitive to AprA ([/gene/DDB_G0281663 aprA])-induced proliferation inhibition [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29440579 (Tang et al. 2018)]. ''Dictyostelium'' cells bind polyphosphate, and polyphosphate inhibits both proliferation and proteasome activity, and induces aggregation in wt cells. ''grlD'' null cells do not bind polyphosphate and are unresponsive to polyphosphate-induced aggregation. In addition, in low nutrient conditions, physiological levels of polyphosphate reduced the proliferation of wild type cells, but not that of ''grlD'' or the small GTPase ''rasC'' ([/gene/DDB_G0281385 rasC]) null cells. In high nutrient conditions, the loss of RasC did not reduce the sensitivity of cells to polyphosphate. Cells lacking GrlD or RasC were unresponsive to polyphosphate-induced proteasome inhibition in all nutrient conditions. Taken together, these results suggest that GrlD is a receptor for extracellular polyphosphate and mediates polyphosphate-induced proliferation inhibition and proteasome inhibition. In addition these results suggest that polyphosphate regulates the proliferation of ''Dictyostelium'' by different signaling pathways depending on nutrient levels [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30785840 (Suess et al. 2019)].
To identify additional components of the polyphosphate proliferation inhibition signaling pathway, available mutants were screened for sensitivity to polyphosphate-induced proliferation inhibition under low-nutrient conditions. In addition to ''grlD'' and ''rasC'' null mutants, cells lacking the G protein component GpbA ([/gene/DDB_G0277143 gpbA]), the Ras guanine nucleotide exchange factor GefA ([/gene/DDB_G0284329 gefA]), phosphatase and tensin homolog (PTEN) ([/gene/DDB_G0286557 pten]), phospholipase C ([/gene/DDB_G0292736 plc]), inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate (IP3) receptor-like protein A (IplA) ([/gene/DDB_G0292564 iplA]), polyphosphate kinase 1 (Ppk1) ([/gene/DDB_G0293524 ppk1]), or the TOR complex 2 component PiaA ([/gene/DDB_G0277399 piaA]) have significantly reduced sensitivity to polyphosphate-induced proliferation inhibition. Polyphosphate also upregulates inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate and cytosolic free Ca2+ levels in wild type ''Dictyostelium'' cells. However, polyphosphate did not significantly affect IP3 levels in null mutant cells of ''grlD'', ''gefA'', ''pten'', ''plC'', and ''piaA'', and polyphosphate did not significantly affect cytosolic free Ca2+ in cells lacking GrlD, GefA, RasC, IplA, Ppk1, or PiaA. Taken together, these results suggest that polyphosphate uses signal transduction pathways including IP3/Ca2+ to inhibit ''Dictyostelium'' proliferation (Tang, et al 2021, PMID:34154396).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 19-AUG-2021 RD

DDB_G0276869.summary: ''psvA'' encodes the spore coat protein SP35 that is stored in prespore vesicles and released during sporulation such that it can bind cellulose to help form the middle of the trilaminar surface layer [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2049876  (Hildebrandt et al. 1991)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9692967  (Zhang, Brown and West 1998)]. There is a signal sequence at the N-terminus that directs transport across membranes. A cDNA clone derived from psvA mRNA, referred to as EB4, was one of the first prespore specific probes [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6301681  (Barklis and Lodish 1983)]. The mRNA starts to accumulate at 11 hrs of development when it is no longer complexed with an antisense transcript [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1995398  (Hildebrandt et al. 1991)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1555240  (Hildebrandt and Nellen 1992)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25887420  (Rosengarten et al. 2015)]. Both the 2.2 kb mRNA and a 1.8 kb antisense transcript from the opposite strand of ''psvA'' are synthesized during early development leading to the formation of double stranded RNA that is unstable. The antisense transcript disappears by 10 hrs of development which allows the mRNA to accumulate [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1555240  (Hildebrandt and Nellen 1992)]. Mutants that fail to accumulate ''psvA'' mRNA have no detectable SP35. No phenotypic aberrations were seen in the mutant lines [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2049876  (Hildebrandt, Saur and Nellen 1991)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 14-DEC-2018 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0270736.summary: ''rasV'' encodes a guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G protein) of the Ras family of small GTPases. G proteins are key components of signal transduction networks in which they function as molecular signaling switches, binding to GDP in the off state while binding GTP in the on state. Guanine nucleotide-exchange factors (GEFs, rasGEFs) promote the exchange of GDP for GTP on Ras GTPases thus activating them, while GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs, rasGAPs) inactivate Ras GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP. An analysis of ''Dictyostelium'' ras family genes reveals that ''rasU'' ([/gene/DDB_G0270138 rasU]), ''rasV'', ''rasW'' ([/gene/DDB_G0270122 rasW]), ''rasX'' ([/gene/DDB_G0270124 rasX]), ''rasY'' ([/gene/DDB_G0270126 rasY]) and ''rasZ'' ([/gene/DDB_G0270140 rasZ]) form a separate phylogenetic clade ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29614268 Park et al. 2018]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 18-MAR-2020 RD

DDB_G0286229.summary:
AlyL belongs to the family of amoeba-type lysozymes, such as [/gene/DDB_G0275123 alyA], which has been shown to have lysozyme activity, and [/gene/DDB_G0275119 alyB], [/gene/DDB_G0275121 alyC]. ''alyD'', which is present in two copies on chromosome 2: [/gene/DDB_G0273197 alyD-1], [/gene/DDB_G0273731 alyD-2], and ''alyL'' are more distantly related to ''alyA'', ''alyB'', and ''alyC''.
In a genetic screen utilizing the growth of mutant amoebae on a variety of bacteria as a phenotypic readout, ''alyL'' has been identified to control growth on Gram-negative bacteria. AlyL has a signal peptide and likely resides in the lysosome or is otherwise secreted. ''alyL'' mutant cells grew poorly on all tested Gram-negative bacterial species such as ''Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa'', or ''E. coli B'', but grew well on Gram-positive bacteria such as ''Bacillus subtitles''. To test wether AlyL is required for feeding on bacteria or for defense against them, the ability to grow on dead Gram-negative cells has been tested. The ''alyL'' mutant cells grew well on the dead bacteria indicating that ''alyL'' is not required for nutritional requirement growing on Gram-negative bacteria, but likely for defense. AlyL, a putative lysozyme seems to fit this role as it is expressed during and required for growth on Gram-negative bacteria [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23664307 (Nasser et al. 2013)].
A comprehensive study classified all lysozymes in ''Dictyostelium''. In addition to the 5 known amoeba type lysozymes ([/gene/DDB_G0275123 alyA], [/gene/DDB_G0275119 alyB], [/gene/DDB_G0275121 alyC], [/gene/DDB_G0273197 alyD-1] and [/gene/DDB_G0286229 alyL] ), two new related lysozymes in this family have been identified, [/gene/DDB_G0282905 alyE] and [/gene/DDB_G0282893 alyF]. These genes are next to each other and almost identical, thus possibly a more recent gene duplication. In the past, gene models for these two new lysozymes gave rise to proteins with one or two transmembrane domains. Thus they first have been named alyTM1 and alyTM2, respectively. However, new sequence analyses resulted in updated gene models coding for proteins containing a signal peptide like the other 5 aly family members. Alignment of the 7 proteins allowed the identification of one conserved Asp and one Glu residue in the C- terminal portion of each protein, which might represent the amoeba lysozyme active site [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/32061941 (Lamrabet et al. 2020)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 22-APR-2020 PF

DDB_G0272036.summary:
DNA-dependent RNA polymerase catalyzes the transcription of DNA into RNA using the four ribonucleoside triphosphates as substrates ([/ontology/go/0003899/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase activity]). Three distinct zinc-containing RNA polymerases are found in eukaryotic nuclei: [/gene/DDB_G0275759 rpa1] for the ribosomal RNA precursor ([/ontology/go/0006360/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase I promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005736/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase I complex]), [/gene/DDB_G0279193 rpb1] for the mRNA precursor ([/ontology/go/0006366/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase II promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005665/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase II, core complex]), and [/gene/DDB_G0277199 rpc1] for 5S and tRNA genes ([/ontology/go/0006383/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase III promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005666/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase III complex]).
RNA polymerase II is composed of 12 subunits: [/gene/DDB_G0279193 rpb1], [/gene/DDB_G0288257 rpb2], [/gene/DDB_G0292244 rpb3], [/gene/DDB_G0282739 rpb4], [/gene/DDB_G0291636 rpb5], [/gene/DDB_G0291037 rpb6], [/gene/DDB_G0284891 rpb7], [/gene/DDB_G0278039 rpb8], [/gene/DDB_G0268306 rpb9], [/gene/DDB_G0272036 rpb10], [/gene/DDB_G0277677 rpb11], and[/gene/DDB_G0283365 rpb12]. Subunits 5, 6, 8, 10, and 12 are common to all threeRNA polymerases (reviewed by [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9618449 Hampsey] in 1998).
Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 09-APR-2004 PG

DDB_G0268636.summary:
''roco11'' encodes a large, multi-domain protein of the Roco family. Roco11 contains an N-terminal leucine-rich repeat (LRR) region, a Roc small GTPase domain, a COR (C-terminal of Roc) domain, and a protein kinase domain. Eleven ''Dictyostelium'' proteins belong to the Roco family: ([/gene/DDB_G0291079 gbpC]), ([/gene/DDB_G0273259 qkgA-1]), ([/gene/DDB_G0269250 pats1]), ([/gene/DDB_G0288251 roco4]), ([/gene/DDB_G0294533 roco5]), ([/gene/DDB_G0279417 roco6]), ([/gene/DDB_G0267472 roco7]), ([/gene/DDB_G0286127 roco8]), ([/gene/DDB_G0288183 roco9]), ([/gene/DDB_G0291710 roco10]) and Roco11.
Roco11 is localized to the cytosol and ''roco11'' is expressed during both growth and development with the highest level of expression during the slug stage of development. ''roco11'' null cells produce fruiting bodies with longer stalks than those of wt cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20348387 van Egmond and van Haastert 2010]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 25-OCT-2021 RD

DDB_G0271984.summary:
''rab5A'' encodes a guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G protein) of the Rab family of small GTPases. G proteins are key components of signal transduction networks in which they function as molecular signaling switches, binding to GDP in the off state while binding GTP in the on state. Guanine nucleotide-exchange factors (GEFs) promote the exchange of GDP for GTP on Rab GTPases thus activating them, while GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) inactivate Rab GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP. Rab5A is an ortholog of human Rab5A. Rab subfamily small GTPases in many organisms are key regulators of intracellular membrane trafficking.
Proteomic analysis revealed that Rab5A is localized to the Legionella-containing vacuole [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24373249 (Hoffmann et al. 2013)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28183814 (Schmolders et al. 2017)] and is associated with ''M. marinum''-containing compartments ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25779329 Barisch, et al. 2015]). Rab5A localizes to the plasma membrane, macropinosomes, and phagosomes. The Rab GAP TbcrA ([/gene/DDB_G0282575 tbcrA]) binds to and has GAP activity towards Rab5A. The PH-domain containing protein PripA ([/gene/DDB_G0275795 pripA]) binds to and forms a protein complex with TbcrA which facilitates Rab5A inactivation and promotes Rab5-to-Rab7 ([/gene/DDB_G0269236 rab7A]) conversion and macropinosome and phagosome maturation (Tu, et al 2022, PMID:35379834).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 15-APR-2022 RD

DDB_G0282147.summary:
The [/gene/DDB_G0285211 fadA] gene was originally identified by [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10504413 Saito and Ochiai (1999)] in a search for ESTs containing the conserved histidine-box domain found in proteins capable of unsaturated fatty acid metabolic processes.. Overexpression of the FadA protein and subsequent analysis by mass spectrometry revealed that thisprotein is specific for 5-Delta desaturation of C16 and C18 fatty acids. A second desaturase,[/gene/DDB_G0282147 fadB], was later identified by [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10712614 Saito and colleagues (2000)].Similar experiments with the FadB protein show a specificity for the 5 position in C18 fatty acids.
Null mutants of ''fadB'' show no detectable phenotype, whereas ''fadA-'' cells have an increased toleranceto higher temperatures during development compared to wild type. This is indicative of the importance of membrane fluidity, which is regulated byfatty acid modification of desaturases such as FadA and FadB ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15632431 Saito et al.2005]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 07-JUN-2021 PF

DDB_G0267490.summary:
The ChLim protein contains a N-terminal Calponin Homology (CH) domain, 3 LIM domains, and 4 LIM-related domains (LRDs). This topology is unique, although there are proteins in other organisms that have both CH and LIM domains.
ChLim was isolated as an interacting partner of [/gene/DDB_G0275157 limF], as was [/gene/DDB_G0286553 rab21], a small GTPase of the Rab subfamily. ChLim and LimF interaction with Rab21 is not dependent on the ability of Rab21 to bind GTP. Mutations in these three genes indicate that ChLim play a role in the [/ontology/go/0050765/annotation/page/1 negative regulation of phagocytosis], while LimF and Rab21 are involved in the [/ontology/go/0050766/annotation/page/1 positive regulation of phagocytosis]. Consistent with this, during phagocytosis, ChLim is found in the [/ontology/go/0001891/annotation/page/1 phagocytic cup] and remains associated with the [/ontology/go/0045335/annotation/page/1 phagocytic vesicle]. The CH domain mediates this localization ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15962002 Khurana et al, 2005]). Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 14-JUL-2005 PG

DDB_G0283265.summary:
''mkkA'' was identified in a PCR screen for MEK kinases, and found to be a single developmentally regulated transcript, not detectable in vegetative cells and induced during early development. The MEKKα protein contains a conserved F-box, known for its role in ubiquitin-mediated protein degradation, followed by 5 WD40 repeats. Compared to wild-type, ''mkkA''-null cells developed more rapidly and formed fruiting bodies ([/ontology/go/0030587/annotation/page/1 sorocarp development]) with longer stalks and smaller sori ([/ontology/go/0009653/annotation/page/1 anatomical structure morphogenesis]). In the slug stage the null mutant shows an increase in the pstO compartment and a concomitant reduction in the prespore domain. Cells expressing a dominant-negative MEKKα containing a L199A mutation in the putative ATP binding site had a similar but stronger morphological phenotype. In contrast, cells overexpressing MEKKα or MEKKαΔWD (lacking the WD40 repeats) showed very delayed development, which often arrested at the mound stage. Cells overexpressing only the F-box/WD40 repeats had a similar but more severe phenotype. Aberrant fruiting body formation and reduced spore production in these mutants suggest that MEKKα plays an important role in prespore cell differentiation.
The Wd40 repeats were shown to target MEKKα to the cortex ([/ontology/go/0005938/annotation/page/1 cell cortex]). Two-hybrid screens using the F-box/WD40 repeats as bait identified two proteins of the ubiqination/deubiquination pathway, [/gene/DDB_G0275021 ubpB], a ubiquitin hydrolase, and [/gene/DDB_G0284865 ubcB], a ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme. ''ubpB'' and ''ubcB'' were shown to differentially control MEKKα through the F-box/WD40 repeats in a cell-type specific and temporally regulated manner [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9832508 (Chung et al., 1998)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 19-OCT-2004 PF

DDB_G0270140.summary: ''rasZ'' encodes a guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G protein) of the Ras family of small GTPases. G proteins are key components of signal transduction networks in which they function as molecular signaling switches, binding to GDP in the off state while binding GTP in the on state. Guanine nucleotide-exchange factors (GEFs, rasGEFs) promote the exchange of GDP for GTP on Ras GTPases thus activating them, while GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs, rasGAPs) inactivate Ras GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP. An analysis of ''Dictyostelium'' ras family genes reveals that ''rasU'' ([/gene/DDB_G0270138 rasU]), ''rasV'' ([/gene/DDB_G0270736 rasV]), ''rasW'' ([/gene/DDB_G0270122 rasW]), ''rasX'' ([/gene/DDB_G0270124 rasX]), ''rasY'' ([/gene/DDB_G0270126 rasY]) and ''rasZ'' form a separate phylogenetic clade ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29614268 Park et al. 2018]). DDB_G0274561.summary:
There are 29 genes encoding actin in ''Dictyostelium'' with amino acid identity greater than 83%, ''act1''-''act29''. Seventeen of these genes encode identical proteins: [/gene/DDB_G0289553 act1], [/gene/DDB_G0274133 act2], [/gene/DDB_G0289005 act4], [/gene/DDB_G0289663 act5], [/gene/DDB_G0274135 act6], [/gene/DDB_G0280545 act7], [/gene/DDB_G0269234 act8], [/gene/DDB_G0274601 act9], [/gene/DDB_G0288879 act11], [/gene/DDB_G0274129 act12], [/gene/DDB_G0274599 act13], [/gene/DDB_G0274137 act14], [/gene/DDB_G0272520 act15], [/gene/DDB_G0272248 act16], [/gene/DDB_G0274727 act19], [/gene/DDB_G0274285 act20], and [/gene/DDB_G0274561 act21], while [/gene/DDB_G0289811 act10], [/gene/DDB_G0275023 act22], and [/gene/DDB_G0289487 act3] respectively have 1, 4 and 11 amino acid differences compared to the 17 identical genes. The proteins encoded by [/gene/DDB_G0274131 act17], [/gene/DDB_G0289489 act18], [/gene/DDB_G0268744 act23] and [/gene/DDB_G0289505 act24]are more divergent.
Actin is a major [/ontology/go/0005200/annotation/page/1 structural constituent of cytoskeleton]. Actin is one of the most abundant proteins in ''Dictyostelium'', constituting approximately 8% of the total protein in vegetative cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/561722 Alton and Lodish et al. 1977]).Actin synthesis is developmentally regulated, peaking shortly after starvation (reviewed by [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6894564 Firtel] in 1981). The different actin genes differ in their levels of expression, with [/gene/DDB_G0274135 act6], [/gene/DDB_G0269234 act8] and [/gene/DDB_G0274129 act12] being highly expressed both during growth and development compared to [/gene/DDB_G0289005 act4], [/gene/DDB_G0289663 act5], [/gene/DDB_G0280545 act7] and [/gene/DDB_G0272248 act16] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6286214 McKeown and Firtel 1981]). DDB_G0291842.summary:
The wee1 family of tyrosine kinases ([/ontology/go/0004713/annotation/page/1 protein-tyrosine kinase activity]) were originally identified in a screen formutants that undergo mitosis at a reduced cell size in the fission yeast ''Schizosaccharomycespombe'' ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7262540 Nurse and Thuriaux 1980]). Since then, members ofthe wee1 family have been shown to play an essential role in cell cycle regulation ([/ontology/go/0000074/annotation/page/1 regulation of progression through cell cycle]) in several other organisms, including thebudding yeast ''Saccharomyces cerevisiae'', the African clawed frog ''Xenopus laevis'', andseveral metazoans ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14625382 reviewed in Kellogg 2003]).
Wee1 phosphorylates a specific tyrosine residue on the mitosis promoting protein Cdk1/Cdc2/Cdc28 ([/gene/DDB_G0272813 cdk1] in ''Dictyostelium''). Phosphorylation of this residue by Wee1 inhibits Cdk1/Cdc2/Cdc28,thereby delaying entry into mitosis from G2. Cdk1/Cdc2/Cdc28 is inactivated by dephosphorylation of thetyrosine residue by the phosphatase Cdc25/Mih1 ([/gene/DDB_G0283617 cdc25] in ''Dictyostelium''), allowingentry into mitosis ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14625382 reviewed in Kellogg 2003]).
Three uncharacterized putative wee1 family members exist in the ''Dictyostelium'' genome: [/gene/DDB_G0291842 DDB_G0291842], [/gene/DDB_G0277539 DDB_G0277539], and [/gene/DDB_G0291133 DDB_G0291133]. Interestingly, ''Schizosaccharomyces pombe'' and animals also have three wee1 family kinases: wee1, mik1, and myt1.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 21-MAY-2004 KP

DDB_G0271980.summary: ''rabR'' encodes a guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G protein) of the Rab family of small GTPases. G proteins are key components of signal transduction networks in which they function as molecular signaling switches, binding to GDP in the off state while binding GTP in the on state. DDB_G0282817.summary: PAT2 is a ''Dictyostelium'' P-type H<sup>+</sup>-ATPase that is very similar to plasma membrane H<sup>+</sup>-transporting ATPases (proton pumps) ([/ontology/go/0015992/annotation/page/1 proton transport]) of plants and fungi. The ''patB'' gene is expressed at low levels in cells growing at neutral pH, but it is up-regulated significantly when cells are shifted to an acidic medium. Immunofluorescence experiments showed PAT2 localization at the plasma [/ontology/go/0016020/annotation/page/1 membrane]. ''patB''-null cells grew and developed normally at neutral pH, but where unable to grow at pH 5. At pH 6.8, wild-type and knock-out cells exhibited similar levels of vanadate-sensitive [/ontology/go/0016887/annotation/page/1 ATPase activity], but when cells were transferred to pH 5 the activity increased rapidly in wild-type, but not in the mutant. These results suggest that PAT2 is an acid-inducible P-type H<sup>+</sup>-ATPase that is essential for survival of ''Dictyostelium'' amoebae in acidic medium [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9421912  (Coukell et al. 1997)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 15-JUL-2005 PF

DDB_G0288047.summary:
There are six subfamilies of DNA methyltransferases. ''Dictyostelium'' has a single cytosine-5-methyltransferase, DnmA, which belongs to the dnmt2 subfamily. Members of this family have weak or undetectable methylase activity. When activity is observed, it is against substrates containing a thymidine 3' of the cytosine, rather than a guanine as other cytosine-5-methyltransferases ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15689527 Ponger and Li, 2005]).
Consistent with these predictions, no methylation has been detected on CG islands in the Dictyostelium genome ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1713034 Smith and Ratner, 1991]). Instead, low levels of DNA methylation has been observed on sites with no obvious sequence preferences. DNA methylation is dependent on the presence of DnmA, as it is greatly reduced in the null mutant, indicating that DnmA has DNA (cytosine-5-)-methyltransferase activity ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16282589 Kuhlmann et al., 2005], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16400165 Katoh et al., 2006]). Kuhlmann and colleagues have noticed that after several passages through growth and development stages, expression of two retrotransposable elements, Skipper and DIRS-1, is greatly increased in the ''dnmA'' null mutant. Null mutants for two other genes involved in RNAi silencing, [/gene/DDB_G0273051 drnA-1] and [/gene/DDB_G0283023 hcpA], also exhibit increased expression of Skipper and DIRS-1. Katoh ''et al.'' report a modest developmental defect of culmination during sorocarp development, as well as a reduction in sporulation efficiency.
DnmA is an active tRNA methyltransferase that modifies C38 in tRNAAsp(GUC) ''in vitro'' and ''in vivo'' ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23877245 Muller, et al. 2013])Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 16-FEB-2005 PG

DDB_G0283391.summary:
[/gene/DDB_G0283391 kinX] and [/gene/DDB_G0289661 kinY] are similar to the kinase domains of the LISK (LIM domain and testis-specific kinase) family of protein kinases ([/ontology/go/0004672/annotation/page/1 protein kinase activity]). Members of the LISK family in metazoans have been shown toplay a role in actin filament dynamics, however, the LISK kinases found in ''Dictyostelium'' do not contain LIMdomains. The ''kinX'' transcript is weakly detected at constant levels throughout development, whereas ''kinY''is expressed at low levels during growth, increasing throughout development with a peak during culmination.Additionally, ''kinY'' is enriched in the prespore cells of slugs ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7857991 Wetterauer et al.1995], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10899639 Wetterauer 2000]).
Seven putative LISK proteins exist in the ''Dictyostelium'' proteome: [/gene/DDB_G0275165 DDB_G0275165], [/gene/DDB_G0271538 DDB_G0271538], [/gene/DDB_G0269298 gefX], [/gene/DDB_G0281745 DDB_G0281745], [/gene/DDB_G0280461 DDB_G0280461], [/gene/DDB_G0271402 DDB_G0271402], [/gene/DDB_G0289859 kxcA].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 04-OCT-2004 KP

DDB_G0273919.summary:
The lectin Discoidin I binds N-acetylgalactosamine and galactose [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/4517669 (Rosen et al. 1973)]. Discoidin I subunits associate to form a tetramer [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/4858710 (Simpson et al. 1974)] and are expressed from a family of 3 different genes: ''dscA'', ''dscC'' ([/gene/DDB_G0273065 dscC-1]) ([/gene/DDB_G0273885 dscC-2]) and ''dscD'' ([/gene/DDB_G0273067 dscD-1]) ([/gene/DDB_G0273887 dscD-2]). [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6279874 (Poole et al. 1981)]. Monomeric discoidin I is located mainly in the cytosol, while the tetrameric form of discoidin I is detected in multilamellar bodies and is externalized during aggregation [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2581974 (Barondes et al. 1985)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8416797 (Fukuzawa et al. 1993)]. Discoidin I gene expression is induced by prestarvation factor (PSF) and conditioned medium factor, ([/gene/DDB_G0275007 cmfA]) but is down-regulated by cAMP [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7641976 (Blusch et al. 1995)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2049883 (Rathi et al. 1991)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1663029 (Gomer et al. 1991)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2196444 (Vauti et al. 1990)]. Mutants defective in discoidin I fail to stream during aggregation, implicating discoidin I in cell-substrate adhesion [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6509552 (Springer et al. 1984)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/4075402 (Crowley et al. 1985)]. In addition, discoidin I is thought to play an intracellular role, as mutants in which discoidin genes are not expressed also have an abnormally centered microtubule organizing center and more rounded cell morphology, suggesting a role for discoidins in cytoskeleton organization during aggregation [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1334012 (Alexander et al. 1992)].
''Dictyostelium discoideum'' strains that carry bacteria secrete approx. 80 times higher levels of DscA and DscC than non-carriers. Secreted DscA binds to ''Klebsiella pneumoniae''. DscA binding protects bacteria from extracellular killing, promotes their internalization and prolongs their retention in both ''Dictyostelium discoideum'' and mammalian cells. Plant lectins induce the same response, suggesting that modified uptake and persistence of lectin-coated bacteria in eukaryotic cells is a general phenomenon, termed lectin-induced modified bacterial internalization [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30049880 (Dinh et al. 2018)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 10-AUG-2018 RD

DDB_G0271806.summary:
RapGAP3 mediates deactivation of Rap1 ([/gene/DDB_G0291237 rapA]) at the late mound stage of development and plays an important role in regulating cell sorting during apical tip formation by controlling cell-cell adhesion and cell migration. RapGAP3 transiently translocates to the cell cortex in response to chemoattractant stimulation, and localizes to the leading edge of migrating cells. Deletion of ''rapgap3'' results in a severely altered morphogenesis of the multicellular organism at the late mound stage ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19284976 Jeon et al. 2009)]. RapGAP3 binds phosphatidylinositol (3,4,5)-triphosphate, and associates with the plasma membrane and the lagging edge of migrating cells. ''rapgap3'' null cells also have defects in chemotaxis to cAMP. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20547830 Zhang et al. 2010)]. The minimal amino acids in the I/LWEQ region required for anterior/posterior localization were investigated by ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24608804 Lee et al. 2014)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28124777 Kim et al. 2017)]. RapGAP3 binds to and is regulated by PI(3,4)P2. Cells lacking RapGAP3 display increased Ras activity, cell spreading and aberrant migratory behavior ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30194235 Li et al. 2018]).

DDB_G0271684.summary: ''grlA'' encodes a member of the evolutionarily conserved family of seven transmembrane receptors that are coupled to G-proteins ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16735079 Prabu and Eichinger 2006)]. GrlA is similar to metazoan gamma aminobutyric acid (GABA) B-type receptors with 7 transmembrane domains and a large extracellular domain. Inactivation of the ''grlA'' gene leads to a delay in development at the post aggregation stage and a reduced number of spores ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17950724 Prabu et al. 2007)]. When steroids such as hydrocortisone bind to GrlA during culmination, GABA is rapidly released to trigger production of the 34 amino acid peptide signal, spore differentiation factor 2 (SDF-2). GrlA uses the trimeric G-protein containing the Galpha4 subunit encoded by gpaD ([/gene/DDB_G0285425 gpaD]). Drugs that inhibit the steroid biosynthetic pathway block the production of SDF-2 and reduce spore viability ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19176583 Anjard et al. 2009)]. Likewise, grlA null and gpaD null mutants fail to release SDF-2 in response to hydrocortisone but respond normally to GABA.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 05-FEB-2017 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0292564.summary:
The [/gene/DDB_G0292564 iplA] gene encodes a protein predicted to have inositol-1,4,5-triphosphate receptor activity by similarity to the human INSP3 receptor. The ''iplA'' transcript is expressed at low levels during growth and peaks at 9 h before declining. A null mutant of ''iplA'' lacks cAMP-stimulated Ca2+ uptake, however, its ability to chemotax towards cAMP is uninhibited ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10970875 Traynor et al. 2000]). Further analysis of ''iplA-'' cells by [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15760480 Schaloske and colleagues (2005)] shows that while influx of extracellular Ca2+ is largely reduced, release of stored Ca2+ into the cytoplasm is intact. Inhibition of capacitative Ca2+ entry does in fact impair the ability of cells to chemotax towards cAMP.
Lam ''et al.'' showed that mutation of the ''iplA'' gene inhibited autophagic cell death, suggesting that Ca2+ flux is necessary to signal this cell death. In addition, ''iplA''/[/gene/DDB_G0292390 atg1] double null cells showed a variable and partial inhibition of necrotic cell death, suggesting a lesser role for iplA in this form of cell death ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18077554 Lam et al. 2008]).
([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22375061 Lusche et al. 2012]) found that IplA localized to cytoplasmic vesicular membranes and to a lesser extent to the plasma membrane. ''iplA'' null cells exhibit defects in Ca2+ mediated chemotaxis, and lack the capacity to reorient in the direction of the aggregation center at the onset of cAMP waves. These results suggest that IplA is either the Ca2+ chemotaxis receptor or an essential component of the Ca2+ chemotaxis regulatory pathway.
Two basic modes of calcium signaling can be distinguished in ''Dictyostelium'': GPCR-dependent signaling (cAMP and folic acid) whose onset is delayed for 5-10 s after the stimulus, and which depends on IplA; and purinergic signalling (ATP and ADP) which has a rapid onset of less than 1 s, is independent of G-beta ([/gene/DDB_G0277143 gpbA]) and IplA, but depends on TrpP ([/gene/DDB_G0272999 pkd2]). ''iplA'' is also required for response to DIF and gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28011630 Traynor et al. 2017]). ''iplA'' is involved in the signal transduction pathway responsible for AprA-dependent ([/gene/DDB_G0281663 aprA]) chemorepulsion ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30462573 Rijal et al. 2018]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 5-MAY-2008 PF

DDB_G0283629.summary: ''zntA'' was identified as a putative zinc transporter by sequence homology and a phylogenetic analysis placed ''zntA'' in a subfamily along with ([/gene/DDB_G0282067 zntB]), ([/gene/DDB_G0269332 zntC]) and ([/gene/DDB_G0291141 zntD]). All four genes are expressed in pstAB cells or at the stalk entrance during culmination, and both ''zntA'' and ''zntC'' are also expressed in pstAB cells in the slug stage. None of the four genes are expressed in a STATa ([/gene/DDB_G0281381 dstA]) null strain [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18415938  (Sunaga et al. 2008)]. ZntA localizes to the contractile vacuole, and, in a ''zntA'' null mutant, Zn2+ transport into the contractile vacuole is abolished. In addition, ''Escherichia coli'' is killed more rapidly in ''zntA'' null mutant cells than in wt, suggesting that accumulation of Zn2+ in phagolysosomes contributes to bacterial killing and that phagolysosomes contain a higher Zn2+ concentration in the ''zntA'' null strain that in wt [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30404827  (Barisch et al. 2018)]. During ''Mycobacterium marinum'' infection, both ZntA and ZntB localize to the Mycobacteria-containing vacuole (MCV), and expression of both genes is increased. In ''zntA'' null cells, MCVs accumulate more Zn2+ than wt cells, and intracellular ''M. marinum'' growth is decreased compared with wt cells, suggesting that ZntB, the main lysosomal and post-lysosomal Zn2+ transporter, might compensate for the absence of ZntA by exporting Zn2+ into all endosomes and MCVs. Taken together, these results suggest that ZntA is the main transporter for delivery of Zn2+ to the contractile vacuole and demonstrate that Zn2+ poisoning of bacteria is a killing strategy of ''Dictyostelium'' for invading bacteria (Hanna, et al. 2021, PMID:33531393).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 02-SEP-2021 RD

DDB_G0281381.summary:
''Dictyostelium'' is the simplest organism known to employ STAT signaling. STAT (signal transducer and activator of transcription) proteins are characterized by a DNA binding domain, an SH2 domain, and a site of tyrosine phosphorylation. A STAT becomes activated when a ligand binds to its receptor, inducing tyrosine phosphorylation of the monomeric STAT molecule. Four STATs have been identified in ''Dictyostelium'', [/gene/DDB_G0281381 dstA], [/gene/DDB_G0268638 dstB], [/gene/DDB_G0293532 dstC] and [/gene/DDB_G0275167 dstD]. STATa was first identified biochemically, as the TTGA-binding factor that binds in vitro to the [/gene/DDB_G0277853 ecmA] activator and [/gene/DDB_G0269132 ecmB] repressor elements (Kawata ''et al.'' [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8670809 1996], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9200609 1997]), and genetically in a REMI screen for mutants that are blocked in fruiting-body formation ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10393118 Mohanty et al. 1999]). During development, STATa is tyrosine phosphorylated in response to cAMP in a [/gene/DDB_G0273397 carA-1]-dependent manner. STATa is downregulated by [/gene/DDB_G0273097 ptpA1-1] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11254360 Early et al. 2001]). The protein kinase DrkA ([/gene/DDB_G0289791 drkA]) phosphorylates and activates STATa ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31002205 Saga et al. 2019]).
''dstA''-null organisms do not culminate and form structures that lack stalk cells and a stalk tube, although the cells differentiate into stalk cells in culture ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10393118 Mohanty et al. 1999]).[http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10821768 (Fukuzawa and Williams 2000)] demonstrated that STATa ([/gene/DDB_G0281381 dstA]), activates ''cudA'' expression in tip-organizer cells of the migrating slug. [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/27125566 (Saga et al. 2016)] demonstrate two distinct signaling pathways for pstA-specific genes downstream of STATa: CudA-dependent and CudA-independent.
Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 28-MAY-2004 PG

DDB_G0269024.summary: ''ate1'' encodes the highly conserved enzyme arginyltransferase which is responsible for the post-translational conjugation of arginine to the N-terminal aspartate or glutamate of a protein. Mass spectrometric analysis identified arginylation sites in actin and several actin-binding proteins, suggesting a role for ''ate1'' in the regulation of cytoskeletal proteins involved in adhesion or migration. DNA-dependent RNA polymerase catalyzes the transcription of DNA into RNA using the four ribonucleoside triphosphates as substrates ([/ontology/go/0003899/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase activity]). Three distinct zinc-containing RNA polymerases are found in eukaryotic nuclei: [/gene/DDB_G0275759 rpa1] for the ribosomal RNA precursor ([/ontology/go/0006360/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase I promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005736/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase I complex]), [/gene/DDB_G0279193 rpb1] for the mRNA precursor ([/ontology/go/0006366/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase II promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005665/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase II, core complex]), and [/gene/DDB_G0277199 rpc1] for 5S and tRNA genes ([/ontology/go/0006383/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase III promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005666/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase III complex]).
RNA polymerase III is a multisubunit complex. The subunits encoded by [/gene/DDB_G0277199 rpc1] (ortholog of ''S. cerevisiae RPO31''), [/gene/DDB_G0293560 rpa2] (''RPC2''), [/gene/DDB_G0268080 rpc3] (''RPC82''),[/gene/DDB_G0277671 rpc4] (''RPC53''), [/gene/DDB_G0271514 rpc5] (''RPC37''), [/gene/DDB_G0272022 rpc34] (''RPC34''), [/gene/DDB_G0273425 rpc25] (''RPC25''), and [/gene/DDB_G0287707 rpc11] (''RPC11'') are unique to RNA polymerase III. Orthologs of ''RPC31'' and ''RPC17'' have not been identified in the ''Dictyostelium'' genome. Two subunits, [/gene/DDB_G0291362 rpc19] and [/gene/DDB_G0282339 rpa5] (''RPC19'' and ''RPC40'' in ''S. cerevisiae''), are common to RNA polymerase I and RNA polymerase III and correspond to subunits 3 and 11 of RNA polymerase II. DDB_G0269102.summary: ''arcD'' encodes the 20 kDa subunit of the Arp2/3 complex [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11807934  (Insall et al. 2001)]. The seven subunits of this 200 kDa complex are encoded by ([/gene/DDB_G0277825 arcA]), ([/gene/DDB_G0282813 arcB]), ([/gene/DDB_G0292804 arcC]), ''arcD'', ([/gene/DDB_G0288319 arcE]), ([/gene/DDB_G0272106 arpB]) and ([/gene/DDB_G0283755 arpC]). The subunits of mammalian Arp2/3 are very similar to ''Dictyostelium'' homologs. Arp2/3 binds to the side of F-actin filaments and initiates polymerization of a new F-actin chain at an angle of 70 degrees leading to a branched actin network that can alter the shape of cells. The ability to nucleate new actin filaments is greatly stimulated by direct interactions with members of the WASP/SCAR family [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11807934  (Insall et al. 2001)]. The Arp2/3 complex largely mediates the actin polymerization response to chemotactic stimulation and contributes to cell motility, pseudopod extension and adhesion in Dictyostelium chemotaxis. The complete Arp2/3 complex is essential for growth; partial loss of activity of either ArcB or ArpB impairs growth and chemotaxis [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17553489  (Langridge and Kay, 2007)]. mRNA from each of the genes encoding Arp2/3 subunits accumulates coordinately to reach a peak at 3 hours of development and gradually decreases thereafter [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25887420  (Rosengarten et al. 2015)]. The Arp2/3 complex interacts with the protein CARMIL, which serves as a scaffold for the assembly of a larger complex of proteins involved in the nucleation and termination of actin filament assembly. The complex consists of CARMIL ([/gene/DDB_G0292386 carmil]), AcpA, ([/gene/DDB_G0267374 acpA]) AcpB, ([/gene/DDB_G0272104 acpB]) the Arp2/3 complex, and type I myosins MyoB ([/gene/DDB_G0289117 myoB]) and MyoC ([/gene/DDB_G0276617 myoC]) [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11425877  (Jung et al. 2001)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 30-MAY-2019 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0293196.summary:
Lam ''et al.'' found that the additional deletion of the pcp gene in an [/gene/DDB_G0292390 atg1] null background does not have any effect on necrotic or autophagic cell death; the phenotype of the double atg1-/pcp- mutant is identical to the phenotype of the single ''atg1''- mutant. Thus, in ''Dictyostelium'', which also appears to have no bcl-2 family members, autophagic cell death and necrotic cell death are independent of caspases and bcl-2 proteins ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17889831 Lam et al., 2007]).
([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23938384 Saheb et al., 2013]) revealed that Pcp was associated with the contractile vacuole membrane, and using a yeast two-hybrid system identified VatM as a protein interacting partner with Pcp. GFP-Pcp over-expressing cells were susceptible to osmotic stress and in hypo-osmotic conditions were rounded and contained more abnormally swollen contractile vacuoles. Their work suggests that Pcp is essential for Dictyostelium osmotic regulation via its functioning in the contractile vacuole system.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 28-AUG-2013 RD

DDB_G0275323.summary: ''tipD'' was isolated from a REMI mutant that was picked because its development was arrested when multiple tips formed on aggregates ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10402673 Stege et al. 1999)]. It encodes a 67 kDa coiled-coil protein with a N-terminal domain that is similar to the yeast autophagy protein ATG16. In yeast, ATG16 associates non-covalently with ATG5-ATG12 to form a complex which acts as an E3 ligase to link Atg8 to phosphatidyl-ethanolamine of the growing membrane of the autophagosome. The product of ''tipD'' has been shown to interact with ATG5 ([/gene/DDB_G0289881 atg5]) in a 2-hybrid yeast assay ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26246495 Mesquita et al. 2015)]. ''tipD'' null mutants have defects in autophagy, phagocytosis and degradation of ubiquitin-marked proteins indicating that this ATG16 homolog may be involved in several steps of membrane trafficking ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25996471 Munoz-Braceras et al. 2015)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25878144 Xiong et al. 2015)]. ''tipD'' null mutants also have abnormal cell sorting behavior and severely reduced fruiting body and spore production. The multitipped phenotype of mutants in tipD is similar to that of mutants in other autophagy genes ''atg6'' ([/gene/DDB_G0269244 atg6A]), ''atg7'' ([/gene/DDB_G0271096 atg7]), ''atg9'' ([/gene/DDB_G0285323 atg9]), ''atg101'' ([/gene/DDB_G0288287 atg101]), and ''tipC'' ([/gene/DDB_G0267422 tipC]). TipD directly interacts with subunits of the proteasomal degradation complex PSMD1 ([/gene/DDB_G0287953 psmD1]) and PSMD2 ([/gene/DDB_G0293752 psmD2]) and mediates their degradation by autophagy, suggesting a role for ''tipD'' in linking autophagy and the ubiquitin proteasome system. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30269947 Xiong et al. 2018)]. Core autophagy genes are upregulated in ''atg12'' ([/gene/DDB_G0282929 atg12]), and ''tipD'' mutants while genes related to cell motility and phagocytosis are down-regulated. An increase in ubiquitin-positive protein aggregates with a corresponding decrease in proteasomal activity in these mutants reveals that the ubiquitin proteasome system (UPS) is dependent on intact autophagy for full activity ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30669443 Fischer et al. 2019)]. ''atg5'' single, ''atg5''/''atg12'' double, and ''atg5''/''atg12''/''tipD'' triple knockout mutants revealed similar defects in the conjugation of ATG8 to phosphatidylethanolamine, development, and cell viability indicating that Atg5, Atg12, and TipD act as a functional unit in canonical autophagy. However, distinct and sometimes opposite phenotypes in growth, macropinocytosis, phagocytosis, and proteasomal activity in these mutants reveal autophagy-independent functions for these genes ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/32397394 Karow et al. 2020)]Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 08-DEC-2020 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis and Ricardo Escalante

DDB_G0277399.summary:
Pianissimo, encoded by the ''piaA'' gene, was identified as a mutant unable to aggregate on bacterial lawns. PiaA is a 130-kD cytosolic protein required for chemotaxis and positive regulation of adenylate cyclase activity ([/gene/DDB_G0281545 acaA]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9389653 Chen et al. 1997]).
The HSB1 mutant harbors a point mutation in the ''piaA'' gene, G917D, that causes a temperature-sensitive developmental phenotype: these cells can undergo aggregation and fruiting body formation at temperatures below 18 degrees C but not above. ''in vivo'' HSB1 mutants have defective G protein-linked adenylyl cyclase activation; transfection with the ''piaA'' but not [/gene/DDB_G0285161 dagA] gene rescues the mutant. PiaA is homogenously distributed in the cytoplasm, even after stimulation with chemoattractants ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12413895 Pergolizzi et al. 2002]).
Using Dictyostelium mutants to investigate the minimal requirements for chemotaxis, [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22081140 Kortholt et al. 2011] identified a basal signaling module consisting of heterotrimeric and monomeric G proteins providing activation of Ras at the leading edge, which is sufficient for chemotaxis. The signalling enzymes PI3K, TorC2, PLA2 and sGC are not required for Ras activation and chemotaxis to folate or to steep gradients of cAMP; however they provide a memory of direction and improved orientation of the cell, which together increase the sensitivity about 150-fold for chemotaxis in shallow cAMP gradients.
PiaA is involved in the signal transduction pathway responsible for AprA-dependent ([/gene/DDB_G0281663 aprA]) chemorepulsion. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30462573 Rijal et al. 2018]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 19-SEP-2003 PG

''roco10'' encodes a large, multi-domain protein of the Roco family. Roco10 contains an N-terminal RhoGAP domain, a leucine-rich repeat (LRR) region, a Roc small GTPase domain, a COR (C-terminal of Roc) domain, a protein kinase domain and a C-terminal Kelch-RGS-Kelch module. Eleven ''Dictyostelium'' proteins belong to the Roco family: ([/gene/DDB_G0291079 gbpC]), ([/gene/DDB_G0273259 qkgA-1]), ([/gene/DDB_G0269250 pats1]), ([/gene/DDB_G0288251 roco4]), ([/gene/DDB_G0294533 roco5]), ([/gene/DDB_G0279417 roco6]), ([/gene/DDB_G0267472 roco7]), ([/gene/DDB_G0286127 roco8]), ([/gene/DDB_G0288183 roco9]), Roco10 and ([/gene/DDB_G0268636 roco11]).
Roco10 is localized to the cytosol and ''roco10'' expression is relatively constant throughout growth and development. Disruption of the ''roco10'' gene did not result in any significant developmental defects ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20348387 van Egmond and van Haastert 2010]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 25-OCT-2021 RD

DDB_G0286521.summary:
DNA-dependent RNA polymerase catalyzes the transcription of DNA into RNA using the four ribonucleoside triphosphates as substrates ([/ontology/go/0003899/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase activity]). Three distinct zinc-containing RNA polymerases are found in eukaryotic nuclei: [/gene/DDB_G0275759 rpa1] for the ribosomal RNA precursor ([/ontology/go/0006360/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase I promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005736/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase I complex]), [/gene/DDB_G0279193 rpb1] for the mRNA precursor ([/ontology/go/0006366/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase II promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005665/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase II, core complex]), and [/gene/DDB_G0277199 rpc1] for 5S and tRNA genes ([/ontology/go/0006383/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase III promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005666/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase III complex]).
RNA polymerase III is a multisubunit complex. The subunits encoded by [/gene/DDB_G0277199 rpc1] (ortholog of ''S. cerevisiae RPO31''), [/gene/DDB_G0293560 rpa2] (''RPC2''), [/gene/DDB_G0268080 rpc3] (''RPC82''),[/gene/DDB_G0277671 rpc4] (''RPC53''), [/gene/DDB_G0271514 rpc5] (''RPC37''), [/gene/DDB_G0286521 rpc9] (''RPC17''), [/gene/DDB_G0272022 rpc34] (''RPC34''), [/gene/DDB_G0273425 rpc25-1] (''RPC25''), and [/gene/DDB_G0287707 rpc11] (''RPC11'') are unique to RNA polymerase III. Orthologs of ''RPC31'' and ''RPC17'' have not been identified in the ''Dictyostelium'' genome. Two subunits, [/gene/DDB_G0291362 rpc19] and [/gene/DDB_G0282339 rpa5] (''RPC19'' and ''RPC40'' in ''S. cerevisiae''), are common to RNA polymerase I and RNA polymerase III and correspond to subunits 3 and 11 of RNA polymerase II. Subunits [/gene/DDB_G0291636 rpb5], [/gene/DDB_G0291037 rpb6], [/gene/DDB_G0278039 rpb8], [/gene/DDB_G0272036 rpb10], and [/gene/DDB_G0283365 rpb12] are common to all three RNA polymerases ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12407181 Peyroche et al. 2002], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12381659 Schramm and Hernandez 2001]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 11-JUN-2009 PG

DDB_G0283907.summary:
''pkaC'' encodes the catalytic subunit of the cAMP dependent protein kinase PKA ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1332055 Mann et al. 1992 ], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8373760 Anjard et al. 1993)]. In the absence of cAMP, PKA ([/gene/DDB_G0283907 pkaC], [/gene/DDB_G0279413 pkaR]) exists as an inactive complex of the catalytic and regulatory subunits. cAMP binds cooperatively to two sites on PkaR which leads to the release of active PkaC. This protein kinase plays multiple roles throughout development ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1728597 Harwood et al. 1992], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9126295 Mann et al. 1997], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9729606 Loomis et al. 1998], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25872182 Loomis et al. 2015]). During normal development on a moist surface, mRNA from ''pkaC'' increases smoothly from an initially low level to reach a peak at 20 hours ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25887420 Rosengarten et al. 2015)]. When cells are developed in suspension with addition of 50 nM cAMP every 6 minutes, the level of ''pkaC'' mRNA stays low throughout development. Very few other genes are repressed by cAMP pulses. The regulatory subunit can reassociate with the catalytic subunit and inhibit it when the phosphodiesterase RegA ([/gene/DDB_G0284331 regA]) hydrolyses cAMP bound to PkaR ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9435289 Shaulsky et al. 1998], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20923972 Moorthy et al. 2011)]. As part of the circuit that generates 6 minute oscillations in cAMP during aggregation, PKA activity blocks ERK2 ([/gene/DDB_G0283903 erkB]) inhibition of RegA as well as CRAC ([/gene/DDB_G0285161 dagA]) activation of ACA ([/gene/DDB_G0281545 acaA]) resulting in rapid decrease in the internal concentration of cAMP and a drop in PKA activity ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9020088 Aubry et al. 1997], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9843585 Laub and Loomis et al. 1998], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15131307 Maeda et al. 2004]). PKA plays a role in gradient sensing and chemotaxis to cAMP by regulating the Ras ([/gene/DDB_G0281385 rasC], [/gene/DDB_G0293434 rasG]), Rap1 ([/gene/DDB_G0291237 rapA]) and TORC2 ([/gene/DDB_G0281569 tor]) signaling pathways in response to cAMP. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28302905 Scavello et al. 2017)]. PKA is also part of the signal transduction pathway by which Prestarvation Factor (PSF) stimulates expression of ''carA'' ([/gene/DDB_G0273397 carA-1], [/gene/DDB_G0273533 carA-2]) and ''acaA'' at the initiation of development ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9584128 Souza et al. 1998)]. PSF activates the protein kinase YakA ([/gene/DDB_G0283605 yakA]) such that it inhibits PufA ([/gene/DDB_G0279735 pufA]) which is the translational inhibitor of ''pkaC'' ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10375515 Souza et al. 1999)]. PkaC increases relative to PkaR resulting in constitutive protein kinase activity. PKA also controls gene expression during culmination by regulating the transcription factor SrfA ([/gene/DDB_G0281387 srfA]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12204259 Escalante et al. 2002)]. The peptide signal that prepares prespore and prestalk cells for terminal differentiation, SDF-1, is phosphorylated by PKA ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9373946 Anjard et al. 1997)].
[http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28057864 (Chen et al. 2017)] demonstrated a role for PKA in stalk cell differentiation. Their investigation into the c-di-GMP signal transduction pathway showed that the stalk-inducing signal cyclic diguanylate (c-di-cGMP) produced by diguanylate cyclase ([/gene/DDB_G0283453 dgcA]) activates cAMP synthesis by adenylate cyclase A (ACA) which is specifically expressed at the apical tip. cAMP then activates PKA which then triggers stalk differentiation. PKA ([/gene/DDB_G0283907 pkaC], [/gene/DDB_G0279413 pkaR]) also mediates the response of several xenobiotic compounds, including valproic acid, a treatment for bipolar disorder, [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16759735 (Boeckeler et al. 2006)] and curcumin [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29135990 (Swatson et al. 2017)]. Results presented in ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29440238 Williams et al. 2018)] argue that macropinocytosis is downregulated in early development because of PKA activation. PkaC is involved in the signal transduction pathway responsible for AprA-dependent ([/gene/DDB_G0281663 aprA]) chemorepulsion. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30462573 Rijal et al. 2018]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 10-DEC-2018 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0290551.summary:
The ''rblA'' gene is the Dictyostelium ortholog of the conserved retinoblastoma susceptibility gene Rb. ''rblA'' overexpression during growth leads to G1 arrest, but as growing ''Dictyostelium'' are overwhelmingly in G2 phase, ''rblA'' does not seem to be important in the normal cell cycle. ''rblA'' is expressed predominantly in pre spore cells and the null mutant shows a preference for the stalk pathway during development [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16495312 (MacWilliams et al. 2006)]. Furthermore, it has been suggested that [/gene/DDB_G0285069 btg] genetically interacts with ''rblA'' in cell fate commitment during development [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20300194 (Conte et al. 2010)].
Using microarray analysis and mRNA-Seq transcriptional profiling, it has been shown that rblA represses genes whose products are involved in S phase and mitosis. ''rblA'' also activates a set of genes unique to Dictyostelids that function in terminal differentiation during development [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22768168 (Strasser et al. 2012)].
Bakthavatsalam and colleagues showed that RblA is necessary for the autocrine proliferation-inhibiting factor AprA ([/gene/DDB_G0281663 aprA]) to inhibit cell proliferation. In addition, RblA is required for AprA-induced chemorepulsion, indicating that in ''Dictyostelium'', Rb is necessary for a pathway mediating the effects of a chalone [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24390142 (Bakthavatsalam et al. 2014)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 09-DEC-2014 PF

DDB_G0273063.summary:
The lectin Discoidin I binds N-acetylgalactosamine and galactose [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/4517669 (Rosen et al. 1973)]. Discoidin I subunits associate to form a tetramer [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/4858710 (Simpson et al. 1974)] and are expressed from a family of 3 different genes: ''dscA'', ''dscC'' ([/gene/DDB_G0273065 dscC-1]) ([/gene/DDB_G0273885 dscC-2]) and ''dscD'' ([/gene/DDB_G0273067 dscD-1]) ([/gene/DDB_G0273887 dscD-2]). [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6279874 (Poole et al. 1981)]. Monomeric discoidin I is located mainly in the cytosol, while the tetrameric form of discoidin I is detected in multilamellar bodies and is externalized during aggregation [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2581974 (Barondes et al. 1985)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8416797 (Fukuzawa et al. 1993)]. Discoidin I gene expression is induced by prestarvation factor (PSF) and conditioned medium factor, ([/gene/DDB_G0275007 cmfA]) but is down-regulated by cAMP [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7641976 (Blusch et al. 1995)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2049883 (Rathi et al. 1991)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1663029 (Gomer et al. 1991)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2196444 (Vauti et al. 1990)]. Mutants defective in discoidin I fail to stream during aggregation, implicating discoidin I in cell-substrate adhesion [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6509552 (Springer et al. 1984)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/4075402 (Crowley et al. 1985)]. In addition, discoidin I is thought to play an intracellular role, as mutants in which discoidin genes are not expressed also have an abnormally centered microtubule organizing center and more rounded cell morphology, suggesting a role for discoidins in cytoskeleton organization during aggregation [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1334012 (Alexander et al. 1992)].
''Dictyostelium discoideum'' strains that carry bacteria secrete approx. 80 times higher levels of DscA and DscC than non-carriers. Secreted DscA binds to ''Klebsiella pneumoniae''. DscA binding protects bacteria from extracellular killing, promotes their internalization and prolongs their retention in both ''Dictyostelium discoideum'' and mammalian cells. Plant lectins induce the same response, suggesting that modified uptake and persistence of lectin-coated bacteria in eukaryotic cells is a general phenomenon, termed lectin-induced modified bacterial internalization [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30049880 (Dinh et al. 2018)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 10-AUG-2018 RD

DDB_G0268760.summary: ''rabQ'' encodes a guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G protein) of the Rab family of small GTPases. G proteins are key components of signal transduction networks in which they function as molecular signaling switches, binding to GDP in the off state while binding GTP in the on state. Guanine nucleotide-exchange factors (GEFs) promote the exchange of GDP for GTP on Rab GTPases thus activating them, while GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) inactivate Rab GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP. A genome-wide DNA microarray analysis revealed that ''rabQ'' expression is down-regulated during phagocytosis ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18559084 Sillo, et al. 2008]), and a proteomic analysis revealed that RabQ is found in lipid droplets ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24036346 Du, et al. 2013]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 27-JAN-2021 RD

DDB_G0269272.summary: ''mtm6'' encodes myotubularin phosphatase, a member of the well conserved myotubularin family. Mtm6 localizes to the leading-edge plasma membrane of migrating cells, as well as to macropinocytic cups. The plasma membrane localization of Mtm6 was abolished in a quintuple PI3K null mutant ([/gene/DDB_G0278727 pikA]), ([/gene/DDB_G0283081 pikB]), ([/gene/DDB_G0275011 pikC]), ([/gene/DDB_G0268548 pikF]), ([/gene/DDB_G0282625 pikG]), but greatly enhanced in ''pten'' ([/gene/DDB_G0286557 pten]) null cells. Mtm6 binds specifically to phosphatidylinositol-3,4,5-trisphosphate (PIP3) and phosphatidylinositol-3,4-bisphosphate (PI(3,4)P2), and has phosphatidylinositol-3,5-bisphosphate phosphatase activity. In ''mtm6'' null cells, the level of trailing edge protein Teep1 ([/gene/DDB_G0277777 teep1]) associated with the plasma membrane is slightly increased. Taken together, these results suggest that Mtm6 likely mediates the removal of PI(3,5)P2 from the front of migrating cells, and the formation of a reverse PI(3,5)P2 gradient on the plasma membrane, which in turn regulates the localization of cell trailing edge membrane proteins (Li, et al 2022, PMID:35186938).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 03-MAR-2022 RD

DDB_G0267432.summary: The ABC superfamily of genes is one of the largest in the genomes of both bacteria and eukaryotes. The proteins encoded by these genes all carry a characteristic 200- to 250-amino-acid ATP-binding cassette that gives them their family name ([/ontology/go/0042626/annotation/page/1 ATPase activity, coupled to transmembrane movement of substances]). In bacteria they are mostly involved in nutrient import, while in eukaryotes many are involved in export ([/ontology/go/0006810/annotation/page/1 transport]). Seven different families have been defined in eukaryotes based on sequence homology, domain topology, and function. Sequences from the well-advanced ''Dictyostelium'' genome project have allowed to recognize 71 members of this superfamily (including one on the chromosome 2 duplication). The ABCG family is characterized by the ABC domain preceding the transmembrane domain ([/ontology/go/0016021/annotation/page/1 integral to membrane]). All of the members of this family in animals are half-transporters while all of the fungal members are full transporters with two ABC-transmembrane units. No members of this family are found in bacteria. ''Dictyostelium'' and ''Arabidopsis'' have members of both types ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12456012 Anjard and Loomis 2002]). Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 18-OCT-2004 PG

DDB_G0291185.summary:
Histones form the nucleosomal core ([/ontology/go/0000786/annotation/page/1 nucleosome]) ([/ontology/go/0006334/annotation/page/1 nucleosome assembly]) that is fundamental to chromatin structure (). The histone octamer is composed of an H3-H4 tetramer (two H3-H4 dimers) coupled with an H2A-H2Btetramer (two H2A-H2B dimers). The histone H1 linker protein plays a role in packaging nucleosomes into the 30 nmfiber found in chromatin ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9177486 Bukenberger et al. 1992]).
In ''Dictyostelium discoideum'' and ''Saccharomyces cerevisiae'', only one copy of histone [/gene/DDB_G0285319 H1] appears to be present, in comparison to other eukaryotes which have multiple copies and subtypes([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7867938 Hauser et al. 1995], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9046096 Ushinsky et al.1997]). Two putative H2A family members, [/gene/DDB_G0279667 H2AX] and [/gene/DDB_G0286747 H2AZ], and three H2Adomain-containing proteins, [/gene/DDB_G0289187 H2Av1], [/gene/DDB_G0289193 H2Av2], [/gene/DDB_G0289197 H2Av3], are present in ''Dictyostelium''. Two H2B domain-containing proteins also exist inthe ''Dicty'' genome: [/gene/DDB_G0293758 H2Bv1] and [/gene/DDB_G0276273 H2Bv2]. There are three histone H3proteins, [/gene/DDB_G0267402 H3a] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9177486 Bukenberger et al. 1992]), [/gene/DDB_G0270838 H3b], and [/gene/DDB_G0271092 H3c], and two H3 domain-containing proteins, [/gene/DDB_G0291185 H3v1] and [/gene/DDB_G0277979 H3v2]. We have also identified two histone H4proteins, [/gene/DDB_G0277183 H4a] and [/gene/DDB_G0276863 H4b], which have identical protein sequences but non-identical nucleotide sequences.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 13-APR-2004 KP

DDB_G0269196.summary: ''tubC'' encodes gamma-tubulin which is localized at the center of the microtubule aster where it forms a complex with Spc98 ([/gene/DDB_G0283909 spc98]) to nucleate polymerization of alpha/beta ??/?? tubulin (tubA, tubB) ([/gene/DDB_G0287689 tubA]), ([/gene/DDB_G0269196 tubB]) dimers [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9275182  (Ueda et al. 1997)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9427688  (Euteneuer et al. 1998)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12018385  (Daunderer and Graf, 2002)]. Microtubules radiate from centrosomes that are found ahead of the nucleus in migrating cells. The centrosome is repositioned shortly after the extension of a new pseudopod. If no reorientation occurs within 30 seconds of the extension, the pseudopod is retracted. Centrosomes appear to stabilize the direction of movement rather than establishing where the cell will go. The morphological changes in centrosomes were followed through the cell cycle by labelling the organelle with GFP fused to gamma- ??-tubulin (Ueda, Schliwa and Euteneuer, 1999 9880333). About 100 different proteins contribute to centrosomal functions including the products of ''tubC'', ([/gene/DDB_G0285849 spc97]), ([/gene/DDB_G0283909 spc98]), ([/gene/DDB_G0288427 cenA]), ([/gene/DDB_G0288375 lis1]), ([/gene/DDB_G0270814 nek2]), ([/gene/DDB_G0283607 eb1]), ([/gene/DDB_G0268616 cepJ]), ([/gene/DDB_G0278809 cepG]). [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15548420  (Graf et al. 2004)]. The abundance of ''tubC'' mRNA is less than 2% that of tubA mRNA in growing cells but increases rapidly between 10 and 14 hours of development, mostly in prestalk cells [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25887420  (Rosengarten et al. 2015)]. ''tubC'' may have a critical role during culmination.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 06-NOV-2017 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis
