DDB_G0273635.summary:
QkgA (Roco2) contains an N-terminal leucine-rich repeat (LRR) motif similar to that of human LRRK2, in addition to the Roc (Ras-like), COR, and kinase domains present in eukaryotic Roco proteins. Eleven ''Dictyostelium'' proteins belong to the Roco family: [/gene/DDB_G0291079 gbpC], [/gene/DDB_G0273259 qkgA-1], [/gene/DDB_G0269250 pats1], [/gene/DDB_G0288251 roco4], [/gene/DDB_G0294533 roco5], [/gene/DDB_G0279417 roco6], [/gene/DDB_G0267472 roco7], [/gene/DDB_G0286127 roco8], [/gene/DDB_G0288183 roco9], [/gene/DDB_G0291710 roco10], and [/gene/DDB_G0268636 roco11]. Disruption of ''qkgA'' causes a marked increase in growth rate, indicating a role in the negative regulation of cell proliferation, and aggregation occurs relatively slowly resulting in abnormally large multicellular structures ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12954783 Abe et al. 2003]). QkgA is involved in a signal transduction network through the autocrine proliferation repressor AprA ([/gene/DDB_G0281663 aprA]). Similar to ''aprA'' and counting factor associated protein CfaD ([/gene/DDB_G0281605 cfaD]) null mutants, ''qkgA'' null cells proliferate to a higher cell density than wild type cells and tend to be multinucleate. In addition, ''qkgA'' null cells are insensitive to exogenous AprA and CfaD, indicating that QkgA is required for AprA and CfaD-mediated inhibition of proliferation ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20709790 Phillips and Gomer, 2010]). Wild-type cells adjacent to a source of recombinant AprA (rAprA) showed a significant bias in displacement away from rApA, whereas G protein alpha 8 ([/gene/DDB_G0284469 gpaH]), ''qkgA'', and ''cfaD'' null cells did not. These results indicate that AprA also functions as a chemorepellent, and that that Galpha8, QkgA, and CfaD are necessary for the chemorepellant effect of AprA ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22711818 Phillips and Gomer, 2012]).
''qkgA'' is a key regulator of the actin cytoskeleton during chemotaxis. QkgA is activated in response to chemoattractant stimulation, localizes to the pseudopodium, and binds to both the rab family GTPase ([/gene/DDB_G0283757 rab1A]) and filamin ([/gene/DDB_G0269100 abpC]). Constitutively active Rab1A pulls down 5 x more Roco2 than wild type Rab1A while dominant-negative Rab1A fails to interact with it, suggesting that activated Rab1A positively regulates Roco2 activity. ''qkgA'' null cells have defects in cell motility and chemotaxis to cAMP, aggregation and cytokinesis. ''qkgA'' null cells also display decreased chemoattractant-mediated F-actin polymerization. These results reveal a signal transduction pathway in which Rab1A activates Roco2 kinase which in turn mediates cell polarization and chemotaxis by regulating cortical F-actin polymerization and pseudopod extension. A major function of Roco2 is to stabilize the nascent pseudopod and enhance F-actin polymerization, in part through its downstream effector filamin ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21551065 Kicka et al. 2011]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 19-OCT-2020 RD

DDB_G0285343.summary:
Transcription factor IIA (TFIIA) is one of several factors that form part of a transcription preinitiation complex along with [/gene/DDB_G0288257 rpb2], the TATA-box-binding protein (TBP, encoded by the [/gene/DDB_G0275617 tbpA] gene)and TBP-associated factors (TAFs) on the TATA-box sequence upstream of the initiation start site. TFIIA binds to TBP to stabilise TBP binding to the TATA element. In yeast, TFIIA is dispensable for accurate initiation of transcription but plays an important role in transcriptional activation, functioning as either an antirepressor or a coactivator.
Human TFIIA and Drosophila TFIIA are composed of three subunits. The two larger subunits (alpha and beta) are encoded by the same gene and appear to be posttranslationally modified forms of a precursor protein. In yeast, two genes TOA1 and TOA2 are homologs of the large and the small subunits, respectively (reviewed by [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9618449 Hampsey] in 1998). In ''Dictyostelium'', [/gene/DDB_G0290327 gtf2a1] encodes the large (alpha/beta) subunits and [/gene/DDB_G0285343 gtf2a2] encodes the small (gamma) subunit. DDB_G0293006.summary: ''gefF'' encodes a Ras guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF, RasGEF). rasGEFs are key components of signaling networks in which they activate Ras family small GTPases by promoting the exchange of GDP for GTP. ''gefF'' is expressed throughout growth and development, with maximum expression at 4 hours. Attempts to knock out ''gefF'' were unsuccessful suggesting that it plays an essential role ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16086850 Wilkins et al. 2005)]. Gain-of-function experiments show that macropinocytosis is stimulated by persistent Ras activation and genetic analysis suggests that RasG ([/gene/DDB_G0293434 rasG]) and RasS ([/gene/DDB_G0283537 rasS]) are the key Ras proteins involved. GefF has GEF activity towards RasG (unpublished results, cited in [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30967009 Williams et al. 2019)]. GefF normally localizes to macropinocytic cups, but is unable to do so in a ''gefF'' knock-in mutant. In addition, a ''gefF'' insertional mutant is defective in fluid phase uptake and macropinosome formation, revealing a role for ''gefF'' in macropinocytosis ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30967009 Williams et al. 2019)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 06-APR-2021 RD

GefG contains two F-box domains, motifs associated with ubiquitination and protein breakdown rather than with upstream signaling. ''gefG'' is weakly expressed, and transcripts could only be detected at 12 and 14 hours of development. Growth, morphology, phototaxis and fruiting body morphology are normal in a ''gefG'' null mutant ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16086850 Wilkins et al. 2005)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 06-APR-2021 RD

DDB_G0282813.summary: ''arcB'' encodes the 34 kDa subunit of the Arp2/3 complex [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11807934  (Insall et al. 2001)]. The seven subunits of this 200 kDa complex are encoded by ([/gene/DDB_G0277825 arcA]), ''arcB'', ([/gene/DDB_G0292804 arcC]), ([/gene/DDB_G0269102 arcD]), ([/gene/DDB_G0288319 arcE]), ([/gene/DDB_G0272106 arpB]) and ([/gene/DDB_G0283755 arpC]). The subunits of mammalian Arp2/3 are very similar to ''Dictyostelium'' homologs. Arp2/3 binds to the side of F-actin filaments and initiates polymerization of a new F-actin chain at an angle of 70 degrees leading to a branched actin network that can alter the shape of cells. The ability to nucleate new actin filaments is greatly stimulated by direct interactions with members of the WASP/SCAR family [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11807934  (Insall et al. 2001)]. The Arp2/3 complex largely mediates the actin polymerization response to chemotactic stimulation and contributes to cell motility, pseudopod extension and adhesion in Dictyostelium chemotaxis. The complete Arp2/3 complex is essential for growth; partial loss of activity of either ArcB or ArpB impairs growth and chemotaxis [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17553489  (Langridge and Kay, 2007)]. mRNA from each of the genes encoding Arp2/3 subunits accumulates coordinately to reach a peak at 3 hours of development and gradually decreases thereafter [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25887420  (Rosengarten et al. 2015)]. The Arp2/3 complex interacts with the protein CARMIL, which serves as a scaffold for the assembly of a larger complex of proteins involved in the nucleation and termination of actin filament assembly. The complex consists of CARMIL ([/gene/DDB_G0292386 carmil]), AcpA, ([/gene/DDB_G0267374 acpA]) AcpB, ([/gene/DDB_G0272104 acpB]) the Arp2/3 complex, and type I myosins MyoB ([/gene/DDB_G0289117 myoB]) and MyoC ([/gene/DDB_G0276617 myoC]) [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11425877  (Jung et al. 2001)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 23-MAY-2019 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0293450.summary: The ABC superfamily of genes is one of the largest in the genomes of both bacteria and eukaryotes. The proteins encoded by these genes all carry a characteristic 200- to 250-amino-acid ATP-binding cassette that gives them their family name ([/ontology/go/0042626/annotation/page/1 ATPase activity, coupled to transmembrane movement of substances]). In bacteria they are mostly involved in nutrient import, while in eukaryotes many are involved in export ([/ontology/go/0006810/annotation/page/1 transport]). Seven different families have been defined in eukaryotes based on sequence homology, domain topology, and function. Sequences from the well-advanced ''Dictyostelium'' genome project have allowed to recognize 71 members of this superfamily (including one on the chromosome 2 duplication). The ABCG family is characterized by the ABC domain preceding the transmembrane domain ([/ontology/go/0016021/annotation/page/1 integral to membrane]). All of the members of this family in animals are half-transporters while all of the fungal members are full transporters with two ABC-transmembrane units. No members of this family are found in bacteria. ''Dictyostelium'' and ''Arabidopsis'' have members of both types ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12456012 Anjard and Loomis 2002]). Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 18-OCT-2004 PG

DDB_G0284171.summary: The CHD (chromodomain-helicase-DNA binding) protein family is one of the major ATP-dependent, chromatin remodeling factors that regulate nucleosome positioning and access of transcription factors and RNA polymerase to the eukaryotic genome. ''chdA'' null cells exhibited a significant delay at the onset of culmination and displayed reduced chemotaxis to cAMP. Genome-wide (RNA-seq) transcriptome profiling for each CHD null strain revealed that the different CHDs regulate distinct gene sets during both growth and development. DDB_G0293524.summary:
''Dictyostelium'' [/gene/DDB_G0293524 ppk1] is highly similar to bacterial PPK, which exhibits polyphosphate kinase activity inresponse to stress and starvation. PPK synthesizes long chains of polyphosphate (poly P), however, the ''ppk1-''mutant retains a low level of polyphospate kinase activity. The remaining kinase activity (DdPKK2 activity) is attributed,interestingly, to three proteins identified using mass spectrometry: [/gene/DDB_G0288937 arpA], [/gene/DDB_G0272106 arpB], and[/gene/DDB_G0289511 act28]. Inhibition of these three actin-related proteins with reagents affecting actinpolymerization (such as phalloidin) concomitantly inhibits poly P formation ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15496465 Gómez-García and Kornberg 2004]).
Disruption of the ''ppk1'' gene results in low levels of poly P and a growth defect attributed to a phagocytosis defect. In addition, the ''ppk1'' mutant exhibits delayed culmination and a significantly reduced number of spore cells. In addition to its functions in development and phagocytosis ppk1 plays a role in the late stages of cytokinesis [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15701689 Zhang et al. 2005]).
[http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26755590 Livermore et al. 2016] also generated a ''ppk1'' null mutant and confirmed that ''ppk1'' is the sole enzyme responsible for polyP synthesis in ''Dictyostelium''. Their investigations revealed that polyP regulates basic metabolism, general fitness, and spore germination. In addition, they discovered a massive increase in the level of polyP during developmental progression which is linked to the accumulation of inositol pyrophosphates. Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 18-JAN-2016 RD

DDB_G0270122.summary: ''rasW'' encodes a guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G protein) of the Ras family of small GTPases. G proteins are key components of signal transduction networks in which they function as molecular signaling switches, binding to GDP in the off state while binding GTP in the on state. Guanine nucleotide-exchange factors (GEFs, rasGEFs) promote the exchange of GDP for GTP on Ras GTPases thus activating them, while GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs, rasGAPs) inactivate Ras GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP. An analysis of ''Dictyostelium'' ras family genes reveals that ''rasU'' ([/gene/DDB_G0270138 rasU]), ''rasV'' ([/gene/DDB_G0270736 rasV]), ''rasW'', ''rasX'' ([/gene/DDB_G0270124 rasX]), ''rasY'' ([/gene/DDB_G0270126 rasY]) and ''rasZ'' ([/gene/DDB_G0270140 rasZ]) form a separate phylogenetic clade ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29614268 Park et al. 2018]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 24-MAR-2020 RD

DDB_G0272208.summary: Isocitrate dehydrogenases are important enzymes of carbohydrate metabolism, which catalyze the oxidative decarboxylation of isocitrate into alpha-ketoglutarate (). IdhC and IdhM are very similar to the corresponding proteins in mammals, which are thought to form homodimers.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 08-FEB-2005 PF

DDB_G0293848.summary:
In mammalian cells, phosducin binds to G proteins and modulate their activity. Phylogenetic analyses revealed that there are three groups of phodsucin proteins. ''Dictyostelium'', like mammalian cells and ''Drosophila'', has one member from each group: [/gene/DDB_G0292850 phlp1], [/gene/DDB_G0285433 phlp2], and [/gene/DDB_G0293848 phlp3]. Phosducins consist of an N-terminal domain containing three helices which binds the alpha subunit of G proteins, and a C-terminal domain which bears similarity to thioredoxin and binds to the beta/gamma subunit of G proteins.
Phlp3 completely lacks the helix involved in G beta/gamma binding. Disruption of the ''phlp3'' gene caused no defect in growth, development, or chemotaxis ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/199357 Blaauw et al. 2003]). Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 18-JUN-2008 PG

DDB_G0288879.summary:
There are 29 genes encoding actin in ''Dictyostelium'' with amino acid identity greater than 83%, ''act1''-''act29''. Seventeen of these genes encode identical proteins: [/gene/DDB_G0289553 act1], [/gene/DDB_G0274133 act2], [/gene/DDB_G0289005 act4], [/gene/DDB_G0289663 act5], [/gene/DDB_G0274135 act6], [/gene/DDB_G0280545 act7], [/gene/DDB_G0269234 act8], [/gene/DDB_G0274601 act9], [/gene/DDB_G0288879 act11], [/gene/DDB_G0274129 act12], [/gene/DDB_G0274599 act13], [/gene/DDB_G0274137 act14], [/gene/DDB_G0272520 act15], [/gene/DDB_G0272248 act16], [/gene/DDB_G0274727 act19], [/gene/DDB_G0274285 act20], and [/gene/DDB_G0274561 act21], while [/gene/DDB_G0289811 act10], [/gene/DDB_G0275023 act22], and [/gene/DDB_G0289487 act3] respectively have 1, 4 and 11 amino acid differences compared to the 17 identical genes. The proteins encoded by [/gene/DDB_G0274131 act17], [/gene/DDB_G0289489 act18], [/gene/DDB_G0268744 act23] and [/gene/DDB_G0289505 act24]are more divergent.
Actin is a major [/ontology/go/0005200/annotation/page/1 structural constituent of cytoskeleton]. Actin is one of the most abundant proteins in ''Dictyostelium'', constituting approximately 8% of the total protein in vegetative cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/561722 Alton and Lodish et al. 1977]).Actin synthesis is developmentally regulated, peaking shortly after starvation (reviewed by [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6894564 Firtel] in 1981). The different actin genes differ in their levels of expression, with [/gene/DDB_G0274135 act6], [/gene/DDB_G0269234 act8] and [/gene/DDB_G0274129 act12] being highly expressed both during growth and development compared to [/gene/DDB_G0289005 act4], [/gene/DDB_G0289663 act5], [/gene/DDB_G0280545 act7] and [/gene/DDB_G0272248 act16] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6286214 McKeown and Firtel 1981]). Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 19-SEP-2003 PG

DDB_G0277829.summary:
A family of four highly related G-protein coupled receptors, CAR1, CAR2, CAR3, and CAR4 (genes ''[/gene/DDB_G0273397 carA-1]'' ''[/gene/DDB_G0288179 carB]'', ''[/gene/DDB_G0277829 carC]'', ''[/gene/DDB_G0277831 carD]'', respectively), mediate developmental responses to cAMP [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2049880 (Saxe et al., 1991]; [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7496377 Ginsburg et al., 1995)]. CAR1 and CAR3 have 56% amino acid identity and show approximately equal affinity to cAMP in vitro [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1537842 (Johnson et al., 1992)]. Both are coupled to trimeric G proteins with the Galpha2 subunit. CAR1 is expressed immediately after the initiation of development while CAR3 onset of expression is in tight aggregates. There are approximately 5,000 CAR3 sites per cell. Disruption of carC does not result in an obvious phenotype [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8382181 (Johnson et al., 1993)]. Disruption of ''carA'' on the other hand results in cells that are unable to aggregate but can still respond to added cAMP by relaying the signal and synthesizing cGMP as long as 100X higher concentrations of cAMP are used than needed for signaling in wild type cells. However, a double ''carA'' / ''carC'' mutant lacking both receptors shows no response to cAMP and an abolished synthesis of cGMP phenotype [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7949426 (Insall et al., 1994)].
CAR3 has a high affinity for cAMP and activates GSK3 (gene ''[/gene/DDB_G0272110 gskA]'') by stimulating the protein tyrosine kinase ZAK1 (gene ''[/gene/DDB_G0276025 zakA]''; [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15380246 Kimmel and Firtel, 2004)]. On the other hand, the lower affinity CAR4 receptor stimulates a protein tyrosine phosphatase that removes the phosphate from GSK3, reducing its activity [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12408804 (Kim et al., 2002]. Thus, CAR3 and CAR4 antagonistically regulate GSK3 to establish cell fate choice. CAR3 signaling favors prespore differentiation and CAR4 signaling favors prestalk differentiation [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12408804 (Kim et al., 2002)]. It has been suggested that cell-type specific expression of receptors with different affinities for cAMP directs pattern formation in response to regional differences in cAMP concentration ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7958880 Louis et al., 1994)]. Further studies indicated that the switching of cAMP receptor subtypes during development enables the organism to respond to changing concentrations of the chemoattractant and thus program morphogenesis appropriately [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9578623 (Kim et al., 1998)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 30-OCT-2015 PF; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0289661.summary:
[/gene/DDB_G0283391 kinX] and [/gene/DDB_G0289661 kinY] are similar to the kinase domains of the LISK (LIM domain and testis-specific kinase) family of protein kinases ([/ontology/go/0004672/annotation/page/1 protein kinase activity]). Members of the LISK family in metazoans have been shown toplay a role in actin filament dynamics, however, the LISK kinases found in ''Dictyostelium'' do not contain LIMdomains. The ''kinX'' transcript is weakly detected at constant levels throughout development, whereas ''kinY''is expressed at low levels during growth, increasing throughout development with a peak during culmination.Additionally, ''kinY'' is enriched in the prespore cells of slugs ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7857991 Wetterauer et al.1995], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10899639 Wetterauer 2000]).
Seven putative LISK proteins exist in the ''Dictyostelium'' proteome: [/gene/DDB_G0275165 DDB_G0275165], [/gene/DDB_G0271538 DDB_G0271538], [/gene/DDB_G0269298 gefX], [/gene/DDB_G0281745 DDB_G0281745], [/gene/DDB_G0280461 DDB_G0280461], [/gene/DDB_G0271402 DDB_G0271402], [/gene/DDB_G0289859 kxcA].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 04-OCT-2004 KP

DDB_G0285427.summary: The ''mkcA'' gene was, along with [/gene/DDB_G0284331 regA], discovered in a screen for genetic suppressors of the [/gene/DDB_G0286119 tagB] mutation. Disruption of ''mkcA'' results in partial suppression of the block to spore formation following the loss of the prestalk gene ''tagB''. Expression of prestalk marker genes [/gene/DDB_G0277853 ecmA] and [/gene/DDB_G0269132 ecmB] in ''mkcA'' null cells is strongly reduced, while the prespore marker [/gene/DDB_G0276761 cotB] is not affected. ''mkcA'' encodes a putative serine/threonine kinase ([/ontology/go/0004674/annotation/page/1 protein serine/threonine kinase activity]) that belongs to the STE20/PAKA family, mitogen-activated protein kinases involved in signalling. Genetic interaction with the ''tagB'' intercellular signalling defects suggest that ''mkcA'' is part of the pathway that regulates cell differentiation ([/ontology/go/0045595/annotation/page/1 regulation of cell differentiation]) in ''Dictyostelium'' [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8986798  (Shaulsky et al., 1996)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 18-OCT-2004 PF

DDB_G0288449.summary:
DNA-dependent RNA polymerase catalyzes the transcription of DNA into RNA using the four ribonucleoside triphosphates as substrates ([/ontology/go/0003899/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase activity]). Three distinct zinc-containing RNA polymerases are found in eukaryotic nuclei: [/gene/DDB_G0275759 rpa1] for the ribosomal RNA precursor ([/ontology/go/0006360/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase I promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005736/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase I complex]), [/gene/DDB_G0279193 rpb1] for the mRNA precursor ([/ontology/go/0006366/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase II promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005665/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase II, core complex]), and [/gene/DDB_G0277199 rpc1] for 5S and tRNA genes ([/ontology/go/0006383/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase III promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005666/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase III complex]).
RNA polymerase III is a multisubunit complex. The subunits encoded by [/gene/DDB_G0277199 rpc1] (ortholog of ''S. cerevisiae RPO31''), [/gene/DDB_G0293560 rpa2] (''RPC2''), [/gene/DDB_G0268080 rpc3] (''RPC82''),[/gene/DDB_G0277671 rpc4] (''RPC53''), [/gene/DDB_G0271514 rpc5] (''RPC37''), [/gene/DDB_G0272022 rpc34] (''RPC34''), [/gene/DDB_G0273425 rpc25-1] (''RPC25''), and [/gene/DDB_G0287707 rpc11] (''RPC11'') are unique to RNA polymerase III. Orthologs of ''RPC31'' and ''RPC17'' have not been identified in the ''Dictyostelium'' genome. Two subunits, [/gene/DDB_G0291362 rpc19] and [/gene/DDB_G0282339 rpa5] (''RPC19'' and ''RPC40'' in ''S. cerevisiae''), are common to RNA polymerase I and RNA polymerase III and correspond to subunits 3 and 11 of RNA polymerase II. Subunits [/gene/DDB_G0291636 rpb5], [/gene/DDB_G0291037 rpb6], [/gene/DDB_G0278039 rpb8], [/gene/DDB_G0272036 rpb10], and [/gene/DDB_G0283365 rpb12] are common to all three RNA polymerases ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12407181 Peyroche et al. 2002], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12381659 Schramm and Hernandez 2001]).
''rpc2'' contains an intein; it is the only gene in the ''Dictyostelium'' genome to have such a feature ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17069655 Goodwin et al. 2006]). Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 11-JUN-2009 PG

DDB_G0286747.summary:
Histones form the nucleosomal core ([/ontology/go/0000786/annotation/page/1 nucleosome]) ([/ontology/go/0006334/annotation/page/1 nucleosome assembly]) that is fundamental to chromatin structure (). The histone octamer is composed of an H3-H4 tetramer (two H3-H4 dimers) coupled with an H2A-H2Btetramer (two H2A-H2B dimers). The histone H1 linker protein plays a role in packaging nucleosomes into the 30 nmfiber found in chromatin ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9177486 Bukenberger et al. 1992]).
In ''Dictyostelium discoideum'' and ''Saccharomyces cerevisiae'', only one copy of histone [/gene/DDB_G0285319 H1] appears to be present, in comparison to other eukaryotes which have multiple copies and subtypes([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7867938 Hauser et al. 1995], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9046096 Ushinsky et al.1997]). Two putative H2A family members, [/gene/DDB_G0279667 H2AX] and [/gene/DDB_G0286747 H2AZ], and three H2Adomain-containing proteins, [/gene/DDB_G0289187 H2Av1], [/gene/DDB_G0289193 H2Av2], [/gene/DDB_G0289197 H2Av3], are present in ''Dictyostelium''. Two H2B domain-containing proteins also exist inthe ''Dicty'' genome: [/gene/DDB_G0293758 H2Bv1] and [/gene/DDB_G0276273 H2Bv2]. There are three histone H3proteins, [/gene/DDB_G0267402 H3a] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9177486 Bukenberger et al. 1992]), [/gene/DDB_G0270838 H3b], and [/gene/DDB_G0271092 H3c], and two H3 domain-containing proteins, [/gene/DDB_G0291185 H3v1] and [/gene/DDB_G0277979 H3v2]. We have also identified two histone H4proteins, [/gene/DDB_G0277183 H4a] and [/gene/DDB_G0276863 H4b], which have identical protein sequences but non-identical nucleotide sequences.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 13-APR-2004 KP

DDB_G0274121.summary: The ABC superfamily of genes is one of the largest in the genomes of both bacteria and eukaryotes. The proteins encoded by these genes all carry a characteristic 200- to 250-amino-acid ATP-binding cassette that gives them their family name ([/ontology/go/0042626/annotation/page/1 ATPase activity, coupled to transmembrane movement of substances]). In bacteria they are mostly involved in nutrient import, while in eukaryotes many are involved in export ([/ontology/go/0006810/annotation/page/1 transport]), ([/ontology/go/0016021/annotation/page/1 integral to membrane]). Seven different families (A to G) have been defined in eukaryotes based on sequence homology, domain topology, and function. ''Dictyostelium'' has 71 ABC transporters (including one on the chromosome 2 duplication) and 11 ABCA family members: [/gene/DDB_G0291994 abcA1], [/gene/DDB_G0267438 abcA2], [/gene/DDB_G0293436 abcA3], [/gene/DDB_G0274121 abcA4], [/gene/DDB_G0274119 abcA5], [/gene/DDB_G0291245 abcA6], [/gene/DDB_G0271140 abcA7], [/gene/DDB_G0271138 abcA8],[/gene/DDB_G0291980 abcA9], [/gene/DDB_G0283387 abcA10], and [/gene/DDB_G0275453 abcA11],One of the defining characteristics of the A family is the presence of a regulatory domain with multiple sites for phosphorylation by various protein kinases in the region after the first ABC domain [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12456012 (Anjard and Loomis 2002)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 16-JUN-2003 PG

DDB_G0273127.summary:
The homeodomain is a sequence-specific DNA binding motif that consists of a helix-turn-helix. Homeobox-containing proteins have transcription factor activity. They have beenidentified in most if not all phyla of eukaryotes. Inmetazoans, homeobox-containing proteins are known to be involvedin regulating the anterior-posterior body plan and in thespecification of certain cell types and anterior-posteriorcompartments (see [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9486804 Han and Firtel 1998] and references therein). There are 14 predicted proteins that contain homeobox domains in ''Dictyostelium'':[/gene/DDB_G0275173 hbx2], [/gene/DDB_G0291075 warA], [/gene/DDB_G0291197 hbx3], [/gene/DDB_G0272967 hbx4], [/gene/DDB_G0273127 hbx5-1] (on the chromosome 2 duplication: [/gene/DDB_G0273645 hbx5-2]), [/gene/DDB_G0277505 hbx6], [/gene/DDB_G0278225 hbx7], [/gene/DDB_G0279257 hbx8], [/gene/DDB_G0280473 hbx9], [/gene/DDB_G0284293 hbx10], [/gene/DDB_G0295787 hbx11], [/gene/DDB_G0286733 hbx12], [/gene/DDB_G0288975 hbx13], and [/gene/DDB_G0289677 hbx14].
[http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25963254 Mishra and Saran 2015] performed a genome-wide classification and comparative genomic analysis of the 14 homeobox genes present in D. discoideum, and found that they could be classified into 3 groups: TALE, OTHER and NOVEL classes, ''hbx5'' belonging to the OTHER class.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 07-JUL-2015 RD

DDB_G0288977.summary: ''iqgC'' encodes a Ras GTPase-activating protein (GAP, rasGAP). RasGAPs are key components of signal transduction networks in which they inactivate Ras GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP. The IQGAP-related protein IqgC contains a Ras GTPase-activating (RasGAP) domain and localizes to macropinosomes and phagosomes. Yeast two-hybrid assay revealed a direct interaction with the active, GTP-bound Ras GTPase RasG ([/gene/DDB_G0293434 rasG]) and IqgC promoted GTPase activity of RasG, confirming that it is a RasGTPase-activating protein that suppresses RasG signaling. ''iqgC'' null cells display an increased rate of macropinocytosis and a slight increase in the size of macropinosomes. ''iqgC'' null cells also have a mild cytokinesis defect and are more efficient in the uptake of both bacteria and yeast than wt cells. These results reveal a role for ''iqgC'' as a negative regulator of macropinocytosis and phagocytosis. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30622175 Marinovic et al. 2019]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 14-MAR-2022 RD

DDB_G0275447.summary:
Besides ''mhcA'' ([/gene/DDB_G0286355 mhcA]) that encodes the classical myosin heavy chain, Dictyostelium carries genes for 12 unconventional myosins. ''myoD'' encodes myosin ID which has an N-terminal motor domain with an actin-activated ATPase and a carboxy terminal domain that is rich in glycine, proline and alanine and can bind actin [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8325874 (Jung et al. 1993)]. MyoD associates with a 16 kDa light chain encoded by ''mlcD'' ([/gene/DDB_G0277917 mlcD]) that has about 48% sequence identity with calmodulin ([/gene/DDB_G0279407 calA]) but has a low affinity for calcium. [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12826013 (De La Roche et al. 2003)] ''myoD'' mRNA is abundant during the first two hours of development, decreases to a minimum at T=7 hrs and then reaccumulates to a peak at T=11 hrs. ''mlcD'' is coordinately expressed with ''myoD'' [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25887420 (Rosengarten et al. 2015)].
The tail homology (TH1) domain of MyoD binds to phosphatidylinositol-3,4,5-trisphosphate (PIP3) which accumulates at the front of cells where the PI3kinases are active and PTEN ([/gene/DDB_G0286557 pten]) is excluded [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22296834 (Chen et al. 2012)]. Although MyoD is found localized to pseudopods at the leading edge of migating cells, cells lacking MyoD showed no obvious growth or developmental defects [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8325874 (Jung et al. 1993)]. However, triple null mutant cells lacking ''myoD'', ''myoE'' ([/gene/DDB_G0288679 myoE]) and ''myoF'' ([/gene/DDB_G0289177 myoF]) are defective in chemotaxis to cAMP, chemoattractant-stimulated actin polymerization and phagocytosis [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22296834 (Chen et al. 2012)]. The amino acid sequences of MyoD, MyoE, and MyoF are more similar to each other than to other myosins; together they form a group of unconventional myosins involved in growth and development.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 26-AUG-2019 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

The GenBank record has a 12 nt insertion at position 1833 that is not present in the Sequencing Center sequence or any of the ESTs.

DDB_G0274383.summary: ''pdeD'' encodes the cGMP-stimulated cGMP phosphodiesterase which has a beta-lactamase catalytic site followed by two cNMP binding sites, the same order of domains found in the cAMP-activated cAMP phosphodiesterase ''pdeE'' ([/gene/DDB_G0276027 pdeE]) [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12429832  (Bosgraaf et al. 2002)]. ''pdeD'' knock-out strains are "streamers" which are characterized by extensive streams during aggregation [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12429831  (Meima et al. 2002)]. ''stmF'' mutants isolated from chemically mutagenized populations are also "streamers" and have greatly reduced cGMP phosphodiesterase activity, but differ from ''pdeD'' null mutants with respect to cAMP-induced calcium uptake [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15878705  (Lusche et al. 2005)]. cGMP accumulates to high levels in ''pdeD'' null mutants leading to the activation of myosin light chain kinase A ([/gene/DDB_G0279925 mlkA]) during aggregation [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12198158  (Bosgraaf et al. 2002)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16546177  (Goldberg et al. 2006)]. cGMP stimulates phosphorylation of both the myosin regulatory light chain and the myosin heavy chain resulting in an increase in suppression of lateral pseudopods and an improvement in chemotaxis to a stable source of cAMP [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12198158  (Bosgraaf et al. 2002)]. However, knockout mutants of ''pdeD'' are defective in chemotaxis to cAMP, and PdeD is phosphorylated by glycogen synthase kinase GskA ([/gene/DDB_G0272110 gskA]), revealing ''pdeD'' to be a component of the GskA signaling pathway coordinating cell migration in response to cAMP [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29626371  (Baumgardner et al. 2018)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 01-NOV-2018 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0282537.summary:
''rabS'' encodes a guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G protein) of the Rab family of small GTPases. G proteins are key components of signal transduction networks in which they function as molecular signaling switches, binding to GDP in the off state while binding GTP in the on state. Guanine nucleotide-exchange factors (GEFs) promote the exchange of GDP for GTP on Rab GTPases thus activating them, while GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) inactivate Rab GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP. Rab2A is associated with both the Golgi membrane and the contractile vacuole system ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/27240981 Maringer et al. 2016)] and dominant-negative (DN) Rab2A cells also localize to lysosomes and endosomes ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29843387 Yarbrough, et al. 2018]). A genome-wide DNA microarray analysis revealed that ''rabS'' expression is down-regulated in response to ''Pseudomas aeruginosa'' expression ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18590548 Carilla-Latorre, et al. 2008]).
''rabS'' is involved in signaling networks that regulate contractile vacuole function and response to osmotic stress, development, endocytosis, and the secretion of lysosomal enzymes. Similar to ''rab2A'' ([/gene/DDB_G0292268 rab2A]) DN cells, ''rabS'' DN cells lack contractile vacuoles. ''rabS'' and ''rab2A'' over-expressing (OE) and mutant cell lines show defects in osmoregulation indicating that both genes are involved in the regulation of cellular response to osmotic stress ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/27240981 Maringer, et al. 2016]). Cells over-expressing ''rabS'' showed an increase in the rate of both phagocytosis and pinocytosis with a corresponding increase in growth rate. These cells also showed a significant increase in cell mortality. Aggregation is severely defective in ''rabS'' OE cells as these cells have decreased cell-cell adhesion and chemotactic response to cAMP. ''rabS'' OE cells are also unable to complete development and could not form fruiting bodies. Dominant negative ''rabS'' cells display increased endocytic recycling and both OE and DN ''rabS'' cell lines over-secreted lysosomal glycosidase enzymes, especially beta-glucosidase ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29843387 Yarbrough, et al. 2018]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 02-FEB-2021 RD

DDB_G0276399.summary: ''rab8B'' encodes a guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G protein) of the Rab family of small GTPases. DDB_G0272756.summary: Three closely related genes, gene ''[/gene/DDB_G0272833 csbA]'', gene ''[/gene/DDB_G0272562 csbB]'' and gene ''[/gene/DDB_G0272756 csbC]'', encode 12 kDa proteins that form contact site B which functions in cell-cell adhesion during early development [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8626027  (Xu et al., 1996)]. Early adhesion can be blocked by 10 mM EDTA and is mediated by contact site B [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8626027  (Xu et al., 1996)]. Early adhesion can be blocked by 10 mM EDTA and is mediated by contact site B [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/5002049  (Gerisch, 1968]; [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/4993098  Beug, et al.1970)]. Early adhesion can also be blocked by antibodies to a glycoprotein, gp24, encoded by gene ''[/gene/DDB_G0285793 cadA]''cadA [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3569662  (Knecht et al., 1987]; [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8663243  Wong et al., 1996)]. Antibodies to gp24 recognize the fusion protein generated by a lamda gt11 expression construct carrying a portion of the ''csbA'' cDNA [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3149564  (Loomis, 1988)]. Deletion of all 3 ''csb'' genes delayed the appearance of EDTA-resistant adhesion by 6 hours [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8626027  (Xu et al., 1996)]. Expression of ''csbA'' and ''csbB'' is stimulated about 3 fold by cAMP during early development, increases to about 24-fold during aggregation and slowly falls after the slug stage to 3-fold at full culmination compared to vegetative cells [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25887420  (Rosengarten et al., 2015)]. DDB_G0291738.summary: ''rabG1'' encodes a guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G protein) of the Rab family of small GTPases. G proteins are key components of signal transduction networks in which they function as molecular signaling switches, binding to GDP in the off state while binding GTP in the on state. Guanine nucleotide-exchange factors (GEFs) promote the exchange of GDP for GTP on Rab GTPases thus activating them, while GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) inactivate Rab GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP. Proteomic analysis revealed that RabG1 is found in lipid droplets ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24036346 Du, et al. 2013]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 04-JAN-2021 RD

DDB_G0288877.summary:
The armadillo repeats that characterize beta-catenin in metazoa are found in the protein encoded by the ''Dictyostelium'' gene ''aarA'' (aardvark). Beta-catenin plays two independent roles in metazoa, as a component in epithelial cell-cell adhesion, and as an intercellular signal transducer in the Wnt signaling pathway. In ''Dictyostelium'' AarA was found to be a component of actin-associated adherens junctions holding cells together around the top of the rising stalk tube. Mutants lacking AarA form weak fruiting bodies that collapse easily. They also express the prespore marker gene [/gene/DDB_G0267412 pspA] at reduced levels [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11130075 (Grimson et al. 2000)]. If beta-catenin is directly acting to regulate transcription, it is doing so in a manner unrelated to the metazoan Wnt signaling pathway. No ortholog of the intercellular signal Wnt can be found in the ''Dictyostelium'' genome. Likewise, the nuclear proteins TCF/LEF that are targeted by beta-catenin in vertebrates are missing in ''Dictyostelium''.
Dickinson and colleagues showed that ''Dictyostelium'' contains a polarized epithelium around the apical tip of the developing fruiting body. The deletion of ''aarA'' resulted in the disruption of this polarized protein organization. Accumulation of cellulose and EcmA/B in the stalk tube is strongly reduced in the mutant. Cellulose synthase ([/gene/DDB_G0269124 dcsA]) and EcmA/B ([/gene/DDB_G0277853 ecmA], [/gene/DDB_G0269132 ecmB]) are mislocalized intracellularly in tip epithelial cells but localization, though weak, is unchanged in stalk cells. This indicates that tip epithelial cells are the primary source of secreted cellulose and EcmA/B in the stalk tube. Aardvark was also shown to bind the ''Dictyostelium'' alpha-catenin ([/gene/DDB_G0285939 ctnnA]; [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21393547 Dickinson et al. 2011)]. Furthermore, both catenins are essential for apical myosin localization ([/gene/DDB_G0286355 mhcA]) during epithelial tube morphogenesis by regulating cortexillin ([/gene/DDB_G0289483 ctxA]) and Ras-GTPase ([/gene/DDB_G0287585 rgaA]) distribution, thus eliciting a signaling function of beta-catenin in ''Dictyostelium'' [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22902739 (Dickinson et al. 2012)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 10-JUN-2015 PF; annotation contributions: PMID 22902739 Daniel Dickinson; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0288247.summary:
''Dictyostelium'' AIF, which is very similar to human AIFM1, has been shown to localize to the mitochondrion in living cells, and to translocate to the nucleus during cell death. The activity of DdAIF was tested by using cytoplasmic extract from Dictyostelium cells, incubating the extract either with human or ''Dictyostelium'' nuclei. In both assays, the extract caused chromosome condensation and DNA degradation. Polyclonal DdAIF antibodies inhibited the nuclear degradation process. These results suggest that like its human counterpart, DdAIF is involve in mitochondrial organization and participates in the cell death pathway [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11598188 (Arnoult et al. 2001)].
Antisense mutants of ''aif'' exhibited slower growth and delayed developmental morphogenesis. ''aif'' antisense cells also contained higher levels of reactive oxygen species (ROS), oxidative DNA damage and calcium levels, but lower intracellular ATP levels. Under oxidative stress, ''aif'' antisense cells showed early mitochondrial membrane depolarization followed by AIF translocation from mitochondria to nucleus. Cells also exhibited necrotic cell death as compared to paraptoptic cell death in control cells. These results suggest that AIF is involved in growth and development in D. discoideum by regulating ROS levels [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/27663234 (Kadam et al. 2016)]. In addition, antisense ''aif'' mutants also exhibited compromised oxidative phosphorylation and lower transcript levels of various subunits of the electron transport chain. ''aif'' downregulation also resulted in increased mitochondrial fission and defects in mitochondrial structure, further revealing the role of ''aif'' in mitochondrial organization and homeostasis [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31991113 (Kadam et al. 2020)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 17-MAR-2020 RD

DDB_G0277199.summary:
DNA-dependent RNA polymerase catalyzes the transcription of DNA into RNA using the four ribonucleoside triphosphates as substrates ([/ontology/go/0003899/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase activity]). Three distinct zinc-containing RNA polymerases are found in eukaryotic nuclei: [/gene/DDB_G0275759 rpa1] for the ribosomal RNA precursor ([/ontology/go/0006360/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase I promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005736/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase I complex]), [/gene/DDB_G0279193 rpb1] for the mRNA precursor ([/ontology/go/0006366/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase II promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005665/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase II, core complex]), and [/gene/DDB_G0277199 rpc1] for 5S and tRNA genes ([/ontology/go/0006383/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase III promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005666/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase III complex]).
RNA polymerase III is a multisubunit complex. The subunits encoded by [/gene/DDB_G0277199 rpc1] (ortholog of ''S. cerevisiae RPO31''), [/gene/DDB_G0293560 rpa2] (''RPC2''), [/gene/DDB_G0268080 rpc3] (''RPC82''),[/gene/DDB_G0277671 rpc4] (''RPC53''), [/gene/DDB_G0271514 rpc5] (''RPC37''), [/gene/DDB_G0286521 rpc9] (''RPC17''), [/gene/DDB_G0272022 rpc34] (''RPC34''), [/gene/DDB_G0273425 rpc25-1] (''RPC25''), and [/gene/DDB_G0287707 rpc11] (''RPC11'') are unique to RNA polymerase III. Orthologs of ''RPC31'' and ''RPC17'' have not been identified in the ''Dictyostelium'' genome. Two subunits, [/gene/DDB_G0291362 rpc19] and [/gene/DDB_G0282339 rpa5] (''RPC19'' and ''RPC40'' in ''S. cerevisiae''), are common to RNA polymerase I and RNA polymerase III and correspond to subunits 3 and 11 of RNA polymerase II. Subunits [/gene/DDB_G0291636 rpb5], [/gene/DDB_G0291037 rpb6], [/gene/DDB_G0278039 rpb8], [/gene/DDB_G0272036 rpb10], and [/gene/DDB_G0283365 rpb12] are common to all three RNA polymerases ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12407181 Peyroche et al. 2002], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12381659 Schramm and Hernandez 2001]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 11-JUN-2009 PG

DDB_G0286191.summary:
The ''atg8'' gene was isolated among several members of the autophagy family of genes, conserved from yeast to man [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12626495 (Otto et al., 2003)]. Macroautophagy is used by eukaryotic cells to recycle non-essential cellular components during starvation and development. In ''atg8''-null cells, survival during nitrogen starvation is reduced. Upon starvation mutant cells show little turnover of cellular components. Development of the mutant is slightly impaired. On bacterial lawns cells aggregate mainly in the center of plaques and not in the periphery, and multi-tipped aggregates form very small fruiting bodies. Axenically grown cells plated on filters form multi-tipped aggregates that develop into small but normal looking fruiting bodies. These fruiting bodies produce few viable, detergent-resistent spores. Wild-type cells in a chimaera do not rescue the developmental defects, showing that the atg8 mutation is autonomous. The phenotype of the ''atg8''-null mutant is almost identical to that of the [/gene/DDB_G0269244 atg6A]-null mutant. Both mutants have the mildest defects when compared to [/gene/DDB_G0292390 atg1], [/gene/DDB_G0289881 atg5], and [/gene/DDB_G0271096 atg7] mutants [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14736886 (Otto et al., 2004)]
Infection of ''Dictyostelium'' by ''Mycobacterium marinum'' triggers an autophagic response, including increased expression of autophagy genes ([/gene/DDB_G0292390 atg1]) and ''atg8a'' autophagosome formation, and recruitment of the bacterium to Mycobacteria-containing vacuole (MCV). However, antagonistically, Mycobacterium also uses its ESX-1 secretion system to repress autophagic flux and support its survival inside the MCV. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28414774 Cardenal-Munoz et al. 2017]).
Generation of single and double knockout mutants of ''atg8a'' and ''atg8b'' ([/gene/DDB_G0290491 atg8b]) revealed unique roles for each protein in autophagy. Knockout of ''atg8b'' displayed only a mild develpmental phenotype, while ''atg8a'' mutants displayed a complex phenotype with delayed development, reduced growth, phagocytosis and cell viability, and an increase in ubiquitinylated proteins and a concomitant decrease in proteasomal activity. However knockout mutants of both genes displayed more severe phenotypes than the single ''atg8a'' mutant, indicating that both proteins function in parallel. Immunofluorescence analysis of knock-out strains suggests a crucial function for ATG8b in autophagosome-lysosome fusion. Atg8b localized around ATG8a and was presumably mainly present on the outer membrane of the autophagosome while Atg8a appears to be mainly associated with the inner membrane. These results suggest that Atg8b predominantly acts as adapter for the autophagy machinery at the outer and Atg8a as cargo receptor at the inner membrane of the autophagosome. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28413119 Messling et al. 2017]).
Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 24-SEP-2004 PF

DDB_G0267466.summary: In a search for genes up-regulated by intracellular calcium ([/ontology/go/0043157/annotation/page/1 response to cation stress]), [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14871937 Coukellet al. (2004)] identified [/gene/DDB_G0277861 patA], a homolog of the yeast vacuolar ATPase PMC1, andseven ''cup'' genes, which encode highly conserved proteins that contain ricin B lectin domains involved incarbohydrate binding. During the developmental program, ''cup transcripts'' are detected at low levels at earlyand late stages and at higher levels during the slug stage. Immunoflourescent staining shows Cup proteinsthroughout the cell in vegetative cells ([/ontology/go/0005737/annotation/page/1 cytoplasm] and [/ontology/go/0005634/annotation/page/1 nucleus]), however, aggregating cells and cellsstressed with 50 mM calcium chloride show increased staining in the [/ontology/go/0005938/annotation/page/1 cell cortex]. Overexpression of [/gene/DDB_G0289815 cupB] antisense mRNA abolishes multicellular development; cells fail to aggregate completely. DDB_G0268638.summary:
''Dictyostelium'' is the simplest organism known to employ STAT signaling. STAT (signal transducer and activator of transcription) proteins are characterized by a DNA binding domain, an SH2 domain, and a site of tyrosine phosphorylation. A STAT becomes activated when a ligand binds to its receptor, inducing tyrosine phosphorylation of the monomeric STAT molecule. Four STATs have been identified in ''Dictyostelium'', [/gene/DDB_G0281381 dstA], [/gene/DDB_G0268638 dstB], [/gene/DDB_G0293532 dstC] and [/gene/DDB_G0275167 dstD].
STATb was isolated by low stringency hybridization using the SH2 domain of STATa as a probe. STATb displays a 15 amino acid insertion in its SH2 domain and the conserved and essential arginine residue,which interacts with phosphotyrosine in all other known SH2 domains, is substituted by leucine. Despite these abnormalities, STATb is biologically functional and is found as a homodimer in the [/ontology/go/0005634/annotation/page/1 nucleus]. ''dstB''-null cells aregradually lost from the population when they are co-culturedwith parental cells ([/ontology/go/0001558/annotation/page/1 regulation of cell growth]). Microarray analysis lead to the identification of several genes that are either underexpressed ([/ontology/go/0016563/annotation/page/1 transcription activator activity]) oroverexpressed ([/ontology/go/0016564/annotation/page/1 transcription repressor activity]) in the ''dstB'' null strain ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14701681 Zhukovskaya et al. 2004]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 28-MAY-2004 PG

DDB_G0285319.summary:
Histones form the nucleosomal core ([/ontology/go/0000786/annotation/page/1 nucleosome]) ([/ontology/go/0006334/annotation/page/1 nucleosome assembly]) that is fundamental to chromatin structure (). The histone octamer is composed of an H3-H4 tetramer (two H3-H4 dimers) coupled with an H2A-H2Btetramer (two H2A-H2B dimers). The histone H1 linker protein plays a role in packaging nucleosomes into the 30 nmfiber found in chromatin ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9177486 Bukenberger et al. 1992]).
In ''Dictyostelium discoideum'' and ''Saccharomyces cerevisiae'', only one copy of histone H1 appears to be present, in comparison to other eukaryotes which have multiple copies and subtypes([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7867938 Hauser et al. 1995], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9046096 Ushinsky et al.1997]). Two putative H2A family members, [/gene/DDB_G0279667 H2AX] and [/gene/DDB_G0286747 H2AZ], and three H2Adomain-containing proteins, [/gene/DDB_G0289187 H2Av1], [/gene/DDB_G0289193 H2Av2], [/gene/DDB_G0289197 H2Av3], are present in ''Dictyostelium''. Two H2B domain-containing proteins also exist inthe ''Dicty'' genome: [/gene/DDB_G0293758 H2Bv1] and [/gene/DDB_G0276273 H2Bv2]. There are three histone H3proteins, [/gene/DDB_G0267402 H3a] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9177486 Bukenberger et al. 1992]), [/gene/DDB_G0270838 H3b], and [/gene/DDB_G0271092 H3c], and two H3 domain-containing proteins, [/gene/DDB_G0291185 H3v1] and [/gene/DDB_G0277979 H3v2]. We have also identified two histone H4proteins, [/gene/DDB_G0277183 H4a] and [/gene/DDB_G0276863 H4b], which have identical protein sequences but non-identical nucleotide sequences.
A functional histone H1 in ''Dictyostelium'' was originally identified by [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3923431 Parish andSchmidlin (1985)]. Through micrococcal nuclease digestion, they showed that a lysine-rich proteinfunctions as an H1 histone to bring the two DNA strands together at their exit point from the nucleosome. HistoneH1 was later cloned by [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7867938 Hauser and colleagues (1995)], who showed throughSouthern blot analysis that H1 exists in a single copy in the ''Dicytostelium'' genome. Their protein sequenceanalysis revealed the presence of the globular domain found higher eukaryotes and a putative cdc2 kinasephosphorylation site. They did not find, however, a nucleotide binding loop or a consensus cAMP-dependent phosphorylationsite. This is consistent with the findings of [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1321059 Heads et al. (1992)], whoshowed that growth-associated H1 histone kinase phosphorylates histone H1 in a cAMP independent manner.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 13-APR-2004 KP

DDB_G0267674.summary: The glycogen synthase encoded by the ''glcS'' gene is very similar to glycogen synthases in yeast and mammals and occurs in both G6P-dependent (D) and independent (I) forms [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9023987  (Williamson et al. 1996)]. It catalyzes the formation of alpha-1,4 glycosidic bonds, adding glucose monomers to growing chains of glycogen (starch). During growth and early development glycogen is the only polysaccharide present [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/5530749  (Ashworth and Watts, 1970)]. The specific activity of glycogen synthase does not change significantly during development but the rate of glycogen synthesis increases during culmination when its substrate UDGP becomes less limiting [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6069170  (Wright and Dalhberg, 1967)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/988019  (Loomis and Thomas, 1976)]. Mutants lacking glycogen synthase had much less glycogen and had greatly delayed morphogenesis resulting in small fruiting bodies [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18424909  (Tresse et al. 2008)]. ''glcS'' null mutant stalk cells were encased in cellulose but had few large vacuoles.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 30-MAR-2017 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0276761.summary: The major spore coat proteins, SP96, SP70, and SP60 ([/gene/DDB_G0276941 cotA], [/gene/DDB_G0276761 cotB], [/gene/DDB_G0277141 cotC], respectively), are coordinately synthesized in prespore cells and stored in prespore vesicles (PSVs) [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/499661  (Orlowski and Loomis, 1979]; [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6352373  Devine et al., 1983]; [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2601718  Fosnaugh and Loomis, 1989], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1646690  1991)]. All three genes are coordinately expressed at the tight aggregate stage. Continued expression is dependent on extracellular cAMP, and positively regulated by protein kinase A [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7713325  (Hopper et al. 1995)]. ''cotB'' encodes SP70 which is glycosylated before being released and positioned in the outer layer of the spore coats [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2471657 (Gonzalez-Yanes et al., 1989)]. The major spore coat proteins are necessary for the integrity of the spore coat [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7813801 (Fosnaugh et al., 1994)]. Expression of ''cotA'' (SP96), ''cotB'' (SP70) and ''cotC'' (SP60) has been used to monitor prespore specific transcription in a large number of studies (e.g., [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11410363  Hata et al., 2001]; [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12204259  Escalante and Sastre, 2002]; [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14729573  Thompson et al., 2004)]. Expression of cotB has been observed in prespore cells by in situ hybridization of whole mounts prepared throughout development [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7556903  (Escalante and Loomis, 1995]; [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15470253  Maruo et al., 2004)].Basic annotations have been added to this gene, 06-AUG-2015 PF; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0270340.summary:
''rapC'' encodes a guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G protein) of the Ras family of small GTPases. G proteins are key components of signal transduction networks in which they function as molecular signaling switches, binding to GDP in the off state while binding GTP in the on state. Guanine nucleotide-exchange factors (GEFs, rasGEFs, rapGEFs) promote the exchange of GDP for GTP on Ras GTPases thus activating them, while GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs, rasGAPs, rapGAPs) inactivate Ras GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP.
''rapC'' plays an important role in controlling cytokinesis, cell migration, and multicellular development in ''Dictyostelium''. RapC is localized to the plasma membrane and intracellular vesicle membranes. ''rapC'' null cells display several defects: increased cell size; multi-nucleated cells; decreased migration speed, increased cell-substrate adhesion, and multiple tip formation during development. [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29614268 (Park et al. 2018)]. Unlike other Ras family GTPases, ''rapC'' has an additional stretch of amino acids in the C-terminal region. Expression of full-length RapC rescues ''rapC'' null phenotypes, but expression of a truncated version of RapC lacking the C-terminal domain in ''rapC'' null cells fails to rescue the phenotypes. Moreover, fusion of the C-terminal domain of RapC onto RapA ([/gene/DDB_G0291237 rapA]) reverses the normal function of RapA, suggesting that the C-terminal residues of RapC may function as a suppressor of Ras signaling (Kim et al. 2021, PMID:34449058). RapA and RapC have opposite roles: RapC is a negative regulator of cell spreading and cell-substrate adhesion, thus increasing cell migration speed; however RapA positively regulates cell spreading and cell-substrate adhesion, thus decreasing cell migration speed (Jeon, et al. 2021, PMID: 34413965).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 21-SEP-2021 RD

DDB_G0274603.summary: ''kif9'' encodes the M-type kinesin that maintains a physical connection between the centrosome and the nuclear envelope [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19286984  (Tikhonenko et al. 2009)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23161062  (Tikhonenko et al. 2012)]. The motor domain that binds microtubules is in the central region and nuclear anchorage is mediated by a transmembrane domain at the carboxyl terminus. The motor domain does not group with specific metazoan kinesins [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14641909  (Kollmar and Glockner 2003)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23213391  (Leo et al. 2012)]. Like [/gene/DDB_G0267404 kif6], the other kinesin with a central motor domain, Kif9 effects an endwise depolymerization of microtubules that may pull the centrosome up against the nucleus to ensure centrosome-nuclear parity in a multinuclear environment [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23161062  (Tikhonenko et al. 2012)].The rate of growth is significantly reduced in ''kif9'' null cells and the microtubule-organizing center (MTOC) that contains the components of the centrosome often becomes disconnected from the nucleus during prophase [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19286984  (Tikhonenko et al. 2009)]. Detached centrosomes cannot produce the spindle-like microtubule arrays in the closed mitotic system of ''Dictyostelium'' that are essential for progress through mitosis [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23213391  (Leo et al. 2012)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 30-JUN-2017 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis; annotation contributions PMID:23161062 Michael Koonce

The homeodomain is a sequence-specific DNA binding motif that consists of a helix-turn-helix. Homeobox-containing proteins have transcription factor activity. There are 14 predicted proteins that contain homeobox domains in ''Dictyostelium'':[/gene/DDB_G0275173 hbx2], [/gene/DDB_G0291075 warA], [/gene/DDB_G0291197 hbx3], [/gene/DDB_G0272967 hbx4], [/gene/DDB_G0273127 hbx5-1] (on the chromosome 2 duplication: [/gene/DDB_G0273645 hbx5-2]), [/gene/DDB_G0277505 hbx6], [/gene/DDB_G0278225 hbx7], [/gene/DDB_G0279257 hbx8], [/gene/DDB_G0280473 hbx9], [/gene/DDB_G0284293 hbx10], [/gene/DDB_G0295787 hbx11], [/gene/DDB_G0286733 hbx12], [/gene/DDB_G0288975 hbx13], and [/gene/DDB_G0289677 hbx14].
[http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25963254 Mishra and Saran 2015] performed a genome-wide classification and comparative genomic analysis of the 14 homeobox genes present in D. discoideum, and found that they could be classified into 3 groups: TALE, OTHER and NOVEL classes, ''hbx8'' belonging to the NOVEL class.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 07-JUL-2015 RD

''stkA'' has been isolated as a "stalky" mutant, in which cells destined to become spores end up as stalk cells ([/ontology/go/0045595/annotation/page/1 regulation of cell differentiation]).The ''stkA'' gene contains GATA-binding transcription factor domains. The StkA protein contains two sequences necessary for localization to the [/ontology/go/0005634/annotation/page/1 nucleus] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8898200 Chang et al. 1996]).
Putative targets for this factor have been identified by differential display of RNA from cells of the culmination stage. In ''stkA'' null mutants, the genes [/gene/DDB_G0277835 cspA], [/gene/DDB_G0292808 cspB], [/gene/DDB_G0282293 rnpA], and [/gene/DDB_G0293364 sigB] fail to be expressed ([/ontology/go/0003700/annotation/page/1 transcription factor activity]), ([/ontology/go/0006355/annotation/page/1 regulation of transcription, DNA-dependent]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11100898 Loughran et al. 2000]). The promoters of ''sigB'' and ''culD'' are also regulated by the MADS box transcription factor [/gene/DDB_G0281387 srfA] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14665466 Escalante et al. 2003]).
GATA transcription factors specifically bind the DNA sequence (A/T)GATA(A/G) in the regulatory regions of genes ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2249770 Yamamoto et al. 1990]).In mammalian cells, GATA-binding transcription factors play important roles in development ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12943715 Tremblay and Viger 2003]). The gene ''hephA'' was identified in a screen for suppressors of the HSB1 mutant, where the gene [/gene/DDB_G0277399 piaA] has been mutated. Pia is part of the TORC2 complex, and the HSB1 (G917A) mutation causes a temperature-sensitive abolished ACA (adenylate cyclase A; [/gene/DDB_G0281545 acaA]) activity, leading to an abolished aggregation phenotype [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12413895 (Pergolizzi et al. 2002)].
The ''hephA'' gene encodes a predicted ubiquitin ligase, containing a HECT and a PH domain in the C-terminal third of the protein (HectPH1). REMI mutants with insertions upstream of those domains rescued the HSB1 phenotype, spontaneous chemotaxis and development were restored. While the obvious developmental phenotypes were rescued in the HSB1/HECTPH-Ko suppressor mutant, ACA stimulation was not restored but bypassed. However, ACB, the adenylate cyclase B ([/gene/DDB_G0267376 acrA]) was shown to play an essential role in the HSB1 rescue. When the ''hephA'' gene is deleted, aggregation is delayed and development is asynchronous, while sensitivity to cAMP is increased. These results indicate that inactivating the HectPH1 ubiquitin ligase increases the cellular sensitivity to cAMP, allowing cell development in response to very low cAMP levels in the HSB1 mutant, thus suggesting that HectPH1 is involved in the desensitization of cAMP signalling [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28049717 (Pergolizzi et al. 2017)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated 21-MAR-2017 PF; annotation contributions: PMID 28049717 Barbara Pergolizzi, Salvo Bozzaro

DDB_G0289325.summary:
Succinyl-CoA synthetase (SCS) is an enzyme in the [/ontology/go/0006099/annotation/page/1 tricarboxylic acid cycle] that catalyzes the formation of succinyl-CoA from succinate with the concomitant hydrolysis of NTP to NDP and phosphate. There are two forms of the enzyme, using either ATP or GTP. The [/gene/DDB_G0289325 scsA] gene encodes the succinyl-CoA synthetase alpha subunit. In eukaryotes one alpha and one beta subunit are thought to form a heterodimer. Anschutzt ''et al.'' determined that in crude [/ontology/go/0016020/annotation/page/1 membrane] extracts ScsA could be phosphorylated by ATP and GTP, but the purified enzyme showed high specificity for GTP ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8448193 Anschutz et al., 1993]).
Only one alpha subunit has been identified in ''Dictyostelium'' ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7771809 Birney and Klein, 1995]). However, two beta subunits are present in the ''Dictyostelium'' genome; [/gene/DDB_G0274449 scsB] is the ortholog of GDP-forming succinyl-CoA ligase beta subunits () and [/gene/DDB_G0271842 scsC] is highly similar to known ADP-forming succinyl-CoA ligase beta subunits ().Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 27-JAN-2005 PF

DDB_G0286733.summary:
The homeodomain is a sequence-specific DNA binding motif that consists of a helix-turn-helix. Homeobox-containing proteins have transcription factor activity. They have beenidentified in most if not all phyla of eukaryotes. Inmetazoans, homeobox-containing proteins are known to be involvedin regulating the anterior-posterior body plan and in thespecification of certain cell types and anterior-posteriorcompartments (see [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9486804 Han and Firtel 1998] and references therein). There are 14 predicted proteins that contain homeobox domains in ''Dictyostelium'':[/gene/DDB_G0275173 hbx2], [/gene/DDB_G0291075 warA], [/gene/DDB_G0291197 hbx3], [/gene/DDB_G0272967 hbx4], [/gene/DDB_G0273127 hbx5-1] (on the chromosome 2 duplication: [/gene/DDB_G0273645 hbx5-2]), [/gene/DDB_G0277505 hbx6], [/gene/DDB_G0278225 hbx7], [/gene/DDB_G0279257 hbx8], [/gene/DDB_G0280473 hbx9], [/gene/DDB_G0284293 hbx10], [/gene/DDB_G0295787 hbx11], [/gene/DDB_G0286733 hbx12], [/gene/DDB_G0288975 hbx13], and [/gene/DDB_G0289677 hbx14].
[http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25963254 Mishra and Saran 2015] performed a genome-wide classification and comparative genomic analysis of the 14 homeobox genes present in D. discoideum, and found that they could be classified into 3 groups: TALE, OTHER and NOVEL classes, ''hbx12'' belonging to the TALE class.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 07-JUL-2015 RD

DDB_G0282931.summary: The ABC superfamily of genes is one of the largest in the genomes of both bacteria and eukaryotes. The proteins encoded by these genes all carry a characteristic 200- to 250-amino-acid ATP-binding cassette that gives them their family name ([/ontology/go/0042626/annotation/page/1 ATPase activity, coupled to transmembrane movement of substances]). In bacteria they are mostly involved in nutrient import, while in eukaryotes many are involved in export([/ontology/go/0006810/annotation/page/1 transport]), ([/ontology/go/0016021/annotation/page/1 integral to membrane]). Seven different families (A to G) have been defined in eukaryotes based on sequence homology, domain topology, and function. ''Dictyostelium'' has 71 ABC transporters (including one on the chromosome 2 duplication) and 11 ABCB family members: [/gene/DDB_G0293416 abcB1], [/gene/DDB_G0293438 abcB2], [/gene/DDB_G0291714 abcB3], [/gene/DDB_G0279915 abcB4],[/gene/DDB_G0292554 abcB5], [/gene/DDB_G0282931 abcB6], [/gene/DDB_G0269720 abcB7], [/gene/DDB_G0293002 tagA], [/gene/DDB_G0286119 tagB], [/gene/DDB_G0286121 tagC], and [/gene/DDB_G0286123 tagD]. The B family includes three main subtypes: full transporters involved in multiple drug resistance (MDR), half-transporters targeted to mitochondria, and half-transporters involved in peptide transport [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12456012 (Anjard and Loomis 2002)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 17-MAY-2004 PG

There are 19 putative bZIP transcription factors in the ''Dictyostelium'' genome: [/gene/DDB_G0278971 dimA], [/gene/DDB_G0291372 dimB], [/gene/DDB_G0279439 bzpC], [/gene/DDB_G0278379 bzpD], [/gene/DDB_G0269338 bzpE], [/gene/DDB_G0279529 bzpF], [/gene/DDB_G0282749 bzpG], [/gene/DDB_G0277681 bzpH], [/gene/DDB_G0290173 bzpI], [/gene/DDB_G0274993 bzpJ], [/gene/DDB_G0282049 bzpK], [/gene/DDB_G0284023 bzpL], [/gene/DDB_G0282047 bzpM], [/gene/DDB_G0286411 bzpN], [/gene/DDB_G0290169 bzpO], [/gene/DDB_G0290303 bzpP], [/gene/DDB_G0288705 bzpQ], [/gene/DDB_G0290165 bzpR], and [/gene/DDB_G0290171 bzpS]
[http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20356373 (Parikh et al. 2010)] identified ''bzpF'' as a component of the PKA pathway based on Bayesian analysis of expression data. [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21810415 (Huang et al. 2011)] extended these findings and demonstrated that BzpF is a CREB-like transcription factor that functions downstream of PKA ([/gene/DDB_G0283907 pkaC], [/gene/DDB_G0279413 pkaR]) during the late stages of Dictyostelium development and regulates sporulation. ''bzpF'' null mutants have severe defects in spore maturation and maintenance.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 02-Nov-2017 RD

DDB_G0273731.summary:
AlyD has been identified in a search of ''Dictyostelium'' sequences similar to [/gene/DDB_G0275123 alyA], which has been shown to have lysozyme activity. There are 3 genes, ''alyA'', [/gene/DDB_G0275119 alyB], and [/gene/DDB_G0275121 alyC], that encode nearly identical proteins; AlyD, however, is more distantly related. These enzymes are not similar to any other known lysozymes. It has been suggested that these proteins represent a new class of lysozymes [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15640146 (Mueller et al., 2005)].
A comprehensive study classified all lysozymes in ''Dictyostelium''. In addition to the 5 known amoeba like lysozymes ([/gene/DDB_G0275123 alyA], [/gene/DDB_G0275119 alyB], [/gene/DDB_G0275121 alyC], [/gene/DDB_G0273197 alyD-1] and [/gene/DDB_G0286229 alyL] ), two new related lysozymes in this family have been identified, [/gene/DDB_G0282905 alyE] and [/gene/DDB_G0282893 alyF]. Because in the past, gene models for these two new lysozymes gave rise to proteins with transmembrane domains, one or two respectively, they first have been named alyTM1 and alyTM2. However, new sequence analyses resulted in updated gene models coding for proteins containing signal peptides like the other 5 members of the aly family. Alignment of the 7 proteins allowed the identification of one conserved Asp and one Glu residue in the C- terminal portion [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/32061941 (Lamrabet et al. 2020)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 29-APR-2020 PF

DDB_G0270124.summary: ''rasX'' encodes a guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G protein) of the Ras family of small GTPases. G proteins are key components of signal transduction networks in which they function as molecular signaling switches, binding to GDP in the off state while binding GTP in the on state. Guanine nucleotide-exchange factors (GEFs, rasGEFs) promote the exchange of GDP for GTP on Ras GTPases thus activating them, while GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs, rasGAPs) inactivate Ras GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP. An analysis of ''Dictyostelium'' ras family genes reveals that ''rasU'' ([/gene/DDB_G0270138 rasU]), ''rasV'' ([/gene/DDB_G0270736 rasV]), ''rasW'' ([/gene/DDB_G0270122 rasW]), ''rasX'', ''rasY'' ([/gene/DDB_G0270126 rasY]) and ''rasZ'' ([/gene/DDB_G0270140 rasZ]) form a separate phylogenetic clade ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29614268 Park et al. 2018]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 12-MAR-2020 RD

DDB_G0284183.summary: MrfA is a transcription factor that regulates expression of the prestalk gene ([/gene/DDB_G0277853 ecmA]) in PstA cells [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22811266  (Senoo et al. 2012)]. MrfA was purified from slug stage nuclear extracts by affinity chromatography to a multimerized 39 bp CA-rich region from the ''ecmA'' promoter which is necessary and sufficient for expression of a reporter gene (''lacZ'') exclusively in anterior prestalk cells. The protein was found to be the product of a partially sequenced random cDNA [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8643615  (Kuspa and Loomis, 1996)]. The DNA binding region of MrfA is found in the middle of the 104 kDa protein and shows sequence similarity to the DNA binding region of human Myelin Regulatory Factor (MRF). There is a peptidase domain near the carboxy terminus followed by a transmembrane domain that is auto-catalytically cleaved releasing the 85 kDa fragment so that it can be localized within nuclei during development [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24046445  (Senoo et al. 2013)]. Nuclear staining is lost from the prespore region when slugs are formed. Cells of ''mrfA'' null strains are delayed in culmination and fail to express the reporter gene linked to the multimerized 39 bp region from the proximal ''ecmA'' promoter [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22811266  (Senoo et al. 2012)]. Prespore and PstO cell specific gene expression are unaffected by the loss of MrfA.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 06-FEB-2018 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0289073.summary: The cell surface glycoprotein CsaA mediates cell-cell adhesion via homophilic binding. ''csaA'' encodes the glycoprotein gp80 that is responsible for Contact Sites A ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16453689 Noegel et al. 1986)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16593709 Wong and Siu et al. 1986)]. It is expressed after 6 hours of development when the cells begin to aggregate. At this time, the cells become mutually adhesive even in the presence of 10 mM EDTA. Antibodies specific to gp80 are able to block this EDTA resistant adhesion ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/5106016 Beug et al. 1971)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7328669 Murray et al. 1981)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3934167 Siu et al. 1985)]. gp80 is stabilized by addition of N-acetylglucosamine to a threonine in a reaction catalyzed by ModB, the product of ([/gene/DDB_G0291241 gnt2]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6717432 Murray et al. 1984)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/4019595 Gerisch et al. 1985)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9092834 Jung et al. 1997)]. gp80 is also phosphorylated ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6178632 Schmidt and Loomis et al. 1982)], and held to the surface membrane by a covalently attached glycosylphosphatidyl-inositol lipid (GPI-anchor) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8081259 Klein et al. 1994)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8294503 Barth et al. 1994)]. Homophilic interactions at the octapeptide YKLNVNDS found near the N-terminus of gp80 are responsible for end-to end adhesion of adjacent cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3320049 Siu et al. 1987)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2582489 Kamboj et al. 1989)]. Disruption of csaA results in loss of EDTA-stable adhesion but does not noticeably affect aggregation ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2515990 Harloff et al. 1989)]. Cells overexpressing csaA formed big slugs that gave rise to unusually large fruiting bodies ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1966011 Kamboj et al. 1990)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 15-JAN-2016 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0289165.summary:
Using comparative genomic hybridizations using DNA microarrays searching for genes that are present in any ''D. discoideum'' member of one mating type but absent or highly diverged in other members lead to the identification of the ''matA'' genes. Single, unrelated genes (''matA'', ''matS'') are sufficient to determine two of the mating types, whereas homologs of both of these genes ''matB''. ''matC'', respectively) are required in the composite type. A type I ''matA'' null mutant was transformed with the type II locus (''matB''. ''matC'' and ''matD'') effectively switching the mating type proving this is the locus for sex determination. MatD plays a possible role in gamete fusion [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21148389 (Bloomfield et al. 2010)].
Unlike haploid dictyostelid cells, zygotes feed cannibalistically on other amoebae of the same species, growing without cell division forming a syncytia and eventually a dormant walled structure called a macrocyst. This large cell is thought to go through meiosis before haploid progeny resumes the mitotic cell cycle. ''Dictyostelium discoideum'' has three mating types: matA for type I, matS for type III, and both matB and matC for type II. However, although matB is genetically compatible with matS, and matA with matC, in specifying sexually compatible pairs, matB and matC are incompatible.
The ''mat'' genes encode proteins with helix-turn-helix folds flanked by largely disordered amino- and carboxyl-terminal tails, resembling homeodomain proteins. For matA and matB it has been shown that they bind DNA in the C-terminal helix, and expression of chimeras showed the C-terminal tail determines mating specificity. [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28879231 (Hedgethorne et al. 2017)].
Genome-wide analysis of progeny from three crosses revealed that recombination is very frequent, with at least one crossover per chromosome. Progeny from each macrocyst are identical, thus only one meiotic product survives. Tree-way crossing of a mating type I , a type II and an excess of matA null cells that cannot produce meiotic progeny showed that a third mating type contributes mitochondrial DNA, but not participating in nuclear DNA cross-overs. Thus fusions of more than two gametes to form transient syncytia lead to frequent triparental inheritance, with haploid meiotic progeny bearing recombined nuclear haplotypes from two parents and the mitochondrial genome from a third [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30670662 (Bloomfield et al. 2019)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 01-MAR-2019 PF

DDB_G0273443.summary: ''atg4'' was isolated together with several other members of the autophagy family of genes, conserved from yeast to man ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12626495 Otto et al. 2003)]. ATG4 is an ortholog of the conserved cysteine protease that processes the ubiquitin-like protein ATG8 ([/gene/DDB_G0286191 atg8a]) to uncover a conserved glycine at the C terminus that can covalently bind to membrane phospholipid with the aid of the E1-type enzyme ATG7 ([/gene/DDB_G0271096 atg7]) and the E2-type enzyme ATG3 ([/gene/DDB_G0277319 atg3]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20603609 Calvo-Garrido et al. 2010)]. There are two copies of the ''atg4'' gene in the chromosome 2 duplication of strain AX4.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 15-FEB-2017 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis and Ricardo Escalante
