DDB_G0273197.summary:
AlyD has been identified in a search of ''Dictyostelium'' sequences similar to [/gene/DDB_G0275123 alyA], which has been shown to have lysozyme activity. There are 3 genes, ''alyA'', [/gene/DDB_G0275119 alyB], and [/gene/DDB_G0275121 alyC], that encode nearly identical proteins; AlyD, however, is more distantly related. These enzymes are not similar to any other known lysozymes. It has been suggested that these proteins represent a new class of lysozymes [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15640146 (Mueller et al., 2005)].
A comprehensive study classified all lysozymes in ''Dictyostelium''. In addition to the 5 known amoeba like lysozymes ([/gene/DDB_G0275123 alyA], [/gene/DDB_G0275119 alyB], [/gene/DDB_G0275121 alyC], [/gene/DDB_G0273197 alyD-1] and [/gene/DDB_G0286229 alyL] ), two new related lysozymes in this family have been identified, [/gene/DDB_G0282905 alyE] and [/gene/DDB_G0282893 alyF]. Because in the past, gene models for these two new lysozymes gave rise to proteins with transmembrane domains, one or two respectively, they first have been named alyTM1 and alyTM2. However, new sequence analyses resulted in updated gene models coding for proteins containing signal peptides like the other 5 members of the aly family. Alignment of the 7 proteins allowed the identification of one conserved Asp and one Glu residue in the C- terminal portion [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/32061941 (Lamrabet et al. 2020)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 29-APR-2020 PF

DDB_G0276863.summary:
Histones form the nucleosomal core ([/ontology/go/0000786/annotation/page/1 nucleosome]) ([/ontology/go/0006334/annotation/page/1 nucleosome assembly]) that is fundamental to chromatin structure (). The histone octamer is composed of an H3-H4 tetramer (two H3-H4 dimers) coupled with an H2A-H2Btetramer (two H2A-H2B dimers). The histone H1 linker protein plays a role in packaging nucleosomes into the 30 nmfiber found in chromatin ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9177486 Bukenberger et al. 1992]).
In ''Dictyostelium discoideum'' and ''Saccharomyces cerevisiae'', only one copy of histone [/gene/DDB_G0285319 H1] appears to be present, in comparison to other eukaryotes which have multiple copies and subtypes([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7867938 Hauser et al. 1995], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9046096 Ushinsky et al.1997]). Two putative H2A family members, [/gene/DDB_G0279667 H2AX] and [/gene/DDB_G0286747 H2AZ], and three H2Adomain-containing proteins, [/gene/DDB_G0289187 H2Av1], [/gene/DDB_G0289193 H2Av2], [/gene/DDB_G0289197 H2Av3], are present in ''Dictyostelium''. Two H2B domain-containing proteins also exist inthe ''Dicty'' genome: [/gene/DDB_G0293758 H2Bv1] and [/gene/DDB_G0276273 H2Bv2]. There are three histone H3proteins, [/gene/DDB_G0267402 H3a] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9177486 Bukenberger et al. 1992]), [/gene/DDB_G0270838 H3b], and [/gene/DDB_G0271092 H3c], and two H3 domain-containing proteins, [/gene/DDB_G0291185 H3v1] and [/gene/DDB_G0277979 H3v2]. We have also identified two histone H4proteins, [/gene/DDB_G0277183 H4a] and [/gene/DDB_G0276863 H4b], which have identical protein sequences but non-identical nucleotide sequences.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 13-APR-2004 KP

DDB_G0284867.summary: The ABC superfamily of genes is one of the largest in the genomes of both bacteria and eukaryotes. The proteins encoded by these genes all carry a characteristic 200- to 250-amino-acid ATP-binding cassette that gives them their family name ([/ontology/go/0042626/annotation/page/1 ATPase activity, coupled to transmembrane movement of substances]). In bacteria they are mostly involved in nutrient import, while in eukaryotes many are involved in export([/ontology/go/0006810/annotation/page/1 transport]), ([/ontology/go/0016021/annotation/page/1 integral to membrane]). Seven different families (A to G) have been defined in eukaryotes based on sequence homology, domain topology, and function. ''Dictyostelium'' has 71 ABC transporters (including one on the chromosome 2 duplication) and 13 ABCC family members: [/gene/DDB_G0280541 abcC1], [/gene/DDB_G0280055 abcC2], [/gene/DDB_G0287691 abcC3], [/gene/DDB_G0286559 abcC5], [/gene/DDB_G0287593 abcC6], [/gene/DDB_G0291243 abcC7], [/gene/DDB_G0284867 abcC8], [/gene/DDB_G0285165 abcC9], [/gene/DDB_G0280977 abcC10], [/gene/DDB_G0280973 abcC12], [/gene/DDB_G0280539 abcC13], [/gene/DDB_G0287589 abcC14], and [/gene/DDB_G0280459 abcC15]. Transporters of the C family have been shown to transport glutathione conjugants as well as to export cadmium ions. They are always found as full transporters with two copies of the transmembrane-ABC unit. Many of the genes of this family in humans and other animals have an additional transmembrane domain at the N terminus [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12456012 (Anjard and Loomis 2002)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 16-JUN-2003 PG

DDB_G0291079.summary: ''gbpC'' (''gefT'') encodes a large multi-domain, high affinity cGMP-binding protein. There is a leucine rich repeat (LRR) at the N-terminus followed by a Ras-related domain and a mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase kinase (MAPKKK) domain; these domains are followed by a RasGEF domain, and two cyclic nucleotide binding domains with a GRAM domain in between [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12011437  (Goldberg et al. 2002)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12952076  (Bosgraaf et al. 2002)]. ''gbpC'' is expressed throughout growth and development, with highest levels of expression between 4 and 12 hours of development ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16086850 Wilkins et al. 2005)]. GbpC is a founding member of the Roco family of proteins (Ras of complex proteins) which includes human leucine rich repeat kinase 2 (LRRK2) that can cause late-onset Parkinson's disease [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14654223  (Bosgraaf and van Haastert 2003)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24981771  (Civiero et al. 2014)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24847205  (Gilsbach and Kortholt 2014)]. ''gbpC'' may have resulted from the fusion of two independent genes, one encoding Ras-MAPKKK and one related to GbpD ([/gene/DDB_G0282373 gbpD]) containing a RasGEF domain and an ancient cAMP-binding (cNB) motif. [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12615006  (Roelof et al. 2003)]. Mutants lacking GbpC have lost all high affinity cGMP binding activity, are unable to polarize, and are greatly impaired in chemotaxis to cAMP gradients [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15827084  (Bosgraaf et al. 2005)]. In wild type cells, cAMP induces rapid phosphorylation of myosin regulatory light chain (RLC) ([/gene/DDB_G0276077 mlcR]) by a cGMP-dependent pathway, however, cAMP induces significantly less phosphorylation of RLC in ''gbpC'' null cells, confirming the role of cGMP in myosin II regulation. When cGMP binds to GbpC, it initiates an intramolecular signaling cascade in which the RasGEF activates Ras which stimulates the protein kinase activity [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18703517  (van Egmond et al. 2008)]. The MAPKKK may then initiate a protein kinase cascade activating the myosin light chain protein kinase MLCK-A ([/gene/DDB_G0279925 mlkA]) that phosphorylates RLC to promote myosin motor activity [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16814425  (Bosgraaf and van Haastert 2006)]. cGMP bound GbpC also leads to actin polymerization [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24136144  (Pfannes et al. 2013)]. Independently of cGMP signaling, cAMP stimulation results in rapid translocation of GbpC from the cytoplasm to the cell perimeter where it may locally phosphorylate effector proteins. The GRAM domain of GbpC is required for membrane association and its function in chemotaxis [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22119747  (Kortholt et al. 2011)]. When developed on filters, ''gbpC''- mutant cells can aggregate slowly by accretion resulting in the delayed formation of mounds which then develop normally.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 08-JUN-2021 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis
DDB_G0291079.note: The sequences from the Sequencing Center and GenBank record AF481923 are identical.

DDB_G0275327.summary: ''rabX'' encodes a guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G protein) of the Rab family of small GTPases. G proteins are key components of signal transduction networks in which they function as molecular signaling switches, binding to GDP in the off state while binding GTP in the on state. Guanine nucleotide-exchange factors (GEFs) promote the exchange of GDP for GTP on Rab GTPases thus activating them, while GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) inactivate Rab GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP. A genome-wide DNA microarray analysis revealed that ''rabX'' expression is down-regulated in response to ''Pseudomas aeruginosa'' expression ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18590548 Carilla-Latorre, et al. 2008]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 16-FEB-2021 RD

DDB_G0280111.summary: Members of the NAK (Numb-associated kinase) family of serine/threonine kinases ([/ontology/go/0004674/annotation/page/1 protein serine/threonine kinase activity]) have been shown toparticipate in diverse cellular processes. The first characterized NAK was the ''Drosophila melanogaster'' NAK,named for its ability to interact with the neuronal differentiation protein Numb, hence the name NAK ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9418906 Chien et al. 1998]). Additional members of this family include AAK1 (AP2-associatedkinase), involved in clathrin-mediated endocytosis ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11877461 Conner and Schmid 2000]),and BIKe (BMP-induced kinase), which plays a role in bone differentiation ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11500515 Kearns et al. 2001]). [/gene/DDB_G0276461 DDB_G0276461] and DDB0229350 are similar to the kinasedomains of AAK1 and BIKe. The NAK family also includes MPSK (myristoylated and palmitoylated serine/threoninekinase), which is fatty acid acylated ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10364453 Berson et al. 1999]) andmay play a role in TGF-beta signaling ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10947953 Ohta et al. 2000]). The mostclosely related protein to MPSK in ''Dictyostelium discoideum'' is [/gene/DDB_G0291350 DDB_G0291350].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 10-MAY-2004 KP

DDB_G0292998.summary:
''rasB'' encodes a guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G protein) of the Ras family of small GTPases. G proteins are key components of signal transduction networks in which they function as molecular signaling switches, binding to GDP in the off state while binding GTP in the on state. Guanine nucleotide-exchange factors (GEFs, rasGEFs) promote the exchange of GDP for GTP on Ras GTPases thus activating them, while GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs, rasGAPs) inactivate Ras GTPases. RasB is activated by the RasGEF Q ([/gene/DDB_G0289665 gefQ]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18504297 Mondal et al. 2008)] and inactivated by the RasGAP DdNF1 ([/gene/DDB_G0271750 nfaA]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18948008 Zhang et al. 2008)].
''rasB'' is expressed at maximum levels during vegetative growth and the first 8 hr of development, and is activated upon cAMP stimulation by rasGEF Q. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8455930 Daniel et al. 1993)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18504297 Mondal et al. 2008)]. RasB is predominantly localized in the nucleus during most of the cell cycle but assumes a diffuse cellular localization during mitosis and cytokinesis ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11606416 Sutherland et al. 2001)]. Constitutively active RasB mutants have an increased proportion of multi-nucleated cells, revealing a defect in cytokinesis. ''rasB'' null cells are unstable and exhibit growth defects, defects in both phagocytosis and macropinocytosis, and decreased F-actin levels in the phagocytic cup ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11606416 Sutherland et al. 2001)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/27821733 Junemann et al. 2016)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30967009 Williams et al. 2019)].
Ras signaling through RasB is a critical mediator of several processes in ''Dictyostelium'': the regulation of myosin II assembly, cytokinesis, and actin assembly during phagocytosis. Both rasGEF Q and constitutively active RasB directly interact with the myosin heavy chain kinase MHCK-A ([/gene/DDB_G0291231 mhkA]) to regulate myosin II assembly ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18504297 Mondal et al. 2008)]. RasB and RasG ([/gene/DDB_G0293434 rasG]) regulate cytokinesis through the protein kinase NdrC ([/gene/DDB_G0284839 ndrC]). ''ndrC'' null cells also display a cytokinesis defect and pull-down assays show that NdrC binds both activated RasG and RasB. The aberrant cytokinesis phenotype of activated RasB suggests that RasB is a negative regulator of cytokinesis ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24986648 Mueller-Taubenberger et al. 2014)]. Null mutants of rasGAP NfaA are also reported to display cytokinesis defects. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18948008 Zhang et al. 2008)]. Similar to the ''rasB'' null mutant phenotype, ablation of the actin filament elongator formin G ([/gene/DDB_G0277175 forG]) results in significantly decreased phagocytosis and aberrant F-actin organization within phagosomes. Constitutively active RasB and RasG accumulate in endocytic cups where they directly interact with and regulate formin G, thus linking Ras GTPase signaling with actin polymerization in phagocytosis and macropinocytosis ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/27821733 Junemann et al. 2016)]. Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 04-MAR-2020 RD

DDB_G0275451.summary:
The ''alxA'' gene was identified as a homolog of mammalian Alix (ALG-2-interacting protein X, alsoreferred to as AIP1), which interacts with ALG-2 (apoptosis-linked gene 2). Mammalian Alix is known tobe involved in many biological processes, including apoptosis, membrane trafficking, and budding of the HIV virus ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15276209 Ohkouchi et al. 2004]). Murine Alix has been shown to interact with ''Dictyostelium'' [/gene/DDB_G0291081 pefA], a calcium-binding EF hand protein similar to mammalian ALG-2, but not with [/gene/DDB_G0293530 pefB] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11927596 Aubry et al. 2002]). The ''alxA'' transcript and encoded protein are expressed throughout development, with higer levels duringgrowth and early development and slightly lower expression during culmination. Immunoflourescence experiments showthat the AlxA protein localizes to the [/ontology/go/0005737/annotation/page/1 cytoplasm] and to the [/ontology/go/0005768/annotation/page/1 endosome] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15708561 Mattei et al. 2005]).
The ''alxA'' null mutant shows no significant phenotype under normal conditions, however, mutant cells display developmentalabnormalities in the presence of LiCl and in low concentrations of Ca2+. In the presence of 5 mM LiCl, ''alxA-'' cellsarrest at the loose aggregate stage or form fruiting body-like structures at the apex of aggregates ([/ontology/go/0009653/annotation/page/1 anatomical structure morphogenesis]). Similarly, ''alxA''null cells arrest at the aggregate stage in the presence of 200µM TMB-8, an antagonist of intracellular Ca2+, and inthe presence of a low concentration of Ca2+. Developmental arrest is of course seen in wild-type cells in the absence offree Ca2+, however, ''alxA-'' cells are hypersensitive to a reduction in free Ca2+ compared to wild-type. Thissuggests that AlxA is somehow involved in calcium signaling in the developmental program, which is interesting in light of thecalcium binding activities of ''Dictyostelium'' PefA and PefB ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15276209 Ohkouchi et al. 2004], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11481037 Ohkouchi et al. 2001]).
A second mutant constructed and analyzed by [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15708561 Mattei et al. (2005)] showssimilar gross phenotypes. At the cellular level, ''alxA-'' cells suppress spore formation ([/ontology/go/0045881/annotation/page/1 positive regulation of sporulation])and promote differentiation into PstB cells, as shown by almost ubiquitous expression of the prestalk markers[/gene/DDB_G0277853 ecmA], [/gene/DDB_G0269132 ecmB], and [/gene/DDB_G0277141 cotC] in migrating slugs.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 10-SEP-2004 KP

DDB_G0289177.summary: Besides ''mhcA'' ([/gene/DDB_G0286355 mhcA]) that encodes the classical myosin heavy chain, ''Dictyostelium'' carries genes for 12 unconventional myosins. The first 5 unconventional myosins: ([/gene/DDB_G0280039 myoA]), ([/gene/DDB_G0289117 myoB]), ([/gene/DDB_G0276617 myoC]), ([/gene/DDB_G0275447 myoD]), ([/gene/DDB_G0288679 myoE]), were isolated from whole genome plasmid clones by low stringency probing with portions of the head region of ''mhcA''. The next 6 unconventional myosins: ([/gene/DDB_G0289177 myoF]), ([/gene/DDB_G0276363 myoG]), ([/gene/DDB_G0289447 myoH]), ([/gene/DDB_G0274455 myoI]), ([/gene/DDB_G0272112 myoJ]), ([/gene/DDB_G0274575 myoK]) were recognized in large YAC clones that represent the whole genome [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7937787  (Titus et al. 1994) ]. The amino acid sequences of MyoD, MyoE, and MyoF are more similar to each other than to other myosins. ''myoF'' encodes myosin 1F that functions together with MyoD and MyoE in growth and development. While mutants lacking MyoF have no obvious growth defects, double mutants lacking both MyoE and MyoF grow more slowly, aggregate more slowly and make misshapen fruiting bodies. Triple mutants cells lacking ''myoD'', ''myoE'' and ''myoF'' are defective in chemotaxis to cAMP, chemoattractant-stimulated actin polymerization and phagocytosis [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7787058  (Titus et al. 1995)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22296834  (Chen et al. 2012)]. Both MyoE and MyoF localize to macropinocytic cups and actin waves [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26801966  (Brzeska et al. 2016)]. The tail domain of MyoF, like that of MyoD and MyoE, binds PIP3 resulting in its accumulation at the front of migrating cells where the PI3kinases are active and PTEN is excluded [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22296834  (Chen et al. 2012)]. Cells lacking MyoF also have difficulty maintaining an elongated polarized shape during chemotaxis in a cAMP gradient [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12953059  (Falk et al. 2003)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 28-AUG-2019 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0275157.summary: LimF was isolated on the basis of its LIM domain, a domain important for cytoskeletal function. A two-hyrbrid screen was performed, which identified two interacting partners, [/gene/DDB_G0267490 ChLim], another LIM domain-containing protein, as well as [/gene/DDB_G0286553 rab21], a small GTPase of the Rab subfamily. The two amino LIM domains of LimF, LIM1 and LIM2, were able to bind ChLIM and Rab21, but not LIM3, the most carboxy LIM domain. ChLim and LimF interaction with Rab21 is not dependent on the ability of Rab21 to bind GTP. Mutations in these three genes indicate that ChLim play a role in the [/ontology/go/0050765/annotation/page/1 negative regulation of phagocytosis], while LimF and Rab21 are involved in the [/ontology/go/0050766/annotation/page/1 positive regulation of phagocytosis]. Consistent with this, during phagocytosis, LimF is found in the [/ontology/go/0001891/annotation/page/1 phagocytic cup] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15962002 Khurana et al, 2005]). DDB_G0272004.summary:
The ''p2xA'' gene is one of 5 ''Dictyostelium'' genes encoding putative P2X receptors. p2xA has been heterologously expressed in human HEK 293 cells and was shown to have ATP-gated cation channel activity. Mutation of conserved lysines (K67A, K289A) or a conserved aspartate (D330A) to alanine rendered the molecule non-functional. This P2X receptor was also found to be sensitive to Cu2+ ions. Deletion of the ''p2xA'' gene in AX4 wild type cells led to extensive swelling of the cells when placed in water, indicating a defect in cellular water homeostasis. Addition to Cu2+ ions recapitulated the swelling phenotype. Expression of a p2xA-GFP construct localized p2xA to the contractile vacuolar membrane and rescued the defect in the null cells [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17625565 (Fountain et al. 2007)].
Using an apoaequorin expressing strain, Ludlow ''et al.'' showed that ''Dictyostelium'' posseses P2X receptors that facilitate rapid Ca2+ influx in response to extracellular ATP and ADP. Deleting ''p2xA'' or [/gene/DDB_G0288061 p2xE] did not influence this behavior, suggesting these genes are not involved. However, this study proposes possible roles for [/gene/DDB_G0275293 p2xB], [/gene/DDB_G0275191 p2xC], or [/gene/DDB_G0288335 p2xD] [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18486207 (Ludlow et al. 2008)].
Ludlow ''et al.'' also showed that P2xB and P2xE, as well as P2xA, have ATP-gated channel activity when expressed in ''Xenopus'' oocytes. However, Na+ inhibited this activity to various degrees in these P2x channels, but K+, and NH4+ ions elicited a large response. Interestingly, P2xA and P2xB, but not P2xE are permeable to Cl- ions. No such ATP-gated channel activity was found for P2xC and P2xD. All ''Dictyostelium'' P2x proteins localize to the contractile vacuolar membrane, and not to the plasma membrane like P2x receptors from other organisms. The transmembrane loop region containing the agonist (ATP) binding site lies within the lumen of the vacuole. Also, A quintuple ''p2xA/B/C/D/E'' null mutant in wild type AX2 shows a reduced response to the calmodulin inhibitor calmidazolium, suggesting a role of the ''Dictyostelium'' proteins in the regulation of calcium-mediated signaling. The quintuple null mutant also shows a slight delay in its hypotonic response when placed in water, however, single mutants in a AX2 background do not show any osmoregulatory defect. Taken together, this study suggests that it is still unclear which molecules are responsible for the extracellular purinergic response in ''Dictyostelium'' and it raises the possibility that the P2x receptors may play a role in the release of intracellular Ca 2+ stores in response to an ATP stimulus from within the contractile vacuole [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19833731 (Ludlow et al. 2009)].
The study by [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22736763 Sivaramakrishnan and Fountain 2012] reported that the P2x receptor ATP binding site faces into the vacuole lumen and ATP translocation triggers P2x receptor-dependent release of calcium. Thus the P2xA receptor in ''Dictyostelium'' is a calcium release channel. In a later study they reported that two commonly used laboratory strains of ''Dictyostelium'' display different phenotypes in response to hypotonic stress.The magnitude of contractile vacuolar calcium, released in response to ATP, differs substantially between AX2 and AX4, with the magnitude of release being significantly smaller in AX2 cells [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23221467 Sivaramakrishnan and Fountain 2013]. The results confirm those from [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19833731 Ludlow et al. 2009] that AX2 cells are not dependent on ''p2xA'' for normal volume regulation, and also substantiate findings from [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17625565 Fountain et al. 2007] that ''p2xA'' is required for normal osmoregulation in AX4 cells.
Activation of P2xA results in calcium efflux required for downregulation of Rab11a (gene [/gene/DDB_G0269238 rab11A]) activity and efficient vacuole fusion. Vacuole fusion and Rab11a downregulation require the activity of CnrF (gene [/gene/DDB_G0276119 cnrF]), an EF-hand-containing Rab GAP found in a complex with Rab11a and P2xA. CnrF Rab GAP activity for Rab11a is enhanced by the presence of calcium and the EF-hand domain. These findings support that P2xA activation results in vacuolar calcium release, which triggers activation of CnrF Rab GAP activity and subsequent downregulation of Rab11a to allow vacuole fusion [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24335649 (Parkinson et al. 2013)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 27-NOV-2015 PF

DDB_G0277075.summary: ''detA'' encodes the homolog of the human DET1 component of E3 ubiquitin ligase that, along with F-box/WD40-repeat-containing proteins, mediate the ubiquitination of proteins to target them for degradation by the proteasome (ubiquitin-protein ligase activity). DetA is found localized to the nucleus, and a plant homolog of DET1 has been shown to bind to the N-terminal tail of histone H2B. The ''Dictyostelium'' ''detA'' gene was disrupted by targeted homologous recombination and the mutation was shown to have rather mild effects on growth and development. The doubling time was extended from 10 hrs to 12 hrs and there was some increase in the proportion of slug cells expressing the prestalk marker ecmAO: GFP. DetA is involved in cell type specification during development, and possibly is responsible for the degradation of a repressor of prestalk genes, although further evidence would be necessary for this conclusion ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21193547 Dubin et al. 2010)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 06-MAR-2019 RD

DDB_G0280921.summary: ''DDB_G0280921'' contains a Phox (PX) homology domain and a P-loop containing nucleoside triphosphate hydrolase domain. Phox domains are involved in phosphoinositide-binding. An RNA-sequencing approach was used to identify mTORC1/AMPK-regulated transcriptional networks and associated signaling pathways that are essential for early developmental induction. A combination of starvation and treatment with rapamycin was used to identify a set of ~500 transcripts upregulated during the transition from growth to development, among which is ''DDB_G0280921''. A ''DDB_G0280921'' null mutant is unable to aggregate and displays reduced expression of CAR1 ([/gene/DDB_G0273397 carA-1]), ([/gene/DDB_G0273533 carA-2]), supporting a role for DDB_G0280921 in the induction of early development [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31319820  (Jaiswal and Kimmel, 2015)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 06-APR-2022 RD

DDB_G0283479.summary: The ABC superfamily of genes is one of the largest in the genomes of both bacteria and eukaryotes. The proteins encoded by these genes all carry a characteristic 200- to 250-amino-acid ATP-binding cassette ([/ontology/go/0042626/annotation/page/1 ATPase activity, coupled to transmembrane movement of substances]) that gives them their family name. In bacteria they are mostly involved in nutrient import, while in eukaryotes many are involved in export([/ontology/go/0006810/annotation/page/1 transport]). Seven different families (A to G) have been defined in eukaryotes based on sequence homology, domain topology, and function. ''Dictyostelium'' has 71 ABC transporters (including one on the chromosome 2 duplication). The ABCH family includes members that do not fit into the seven eukaryotic families and are not necessarily related to each other. ''Dictyostelium'' has five genes that compose this group: [/gene/DDB_G0292384 abcH1], [/gene/DDB_G0267428 abcH2], [/gene/DDB_G0275697 abcH3], [/gene/DDB_G0283479 abcH4], and[/gene/DDB_G0293528 arsA]. The ''Dictyostelium'' [/gene/DDB_G0292384 abcH1] and [/gene/DDB_G0267428 abcH2] genes have a single ABC domain and no TM domain. They cluster with ABC transporters involved in the uptake of polar amino acids[http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12456012  (Anjard and Loomis 2002)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 17-MAY-2004 PG

DDB_G0269236.summary:
''rab7A'' encodes a guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G protein) of the Rab family of small GTPases. G proteins are key components of signal transduction networks in which they function as molecular signaling switches, binding to GDP in the off state while binding GTP in the on state. Guanine nucleotide-exchange factors (GEFs) promote the exchange of GDP for GTP on Rab GTPases thus activating them, while GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) inactivate Rab GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP. RabGAP Rbg3 ([/gene/DDB_G0281891 rbg3]) is a possible RabGAP for Rab7A ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24349132 Kuwayama et al. 2013]). Rab7A interacts with TipC ([/gene/DDB_G0267422 tipC]) [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30709847 (Munoz-Braceras et al. 2019)], and with the PH domain-containing protein PripA ([/gene/DDB_G0275795 pripA]) (Tu, et al 2022, PMID:35379834). ''rab7A'' is expressed at a relatively high level throughout both growth and development (unpublished results cited in [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9243512 Buczynski et al. 1997]). Rab7A localizes to the plasma membrane, macropinosomes, lysosomes, post-lysosomes, and maturing phagosomes ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7929276 Temesvari et al. 1994], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7593293 Adessi et al. 1995]), ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9243512 Buczynski et al. 1997]), ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11553719 Rupper et al. 2001]), (Tu, et al 2022, PMID:35379834). Proteomic analysis reveals that Rab7A also localizes to prespore secretory vesicles ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11990506 Srinivasan et al. 2001]) and the Legionella-containing vacuole ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18980612 Urwyler et al. 2009]), ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24373249 Hoffmann et al. 2013]), [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28183814 (Schmolders et al. 2017)]. Rab7A is also associated with ''M. marinum''-containing compartments ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25779329 Barisch, et al. 2015]).
Rab7A is a key regulator of endo-lysosomal trafficking and plays a role in macropinosome and phagosome maturation. Dominant-negative ''rab7A'' cells display a decrease in both the rate of pinocytosis and the efflux rate of fluid phase material compared with wt cells. In addition, the phagocytosis rate is reduced by approximately a third in dominant-negative ''rab7A'' cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9243512 Buczynski et al. 1997]). Rab7 positively regulates macropinocytosis: expression of dominant-negative ''rab7A'' results in the almost complete abolishment of macropinocytosis ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11553719 Rupper et al. 2001]). Rab7 also plays a role in phagosome maturation. Delivery of alpha-mannosidase ([/gene/DDB_G0292206 manA]) to early phagosomes is abolished and delivery of the lysosomal membrane glycoprotein LmpA ([/gene/DDB_G0267406 lmpA]) is decreased in dominant-negative ''rab7A'' cells. Full-sized phagosomes still form in dominant-negative ''rab7A'' cells; however, the regulation of phagosomal pH is aberrant ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11559753 Rupper et al. 2001]). The Rab7A interactor PripA also binds phosphatidylinositol-3,4-bisphosphate and forms a complex with the Rab GAP TbcrA ([/gene/DDB_G0282575 tbcrA]), which has GAP activity towards Rab5A ([/gene/DDB_G0271984 rab5A]). The PripA-TbcrA complex thus promotes Rab5-to-Rab7 conversion and macropinosome and phagosome maturation (Tu, et al 2022, PMID:35379834).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 18-APR-2022 RD

DDB_G0289121.summary: ''pde4'' encodes a type 1 phosphodiesterase which participates along with PdsA ([/gene/DDB_G0285995 pdsA]) in breaking down extracellular cAMP during the slug stage. Pde4 has a lower affinity for cAMP than PdsA but accounts for most of the extracellular activity after aggregation [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16644729  (Bader et al. 2006)],[http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17040207  (Bader et al. 2007)]. A signal sequence for secretion of Pde4 across membranes occurs at the N-terminus followed by two transmembrane domains that leave the catalytic domain in the extracellular environment. ''pde4'' is not expressed in growing cells or during early development but is active between 6 and 16 hours of development. This transcriptional pattern is identical to that of ''pdeE'' ([/gene/DDB_G0276027 pdeE]) which encodes an internal cAMP phosphodiesterase found at the slug stage [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25887420  (Rosengarten et al. 2015)]. Deletion of ''pde4'' results in mutant strains that aggregate normally but then are arrested at the mound stage [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16644729  (Bader et al. 2006)]. It appears that Pde4 controls the extracellular levels of cAMP that regulate morphogenesis in mounds and slugs.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 07-NOV-2018 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis
phenotypes: increased number of early culminant tips

DDB_G0269176.summary:
''racF1'' encodes a guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G protein) of the Rho family of small GTPases. G proteins are key components of signal transduction networks in which they function as molecular signaling switches, binding to GDP in the off state while binding GTP in the on state. Guanine nucleotide-exchange factors (GEFs) promote the exchange of GDP for GTP on Ras GTPases thus activating them, while GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) inactivate Ras GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP. The Rac GEF GxcT ([/gene/DDB_G0269610 gxcT]) binds to and may also activate RacE ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24248334 Wang et al. 2013]). The myosin heavy chain kinase PakB ([/gene/DDB_G0276459 pakB]) interacts with and is a potential downstream effector of RacF1 ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15509655 de la Roche et al. 2005]).
RacF1 shares 94 percent sequence identity with another ''Dictyostelium'' Rho GTPase, RacF2 ([/gene/DDB_G0276967 racF2]). ''racF1'' mRNA is expressed throughout the life cycle: a 0.7 kb transcript is present in vegetative cells, and a 0.9 kb transcript is constitutively expressed throughout the developmental cycle. RacF1 is distributed uniformly in the cytosol and is transiently associated with macropinosomes and phagosomes. When two cells come in contact, RacF1 is strongly enriched in the cortex in the contact area as long as the cells remain attached. ''racF1'' null mutant cells display no prominent phenotypes, and RacF1 does not appear to be essential for endocytosis, cytokinesis or development ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10198067 Rivero et al. 1999)]. RacF1 and RacF2 are likely to have redundant roles in sexual cell fusion. Analysis of ''racF2'' null and overexpression mutants suggest that the gene affects sexual cell fusion and asexual development through the regulation of EDTA-sensitive cell-cell adhesion. ''racF1'' is also induced during sexual cell maturation, although to a lesser extent than ''racF2'', and the RacF1 protein accumulates transiently at cell-cell contact sites, compatible with a role in cell-cell adhesion regulation ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16573737 Muramoto et al. 2006]), ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26940518 Rivero et al. 2016]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 19-MAY-2020 RD

DDB_G0272002.summary: The ''egeA'' gene was identified during a REMI screen for mutants defective in early development. EgeA was found to be a cytosolic, C2 domain-containing protein. ''egeA'' mRNA is expressed in vegetative and early development cells, with expression reaching a maximum at the 2 hr. developmental stage. ''egeA'' null cells fail to form aggregates and do not enter development. Further, the ''egeA'' null mutant expresses pre-starvation genes, but fails to express early developmental genes required for aggregation, such as cAR1 and GP80. EgeA over expressing cells display a similar phenotype to ''egaA'' null cells, suggesting that an optimal level of Ege A is required for proper function. These results suggest that ''egeA'' is a novel cytosolic protein required for the induction of GPCR-mediated early gene expression [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12142016  (Zhang et al. 2002)]. Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 19-JAN-2015 RD

DDB_G0279823.summary: Sey1 is an ortholog of yeast SEY1, a dynamin-like GTPase that mediates homotypic endoplasmic reticulum (ER) fusion. Sey1 consists of a large N-terminal guanosine triphosphatase (GTPase) domain, followed by a three-helix bundle (3HB) domain, two adjacent transmembrane motifs (TMs), and a cytosolic C-terminal domain. Sey1 localizes to the ER as well as to ''Legionella''-containing vacuoles (LCV). ''sey1'' mutants reveal a role for Sey1 in ''Legionella pneumophila'' replication. Over-expression of Sey1 promotes the intracellular replication of ''L. pneumophila'' and LCVs with an enlarged diameter, whereas ''L. pneumophila'' growth is substantially decreased, and the diameter of LCVs is reduced in ''sey1'' mutant cells with abolished GTPase activity. In addition, the ER fails to accumulate around LCVs in catalytically inactive ''sey1'' mutants. These results reveal that Sey1 promotes intracellular replication of L. pneumophila by remodeling the ER connecting with the pathogen vacuole [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28835546  (Steiner et al. 2017)]. ''sey1'' null mutants have an altered ER architecture, with a partially disrupted tubular ER network. ''sey1'' null mutants also exhibit defects in lysosomal enzyme exocytosis, intracellular proteolysis, and cell motility, resulting in impaired growth on bacterial lawns. In ''sey1'' null mutants, the expansion of the LCV is inhibited at early stages of infection, the ER is less efficiently recruited to the LCV, and ''L. pneumophila'' replicates less efficiently and shows a severe growth defect compared with growth in wild type cells. These results further reveal a role for Sey1 in maintenance of the ER architecture and intracellular replication by ''L. pneumophila'' (Husler, et al. 2021, PMID:33583106).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 28-OCT-2021 RD

DDB_G0286183.summary:
''agps'' is an oxidoreductase with [/ontology/go/0008609/annotation/page/1 alkylglycerone-phosphate synthase activity], responsible for the formation of alkyldihydroxyacetonephosphate (alkyl-DHAP) through the exchange of the acyl moiety of acyl-DHAP with a fatty alcohol. This reaction required FAD. This essential reaction generates the ether bond in the [/ontology/go/0008611/annotation/page/1 ether lipid biosynthetic process]. In other organisms, this takes place in the [/ontology/go/0005777/annotation/page/1 peroxisome]. Consistent with this, the ''Dictyostelium'' protein has a type 1 peroxisomal targeting signal at the C terminus.
The ''Dictyostelium'' Agps protein has been crystallized ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17562315 Razeto et al., 2007], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17601746 Razeto et al., 2007]). The catalytic site contains five conserved residues: Asp237, Arg352,Arg447, Glu461, and Tyr508. Mutagenesis of the Arg352 residue diminishes agps activity, while mutation of Tyr508 abolishes the activity.
Defects in human ''AGPS'' causes rhizomelic chondrodysplasia punctata (RCDP), a peroxisomal disorder defined by the inability of patients to synthesize ether phospholipids. This results in serious developmental defects and death before 10 years of age.
Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 18-DEC-2007 PG

DDB_G0276273.summary:
Histones form the nucleosomal core ([/ontology/go/0000786/annotation/page/1 nucleosome]) ([/ontology/go/0006334/annotation/page/1 nucleosome assembly]) that is fundamental to chromatin structure (). The histone octamer is composed of an H3-H4 tetramer (two H3-H4 dimers) coupled with an H2A-H2Btetramer (two H2A-H2B dimers). The histone H1 linker protein plays a role in packaging nucleosomes into the 30 nmfiber found in chromatin ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9177486 Bukenberger et al. 1992]).
In ''Dictyostelium discoideum'' and ''Saccharomyces cerevisiae'', only one copy of histone [/gene/DDB_G0285319 H1] appears to be present, in comparison to other eukaryotes which have multiple copies and subtypes([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7867938 Hauser et al. 1995], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9046096 Ushinsky et al.1997]). Two putative H2A family members, [/gene/DDB_G0279667 H2AX] and [/gene/DDB_G0286747 H2AZ], and three H2Adomain-containing proteins, [/gene/DDB_G0289187 H2Av1], [/gene/DDB_G0289193 H2Av2], [/gene/DDB_G0289197 H2Av3], are present in ''Dictyostelium''. Two H2B domain-containing proteins also exist inthe ''Dicty'' genome: [/gene/DDB_G0293758 H2Bv1] and [/gene/DDB_G0276273 H2Bv2]. There are three histone H3proteins, [/gene/DDB_G0267402 H3a] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9177486 Bukenberger et al. 1992]), [/gene/DDB_G0270838 H3b], and [/gene/DDB_G0271092 H3c], and two H3 domain-containing proteins, [/gene/DDB_G0291185 H3v1] and [/gene/DDB_G0277979 H3v2]. We have also identified two histone H4proteins, [/gene/DDB_G0277183 H4a] and [/gene/DDB_G0276863 H4b], which have identical protein sequences but non-identical nucleotide sequences.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 13-APR-2004 KP

DDB_G0277721.summary: In bacteria, the protein FtsZ is the principal component of FtsZ cytokinetic ring (the Z-ring), a ring that constricts the cell at division. The precise role of FtsZ is not know. A protein related to FtsZ is found in some organelles of certain eukaryotes. ''Dictyostelium'' has two nuclearly encoded FtsZs, [/gene/DDB_G0277721 fszA] and [/gene/DDB_G0269224 fszB], that are targeted to the [/ontology/go/0005759/annotation/page/1 mitochondrial matrix]. The two proteins have different distributions in the mitochondria, suggesting that they have divergent roles in [/ontology/go/0007005/annotation/page/1 mitochondrion organization and biogenesis]. Null mutations in ''fszA'' and ''fszB'' results in a higher fraction of cells with tubular mitochondrial morphology ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14665465 Gilson et al. 2003]). Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 03-MAY-2004 PG

DDB_G0275697.summary: The ABC superfamily of genes is one of the largest in the genomes of both bacteria and eukaryotes. The proteins encoded by these genes all carry a characteristic 200- to 250-amino-acid ATP-binding cassette ([/ontology/go/0042626/annotation/page/1 ATPase activity, coupled to transmembrane movement of substances]) that gives them their family name. In bacteria they are mostly involved in nutrient import, while in eukaryotes many are involved in export ([/ontology/go/0006810/annotation/page/1 transport]). Seven different families (A to G) have been defined in eukaryotes based on sequence homology, domain topology, and function. ''Dictyostelium'' has 71 ABC transporters (including one on the chromosome 2 duplication). The ABCH family includes members that do not fit into the seven eukaryotic families and are not necessarily related to each other. ''Dictyostelium'' has five genes that compose this group: [/gene/DDB_G0292384 abcH1], [/gene/DDB_G0267428 abcH2], [/gene/DDB_G0275697 abcH3], [/gene/DDB_G0283479 abcH4], and[/gene/DDB_G0293528 arsA]. The ''Dictyostelium'' [/gene/DDB_G0292384 abcH1] and [/gene/DDB_G0267428 abcH2] genes have a single ABC domain and no TM domain. They cluster with ABC transporters involved in the uptake of polar amino acids[http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12456012  (Anjard and Loomis 2002)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 16-JUN-2003 PG

DDB_G0289827.summary: ''rab18'' encodes a guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G protein) of the Rab family of small GTPases. G proteins are key components of signal transduction networks in which they function as molecular signaling switches, binding to GDP in the off state while binding GTP in the on state. Guanine nucleotide-exchange factors (GEFs) promote the exchange of GDP for GTP on Rab GTPases thus activating them, while GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) inactivate Rab GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP. Rab subfamily small GTPases in many organisms are key regulators of intracellular membrane trafficking. Rab18 is similar to human RAB18, which is involved in lipid droplet formation. In addition, proteomic analysis revealed that Rab18 is localized to lipid droplets ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24036346 Du, et al. 2013]), suggesting a possible role for ''Dictyostelium'' ''rab18''. Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 20-SEP-2020 RD

DDB_G0292354.summary:
Members of the casein kinase I (CK1) family ([/ontology/go/0004681/annotation/page/1 casein kinase I activity]) of serine/threonine kinases have been implicated in manycellular processes. Casein kinases have been shown to phosphorylate the 14-3-3 ([/gene/DDB_G0269138 fttB]) protein inmammals, play a role in Wnt signaling in ''Xenopus laevis'' and ''Caenorhabditis elegans'', and maintaincircadian rhythms in ''Drosophila melanogaster''. Additionally, CK1 plays a role in DNA repair ([/ontology/go/0006281/annotation/page/1 DNA repair])in ''Saccharomyces cerevisiae'' and ''Schizosaccharomyces pombe'' ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10880352 Moreno-Bueno et al. 2000]).
Two casein kinase I family members have been identified in ''Dictyostelium discoideum'', [/gene/DDB_G0273059 cak1] and''DDB0216336''. Cak1 is highly similar to CK1s in yeast and in metazoans. DDB0216336 is a putative casein kinase Ithat is highly similar to the CK1 subfamily tau-tubulin kinase (TTBK) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12471243 Manning etal. 2002]). The Cak1 protein has been shown to phosphorylate casein when it is expressed in ''E.coli'' cells, and localizes to both the cytoplasm ([/ontology/go/0005737/annotation/page/1 cytoplasm]) and the nucleus ([/ontology/go/0005634/annotation/page/1 nucleus]) inimmunofluorescence assays. Null mutations and overexpression of a dominant-negative form of Cak1 fail to produce viable cells, indicating that this protein may be essential for growth. Overexpression of wild-type Cak1 results in decreased sensitivity to the DNA-damaging agent hydroxyurea; this suggests a role for Cak1 in DNA repair ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10880352 Moreno-Bueno et al. 2000]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 05-MAY-2004 KP

DDB_G0292220.summary: ''ecmH'' encodes a 14 kDa protein that contains a cellulose-binding domain. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15309638 Shimada et al. 2004)]. There are 14 other proteins in the ''Dictyostelium'' genome that carry a cellulose-binding domain. Genes encoding 4 of the small cellulose-binding proteins are tightly clustered on chromosome 6 and another 4 are clustered on chromosome 1. mRNA from ''ecmH'' is not found in growing cells or during aggregation; however it accumulates more than 50 fold in prestalk cells between 16 and 22 hrs of development ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25887420 Rosengarten et al. 2015)]. Expression of ecmH as well as the other family members on chromosome 6 ([/gene/DDB_G0291291 ecmF], [/gene/DDB_G0292224 ecmG], [/gene/DDB_G0292222 ecmI], [/gene/DDB_G0292218 st15]) is regulated by the transcription factor STATa ([/gene/DDB_G0281381 dstA]). ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15309638 Shimada et al. 2004)]. Since the slug sheath is made for several hours before ''ecmH'' is expressed, it is unlikely that EcmH is an essential sheath component, and more likely that it is involved in culmination.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 12-NOV-2015 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0279175.summary:
Hspc300 (brk1) is a member of the Scar/WAVE complex, consisting of (Scar) ([/gene/DDB_G0285253 scrA]), Hspc300, ([/gene/DDB_G0267956 abiA]), (PIR121) ([/gene/DDB_G0287855 pirA]), and ([/gene/DDB_G0274519 napA]). In migrating cells, the Scar/WAVE complex regulates the production of lamellipods and pseudopods through Arp2/3 complex activation. The Scar/WAVE complex localizes to the front of pseudopods and the tips of filopods, cell-cell contact zones, and the cell leading edge. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22891261 Veltman et al. 2012]). Hspc300 interacts directly with Scar ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17314411 Caracino et al. 2007]), forms homotrimers and interacts with Scar and AbiA ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21701600 Linkner et al. 2011]).
Disruption of ''hspc300'' leads to a complete loss of Scar protein and PIR121 fails to localize to the leading edge of actin pseudopods as in wild type cells. ''hspc300'' null mutants have phenotypes similar to ''scrA'' null mutants, including decreased cell motility speed and smaller, more rounded cells with smaller protrusions. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19228419 Pollitt and Insall 2009]). ''hspc300'' null cells are also multinucleate revealing a cytokinesis defect ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20530573 King et al. 2010]). Deletion of ''hspc300'' in an AX2 background (''hspc300''/AX2 null) revealed additional phenotypes. In ''hspc300''/AX2 null cells Scar and AbiA levels are severely decreased. ''hspc300''/AX2 null cells largely lacked macropinocytic cups and have a moderate decrease in filopodium formation. ''hspc300''/AX2 null cells have both a reduced cell speed and directionality of movement. Although ''hspc300''/AX2 single null cells lack developmental defects, ''hspc300''/''vasP''/AX2 ([/gene/DDB_G0289541 vasP]) double null cells have severe developmental defects and on PB agar plates development did not advance beyond the slug stage. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28889942 Litschko et al. 2017]).
Biochemical analysis and X-ray crystallography studies suggest a model in which Hspc300 serves as an adaptor protein to promote assembly of the mature Scar complex. Homotrimeric Hspc300 maintains a dynamic pool of Hspc300 monomers which associate with Scar and AbiA to form a heterotrimeric subcomplex. In the final assembly step, Hspc300 then serves as an adaptor protein to stabilize and coordinate the assembly of the Scar/AbiA/Hspc300 with heterodimeric NapA/PirA to form the mature Scar/WAVE complex ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21701600 Linkner et al. 2011]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 12-JAN-2022 RD

DDB_G0282923.summary: Genetic complementation studies were used to assign a series of rapid developing mutants of Dictyostelium to one or another of 3 rde loci. Those carrying mutations in ''rdeA'' were found to have high levels of cAMP ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6298035 Abe et al. 1983)]. Sequence comparisons and phenotypic characterizations showed that RdeA is a component of phosphorelay pathways controlling internal cAMP phosphodiesterase activity ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9582274 Chang et al. 1998)]. A histidine moeity in the 28 kDa RdeA protein accepts a phosphate from an aspartate in histidine kinases, and relays it to an aspartate in the response regulator region of the cAMP phosophodiesterase RegA ([/gene/DDB_G0284331 regA]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10488068 Thomason et al. 1999)]. RdeA also facilitates dephosphorylation of RegA when DhkA ([/gene/DDB_G0280961 dhkA]) is converted to a phosphatase after it has bound SDF-2 ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10373524 Wang et al. 1999)]. The signaling molecule differentiation-inducing factor 2 (DIF-2) modulates chemotaxis to cAMP via the DhkC ([/gene/DDB_G0274191 dhkC])-RegA-RdeA signaling pathway. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26919666 Kuwayama and Kubohara 2016)]Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 24-JAN-2017 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0289389.summary: The ''dtfA'' gene was identified by screening a bank of REMI mutants for clones that could not form tipped mounds during development. The ''dftA'' protein DFTA lacks extensive sequence homology to other proteins, but contains four short motifs which show partial homology to repeats found in mammalian mucins. These results suggest that ''dtfA'' may form part of a cell-cell adhesion system that is needed both for optimal aggregation and efficient cell sorting during development. DDB_G0291714.summary:
The ABC superfamily of genes is one of the largest in the genomes of both bacteria and eukaryotes. The proteins encoded by these genes all carry a characteristic 200- to 250-amino-acid ATP-binding cassette that gives them their family name ATPase activity, coupled to transmembrane movement of substances. In bacteria they are mostly involved in nutrient import, while in eukaryotes many are involved in export. Seven different families (A to G) have been defined in eukaryotes based on sequence homology, domain topology, and function. ''Dictyostelium'' has 71 ABC transporters (including one on the chromosome 2 duplication) and 11 ABCB family members: [/gene/DDB_G0293416 abcB1], [/gene/DDB_G0293438 abcB2], [/gene/DDB_G0291714 abcB3], [/gene/DDB_G0279915 abcB4],[/gene/DDB_G0292554 abcB5], [/gene/DDB_G0282931 abcB6], [/gene/DDB_G0269720 abcB7], [/gene/DDB_G0293002 tagA], [/gene/DDB_G0286119 tagB], [/gene/DDB_G0286121 tagC], and [/gene/DDB_G0286123 tagD]. The B family includes three main subtypes: full transporters involved in multiple drug resistance (MDR), half-transporters targeted to mitochondria, and half-transporters involved in peptide transport [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12456012 (Anjard and Loomis 2002)].
[http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25448698 Miranda et al. 2014] show pharmacologically and genetically that ABC transporters mediate cAMP export. They identified several candidates and further characterized one, ''abcB3'', in detail. RNAi-mediated knockdown of abcB3 results in delayed development and decreased extracellular cAMP levels. In addition, ectopic expression of ''abcB3'' is sufficient to increase cAMP export in mammalian cells, suggesting that AbcB3 is a component of the cAMP export mechanism in D. discoideum development. Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 10-DEC-2014 RD

DDB_G0282339.summary:
DNA-dependent RNA polymerase catalyzes the transcription of DNA into RNA using the four ribonucleoside triphosphates as substrates ([/ontology/go/0003899/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase activity]). Three distinct zinc-containing RNA polymerases are found in eukaryotic nuclei: [/gene/DDB_G0275759 rpa1] for the ribosomal RNA precursor ([/ontology/go/0006360/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase I promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005736/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase I complex]), [/gene/DDB_G0279193 rpb1] for the mRNA precursor ([/ontology/go/0006366/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase II promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005665/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase II, core complex]), and [/gene/DDB_G0277199 rpc1] for 5S and tRNA genes ([/ontology/go/0006383/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase III promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005666/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase III complex]).
RNA polymerase I is a multisubunit complex. The subunits encoded by [/gene/DDB_G0275759 rpa1] (ortholog of ''S. cerevisiae RPA190''), [/gene/DDB_G0288449 rpc2] (''RPA135''), [/gene/DDB_G0268198 rpa43] (''RPA43''), [/gene/DDB_G0290909 rpa49] (''RPA49''), and [/gene/DDB_G0278263 rpa12] (''RPA12'') are unique to RNA polymerase I. Two subunits, [/gene/DDB_G0291362 rpc19] and [/gene/DDB_G0282339 rpa5] (''RPC19'' and ''RPC40'' in ''S. cerevisiae''), are common to RNA polymerase I and RNA polymerase III and correspond to subunits 3 and 11 of RNA polymerase II. Subunits [/gene/DDB_G0291636 rpb5], [/gene/DDB_G0291037 rpb6], [/gene/DDB_G0278039 rpb8], [/gene/DDB_G0272036 rpb10], and [/gene/DDB_G0283365 rpb12] are common to all three RNA polymerases. Yeast has two additional subunits, ''RPA34'' and ''RPA14'', that do not have clear orthologs in other species, including in ''Dictyostelium'' ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12407181 Peyroche et al. 2002], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12381659 Schramm and Hernandez 2001]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 13-APR-2004 PG

DDB_G0273737.summary:
Members of the casein kinase I (CK1) family of serine/threonine kinases have been implicated in many cellular processes. Casein kinases have been shown to phosphorylate the 14-3-3 ([/gene/DDB_G0269138 fttB]) protein in mammals, play a role in Wnt signaling in ''Xenopus laevis'' and ''Caenorhabditis elegans'', and maintain circadian rhythms in ''Drosophila melanogaster''. Additionally, CK1 plays a role in DNA repair in ''Saccharomyces cerevisiae'' and ''Schizosaccharomyces pombe'' ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10880352 Moreno-Bueno et al. 2000]).
Two casein kinase I family members have been identified in ''Dictyostelium discoideum'', ''cak1'' and [/gene/DDB_G0292354 DDB_G0292354]. Cak1 is highly similar to CK1s in yeast and in metazoans. DDB0216336 is a putative casein kinase I that is highly similar to the CK1 subfamily tau-tubulin kinase (TTBK) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12471243 Manninget al. 2002]). The Cak1 protein has been shown to phosphorylate casein when it is expressed in ''E. coli'' cells, and localizes to both the cytoplasm and the nucleus in immunofluorescence assays. Null mutations and overexpression of a dominant-negative form of Cak1 fail to produce viable cells, indicating that this protein may be essential for growth. Overexpression of wild-type Cak1 results in decreased sensitivity to the DNA-damaging agent hydroxyurea; this suggests a role for Cak1 in DNA repair ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10880352 Moreno-Bueno et al. 2000]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 05-MAY-2004 KP

DDB_G0277979.summary:
Histones form the nucleosomal core ([/ontology/go/0000786/annotation/page/1 nucleosome]) ([/ontology/go/0006334/annotation/page/1 nucleosome assembly]) that is fundamental to chromatin structure (). The histone octamer is composed of an H3-H4 tetramer (two H3-H4 dimers) coupled with an H2A-H2Btetramer (two H2A-H2B dimers). The histone H1 linker protein plays a role in packaging nucleosomes into the 30 nmfiber found in chromatin ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9177486 Bukenberger et al. 1992]).
In ''Dictyostelium discoideum'' and ''Saccharomyces cerevisiae'', only one copy of histone [/gene/DDB_G0285319 H1] appears to be present, in comparison to other eukaryotes which have multiple copies and subtypes([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7867938 Hauser et al. 1995], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9046096 Ushinsky et al.1997]). Two putative H2A family members, [/gene/DDB_G0279667 H2AX] and [/gene/DDB_G0286747 H2AZ], and three H2Adomain-containing proteins, [/gene/DDB_G0289187 H2Av1], [/gene/DDB_G0289193 H2Av2], [/gene/DDB_G0289197 H2Av3], are present in ''Dictyostelium''. Two H2B domain-containing proteins also exist inthe ''Dicty'' genome: [/gene/DDB_G0293758 H2Bv1] and [/gene/DDB_G0276273 H2Bv2]. There are three histone H3proteins, [/gene/DDB_G0267402 H3a] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9177486 Bukenberger et al. 1992]), [/gene/DDB_G0270838 H3b], and [/gene/DDB_G0271092 H3c], and two H3 domain-containing proteins, [/gene/DDB_G0291185 H3v1] and [/gene/DDB_G0277979 H3v2]. We have also identified two histone H4proteins, [/gene/DDB_G0277183 H4a] and [/gene/DDB_G0276863 H4b], which have identical protein sequences but non-identical nucleotide sequences.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 13-APR-2004 KP

DDB_G0269250.summary:
''pats1'' encodes a large, multi-domain protein of the Roco family. Pats1contains N-terminal myotubulin-related and catalytic protein tyrosine phosphatase (PTP) domains, a leucine-rich repeat (LRR) region, a Roc small GTPase domain, a COR (C-terminal of Roc) domain, a protein kinase domain and a WD40 repeat domain in the C-terminal region. ''pats1'' is an ortholog of human LRRK2, mutations in which are associated with Parkinson disease. Eleven ''Dictyostelium'' proteins belong to the Roco family: ([/gene/DDB_G0291079 gbpC]), ([/gene/DDB_G0273259 qkgA-1]), Pats1, ([/gene/DDB_G0288251 roco4]), ([/gene/DDB_G0294533 roco5]), ([/gene/DDB_G0279417 roco6]), ([/gene/DDB_G0267472 roco7]), ([/gene/DDB_G0286127 roco8]), ([/gene/DDB_G0288183 roco9]), ([/gene/DDB_G0291710 roco10]) and ([/gene/DDB_G0268636 roco11]).
''pats1'' was identified in a REMI mutagenesis screen designed to isolate genes required for cytokinesis. Pats1 localizes to the cytosol and interacts with the actin cytoskeleton. ''pats1'' is expressed during both growth and development with the highest level of expression during the slug stage of development. Both ''pats1'' null mutants and cells overexpressing ''pats1'' have a severe cytokinesis defect, indicating that ''pats1'' is an important regulator of cytokinesis in ''Dictyostelium''. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12529423 Abysalh et al. 2003]), ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20348387 van Egmond and van Haastert 2010]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 13-OCT-2021 RD

DDB_G0275699.summary:
GNT1 is the first of three glycosyltransferases to modify Skp1. ''Dictyostelium'' acetylglucosaminyltransferase activity was originally identified in the cytoplasm ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10593934 Teng-umnuay et al. 1999]). This activity was later attributed to the [/gene/DDB_G0275699 gnt1] gene ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12244115 van der Wel et al. 2002]). GNT1 specifically adds GlcNAc (N-acetylglucosamine) to Skp1 ([/gene/DDB_G0269230 fpaA]/[/gene/DDB_G0273251 fpaB-1])
Glycosylation of Skp1 has been extensively studied in ''Dictyostelium''. The initial step in Skp1 glycosylation involves the hydroxylation of Pro143 by a proline hydroxylase ([/gene/DDB_G0277759 phyA], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9660787 Teng-umnuay et al. 1998]). HyPro143 is then modified by the glycosyltransferase [/gene/DDB_G0275699 gnt1], which transfers a GlcNAc (N-acetylglucosamine) to the Skp1 protein ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10593934 Teng-umnuay et al. 1999]). The Skp1-GlcNAc is extended by a bifunctional diglycosyltransferase, [/gene/DDB_G0283761 pgtA], which processively adds galactose and fucose ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11423539 van der Wel et al. 2001], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12244067 van der Wel et al. 2002]). Subsequently two additional galactose residues are added by [/gene/DDB_G0283005 agtA] to yield the Skp1 pentasaccharide (GGFGGnOSkp1; [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16495217 Ercan et al. 2006], reviewed in [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31128470 West and Kim 2019]).
Genetic disruption of ''gnt1'' results in an oxygen requirement for culmination that lies between that of the phyA-KO (gene [/gene/DDB_G0277759 phyA]) and wild type cells, but also yields morphologically defective fruiting bodies at any oxygen level ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22128189 Zhang et al. 2011]). Further investigations showed that full SKP1 glycosylation is required for optimal oxygen sensing during development, for example [/gene/DDB_G0283005 agtA] knockout and overexpression mutants require an elevated oxygen level to culminate, similar to the phenotype of the [/gene/DDB_G0277759 phyA] mutant ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19687007 Wang et al. 2009], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22128189 Zhang et al. 2011], reviewed in [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25988702 West and Blader 2015]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 19-MAR-2020 PF

DDB_G0290529.summary: ''Dictyostelium cpnE'' belongs to the highly conserved copines, a family of ubiquitious Ca(2+)-dependent phospholipid-binding ([/ontology/go/0005544/annotation/page/1 calcium-dependent phospholipid binding]) proteins. In their N-terminal half, copines contain two Ca(2+)- and phospholipid-binding domains (C2 domains) present in such proteins as phospholipase C and protein kinase C. Much of the C-terminal half consists of a von Willebrand Factor type A domain (VWFA) typically found in the extracellular portions of membrane proteins like integrins. Thus copines represent a fusion of intracellular (C2) and extracellular (VWFA) domains. However, there are no signal sequence or hydrophobic transmembrane sequences in the predicted proteins suggesting copines are intracellular proteins. Copines are thought to be involved in membrane trafficking. It is of particular interest that copines, first found in the highly phagocytic protozoan ''Paramecium'' and then isolated from mammalian spleen and liver, seem to be abundant in cells and organs that are, or contain, phagocytes. In this context it comes as no surprise that phagocytic ''Dictyostelium'' has a total of six copine genes[http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16343335  (Damer et al. 2005)]. The widespread distribution of copines from protozoans to mammals and their high similarity suggest they play important role(s) in eukaryotic biology. Reviewed in [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12440769  (Tomsig and Creutz, 2001)]Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 05-APR-2004 PF

DDB_G0282055.summary: ''c2gapB'' encodes a putative Ras GTPase-activating protein (GAP, rasGAP). RasGAPs are key components of signal transduction networks in which they inactivate Ras GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP. C2gapB contains an N-terminal C2 domain followed by a C-terminal Ras GTPase-activating domain. C2gapB localizes to the membrane, at the base of macropinocytotic crowns and nascent macropinosomes, and is also associated strongly with the rear of cells. C2gapB binds phosphatidylinositol-3,4-bisphosphate. In ''c2gapB'' null cells, active Ras patches cover most the cell perimeter instead of restricted localization as in wild type cells and Ras activity is significantly increased; however, a specific target Ras GTPase has not been identified. Elevated Ras activity in the null mutants results in a significant increase in random cell motility. These results indicate that C2gapB inhibits Ras activity at the rear of the cell and suggest that it is an important regulator of protrusion dynamics and motility. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30194235 Li et al. 2018]), (Erratum, Li, et al. 2018, PMID: 30322942).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 16-MAR-2022 RD

DDB_G0269224.summary: In bacteria, the protein FtsZ is the principal component of FtsZ cytokinetic ring (the Z-ring), a ring that constricts the cell at division. The precise role of FtsZ is not know. A protein related to FtsZ is found in some organelles of certain eukaryotes. ''Dictyostelium'' has two nuclearly encoded FtsZs, [/gene/DDB_G0277721 fszA] and [/gene/DDB_G0269224 fszB], that are targeted to the [/ontology/go/0005759/annotation/page/1 mitochondrial matrix]. The two proteins have different distributions in the mitochondria, suggesting that they have divergent roles in [/ontology/go/0007005/annotation/page/1 mitochondrion organization and biogenesis]. Null mutations in ''fszA'' and ''fszB'' results in a higher fraction of cells with tubular mitochondrial morphology ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14665465 Gilson et al. 2003]). Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 03-MAY-2004 PG

DDB_G0273251.summary:
The [/gene/DDB_G0269230 fpaA] and [/gene/DDB_G0273251 fpaB-1]/[/gene/DDB_G0273615 fpaB-2] genes encode nearly identical proteins, differing by one intron, 33 nucleotides, and one amino acid ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9373134 West et al. 1997]). The ''fpa'' genes encode the Skp1 protein, which in ''Dictyostelium'' and other protists forms the SCF ubiquitin ligase complex (reviewed in [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15238247 West et al. 2004]) Both FpaA and FpaB proteins are found in the cytoplasm and enriched in the nucleus in immunocytochemistry experiments.During development, expression persists in the nucleus but also increases at the cell cortex. Glycosylation is required for nuclear enrichment ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11358877 Sassi et al. 2001]).
Glycosylation of Skp1 has been extensively studied in ''Dictyostelium''. The initial step in Skp1 glycosylation involves the hydroxylation of Pro143 by a proline hydroxylase ([/gene/DDB_G0277759 phyA], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9660787 Teng-umnuay et al. 1998]). HyPro143 is then modified by the glycosyltransferase [/gene/DDB_G0275699 gnt1], which transfers a GlcNAc (N-acetylglucosamine) to the Skp1 protein ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10593934 Teng-umnuay et al. 1999]). The Skp1-GlcNAc is extended by a bifunctional diglycosyltransferase, [/gene/DDB_G0283761 pgtA], which processively adds galactose and fucose ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11423539 van der Wel et al. 2001], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12244067 van der Wel et al. 2002]). Subsequently two additional galactose residues are added by [/gene/DDB_G0283005 agtA] to yield the Skp1 pentasaccharide (GGFGGnOSkp1; [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16495217 Ercan et al. 2006], reviewed in [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31128470 West and Kim 2019]).
West and colleagues reported that the proline hydroxylase ([/gene/DDB_G0277759 phyA]) performing the first SKP1 modification mediates oxygen signaling during ''Dictyostelium'' development. ''phyA''-null cells need strongly elevated oxygen levels to culminate ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17699611 West et al. 2007]). Mutant analyses showed not only is Skp1 a substrate for PhyA it is also a functional mediator of PhyA activity in cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20969846 Wang et al. 2011]). Further investigations showed that full SKP1 glycosylation is required for optimal oxygen sensing during development, for example [/gene/DDB_G0283005 agtA] knockout and overexpression mutants require elevated oxygen levels to culminate ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19687007 Wang et al. 2009], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22128189 Zhang et al. 2011], reviewed in [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25988702 West and Blader 2015]).
The ''Dictyostelium'' unmodified Skp1 seems to form a dimer. The SCF ubiquitin ligase complex has been investigated and binding to F-box protein seems to dissociate the dimer. Free Skp1 forms a complex with a CullinA homolog ([/gene/DDB_G0278991 culE]), and the F-box protein ([/gene/DDB_G0292312 fbxD]; [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24550398 Shafer et al. 2014], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25341530 Sheik et al. 2015]). Co-immunoprecipitation and proteomic analysis also showed the F-box protein [/gene/DDB_G0276887 fbxA] binding to Skp1. CulE binds proteins such as the RING box protein [/gene/DDB_G0287629 rbx1] and the cullin-associated neddylation-disassociated protein [/gene/DDB_G0274167 cand1]. F-box proteins preferentially associate with fully glycosylated Skp1 compared to unmodified Skp1. Thus low oxygen levels are rate limiting for the hydroxylation of nascent Skp1 in cells, and demonstrates that full Skp1 hydroxylation/glycosylation is to alter the repertoire of the F-box proteins with which it associates ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24506136 Sheik et al. 2014], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25341530 Sheikh et al. 2015]). Furthermore NMR and mass spec analyses showed that Skp1 complete glycolysation modifies the originally disordered protein conformation resulting in enhanced F-box protein binding ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28928219 Sheikh et al. 2017]; [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29251491 Xu et al. 2018], reviewed in [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31128470 West and Kim 2019]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 06-MAR-2020 PF
DDB_G0273251.note: Two genes encode the Skp1 protein, named fpaA and fpaB, differing by 1 intron, 33 nt, and 1 aa.

DDB_G0285321.summary:
SplB (Pyk2) was initially characterized by [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22699506 Araki et. al 2012 ] and shown to be a direct, constitutive activator of STATc. In a null mutant for SplB, exposure to DIF-1 does not activate STATc. Conversely, overexpression of SplB causes constitutive STATc activation. SplB phosphorylates STATc on Tyr922 in vitro and complexes with STATc both in vitro and in vivo.
The tyrosine kinase like enzymes SplB and Pyk3 were shown to be involved in the hyper osmotic-induced activation of STATc. A double mutant of ''splB'' and ''pyk3'' is completely unresponsive to hyperosmotic stress-induced activation of STATc. Both SplB and Pyk3 undergo increased autocatalytic phosphorylation when cells are stressed. In addition, under stress Pyk3 and SplB accumulate in different parts of the cell: Pyk3 moves from the cytosol to the cortex, whereas SplB accumulates in cytosolic granules that colocalize with PTP3. [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25143406 (Araki et. al 2014)] Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 09-APR-2015 RD

DDB_G0291350.summary: Members of the NAK (Numb-associated kinase) family of serine/threonine kinases ([/ontology/go/0004674/annotation/page/1 protein serine/threonine kinase activity]) have been shown toparticipate in diverse cellular processes. The first characterized NAK was the ''Drosophila melanogaster'' NAK,named for its ability to interact with the neuronal differentiation protein Numb, hence the name NAK ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9418906 Chien et al. 1998]). Additional members of this family include AAK1 (AP2-associatedkinase), involved in clathrin-mediated endocytosis ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11877461 Conner and Schmid 2000]),and BIKe (BMP-induced kinase), which plays a role in bone differentiation ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11500515 Kearns et al. 2001]). [/gene/DDB_G0276461 DDB_G0276461] and [/gene/DDB_G0280111 DDB_G0280111] are similar to the kinasedomains of AAK1 and BIKe. The NAK family also includes MPSK (myristoylated and palmitoylated serine/threoninekinase), which is fatty acid acylated ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10364453 Berson et al. 1999]) andmay play a role in TGF-beta signaling ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10947953 Ohta et al. 2000]). The mostclosely related protein to MPSK in ''Dictyostelium discoideum'' is DDB0216373.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 10-MAY-2004 KP

DDB_G0274695.summary: The role of Nwk/Bzz1p-like protein (NLP) and Syndapin-like protein (SLP), in the regulation of the formation and trafficking of WASP-vesicles during chemotaxis was investigated by [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19409937  Lee et al. 2009]. Deletion mutants of either ''nlp'' or ''slp'' did not cause significant defects, but deletion of both genes causes the loss of polararized F-actin organization and significant defects in chemotaxis. WASP and NLP are colocalized on vesicles and interactions between the two are required for vesicle formation from Golgi. Microtubules are required for polarized trafficking of these vesicles as vesicles showing high directed mobility are absent in cells treated with nocodazole. Our results suggest that interaction of WASP with NLP/SLP is required for the formation and trafficking of vesicles from Golgi to the membrane, which might play a central role in the establishment of cell polarity during chemotaxis. Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 13-JAN-2015 RD

DDB_G0281337.summary:
''rab14'' (''rabD'') encodes a guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G protein) of the Rab family of small GTPases. G proteins are key components of signal transduction networks in which they function as molecular signaling switches, binding to GDP in the off state while binding GTP in the on state. Guanine nucleotide-exchange factors (GEFs) promote the exchange of GDP for GTP on Rab GTPases thus activating them, while GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) inactivate Rab GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP. DRG ([/gene/DDB_G0291978 xacA]) contains both GAP and GEF domains and displays GAP activity for Rab14 ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11285226 Manstein et al. 2001]). Disgorgin ([/gene/DDB_G0280955 dsgg]) exhibits weak GAP activity toward Rab14 while drainin ([/gene/DDB_G0269130 phgA]) binds but does not exhibit GAP activity to Rab14 ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18636095 Du et al. 2008 ]). ''rab14'' is expressed at a relatively constant level throughout growth and development and is associated with the lysosomal membrane and the contractile vacuole complex [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7876348 (Bush et al. 1994)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7929276 (Temesvari et al. 1994)]. Rab14 also localizes to the Legionella-containing vacuole [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18980612 (Urwyler et al. 2009)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28183814 (Schmolders et al. 2017)].
''rab14'' is involved in signaling networks that regulate membrane traffic between the endosomal pathway and the contractile vacuole. ''rab14'' regulates phagocytosis and plays a role in the regulation of lysosome and phagosome fusion. Cells overexpressing dominant negative Rab14 swell and lyse when placed in water, and have an aberrant contractile vacuole morphology. Constitutively active ''rab14'' localizes to the membranes of large acidic lysosomes and these cells show an increased rate of fusion of early endosomes. In addition, in constitutively active ''rab14'' cells the phagocytosis rate was more than twice that of wt cells and phagosome-phagosome fusion occurred at five times the rate of wt cells. Dominant-negative ''rab14'' cells have opposing phenotypes with a decrease in both the rate of phagocytosis and the rate of phagosome-phagosome fusion [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8898366 (Bush et al. 1996)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12186956 (Harris and Cardelli 2002]). ''lvsB'' ([/gene/DDB_G0271504 lvsB]) null mutants have defects in lysosome organization and biogenesis, and LvsB contributes to lysosome function by antagonizing the function of Rab14. Expression of activated Rab14 phenocopies the loss of LvsB, causing inappropriate heterotypic fusion between lysosomes and post-lysosomes, while expression of inactivated Rab14 suppresses the phenotype of LvsB null cells and restores their lysosomal size and segregation from post-lysosomes. These results suggest that LvsB binds to late lysosomes and promotes the inactivation of Rab14, which then allows the lysosomes to mature into post-lysosomes for eventual secretion ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23387437 Kypri et al. 2013]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 18-AUG-2020 RD
