DDB_G0288679.summary: Besides ''mhcA'' ([/gene/DDB_G0286355 mhcA]) that encodes the classical myosin heavy chain, ''Dictyostelium'' carries genes for 12 unconventional myosins. ''myoE'' encodes myosin 1E that, like myosin 1A ([/gene/DDB_G0280039 myoA]), has a truncated tail domain that does not bind F-actin [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8504170  (Urrutia et al. 1993)]. However, the tail region of MyoE, like that of MyoD ([/gene/DDB_G0275447 myoD]) and MyoF ([/gene/DDB_G0289177 myoF]), binds phosphatidylinositol-3,4,5-trisphosphate (PIP3) resulting in its accumulation at the front of migrating cells where the PI3kinases are active and PTEN ([/gene/DDB_G0286557 pten]) is excluded [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22296834  (Chen et al. 2012)]. MyoE, like MyoA, uses multifunctional calmodulin ([/gene/DDB_G0279407 calA]) as a light chain [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21671662  (Crawley et al. 2011)]. Neither growth nor development are noticably affected by null mutations in ''myoE'' but double mutants carrying either ''myoD''-/''myoE''- and ''myoE''-/''myoF''- grow more slowly, aggregate more slowly and make misshapen fruiting bodies. Triple mutant cells lacking ''myoD'', ''myoE'' and ''myoF'' are defective in chemotaxis to cAMP, chemoattractant-stimulated actin polymerization and phagocytosis [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22296834  (Chen et al. 2012)]. Both MyoE and MyoF localize to macropinocytic cups and actin waves [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26801966  (Brzeska et al. 2016)]. The amino acid sequences of MyoD, MyoE, and MyoF are more similar to each other than to other myosins; together they form a group of unconventional myosins involved in growth and development. Like ''myoD'' mRNA, ''myoE'' mRNA is abundant during the first two hours of development, decreases to a minimum at T=7 hrs and then reaccumulates to a peak at T=11 hrs. ''myoF'' mRNA is much less abundant [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25887420  (Rosengarten et al. 2015)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 27-AUG-2019 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis
DDB_G0288679.note: There is a discrepancy between the sequence from the Sequencing Center and the sequence in GenBank record L06805, however, the sequence from the Sequencing Center has been verified.

DDB_G0293084.summary: ''zizB'' encodes a Rho guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF, RhoGEF). RhoGEFs are key components of signaling networks in which they activate Rho family GTPases by promoting the exchange of GDP for GTP. ''zizB'' is highly expressed throughout growth and development. ZizB is localized to the cytosol and enriched at the cell cortex and is excluded from the trailing edge during cell migration. In ''zizB'' null cells, development is delayed, and the cells have sparse, collapsed fruiting bodies with thickened stalks. In addition, ''zizB'' null cells displayed a significant reduction in both directionality and velocity during chemotaxis to cAMP. Cells overexpressing ''zizB'' show a twofold increase in filopodia formation and also have defects in cytokinesis. ZizB has multiple binding partners, including the Rho GTPases Rac1A ([/gene/DDB_G0277869 rac1A]), RacA ([/gene/DDB_G0286555 racA]), RacC ([/gene/DDB_G0293526 racC]), and RacG ([/gene/DDB_G0269178 racG]). In addition, ZizB co-immunoprecipitates with a number of actin or myosin-associated proteins, including the tubulins TubA ([/gene/DDB_G0287689 tubA]), TubB ([/gene/DDB_G0269196 tubB]), the actin filament nucleator ForA ([/gene/DDB_G0279607 forA]), F-actin capping protein subunits AcpA ([/gene/DDB_G0267374 acpA]) and AcpB ([/gene/DDB_G0272104 acpB]) and the Arp2/3 complex proteins ArcA ([/gene/DDB_G0277825 arcA]) and ArcB ([/gene/DDB_G0282813 arcB]). The ''zizB'' mutant phenotypes and ZizB binding partners suggest a central role for ZizB in actin cytoskeletal organization and cortical stabilization. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22366457 Pakes et al. 2012]), ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23247359 Pakes et al. 2012]). Overexpression of ZizB phenocopies the effects of Rac1A overexpression, suggesting that ZizB functions as RhoGEF for ''rac1A''. In addition, ZizB may also function as a RhoGEF for ''racA'', ''racC'', and ''racG'' ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26940518 Rivero et al. 2016]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 26-MAY-2021 RD

DDB_G0276945.summary: In search for ''Dictyostelium'' clathrin adaptor complexes (APs) cDNAs ''apm4'', [/gene/DDB_G0289247 apm1], and [/gene/DDB_G0277901 apm3], encoding proteins homologous to mammalian medium chain (mu) subunits, have been cloned. All APs are comprised of two large subunits, one medium size subunit, and one small subunit. ''Apm4'' encodes the medium chain of AP-4 ([/ontology/go/0030124/annotation/page/1 AP-4 adaptor complex]), which seems to be associated with the Golgi apparatus ([/ontology/go/0005794/annotation/page/1 Golgi apparatus]). The ''apm4'' protein (mu4) is 26% identical with the human mu4A, and is slightly larger (59 kD versus 50 kD). However, the existance of several other partial sequences homologous to AP-4 complexes in the ''Dictyostelium'' database and the presence of conserved residues potentially interacting with tyrosine-based sorting signals suggest that ''amp4'' truly encodes an AP-4 medium chain. Expression of ''apm4'' is developmentally regulated, sharply increasing at 12 hours, and peaking at 16 hours development [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11179674  (de Chassey et al., 2001)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 19-SEP-2003 PF

DDB_G0272138.summary: ''rab2B'' encodes a guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G protein) of the Rab family of small GTPases. G proteins are key components of signal transduction networks in which they function as molecular signaling switches, binding to GDP in the off state while binding GTP in the on state. Guanine nucleotide-exchange factors (GEFs) promote the exchange of GDP for GTP on Rab GTPases thus activating them, while GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) inactivate Rab GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP. Rab subfamily small GTPases in many organisms are key regulators of intracellular membrane trafficking. Proteomic analysis revealed that Rab2B is localized to lipid droplets ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24036346 Du, et al. 2013]) and also to the Legionella-containing vacuole [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28183814  (Schmolders et al. 2017)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 20-SEP-2020 RD

DDB_G0286559.summary: The ABC superfamily of genes is one of the largest in the genomes of both bacteria and eukaryotes. The proteins encoded by these genes all carry a characteristic 200- to 250-amino-acid ATP-binding cassette that gives them their family name ([/ontology/go/0042626/annotation/page/1 ATPase activity, coupled to transmembrane movement of substances]). In bacteria they are mostly involved in nutrient import, while in eukaryotes many are involved in export([/ontology/go/0006810/annotation/page/1 transport]), ([/ontology/go/0016021/annotation/page/1 integral to membrane]). Seven different families (A to G) have been defined in eukaryotes based on sequence homology, domain topology, and function. ''Dictyostelium'' has 71 ABC transporters (including one on the chromosome 2 duplication) and 13 ABCC family members: [/gene/DDB_G0280541 abcC1], [/gene/DDB_G0280055 abcC2], [/gene/DDB_G0287691 abcC3], [/gene/DDB_G0286559 abcC5], [/gene/DDB_G0287593 abcC6], [/gene/DDB_G0291243 abcC7], [/gene/DDB_G0284867 abcC8], [/gene/DDB_G0285165 abcC9], [/gene/DDB_G0280977 abcC10], [/gene/DDB_G0280973 abcC12], [/gene/DDB_G0280539 abcC13], [/gene/DDB_G0287589 abcC14], and [/gene/DDB_G0280459 abcC15]. Transporters of the C family have been shown to transport glutathione conjugants as well as to export cadmium ions. They are always found as full transporters with two copies of the transmembrane-ABC unit. Many of the genes of this family in humans and other animals have an additional transmembrane domain at the N terminus [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12456012 (Anjard and Loomis 2002)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 16-JUN-2003 PG

DDB_G0285973.summary: ''ttpA'' encodes an mRNA-binding protein of the tristetraproline (TTP) family. Eukaryotic orthologs of ''ttpA'' bind to AU-rich motifs in the 3 prime untranslated region (UTR) of mRNA, promoting mRNA de-adenylation and decay and inhibition of translation. ''Dictyostelium'' TtpA contains two tandem zinc-finger domains and was demonstrated to bind RNA. When ectopically expressed in mammalian cells, ''Dictyostelium'' TtpA promotes the decay of mRNA transcripts containing AU-rich binding motifs in their 3 prime UTRs. When grown in shaking liquid culture, ''ttpA'' null and loss-of-function mutants display a decrease in cell proliferation and enlarged nuclei; however, these phenotypes were not observed when the mutants were grown on plastic surfaces. The expression level of 3 genes was increased manyfold in ''ttpA'' null and loss-of-function mutants: ([/gene/DDB_G0283095 DD3-3]), ([/gene/DDB_G0281067 DDB_G0281067]) and ([/gene/DDB_G0282993 sodC]). In addition, ([/gene/DDB_G0289653 noxA]), ([/gene/DDB_G0267460 cybA]) and ([/gene/DDB_G0278313 DDB_G0278313]) expression levels were consistently elevated in the mutant cells. All six target transcripts encode putative membrane proteins and contain multiple TTP binding motifs (UUAUUUAUU) in their 3 prime UTRs. These results suggest that ''ttpA'' promotes mRNA de-adenylation and decay in a specific mRNA subclass and thus post-transcriptionally regulates the expression of functionally related proteins. (Bai, et al. 2021, PMID:34718768).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 04-NOV-2021 RD

DDB_G0285793.summary:
''cadA'' encodes the glycoprotein gp24 or DdCAD-1 that has been implicated in cell-cell adhesion during early development [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3569662 (Knecht et al., 1987]; [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8663243 Wong et al., 1996)]. It is synthesized in the cytoplasm and transported to the plasma membrane by contractile vacuoles [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9265658 (Sesaki et al., 1997)]. DdCAD-1 binds Ca(2+) activated calmodulin, which promotes its transport to the contractile vacuole [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23441816 (Sriskanthadevan et al., 2013)].
Early adhesion can be blocked by 10 mM EDTA and is mediated by contact site B [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/5002049 (Gerisch, 1968]; [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/4993098 Beug, et al.1970)]. High levels of EDTA or other dicarboxylic acids block contact site B adhesion other than by chelating calcium since early developing cells will stick to each other without added calcium even in the presence of 1 mM EDTA [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3569662 (Knecht et al., 1987)]. Moreover, Ca(2+) does not induce major conformational changes in DdCAD-1 [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17057715 (Lin et al., 2006)]. Mutant strains in which ''cadA'' is disrupted show reduced EDTA-sensitive adhesion but can, despite some milder defects, complete development and form fruiting bodies [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12135922 (Wong et al., 2002)].
DdCAD-1 localizes to membrane ruffles at the anterior of the migrating cell during early development [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8806827 (Sesaki and Siu, 1996]; [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11792801 Coates and Harwood, 2001)]. Furthermore, Sriskanthadevan and colleagues developed ''cadA'' knockout cells as chimeras with wild type on non-nutrient agar and found that the mutant cells sorted to be spores in the fruiting body, behaving like facultative cheaters. On soil plates the same chimeras showed the opposite effect but this was found to be due to the soil particles preventing effective adhesion of the ''cadA'' null mutant and as a result these cells did not mix well with wild type [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21561987 (Sriskanthadevan et al., 2011)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 26-SEP-2019 PF; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0280535.summary: Succinate dehydrogenase, also known as complex II ([/ontology/go/5749/annotation/page/1 mitochondrial respiratory chain complex II]), catalyzes the oxidation of succinate to fumarate while FAD is reduced to FADH<sub>2</sub>. The enzyme contains 4 subunits: a flavoprotein (FP) ([/gene/DDB_G0280535 sdhA]), an iron-sulfur protein (IP) ([/gene/DDB_G0270120 sdhB]), and a cytochrome b composed of two integral membrane proteins ([/ontology/go/16021/annotation/page/1 integral to membrane]) ([/gene/DDB_G0275115 sdhC] and [/gene/DDB_G0278157 sdhD]). The 4 subunit complex is bound in the [/ontology/go/5740/annotation/page/1 mitochondrial envelope] and provides a link between the the [/ontology/go/6099/annotation/page/1 tricarboxylic acid cycle] and the membrane-bound [/ontology/go/6118/annotation/page/1 electron transport] system. It is part of the respiratory chain and repressed in anaerobic respiration.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 31-JAN-2005 PF

DDB_G0275437.summary:
The [/gene/DDB_G0275437 7E] and [/gene/DDB_G0280847 2C] genes encode polypeptides of similar size, 9220 and 10573 Da, respectively. They both contain an unusually high proportion of serine plus glycine residues (41% and 59%, respectively). Computer analysis indicates that both gene products are probably [/ontology/go/0005622/annotation/page/1 intracellular] that form extended coil structures. 2C and 7E are expressed in all cell types during development. Expression ceases upon cell disaggregation but is restored by exogenous cAMP ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2157129 Ramji et al. 1990], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2177818 Richards et al. 1990]).
The regulatory elements of the 7E promoter have been analyzed. The 7E gene is expression within anterior prestalk cells at approximately 18 h of development. Subsequently, the promoter activity is independently regulated in subpopulations of prestalk cells by different promoter elements ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11683490 Seager et al. 2001]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 30-AUG-2004 PG

DDB_G0290901.summary: ''gefK'' encodes a Ras guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF, RasGEF). rasGEFs are key components of signaling networks in which they activate Ras family small GTPases by promoting the exchange of GDP for GTP. ''gefK'' is expressed during both growth and development, with maximum expression at 12 hours of development. Growth, morphology, phototaxis and fruiting body morphology are normal in a ''gefK'' null mutant ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16086850 Wilkins et al. 2005)]. A REMI insertional mutant in the intergenic region between ''gefK'' and ''gacL'' ([/gene/DDB_G0290891 gacL]) grows well on Gram positive bacteria but poorly on Gram negative bacteria, and also displays density-dependent growth. These and further results from additional mutants support the hypothesis that ''Dictyostelium discoideum'' is a cooperative predator ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30625171 Rubin et al. 2019)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 16-APR-2021 RD

DDB_G0271140.summary: The ABC superfamily of genes is one of the largest in the genomes of both bacteria and eukaryotes. The proteins encoded by these genes all carry a characteristic 200- to 250-amino-acid ATP-binding cassette that gives them their family name ([/ontology/go/0042626/annotation/page/1 ATPase activity, coupled to transmembrane movement of substances]). In bacteria they are mostly involved in nutrient import, while in eukaryotes many are involved in export ([/ontology/go/0006810/annotation/page/1 transport]), ([/ontology/go/0016021/annotation/page/1 integral to membrane]). Seven different families (A to G) have been defined in eukaryotes based on sequence homology, domain topology, and function. ''Dictyostelium'' has 71 ABC transporters (including one on the chromosome 2 duplication) and 11 ABCA family members: [/gene/DDB_G0291994 abcA1], [/gene/DDB_G0267438 abcA2], [/gene/DDB_G0293436 abcA3], [/gene/DDB_G0274121 abcA4], [/gene/DDB_G0274119 abcA5], [/gene/DDB_G0291245 abcA6], [/gene/DDB_G0271140 abcA7], [/gene/DDB_G0271138 abcA8],[/gene/DDB_G0291980 abcA9], [/gene/DDB_G0283387 abcA10], and [/gene/DDB_G0275453 abcA11],One of the defining characteristics of the A family is the presence of a regulatory domain with multiple sites for phosphorylation by various protein kinases in the region after the first ABC domain [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12456012 (Anjard and Loomis 2002)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 16-JUN-2003 PG

DDB_G0268068.summary: ''rab6'' encodes a guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G protein) of the Rab family of small GTPases. G proteins are key components of signal transduction networks in which they function as molecular signaling switches, binding to GDP in the off state while binding GTP in the on state. Guanine nucleotide-exchange factors (GEFs) promote the exchange of GDP for GTP on Rab GTPases thus activating them, while GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) inactivate Rab GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP. Rab subfamily small GTPases in many organisms are key regulators of intracellular membrane trafficking. Rab6 is an ortholog of human Rab6A and Rab6B. Proteomic analysis revealed that Rab6 is localized to the Legionella-containing vacuole [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24373249  (Hoffmann et al. 2013)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28183814  (Schmolders et al. 2017)], and also to lipid droplets ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24036346 Du, et al. 2013]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 12-NOV-2020 RD

DDB_G0283005.summary:
AgtA is a ''Dictyostelium'' galactosyltransferase involved in modifying Skp1 ([/gene/DDB_G0269230 fpaA] and [/gene/DDB_G0273251 fpaB-1]/[/gene/DDB_G0273615 fpaB-2] genes), which is part of the SCF ubiquitin ligase complex. The initial step in Skp1 glycosylation involves the hydroxylation of Pro143 by a proline hydroxylase ([/gene/DDB_G0277759 phyA], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9660787 Teng-umnuay et al. 1998]). HyPro143 is then modified by the glycosyltransferase [/gene/DDB_G0275699 gnt1], which transfers a GlcNAc (N-acetylglucosamine) to the Skp1 protein ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10593934 Teng-umnuay et al. 1999]). The Skp1-GlcNAc is extended by a bifunctional diglycosyltransferase, [/gene/DDB_G0283761 pgtA], which processively adds galactose and fucose ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11423539 van der Wel et al. 2001], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12244067 van der Wel et al. 2002]). Subsequently two additional galactose residues are added by [/gene/DDB_G0283005 agtA] to yield the Skp1 pentasaccharide (GGFGGnOSkp1). Also, Skp1 is the only substrate of AgtA ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16495217 Ercan et al. 2006], reviewed in [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31128470 West and Kim 2019]).
SKP1 glycosylation is required for optimal oxygen sensing during development. West and colleagues reported that the proline hydroxylase ([/gene/DDB_G0277759 phyA]) performing the first SKP1 modification mediates oxygen signaling during ''Dictyostelium'' development. ''phyA''-null cells need strongly elevated oxygen levels to culminate ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17699611 West et al. 2007]). Furthermore, ''agtA'' knockout and overexpression mutants were shown to require elevated oxygen levels to culminate. In addition the high oxygen requirement of ''agtA'' null cells is ameliorated by reduction of Skp1 levels ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19687007 Wang et al. 2009], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22128189 Zhang et al. 2011], reviewed in [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25988702 West and Blader 2015]). AgtA contains a C-terminal WD40 repeat domain in addition to its single catalytic domain that confers a salt-sensitive second-site binding interaction with Skp1. AgtA binds similarly well to precursor forms of Skp1, which competes with Skp1-F-box protein binding. When AgtA glycosylates Skp1,WD-40 domain binding is diminished. These results and mutant analyses suggest that AgtA mediates non-enzymatic control of unmodified and substrate precursor forms of Skp1. This binding mechanism is then relieved by switch-like activation of its glycosylation function This attests to a complex regulation of SKP1 modification and function ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24550398 Shafer et al. 2014]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 09-MAR-2020 PF

DDB_G0289075.summary: ''spiA'' encodes a 31 kDa protein that is added to the inner face of spore coats to keep spores viable ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2010032 Richardson et al. 1991)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1592257 Richardson and Loomis, 1992)]. Transcription starts very late in development as the cells are beginning to culminate (T=18 hrs). Expression is dependent on the MADS-box transcription factor SrfA ([/gene/DDB_G0281387 srfA]) and the GATA-binding transcription factor StkA ([/gene/DDB_G0277147 stkA]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9729488 Escalante and Sastre, 1998)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15075287 Escalante et al. 2004)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2010032 Richardson et al. 1991)]. Transcription starts in the rising culminant at the interface of prestalk and prespore cells and then spreads down through the underlying prespore cells in the sorus ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7607079 Richardson et al. 1994)]. This spatial pattern of expression is the result of stimulation of PKA ([/gene/DDB_G0283907 pkaC], [/gene/DDB_G0279413 pkaR]) activity by diffusible signals generated by prestalk cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7937993 Mann et al. 1994)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12204259 Escalante and Sastre, 2002)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15897458 Anjard and Loomis, 2005)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 11-MAY-2016 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0274449.summary:
Succinyl-CoA synthetase (SCS) is an enzyme in the [/ontology/go/0006099/annotation/page/1 tricarboxylic acid cycle] that catalyzes the formation of succinyl-CoA from succinate with the concomitant hydrolysis of NTP to NDP and phosphate. There are two forms of the enzyme, using either ATP or GTP. The [/gene/DDB_G0289325 scsA] gene encodes the succinyl-CoA synthetase alpha subunit. In eukaryotes one alpha and one beta subunit are thought to form a heterodimer. Anschutzt ''et al.'' determined that in crude [/ontology/go/0016020/annotation/page/1 membrane] extracts ScsA could be phosphorylated by ATP and GTP, but the purified enzyme showed high specificity for GTP ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8448193 Anschutz et al., 1993]).
Only one alpha subunit has been identified in ''Dictyostelium'' ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7771809 Birney and Klein, 1995]). However, two beta subunits are present in the ''Dictyostelium'' genome; [/gene/DDB_G0274449 scsB] is the ortholog of GDP-forming succinyl-CoA ligase beta subunits () and [/gene/DDB_G0271842 scsC] is highly similar to known ADP-forming succinyl-CoA ligase beta subunits ().Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 27-JAN-2005 PF

DDB_G0290963.summary: ''kif1'' encodes a large, 248 kDa kinesin that functions as the major molecular motor for transport of organelles to the plus-ends of microtubules [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10545495  (Pollock et al. 1999)]. Kif1 has an N-terminal motor domain highly similar to human kinesin KIF1B and ''Caenorhabditis elegans'' ''unc104'' motor domain that is followed by a Forkhead-associated domain that can bind phosphoproteins, and a Pleckstrin homology domain that can bind membrane-associated phosphatidylinositol (4,5) bisphosphate (PIP2). In ''Dictyostelium'', Kif1 functions as a dimer and appears to cluster in PIP2 containing rafts [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12015984  (Klopfenstein et al. 2002)]. Kinesins move along microtubules by a "hand-over-hand" mechanism in which they tilt over to allow the motor domains to step past one another using the energy of ATP hydrolysis. Endosomes are transported along microtubules with frequent reversals in direction due to a tug-of-war between kinesin (kif1) pulling to the plus-end and dynein ([/gene/DDB_G0276355 dhcA]) pulling to the minus-end [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19864630  (Soppina et al. 2009)]. A knockout of ''kif1'' results in a 60% decrease in organelle transport, but the cells can still grow [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10545495  (Pollock et al. 1999)]. ''kif1'' is transcribed throughout development. Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 24-MAY-2017 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0281663.summary:
The gene product encoded by [/gene/DDB_G0281663 aprA] is a secreted protein that exists in a 150 kDa protein complex. The AprA protein contains the PhoPQ-activated pathogenicity-related protein domain, which is thought to play a role in virulence of Salmonella. From its mutant phenotype,AprA functions in negative regulation of cell proliferation and is also clearly important for sporulation. Although it plays a role in cell proliferation, AprA does not have an effect on cell growth, as evidenced by an unchanged mass per number of cells in comparison to wild-type. Four proteins in the ''Dictyostelium'' genome are highly similar to AprA: [/gene/DDB_G0286625 DDB_G0286625], [/gene/DDB_G0277031 DDB_G0277031], [/gene/DDB_G0276897 DDB_G0276897], [/gene/DDB_G0282135 DDB_G0282135] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16176950 Brock and Gomer 2005]).
It has been demonstrated that Galpha8 (gene [/gene/DDB_G0284469 gpaH]) and Gbeta (gene [/gene/DDB_G0277143 gpbA]) are part of a signaling pathway used by AprA to inhibit cell proliferation but not growth, while Galpha9 (gene [/gene/DDB_G0283419 gpaI]) is part of a different pathway that regulates both proliferation and growth. Similar to aprA- and [/gene/DDB_G0281605 cfaD] null mutants, cells lacking these G-proteins proliferate faster than wild type ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19635129 Bakthavatsalam et al. 2009]).
In 2012 AprA has been found to also function as a chemorepellant. Wild-type cells at the edge of a colony showed directed movement outward from the colony, whereas cells lacking AprA did not. Starved cells are not repelled by recombinant AprA, suggesting that aggregation-phase cells are not sensitive to the chemorepellant effect. The secreted protein CfaD, the G protein Galpha8, and the kinase QkgA are necessary for the chemorepellant activity of AprA as well as its proliferation-inhibiting activity ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22711818 Philips et al. 2012]). The Retinoblastoma protein (gene [/gene/DDB_G0290551 rblA]) has been implicated in AprA function as recombinant AprA inhibits the proliferation of wild type cells, but not that of rblA- cells, and RblA is required for chemorepulsion ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24390142 Bakthavatsalam et al. 2014]).
([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29440579 Tang et al. 2018]) identified four mutants that show insensitivity to AprA: ([/gene/DDB_G0271686 grlB]), ([/gene/DDB_G0286895 grlD]), ([/gene/DDB_G0291356 grlE]), and ([/gene/DDB_G0282459 grlH]). Among these, cells lacking GrlH show most of the phenotypes expected for cells lacking the AprA receptor, including reduced binding to AprA, suggesting that GrlH is an AprA receptor.
The P21 activated protein kinase D (gene [/gene/DDB_G0269696 pakD]) was identified to being required for AprA dependent chemorepulsion ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24797076 Philips et al. 2014]). A comprehensive study comparing the pathways mediating AprA chemorepulsion to the cAMP chemoattraction pathways has delineated components of the AprA chemorepulsion pathway. Both cAMP chemotaxis and AprA chemorepulsion use G protein-coupled receptors, G proteins, and Ras, and both involve receptor-mediated activation of Ras. AprA uses a subset of chemoattraction signal transduction pathways including Ras, protein kinase A, TOR, phospholipase A, and ERK1, but does not require the PI3 kinase/Akt/PKB and guanylyl cyclase pathways to induce chemorepulsion. Genes involved in ArpA-mediated chemorepulsion include ([/gene/DDB_G0282459 grlH]), ([/gene/DDB_G0284469 gpaH]), ([/gene/DDB_G0277143 gpbA]), ([/gene/DDB_G0281385 rasC]), ([/gene/DDB_G0293434 rasG]), ([/gene/DDB_G0285161 dagA]), ([/gene/DDB_G0283907 pkaC]), ([/gene/DDB_G0286557 pten]), ([/gene/DDB_G0277399 piaA]), ([/gene/DDB_G0292592 lst8]), ([/gene/DDB_G0292564 iplA]), ([/gene/DDB_G0278525 plaA]), ([/gene/DDB_G0288147 pkcA]), ([/gene/DDB_G0286353 erkA]), ([/gene/DDB_G0293526 racC]), ([/gene/DDB_G0285253 scrA]), ([/gene/DDB_G0269696 pakD]) and ([/gene/DDB_G0287969 cnrN]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30462573 Rijal et al. 2018]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 22-DEC-2014 PF

DDB_G0294533.summary:
''roco5'' encodes a large, multi-domain protein of the Roco family. Roco5 contains an N-terminal Rho-GEF domain followed by a PH domain, a leucine-rich repeat (LRR) region, a Roc small GTPase domain, a COR (C-terminal of Roc) domain, and a protein kinase domain in the C-terminal region. Roco5 has sequence similarity to human LRRK2, mutations in which are associated with Parkinson disease. Eleven ''Dictyostelium'' proteins belong to the Roco family: ([/gene/DDB_G0291079 gbpC]), ([/gene/DDB_G0273259 qkgA-1]), ([/gene/DDB_G0269250 pats1]), ([/gene/DDB_G0288251 roco4]), Roco5, ([/gene/DDB_G0279417 roco6]), ([/gene/DDB_G0267472 roco7]), ([/gene/DDB_G0286127 roco8]), ([/gene/DDB_G0288183 roco9]), ([/gene/DDB_G0291710 roco10]) and ([/gene/DDB_G0268636 roco11]).
Roco5 is localized to the cytosol and ''roco5'' expression is relatively constant throughout growth and development. Disruption of the ''roco5'' gene did not result in any significant developmental defects ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20348387 van Egmond and van Haastert 2010]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 14-OCT-2021 RD

DDB_G0275011.summary: To investigate the minimal requirements for chemotaxis, [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22081140  Kortholt et al. 2011] obtained quantitative data on Ras activation and chemotaxis in cAMP and folic acid gradients using a variety of Dictyostelium mutant cell lines from the four signaling pathways that contribute to chemotaxis: PI3K, TorC2, PLA2, and sGC. Their results demonstrate that Ras is activated at the leading edge, through a pathway consisting of G-alpha/beta/gamma, which does not depend on either of the four pathways. The authors measured chemotaxis of mutant cells exposed to cAMP gradients with different steepness and found that many mutants will chemotax in shallow gradients, despite a reduced sensitivity. Expression of multiple pathways increases sensitivity, with some combinations of pathways exhibiting weak amplification while others produce good chemotaxis with strong signal amplification. The results of cluster analysis revealed that one cluster of signaling pathways, including PI3K + TorC2 + sGC, is involved in inducing orientation of the cell towards the gradient, while a second cluster consists of cGMP + PLA2 and functions as a memory of current direction. Thus one individual pathway does not contribute strongly to chemotaxis, but it can synergize with other pathways, which together increases the sensitivity about 150-fold. These results suggest a conceptual model of chemotaxis in which a basal signaling module consisting of heterotrimeric and monomeric G proteins provides activation of Ras at the leading edge, which is sufficient for chemotaxis.Basic annotations have been added to this gene, 22-DEC-2014 RD

DDB_G0285433.summary:
In mammalian cells, phosducin binds to G proteins and modulate their activity. Phylogenetic analyses revealed that there are three groups of phodsucin proteins. ''Dictyostelium'', like mammalian cells and ''Drosophila'', has one member from each group: [/gene/DDB_G0292850 phlp1], [/gene/DDB_G0285433 phlp2], and [/gene/DDB_G0293848 phlp3]. Phosducins consist of an N-terminal domain containing three helices which binds the alpha subunit of G proteins, and a C-terminal domain which bears similarity to thioredoxin and binds to the beta/gamma subunit of G proteins.
Phlp2 lack many residues in the C-terminal region that are expected to be required for G beta/gamma binding. The cellular role of Phlp2 is unknown, but appears to be essential for growth: null mutants divide for a few generations and die. The putative ortholog from ''S. cerevisiae'', ''plp2'', is also essential ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/199357 Blaauw et al.2003]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 18-JUN-2008 PG

DDB_G0288427.summary: ''cenA'' encodes an EF-hand centrin that is an integral component of isolated centrosomes as well as concentrated at centromeres in the nucleus [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11713866  (Daunderer et al. 2001)]. During interphase cytosolic centrosomes are connected to nuclei by fibrous bridges which carry CenA at both ends. The bridges disappear at metaphase when centrosomes enter fenestra in the nuclear envelope to organize microtubule spindles [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15548420  (Graf et al. 2004)]. CenA may help maintain association of the nucleus-associated centrosome with clustered chromosomal centromeres within the nucleus [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25952183  (Graf et al. 2015)]. About 100 different proteins contribute to centrosomal functions including the products of ([/gene/DDB_G0271738 tubC]), ([/gene/DDB_G0285849 spc97]), ([/gene/DDB_G0283909 spc98]), ''cenA'', ([/gene/DDB_G0288375 lis1]), ([/gene/DDB_G0270814 nek2]), ([/gene/DDB_G0283607 eb1]), ([/gene/DDB_G0268616 cepJ]) and ([/gene/DDB_G0278809 cepG]). [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15548420  (Graf et al. 2004)]. Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 18-DEC-2017 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0269174.summary: ''rab1C'' encodes a guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G protein) of the Rab family of small GTPases. G proteins are key components of signal transduction networks in which they function as molecular signaling switches, binding to GDP in the off state while binding GTP in the on state. Guanine nucleotide-exchange factors (GEFs) promote the exchange of GDP for GTP on Rab GTPases thus activating them, while GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) inactivate Rab GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP. Rab1C is similar to human RAB1A, which is a key regulator of intracellular membrane trafficking. Expression of ''rab1C'' is upregulated in response to intracellular ''Mycobacterium marinum'' infection ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31823727 Kjellin et al. 2019]). Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 01-SEP-2020 RD

DDB_G0280541.summary: The ABC superfamily of genes is one of the largest in the genomes of both bacteria and eukaryotes. The proteins encoded by these genes all carry a characteristic 200- to 250-amino-acid ATP-binding cassette that gives them their family name ([/ontology/go/0042626/annotation/page/1 ATPase activity, coupled to transmembrane movement of substances]). In bacteria they are mostly involved in nutrient import, while in eukaryotes many are involved in export([/ontology/go/0006810/annotation/page/1 transport]), ([/ontology/go/0016021/annotation/page/1 integral to membrane]). Seven different families (A to G) have been defined in eukaryotes based on sequence homology, domain topology, and function. ''Dictyostelium'' has 71 ABC transporters (including one on the chromosome 2 duplication) and 13 ABCC family members: [/gene/DDB_G0280541 abcC1], [/gene/DDB_G0280055 abcC2], [/gene/DDB_G0287691 abcC3], [/gene/DDB_G0286559 abcC5], [/gene/DDB_G0287593 abcC6], [/gene/DDB_G0291243 abcC7], [/gene/DDB_G0284867 abcC8], [/gene/DDB_G0285165 abcC9], [/gene/DDB_G0280977 abcC10], [/gene/DDB_G0280973 abcC12], [/gene/DDB_G0280539 abcC13], [/gene/DDB_G0287589 abcC14], and [/gene/DDB_G0280459 abcC15]. Transporters of the C family have been shown to transport glutathione conjugants as well as to export cadmium ions. They are always found as full transporters with two copies of the transmembrane-ABC unit. Many of the genes of this family in humans and other animals have an additional transmembrane domain at the N terminus [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12456012 (Anjard and Loomis 2002)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 16-JUN-2003 PG

DDB_G0273887.summary:
The lectin Discoidin I binds N-acetylgalactosamine and galactose [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/4517669 (Rosen et al. 1973)]. Discoidin I subunits associate to form a tetramer [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/4858710 (Simpson et al. 1974)] and are expressed from a family of 3 different genes: ''dscA'' ([/gene/DDB_G0273063 dscA-1]) ([/gene/DDB_G0273919 dscA-2]), ''dscC'' ([/gene/DDB_G0273065 dscC-1]) ([/gene/DDB_G0273885 dscC-2]) and ''dscD''. [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6279874 (Poole et al. 1981)]. Monomeric discoidin I is located mainly in the cytosol, while the tetrameric form of discoidin I is detected in multilamellar bodies and is externalized during aggregation [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2581974 (Barondes et al. 1985)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8416797 (Fukuzawa et al. 1993)]. Discoidin I gene expression is induced by prestarvation factor (PSF) and conditioned medium factor, ([/gene/DDB_G0275007 cmfA]) but is down-regulated by cAMP [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7641976 (Blusch et al. 1995)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2049883 (Rathi et al. 1991)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1663029 (Gomer et al. 1991)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2196444 (Vauti et al. 1990)]. Mutants defective in discoidin I fail to stream during aggregation, implicating discoidin I in cell-substrate adhesion [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6509552 (Springer et al. 1984)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/4075402 (Crowley et al. 1985)]. In addition, discoidin I is thought to play an intracellular role, as mutants in which discoidin genes are not expressed also have an abnormally centered microtubule organizing center and more rounded cell morphology, suggesting a role for discoidins in cytoskeleton organization during aggregation [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1334012 (Alexander et al. 1992)].
''Dictyostelium discoideum'' strains that carry bacteria secrete approx. 80 times higher levels of DscA and DscC than non-carriers. Secreted DscA binds to ''Klebsiella pneumoniae''. DscA binding protects bacteria from extracellular killing, promotes their internalization and prolongs their retention in both ''Dictyostelium discoideum'' and mammalian cells. Plant lectins induce the same response, suggesting that modified uptake and persistence of lectin-coated bacteria in eukaryotic cells is a general phenomenon, termed lectin-induced modified bacterial internalization [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30049880 (Dinh et al. 2018)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 24-AUG-2018 RD

DDB_G0279343.summary:
The Aurora family of serine/threonine protein kinases ([/ontology/go/0004674/annotation/page/1 protein serine/threonine kinase activity]) were originally identified in ''Drosophila melanogaster''mutants defective in spindle-pole behavior. The name "Aurora" stems from the auroraphenomenon observed in the night sky over the polar regions. Both Aurora A and Aurora B kinases have been found in metazoans, while only one Aurora kinase has been identified in ''Saccharomyces cerevisiae'', ''Schizosaccharomyces pombe'' and ''Dictyostelium discoideum''. Aurora A kinases associate with the centrosome during mitosis and have been shown to be involved in proper centrosome positioning and spindle assembly. Aurora B kinases are localized to the equator of the mitotic spindle and are thought to play a role in kinetochore attachment to the microtubule spindle and other important events in mitosis.
The ''Dictyostelium'' Aurora kinase has been shown to have properties of both Aurora A and Aurora B kinases. Like Aurora A, it localizes at to the [/ontology/go/0000922/annotation/page/1 spindle pole]s in early mitosis. Like Aurora B, it binds to [/gene/DDB_G0267690 icpA] (DdINCENP) and localizes to the [/ontology/go/0005813/annotation/page/1 centrosome], the [/ontology/go/0051233/annotation/page/1 spindle midzone], and the late [/ontology/go/0032154/annotation/page/1 cleavage furrow] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18326585 Li et al., 2008]).This gene has been comprehensively annotated, 12-NOV-2008 PF

DDB_G0279605.summary:
''racB'' encodes a guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G protein) of the Rho family of small GTPases. G proteins are key components of signal transduction networks in which they function as molecular signaling switches, binding to GDP in the off state while binding GTP in the on state. Guanine nucleotide-exchange factors (GEFs) promote the exchange of GDP for GTP on Ras GTPases thus activating them, while GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) inactivate Ras GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP. RacGEF1 ([/gene/DDB_G0277987 gxcA]) is a GEF for RacB ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15470506 Park et al. 2004]). Additional potential GEFs for racB include ''gflB'' ([/gene/DDB_G0286773 gflB]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/27009206 Senoo et al. 2016]), DockC ([/gene/DDB_G0292004 docC]) and ZizA ([/gene/DDB_G0275035 zizA]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22264729 Yan et al. 2012]). GAPA binds weakly to RacB and may function as a GAP for it ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26940518 Rivero et al. 2016]).
RacB has multiple binding partners that may function as downstream effectors. These include: protein kinases PakA ([/gene/DDB_G0269166 pakA]) and PakC ([/gene/DDB_G0267450 pakC]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15470506 Park et al. 2004]), ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15483055 Lee et al. 2004]), myosin heavy chain kinase PakB ([/gene/DDB_G0276459 pakB]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15509655 de la Roche et al. 2005]), WASP ([/gene/DDB_G0293834 wasA]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16968699 Han et al. 2006]), WASP-B ([/gene/DDB_G0272811 wasB]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23791739 Chung et al. 2013]) and coronin A ([/gene/DDB_G0267382 corA]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24347642 Swaminathan et al. 2013]). RacB also binds to the Rho GDP-dissociation inhibitor 1 RhoGDI1 ([/gene/DDB_G0291077 rdiA]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12163018 Imai et al. 2002]).
''racB'' mRNA is expressed at a relatively constant level during the growth phase. Expression levels decrease significantly at the beginning of aggregation; approximately 10% of growth phase levels remained in cells late during development ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8294042 Bush et al. 1993]). RacB is activated upon cAMP stimulation and activation is partially controlled by PI3K ([/gene/DDB_G0278727 pikA], [/gene/DDB_G0283081 pikB]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15470506 Park et al. 2004]), ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26940518 Rivero et al. 2016]). Constitutively active ''racB'' mutants have a flattened morphology and display increased F-actin polymerization and F-actin levels. The mutants also have defects in growth and cytokinesis and have dramatically reduced rates of endocytosis, phagocytosis, and endosomal efflux ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12796292 Lee et al. 2003]). ''racB'' null mutants have complementary phenotypes: decreased cAMP-stimulated F actin polymerization and F-actin levels, and decreased myosin II assembly. In addition, ''racB'' null mutants have a decreased chemotaxis rate and delayed aggregation. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15470506 Park et al. 2004]). These results reveal a role for ''racB'' in signaling networks regulating F-actin polymerization and chemotaxis. Through its interaction with the adaptor protein ElmoE, ([/gene/DDB_G0279657 elmoE]) RacB is involved in a protein complex and signaling pathway linking G-protein coupled receptors on the cell surface to the actin cytoskeleton. cAMP stimulated activation of cAR1 ([/gene/DDB_G0273397 carA-1]), ([/gene/DDB_G0273533 carA-2]) promotes the association between ElmoE, Gbeta ([/gene/DDB_G0277143 gpbA]) and Ggamma ([/gene/DDB_G0274125 gpgA]). ElmoE also interacts with Arp 2/3 components ArcB ([/gene/DDB_G0282813 arcB]), ArcC ([/gene/DDB_G0292804 arcC]), as well as actin ([/gene/DDB_G0275023 act22]). In addition, ElmoE associates with RacB and potential GEFs DocC ([/gene/DDB_G0292004 docC]) and (or) ZizA ([/gene/DDB_G0275035 zizA]) to form the evolutionarily conserved Elmo/Dock complex that likely serves as the GEF to activate RacB. Thus cAMP-stimulated activation of cAR1 results in ELMOE-mediated activation of RacB, which in turn promotes actin polymerization at the leading front of migrating cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22754623 Yan et al. 2012]), ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22754623 Yan et al. 2012]), ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28641070 Xu et al. 2017]). Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 30-APR-2020 RD

DDB_G0274519.summary:
NapA (Nap1) is a member of the Scar/WAVE complex, consisting of (Scar) ([/gene/DDB_G0285253 scrA]), ([/gene/DDB_G0287855 pirA]), ([/gene/DDB_G0279175 hspc300]), ([/gene/DDB_G0267956 abiA]), and NapA. In migrating cells, the Scar/WAVE complex regulates the production of lamellipods and pseudopods through Arp2/3 complex activation. The Scar/WAVE complex localizes to the front of pseudopods and the tips of filopods, cell-cell contact zones, and the cell leading edge ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22891261 Veltman et al. 2012]). NapA and PirA interact to form an independent heterodimeric subcomplex prior to formation of the mature Scar/WAVE complex ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21701600 Linkner et al. 2011]).
In ''napA'' null mutants in an AX3 background, Scar protein levels are reduced approximately 10-fold, and PirA levels are reduced by approximately half. ''napA'' null mutant cells move more slowly toward the chemoattractant folate, appear more rounded, and extend much smaller protrusions than wild type (wt) cells. ''napA'' null mutant cells are also much smaller and have a large reduction in F-actin levels. In addition, ''napA'' null mutants have defects in cell-substrate adhesion and development, including delayed aggregation and slugs which are defective in phototaxis. ''pirA''/''napA'' double null phenotypes reveal that that NapA is required for ''pirA'' null phenotypes ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16581519 Ibarra et al. 2006]). Disruption of ''napA'' in an AX2 background (''napA''/AX2 null) leads to a drastic decrease or disappearance of the other four SCAR/WAVE complex components. ''napA''/AX2 null cells are more spread than wt cells and form broad areas of membrane ruffle-like structures at their peripheries. ''napA''/AX2 null cells also move more slowly than wt cells and have defects in cytokinesis ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28889942 Litschko et al. 2017]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 20-JAN-2022 RD

DDB_G0287593.summary: The ABC superfamily of genes is one of the largest in the genomes of both bacteria and eukaryotes. The proteins encoded by these genes all carry a characteristic 200- to 250-amino-acid ATP-binding cassette that gives them their family name ([/ontology/go/0042626/annotation/page/1 ATPase activity, coupled to transmembrane movement of substances]). In bacteria they are mostly involved in nutrient import, while in eukaryotes many are involved in export([/ontology/go/0006810/annotation/page/1 transport]), ([/ontology/go/0016021/annotation/page/1 integral to membrane]). Seven different families (A to G) have been defined in eukaryotes based on sequence homology, domain topology, and function. ''Dictyostelium'' has 71 ABC transporters (including one on the chromosome 2 duplication) and 13 ABCC family members: [/gene/DDB_G0280541 abcC1], [/gene/DDB_G0280055 abcC2], [/gene/DDB_G0287691 abcC3], [/gene/DDB_G0286559 abcC5], [/gene/DDB_G0287593 abcC6], [/gene/DDB_G0291243 abcC7], [/gene/DDB_G0284867 abcC8], [/gene/DDB_G0285165 abcC9], [/gene/DDB_G0280977 abcC10], [/gene/DDB_G0280973 abcC12], [/gene/DDB_G0280539 abcC13], [/gene/DDB_G0287589 abcC14], and [/gene/DDB_G0280459 abcC15]. Transporters of the C family have been shown to transport glutathione conjugants as well as to export cadmium ions. They are always found as full transporters with two copies of the transmembrane-ABC unit. Many of the genes of this family in humans and other animals have an additional transmembrane domain at the N terminus [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12456012 (Anjard and Loomis 2002)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 16-JUN-2003 PG

DDB_G0268632.summary:
The ''abpA'' gene encodes alpha-actinin, a 95 kD protein originally isolated from the cell cortex. It forms a dimer, crosslinks actin filaments into lateral arrays, and increases the actin-stimulated Mg ATPase of myosin. Both activities are regulated by Ca2+ [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6746725 (Condeelis et al. 1984)]. The alpha-actinin molecule carries two characteristic EF-hand structures. The calcium-binding loops form the structural basis for the calcium sensitivity [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3622778 (Noegel et al. 1987)]. It was shown that EF hand I has a low affinity for Ca2+ and EF hand II a high affinity, implying a regulatory function of EF hand I in the inhibition of F-actin cross-linking activity [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8486739 (Witke et al. 1993)]. This was confirmed when the viscoelastic properties of F-actin solutions in the presence of mutated EF hand structures was tested, and it was concluded that the first EF hand of alpha-actinin is crucial for its crosslinking function [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8561496 (Janssen et al. 1996)].
The phenotype of an alpha-actinin mutant, HG1130, which retained only trace amounts of alpha-actinin, appeared to be normal [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3956480 (Wallraff et al. 1986)]. The lack of alpha-actinin was shown to only slightly affect cell substrate adhesion [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10411959 (Weber 1996)], growth and pinocytosis [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10413681 (Rivero et al. 1999)], and development [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10704840 (Ponte et al. 2000)]. A redundancy in the microfilament system was suggested when two cytoskeletal genes, ''abpA'' and [/gene/DDB_G0269100 abpC], were disrupted. The loss of both proteins severely affected growth and resistance to osmotic stress. It also resulted in reduced motility and phagocytosis rates, and heavily impaired development. These changes were reversed by expressing either ''abpA'' or ''abpC'', showing the defects to be due to the absence of the two F-actin cross-linking proteins [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1732064 (Witke et al. 1992)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8937986 (Rivero et al. 1996)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 24-NOV-2014 PF

DDB_G0282067.summary: ''zntB'' was identified as a putative zinc transporter by sequence homology and a phylogenetic analysis placed ''zntB'' in a subfamily along with ([/gene/DDB_G0283629 zntA]), ([/gene/DDB_G0269332 zntC]) and ([/gene/DDB_G0291141 zntD]). All four genes are expressed in pstAB cells or at the stalk entrance during culmination, but none of the four genes are expressed in a STATa ([/gene/DDB_G0281381 dstA]) null strain [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18415938  (Sunaga et al. 2008)]. ZntB localizes to organelles of the endosomal pathway, including zinc-containing endosomes, phagosomes, and recycling endosomes and/or the Golgi apparatus. ZntB also localizes to ''Mycobacterium smegmatis''-containing vacuoles (MCV), and Zn2+ accumulates inside the MCV at the same time. In ''zntB'' null cells, there is a 60% reduction in Zn2+ ion transport into the phagosome compared with wt, suggesting that ZntB is the main Zn2+ transporter into lysosomes and post-lysosomes [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30404827  (Barisch et al. 2018)]. During ''Mycobacterium marinum'' infection, both ZntB and ZntA localize to the Mycobacteria-containing vacuole, and expression of both genes is increased. In ''zntB'' null cells, MCVs accumulate less Zn2+ than in wt, however intracellular ''M. marinum'' growth is decreased compared with wt cells. This result suggests that additional Zn2+ dependent defense mechanisms may be employed by ''Dictyostelium'' against bacterial infection (Hanna, et al. 2021, PMID:33531393).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 02-SEP-2021 RD

DDB_G0292244.summary:
DNA-dependent RNA polymerase catalyzes the transcription of DNA into RNA using the four ribonucleoside triphosphates as substrates ([/ontology/go/0003899/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase activity]). Three distinct zinc-containing RNA polymerases are found in eukaryotic nuclei: [/gene/DDB_G0275759 rpa1] for the ribosomal RNA precursor ([/ontology/go/0006360/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase I promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005736/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase I complex]), [/gene/DDB_G0279193 rpb1] for the mRNA precursor ([/ontology/go/0006366/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase II promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005665/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase II, core complex]), and [/gene/DDB_G0277199 rpc1] for 5S and tRNA genes ([/ontology/go/0006383/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase III promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005666/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase III complex]).
RNA polymerase II is composed of 12 subunits: [/gene/DDB_G0279193 rpb1], [/gene/DDB_G0288257 rpb2], [/gene/DDB_G0292244 rpb3], [/gene/DDB_G0282739 rpb4], [/gene/DDB_G0291636 rpb5], [/gene/DDB_G0291037 rpb6], [/gene/DDB_G0284891 rpb7], [/gene/DDB_G0278039 rpb8], [/gene/DDB_G0268306 rpb9], [/gene/DDB_G0272036 rpb10], [/gene/DDB_G0277677 rpb11], and[/gene/DDB_G0283365 rpb12]. Subunits 5, 6, 8, 10, and 12 are common to all threeRNA polymerases (reviewed by [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9618449 Hampsey] in 1998).
Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 09-APR-2004 PG

DDB_G0283389.summary:
Rhesus proteins (Rh) are glycoproteins present on the cell surface of red blood cells in mammals and are involved in ammonium ion export ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12846905 Hemker et al., 2003]).

However, analysis of a null mutant has not revealed any defect is the response to osmotic stress ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11220631 Benghezal et al., 2001]). DDB_G0273175.summary:
Developing ''Dictyostelium'' cells aggregate to form fruiting bodies containing typically 2 x 10(4) cells. To prevent the formation of an excessively large fruiting body, streams of aggregating cells break up into groups if there are too many cells. The breakup is regulated by a secreted complex of polypeptides called counting factor (CF). CF is composed of 4 polypeptides, including Countin (encoded by the [/gene/DDB_G0274597 ctnA] gene), cf50, [/gene/DDB_G0269248 cf45-1] and [/gene/DDB_G0284363 cf60]. CF50 is 30% identical to lysozymes (but has very little lysozyme activity) and contains distinctive serine-glycine motifs. Transformants with a disrupted cf50 gene, like ''ctnA-'' cells, form abnormally large groups, exhibit increased levels of cytosolic glucose, increased cell-cell adhesion and decreased cell motility. CF50 is present in the same conditioned medium sieve column fraction as the 450 kDa CF complex. In the absence of CF50, secreted countin is degraded, suggesting that one function of CF50 may be to protect countin from degradation. However, unlike''ctnA-'' cells, ''cf50-'' cells differentiate into an abnormally high percentage of cells expressing [/gene/DDB_G0276761 cotB] (a marker expressed in a subset of prespore cells). Also unlike countin, addition of recombinant CF50 decreases the cAMP pulse following stimulation with cAMP. Countin and CF50 require each other's presence to affect group size, but the presence of countin is not necessary for CF50 to bind to cells, and CF50 is not necessary for countin to bind to cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12117815 Brock et al.2002], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12912898 Brock et al. 2003]). CF and group size have also been mathematically modeled [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16371424 (Dallon et al. 2006)], which together with experimental evidence has been reviewed in [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18426773 Jang and Gomer 2008].
Recent studies classified all lysozymes in ''Dictyostelium''. CF50 and CF45-1 have been assigned to belong to the Entamoeba-type lysozyme family that contain a GH25 domain. Like the other family members ([/gene/DDB_G0274181 lyEh1], [/gene/DDB_G0293492 lyEh2], [/gene/DDB_G0293566 lyEh3], [/gene/DDB_G0276439 lyEh4]), CF50 and CF45-1 have the three conserved Asp and Glu residues, though these counting factor proteins have shown only little, if any lysozyme activity [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/32061941 (Lamrabet et al. 2020)]Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 13-APR-2020 PF

DDB_G0286353.summary: ''erkA'' encodes a protein kinase that is a member of the MAP kinase family ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7935416 Gaskins et al. 1994)]. A REMI mutant was isolated in which ''erkA'' was disrupted by the inserted plasmid. Cells lacking ERK1 exhibit chemotaxis defects and make small aggregates that form tips only after a considerable delay. This phenotype is also seen in mutants lacking the MAP kinase kinase MEK1 ([/gene/DDB_G0269152 mekA]), suggesting that MEK1 and ERK1 are in the same regulatory cascade ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12062087 Sobko et al. 2002)]. In addition, ERK1 was shown to function in Galpha5 ([/gene/DDB_G0286185 gpaE]) subunit-mediated signal transduction. ERK1 was specifically required for Galpha5-mediated tip morphogenesis, suggesting this cascade might be responsible for production of signals necessary for tip formation ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20079430 Nquyen et al. 2010)] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20019085 Raisley et al. 2010)]. ErkA is also involved in polyphosphate signal transduction ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28584190 Seus et al. 2017)] and in the signal transduction pathway responsible for AprA-dependent ([/gene/DDB_G0281663 aprA]) chemorepulsion. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30462573 Rijal et al. 2018]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 11-DEC-2018 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0292996.summary:
''rasD'' encodes a G protein of the Ras family of small GTPases. G proteins are key components of signal transduction networks in which they function as molecular signaling switches, binding to GDP in the off state while binding GTP in the on state. Guanine nucleotide-exchange factors (GEFs, rasGEFs) promote the exchange of GDP for GTP on Ras GTPases thus activating them, while GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs, rasGAPs) inactivate Ras GTPases. RasD is activated by the RasGEF E ([/gene/DDB_G0269252 gefE]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24282234 Chattwood et al. 2013)] RasD and GefE together regulate phototaxis, thermotaxis and cell lineage priming. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10837033 Wilkins et al. 2000)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16086850 Wilkins et al. 2005)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24282234 Chattwood et al. 2013)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30473004 Gruenheit et al. 2018)].
The ''rasD'' gene is inducible by cAMP. ''rasD'' mRNA accumulates to a low level during growth, is reduced during during early development and then re-accumulates during aggregation ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1703508 Esch et al. 1991)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6091907 Reymond et al. 1984)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2644652 Robbins et al. 1989)]. Expression of ''rasD'' is upregulated in response to intracellular ''Mycobacterium marinum'' and ''Legionella pneumophila'' infection ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31823727 Kjellin et al. 2019]). During development ''rasD'' is first expressed during aggregation and by the time of slug development RasD expression is enriched in prestalk cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3749127 Reymond et al. 1986)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3443054 Jermyn et al. 1987)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3749127 Reymond et al. 1986)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7641977 Jermyn and Williams 1995)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1703508 Esch et al. 1991)]. RasD is capable of correcting some, but not all of ''rasG'' ([/gene/DDB_G0293434 rasG]) null phenotypes, suggesting some overlap in function between RasD and RasG ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10725225 Khosla et al. 2000)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20833893 Bolourani et al. 2010)].
In constitutively active ''rasD'' mutants, cells aggregate into mounds with multiple tips, followed in most cases by developmental arrest. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3093890 Reymond et al. 1986)]. Additional phenotypes of constitutively active RasD mutants include enhanced expression of prestalk cell-specific genes, repressed expression of prespore cell-specific genes, and decreased Erk2 ([/gene/DDB_G0283903 erkB]) activation ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9190209 Louis et al. 1997)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9020088 Aubry et al. 1997)]. ''rasD'' null mutants cells have no developmental defects, however they have significant defects in both phototaxis and thermotaxis, indicating that RasD plays a role in the regulation of both phototaxis and thermotaxis of multicellular slugs ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10837033 Wilkins et al. 2000)]. RasD interacts with several proteins to form a phototactic signaling complex: filamin ([/gene/DDB_G0269100 abpC]), ERK2, PKB ([/gene/DDB_G0268620 pkbA]) and a gelsolin-related protein ([/gene/DDB_G0291125 gnrA]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16735078 Bandala-Sanchez et al. 2006)]. Ras signaling through RasD is also involved in cell fate bias. ''rasD'' null cells exhibit a spore bias in chimeric mixtures with wild type cells, while constitutively active ''rasD'' cells exhibit a strong stalk bias. A genetic screen for modulators of lineage bias identified GefE. Expression of GefE is required to activate RasD in a subset of cells, which in turn sets the intrinsic response threshold at which these cells respond to the pstB/pstO differentiation-inducer DIF, indicating that GefE acts through rasD to promote prestalk cell fate choice ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24282234 Chattwood et al. 2013)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30473004 Gruenheit et al. 2018)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 24-FEB-2020 RD

DDB_G0275445.summary:
Members of the Myb family of transcription factors are typically composed of two orthree imperfect repeats each of about 50 amino acids. These repeats fold into a variant ofthe helix-turn-helix motif and bind DNA ([/ontology/go/0003677/annotation/page/1 DNA binding]).The Myb motif has been well conserved during evolution (see [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10331990 Guo et al. 1999] and references therein).
''mybB'' was isolated a REMI mutant that does not aggregate upon starvation ([/ontology/go/0031152/annotation/page/1 aggregation involved in sorocarp development]). It has undetectable levels of [/gene/DDB_G0281545 acaA] transcript and no cAMP production. The expression pattern of ''mybB'' is consistent with its role in early development, peaking 2 hours after starvation. MybB functions in [/ontology/go/0043193/annotation/page/1 positive regulation of gene-specific transcription], being specifically required for the induction of adenylate cyclase expression in early development. Adenylate cyclase is responsible for cAMP production which mediates signaling during development ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9620859 Otsuka and Van Haastert 1998]).Overexpression of ''mybB'' rescues the developmental arrest of [/gene/DDB_G0282375 amiB] cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10651904 Kon et al. 2000]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 07-MAY-2004 PG
DDB_G0275445.note: The Curated Model is based on GenBank record AJ002383. The Sequencing Center predicts an 86 nt intron at nt 991, but analyses in PMID 9620859 indicates that this sequence is present in cDNAs.
phenotypes: decreased activation of adenylate cyclase activity

DDB_G0267472.summary:
''roco7'' encodes a large, multi-domain protein of the Roco family. Roco7 contains a Roc small GTPase domain, a COR (C-terminal of Roc) domain, a protein kinase domain and a C-terminal WD40 repeat domain. ''roco7'' is an ortholog of human LRRK2, mutations in which are associated with Parkinson disease. Eleven ''Dictyostelium'' proteins belong to the Roco family: ([/gene/DDB_G0291079 gbpC]), ([/gene/DDB_G0273259 qkgA-1]), ([/gene/DDB_G0269250 pats1]), ([/gene/DDB_G0288251 roco4]), ([/gene/DDB_G0294533 roco5]), ([/gene/DDB_G0279417 roco6]), Roco7, ([/gene/DDB_G0286127 roco8]), ([/gene/DDB_G0288183 roco9]), ([/gene/DDB_G0291710 roco10]) and ([/gene/DDB_G0268636 roco11]).
Roco7 is localized to the cytosol and ''roco7'' is expressed during both growth and development with the highest level of expression during aggregation. Disruption of the ''roco7'' gene did not result in any significant developmental defects ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20348387 van Egmond and van Haastert 2010]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 15-OCT-2021 RD

DDB_G0289067.summary: The [/gene/DDB_G0289067 smkA] gene was first identified as a suppressor of the [/gene/DDB_G0269152 mekA] null chemotaxis phenotype.In addition to a chemotaxis phenotype, cells lacking ''smkA'' are defective in cytokinesis when grown in suspension andhave greatly reduced levels of myosin II ([/gene/DDB_G0286355 mhcA]). The ''smkA'' gene product, SMEK, is highly conservedacross species and contains an EVH1 domain, however, its function is unknown. SMEK localizes to the [/ontology/go/0005938/annotation/page/1 cell cortex] duringgrowth and translocates to the [/ontology/go/0005634/annotation/page/1 nucleus] during development via its NLS ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16107728 Mendoza et al. 2005]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 07-SEP-2005 KP

DDB_G0269230.summary:
The [/gene/DDB_G0269230 fpaA] and [/gene/DDB_G0273251 fpaB-1]/[/gene/DDB_G0273615 fpaB-2] genes encode nearly identical proteins, differing by one intron, 33 nucleotides, and one amino acid ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9373134 West et al. 1997]). The ''fpa'' genes encode the Skp1 protein, which in ''Dictyostelium'' and other protists forms the SCF ubiquitin ligase complex (reviewed in [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15238247 West et al. 2004]) Both FpaA and FpaB proteins are found in the cytoplasm and enriched in the nucleus in immunocytochemistry experiments.During development, expression persists in the nucleus but also increases at the cell cortex. Glycosylation is required for nuclear enrichment ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11358877 Sassi et al. 2001]).
Glycosylation of Skp1 has been extensively studied in ''Dictyostelium''. The initial step in Skp1 glycosylation involves the hydroxylation of Pro143 by a proline hydroxylase ([/gene/DDB_G0277759 phyA], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9660787 Teng-umnuay et al. 1998]). HyPro143 is then modified by the glycosyltransferase [/gene/DDB_G0275699 gnt1], which transfers a GlcNAc (N-acetylglucosamine) to the Skp1 protein ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10593934 Teng-umnuay et al. 1999]). The Skp1-GlcNAc is extended by a bifunctional diglycosyltransferase, [/gene/DDB_G0283761 pgtA], which processively adds galactose and fucose ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11423539 van der Wel et al. 2001], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12244067 van der Wel et al. 2002]). Subsequently two additional galactose residues are added by [/gene/DDB_G0283005 agtA] to yield the Skp1 pentasaccharide (GGFGGnOSkp1; [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16495217 Ercan et al. 2006], reviewed in [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31128470 West and Kim 2019]).
West and colleagues reported that the proline hydroxylase ([/gene/DDB_G0277759 phyA]) performing the first SKP1 modification mediates oxygen signaling during ''Dictyostelium'' development. ''phyA''-null cells need strongly elevated oxygen levels to culminate ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17699611 West et al. 2007]). Mutant analyses showed not only is Skp1 a substrate for PhyA it is also a functional mediator of PhyA activity in cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20969846 Wang et al. 2011]). Further investigations showed that full SKP1 glycosylation is required for optimal oxygen sensing during development, for example [/gene/DDB_G0283005 agtA] knockout and overexpression mutants require elevated oxygen levels to culminate ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19687007 Wang et al. 2009], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22128189 Zhang et al. 2011], reviewed in [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25988702 West and Blader 2015]).
The ''Dictyostelium'' unmodified Skp1 seems to form a dimer. The SCF ubiquitin ligase complex has been investigated and binding to F-box protein seems to dissociate the dimer. Free Skp1 forms a complex with a CullinA homolog ([/gene/DDB_G0278991 culE]), and the F-box protein ([/gene/DDB_G0292312 fbxD]; [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24550398 Shafer et al. 2014], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25341530 Sheik et al. 2015]). Co-immunoprecipitation and proteomic analysis also showed the F-box protein [/gene/DDB_G0276887 fbxA] binding to Skp1. CulE binds proteins such as the RING box protein [/gene/DDB_G0287629 rbx1] and the cullin-associated neddylation-disassociated protein [/gene/DDB_G0274167 cand1]. F-box proteins preferentially associate with fully glycosylated Skp1 compared to unmodified Skp1. Thus low oxygen levels are rate limiting for the hydroxylation of nascent Skp1 in cells, and demonstrates that full Skp1 hydroxylation/glycosylation is to alter the repertoire of the F-box proteins with which it associates ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24506136 Sheik et al. 2014], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25341530 Sheikh et al. 2015]). Furthermore NMR and mass spec analyses showed that Skp1 complete glycolysation modifies the originally disordered protein conformation resulting in enhanced F-box protein binding ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28928219 Sheikh et al. 2017]; [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29251491 Xu et al. 2018], reviewed in [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31128470 West and Kim 2019]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 06-MAR-2020 PF

DDB_G0286187.summary: Profilins are small, well-conserved, actin-binding proteins that also bind other proteins as well as phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2). Dictyostelium has three genes encoding profilin, ([/gene/DDB_G0287125 proA]), ''proB'' and ([/gene/DDB_G0271142 proC]) [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1725525  (Haugwitz et al. 1991)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17467078  (Arasada et al. 2007)]. ''proB'' is expressed in vegetative cells as well as during early development giving a peak of mRNA abundance at T=11 hrs [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25887420  (Rosengarten et al. 2015)]. ''In vitro'', profilin II raises the critical concentration of G-actin necessary for F-actin formation and delays the onset of elongation of F-actin more than profilin I, perhaps as the consequence of having a higher affinity to G-actin [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1725525  (Haugwitz et al. 1991)]. When profilin II binds G-actin it stimulates the exchange of ADP by ATP in G-actin which allows it to polymerize. Single mutants in which ''proB'' is inactivated show no significant defects, but double mutants with null mutations in both ''proA'' and ''proB'' have growth and developmental defects. The cells do not grow in suspension and become multinucleated when grown on solid supports. Aggregation proceeds well but mounds do not culminate and spores are not formed by the double mutants. F-actin is 60% more abundant in the double mutants than in wild type cells. [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7954798  (Haugwitz et al. 1994)]. In addition, profilin double mutants are defective in macropinocytosis, fluid phase efflux, and secretion of lysosomal enzymes, but are more efficient in phagocytosis than wt cells. Disruption of the ''lmpA'' ([/gene/DDB_G0267406 lmpA]) gene in the profilin double null background suppressed the endocytic defects and phagocytic increases, suggesting that LmpA may act as a negative regulator of profilin [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10848626  (Temesvari et al. 2000)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11683394  (Seastone et al. 2001)]. Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 17-DEC-2019 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0276043.summary:
Initiation of protein translation in eukaryotes is regulated by phosphorylation of the alpha subunit of eukaryotictranslation initiation factor 2 (eIF2alpha). During periods of amino acid starvation, eIF2alpha is inactivated viaphosphorylation by the serine/threonine kinase ([/ontology/go/0004674/annotation/page/1 protein serine/threonine kinase activity]) GCN2 (general control nonderepressible), also known asPEK (pancreatic eukaryotic translation initiation factor kinase). The PEK family of protein kinases is highly conservedfrom yeast to humans, however, the effect on translation in metazoans is global whereas GCN2 in yeast acts to inhibittranslation of specific species of mRNA ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7855893 reviewed in Wek 1994]).
In ''Dictyostelium'', two members of the PEK family of protein kinases have been identified: [/gene/DDB_G0272837 ifkA] and[/gene/DDB_G0276829 ifkB]. Putative proteins belonging to the PEK family are: [/gene/DDB_G0276043 ifkC], [/gene/DDB_G0283065 DDB_G0283065], [/gene/DDB_G0268642 DDB_G0268642], [/gene/DDB_G0292734 DDB_G0292734], and [/gene/DDB_G0292734 DDB_G0292734].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 17-SEP-2004 KP

DDB_G0275191.summary:
Using an apoaequorin expressing strain, Ludlow ''et al.'' showed that ''Dictyostelium'' posseses P2X receptors that facilitate rapid Ca2+ influx in response to extracellular ATP and ADP. Deleting [/gene/DDB_G0272004 p2xA] or [/gene/DDB_G0288061 p2xE] did not influence this behavior, suggesting these genes are not involved. However, this study proposes possible roles for [/gene/DDB_G0275293 p2xB], [/gene/DDB_G0275191 p2xC], or [/gene/DDB_G0288335 p2xD] [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18486207 (Ludlow et al. 2008)].
Most recently, Ludlow ''et al.'' showed that p2xB and p2xE, as well as p2xA, have ATP-gated channel activity when expressed in ''Xenopus'' oocytes. However, Na+ rather inhibited this activity to various degrees in these P2x channels, but K+, and NH4+ ions elicited a large response. Interestingly, p2xA and p2xB, but not p2xE are permeable to Cl- ions. No such ATP-gated channel activity was found for p2xC and p2xD. All ''Dictyostelium'' P2x proteins localize to the [/ontology/go/0031164/annotation/page/1 contractile vacuolar membrane], and not to the plasma membrane like P2X receptors from other organisms. By using a protease protection assay on tagged receptors the authors demonstrated that the transmembrane loop region containing the agonist (ATP) binding site lies within the lumen of the vacuole. A quintuple p2xA/B/C/D/E null mutant in wild type background AX2 shows a reduced response to the calmodulin inhibitor calmidazolium, suggesting a role of the ''Dictyostelium'' proteins in the [/ontology/go/0050848/annotation/page/1 regulation of calcium-mediated signaling]. The quintuple null mutant also shows a slight delay in its [/ontology/go/0006971/annotation/page/1 hypotonic response] when placed in water, however, single mutants in a AX2 background do not show any osmoregulatory defect. Taken together, this study suggests that it is still unclear which molecules are responsible for the extracellular purinergic response in ''Dictyostelium'' and it raises the possibility that the P2x receptors may play a role in the release of intracellular Ca 2+ stores in response to an ATP stimulus from within the contractile vacuole [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19833731 (Ludlow et al. 2009)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 11-MAR-2010 PF

DDB_G0286553.summary:
''rab21'' (''rabB'') encodes a guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G protein) of the Rab family of small GTPases. G proteins are key components of signal transduction networks in which they function as molecular signaling switches, binding to GDP in the off state while binding GTP in the on state. Guanine nucleotide-exchange factors (GEFs) promote the exchange of GDP for GTP on Rab GTPases thus activating them, while GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) inactivate Rab GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP. ''rab21'' is expressed at a relatively constant level throughout growth and development [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8294041 (Bush et al. 1993)]. Proteomic analysis revealed that Rab2A is localized to lipid droplets ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24036346 Du, et al. 2013]) and also to the Legionella-containing vacuole [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28183814 (Schmolders et al. 2017)].
''rab21'' is involved in a signaling pathway that regulates phagocytosis. Rab21 interacts with two LIM-domain containing proteins: ([/gene/DDB_G0267490 ChLim]) and ([/gene/DDB_G0275157 limF]). Expression of constitutively active Rab21, overexpression of LimF, or deletion of ChLim increases the rate of phagocytosis above that of wild type; conversely, expression of a dominant-negative Rab21, deletion of LimF, or overexpression of ChLim inhibits phagocytosis. These results suggest a complex interactive relationship in which the three proteins function as a regulatory unit to direct phagocytic uptake: activated Rab21 positively regulates phagocytosis, ChLim serves to inhibit the activating function of Rab21, while LimF is required for the activating function of Rab21 [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15962002 (Khurana et al. 2005)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 30-SEP-2020 RD

DDB_G0275035.summary: ''zizA'' encodes a Rho guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF, RhoGEF). RhoGEFs are key components of signaling networks in which they activate Rho family GTPases by promoting the exchange of GDP for GTP. ''zizA'' is expressed throughout growth and development. ZizA is distributed throughout the cytosol with enrichment at the microtubule organizing center (MTOC). ZizA does not show chemoattractant-induced localization or cause any alterations in cell movement or filopod formation. ''zizA'' null mutant cells do not have defects in development or cytokinesis ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22366457 Pakes et al. 2012]). The adaptor protein ElmoE ([/gene/DDB_G0279657 elmoE]) associates with the Rho GTPase RacB ([/gene/DDB_G0279605 racB]) as well as with both ZizA and DocC ([/gene/DDB_G0292004 docC]), suggesting that ElmoE, DocC, and ZizA may form an evolutionarily conserved Elmo/Dock complex to serve as a GEF for RacB ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22264729 Yan et al. 2012]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 21-MAY-2021 RD
