DDB_G0289653.summary: NoxA, NoxB ([/gene/DDB_G0287101 noxB]), and NoxC ([/gene/DDB_G0291117 noxC]), are homologs of the heme-containing subunit of NADPH oxidase flavocytochromes that generate superoxide for defense and signaling. Each of them has 6 predicted transmembrane regions and uses 4 histidine moieties to bind 2 heme groups. Mutations that inactivate the ''nox'' genes in the genetic background of strain JH10 result in a developmental block at the tipped mound stage, but have no effect on growth in association with bacteria. [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15950752  (Lardy et al. 2005)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16367873  (Benghezal et al. 2006)]. A triple mutant in which ''noxA'', ''noxB'', and ''noxC'' are disrupted in the genetic background of strain AX2 develops normally, but has defects in the defense response to bacteria. The Sentinel cells that normally provide innate immunity in slugs are unable to generate superoxide when all 3 of the ''nox'' genes are deleted. Reactive oxygen species (ROS) stimulate S cells to take up bacteria by phagocytosis and to release mitochondrial DNA nets that trap extracellular bacteria. ''noxA''/''noxB''/''noxC'' triple null mutants release very few DNA nets and fail to clear bacteria from the slugs. [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26927887  (Zhang et al. 2016)]. ''noxA'' is expressed at high levels in vegetative cells and at lower levels during development. ''noxB'' and ''noxC'' are only expressed after 6 hrs of development [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15950752  (Lardy et al. 2005)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 20-DEC-2018 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0272324.summary: Shwachman-Diamond syndrome (SDS) is characterized by exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, bone marrow failure and skeletal abnormalities, and is caused by mutations in the highly conserved SBDS gene. ''Dictyostelium'' ''sbds'' encodes the ortholog of human SBDS with which it exhibits an overall identity of 38% and similarity of 69%. Attempts to create null mutants of ''sbds'' were unsuccessful, but conditional mutants using temperature-sensitive self-splicing inteins were engineered and introduced into the ''sbds'' gene to assess its function. In ''sbds'' conditional mutants, growth is abolished at the restrictive temperature and development arrests at the loose mound stage. In addition, the mutants have increased levels of free 40S and 60S ribosomal subunits and decreased levels of mature 80S ribosomes, indicating that SbdS has a conserved function in ribosomal subunit joining. These phenotypes can all be complemented by expression of human SBDS. Overexpression of ''eIF6'' ([/gene/DDB_G0276493 eIF6]) also impairs ribosomal subunit joining. eIF6 binds pre-60S subunits in the nucleus and is exported with them into the cytoplasm. The ribosomal subunit joining defect in ''sbds'' mutants, as well as their growth and developmental phenotypes, can also be suppressed by expressing a mutant form of eIF6 with reduced affinity for 60S ribosomal subunits. SBDS and Elongation factor-like GTPase EFL1 ([/gene/DDB_G0279689 eftud1]) interact directly ''in vivo'' and are bound in close physical proximity on the surface of the 60S ribosomal subunit, where they activate nascent 60S ribosomal subunits for translation by catalyzing eviction of the anti-association factor eIF6 from nascent 60S ribosomal subunits. These findings support the hypothesis that SDS is a ribosomopathy caused by impaired release of eIF6 and defective ribosomal subunit joining due to mutations in the ribosome assembly factor SBDS [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21803848  (Wong et al. 2011)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26479198  (Weis et al. 2015)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 15-OCT-2020 RD

DDB_G0286069.summary: DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) can be repaired by either non-homologous end-joining (NHEJ) or homologous recombination (HR). In vertebrates, NHEJ is initated when Ku70/Ku80 heterodimers bind to DNA ends and recruit the catalytic subunit of DNA-dependent protein kinase (DNA-PKcs). Homologs of these components in Dictyostelium are encoded by ''ku70'', ''ku80'' ([/gene/DDB_G0286303 ku80]),and ''dnapkcs'' ([/gene/DDB_G0281167 dnapkcs]) [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16243037  (Hudson et al. 2005)]. Both Ku70 and Ku80 are members of the family of ATP-dependent DNA helicases and are coordinately expressed during growth and early development [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16112620  (Block and Lees-Miller, 2005)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25887420  (Rosengarten et al. 2015)]. Poly ADP-ribose is generated by the polymerase Adprt1a ([/gene/DDB_G0278741 adprt1A]) at sites of DNA DSBs. Poly ADP-ribose polymers promote NHEJ by binding Ku70 at DSBs and attaching Ku80 [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21807880  (Couto et al. 2011)]. Ku80 has a C-terminal domain that binds DNA-PKcs together with the homolog of the DNA repair endonuclease Artemis, Dclre1 ([/gene/DDB_G0277755 dclre1]), that is essential for NHEJ [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16112620  (Block and Lees-Miller, 2005)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16582628  (Hsu et al. 2006)]. Null mutations in either ''ku70'' or ''dnapkcs'' render recently germinated cells unusually sensitive to the DSB-inducing agent bleomycin. However, these mutations have no effect on bleomycin sensitivity of populations of growing cells, probably because DSBs can be repaired by the HR pathway in cells with two copies of each gene. Haploid cells emerge from spores in the G1 phase of the cell cycle where HR is inoperable; however, growing cells are in G2 where HR can compensate for loss of NHEJ [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16243037  (Hudson et al. 2005)]. The DNA joining events that result in integration of plasmid sequences at random sites of double-strand cleavage during REMI mutagenesis appear to depend on the NHEJ pathway, since ''ku70'', ''ku80'', ''adprt1a'' and ''dclre1'' null mutants do not show the increase in plasmid integration seen in wild type cells transformed together with restriction enzymes [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21807880  (Couto et al. 2011)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21536833  (Hsu et al. 2011)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 04-JAN-2019 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0284331.summary: The major intracellular cAMP phosphodiesterase is encoded by ''regA'' ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8986798 Shaulsky et al. 1996)]. RegA associates with PkaR ([/gene/DDB_G0279413 pkaR]) and catalyzes the hydrolysis of bound cAMP ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9435289 Shaulsky et al. 1998)]. The catalytic subunit of PKA ([/gene/DDB_G0283907 pkaC]) then displaces RegA and reforms the inactive PKA complex ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20923972 Moorthy et al. 2011)]. RegA carries a response regulator domain at the N-terminus that accepts phosphate from the H2 relay protein RdeA ([/gene/DDB_G0282923 rdeA]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9582274 Chang et al. 1998], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10488068  Thomason et al. 1999)]. Phosphorylation of the response regulator domain of RegA allosterically activates the catalytic domain found near the carboxy-terminus ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22326871 Moorthy et al. 2012)]. Multiple histidine kinases relay phosphate to RdeA and can thereby modulate cAMP levels by controlling the phosphodiesterase activity. DhkA ([/gene/DDB_G0280961 dhkA]) is a receptor histidine kinase that acts in a two-component system with RegA ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8670894 Wang et al. 1996], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10373524 Wang et al. 1999)]. When DhkA binds its peptide ligand, SDF-2, it acts as a phosphatase to remove phosphate from RdeA which can then dephosphorylate RegA and reduce its activity ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9191038 Loomis et al. 1997], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9582277 Thomason et al. 1998)]. RegA is part of the circuit that generates 6 minute oscillations in cAMP during aggregation ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9843585 Laub et al. 1998], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15131307 Maeda et al. 2004)]. When external cAMP binds to the CAR1 ([/gene/DDB_G0273397 carA-1]), ([/gene/DDB_G0273533 carA-2]) receptor, ERK2 ([/gene/DDB_G0283903 erkB]) is activated and then associates with and inhibits RegA ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31730032 Adhikari et al. 2019)]. cAMP can then rapidly build up until it activates the cAMP dependent protein kinase PKA which blocks ERK2 inhibition of RegA; the resulting RegA activity drives the concentration of cAMP back down. Cells in which ''regA'' is disrupted develop precociously much like cells in which ''pkaR'' is disrupted ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9435289 Shaulsky et al. 1998)]. These mutant cells are also impaired in chemotaxis as the result of being unable to suppress lateral pseudopods in the front of natural cAMP waves ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10930471 Wessels et al. 2000)]. The signaling molecule differentiation-inducing factor 2 (DIF-2) modulates chemotaxis to cAMP via the DhkC ([/gene/DDB_G0274191 dhkC])-RegA-RdeA signaling pathway. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26919666 Kuwayama and Kubohara 2016)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 24-JAN-2017 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis; annotation contributions: PMID:24511612, Jeff Hadwiger

DDB_G0283385.summary: Tyrosine phosphorylation regulates many eukaryotic proteins. Protein-tyrosine kinase genes were recognized by screening cDNA expression libraries with anti-phosphotyrosine antibody [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1972546  (Tan and Spudich, 1990)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8898113  (Adler et al. 1996)]. One of the tyrosine kinases found in this screen, SplA, was shown to be essential for spore differentiation. Mutant cells lacking SplA develop normally and make fruiting bodies, but prespore cells fail to assemble spore coats and spontaneously lyse in the sorus. It was suggested that SplA might play an essential role in triggering exocytosis of prespore vesicles during culmination. [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8898241  (Nuckolls et al. 1996)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 30-JAN-2018 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0282145.summary: The ''ptpC'' gene encodes protein tyrosine phosphatase PTP3. PTP3 is expressed in anterior-like and prestalk cell types. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1423620 Howard et al. 1992)]. The responses to the stalk inducer DIF-1 as well as to hyper-osmotic stress that are mediated by the DNA-binding protein STATc ([/gene/DDB_G0293532 dstC]) are controlled by inhibition of PTP3 ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10207040 Gamper et al. 1999)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18840649 Langenick et al. 2008)]. PTP3 dephosphorylates and inhibits STATc by removing a phosphate necessary for its nuclear localization. PTP3 is itself inhibited in response to changes to the cortical cytoskeleton. The protein kinase Phg2 ([/gene/DDB_G0283699 phg2]) inhibits PTP3 by phosphorylating it at S747, while an as yet unknown protein kinase phosphorylates PTP3 on S448. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18305004 Araki et al. 2008)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22365144 Araki et al. 2012)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24587195 Vu et al. 2014)]. Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 14-JUL-2016 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

G proteins are key components of signal transduction networks in which they function as molecular signaling switches, binding to GDP in the off state while binding GTP in the on state. Guanine nucleotide-exchange factors (GEFs) promote the exchange of GDP for GTP on Rab GTPases thus activating them, while GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) inactivate Rab GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP. DDB_G0274285.summary:
There are 29 genes encoding actin in ''Dictyostelium'' with amino acid identity greater than 83%, ''act1''-''act29''. Seventeen of these genes encode identical proteins: [/gene/DDB_G0289553 act1], [/gene/DDB_G0274133 act2], [/gene/DDB_G0289005 act4], [/gene/DDB_G0289663 act5], [/gene/DDB_G0274135 act6], [/gene/DDB_G0280545 act7], [/gene/DDB_G0269234 act8], [/gene/DDB_G0274601 act9], [/gene/DDB_G0288879 act11], [/gene/DDB_G0274129 act12], [/gene/DDB_G0274599 act13], [/gene/DDB_G0274137 act14], [/gene/DDB_G0272520 act15], [/gene/DDB_G0272248 act16], [/gene/DDB_G0274727 act19], [/gene/DDB_G0274285 act20], and [/gene/DDB_G0274561 act21], while [/gene/DDB_G0289811 act10], [/gene/DDB_G0275023 act22], and [/gene/DDB_G0289487 act3] respectively have 1, 4 and 11 amino acid differences compared to the 17 identical genes. The proteins encoded by [/gene/DDB_G0274131 act17], [/gene/DDB_G0289489 act18], [/gene/DDB_G0268744 act23] and [/gene/DDB_G0289505 act24]are more divergent.
Actin is a major [/ontology/go/0005200/annotation/page/1 structural constituent of cytoskeleton]. Actin is one of the most abundant proteins in ''Dictyostelium'', constituting approximately 8% of the total protein in vegetative cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/561722 Alton and Lodish et al. 1977]).Actin synthesis is developmentally regulated, peaking shortly after starvation (reviewed by [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6894564 Firtel] in 1981). The different actin genes differ in their levels of expression, with [/gene/DDB_G0274135 act6], [/gene/DDB_G0269234 act8] and [/gene/DDB_G0274129 act12] being highly expressed both during growth and development compared to [/gene/DDB_G0289005 act4], [/gene/DDB_G0289663 act5], [/gene/DDB_G0280545 act7] and [/gene/DDB_G0272248 act16] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6286214 McKeown and Firtel 1981]). Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 19-SEP-2003 PG

DDB_G0280055.summary: The ABC superfamily of genes is one of the largest in the genomes of both bacteria and eukaryotes. The proteins encoded by these genes all carry a characteristic 200- to 250-amino-acid ATP-binding cassette that gives them their family name ([/ontology/go/0042626/annotation/page/1 ATPase activity, coupled to transmembrane movement of substances]). In bacteria they are mostly involved in nutrient import, while in eukaryotes many are involved in export([/ontology/go/0006810/annotation/page/1 transport]), ([/ontology/go/0016021/annotation/page/1 integral to membrane]). Seven different families (A to G) have been defined in eukaryotes based on sequence homology, domain topology, and function. ''Dictyostelium'' has 71 ABC transporters (including one on the chromosome 2 duplication) and 13 ABCC family members: [/gene/DDB_G0280541 abcC1], [/gene/DDB_G0280055 abcC2], [/gene/DDB_G0287691 abcC3], [/gene/DDB_G0286559 abcC5], [/gene/DDB_G0287593 abcC6], [/gene/DDB_G0291243 abcC7], [/gene/DDB_G0284867 abcC8], [/gene/DDB_G0285165 abcC9], [/gene/DDB_G0280977 abcC10], [/gene/DDB_G0280973 abcC12], [/gene/DDB_G0280539 abcC13], [/gene/DDB_G0287589 abcC14], and [/gene/DDB_G0280459 abcC15]. Transporters of the C family have been shown to transport glutathione conjugants as well as to export cadmium ions. They are always found as full transporters with two copies of the transmembrane-ABC unit. Many of the genes of this family in humans and other animals have an additional transmembrane domain at the N terminus [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12456012 (Anjard and Loomis 2002)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 16-JUN-2003 PG

DDB_G0290833.summary: ''rabK1'' encodes a guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G protein) of the Rab family of small GTPases. G proteins are key components of signal transduction networks in which they function as molecular signaling switches, binding to GDP in the off state while binding GTP in the on state. Guanine nucleotide-exchange factors (GEFs) promote the exchange of GDP for GTP on Rab GTPases thus activating them, while GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) inactivate Rab GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP. Basic annotations have been added to this gene, 14-JAN-2021 RD

DDB_G0276027.summary: ''pdeE'' encodes a cAMP-stimulated cAMP phosphodiesterase which participates along with RegA ([/gene/DDB_G0284331 regA]) in breaking down intracellular cAMP. The affinity of PdeE for cAMP is much lower than the affintity of RegA for cAMP [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17040207  (Bader et al. 2007)]. PdeE has a beta-lactamase catalytic site followed by two cNMP binding sites, the same order of domains found in the highly related cGMP-activated cGMP phosphodiesterase PdeD ([/gene/DDB_G0274383 pdeD]) [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12429832  (Bosgraaf et al. 2002)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12574165  (Meima et al. 2003)]. cGMP is also hydrolyzed by PdeE but much more slowly than cAMP. '' pdeE'' is expressed between 6 and 16 hours of development when it could regulate PKA ([/gene/DDB_G0283907 pkaC], [/gene/DDB_G0279413 pkaR]) activity affecting post-aggregation differentiation [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25887420  (Rosengarten et al. 2015)]. ''pdeE'' knock-out strains have high levels of cAMP and are sporogenous much like ''regA'' nulls. Over-expression of ''pdeE'' leads to very slow aggregation [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12429832  (Bosgraaf et al. 2002)]. In shallow cAMP gradients, the stalk cell differentiation factor, differentiation-inducing factor 1 (DIF-1), inhibits chemotaxis through a ''pdeE''-dependent pathway [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19684855  (Kuwayama and Kubohara, 2009)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28619991  (Kubohara et al. 2017)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 02-NOV-2018 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0272242.summary: In a search for genes up-regulated by intracellular calcium ([/ontology/go/0043157/annotation/page/1 response to cation stress]), [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14871937 Coukellet al. (2004)] identified [/gene/DDB_G0277861 patA], a homolog of the yeast vacuolar ATPase PMC1, andseven ''cup'' genes, which encode highly conserved proteins that contain ricin B lectin domains involved incarbohydrate binding. During the developmental program, ''cup transcripts'' are detected at low levels at earlyand late stages and at higher levels during the slug stage. Immunoflourescent staining shows Cup proteinsthroughout the cell in vegetative cells ([/ontology/go/0005737/annotation/page/1 cytoplasm] and [/ontology/go/0005634/annotation/page/1 nucleus]), however, aggregating cells and cellsstressed with 50 mM calcium chloride show increased staining in the [/ontology/go/0005938/annotation/page/1 cell cortex]. Overexpression of [/gene/DDB_G0289815 cupB] antisense mRNA abolishes multicellular development; cells fail to aggregate completely. The sevencalcium up-regulated ''cup'' genes identified are: [/gene/DDB_G0267466 cupA], [/gene/DDB_G0289815 cupB], [/gene/DDB_G0289283 cupC], [/gene/DDB_G0293536 cupD], [/gene/DDB_G0294531 cupE], [/gene/DDB_G0289813 cupF], and [/gene/DDB_G0289883 cupG] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14871937 Coukell et al. 2004]). There are three other related genes, [/gene/DDB_G0290563 cupH], [/gene/DDB_G0272242 cupI], and [/gene/DDB_G0277959 cupJ]. Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 24-MAR-2008 PG

DDB_G0276155.summary:
The ''spnA'' gene was identified as a developmentally essential gene in a REMI screen. SpnA- cells aggregate and form mounds but fail to continue through morphogenesis ([/ontology/go/0006953/annotation/page/1 acute-phase response]). However, at 16 hours of development the mounds disaggregate to eventually form many small finger-like structures. Analysis of cell-type differentiation ([/ontology/go/0030154/annotation/page/1 cell differentiation]) showed that SpnA function is cell autonomous for prestalk differentiation, and cell non-autonomous for prespore differentiation.
''SpnA,'' encodes a bimodular protein with an N-terminal domain that shares substantial sequence homology with the heterotrimeric Galpha subunit family of GTP binding proteins ([/ontology/go/0005525/annotation/page/1 GTP binding]). The C-terminal domain shows strong homology to the Ser/Thr phosphatases of the PPC2 class. SpnA was shown to have Ser/Thr phosphatase activity ([/ontology/go/0004722/annotation/page/1 protein serine/threonine phosphatase activity]) in vitro, and mutational analysis identified the PPC2 domain to be essential for spnA function. The Galpha-like domain, on the other hand, seems to be required for ''spnA'' regulation and its targeting to membrane ruffles ([/ontology/go/0001726/annotation/page/1 ruffle]). These results suggest that spnA works as a GTP-regulated molecular switch in ''Dictyostelium'' development [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9585512 (Aubry and Firtel, 1998)]. Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 19-SEP-2003 PF

DDB_G0281387.summary:
''srfA'' encodes a MADS-box transcription factor ([/ontology/go/0003700/annotation/page/1 transcription factor activity]), ([/ontology/go/0006357/annotation/page/1 regulation of transcription from RNA polymerase II promoter]). The expression of ''srfA'' is developmentally regulated. The mRNA is present in vegetative cells, undetectable in aggregating cells up to the mound stage, and peaks in the late culminant.''srfA'' expression is controlled by alternative promoters in prestalk and prespore cells and is dependent on [/gene/DDB_G0283907 pkaC] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9729488 Escalante and Sastre 1998], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11437439 Escalante et al. 2001], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12204259 Escalante and Sastre 2002])
Disruption of ''srfA'' leads to defects in [/ontology/go/0030435/annotation/page/1 sporulation] that affects spore viability. Spores have lower cellulose levels [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9729488 (Escalante and Sastre 1998)]. Moreover, ''srfA'' null cells have defects in [/ontology/go/0030036/annotation/page/1 actin cytoskeleton organization and biogenesis], including reduced phosphorylation of actin ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14706699 Escalante et al. 2004]).
Microarray analysis lead to the identificationof several genes that fail to be expressed, or are expressed at reduced levels in the ''srfA'' null mutant. Many of these genes are required for spore maturation processes and include: [/gene/DDB_G0288359 dcd3A], [/gene/DDB_G0269108 catB], [/gene/DDB_G0291970 cofB],[/gene/DDB_G0283621 cutA], [/gene/DDB_G0290187 hspH], [/gene/DDB_G0269254 sigJ],[/gene/DDB_G0271922 mcfI], [/gene/DDB_G0292736 pipA], [/gene/DDB_G0277275 poxA], [/gene/DDB_G0275177 sigI], [/gene/DDB_G0277921 sigE],[/gene/DDB_G0289885 sigF], [/gene/DDB_G0290071 sigG], [/gene/DDB_G0282293 rnpA], [/gene/DDB_G0272524 malA], [/gene/DDB_G0293364 sigB], [/gene/DDB_G0277273 phg1b] (sigC),[/gene/DDB_G0267474 sigD], [/gene/DDB_G0289075 spiA], [/gene/DDB_G0280061 sybA],[/gene/DDB_G0286563 sigM], [/gene/DDB_G0273261 sigL], and [/gene/DDB_G0267476 sigK] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14665466 Escalante et al. 2003], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15075287 Escalante et al. 2004]).
The MADS-box (for the initials of the first identified members: MCM1, ARG80 from yeast, Deficient from Arabidopsis and SRF from humans) is a in a highly conserved60 amino-acid region that contain a dimerization and a DNA-binding domain. The serum response factor (SRF) is a DNA-binding proteininvolved in the transcriptional activation ofgenes in response to serum in cultured mammalian cells (see [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9729488 Escalante and Sastre 1998] and references therein).There are 4 predicted proteins that contain MADS-box in the ''Dictyostelium'' genome: [/gene/DDB_G0281387 srfA], [/gene/DDB_G0282835 srfB], [/gene/DDB_G0268920 srfC], and [/gene/DDB_G0283483 srfD].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 28-APR-2004 PG

DDB_G0293920.summary: The leucine-rich repeat domain-containing protein Leep1 was identified through a proteomic screen designed to identify proteins involved in the regulation of polarity. Leep1 localizes to the plasma membrane at the cell leading edge. In developing cells, Leep1 transiently redistributes to the cell periphery following both cAMP and folic acid stimulation. In vegetative-stage cells undergoing macropinocytosis, Leep1 is enriched at membrane patches that form macropinocytic cups. Leep1 is also associated with phagocytic cups. Leep1 associates with phosphatidylinositol (3,4,5)-trisphosphate (PIP3), which is responsible for recruiting Leep1 to the leading edge. ''leep1'' null mutants have a decreased rate of macropinocytosis and a reduction in the formation of macropinocytic cups. The mutant cells have an increased generation time when grown in liquid medium. Cell migration is only marginally affected in ''leep1'' null mutants, but the mutants generated fewer pseudopod splitting events compared with wild type cells, suggesting that ''leep1'' also plays a role in pseudopod dynamics. Overexpression of ''leep1'' results in increased filopodia formation and altered cytoskeletal rearrangement. Leep1 interacts with the Scar/WAVE complex, and both ScrA ([/gene/DDB_G0285253 scrA]) and PirA ([/gene/DDB_G0287855 pirA]) coimmunoprecipitate with Leep1. A ''leep1'' mutant with a truncated carboxyl-terminus does not interact with ScrA and also fails to promote increased filopodia formation, demonstrating that the ability to interact with the Scar complex underlies the cellular activity of Leep1. The similarity in phenotypes between overexpression of Leep1 and disruption of Scar implies that Leep1acts as a negative regulator of the Scar/WAVE complex in modulating leading edge dynamics. DDB_G0289555.summary:
The ''arkA'' gene was identified in a screen for suppressors of the protein phosphatase [/gene/DDB_G0276155 spnA]mutant ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14597204 Aubry et al. 2003]). ArkA contains several functionaldomains, including a protein kinase domain ([/ontology/go/0004672/annotation/page/1 protein kinase activity]) that is classified in the tyrosine kinase-like (TKL)group of protein kinases. The ''arkA'' transcript is developmentally regulated such that two peaks inexpression are detected by Northern blot at 8 hours and 15 hours after starvation. Spatial expression of thetranscript is highly enriched in the prestalk region in the slug and in the stalk and the tip of the fruitingbody. Subcellular localization is detected in the cortex, most likely associated with the cytoskeleton ([/ontology/go/0030863/annotation/page/1 cortical cytoskeleton]).
Disruption of the ''arkA'' gene results in abnormal fruiting bodies, whereas overexpression results in severemorphological defects ([/ontology/go/0007275/annotation/page/1 multicellular organismal development]). Expression levels of developmental markers [/gene/DDB_G0280531 lagC], [/gene/DDB_G0277853 ecmA],and [/gene/DDB_G0277141 cotC] are not affected in ''arkA-'' cells, however, the spore-specific [/gene/DDB_G0289075 spiA] transcript is elevated in comparison to wild-type. Additionally, yeast two-hybrid analysis showsthat ArkA interacts with 14-3-3 ([/gene/DDB_G0269138 fttB]) and [/gene/DDB_G0292998 rasB] but not with [/gene/DDB_G0292996 rasD], [/gene/DDB_G0293434 rasG], or [/gene/DDB_G0283537 rasS] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14597204 Aubry et al.2003]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 09-NOV-2004 KP

DDB_G0275689.summary:
''abcG2'' and [/gene/DDB_G0275687 abcG18] are present in the ''Dictyostelium'' genome as a tandem. In insertional mutant that disrupts both ''abcG2'' and [/gene/DDB_G0275687 abcG18] (''mdrA1/mdrA2'') results in release from the developmental block and the suppression of the defect in initial cell type choice caused by loss of the [/gene/DDB_G0271916 rtoA] gene. AbcG2 is localized to the endosome ([/ontology/go/0005768/annotation/page/1 endosome]). ''abcG2-/abcG18-'' cells have an endocytosis rate roughly 70% that of wild-type ([/ontology/go/0006897/annotation/page/1 endocytosis]). The triple null ''abcG2-/abcG18-/rtoA-'' has even lower endocytosis rates, about 20% that of wild type cells. The exocytosis rates of ''abcG2-/abcG18-''and ''abcG2-/abcG18-/rtoA-'' are roughly that of wild-type. ''abcG2-/[/gene/DDB_G0275687 abcG18]-'' endosomes have an unusually high pH ([/ontology/go/0030641/annotation/page/1 regulation of cellular pH]), whereas ''abcG2-/abcG18-/rtoA-'' endosomes have an almost normal pH [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11719559 (Brazill et al. 2000)].
The ABC superfamily of genes is one of the largest in the genomes of both bacteria and eukaryotes. The proteins encoded by these genes all carry a characteristic 200- to 250-amino-acid ATP-binding cassette that gives them their family name ([/ontology/go/0042626/annotation/page/1 ATPase activity, coupled to transmembrane movement of substances]). In bacteria they are mostly involved in nutrient import, while in eukaryotes many are involved in export([/ontology/go/0006810/annotation/page/1 transport]), ([/ontology/go/0016021/annotation/page/1 integral to membrane]). Seven different families (A to G) have been defined in eukaryotes based on sequence homology, domain topology, and function. ''Dictyostelium'' has 71 ABC transporters (including one on the chromosome 2 duplication) and 23 ABCG family members: [/gene/DDB_G0269214 abcG1], [/gene/DDB_G0275689 abcG2], [/gene/DDB_G0287461 abcG3], [/gene/DDB_G0289657 abcG4], [/gene/DDB_G0281391 abcG5], [/gene/DDB_G0281389 abcG6], [/gene/DDB_G0289655 abcG7], [/gene/DDB_G0274117 abcG8], [/gene/DDB_G0293450 abcG9], [/gene/DDB_G0292986 abcG10], [/gene/DDB_G0269212 abcG11], [/gene/DDB_G0274115 abcG12], [/gene/DDB_G0269210 abcG14], [/gene/DDB_G0267432 abcG15], [/gene/DDB_G0289331 abcG16], [/gene/DDB_G0273073 abcG17-1], [/gene/DDB_G0275687 abcG18], [/gene/DDB_G0269208 abcG19], [/gene/DDB_G0267430 abcG20], [/gene/DDB_G0269206 abcG21], [/gene/DDB_G0270826 abcG22], [/gene/DDB_G0269026 abcG23], and [/gene/DDB_G0282103 abcG24]. The ABCG family is characterized by the ABC domain preceding the transmembrane domain. All of the members of this family in animals are half-transporters while all of the fungal members are full transporters with two ABC-transmembrane units. No members of this family are found in bacteria. ''Dictyostelium'' and ''Arabidopsis'' have members of both types [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12456012 (Anjard and Loomis 2002)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 17-MAY-2004 PG

DDB_G0293012.summary: The CHD (chromodomain-helicase-DNA binding) protein family is one of the major ATP-dependent, chromatin remodeling factors that regulate nucleosome positioning and access of transcription factors and RNA polymerase to the eukaryotic genome. ''Dictyostelium discoideum'' contains three CHD orthologs (ChdA ([/gene/DDB_G0284171 chdA]), ChdB ([/gene/DDB_G0280705 chdB]) and ChdC) which are expressed throughout development, but with unique patterns. ''chdC'' has peak abundance between 8 and 10 hrs. of development. ''chdC'' null cells exhibited developmental arrest at the multicellular mound stage at approx. 12 hrs. and development failed to progress to the tipped mound stage. ''chdC'' null cells also displayed a reduced chemotaxis to cAMP, and the vegetative growth rate for ''chdC'' null cells was about half that of wt cells. Genome-wide (RNA-seq) transcriptome profiling for each CHD null strain revealed that the different CHDs regulate distinct gene sets during both growth and development. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24301467 Platt et al. 2013]). [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28330902 Platt et al. 2017] further demonstrated major nucleosome positional changes associated with developmental gene regulation in wild type cells. Loss of ''chdC'' caused an increase of nucleosome spacing in a large set of genes, and down regulation of developmental genes, affecting approximately 50 percent of the genes up-regulated in wild type during early development ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28330902 Platt et al. 2017]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 28-JAN-2022 PF

DDB_G0288335.summary:
Using an apoaequorin expressing strain, Ludlow ''et al.'' showed that ''Dictyostelium'' posseses P2X receptors that facilitate rapid Ca2+ influx in response to extracellular ATP and ADP. Deleting [/gene/DDB_G0272004 p2xA] or [/gene/DDB_G0288061 p2xE] did not influence this behavior, suggesting these genes are not involved. However, this study proposes possible roles for [/gene/DDB_G0275293 p2xB], [/gene/DDB_G0275191 p2xC], or [/gene/DDB_G0288335 p2xD] [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18486207 (Ludlow et al. 2008)].
Most recently, Ludlow ''et al.'' showed that p2xB and p2xE, as well as p2xA, have ATP-gated channel activity when expressed in ''Xenopus'' oocytes. However, Na+ rather inhibited this activity to various degrees in these P2x channels, but K+, and NH4+ ions elicited a large response. Interestingly, p2xA and p2xB, but not p2xE are permeable to Cl- ions. No such ATP-gated channel activity was found for p2xC and p2xD. All ''Dictyostelium'' P2x proteins localize to the [/ontology/go/0031164/annotation/page/1 contractile vacuolar membrane], and not to the plasma membrane like P2X receptors from other organisms. By using a protease protection assay on tagged receptors the authors demonstrated that the transmembrane loop region containing the agonist (ATP) binding site lies within the lumen of the vacuole. A quintuple p2xA/B/C/D/E null mutant in wild type background AX2 shows a reduced response to the calmodulin inhibitor calmidazolium, suggesting a role of the ''Dictyostelium'' proteins in the [/ontology/go/0050848/annotation/page/1 regulation of calcium-mediated signaling]. The quintuple null mutant also shows a slight delay in its [/ontology/go/0006971/annotation/page/1 hypotonic response] when placed in water, however, single mutants in a AX2 background do not show any osmoregulatory defect. Taken together, this study suggests that it is still unclear which molecules are responsible for the extracellular purinergic response in ''Dictyostelium'' and it raises the possibility that the P2x receptors may play a role in the release of intracellular Ca 2+ stores in response to an ATP stimulus from within the contractile vacuole [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19833731 (Ludlow et al. 2009)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 11-MAR-2010 PF

DDB_G0267406.summary: A REMI screen to find suppressor mutants for the developmental phenotype of profilin null cells identified the ''lmpA'' gene. LmpA is homologous to mammalian CD36/LIMP-II, a member of the class B of scavenger receptors. LmpA specifically binds to phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP<sub>2</sub>) [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10189376  (Karakesisoglou et al. 1999)]. Disruption of ''lmpA'' in the profilin double null background ([/gene/DDB_G0287125 proA], [/gene/DDB_G0286187 proB]) suppressed the profilin null endocytic defects and phagocytic increases, suggesting that LmpA may act as a negative regulator of profilin [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10848626  (Temesvari et al. 2000)]. ''lmpA'' knockout mutants reveal a role for ''lmpA'' in phagocytosis and phagolysosome biosynthesis. ''lmpA'' null cells are highly affected by actin-dependent processes such as bacterial particle uptake and cell motility. The cells are also impaired in pinocytosis, phagosomal acidification, reneutralization and proteolysis, and also contain a reduced level of lysosomal hydrolases. In addition, ''lmpA'' null cells are more susceptible to infection by pathogenic ''Mycobacterium marinum''. Lmp localizes to macropinosomes, lysosomes, post-lysosomes and ''M. marinum''-containing vacuoles, further supporting its role in phagocytosis and host cell defense [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30054386  (Sattler et al. 2018)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10848626  (Temesvari et al. 2000)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 19-DEC-2019 RD

The ''cbpA'' gene encodes a [/ontology/go/0005509/annotation/page/1 calcium ion binding] protein, CBP1 ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7729526 Coukell et al. 2000]). CBP1 associates with the [/ontology/go/0015629/annotation/page/1 actin cytoskeleton] during development. ''cbpA''-null cells grow normally, but exhibits delayed aggregation when developed in submerged conditions. This defect in aggregation appears to be related to a general reduction in [/ontology/go/0006928/annotation/page/1 cell motility] rather than to defect in the cAMP signaling cascade. Together, these results suggest that CBP1 might function to help regulate the reorganization of the ''Dictyostelium'' actin cytoskeleton during aggregation ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10896781 Dharamsi et al. 2000]).
CBP1 has been shown to interact with two other calcium-binding proteins, encoded by [/gene/DDB_G0283153 cbpD1] and [/gene/DDB_G0283083 cbpD2] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10771103 Dorywalskal et al. 2000]). It also interacts with protovilin ([/gene/DDB_G0276453 vilB]) and EF-1 alpha ([/gene/DDB_G0269134 efaAI]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10896781 Dharamsi et al. 2000]). DDB_G0285939.summary:
The ''Dictyostelium'' alpha-catenin was first identified in a screen for proteins involved in adhesion during cytokinesis and described as a vinculin (''vinA'') with which it shares considerable similarities. It was found to colocalize with [/gene/DDB_G0274109 paxB] in focal adhesion-like complexes. Mutant analysis showed that its involvement in adhesion dependent cytokinesis, or cytokinesis B. Myosin II is required for the contractile ring-dependent cytokinesis (cytokinesis A). A double mutant with mhcA disrupted adhesion on solid substrate completely, as both cytokinesis A were B are disrupted [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19065153 (Nagasaki et al. 2009)].
Dickinson and colleagues analyzed the structural similarity of the ''Dictyostelium'' protein with vinculins and alpha-catenins and found that it represents one of the earliest members before the branching of vinculins and alpha-catenins. everal experimental results were convincing that this protein is the ''Dictyostelium'' alpha-catenin homolog and the gene was named ''ctnnA''. CtnnA binds AarA, the ''Dictyostelium'' beta-catenin ([/gene/DDB_G0288877 aarA]), as well as the human beta-catenin. Depletion of ''ctnnA'' through RNAi resulted in a disruption of the polarized tip epithelium organization during development. Cellulose synthase ([/gene/DDB_G0269124 dcsA]) and EcmA/B ([/gene/DDB_G0277853 ecmA], [/gene/DDB_G0269132 ecmB]) are mislocalized intracellularly in tip epithelial cells but localization, though weak, is unchanged in stalk cells. This indicates that tip epithelial cells are the primary source of secreted cellulose and EcmA/B in the stalk tube [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21393547 Dickinson et al. 2011)]. Furthermore, both catenins are essential for apical myosin localization ([/gene/DDB_G0286355 mhcA]) during epithelial tube morphogenesis by regulating cortexillin ([/gene/DDB_G0289483 ctxA]) and Ras-GTPase ([/gene/DDB_G0287585 rgaA]) distribution, thus eliciting a signaling function of alpha-catenin in ''Dictyostelium'' [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22902739 (Dickinson et al. 2012)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 11-JUN-2015 PF; annotation contributions: PMID 22902739 Daniel Dickinson.

DDB_G0278263.summary:
DNA-dependent RNA polymerase catalyzes the transcription of DNA into RNA using the four ribonucleoside triphosphates as substrates ([/ontology/go/0003899/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase activity]). Three distinct zinc-containing RNA polymerases are found in eukaryotic nuclei: [/gene/DDB_G0275759 rpa1] for the ribosomal RNA precursor ([/ontology/go/0006360/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase I promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005736/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase I complex]), [/gene/DDB_G0279193 rpb1] for the mRNA precursor ([/ontology/go/0006366/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase II promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005665/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase II, core complex]), and [/gene/DDB_G0277199 rpc1] for 5S and tRNA genes ([/ontology/go/0006383/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase III promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005666/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase III complex]).
RNA polymerase I is a multisubunit complex. The subunits encoded by [/gene/DDB_G0275759 rpa1] (ortholog of ''S. cerevisiae RPA190''), [/gene/DDB_G0288449 rpc2] (''RPA135''), [/gene/DDB_G0268198 rpa43] (''RPA43''), [/gene/DDB_G0290909 rpa49] (''RPA49''), and [/gene/DDB_G0278263 rpa12] (''RPA12'') are unique to RNA polymerase I. Two subunits, [/gene/DDB_G0291362 rpc19] and [/gene/DDB_G0282339 rpa5] (''RPC19'' and ''RPC40'' in ''S. cerevisiae''), are common to RNA polymerase I and RNA polymerase III and correspond to subunits 3 and 11 of RNA polymerase II. Subunits [/gene/DDB_G0291636 rpb5], [/gene/DDB_G0291037 rpb6], [/gene/DDB_G0278039 rpb8], [/gene/DDB_G0272036 rpb10], and [/gene/DDB_G0283365 rpb12] are common to all three RNA polymerases. Yeast has two additional subunits, ''RPA34'' and ''RPA14'', that do not have clear orthologs in other species, including in ''Dictyostelium'' ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12407181 Peyroche et al. 2002], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12381659 Schramm and Hernandez 2001]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 13-APR-2004 PG

DDB_G0275637.summary: The ABC superfamily of genes is one of the largest in the genomes of both bacteria and eukaryotes. The proteins encoded by these genes all carry a characteristic 200- to 250-amino-acid ATP-binding cassette that gives them their family name. In bacteria they are mostly involved in nutrient import, while in eukaryotes many are involved in export. Seven different families (A to G) have been defined in eukaryotes based on sequence homology, domain topology, and function. ''Dictyostelium'' has 71 ABC transporters (including one on the chromosome 2 duplication) and 4 ABCF family members: [/gene/DDB_G0285997 abcF1], [/gene/DDB_G0284047 abcF2], [/gene/DDB_G0275637 abcF3] and [/gene/DDB_G0267436 abcF4]. The ABCF family is characterized by two ABC domains and no transmembrane domains. [/gene/DDB_G0285997 abcF1] and [/gene/DDB_G0267436 abcF4] are the most closely related to GCN20 from yeast and so are candidates for translational regulators [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6420574 (Anjard and Loomis 2002)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 16-JUN-2003 PG

DDB_G0282247.summary:
''rapgapB'' encodes a Rap GTPase-activating protein (GAP, rapGAP). RapGAPs are key components of signal transduction networks in which they inactivate Rap GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP. RapGAPB belongs to the Rap/Ran-GAP superfamily. ''rapGAPB'' is expressed during multicellular development and is enriched in prestalk cells with highest expression in the prestalk (pstO) region of slugs and in the upper and lower cups of culminants. In response to cAMP stimulation, ''rapgapB'' null cells display increased levels of active Rap GTPase RapA (Rap1) ([/gene/DDB_G0291237 rapA]) and the time course of RapA deactivation is dramatically decreased, indicating that RapGAPB has specific GAP activity for RapA.
''rapgapB'' null cells attach more strongly to the substratum than wild-type (wt) cells and display aberrant actin filament organization, with actin decorating the periphery of cells within filopodia. Aggregation is aberrant in ''rapgapB'' null cells with aggregation streams tending to break up resulting in large numbers of small mounds. The mutants form large numbers of misshapen tipped mound structures, and appear unable to form migratory slugs although small, twisted fruiting bodies eventually form. ''rapgapB'' null cells also have defects in pre-stalk cell patterning, as both pstA and pstO cells are mislocalized in the mutant cells. In addition, ''rapgapB'' null cells exhibit defects in cell-type-specific cell-cell adhesion: null mutant prestalk cells are less adhesive than wt prestalk cells but null mutant prespore cells are more adhesive than wt prespore cells, suggesting that changes in cell adhesion may underlie the ''rapgapB'' null mutant sorting defects. These results indicate that ''rapgapB'' is involved in the regulation of cell-substrate adhesion, aggregation and actin filament organization through the mediation of RapA activation ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19126673 Parkinson et al. 2009]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 30-MAR-2022 RD

[/gene/DDB_G0293002 tagA], [/gene/DDB_G0286119 tagB], [/gene/DDB_G0286121 tagC], and [/gene/DDB_G0286123 tagD] are members of the B family of ABC transporters. They encode proteins that are more than 65% identical, with the differences located mostly in the terminal regions. DDB_G0277777.summary: ''teep1'' was identified in a screen for pleckstrin homology (PH) domain-containing proteins exhibiting polarized distribution. Teep1 localizes to the trailing edge membrane of migrating, vegetative cells. In developing cells in response to cAMP stimulation, Teep1 transiently translocates from the plasma membrane to the cytosol. The localization pattern of Teep1 resembles that of Pten ([/gene/DDB_G0286557 pten]). Analysis of truncated ''teep1'' mutants reveal that the two N-terminal PH domains are responsible for targeting Teep1 to the rear of cells. Teep1 interacts with talin B ([/gene/DDB_G0287505 talB]) and binds to both phosphatidylinositol-4,5-bisphosphate (PI(4,5)P2) and phosphatidylinositol-3,5-bisphosphate (PI(3,5)P2). Deletion of enzymes responsible for production of PI(4,5)P2 (PikI) ([/gene/DDB_G0267588 pikI]) and PI(3,5)P2 (PIKfyve) ([/gene/DDB_G0279149 pip5k3]) reduce the plasma membrane association of Teep1, indicating that PI(4,5)P2 and PI(3,5)P2 regulate the posterior accumulation of Teep1 by jointly shaping the back state of the plasma membrane. In addition, the level of Teep1 associated with the plasma membrane is slightly increased in null cells of a myotubularin phosphatase, Mtm6 ([/gene/DDB_G0269272 mtm6]). Mtm6 localizes to the cell leading edge and is capable of degrading PI(3,5)P2, and likely mediates the removal of PI(3,5)P2 from the front and the formation of a reverse PI(3,5)P2 gradient. ''teep1'' null cells have a defect in cell motility and migrate at a significantly decreased speed compared with wt cells, but do not exhibit a defect in directed cell migration to either folic acid or cAMP. (Li, et al 2022, PMID:35186938).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 02-MAR-2022 RD

''roco6'' encodes a large, multi-domain protein of the Roco family. Roco6 contains an N-terminal leucine-rich repeat (LRR) region, a Roc small GTPase domain, a COR (C-terminal of Roc) domain, and a protein kinase domain, and two WD40 repeat domains and a PH domain in the C-terminal region. Eleven ''Dictyostelium'' proteins belong to the Roco family: ([/gene/DDB_G0291079 gbpC]), ([/gene/DDB_G0273259 qkgA-1]), ([/gene/DDB_G0269250 pats1]), ([/gene/DDB_G0288251 roco4]), ([/gene/DDB_G0294533 roco5]), Roco6, ([/gene/DDB_G0267472 roco7]), ([/gene/DDB_G0286127 roco8]), ([/gene/DDB_G0288183 roco9]), ([/gene/DDB_G0291710 roco10]) and ([/gene/DDB_G0268636 roco11]).
Roco6 is localized to the cytosol and ''roco6'' is expressed during both growth and development with the highest level of expression during the slug stage of development. Disruption of the ''roco6'' gene did not result in any significant developmental defects ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20348387 van Egmond and van Haastert 2010]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 14-OCT-2021 RD

DDB_G0272875.summary: ''Dictyostelium cpnB'' belongs to the highly conserved copines, a family of ubiquitious Ca(2+)-dependent phospholipid-binding ([/ontology/go/0005544/annotation/page/1 calcium-dependent phospholipid binding]) proteins. In their N-terminal half, copines contain two Ca(2+)- and phospholipid-binding domains (C2 domains) present in such proteins as phospholipase C and protein kinase C. Much of the C-terminal half consists of a von Willebrand Factor type A domain (VWFA) typically found in the extracellular portions of membrane proteins like integrins. Thus copines represent a fusion of intracellular (C2) and extracellular (VWFA) domains. However, there are no signal sequence or hydrophobic transmembrane sequences in the predicted proteins suggesting copines are intracellular proteins. Copines are thought to be involved in membrane trafficking. It is of particular interest that copines, first found in the highly phagocytic protozoan ''Paramecium'' and then isolated from mammalian spleen and liver, seem to be abundant in cells and organs that are, or contain, phagocytes. In this context it comes as no surprise that phagocytic ''Dictyostelium'' has a total of six copine genes[http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16343335  (Damer et al. 2005)]. The widespread distribution of copines from protozoans to mammals and their high similarity suggest they play important role(s) in eukaryotic biology. Reviewed in [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12440769  (Tomsig and Creutz, 2001)]Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 05-APR-2004 PF

DDB_G0271916.summary:
''rtoA'' was initially isolated by shotgun antisense cDNA as a gene required for [/ontology/go/0030587/annotation/page/1 sorocarp development] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8643519 Spann et al., 1996]). Defects in ''rtoA'' results in cells that have an abnormally high percentage of prestalk cells. Unlike wild type cells, ''rtoA'' mutant cells' propensity to differentate into prestalk or prespore cells is independent of their position in the cell cycle at starvation ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8951083 Wood et al., 1996]). RtoA levels vary during the cell cycle. During development, expression of RtoA is restricted to prespore cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10747962 Brazill et al., 2000]). ''rtoA''- cells have aberrant regulation of calcium levels during the cell cycle, indicating that [/ontology/go/0006874/annotation/page/1 cellular calcium ion homeostasis] may be linked to the [/ontology/go/0045595/annotation/page/1 regulation of cell differentiation] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11330860 Azhar et al., 2001]). The ''rtoA''- mutation affects the [/ontology/go/0006885/annotation/page/1 regulation of pH] in the cytosol as well as in the endocytic and exocytic vesicles. The RtoA protein contains several repeats of a serine-rich motif, which catalyzes the fusion of phospholipid vesicles ''in vitro''. Consistent with a role in [/ontology/go/0006944/annotation/page/1 membrane fusion], ''rtoA''- cells have a defect in the fusion of endocytic vesicles and decreased [/ontology/go/0006887/annotation/page/1 exocytosis] rates ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10747962 Brazill et al., 2000]).
Partial uppression of the ''rtoA'' phenotype can be observed in an insertional mutant that disrupts both [/gene/DDB_G0275689 abcG2] and [/gene/DDB_G0275687 abcG18] (''mdrA1/mdrA2''). The triple null ''abcG2-/abcG18-/rtoA-'' has greatly reduced endocytosis rates. Also, the cytosolic and endosomal pH of ''abcG2-/abcG18-/rtoA-'' are abnormal, indicating that the product of these genes are required for proper [/ontology/go/0048388/annotation/page/1 endosomal lumen acidification] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11719559 Brazill et al., 2001]).
''rtoA''- cells are more resistant to infection by the pathogen ''Legionella pneumophila'', probably because due to their defect in endocytic vesicles fusion ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15679845 Li et al., 2005]). It is also less efficient at phagocytosing the fungus ''Cryptococcus neoformans'', although once ingested, ''C. neoformans'' replicates as well in ''rtoA-'' mutants as in wild type cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12933827 Steenbergen et al., 2001]).
A region of the ''rtoA'' promoter necessary for the response to osmotic stress have been identified (Tsujioka and Williams 2007, personnal communication to dictyBase; the complete communication is available on the '''rtoA Community Annotation Page''', see link just above the Summary). The region between -144 and 256 relative to the start codon of the Curated Model is essential for up-regulation of ''rtoA'' following exposure to 100 mM sorbitol. Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 19-SEP-2003 PG
DDB_G0271916.note:
The Curated Model is based on the Sequencing Center gene prediction. GenBank record U48298 indicates the presence of an additional 431 nt intron 5' of the gene. Due to discrepancies between the sequence from GenBank and the sequence from the Sequencing Center, that first exon cannot be reconstituted.
Moreover, there are promoter elements located between -144 and -256 from the start codon of the Curated Model (see rtoA Community Annotations), providing additional support for the Curated Model.

DDB_G0276371.summary: ''gefL'' encodes a Ras guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF, RasGEF). rasGEFs are key components of signaling networks in which they activate Ras family small GTPases by promoting the exchange of GDP for GTP. ''gefL'' is expressed throughout both growth and development. A ''gefL'' null mutant is defective in phototaxis, with shorter and less accurate slug migration toward the light source. The mutant slugs are also defective in thermotaxis, displaying an insensitivity to temperature gradients. However, growth, morphology and fruiting body morphology are normal in ''gefL'' null mutants ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16086850 Wilkins et al. 2005)]. A high-throughput analysis also suggests defects in development and slug migration in ''gefL'' mutants ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17659086 Sawai et al. 2007)]. In addition to RasGEF and leucine-rich repeat domains, GefL also contains a GBD/FH3 domain, which suggests that it may potentially bridge Rho and Ras signaling pathways ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26940518 Rivero et al. 2016)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 20-APR-2021 RD

DDB_G0292310.summary: ''Dictyostelium'' contains orthologs of the core components of the presenilin/gamma-secretase complex: presenilin A ([/gene/DDB_G0291352 psenA]), presenilin B ([/gene/DDB_G0292310 psenB]), Aph-1 ([/gene/DDB_G0267976 aph1]) and nicastrin ([/gene/DDB_G0287801 ncstn]) which are capable of amyloidogenic processing of ectopically expressed human amyloid precursor protein (APP) to generate amyloid-beta peptides. Gamma-secretase activity is required for phagocytosis in Dictyostelium, and gamma-secretase mutants have primary defects in pre-spore/spore differentiation [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20699477  (McMains et al. 2010)]. A double null mutant lacking both presenilin A and presenilin B genes is blocked at the aggregation stage prior to morphogenesis. Either PsenB or human Psen1 can rescue the developmental phenotype of this mutant. In addition, presenilin loss in Dictyostelium results in elevated cAMP levels and enhanced stimulation-induced calcium release, suggesting that presenilins regulate these intracellular signalling pathways. [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24463814  (Ludtmann et al. 2014)]. ''Dictyostelium'' orthologs of the gamma-secretase complex PsenA, PsenB, Aph-1, and Nicastrin are necessary for macropinocytosis, phagocytosis, and autophagy, indicating roles in a general defect in lysosomal trafficking and degradation. In addition, loss of psenA/psenB and Aph-1 leads to an accumulation of ubiquitinated proteins, suggesting impaired protein degradation in these mutants. All of the endocytic defects in PSEN ortholog mutants can be fully restored by proteolytically inactive ''Dictyostelium'' PsenB and human PSEN1, demonstrating an evolutionarily conserved non-proteolytic role for presenilin in lysosomal trafficking and autophagy. [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30806144  (Sharma et al. 2019)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 23-JUL-2019 RD; annotation contributions: PMID:24463814 Grant Otto

DDB_G0267402.summary:
Histones form the nucleosomal core ([/ontology/go/0000786/annotation/page/1 nucleosome]) ([/ontology/go/0006334/annotation/page/1 nucleosome assembly]) that is fundamental to chromatin structure (). The histone octamer is composed of an H3-H4 tetramer (two H3-H4 dimers) coupled with an H2A-H2Btetramer (two H2A-H2B dimers). The histone H1 linker protein plays a role in packaging nucleosomes into the 30 nmfiber found in chromatin ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9177486 Bukenberger et al. 1992]).
In ''Dictyostelium discoideum'' and ''Saccharomyces cerevisiae'', only one copy of histone [/gene/DDB_G0285319 H1] appears to be present, in comparison to other eukaryotes which have multiple copies and subtypes([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7867938 Hauser et al. 1995], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9046096 Ushinsky et al.1997]). Two putative H2A family members, [/gene/DDB_G0279667 H2AX] and [/gene/DDB_G0286747 H2AZ], and three H2Adomain-containing proteins, [/gene/DDB_G0289187 H2Av1], [/gene/DDB_G0289193 H2Av2], [/gene/DDB_G0289197 H2Av3], are present in ''Dictyostelium''. Two H2B domain-containing proteins also exist inthe ''Dicty'' genome: [/gene/DDB_G0293758 H2Bv1] and [/gene/DDB_G0276273 H2Bv2]. There are three histone H3proteins, [/gene/DDB_G0267402 H3a] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9177486 Bukenberger et al. 1992]), [/gene/DDB_G0270838 H3b], and [/gene/DDB_G0271092 H3c], and two H3 domain-containing proteins, [/gene/DDB_G0291185 H3v1] and [/gene/DDB_G0277979 H3v2]. We have also identified two histone H4proteins, [/gene/DDB_G0277183 H4a] and [/gene/DDB_G0276863 H4b], which have identical protein sequences but non-identical nucleotide sequences.
The three H3 histones present in the ''Dictyostelium'' genome are highly similar to H3 histones in othereukaryotes, including mammalian sequences. [/gene/DDB_G0270838 H3b] and [/gene/DDB_G0271092 H3c] encode proteins 136 amino acids in length, theconserved length for H3, whereas [/gene/DDB_G0267402 H3a] has a 3 amino acid insert compared to other sequences ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9177486 Bukenberger et al. 1992]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 13-APR-2004 KP

DDB_G0273935.summary: ''rabF1'' encodes a guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G protein) of the Rab family of small GTPases. DDB_G0276885.summary:
CK2 (casein kinase II), a ubiquitous serine/threonine kinase, is one of the most highly conserved proteins in eukaryotic cells. The protein kinase usually forms a tetramer, comprised of two catalytic alpha or alpha' subunits, and two regulatory beta subunits. The ''Dictyostelium'' ''casK'' gene encodes a previously cloned CK2 alpha chain [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1448100 (Kikkawa et al., 1992)]. In addition, the ''Dictyostelium'' genome contains another putative alpha chain, [/gene/DDB_G0286481 DDB_G0286481], and a single ortholog of the CK2 beta chain, [/gene/DDB_G0284601 csnk2b].
The CK2 alpha chain encoded by ''casK'' has been identified by PCR, based on similarity. Northern blot analysis of ''casK'' during development, as well as CK2 activity ([/ontology/go/0004682/annotation/page/1 protein kinase CK2 activity]) throughout development both show a constitutive expression and presence of CK2 during the ''Dictyostelium'' life cycle. Attempts to delete the ''casK'' gene failed, indicating that it is an essential gene [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1448100 (Kikkawa et al., 1992)]. However, in yeast, which has two CK2 genes, only (haploid) cells carrying disruptions in both CK2 alpha chains are inviable [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2196445 (Padmanabha et al., 1990)].
Protein kinase CK2 represents a family of closely related kinases with broad specifity. There are hundreds of target molecules, implicating CK2 in many signalling pathways ([/ontology/go/0007165/annotation/page/1 signal transduction]), including such involved in cell survival. For recent reviews see [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12396231 (Litchfield, 2003)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12631575 (Meggio & Pinnal, 2003)], and [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12062170 (Ahmed et al., 2002)].
The presence of a second putative CK2 alpha- and one putative CK2 beta chain in ''Dictyostelium'' suggests that the tetrameric holoenzyme in this organism consists of two different alpha chains and two identical beta chains. However, currently there is no eperimental evidence that these putative genes are expressed and further investigation is necessary.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 10-MAY-2004 PF

DDB_G0291916.summary: ''argJ'' is the ''Dictyostelium'' member of the ArgJ family that catalyzes the first and fifth steps in [/ontology/go/0006526/annotation/page/1 arginine biosynthetic process]. These are evolutionarily related enzymes found in bacteria, yeast, fungi, and plants. Some but not all appear bifunctional, catalyzing the synthesis of acetlyglutamate from glutamate and acetyl-CoA ([/ontology/go/0004358/annotation/page/1 glutamate N-acetyltransferase activity]), and of ornithine by transacetylation between acetylornithine and glutamate ([/ontology/go/0006592/annotation/page/1 ornithine biosynthetic process]). The yeast enzyme, ARG7, which has been shown to be bifunctional [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9428669  (Crabeel et al., 1997)], is 41% identical to the ''Dictyostelium'' protein.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 08-FEB-2005 PF

These conventional kinesins are involved in transport of diverse organelles to the plus ends of microtubules. Kif7 is localized around nuclei but can be easily washed off following cell lysis. Cells lacking Kif7 because of a mutation in ''kif7'' grow and develop normally suggesting that this kinesin is dispensible for common functions. DDB_G0287053.summary: The LSM (like-Sm) proteins are a conserved group known to function in mRNA splicing and mRNA degradation.Complexes containing Lsm2-8 function in [/ontology/go/0000398/annotation/page/1 nuclear mRNA splicing, via spliceosome] in association with [/ontology/go/0005688/annotation/page/1 snRNP U6]. Complexes consistingof Lsm1-7, on the other hand, are believed to function in [/ontology/go/0006402/annotation/page/1 mRNA catabolic process] (reviewed in [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15916535 Beggs 2005]). In ''Dictyostelium'', clear orthologs of the Lsm proteins exist:[/gene/DDB_G0279837 lsm1], [/gene/DDB_G0281779 lsm2], [/gene/DDB_G0277107 lsm3], [/gene/DDB_G0287053 lsm4], [/gene/DDB_G0268716 lsm5],[/gene/DDB_G0275719 lsm6], [/gene/DDB_G0289499 lsm7], and [/gene/DDB_G0288479 lsm8]. Additionally, the ''Dictyostelium''genome contains putative orthologs of human LSM10 ([/gene/DDB_G0291015 DDB_G0291015]), LSM11 ([/gene/DDB_G0289453 DDB_G0289453]), and LSM12 ([/gene/DDB_G0270402 DDB_G0270402]). LSM10 and LSM11 associate with the U7snRNA, whereas LSM12 is hypothesized to be involved in RNA methylation ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11574479 Pillai et al. 2001], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15225602 Albrecht and Lengauer 2004]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 13-MAR-2006 KP

DDB_G0279977.summary: Members of the p53-related/BUD32 family of serine/threonine protein kinases ([/ontology/go/0004674/annotation/page/1 protein serine/threonine kinase activity]) are amongst theshortest protein kinases, with protein lengths less than 300 amino acids. BUD32 was first identified in ''Saccharomyces cerevisiae'' in a severe growth mutant, and it has been shown experimentally to phosphorylatecasein and osteopontin in a Mn2+ dependent manner ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9305753 Stocchetto et al.1997]). A highly related protein was later found in mammalian systems, however, it is not functionallycomplementary to yeast BUD53. This protein, named p53-related protein kinase (PRPK), phosphorylates the tumorsuppresor p53 ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11546806 Abe et al. 2001]). DDB0216402 in ''Dictyostelium''is highly similar to both BUD32 and PRPK.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 13-SEP-2004 KP

''Dictyostelium'' has three genes encoding actobindin, [/gene/DDB_G0270884 abnA], [/gene/DDB_G0269518 abnB], and [/gene/DDB_G0269520 abnC]. While proteins are identical for ''abnB'' and ''abnC'', both are 72% identical to ''abnA''. All three ''Dictyostelium'' actobindins are 50 to 51% identical to the ''Acanthamoeba'' protein.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 06-APR-2005 PF

DDB_G0271842.summary:
Succinyl-CoA synthetase (SCS) is an enzyme in the [/ontology/go/0006099/annotation/page/1 tricarboxylic acid cycle] that catalyzes the formation of succinyl-CoA from succinate with the concomitant hydrolysis of NTP to NDP and phosphate. There are two forms of the enzyme, using either ATP or GTP. The [/gene/DDB_G0289325 scsA] gene encodes the succinyl-CoA synthetase alpha subunit. In eukaryotes one alpha and one beta subunit are thought to form a heterodimer. Anschutzt ''et al.'' determined that in crude [/ontology/go/0016020/annotation/page/1 membrane] extracts ScsA could be phosphorylated by ATP and GTP, but the purified enzyme showed high specificity for GTP ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8448193 Anschutz et al., 1993]).
Only one alpha subunit has been identified in ''Dictyostelium'' ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7771809 Birney and Klein, 1995]). However, two beta subunits are present in the ''Dictyostelium'' genome; [/gene/DDB_G0274449 scsB] is the ortholog of GDP-forming succinyl-CoA ligase beta subunits () and [/gene/DDB_G0271842 scsC] is highly similar to known ADP-forming succinyl-CoA ligase beta subunits ().Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 27-JAN-2005 PF

DDB_G0289247.summary:
In search for ''Dictyostelium'' clathrin adaptor complexes (APs) cDNAs ''apm1'', [/gene/DDB_G0277901 apm3], and [/gene/DDB_G0276945 apm4], encoding proteins homologous to mammalian medium chain (mu) subunits, have been cloned. All APs are comprised of two large subunits, one medium size subunit, and one small subunit. ''Apm1'' encodes the medium chain of AP-1 ([/ontology/go/0030121/annotation/page/1 AP-1 adaptor complex]), which is known to be associated with clathrin coated vesicles from the trans-Golgi network ([/ontology/go/0030130/annotation/page/1 clathrin coat of trans-Golgi network vesicle]). The ''apm1'' encoded protein (mu1) shares 69% identity with the mouse mu1A, and is very similar in size (49 kD). This, and the presence of conserved residues potentially interacting with tyrosine-based sorting signals indicates that ''apm1'' truly encodes an AP-1 medium chain. Expression levels of ''apm1'' remain constant throughout development [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11179674 (de Chassey et al., 2001)].
Deletion of ''apm1'' causes defects in growth and spore germination, and a delay in development ([/ontology/go/0007275/annotation/page/1 multicellular organismal development]). Two lysosomal enzymes are secreted as precursors, indicating that lysosomal transport ([/ontology/go/0007041/annotation/page/1 lysosomal transport]) is impaired. Investigation of the endosome membrane marker [/gene/DDB_G0287297 p80] in apm1- cells showed the correct localization, but the size of endosomes appeared smaller and their number was significantly increased compaired to wild-type ([/ontology/go/0007032/annotation/page/1 endosome organization and biogenesis]). This result was confirmed by electron microscopy. Amp1- cells also failed to adjust to hypotonic stress ([/ontology/go/0006971/annotation/page/1 hypotonic response]), and while two markers for the contractile vacuole failed to localize correctly, no contractile vacuole could be identified by electron microscopy. Together with the studies of the AP-1 large subunit [/gene/DDB_G0281957 ap1g1] these data elucidate the functions of the AP-1 vesicular coat protein [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12802059 (Lefkir et al., 2003)]. Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 19-SEP-2003 PF

DDB_G0276363.summary: Besides ''mhcA'' ([/gene/DDB_G0286355 mhcA] that encodes the classical myosin heavy chain, ''Dictyostelium'' carries genes for 12 unconventional myosins. The first 5 unconventional myosins ([/gene/DDB_G0280039 myoA]), ([/gene/DDB_G0289117 myoB]), ([/gene/DDB_G0276617 myoC]), ([/gene/DDB_G0275447 myoD]), ([/gene/DDB_G0288679 myoE]), were isolated from whole genome plasmid clones by low stringency probing with portions of the head region of ''mhcA''. The next 6 unconventional myosins ([/gene/DDB_G0289177 myoF]), ''myoG'', ([/gene/DDB_G0289447 myoH]), ([/gene/DDB_G0274455 myoI]), ([/gene/DDB_G0272112 myoJ]), ([/gene/DDB_G0274575 myoK]) were recognized in large YAC clones that represent the whole genome [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7937787  (Titus et al. 1994)]. ''myoG'' encodes MyoG that carries a somewhat diverged version of the N-terminal motor domain, an IQ region for calmodulin ([/gene/DDB_G0279407 calA]) binding and a novel tail region which has two myosin tail homology domains (MyTH4) adjacent to a FERM domain [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20351273  (Breshears et al. 2010)]. MyoG is currently considered an orphan myosin. Strains with null mutations in ''myoG'' fail to develop and remain as smooth lawns; they appear to have cell autonomous defects in polarization and chemotaxis to cAMP and fail to activate PI3K at the anterior as occurs in wild type cells [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20351273  (Breshears et al. 2010)]. MyoG may play a role in membrane localization of RasGEF that limits its diffusion. Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 02-SEP-2019 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0273425.summary:
DNA-dependent RNA polymerase catalyzes the transcription of DNA into RNA using the four ribonucleoside triphosphates as substrates ([/ontology/go/0003899/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase activity]). Three distinct zinc-containing RNA polymerases are found in eukaryotic nuclei: [/gene/DDB_G0275759 rpa1] for the ribosomal RNA precursor ([/ontology/go/0006360/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase I promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005736/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase I complex]), [/gene/DDB_G0279193 rpb1] for the mRNA precursor ([/ontology/go/0006366/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase II promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005665/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase II, core complex]), and [/gene/DDB_G0277199 rpc1] for 5S and tRNA genes ([/ontology/go/0006383/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase III promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005666/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase III complex]).
RNA polymerase III is a multisubunit complex. The subunits encoded by [/gene/DDB_G0277199 rpc1] (ortholog of ''S. cerevisiae RPO31''), [/gene/DDB_G0293560 rpa2] (''RPC2''), [/gene/DDB_G0268080 rpc3] (''RPC82''),[/gene/DDB_G0277671 rpc4] (''RPC53''), [/gene/DDB_G0271514 rpc5] (''RPC37''), [/gene/DDB_G0286521 rpc9] (''RPC17''), [/gene/DDB_G0272022 rpc34] (''RPC34''), [/gene/DDB_G0273425 rpc25-1] (''RPC25''), and [/gene/DDB_G0287707 rpc11] (''RPC11'') are unique to RNA polymerase III. Orthologs of ''RPC31'' and ''RPC17'' have not been identified in the ''Dictyostelium'' genome. Two subunits, [/gene/DDB_G0291362 rpc19] and [/gene/DDB_G0282339 rpa5] (''RPC19'' and ''RPC40'' in ''S. cerevisiae''), are common to RNA polymerase I and RNA polymerase III and correspond to subunits 3 and 11 of RNA polymerase II. Subunits [/gene/DDB_G0291636 rpb5], [/gene/DDB_G0291037 rpb6], [/gene/DDB_G0278039 rpb8], [/gene/DDB_G0272036 rpb10], and [/gene/DDB_G0283365 rpb12] are common to all three RNA polymerases ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12407181 Peyroche et al. 2002], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12381659 Schramm and Hernandez 2001]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 11-JUN-2009 PG

DDB_G0278077.summary: The CRTF protein was isolated from nuclear extracts ([/ontology/go/0005634/annotation/page/1 nucleus]) by its ability to bind the [/gene/DDB_G0273397 carA-1] promoter. The deduced CRTFprotein is ~100 kDa with a C-terminal, zinc finger-likemotif required for DNA binding ([/ontology/go/0042156/annotation/page/1 zinc-mediated transcriptional activator activity]). ''crtf''-null strains fail to developunder standard conditions ([/ontology/go/0007275/annotation/page/1 multicellular organismal development]) or to exhibit induced expressionof ''carA'' or other cAMP-regulated genes ([/ontology/go/0045941/annotation/page/1 positive regulation of transcription]). Furthermore,''crtf''-nulls fail to sporulate ([/ontology/go/0030435/annotation/page/1 sporulation]), even under conditions thatbypass the dependence on early cAMP signaling pathways.Early developmental events of ''crtf''-null strainscan be rescued with exogenous cAMP treatment,constitutive expression of CAR1 or co-development withwild-type cells; however, these treatments are insufficientto promote sporulation. This suggests a cell-autonomousrole for CRTF during late development that is separatefrom its capacity to control ''carA'' expression ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11493573 Mu et al. 2001]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 28-MAY-2004 PG

DDB_G0269160.summary:
Annexins are evolutionarily conserved calcium/phospholipid binding proteins consisting of a core domain made up of tandem repeats, of approximately 70 residues. ''nxnA'' is homologous to human ANXA7, and encodes annexin VII, one of two annexin genes in the ''Dictyostelium'' genome. ''nxnA'' mRNA is expressed during both growth and development, with the level of ''nxnA'' mRNA increasing 5 fold during development and reaching a peak at approximately 16 hrs. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1832674 Doring et al. 1991]), ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1826615 Greenwood et al. 1991]), ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7862106 Bonfils et al. 1994]). Annexin VII (NxnA) localizes to the plasma membrane, cytoplasm and nucleus ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7657724 Doring et al. 1995]). Proteomic analyses reveal that NxnA also localizes to the phagosome ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16926386 Gotthardt et al. 2006]) and to Legionella-containing phagosomes ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19482547 Shevchuk et al. 2009]). Annexin VII binds to phosphatidylserine in a calcium ion-dependent manner ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1824843 Gerke et al. 1991]), ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7862106 Bonfils et al. 1994]). Annexin VII interacts with the calcium-binding proteins Cbp2 ([/gene/DDB_G0267456 cbp2]) and Alg-2 ([/gene/DDB_G0293530 pefB]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16762449 Marko et al. 2006]).
Annexin VII plays a role in cellular calcium ion homeostasis. On non-nutrient agar, development was delayed in ''nxnA'' null cells and a significant number of aggregates failed to form fruiting bodies. Growth, pinocytosis, phagocytosis, chemotaxis, and motility were not significantly affected when ''nxnA'' null cells were grown in axenic medium. However, when Ca2+ chelator EGTA was added to the growth medium to reduce Ca2+ concentration, ''nxnA'' cells were severely impaired in growth, motility and chemotaxis. Exocytosis of secreted enzymes was not significantly altered in EGTA-treated ''nxnA'' null cells compared with wt; however, the total amounts of these enzymes were lower in the mutant than in the wild type. These results suggest that annexin VII is not required for membrane fusion, but rather for cellular Ca2+ homeostasis. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7657724 Doring et al. 1995]). Annexin VII accumulates at cell membrane wound sites, and in ''nxnA'' cells, there is defective cell membrane wound repair suggesting a role for NxnA in this process ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29789591 Pervin et al. 2018]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 03-MAR-2021 RD

DDB_G0271738.summary: Gamma-tubulin is localized at the center of the microtubule aster where it forms a complex with Spc98 ([/gene/DDB_G0283909 spc98]) to nucleate polymerization of alpha/beta tubulin ([/gene/DDB_G0287689 tubA]), ([/gene/DDB_G0269196 tubB]) dimers [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9275182  (Ueda et al. 1997)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9427688  (Euteneuer et al. 1998)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12018385  (Daunderer and Graf, 2002)]. Microtubules radiate from centrosomes that are found ahead of the nucleus in migrating cells. The centrosome is repositioned shortly after the extension of a new pseudopod. If no reorientation occurs within 30 seconds of the extension, the pseudopod is retracted. Centrosomes appear to stabilize the direction of movement rather than establishing where the cell will go. The morphological changes in centrosomes were followed through the cell cycle by labelling the organelle with GFP fused to gamma-tubulin [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9880333  (Ueda et al. 1999)]. About 100 different proteins contribute to centrosomal functions including the products of ''tubC'', ([/gene/DDB_G0285849 spc97]), ([/gene/DDB_G0283909 spc98]), ([/gene/DDB_G0288427 cenA]), ([/gene/DDB_G0288375 lis1]), ([/gene/DDB_G0270814 nek2]), ([/gene/DDB_G0283607 eb1]), ([/gene/DDB_G0268616 cepJ]) and ([/gene/DDB_G0278809 cepG]). [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15548420  (Graf et al. 2004)]. The abundance of ''tubC'' mRNA is less than 2% that of tubA mRNA in growing cells but increases rapidly between 10 and 14 hours of development, mostly in prestalk cells [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25887420  (Rosengarten et al. 2015)]. ''tubC'' may have a critical role during culmination.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 17-NOV-2017 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0271736.summary: ''rabC'' encodes a guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G protein) of the Rab family of small GTPases. G proteins are key components of signal transduction networks in which they function as molecular signaling switches, binding to GDP in the off state while binding GTP in the on state. Guanine nucleotide-exchange factors (GEFs) promote the exchange of GDP for GTP on Rab GTPases thus activating them, while GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) inactivate Rab GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP. Northern analysis revealed that ''rabC'' is expressed at detectable levels in axenically growing cells, and that the expression level did not significantly change during development ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8294041 Bush et al. 1993]). Proteomic analysis revealed that RabC is found in lipid droplets ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24036346 Du, et al. 2013]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 16-DEC-2020 RD
