DDB_G0293918.summary: Telomerase reverse transcriptase is a ribonucleoprotein enzyme responsible for telomere maintenance in most eukaryotes. Dictyostelium ''tert'' shares 22% identity with human TERT, but contains a Poly A stretch within the catalytic domain that could impair enzymatic activity. The expression level of the ''tert'' gene appears to be extremely low (MacWilliams, pers. communication). A telomerase activity assay did not detect telomerase activity in cell extracts, and ''tert'' null cells displayed developmental defects suggesting a non-canonical role for Tert in ''Dictyostelium'' ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31237867 Nassir, et al. 2019]). Several genes involved in DNA recombination: ([/gene/DDB_G0292786 rad50]), ([/gene/DDB_G0273139 rad51-1]), ([/gene/DDB_G0273611 rad51-2]), ([/gene/DDB_G0288993 smc6]) and ([/gene/DDB_G0293546 mre11]) are upregulated in ''tert'' null cells, suggesting that a mechanism of telomere extension other than telomere elongation by telomerase may be used in ''Dictyostelium''. However, a putative telomerase activity was detected, and ''tert'' null strains have a modified telomere structure, indicating that ''tert'' is involved in telomere maintenance. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31550289 Rodriguez-Centeno, et al. 2019]). Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 24-SEP-2020 RD

The homeodomain is a sequence-specific DNA binding motif that consists of a helix-turn-helix. Homeobox-containing proteins have transcription factor activity. They have beenidentified in most if not all phyla of eukaryotes. Inmetazoans, homeobox-containing proteins are known to be involvedin regulating the anterior-posterior body plan and in thespecification of certain cell types and anterior-posteriorcompartments (see [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9486804 Han and Firtel 1998] and references therein). There are 14 predicted proteins that contain homeobox domains in ''Dictyostelium'':[/gene/DDB_G0275173 hbx2], [/gene/DDB_G0291075 warA], [/gene/DDB_G0291197 hbx3], [/gene/DDB_G0272967 hbx4], [/gene/DDB_G0273127 hbx5-1] (on the chromosome 2 duplication: [/gene/DDB_G0273645 hbx5-2]), [/gene/DDB_G0277505 hbx6], [/gene/DDB_G0278225 hbx7], [/gene/DDB_G0279257 hbx8], [/gene/DDB_G0280473 hbx9], [/gene/DDB_G0284293 hbx10], [/gene/DDB_G0295787 hbx11], [/gene/DDB_G0286733 hbx12], [/gene/DDB_G0288975 hbx13], and [/gene/DDB_G0289677 hbx14].
[http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25963254 Mishra and Saran 2015] performed a genome-wide classification and comparative genomic analysis of the 14 homeobox genes present in D. discoideum, and found that they could be classified into 3 groups: TALE, OTHER and NOVEL classes, ''hbx5'' belonging to the OTHER class.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 07-JUL-2015 RD

DDB_G0274455.summary: Besides ''mhcA'' ([/gene/DDB_G0286355 mhcA]) that encodes the classical myosin heavy chain, ''Dictyostelium'' carries genes for 12 unconventional myosins. The first 5 unconventional myosins ([/gene/DDB_G0280039 myoA]), ([/gene/DDB_G0289117 myoB]), ([/gene/DDB_G0276617 myoC]), ([/gene/DDB_G0275447 myoD]), ([/gene/DDB_G0288679 myoE]), were isolated from whole genome plasmid clones by low stringency probing with portions of the head region of ''mhcA''. The next 6 unconventional myosins ([/gene/DDB_G0289177 myoF]), ([/gene/DDB_G0276363 myoG]), ([/gene/DDB_G0289447 myoH]), ''myoI'', ([/gene/DDB_G0272112 myoJ]), ([/gene/DDB_G0274575 myoK]) were recognized in large YAC clones that represent the whole genome [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7937787  (Titus et al. 1994)]. ''myoI'' encodes a class VII unconventional myosin, MyoI, that is involved in phagocytosis [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7937787  (Titus et al. 1994)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10574761  (Titus, 1999)]. Like MyoG, there are two MyTH4 domains and a FERM domain in MyoI that can bind to both F-actin and microtubules [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21875595  (Moen et al. 2011)]. MyoI is enriched in filopods and phagocytic cups and is found at the leading edge of migrating cells [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11267868  (Tuxworth et al. 2001)]. MyoI appears to play a role in adhesion to particles as well as to the substratum through its direct interaction with talin A ([/gene/DDB_G0290481 talA]) [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16355532  (Titus, 2005)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15826949  (Tuxworth et al. 2005)]. ''myoI'' mRNA is relatively abundant throughout early development and only decreases after 11 hrs of development [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25887420  (Rosengarten et al. 2015)]. ''myoI'' is induced during early germination and plays a role in spore swelling [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15470238  (Xu et al. 2004)]. ''myoI'' null mutants have defects in spore germination, phagocytosis, filopodium formation and both cell-cell and cell-substrate adhesion. [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15470238  (Xu et al. 2004)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10574761  (Titus, 1999)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11267868  (Tuxworth et al. 2001)]. MyoI fails to target efficiently to the cell cortex in ''vasP'' ([/gene/DDB_G0289541 vasP]) null cells. The actin regulator VasP produces a cortical actin network at the leading-edge cortex that activates MyoI, and together, VasP and MyoI drive filopodia initiation by further bundling and polymerizing actin. (Arthur, et al 2021, PMID: 34042588).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 27-JAN-2022 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0273805.summary:
''ndkC'' encodes the cytosolic form of nucleoside diphosphate (NDP) kinase (EC 2.7.4.6). The related [/gene/DDB_G0279911 ndkM] gene encodes a mitochondrial NDP kinase ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8244981 Troll et al. 1993]). This enzyme is responsible for the phosphorylation of nucleoside or deoxynucleoside diphosphates into the corresponding triphosphates at the expense of ATP ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8931563 Deville-Bonne et al. 1996]). NDP kinase is transiently phosphorylated on an active site histidine as part of the catalytic process (see [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9786875 Schneider et al. 1998 and references therein]).
This enzyme plays a crucial role in equilibrating the cellular nucleotide pools (see [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9786875 Schneider et al. 1998 and references therein]). Besides this role in intermediate nucleotide metabolism, NDP kinase has been implicated in a large number of cellular functions. Part of the cellular NDP kinase is associated with the plasma membrane and stimulated by cell surface cAMP receptors. The GTP produced by the action of NDP kinase is capable of activating G-proteins as monitored by altered G-protein-receptor interaction and the activation of the effector enzyme phospholipase C ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8389692 Bominaar et al. 1993]). Nucleoside diphosphate kinase is also associated with the cytoskeleton where it channels ATP to the myosin molecule ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8816286 Aguado-Velasco et al. 1996]). Yet another role for NDP kinase is to feed GTP into the translation machinery, as inferred by its association with active ribosomes ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7733916 Sonnemann and Mutzel 1995]). Knock down of NDP kinase expression suppressed the phenotypic defects that are caused by AMPK ([/gene/DDB_G0277905 snfA]), hyperactivity resulting either from overexpression of AMP alpha T or from mitochondrial dysfunction. These included rescue of defects in slug phototaxis, fruiting body morphology and growth in a liquid medium. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21374069 Annesley et al. 2011]).
The X-ray structure of nucleoside diphosphate kinase (NDP kinase) from ''Dictyostelium discoideum'' has been determined ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1846924 Dumas et al. 1991], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7966307 Morera et al. 1994]). The protein is a hexamer with D3 symmetry. The X-ray structure of wild type and several mutants nucleoside diphosphate kinase bound to substrates, co-factors and inhibitors has also been determined (see [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12171931 Gallois-Montbrun et al. 2002], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11277918 Schneider et al. 2001], and references therein).
Nucleoside analogs are currently used in antiretrovirus therapies. The best known example is AZT, one of the first drugs to be used for the treatment of AIDS. However, only the triphosphate derivatives of these compounds act as substrates of the viral reverse transcriptase. Since these compounds cannot enter cells, nucleoside analogs are administered and phosphorylated by cellular kinases, including nucleoside diphosphate (NDP) kinase. Studies of the enzymatic mechanism of this enzyme provide essential information for the design of new nucleoside analogs with increased efficiency in antiretroviral therapies ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11768316 Schneider et al. 2000]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 16-JUN-2003 PG

DDB_G0280689.summary:
''tgrB1'' is a member of a family of genes with a high degree of natural polymorphism [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19285397 (Benabentos et al. 2009)]. ''tgrB1'' encodes a cell surface glycoprotein that acts in conjunction with TgrC1 ([/gene/DDB_G0280531 tgrC1]) to mediate post-aggregation EDTA-resistant cell-cell adhesion and kin recognition [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21700835 (Hirose et al. 2011]; [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23477311 Chen et al. 2013]; [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24490801 Chen et al. 2014)]. Signal transduction from TgrB1/TgrC1 regulates expression of post-aggregative genes and thereby synchronizes temporal aspects of differentiation [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16386729 (Iranfar et al. 2006]; [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21700835 Hirose et al. 2011)].
Independent isolates from nature show a high degree of polymorphism of TrgB1 and TgrC1. Cells with compatible TgrB1 / TgrC1 pairs form common aggregates but distant kin that express variants are excluded. This mechanism of kin recognition protects from potential cheaters that fail to make their fair share of stalk cells [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23910661 (Ho et al. 2013]; [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26018043 Ho and Shaulsky 2015)]. ''tgrB1'' and ''tgrC1'' are coordinately transcribed between 2 and 8 hours of development [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25887420 (Rosengarten et al. 2015)]. Transcriptome analysis of several ''tgrB1'' / ''tgrC1'' gene replacement strains revealed 68 differentially expressed genes at 8 hours and 85 genes at 12 hours development (only one gene differentially expressed at both time points). This underlines the necessity of allorecognition facilitating the transition to multicellularity during development [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26395484 (Hirose et al. 2015)]. TgrB1/TgrC1 mediated development but not allorecognition is regulated by N-glycosylation through Alg9 ([/gene/DDB_G0279349 alg9]), a putative mannosyl transferase [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26359303 (Li et al. 2015)]. Cells lacking all three adenylate cyclase genes ([/gene/DDB_G0281545 acaA], [/gene/DDB_G0267376 acrA], [/gene/DDB_G0274569 acgA]) and overexpressing PKA ([/gene/DDB_G0283907 pkaC], [/gene/DDB_G0279413 pkaR]) exhibited cell polarization, tissue formation and cooperation when mixed with allotype-compatible wild-type cells, but not with incompatible ''tgrB1''-/''tgrC1''-/QS31 cells, indicating that TgrB1/TgrC1-mediated allorecognition and tissue formation do not require cAMP production as long as PKA is active (Hirose, et al 2021, PMID: 34169317).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 10-June-2016 PF; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0276897.summary: The gene product encoded by [/gene/DDB_G0281663 aprA] is a secreted protein that exists in a 150 kDa protein complex. The AprA protein contains the PhoPQ-activated pathogenicity-related protein domain, which is thought to play a role in virulence of Salmonella. From its mutant phenotype,AprA functions in negative regulation of cell proliferation and is also clearly important for sporulation. Although it plays a role in cellproliferation, AprA does not have an effect on cell growth, as evidenced by an unchanged mass per number of cells in comparison to wild-type. Four proteins in the ''Dictyostelium'' genome are highly similar to AprA: [/gene/DDB_G0286625 DDB_G0286625], [/gene/DDB_G0277031 DDB_G0277031], [/gene/DDB_G0276897 DDB_G0276897], [/gene/DDB_G0282135 DDB_G0282135]([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16176950 Brock and Gomer 2005]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 06-FEB-2006 KP

DDB_G0272106.summary: ''arpB'' encodes the 44 kDa actin-related subunit of the Arp2/3 complex [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11807934  (Insall et al. 2001)]. The seven subunits of this 200 kDa complex are encoded by ([/gene/DDB_G0277825 arcA]), ([/gene/DDB_G0282813 arcB]), ([/gene/DDB_G0292804 arcC]), ([/gene/DDB_G0269102 arcD]), ([/gene/DDB_G0288319 arcE]), ''arpB'' and ([/gene/DDB_G0283755 arpC]). The subunits of mammalian Arp2/3 are very similar to their ''Dictyostelium'' homologs. Arp2/3 binds to the side of F-actin filaments and initiates polymerization of a new F-actin chain at an angle of 70 degrees leading to a branched actin network that can alter the shape of cells. The ability to nucleate new actin filaments is greatly stimulated by direct interactions with members of the WASP/SCAR family [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11807934  (Insall et al. 2001)]. The Arp2/3 complex largely mediates the actin polymerization response to chemotactic stimulation and contributes to cell motility, pseudopod extension and adhesion in Dictyostelium chemotaxis. The complete Arp2/3 complex is essential for growth; partial loss of activity of either ArcB or ArpB impairs growth and chemotaxis [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17553489  (Langridge and Kay, 2007)]. mRNA from each of the genes encoding Arp2/3 subunits accumulates coordinately to reach a peak at 3 hours of development and gradually decreases thereafter [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25887420  (Rosengarten et al. 2015)]. ArpB is also a component of polyphosphate kinase that forms an actin-like fiber concurrent with the synthesis of a poly-phosphate chain in acidocalcisomes [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15496465  (Gomez-Garcia et al. 2004)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19344251  (Rao et al. 2009)]. The Arp2/3 complex interacts with the protein CARMIL, which serves as a scaffold for the assembly of a larger complex of proteins involved in the nucleation and termination of actin filament assembly. The complex consists of CARMIL ([/gene/DDB_G0292386 carmil]), AcpA, ([/gene/DDB_G0267374 acpA]) AcpB, ([/gene/DDB_G0272104 acpB]) the Arp2/3 complex, and type I myosins MyoB ([/gene/DDB_G0289117 myoB]) and MyoC ([/gene/DDB_G0276617 myoC]) [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11425877  (Jung et al. 2001)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 10-JUN-2019 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis; annotation contributions PMID:23223240 Changhoon Choi

DDB_G0281561.summary: Disruption of ''tipA'' by REMI mutagenesis resulted in cells that aggregated normally but were blocked at the mound ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9169048 Stege et al. 1997)]. The gene encodes a prestalk enriched protein that has a conserved PP 2C domain also found in protein phosphatases but is otherwise unrelated to previously characterized proteins. Prestalk cells differentiate in tipA- aggregates but fail to sort out to form an apical tip. They remain as small clumps scattered throughout the mounds. TipA appears to be responsible for cell autonomous sorting of the initial cell types.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 12-MAY-2016 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0272590.summary: Nascent proteins that contain a signal peptide, and are therefore secreted, are recognized by the[/ontology/go/0005786/annotation/page/1 signal recognition particle, endoplasmic reticulum targeting] (SRP), which is composed of 7S RNA plus [/gene/DDB_G0267622 srp9], [/gene/DDB_G0272590 srp14-1],[/gene/DDB_G0275211 srp19], [/gene/DDB_G0275455 srp54], [/gene/DDB_G0285821 srp68], and [/gene/DDB_G0291412 srp72]. The SRPcontains two domains: the Alu domain (SRP9/14) functions to arrest translational elongation and the Sdomain (SRP54, SRP19, and SRP68/72) plays a role in ribosome-nascent chain (RNC) recognition and SRP receptorbinding. After the RNC is bound, the SRP binds via SRP54 to the SRP receptor, an alpha/beta heterodimermade up of [/gene/DDB_G0277377 srpR] and [/gene/DDB_G0278543 srpRB] in the [/ontology/go/0005783/annotation/page/1 endoplasmic reticulum] (reviewed in [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15718142 Halic and Beckmann 2005] and [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16092520 Pool2005]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 17-NOV-2005 KP

DDB_G0269252.summary:
''gefE'' encodes a Ras guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF, RasGEF). rasGEFs are key components of signaling networks in which they activate Ras family small GTPases by promoting the exchange of GDP for GTP. The level of activated RasD ([/gene/DDB_G0292996 rasD]) is significantly lower in ''gefE'' null mutant cells, indicating that GefE has GEF activity towards RasD ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24282234 Chattwood et al. 2013)].
RasD and GefE together regulate phototaxis, thermotaxis and cell fate bias. ''gefE'' null mutant slugs are defective in both thermotaxis and phototaxis, migrating similar distances as wild type, but far less accurately towards the light source ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16086850 Wilkins et al. 2005)], similar to the phenotype of ''rasD'' null mutants ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10837033 Wilkins et al. 2000)]. To investigate the molecular basis of lineage priming and how it leads to reproducible cell type proportioning ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24282234 Chattwood et al. 2013) ] employed a genetic screen and identified two bias genes, ''gefE'' and ''rasD''. ''gefE'' null mutants formed more spores than wt cells, and in chimeric slugs labelled mutants are enriched in the prespore region, while cells expressing higher levels of GefE are found in prestalk regions of the slug. ''gefE'' null mutants are also less sensitive to DIF than wt ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24282234 Chattwood et al. 2013)]. ''rasD'' mutants exhibit similar phenotypes: ''rasD'' null cells exhibit a spore bias in chimeric mixtures with wild type cells, while constitutively active ''rasD'' cells exhibit a strong stalk bias ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30473004 Gruenheit et al. 2018)]. Expression of GefE is required to activate RasD in a subset of cells, which in turn sets the threshold at which these cells respond to the pstB/pstO differentiation inducer DIF, indicating that GefE acts through ''rasD'' to promote prestalk cell fate choice. Although ''gefE'' expression is uniform in all cells during growth, transcription of ''rasD'' is both heterogeneous and dynamic, thus providing a novel mechanism for heterogeneity generation and position-independent differentiation ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24282234 Chattwood et al. 2013)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30473004 Gruenheit et al. 2018)]. The confinement of Ras activation to the membrane region at the source of cAMP stimulus is abolished in both ''gefD'' ([/gene/DDB_G0289667 gefD]) and ''gefE'' null mutants, suggesting that ''gefD'' and ''gefE'' contribute to restrict activation of Ras to the front of chemotaxing cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23886948 Kortholt et al. 2013]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 30-MAR-2021 RD

DDB_G0291982.summary: The psi factor (prespore-inducing factor) is a secreted factor that has the ability to induce pre-spore cell differentiation under the appropriate conditions. The psi factor is a glycoprotein with an apparent molecular mass of 106 kDa, and with a predicted molecular mass of 60 kDA for the mature secreted protein. The ''psiA'' gene is maximally expressed at the loose mound stage. ''psiA'' knockout mutant strains develop normally; however, conditioned medium from these mutants shows reduced prespore-cell-inducing activity and reduced prespore cell division-inducing activity, suggesting that PsiA plays a role in the positive regulation of spore cell differentiation ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15367206 Kawata et al. 2004]). The ''psiA'' gene is highly expressed in scattered cells at the mound stage and in prespore cells at the onset of culmination. During development, ''psiA'' overexpression delayed expression of the prestalk-specific gene ''ecmB'' ([/gene/DDB_G0269132 ecmB]), while ''ecmB'' was expressed precociously in ''psiA'' null cells. In addition, ''psiA'' overexpression inhibited DIF-1-induced stalk formation in monolayer cultures, indicating that PsiA is also involved in prestalk cell differentiation ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20500764 Yamada et al. 2010]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 19-NOV-2020 RD

DDB_G0291081.summary:
The [/gene/DDB_G0291081 pefA] and [/gene/DDB_G0293530 pefB] genes were identified as homologs of mammalian ALG-2 (apoptosis-linked gene 2), which is involved in programmed cell death, as its name suggests. The pefA and pefB proteins eachcontain five calcium-binding ([/ontology/go/0005509/annotation/page/1 calcium ion binding]) EF hand motifs ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11481037 Ohkouchi et al.2001], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11927596 Aubry et al. 2002]).
Expression of ''pefA'' mRNA is developmentally regulated, however, two separate Northern blot experiments show differentpatterns of expression. [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11481037 Ohkouchi and colleagues (2001)] show that ''pefA'' expressionis low during growth and gradually increases through the developmental program, whereas [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11927596 Aubry et al.(2002)] report a peak in ''pefA'' expression at 4 hours followed by a rapid decline. PefA has been shown tolocalize intracellularly to the cytoplasm ([/ontology/go/0005737/annotation/page/1 cytoplasm]) and, in the presence of calcium, to the membrane fraction ([/ontology/go/0005624/annotation/page/1 membrane fraction]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11481037 Ohkouchi et al. 2001], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11927596 Aubry et al.2002]). Additionally, in situ hybridization analysis of ''pefA'' shows expression in the posterior presporeregion ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11481037 Ohkouchi et al. 2001]).
In surface plasmon resonance experiments, [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11927596 Aubry and colleagues (2002)] demonstrate thatPefA is capable of dimerizing with itself ([/ontology/go/0042803/annotation/page/1 protein homodimerization activity]), PefB ([/ontology/go/0046982/annotation/page/1 protein heterodimerization activity]), and with murine Alix (ALG-2 interacting protein X, homolog of ''Dictyostelium'' [/gene/DDB_G0275451 alxA]). PefB, on the other hand, heterodimerizes ([/ontology/go/0046982/annotation/page/1 protein heterodimerization activity]) with PefA but fails to dimerize with murineAlix. Additionally, they show that null mutants of both '' pefA'' and ''pefB'' and double mutants ''pefA-''/''pefB-'' have no detectable developmental phenotype.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 08-SEP-2004 KP

DDB_G0275173.summary:
Two homeobox-containing proteins have been cloned and analyzed in ''Dictyostelium'', [/gene/DDB_G0291075 warA] and [/gene/DDB_G0275173 hbx2]. Their expression is developmentally regulatedstarting at the mound stage in response to cAMP and require the transcription factor [/gene/DDB_G0288755 gbfA].
''hbx2'' null mutants are morphologically indistinguishable from wild type cells. The double ''warA/hbx2'' knock out has a phenotype similar to the ''warA'' null mutant, with a slightly enhanced morphological phenotype. Many of the multicellular structures formed arrest at the mound stage,while the remainder proceed through development and form fruiting bodies with anenlarged basal disc and lower portion of the stalk, suggestingthere is an increase in the number of basal disc and stalk cells. This is supported by the observation that the pstO region of ''warA'' null cells is about twice the size of that of wild type cells, with a corresponding decrease in the proportion of prespore cells [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9486804 (Han and Firtel 1998)].
The homeodomain is a sequence-specific DNA binding motif that consists of a helix-turn-helix. Homeobox-containing proteins have transcription factor activity. They have beenidentified in most if not all phyla of eukaryotes. Inmetazoans, homeobox-containing proteins are known to be involvedin regulating the anterior-posterior body plan and in thespecification of certain cell types and anterior-posteriorcompartments (see [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9486804 Han and Firtel 1998] and references therein). There are 14 predicted proteins that contain homeobox domains in ''Dictyostelium'':[/gene/DDB_G0275173 hbx2], [/gene/DDB_G0291075 warA], [/gene/DDB_G0291197 hbx3], [/gene/DDB_G0272967 hbx4], [/gene/DDB_G0273127 hbx5-1] (on the chromosome 2 duplication: [/gene/DDB_G0273645 hbx5-2]), [/gene/DDB_G0277505 hbx6], [/gene/DDB_G0278225 hbx7], [/gene/DDB_G0279257 hbx8], [/gene/DDB_G0280473 hbx9], [/gene/DDB_G0284293 hbx10], [/gene/DDB_G0295787 hbx11], [/gene/DDB_G0286733 hbx12], [/gene/DDB_G0288975 hbx13], and [/gene/DDB_G0289677 hbx14].
[http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25963254 Mishra and Saran 2015] performed a genome-wide classification and comparative genomic analysis of the 14 homeobox genes present in D. discoideum, and found that they could be classified into 3 groups: TALE, OTHER and NOVEL classes, with ''hbx2'' belonging to the OTHER class. Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 07-JUL-2015 RD

DDB_G0279483.summary:
Phospholipase D hydrolyzes the membrane phospholipid phosphatidylcholine, producing choline and a phosphatidate. Three orthologs of mammalian phospholipase D1 (PLD1) are present in ''Dictyostelium'': ([/gene/DDB_G0281031 pldA]), ''pldB'' and ([/gene/DDB_G0277949 pldC]).
The ''pldB'' transcript first appears at the onset of development, peaking around 20 hr. Deletion of the ''pldB'' gene results in cells that are unable to sense cell density and aggregate at low cell concentrations. Conversely, cells over-expressing ''pldB'' do not aggregate, even at high cell densities. Additionally, ''pldB'' null cells develop precociously in submerged culture and on filter pads ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15821129 Chen et al. 2005]). PldB regulates chemotaxis and cell sorting, and was also found to mediate CMF-dependent quorum sensing by regulating G protein signaling ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20950684 Ray et al. 2011]). PldB and ([/gene/DDB_G0274109 paxB]) functionally interact to regulate the organization of the actin cytoskeleton ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21531871 Pribic et al. 2011]). The protein kinase ''pkcA'' ([/gene/DDB_G0288147 pkcA]) positively regulates phospholipase D activity, and PkcA and PldB functionally interact to regulate aggregation, differentiation, and cell-cell adhesion during development. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28257811 Singh et al. 2017)]Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 09-MAY-2017 RD

DDB_G0283757.summary:
''rab1A'' encodes a guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G protein) of the Rab family of small GTPases. G proteins are key components of signal transduction networks in which they function as molecular signaling switches, binding to GDP in the off state while binding GTP in the on state. Guanine nucleotide-exchange factors (GEFs) promote the exchange of GDP for GTP on Rab GTPases thus activating them, while GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) inactivate Rab GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP. Rab1A binds to the leucine-rich repeat kinase Roco2 ([/gene/DDB_G0273259 qkgA-1]), ([/gene/DDB_G0273635 qkgA-2]) which serves as a downstream effector of Rab1A ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21551065 Kicka et al. 2011]). ''rab1A'' is expressed at detectable levels in growing cells and expression remains constant at approximately the same level during development ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8294041 Bush et al. 1993]). Rab1A localizes to the pseudopodium ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21551065 Kicka et al. 2011]) and the Legionella-containing vacuole [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18980612 (Urwyler et al. 2009)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29602783 (Welin et al. 2018)]. Rab1A is highly similar to human Rab1A and Rab1B, which are key regulators of intracellular membrane trafficking.
''rab1A'' is involved in a signaling pathway that controls the actin cytoskeleton and pseudopod extension, and thereby, cell polarity and motility. Roco2 is activated in response to chemoattractant stimulation, localizes to the pseudopodium, and binds to both Rab1A and filamin ([/gene/DDB_G0269100 abpC]). Constitutively active Rab1A pulls down 5 x more Roco2 than wild type Rab1A while dominant-negative Rab1A fails to interact with it, suggesting that activated Rab1A positively regulates Roco2 activity. Both Roco2 null mutants and dominant-negative Rab1A cells have defects in chemotaxis to cAMP and aberrant chemoattractant-mediated F-actin polymerization, and constitutively active Rab1A cells produce extended pseudopodia and make an increased number of turns during chemotaxis. These results reveal a signal transduction pathway in which Rab1A activates Roco2 kinase which in turn mediates cell polarization and chemotaxis by regulating cortical F-actin polymerization and pseudopod extension. Filamin serves as a downstream effector of Roco2 to control pseudopod extension ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21551065 Kicka et al. 2011]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 26-AUG-2020 RD

DDB_G0275293.summary:
Using an apoaequorin expressing strain, Ludlow ''et al.'' showed that ''Dictyostelium'' posseses P2X receptors that facilitate rapid Ca2+ influx in response to extracellular ATP and ADP. Deleting [/gene/DDB_G0272004 p2xA] or [/gene/DDB_G0288061 p2xE] did not influence this behavior, suggesting these genes are not involved. However, this study proposes possible roles for [/gene/DDB_G0275293 p2xB], [/gene/DDB_G0275191 p2xC], or [/gene/DDB_G0288335 p2xD] [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18486207 (Ludlow et al. 2008)].
Most recently, Ludlow ''et al.'' showed that p2xB and p2xE, as well as p2xA, have ATP-gated channel activity when expressed in ''Xenopus'' oocytes. However, Na+ rather inhibited this activity to various degrees in these P2x channels, but K+, and NH4+ ions elicited a large response. Interestingly, p2xA and p2xB, but not p2xE are permeable to Cl- ions. No such ATP-gated channel activity was found for p2xC and p2xD. All ''Dictyostelium'' P2x proteins localize to the [/ontology/go/0031164/annotation/page/1 contractile vacuolar membrane], and not to the plasma membrane like P2X receptors from other organisms. By using a protease protection assay on tagged receptors the authors demonstrated that the transmembrane loop region containing the agonist (ATP) binding site lies within the lumen of the vacuole. A quintuple p2xA/B/C/D/E null mutant in wild type background AX2 shows a reduced response to the calmodulin inhibitor calmidazolium, suggesting a role of the ''Dictyostelium'' proteins in the [/ontology/go/0050848/annotation/page/1 regulation of calcium-mediated signaling]. The quintuple null mutant also shows a slight delay in its [/ontology/go/0006971/annotation/page/1 hypotonic response] when placed in water, however, single mutants in a AX2 background do not show any osmoregulatory defect. Taken together, this study suggests that it is still unclear which molecules are responsible for the extracellular purinergic response in ''Dictyostelium'' and it raises the possibility that the P2x receptors may play a role in the release of intracellular Ca 2+ stores in response to an ATP stimulus from within the contractile vacuole [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19833731 (Ludlow et al. 2009)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 11-MAR-2010 PF

DDB_G0277215.summary: Isopentenyltransferase catalyzes the condensation of isopentenyl pyrophosphate with AMP, ADP or ATP ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7363945 Ihara et al. 1980)]. After dephosphorylation, the ribose moiety is removed to generate the cytokinin isopentenyl adenine that can be further modified to make the germination inhibitor, discadenine ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/566219 Taya et al. 1978)]. Isopentenyl adenine is also generated by post-transcriptional addition of an isopentenyl group to adenosine groups in tRNA. ''iptA'' encodes the condensing enzyme while iptB ([/gene/DDB_G0291528 iptB]) and iptC ([/gene/DDB_G0273039 iptC-1]), ([/gene/DDB_G0274017 iptC-2]) encode homologs of transferases that modify tRNA ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18216168 Anjard and Loomis et al. 2008)]. Mutants lacking IptA have less than 10% of the wild type level of isopentenyl adenine or discadenine during culmination and sporulate poorly. The phenotype is non-cell autonomous as expected from the ability of secreted cytokinins to induce sporulation. Cellular responses to cytokinins depend on a two component system that includes the adenylyl cyclase with a receiver domain, ACR, ([/gene/DDB_G0267376 acrA]) and the histidine kinase, DhkB, ([/gene/DDB_G0277845 dhkB]) but not the H2 intermediate, RdeA ([/gene/DDB_G0282923 rdeA]). It appears that cytokinins activate adenylyl cyclase activity by direct phosphorelay from DhkB to ACR ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18216168 Anjard and Loomis et al. 2008)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 20-JAN-2017 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0276883.summary: The catalytic subunit of calcineurin is encoded by ''canA''. The primary sequence of this calcium/calmodulin dependent protein phosphatase is very similar to the sequences of calcineurin A in mammals [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8735922  (Malchow et al. 1996)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8681950  (Dammann et al. 1996)]. In the absence of calcium, calcineurin A forms inactive heterodimers with the regulatory subunit calcineurin B ([/gene/DDB_G0267446 cnbA]) that are converted to active heterotetramers when they bind Ca++/calmodulin [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25518940  (Sugden et al. 2014)]. RNA-seq studies have shown that canA and cnbA are coordinately expressed during early aggregation and reach a peak at 11 hrs of development [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25887420  (Rosengarten et al. 2015)]. Inhibition of the enzyme activity by cyclosporin A has little effect on growth or aggregation but results in reduced expression of prestalk and prespore specific genes [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8855370  (Horn and Gross, 1996)]. Inhibition of calcineurin activity with the polyphenolic aldehyde, gossypol, reduces the rate of growth and the number of aggregates formed after 24 hrs of development [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15621416  (Weissenmayer et al. 2005)]. cAMP relay is inhibited within 10 minutes of addition of 10 microM gossypol. Gossypol also stimulates nuclear translocation of the prestalk transcription factor DimB ([/gene/DDB_G0291372 dimB]) within a few minutes and blocks nuclear translocation of the transcription factor TacA ([/gene/DDB_G0291342 tacA]) in response to calcium indicating that calcineurin mediates these responses [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22944283  (Thewes et al. 2012)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25518940  (Sugden et al. 2014)]. Cells lacking calcineurin as the result of expression of RNAi for either ''canA'' or ''cnbA'' form a reduced number of fruiting bodies with short stalks [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16512895  (Boeckeler et al. 2006)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23686520  (Thewes et al. 2013)]. These mutant strains are also hypersensitive to high levels of cations showing that calcineurin is responsible for stress responses as in other organisms.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 22-MAR-2018 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis; annotation contributions PMID:23686520 Sascha Thewes

DDB_G0290483.summary: The ABC superfamily of genes is one of the largest in the genomes of both bacteria and eukaryotes. The proteins encoded by these genes all carry a characteristic 200- to 250-amino-acid ATP-binding cassette that gives them their family name. In bacteria they are mostly involved in nutrient import, while in eukaryotes many are involved in export. Seven different families (A to G) have been defined in eukaryotes based on sequence homology, domain topology, and function. ''Dictyostelium'' has 71 ABC transporters (including one on the chromosome 2 duplication) and a single ABCE family member. The ABCE family is characterized by the presence of a conserved ferredoxin motif (pfam00037) at the N terminus, a motif found in nucleic acid binding proteins. They contain two ABC domains but no transmembrane domains and so are unlikely to act as transporters. In animals, ABCE protein has been shown to inhibit RNase L, the double-stranded RNA nuclease, and is referred to as RLi [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6420574  (Anjard and Loomis 2002)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 19-SEP-2003 PG

DDB_G0274137.summary:
There are 29 genes encoding actin in ''Dictyostelium'' with amino acid identity greater than 83%, ''act1''-''act29''. Seventeen of these genes encode identical proteins: [/gene/DDB_G0289553 act1], [/gene/DDB_G0274133 act2], [/gene/DDB_G0289005 act4], [/gene/DDB_G0289663 act5], [/gene/DDB_G0274135 act6], [/gene/DDB_G0280545 act7], [/gene/DDB_G0269234 act8], [/gene/DDB_G0274601 act9], [/gene/DDB_G0288879 act11], [/gene/DDB_G0274129 act12], [/gene/DDB_G0274599 act13], [/gene/DDB_G0274137 act14], [/gene/DDB_G0272520 act15], [/gene/DDB_G0272248 act16], [/gene/DDB_G0274727 act19], [/gene/DDB_G0274285 act20], and [/gene/DDB_G0274561 act21], while [/gene/DDB_G0289811 act10], [/gene/DDB_G0275023 act22], and [/gene/DDB_G0289487 act3] respectively have 1, 4 and 11 amino acid differences compared to the 17 identical genes. The proteins encoded by [/gene/DDB_G0274131 act17], [/gene/DDB_G0289489 act18], [/gene/DDB_G0268744 act23] and [/gene/DDB_G0289505 act24]are more divergent.
Actin is a major [/ontology/go/0005200/annotation/page/1 structural constituent of cytoskeleton]. Actin is one of the most abundant proteins in ''Dictyostelium'', constituting approximately 8% of the total protein in vegetative cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/561722 Alton and Lodish et al. 1977]).Actin synthesis is developmentally regulated, peaking shortly after starvation (reviewed by [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6894564 Firtel] in 1981). The different actin genes differ in their levels of expression, with [/gene/DDB_G0274135 act6], [/gene/DDB_G0269234 act8] and [/gene/DDB_G0274129 act12] being highly expressed both during growth and development compared to [/gene/DDB_G0289005 act4], [/gene/DDB_G0289663 act5], [/gene/DDB_G0280545 act7] and [/gene/DDB_G0272248 act16] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6286214 McKeown and Firtel 1981]). Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 19-SEP-2003 PG

DNA-dependent RNA polymerase catalyzes the transcription of DNA into RNA using the four ribonucleoside triphosphates as substrates ([/ontology/go/0003899/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase activity]). Three distinct zinc-containing RNA polymerases are found in eukaryotic nuclei: [/gene/DDB_G0275759 rpa1] for the ribosomal RNA precursor ([/ontology/go/0006360/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase I promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005736/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase I complex]), [/gene/DDB_G0279193 rpb1] for the mRNA precursor ([/ontology/go/0006366/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase II promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005665/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase II, core complex]), and [/gene/DDB_G0277199 rpc1] for 5S and tRNA genes ([/ontology/go/0006383/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase III promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005666/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase III complex]).
RNA polymerase II is composed of 12 subunits: [/gene/DDB_G0279193 rpb1], [/gene/DDB_G0288257 rpb2], [/gene/DDB_G0292244 rpb3], [/gene/DDB_G0282739 rpb4], [/gene/DDB_G0291636 rpb5], [/gene/DDB_G0291037 rpb6], [/gene/DDB_G0284891 rpb7], [/gene/DDB_G0278039 rpb8], [/gene/DDB_G0268306 rpb9], [/gene/DDB_G0272036 rpb10], [/gene/DDB_G0277677 rpb11], and[/gene/DDB_G0283365 rpb12]. Subunits 5, 6, 8, 10, and 12 are common to all threeRNA polymerases (reviewed by [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9618449 Hampsey] in 1998).

DDB_G0269132.summary:
The ''ecmB'' gene encodes an extracellular matrix protein that is a structural component of the stalk tube([/ontology/go/0005201/annotation/page/1 extracellular matrix structural constituent]), ([/ontology/go/0030198/annotation/page/1 extracellular matrix organization and biogenesis]), ([/ontology/go/0005578/annotation/page/1 proteinaceous extracellular matrix]) . [/gene/DDB_G0277853 ecmA], ''ecmB'', and [/gene/DDB_G0294473 staA] were isolated as prestalk-specific, DIF-inducible genes. ''ecmB'' null cells undergo apparently normal development, suggesting a functional redundancy between [/gene/DDB_G0277853 ecmA] and ''ecmB'' [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8200481 (Morrison et al. 1994)].
Differential expression of ''ecmA'' and ''ecmB'' in the anterior zone has led to the identification of several different prestalk cell types: the pstA cells, located at the anterior-most region of the prestalk zone and characterized by high expression of the ''ecmA'' gene directed by the proximal part of its promoter (''ecmA'' promoter), the pstAB cells, forming a cone-shaped area of the prestalk zone that occupies a core among the pstA region in which cells express both the ecmA and ecmB genes, and the pstO cells, located posterior to the pstA zone and characterized by low expression of the ''ecmA'' gene directed by the distal part of its promoter (ecmO promoter) (reviewed by [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8016318 Williams and Morrison] in 1994). Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 23-OCT-2003 PG

DDB_G0272833.summary: Three closely related genes, gene ''[/gene/DDB_G0272833 csbA]'', gene ''[/gene/DDB_G0272562 csbB]'' and gene ''[/gene/DDB_G0272756 csbC]'', encode 12 kDa proteins that form contact site B which functions in cell-cell adhesion during early development [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8626027  (Xu et al., 1996)]. Early adhesion can be blocked by 10 mM EDTA and is mediated by contact site B [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8626027  (Xu et al., 1996)]. Early adhesion can be blocked by 10 mM EDTA and is mediated by contact site B [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/5002049  (Gerisch, 1968]; [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/4993098  Beug, et al.1970)]. Early adhesion can also be blocked by antibodies to a glycoprotein, gp24, encoded by gene ''[/gene/DDB_G0285793 cadA]''cadA [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3569662  (Knecht et al., 1987]; [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8663243  Wong et al., 1996)]. Antibodies to gp24 recognize the fusion protein generated by a lamda gt11 expression construct carrying a portion of the ''csbA'' cDNA [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3149564  (Loomis, 1988)]. Deletion of all 3 ''csb'' genes delayed the appearance of EDTA-resistant adhesion by 6 hours [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8626027  (Xu et al., 1996)]. Expression of ''csbA'' and ''csbB'' is stimulated about 3 fold by cAMP during early development, increases to about 24-fold during aggregation and slowly falls after the slug stage to 3-fold at full culmination compared to vegetative cells [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25887420  (Rosengarten et al., 2015)]. DDB_G0283349.summary: G proteins are evolutionarily conserved heterotrimeric GTP binding proteins that can act as molecular switches. ''gpaA'' encodes G-alpha 1, one of the dozen alpha subunits that associate with the unique G-beta and G-gamma subunits ([/gene/DDB_G0277143 gpbA], [/gene/DDB_G0274125 gpgA]) [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2500658  (Pupillo et al. 1989)]. G-alpha 1 expression is cell-type-specific, being preferentially expressed in the anterior prestalk AB cells and anterior-like cells. Cells lacking G-alpha 1 grow and develop reasonably well although they tend to make fruiting bodies with elongated stalks. Strains overexpressing G-alpha 1 culminate abnormally with an aberrant stalk differentiation suggesting that G-alpha 1-mediated signaling pathways play an essential role in regulating development by controlling prestalk morphogenesis [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1670774  (Kumagai et al. 1991)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7821221  (Dharmawardhane et al. 1994)]. Several lines of evidence indicate that G-alpha 1 plays a role in regulating the activity of phospholipase C ([/gene/DDB_G0292736 plc]) during early development, most likely in conjunction with an unknown receptor [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8280098  (Bominaar and van Haastert, 1994)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9525920  (Brazill et al. 1998)]. Later in development, G-alpha 1 plays a role in the signal transduction pathway by which the polyketide 4-methyl-5-pentylbenzene-1,3 diol (MPBD) stimulates production of the phosphopeptide signaling molecule, spore differentiation factor 1 (SDF-1) [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21602484  (Anjard et al. 2011)]. The surface receptor for MPBD is CrlA ([/gene/DDB_G0280983 crlA]), a GPCR similar to the cAMP receptor CAR1 ([/gene/DDB_G0273397 carA-1], [/gene/DDB_G0273533 carA-2]). It appears to be coupled to a trimeric G protein containing the G-alpha 1 subunit. After exchange of GTP for GDP on G-alpha 1, the protein kinase GskA ([/gene/DDB_G0272110 gskA]) is either directly or indirectly inhibited [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21602484  (Anjard et al. 2011)]. When GskA is inhibited, the SDF-1 precursor can be released to generate SDF-1 in the surrounding fluid.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 18-APR-2019 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0268402.summary: ''rab24'' encodes a putative guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G protein) of the Rab family of small GTPases. G proteins are key components of signal transduction networks in which they function as molecular signaling switches, binding to GDP in the off state while binding GTP in the on state. Guanine nucleotide-exchange factors (GEFs) promote the exchange of GDP for GTP on Rab GTPases thus activating them, while GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) inactivate Rab GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP. Rab24 is similar to human RAB24, which has low GTPase activity due to lack of a conserved glutamine in a nucleotide binding region. ''Dictyostelium'' Rab24 also lacks a glutamine residue at the corresponding position suggesting that it may also have low intrinsic GTPase activity.  Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 01-OCT-2020 RD

DDB_G0293434.summary:
''rasG'' encodes a G protein of the Ras family of small GTPases. G proteins are key components of signal transduction networks in which they function as molecular signaling switches, binding to GDP in the off state while binding GTP in the on state. Guanine nucleotide-exchange factors (GEFs, rasGEFs) promote the exchange of GDP for GTP on Ras GTPases thus activating them, while GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs, rasGAPs) inactivate Ras GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP. RasG activation is reduced in ''gefR'' ([/gene/DDB_G0274605 gefR]) and ''gflB'' ([/gene/DDB_G0286773 gflB]) null mutant strains, indicating that these rasGEFs activate rasG. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17380187 Kae et al. 2007)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/27009206 Senoo et al. 2016)]. In addition, rasGEF GefF ([/gene/DDB_G0293006 gefF]) is also reported to activate RasG ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30967009 Williams et al. 2019)]. At least three RasGAPs inactivate ''rasG'': DdNF1 ([/gene/DDB_G0271750 nfaA]), C2GAP1 ([/gene/DDB_G0278483 ngap]) and IqgC ([/gene/DDB_G0288977 iqgC]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18948008 Zhang et al. 2008)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29109256 Xu et al. 2017)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30622175 Marinovic et al. 2019)]. ''rasG'' is expressed only during growth and early development, although a quantity of the RasG protein is present throughout development ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2644652 Robbins et al. 1989]), ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2154684 Khosla et al. 1990]), ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10837033 Wilkins et al. 2000]). ''rasG'' is activated by cAMP, and this activation does not occur in a number of cAMP signaling mutants. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15143344 Kae et al. 2004)].
RasG, either alone or in combination with other Ras proteins, is involved in mediating chemotaxis to cAMP, PI3K signaling, cytokinesis, and macropinocytosis. ''rasG'' null cells are multinucleate and display a wide range of defects in control of the actin cytoskeleton, including defective cell movement, loss of cell polarity, absence of normal lamellipodia, formation of unusual polymerized actin structures and abnormally long filopodia. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9245789 Tuxworth et al. 1997]). ''rasG'' null mutants display decreased PKB ([/gene/DDB_G0268620 pkbA]) activation, decreased cell polarity and decreased F-actin polymerization ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15534002 Sasaki et al. 2004)]. ''rasG'' null cells also have a defect in fluid uptake ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/27960076 Veltman et al. 2016)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30967009 Williams et al. 2019)]. Cells overexpressing an activated form of RasG fail to aggregate ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8754814 Khosla et al. 1996]).
RasG and RasC ([/gene/DDB_G0281385 rasC]) are critical mediators of the chemotactic response to cAMP with some overlap of function between the two genes. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16885420 Bolourani et al. 2006)]. RasG controls cAMP-mediated chemotaxis in part by regulating the activation of phosphoinositol 3-kinase (PI3Ks) and controlling the site of F-actin polymerization and the direction of migration. A feedback loop, mediated through localized F-actin polymerization, recruits cytosolic PI3K to the leading edge to amplify the chemotactic signal. RasG also regulates the plasma membrane recruitment and activation of downstream effectors including Akt/PKB. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16885420 Bolourani et al. 2006)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15534002 Sasaki et al. 2004)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18948008 Zhang et al. 2008)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29626371 Baumgardner et al. 2018)]. The RasGAPs ''nfaA'' and ''ngap'' act as regulators of RasG chemotactic signaling ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18948008 Zhang et al. 2008)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29109256 Xu et al. 2017)]. RasG and RasB ([/gene/DDB_G0292998 rasB]) regulate cytokinesis through the protein kinase NdrC ([/gene/DDB_G0284839 ndrC]). NdrC binds both RasG and RasB, and ''ndrC'' null cells display both a cytokinesis defect and increased levels of activated RasB and RasG. The multinucleate phenotype of ''rasG'' cells suggests a role for RasG in activating NdrC ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24986648 Mueller-Taubenberger et al. 2014)]. RasG and RasS ([/gene/DDB_G0283537 rasS]) are the most important Ras proteins involved in the regulation of macropinocytosis. The rasGEF GefF activates ''rasG'', and a ''gefF'' knock-in mutant also displays defects in fluid uptake, suggesting that it is involved in regulation of macropinocytosis through activation of ''rasG'' ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23843627 Hoeller et al. 2013)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/27960076 Veltman et al. 2016)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30967009 Williams et al. 2019)], while the RasGAP IqgC binds RasG and acts as a negative regulator of macropinocytosis ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30622175 Marinovic et al. 2019)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 30-JAN-2020 RD; annotation contributions: PMID:24742374 Alex Chattwood

DDB_G0289487.summary:
There are 29 genes encoding actin in ''Dictyostelium'' with amino acid identity greater than 83%, ''act1''-''act29''. Seventeen of these genes encode identical proteins: [/gene/DDB_G0289553 act1], [/gene/DDB_G0274133 act2], [/gene/DDB_G0289005 act4], [/gene/DDB_G0289663 act5], [/gene/DDB_G0274135 act6], [/gene/DDB_G0280545 act7], [/gene/DDB_G0269234 act8], [/gene/DDB_G0274601 act9], [/gene/DDB_G0288879 act11], [/gene/DDB_G0274129 act12], [/gene/DDB_G0274599 act13], [/gene/DDB_G0274137 act14], [/gene/DDB_G0272520 act15], [/gene/DDB_G0272248 act16], [/gene/DDB_G0274727 act19], [/gene/DDB_G0274285 act20], and [/gene/DDB_G0274561 act21], while [/gene/DDB_G0289811 act10], [/gene/DDB_G0275023 act22], and [/gene/DDB_G0289487 act3] respectively have 1, 4 and 11 amino acid differences compared to the 17 identical genes. The proteins encoded by [/gene/DDB_G0274131 act17], [/gene/DDB_G0289489 act18], [/gene/DDB_G0268744 act23] and [/gene/DDB_G0289505 act24]are more divergent.
Actin is a major [/ontology/go/0005200/annotation/page/1 structural constituent of cytoskeleton]. Actin is one of the most abundant proteins in ''Dictyostelium'', constituting approximately 8% of the total protein in vegetative cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/561722 Alton and Lodish et al. 1977]).Actin synthesis is developmentally regulated, peaking shortly after starvation (reviewed by [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6894564 Firtel] in 1981). The different actin genes differ in their levels of expression, with [/gene/DDB_G0274135 act6], [/gene/DDB_G0269234 act8] and [/gene/DDB_G0274129 act12] being highly expressed both during growth and development compared to [/gene/DDB_G0289005 act4], [/gene/DDB_G0289663 act5], [/gene/DDB_G0280545 act7] and [/gene/DDB_G0272248 act16] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6286214 McKeown and Firtel 1981]). Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 19-SEP-2003 PG

DDB_G0292262.summary: Besides ''mhcA'' that encodes the classical myosin heavy chain, ''Dictyostelium'' carries genes for 12 unconventional myosins. ''myoM'', the last unconventional myosin gene discovered, encodes a large protein with a N-terminal myosin motor domain and a C-terminal RhoGEF domain [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10403059  (Schwarz et al. 1999)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10828443  (Oishi et al. 2000)]. There is also a PH-domain at the C-terminal that could localize MyoM to acidic membrane lipids such as PIP2. The C-terminal domain was directly shown to catalyze nucleotide exchange and activation of Rac1 GTPases that induce actin-driven surface protrusions [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11208126  (Geissler et al. 2000)]. Mutant strains lacking MyoM had no observable defects in either growth or development [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10828443  (Oishi et al. 2000)]. However mutant strains overexpressing MyoM displayed defects in growth and development, and an aberrant response to osmotic stress. The combination of a myosin motor domain and an active Rac-GEF domain suggests a possible role for MyoM at the interface of Rac-mediated signal transduction and remodeling of the actin cytoskeleton [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11208126  (Geissler et al. 2000)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 17-SEP-2019 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0268080.summary:
DNA-dependent RNA polymerase catalyzes the transcription of DNA into RNA using the four ribonucleoside triphosphates as substrates ([/ontology/go/0003899/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase activity]). Three distinct zinc-containing RNA polymerases are found in eukaryotic nuclei: [/gene/DDB_G0275759 rpa1] for the ribosomal RNA precursor ([/ontology/go/0006360/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase I promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005736/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase I complex]), [/gene/DDB_G0279193 rpb1] for the mRNA precursor ([/ontology/go/0006366/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase II promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005665/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase II, core complex]), and [/gene/DDB_G0277199 rpc1] for 5S and tRNA genes ([/ontology/go/0006383/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase III promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005666/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase III complex]).
RNA polymerase III is a multisubunit complex. The subunits encoded by [/gene/DDB_G0277199 rpc1] (ortholog of ''S. cerevisiae RPO31''), [/gene/DDB_G0293560 rpa2] (''RPC2''), [/gene/DDB_G0268080 rpc3] (''RPC82''),[/gene/DDB_G0277671 rpc4] (''RPC53''), [/gene/DDB_G0271514 rpc5] (''RPC37''), [/gene/DDB_G0286521 rpc9] (''RPC17''), [/gene/DDB_G0272022 rpc34] (''RPC34''), [/gene/DDB_G0273425 rpc25-1] (''RPC25''), and [/gene/DDB_G0287707 rpc11] (''RPC11'') are unique to RNA polymerase III. Orthologs of ''RPC31'' and ''RPC17'' have not been identified in the ''Dictyostelium'' genome. Two subunits, [/gene/DDB_G0291362 rpc19] and [/gene/DDB_G0282339 rpa5] (''RPC19'' and ''RPC40'' in ''S. cerevisiae''), are common to RNA polymerase I and RNA polymerase III and correspond to subunits 3 and 11 of RNA polymerase II. Subunits [/gene/DDB_G0291636 rpb5], [/gene/DDB_G0291037 rpb6], [/gene/DDB_G0278039 rpb8], [/gene/DDB_G0272036 rpb10], and [/gene/DDB_G0283365 rpb12] are common to all three RNA polymerases ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12407181 Peyroche et al. 2002], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12381659 Schramm and Hernandez 2001]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 11-JUN-2009 PG

DDB_G0292810.summary: beta-glucosidase was one of the first developmentally regulated enzymes to be used as a stage specific marker in ''Dictyostelium''. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/4982890 Coston and Loomis 1969)]. Two electrophoretically separable isozymes were found to accumulate at different stages of development. Mutations in the ''gluA'' locus affected both the early and the late isozyme that appear to differ in post-translational modifications ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/57116 Dimond and Loomis 1976)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6162850 Knecht and Dimond 1981)]. mRNA from the ''gluA'' locus is present between 2 and 6 hours of development and then remains at a low level until 16 hours when it accumulates again to reach a peak at 22 hours that is three fold higher than the early developmental peak ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8288612 Bush et al. 1976)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25887420 Rosengarten et al. 2015)]. The GluA protein has a signal sequence at the N-terminus for secretion followed by a stretch of 49 polar amino acids that is cleaved off to generate the mature protein. Like other acid hydrolases in growing cells, beta-glucosidase is found in lysosomes and secreted into the surrounding medium. During culmination ''gluA'' is expressed uniquely in the Pst 0 region of prestalk cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12796308 Maeda et al. 2003)]. Analyses of ''gluA'' null mutants indicate that beta-glucosidase acts as a block to selfing in macrocyst formation ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/57116 Dimond and Loomis 1976)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 20-JAN-2016 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0277505.summary:
The homeodomain is a sequence-specific DNA binding motif that consists of a helix-turn-helix. Homeobox-containing proteins have transcription factor activity. They have beenidentified in most if not all phyla of eukaryotes. Inmetazoans, homeobox-containing proteins are known to be involvedin regulating the anterior-posterior body plan and in thespecification of certain cell types and anterior-posteriorcompartments (see [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9486804 Han and Firtel 1998] and references therein). There are 14 predicted proteins that contain homeobox domains in ''Dictyostelium'':[/gene/DDB_G0275173 hbx2], [/gene/DDB_G0291075 warA], [/gene/DDB_G0291197 hbx3], [/gene/DDB_G0272967 hbx4], [/gene/DDB_G0273127 hbx5-1] (on the chromosome 2 duplication: [/gene/DDB_G0273645 hbx5-2]), [/gene/DDB_G0277505 hbx6], [/gene/DDB_G0278225 hbx7], [/gene/DDB_G0279257 hbx8], [/gene/DDB_G0280473 hbx9], [/gene/DDB_G0284293 hbx10], [/gene/DDB_G0295787 hbx11], [/gene/DDB_G0286733 hbx12], [/gene/DDB_G0288975 hbx13], and [/gene/DDB_G0289677 hbx14].
[http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25963254 Mishra and Saran 2015] performed a genome-wide classification and comparative genomic analysis of the 14 homeobox genes present in D. discoideum, and found that they could be classified into 3 groups: TALE, OTHER and NOVEL classes, ''hbx6'' belonging to the NOVEL class.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 07-JUL-2015 RD

DDB_G0291768.summary: TSET is the latest addition to trafficking proteins, which is ancient but frequently lost or reduced in evolution. The TSET complex is a heterohexamer and was named for the protein subunits in the complex, TSPOON (sigma-like), TPLATE (beta-like), TCUP (mu-like), TSAUCER (alpha, beta, gamma, delta, epsilon, zeta-like), TTRAY1, and TTRAY2. This ancient adaptor complex (AP) was identified in organisms such as Dictyostelids and land plants, such as ''Arabidopsis''. Only the TCUP subunit has been retained in fungi and animals, in mammals it has evolved into the cargo adaptor muniscin. A TSPOON-GFP fusion (gene tstD) has been shown to physically bind the 5 other TSET subunits. The TTRAY subunits form the scaffold for the TSPOON, TPLATE, TCUP, TSAUCER, heterotetramer. TIRF microscopy showed a punctate temporary localization of the complex to the plasma membran. The C-terminal domain of TCUP is homologous to the C-terminal domains of the muniscins, proteins in opisthokonts some of which are involved in the endocytic pathway [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24867644  (Hirst et al. 2014)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated,, 07-DEC-2018 PF

DDB_G0287691.summary: The ABC superfamily of genes is one of the largest in the genomes of both bacteria and eukaryotes. The proteins encoded by these genes all carry a characteristic 200- to 250-amino-acid ATP-binding cassette that gives them their family name ([/ontology/go/0042626/annotation/page/1 ATPase activity, coupled to transmembrane movement of substances]). In bacteria they are mostly involved in nutrient import, while in eukaryotes many are involved in export([/ontology/go/0006810/annotation/page/1 transport]), ([/ontology/go/0016021/annotation/page/1 integral to membrane]). Seven different families (A to G) have been defined in eukaryotes based on sequence homology, domain topology, and function. ''Dictyostelium'' has 71 ABC transporters (including one on the chromosome 2 duplication) and 13 ABCC family members: [/gene/DDB_G0280541 abcC1], [/gene/DDB_G0280055 abcC2], [/gene/DDB_G0287691 abcC3], [/gene/DDB_G0286559 abcC5], [/gene/DDB_G0287593 abcC6], [/gene/DDB_G0291243 abcC7], [/gene/DDB_G0284867 abcC8], [/gene/DDB_G0285165 abcC9], [/gene/DDB_G0280977 abcC10], [/gene/DDB_G0280973 abcC12], [/gene/DDB_G0280539 abcC13], [/gene/DDB_G0287589 abcC14], and [/gene/DDB_G0280459 abcC15]. Transporters of the C family have been shown to transport glutathione conjugants as well as to export cadmium ions. They are always found as full transporters with two copies of the transmembrane-ABC unit. Many of the genes of this family in humans and other animals have an additional transmembrane domain at the N terminus [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12456012 (Anjard and Loomis 2002)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 16-JUN-2003 PG

DDB_G0293900.summary:
Members of the Myb family of transcription factors are typically composed of two orthree imperfect repeats each of about 50 amino acids. These repeats fold into a variant ofthe helix-turn-helix motif and bind DNA. The Myb motif has been well conserved during evolution (see [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10331990 Guo et al. 1999] and references therein).
The putative DNA-binding domain of ''Dictyostelium mybA'' is as closely related to vertebrate c-Myb as is ''Drosophila'' Myb (65% identity), whereas the known Myb-related proteins of plants and yeast are more distantly related. The conserved domain of ''Dictyostelium'' MybA is capable of binding to the same DNA sequence as the vertebrate and ''Drosophila'' Myb proteins. The remainder of the deduced amino acid sequence of ''Dictyostelium'' MybA shows no homology to the divergent domains of the known animal, plant and yeast Myb-related proteins. Evolutionary analysis implies that the duplications that generated the repeats of the Myb DNA-binding domain began prior to the divergence of animals, plants, cellular slime molds and yeast [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1549373 (Stober-Grasser et al. 1992)]
In electrophoretic shift assays, MybA binds specifically to a sequence from the [/gene/DDB_G0269112 celB] promoter containing the Myb consensus binding site TAACTGA ([/ontology/go/0003677/annotation/page/1 DNA binding]). Mutation of Myb binding sites of the [/gene/DDB_G0271134 celA] and [/gene/DDB_G0269112 celB] promoters results in aberrant expression of these genes ([/ontology/go/0000122/annotation/page/1 negative regulation of transcription from RNA polymerase II promoter])([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7659526 Ramalingam and Ennis 1995], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7659526 Ramalingam and Ennis 1995]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 07-MAY-2004 PG

DDB_G0291974.summary: ''docA'' encodes a Rho guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF, RhoGEF). RhoGEFs are key components of signaling networks in which they activate Rho family GTPases by promoting the exchange of GDP for GTP. Microarray analysis revealed that ''docA'' is expressed in prestalk cells, with expression being maintained in all prestalk cells by early culmination ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12796308 Maeda et al. 2003]). A genome-wide screen for cheater mutants identified ''docA'' as a cheater. In ''docA'' null cells sporulation is reduced compared with wild-type cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18272966 Santorelli et al. 2008]). ''docA'' null mutant cells exhibit no growth or developmental defects. However developmentally competent ''docA'' null mutants chemotax with a slightly lower speed and directionality than wild-type cells in a cAMP gradient. The chemotaxis defect is more pronounced in ''docA''/''docD'' ([/gene/DDB_G0284725 docD]) double null mutants which have a polarity defect and a further reduction in speed. Vegetative stage ''docD'' null mutants have a significant decrease in random cell motility compared to wild type cells whereas ''docA'' null mutants show no significant decrease, and ''docA''/''docD'' double null mutant cells have only a slight decrease in speed compared with ''docD'' null mutants. However, expression of either DocA or DocD in the double null mutants rescues the phenotype, suggesting that DocA and DocD may function redundantly. Loss of DocA and DocD also affects the distribution of F-actin polymerization, as the vegetative double null cells appeared incapable of localizing F-actin accumulation at restricted regions of the cortex to create effective membrane protrusions. Taken together, these results suggest that DocA and DocD regulate the actin cytoskeleton and cell motility ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19037099 Para et al. 2009]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 02-JUN-2021 RD

DDB_G0275009.summary: The sequence and structure of the membrane bound guanylyl cyclase, GCA, encoded by ''gcA'', is similar to 12-transmembrane adenylyl cyclases, but the enzyme specifically catalyzes the synthesis of cGMP [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11237875  (Roelofs et al. 2001)]. Strains carrying null mutations in ''gcA'' aggregate and develop normally. ''In vivo'' GCA seems to account for less than 10% of the cAMP-induced cGMP and the remainder comes from the soluble guanylyl cyclase, sGC ([/gene/DDB_G0276269 sgcA]) [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11777934  (Roelofs and van Haastert 2002)]. Unlike the vertebrate guanylyl cyclases but similar to the adenylyl cyclase ACA, the Dictyostelium guanylyl cyclases are activated by receptor coupled heterotrimeric G-proteins [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15769639  (Schaap 2005)]. There may be relatively frequent conversion between adenylyl cyclases and guanylyl cyclases during evolution. Double mutants lacking both GCA and sGC have no measurable cGMP at any stage of development and yet show few defects in growth or development [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11777934  (Roelofs and van Haastert 2002)]. GCA and sGC double mutants contain significant defects in chemotaxis to cAMP, but sGC rather than GCA is responsible for this phenotype [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18299345  (Veltman et al. 2008)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 13-DEC-2018 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0287033.summary: ''nagA'' encodes the lysosomal acid hydrolase beta-N-acetylglucosaminidase ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/640375 Loomis et al. 1978)]. Measurements of the specific activity using a p-nitrophenol linked susbstrate in wild type and mutant strains showed that the initiation and termination of synthesis of the enzyme are controlled by the developmental program ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/5813341 Loomis et al. 1969)]. Expression of ''nagA'' does not occur until the density of growing cells exceeds 10<sup>6</sup>/ml when a secreted quorum sensing signal reaches threshold ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/567142 Grabel and Loomis et al. 1978)].The mRNA reaches peak at 6 hours of development and declines thereafter ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2972716 Graham et al. 1988)].Since beta-N-acetylglucosaminidase can be efficiently assayed along with other developmentally regulated acid hydrolases in wild type and mutant strains, it has been used to establish an early dependent sequence of developmental events in Dictyostelium ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1033094 Loomis et al. 1976)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 21-MAR-2016 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0275795.summary: ''pripA'' encodes a pleckstrin homology (PH) domain-containing protein. PripA was identified during a screen for proteins that localize to the macropinosome during the macropinosome maturation process, specifically the fusion of Rab5 ([/gene/DDB_G0271984 rab5A])-marked early macropinosomes to Rab7 ([/gene/DDB_G0269236 rab7A])-marked late macropinosomes. PripA localizes to both macropinosomes and phagosomes, and PripA localizes to newly formed macropinosomes by interacting with phosphatidylinositol-3,4-bisphosphate (PI(3,4)P2) via the PH domain. PripA colocalizes with Rab5A on macropinosomes. PripA forms a complex with the Rab GAP TbcrA ([/gene/DDB_G0282575 tbcrA]) that has GAP activity towards the Rab GTPase Rab5A. PripA also interacts specifically with the constitutively active form of Rab GTPase 7A, suggesting that PI(3,4)P2 and Rab7A mediate the recruitment of PripA to macropinosomes. In both ''pripA'' and ''tbcrA'' null cells, there is decreased inactivation of Rab5A, suggesting that PripA and TbcrA function in a complex. In ''pripA'' null cells there is also decreased localization of TbcrA to macropinosomes and phagosomes, as well as delayed macropinocytic and phagocytic cargo degradation. Taken together, these results support a role for the PripA-TbcrA complex in regulating macropinosome maturation by linking early and late macropinocytic compartments and promoting Rab conversion (Tu, et al 2022, PMID:35379834).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 19-APR-2022 RD

Seventeen of these genes encode identical proteins: [/gene/DDB_G0289553 act1], [/gene/DDB_G0274133 act2], [/gene/DDB_G0289005 act4], [/gene/DDB_G0289663 act5], [/gene/DDB_G0274135 act6], [/gene/DDB_G0280545 act7], [/gene/DDB_G0269234 act8], [/gene/DDB_G0274601 act9], [/gene/DDB_G0288879 act11], [/gene/DDB_G0274129 act12], [/gene/DDB_G0274599 act13], [/gene/DDB_G0274137 act14], [/gene/DDB_G0272520 act15], [/gene/DDB_G0272248 act16], [/gene/DDB_G0274727 act19], [/gene/DDB_G0274285 act20], and [/gene/DDB_G0274561 act21], while [/gene/DDB_G0289811 act10], [/gene/DDB_G0275023 act22], and [/gene/DDB_G0289487 act3] respectively have 1, 4 and 11 amino acid differences compared to the 17 identical genes. Actin is a major [/ontology/go/0005200/annotation/page/1 structural constituent of cytoskeleton]. DDB_G0269208.summary: The ABC superfamily of genes is one of the largest in the genomes of both bacteria and eukaryotes. The proteins encoded by these genes all carry a characteristic 200- to 250-amino-acid ATP-binding cassette that gives them their family name ([/ontology/go/0042626/annotation/page/1 ATPase activity, coupled to transmembrane movement of substances]). In bacteria they are mostly involved in nutrient import, while in eukaryotes many are involved in export ([/ontology/go/0006810/annotation/page/1 transport]). Seven different families have been defined in eukaryotes based on sequence homology, domain topology, and function. Sequences from the well-advanced ''Dictyostelium'' genome project have allowed to recognize 71 members of this superfamily (including one on the chromosome 2 duplication). The ABCG family is characterized by the ABC domain preceding the transmembrane domain ([/ontology/go/0016021/annotation/page/1 integral to membrane]). All of the members of this family in animals are half-transporters while all of the fungal members are full transporters with two ABC-transmembrane units. No members of this family are found in bacteria. ''Dictyostelium'' and ''Arabidopsis'' have members of both types ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12456012 Anjard and Loomis 2002]). DDB_G0281391.summary: The ABC superfamily of genes is one of the largest in the genomes of both bacteria and eukaryotes. The proteins encoded by these genes all carry a characteristic 200- to 250-amino-acid ATP-binding cassette that gives them their family name ([/ontology/go/0042626/annotation/page/1 ATPase activity, coupled to transmembrane movement of substances]). In bacteria they are mostly involved in nutrient import, while in eukaryotes many are involved in export ([/ontology/go/0006810/annotation/page/1 transport]). Seven different families have been defined in eukaryotes based on sequence homology, domain topology, and function. Sequences from the well-advanced ''Dictyostelium'' genome project have allowed to recognize 71 members of this superfamily (including one on the chromosome 2 duplication). The ABCG family is characterized by the ABC domain preceding the transmembrane domain ([/ontology/go/0016021/annotation/page/1 integral to membrane]). All of the members of this family in animals are half-transporters while all of the fungal members are full transporters with two ABC-transmembrane units. No members of this family are found in bacteria. ''Dictyostelium'' and ''Arabidopsis'' have members of both types ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12456012 Anjard and Loomis 2002]). Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 18-OCT-2004 PG

DDB_G0281891.summary: ''rbg3'' encodes a putative Rab GTPase-activating protein (GAP, rabGAP). RabGAPs are key components of signal transduction networks in which they inactivate Rab GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP. Rbg3 belongs to the Rab-GTPase-TBC domain superfamily. Rbg3 was identified in a yeast two hybrid (Y2H) screen in which the active form of G-protein subunit alpha 2 ([/gene/DDB_G0276267 gpaB]) was used as bait. ''rbg3'' is expressed at low levels in the vegetative stage with a marginal increase during development; however Rbg3 protein levels remain constant throughout the life cycle. Rbg3 is localized to the cytosol, but in a cAMP gradient Rbg3 transiently localizes inside of the leading edge. Rbg3 interacts with G-protein subunit alpha 2 and G-protein subunit alpha 9 ([/gene/DDB_G0283419 gpaI]) suggesting that Rbg3 is potentially regulated via the activity of G-alpha 9 during growth and that of G-alpha 2 during development. Rbg3 is a possible RabGAP for ''rab7A'' ([/gene/DDB_G0269236 rab7A]). ''rbg3'' null cells have an increased growth rate, with increased cell numbers and increased cell density at stationary phase compared with wild type (wt). ''rbg3'' null cells develop precociously, completing development 4 hours faster than wt cells. ''rbg3'' null cells also showed enhanced cAMP levels. In contrast, ''rbg3'' overexpression mutants have a decreased growth rate and delayed development compared with wt cells. In addition, the size of lysosomes is increased in ''rbg3'' overexpression mutants. Both human and C. elegans ''rbg3'' homologs complemented the growth and development ''rbg3'' phenotypes in ''D. discoideum'', suggesting that a common functional role may exist for Rbg3 among multicellular organisms. These results suggest that ''rbg3'' is involved in signal transduction networks regulating growth, lysosome function and life-cycle duration ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24349132 Kuwayama et al. 2013]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 25-MAR-2022 RD; annotation contributions: PMID:24349132 Hidekazu Kuwayama
