There are 29 genes encoding actin in ''Dictyostelium'' with amino acid identity greater than 83%, ''act1''-''act29''. Seventeen of these genes encode identical proteins: [/gene/DDB_G0289553 act1], [/gene/DDB_G0274133 act2], [/gene/DDB_G0289005 act4], [/gene/DDB_G0289663 act5], [/gene/DDB_G0274135 act6], [/gene/DDB_G0280545 act7], [/gene/DDB_G0269234 act8], [/gene/DDB_G0274601 act9], [/gene/DDB_G0288879 act11], [/gene/DDB_G0274129 act12], [/gene/DDB_G0274599 act13], [/gene/DDB_G0274137 act14], [/gene/DDB_G0272520 act15], [/gene/DDB_G0272248 act16], [/gene/DDB_G0274727 act19], [/gene/DDB_G0274285 act20], and [/gene/DDB_G0274561 act21], while [/gene/DDB_G0289811 act10], [/gene/DDB_G0275023 act22], and [/gene/DDB_G0289487 act3] respectively have 1, 4 and 11 amino acid differences compared to the 17 identical genes. The proteins encoded by [/gene/DDB_G0274131 act17], [/gene/DDB_G0289489 act18], [/gene/DDB_G0268744 act23] and [/gene/DDB_G0289505 act24]are more divergent.
Actin is a major [/ontology/go/0005200/annotation/page/1 structural constituent of cytoskeleton]. Actin is one of the most abundant proteins in ''Dictyostelium'', constituting approximately 8% of the total protein in vegetative cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/561722 Alton and Lodish et al. 1977]).Actin synthesis is developmentally regulated, peaking shortly after starvation (reviewed by [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6894564 Firtel] in 1981). The different actin genes differ in their levels of expression, with [/gene/DDB_G0274135 act6], [/gene/DDB_G0269234 act8] and [/gene/DDB_G0274129 act12] being highly expressed both during growth and development compared to [/gene/DDB_G0289005 act4], [/gene/DDB_G0289663 act5], [/gene/DDB_G0280545 act7] and [/gene/DDB_G0272248 act16] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6286214 McKeown and Firtel 1981]). DDB_G0282365.summary:
''rac1C'' encodes a guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G protein) of the Rho family of small GTPases. G proteins are key components of signal transduction networks in which they function as molecular signaling switches, binding to GDP in the off state while binding GTP in the on state. Guanine nucleotide-exchange factors (GEFs) promote the exchange of GDP for GTP on Ras GTPases thus activating them, while GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) inactivate Ras GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP. Rac GEF gxcT ([/gene/DDB_G0269610 gxcT]) interacts with and may also activate Rac1C ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24248334 Wang et al. 2013]). DGAP1 ([/gene/DDB_G0287585 rgaA]) and GAPA ([/gene/DDB_G0269140 gapA]) are possible GAPs for Rac1C ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10825297 Dumontier et al. 2000]), ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20375144 Lee et al. 2010]). Rac1C has multiple binding partners that may function as downstream effectors, including protein kinase PakA ([/gene/DDB_G0269166 pakA]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15470506 Park et al. 2004]), myosin heavy chain kinase PakB ([/gene/DDB_G0276459 pakB]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15509655 de la Roche et al. 2005]) and protein kinase PakC ([/gene/DDB_G0267450 pakC]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15470506 Park et al. 2004]). Rac1C also binds to the Rho GDP-dissociation inhibitor 1 RhoGDI1 ([/gene/DDB_G0291077 rdiA]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12163018 Imai et al. 2002]). ''rac1C'' is induced during sexual maturation but expression is reduced immediately after cell fusion, suggesting that Rac1C may be involved in cell/cell interactions during the sexual cycle ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16573737 Muramoto et al. 2005]). Expression of ''rasD'' is upregulated in response to intracellular ''Mycobacterium marinum'' infection ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31823727 Kjellin et al. 2019]).
''rac1C'' is highly similar to two additional ''Dictyostelium'' rho GTPases: ''rac1A'' ([/gene/DDB_G0277869 rac1A]) and ''rac1B'' ([/gene/DDB_G0268622 rac1B]). Expression of the three ''rac1'' genes is low during growth but increases 3-fold during aggregation before again declining to growth-stage levels during the slug stage ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8294042 Bush et al. 1993]). Overexpression of ''rac1'' genes results in increased filopodium formation, while constitutively active Rac1A and Rac1C mutants are severely impaired in growth, motility and endocytosis. In addition, these mutants are delayed in development and display defects in cytokinesis and F-actin organization. These results indicate that the Rac1 GTPases mediate signaling cascades regulating processes such as cell motility, endocytosis and cytokinesis that depend on the reorganization of the actin cytoskeleton in ''Dictyostelium'' ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10825297 Dumontier et al. 2000]). At the leading edge of migrating cells activated Rac1 participates in Scar/WAVE ([/gene/DDB_G0285253 scrA])-mediated actin polymerization and pseudopod extension. At the trailing edge activated Rac1 forms a complex with DGAP1 and the actin-binding proteins cortexillin I ([/gene/DDB_G0289483 ctxA]) and cortexillin II ([/gene/DDB_G0276893 ctxB]) enabling proper cell retraction ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20375144 Lee et al. 2010]), ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22891261 Veltman et al. 2012]), ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23503127 Faix et al. 2013]), ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26940518 Rivero et al. 2016]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 21-APR-2020 RD

DDB_G0280955.summary:
''dsgg'' encodes a Disgorgin, a Rab GTPase-activating protein (GAP, rabGAP). RabGAPs are key components of signal transduction networks in which they inactivate Rab GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP. Disgorgin localizes to the contractile vacuole (CV) membrane during the late charging phase. Disgorgin binds to and has strong GAP activity towards Rab GTPase 8A ([/gene/DDB_G0280043 rab8A]), which also localizes to the contractile vacuole. Disgogrin also binds to a dominant negative Rab11A ([/gene/DDB_G0269238 rab11A]) mutant. ''dsgg'' null cells have enlarged contractile vacuoles as a result of impaired contractile vacuole-plasma membrane fusion.
Disgorgin, along with Drainin ([/gene/DDB_G0269130 phgA]), Rab8A and Rab11A function in a signaling pathway to regulate CV fusion with the plasma membrane and subsequent CV discharging. In response to hypo-osmotic stress, Rab GTPase Rab11A is activated and recruits Drainin to the contractile vacuole membrane. Disgorgin and Rab8A function downstream of Drainin and rab11A to mediate contractile vacuole-plasma membrane fusion which is then followed by the discharge of water out of the cell. The strong interaction between Disgorgin and dominant-negative Rab11A suggests a possible feedback pathway between the two. In addition, LvsA ([/gene/DDB_G0269150 lvsA]) and LvsD ([/gene/DDB_G0271502 lvsD]) are also involved in the regulation of CV formation. Disrupting ''lvsA'' or overexpressing LvsD suppresses the large CV phenotype in ''dsgg'' null cells, whereas overexpressing LvsA or disrupting ''lvsD'' leads to the extended enlargement of CVs in ''dsgg'' null cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18636095 Du et al. 2008]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 19-NOV-2021 RD

DDB_G0291976.summary:
''racD'' encodes a guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G protein) of the Rho family of small GTPases. G proteins are key components of signal transduction networks in which they function as molecular signaling switches, binding to GDP in the off state while binding GTP in the on state. Guanine nucleotide-exchange factors (GEFs) promote the exchange of GDP for GTP on Ras GTPases thus activating them, while GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) inactivate Ras GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP.
''racD'' mRNA is expressed during the growth phase, with a slight increase in expression during early development, but then mRNA levels slowly decrease at the start of aggregation until the end of development ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8294042 Bush et al. 1993]). RacD is an atypical member of the Rho GTPase family. RacD lacks a C-terminal prenylation motif, a signal for attachment of a lipid moiety, geranylgeranyl or farnesyl, characteristic of other Rho proteins. The prenylation motif has been demonstrated to contribute to the association of Rho proteins with membranes ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11222756 Rivero et al. 2001]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 08-MAY-2020 RD
DDB_G0291976.note: The sequences from the Sequencing Center and GenBank record L11594 are identical.

DDB_G0271138.summary: The ABC superfamily of genes is one of the largest in the genomes of both bacteria and eukaryotes. The proteins encoded by these genes all carry a characteristic 200- to 250-amino-acid ATP-binding cassette that gives them their family name ([/ontology/go/0042626/annotation/page/1 ATPase activity, coupled to transmembrane movement of substances]). In bacteria they are mostly involved in nutrient import, while in eukaryotes many are involved in export ([/ontology/go/0006810/annotation/page/1 transport]), ([/ontology/go/0016021/annotation/page/1 integral to membrane]). Seven different families (A to G) have been defined in eukaryotes based on sequence homology, domain topology, and function. ''Dictyostelium'' has 71 ABC transporters (including one on the chromosome 2 duplication) and 11 ABCA family members: [/gene/DDB_G0291994 abcA1], [/gene/DDB_G0267438 abcA2], [/gene/DDB_G0293436 abcA3], [/gene/DDB_G0274121 abcA4], [/gene/DDB_G0274119 abcA5], [/gene/DDB_G0291245 abcA6], [/gene/DDB_G0271140 abcA7], [/gene/DDB_G0271138 abcA8],[/gene/DDB_G0291980 abcA9], [/gene/DDB_G0283387 abcA10], and [/gene/DDB_G0275453 abcA11],One of the defining characteristics of the A family is the presence of a regulatory domain with multiple sites for phosphorylation by various protein kinases in the region after the first ABC domain [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12456012 (Anjard and Loomis 2002)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 16-JUN-2003 PG

DDB_G0286773.summary:
GflB has been identified as a novel RacE-binding protein which contains an N-terminal lipid- binding domain, a Ras GEF domain, and a Rho GAP domain. GflB interacts with both Rho and Ras GTPases and controls their activities in response to cAMP. A ''gflB'' knockout shows that GflB is important for spatially restricting intracellular chemotactic signals at the leading edge of migrating cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/27009206 Senoo et al. 2016)].
GflB directly couples the cAMP receptor to Rap1 ([/gene/DDB_G0291237 rapA]). Localizing to the leading edge it binds active (GTP-bound) G-alpha 2. GflB functions as a Ga2-activated, Rap1-specific guanine nucleotide exchange factor, required to balance Ras and Rap signaling. The nucleotide exchange on Rap1 induces a major rearrangement of the cytoskeleton and results in the recruitment of additional GflB to the leading edge.The kinetics of GflB translocation to the leading edge of chemotaxing cells are fine-tuned by GSK3 phosphorylation ([/gene/DDB_G0272110 gskA]; [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/27237792 Liu et al. 2016)].
During vegetative growth, ''gflB''-knockout cells are flatter and more polarized, whereas GflB-overproducing cells are rounder. The ''gflB''- cells exhibited impaired crown formation and particularly retraction, resulting in more crowns (macropinocytic cups) per cell and longer crown lifetimes. Accordingly, ''gflB''- cells showed defects in macropinocytosis, phagocytosis and cytokinesis. An N-terminal region was shown to bind F-actin directly. Expressing several deletion constructs found the N-terminal region essential for cortical localization including crowns, a downstream basic region might recruit the protein to the cortex through its lipid binding property. Both the RasGEF domain and NKD (nankyrin domain)) are important for GflB function, the NKD may modulate the cortical binding. Thus GflB acts as a key regulator of actin-driven membrane protrusions during processes such as phagocytosi and cytokinesis, possibly by modulating Rap1 signaling pathways ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28778987 Inaba et al. 2017)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 08-MAR-2019 PF

DDB_G0277589.summary:
''gtaC'' was identified as a DIF-1 insensitive mutant, dimC, that fail to make stalk cells in response to DIF in the 8-Br-cAMP monolayer assay. ''gtaC'' is expressed in the lower and upper cups and the basal disc;, and consistent with that pattern of expression, mutant phenotypes show that it is involved in DIF signaling leading to pstB cell sorting and basal disc formation.
''gtaC'' is maximally expressed during aggregation, and localizes to the nucleus upon DIF stimulation ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22008230 Keller and Thompson 2008]).
GATA transcription factors specifically bind the DNA sequence (A/T)GATA(A/G) in the regulatory regions of genes ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2249770 Yamamoto et al. 1990]).In mammalian cells, GATA-binding transcription factors play important roles in development ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12943715 Tremblay and Viger 2003]). In ''Dictyostelium'', there are 24 predicted proteins that contain GATA-type zinc fingers: [/gene/DDB_G0277147 stkA], [/gene/DDB_G0280547 comH], [/gene/DDB_G0277589 gtaC], [/gene/DDB_G0286855 gtaD],[/gene/DDB_G0267640 gtaE],[/gene/DDB_G0268792 gtaF],[/gene/DDB_G0270756 gtaG],[/gene/DDB_G0277591 gtaH],[/gene/DDB_G0281661 gtaI],[/gene/DDB_G0281829 gtaJ],[/gene/DDB_G0282811 gtaK],[/gene/DDB_G0285139 gtaL],[/gene/DDB_G0286837 gtaM],[/gene/DDB_G0287057 gtaN],[/gene/DDB_G0289651 gtaO],[/gene/DDB_G0295707 gtaP],[/gene/DDB_G0286843 gtaQ],[/gene/DDB_G0279331 gtaR],[/gene/DDB_G0280627 gtaS],[/gene/DDB_G0280639 gtaT],[/gene/DDB_G0280853 gtaU],[/gene/DDB_G0281087 gtaV],[/gene/DDB_G0286839 gtaW], and[/gene/DDB_G0290665 gtaX].
GtaC exhibits oscillatory nucleocytoplasmic shuttling in response to periodic cAMP waves during early development. This behavior requires a negative regulation of an intrinsic nuclear localization signal and cAMP receptor-mediated phosphorylation of GtaC by [/gene/DDB_G0272110 gskA]. GtaC shuttling controls the proper expression of early development genes and inhibition of its nuclear exit leads to precocious gene expression and aberrant development. Consistent with the shuttling behavior, cAMP cycles generate bursts of GtaC-dependent transcription, indicating that GtaC is responsible for relaying oscillatory cAMP signaling ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24653039 Cai, et al. 2014]). Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 03-NOV-2014 PF

DDB_G0267422.summary: ''tipC'' was isolated from a REMI mutant that was picked because its development was arrested when multiple tips formed on aggregates ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10402673 Stege et al. 1999)]. It encodes a large protein with a C-terminal domain similar to the one in yeast and human vacuolar sorting protein VPS13. This protein is involved in the transport of proteins to the vacuole in yeast. The human protein VPS13A is mutated in the neurodegenerative disease chorea-acanthocytosis. ''tipC'' null mutants have a reduced number of autophagosomes as visualized by punctate GFP-ATG8 and GFP-ATG18 as well as defects in autophagy flux ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25996471 Munoz-Braceras et al. 2015)]. Further analysis of VPS13 in human cells confirmed the participation of the human protein in autophagy.'' tipC'' null mutants have abnormal cell sorting behavior and severely reduced fruiting body and spore production. The multi-tipped phenotype of ''tipC'' null mutants is similar to that of mutants in other autophagy genes ''atg6'' ([/gene/DDB_G0269244 atg6A]), ''atg7'' ([/gene/DDB_G0271096 atg7]), ''atg9'' ([/gene/DDB_G0285323 atg9]), ''atg101'' ([/gene/DDB_G0288287 atg101]), and ''tipD'' ([/gene/DDB_G0275323 tipD]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 23-FEB-2017 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis and Ricardo Escalante

DDB_G0267384.summary: CulB is a member of the cullin family of proteins that function as scaffolds that, along with F- box/WD40-repeat-containing proteins, mediate the ubiquitination of proteins to target them for degradation by the proteasome. ''culB'' was isolated in a screen of REMI mutants that form aberrant fruiting bodies ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12455979 Wang and Kuspa, 2002)]. When ''culB'' is knocked out in a wild type background, the cells develop into multi-tipped mounds that each give rise to a small fruiting body. Only about 17% of the wild-type number of viable spores are formed. When allowed to develop together with mostly wild type cells, ''culB'' mutant cells are distributed in the stalk, the basal disk, upper and lower cups, but rarely among the spores in the sorus. The prestalk marker ''ecmA'', ([/gene/DDB_G0277853 ecmA]) which is normally only expressed after 12 hours of development, is strongly expressed after 4 hours of development in ''culB'' mutant cells. It appears that CulB normally delays prestalk cell differentiation until the optimal proportion of prestalk and prespore cells can be established. When the rate of development is accelerated by inactivation of the regulatory subunit of PKA, ([/gene/DDB_G0279413 pkaR]) the effects of loss of CulB are amplified; almost no spores are formed in ''culB''/''pkaR'' double null cells and most mutant cells vacuolize and lay down cellulosic cell walls like stalk cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12455979 Wang and Kuspa, 2002)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 21-FEB-2019 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0288181.summary: ''Dictyostelium'' responds to heat shock like most eukaryotes by inducing the synthesis of a small number of specific genes. One of these heat shock genes, hspA, encodes the 60 kDa protein Hsp60 [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6775994  (Loomis and Wheeler, 1980)]. Hsp60 is imported into mitochondria where it can act as a molecular chaperonin [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12952082  (Kotsifas et al., 2002)]. Antisense inhibition of ''hspA'' was used to generate cells with a deficiency of Hsp60 that were shown to have defects in growth and multicellular morphogenesis. These symptoms could be overcome by reducing the activity of the AMP dependent protein kinase AMPK [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17332500  (Bokko et al., 2007)]. The investigators suggest that mitochondrial disease is caused by chronic AMPK signaling rather than by insufficient ATP. Furthermore, Francione and colleagues found in mitochondrially diseased cells mutated in gene ''hspA'' or gene ''[/gene/DDB_G0294034 rnlA]'' these mutations also secondarily cause increased AMPK signaling, resulting in an enhanced ''Legionella pneumophila'' infection rate [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19638422  (Francione et al., 2009)]. Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 23-SEP-2019 PF; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0291342.summary: TacA is a homolog of the budding yeast ''S. cerevisiae'' zinc finger transcription factor, Crz1. TacA is translocated from the cytosol to the nucleus after dephosphorylation by the calcium-activated protein phosphatase calcineurin ([/gene/DDB_G0276883 canA]) [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22944283  (Thewes et al. 2012)]. TacA translocates to the nucleus of ''D. discoideum'' within 3 minutes after addition of 100 mM CaCl2. The effect of calcium on TacA can be blocked by inhibition of calcineurin with 50 mM gossypol. Cells with reduced TacA as the result of expression of tacA-RNAi are delayed in aggregation and form very small fruiting bodies. Expression of prestalk genes ([/gene/DDB_G0277853 ecmA]) and ([/gene/DDB_G0269132 ecmB]), prespore gene ([/gene/DDB_G0267412 pspA]), and calcium up-regulated genes ([/gene/DDB_G0289283 cupC]) and ([/gene/DDB_G0277861 patA]) showed no clear effect of reduction of TacA in the mutant strain [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22944283  (Thewes et al. 2012)]. It is likely that the major roles of TacA occur during early development.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 15-FEB-2018 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis; annotation contribution: PMID 22944283 Sascha Thewes

DDB_G0277845.summary: ''dhkB'' is involved in the cytokinin signal transduction pathway regulating spore germination. ''dhkB'' encodes a histidine kinase with several potential transmembrane domains but no extracellular loops of more than 10 amino acids. Spores from ''dhkB'' null cells germinate precociously, a phenotype that is suppressed by ectopic activation of or expression of protein kinase A (PKA) ([/gene/DDB_G0283907 pkaC], [/gene/DDB_G0279413 pkaR]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9576830 Zinda and Singleton 1998)]. Spores lacking DhkB germinate precociously because they do not respond to the cytokinin germination inhibitor, discadenine, by an increase in internal cAMP. Cytokinins accelerate sporulation in wild type cells, but not in dhkB null mutants ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18216168 Anjard and Loomis 2008)]. The same phenotype is observed in mutants lacking the late adenylyl cyclase AcrA ([/gene/DDB_G0267376 acrA]), that can function as part of a two-component system by accepting a phosphate in its response regulator region. The response to cytokinins is independent of the sole H2 protein of Dictyostelium, RdeA ([/gene/DDB_G0282923 rdeA]), and so does not use the standard phosphorelay pathway. It is possible that cytokinins stimulate direct phosphorelay between DhkB and AcrA which results in an increase in the level of cAMP. Pharmaceutical stimulation of cAMP and PKA activity accelerates sporulation in both dhkB- and acrA- mutants. The cytokinin receptor does not appear to be either DhkB or AcrA since culmination-stage mutants lacking these products bind radiolabelled cytokinin just as well as wild type cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18216168 Anjard and Loomis 2008)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 26-OCT-2015 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

The E3 enzyme [/gene/DDB_G0291648 lpd] is adihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase ([/ontology/go/0004148/annotation/page/1 dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase activity]) that is shared by three 2-oxoacid dehydrogenase complexes and the glycine cleavage system. DDB_G0291197.summary:
The homeodomain is a sequence-specific DNA binding motif that consists of a helix-turn-helix. Homeobox-containing proteins have transcription factor activity. They have beenidentified in most if not all phyla of eukaryotes. Inmetazoans, homeobox-containing proteins are known to be involvedin regulating the anterior-posterior body plan and in thespecification of certain cell types and anterior-posteriorcompartments (see [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9486804 Han and Firtel 1998] and references therein). There are 14 predicted proteins that contain homeobox domains in ''Dictyostelium'':[/gene/DDB_G0275173 hbx2], [/gene/DDB_G0291075 warA], [/gene/DDB_G0291197 hbx3], [/gene/DDB_G0272967 hbx4], [/gene/DDB_G0273127 hbx5-1] (on the chromosome 2 duplication: [/gene/DDB_G0273645 hbx5-2]), [/gene/DDB_G0277505 hbx6], [/gene/DDB_G0278225 hbx7], [/gene/DDB_G0279257 hbx8], [/gene/DDB_G0280473 hbx9], [/gene/DDB_G0284293 hbx10], [/gene/DDB_G0295787 hbx11], [/gene/DDB_G0286733 hbx12], [/gene/DDB_G0288975 hbx13], and [/gene/DDB_G0289677 hbx14].
[http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25963254 Mishra and Saran 2015] performed a genome-wide classification and comparative genomic analysis of the 14 homeobox genes present in D. discoideum, and found that they could be classified into 3 groups: TALE, OTHER and NOVEL classes, ''hbx3'' belonging to the TALE class.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 07-JUL-2015 RD

DDB_G0278483.summary: ''ngaP'' encodes a Ras GTPase-activating protein (GAP, rasGAP). RasGAPs are key components of signal transduction networks in which they inactivate Ras GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP. ''ngap'' is expressed during development with highest expression at the cAMP chemotactic-competent stage. cAMP stimulation promotes an association between RasC ([/gene/DDB_G0281385 rasC]) and RasG ([/gene/DDB_G0293434 rasG]) and causes the transient translocation of Ngap from the cytosol to the leading edge membrane. Dominant negative RasC(S17N) or RasG(S17N) showed significantly reduced cAMP-mediated membrane translocation of NgaP, while constitutively active RasC(G12V) significantly enhanced the membrane translocation of NgaP, indicating that NgaP membrane localization is dependent on activated Ras. ''ngap'' null mutant cells have multiple phenotypes, including impaired aggregation, a decreased number of fruiting bodies, and a higher level of activated Ras. In response to persistent cAMP stimulation, ''ngap'' null mutants display the same initial, transient Ras activation as wild type (wt) cells, but fail to adapt persistently to the stimulation. In addition, ''ngap'' null cells have a chemotaxis defect, exhibiting poor directionality, decreased speed and a shorter travel path compared with wt cells at higher (10 microM) levels of cAMP, but normal chemotaxis at lower (100 nanoMolar) levels of cAMP. These results reveal that ''ngap'' null cells are unable to generate proper responses to cAMP gradients and indicate that NgaP is a negative regulator of Ras signaling required for adaptation and chemotaxis ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29109256 Xu et al. 2017]). In the presence of high [Ca2+], there is a decreased membrane localization of NgaP. ''iplA'' null cells ([/gene/DDB_G0292564 iplA]), which lack a [Ca2+ ] increase in response to cAMP stimulation, displayed an increased, prolonged membrane translocation of NgaP, while ''cbpG'' ([/gene/DDB_G0283609 cbpG]) null cells with higher basal [Ca2+ ] levels upon cAMP stimulation exhibited little membrane translocation of NgaP, indicating that calcium negatively mediates the membrane targeting of NgaP. Further investigation of chemotactic response in a range of low cAMP concentrations revealed that ''ngap'' null cells display defective chemotaxis in high-concentration gradients but improved chemotaxis compared to wt cells in low- or sub-sensitive-concentration gradients (Xu, et al 2021, PMID: 34395450).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 01-OCT-2021 RD

DDB_G0276461.summary: Members of the NAK (Numb-associated kinase) family of serine/threonine kinases ([/ontology/go/0004674/annotation/page/1 protein serine/threonine kinase activity]) have been shown toparticipate in diverse cellular processes. The first characterized NAK was the ''Drosophila melanogaster'' NAK,named for its ability to interact with the neuronal differentiation protein Numb, hence the name NAK ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9418906 Chien et al. 1998]). Additional members of this family include AAK1 (AP2-associatedkinase), involved in clathrin-mediated endocytosis ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11877461 Conner and Schmid 2000]),and BIKe (BMP-induced kinase), which plays a role in bone differentiation ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11500515 Kearns et al. 2001]). DDB0229347 and [/gene/DDB_G0280111 DDB_G0280111] are similar to the kinasedomains of AAK1 and BIKe. The NAK family also includes MPSK (myristoylated and palmitoylated serine/threoninekinase), which is fatty acid acylated ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10364453 Berson et al. 1999]) andmay play a role in TGF-beta signaling ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10947953 Ohta et al. 2000]). The mostclosely related protein to MPSK in ''Dictyostelium discoideum'' is [/gene/DDB_G0291350 DDB_G0291350].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 10-MAY-2004 KP

DDB_G0289657.summary: The ABC superfamily of genes is one of the largest in the genomes of both bacteria and eukaryotes. The proteins encoded by these genes all carry a characteristic 200- to 250-amino-acid ATP-binding cassette that gives them their family name ([/ontology/go/0042626/annotation/page/1 ATPase activity, coupled to transmembrane movement of substances]). In bacteria they are mostly involved in nutrient import, while in eukaryotes many are involved in export ([/ontology/go/0006810/annotation/page/1 transport]). Seven different families have been defined in eukaryotes based on sequence homology, domain topology, and function. Sequences from the well-advanced ''Dictyostelium'' genome project have allowed to recognize 71 members of this superfamily (including one on the chromosome 2 duplication). The ABCG family is characterized by the ABC domain preceding the transmembrane domain ([/ontology/go/0016021/annotation/page/1 integral to membrane]). All of the members of this family in animals are half-transporters while all of the fungal members are full transporters with two ABC-transmembrane units. No members of this family are found in bacteria. ''Dictyostelium'' and ''Arabidopsis'' have members of both types ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12456012 Anjard and Loomis 2002]). Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 18-OCT-2004 PG

DDB_G0289875.summary: The increased rate of polysaccharide synthesis during culmination is dependent on uridine diphosphate glucose pyrophosphorylase (UDP-glucose pyrophosphorylase) activity to generate the needed substrate, UDP-glucose. Biochemical assays found a 10 fold increase in pyrophosphorylase activity between 10 and 20 hours of development ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6067273 Ashworth and Sussman, 1967)]. Mutant strains lacking this enzyme activity develop well until culmination but then arrest as gnarled fingers ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/944665 Dimond et al. 1976)]. Characterization of cDNA and genomic clones of ''uppA'' showed that it encodes UDP-glucose pyrophosphorylase ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2991046 Fishel et al. 1985)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3035502 Ragheb et al. 1987)]. However, most of the UDP-glucose pyrophosphorylase activity during development is produced by the related gene ''ugpB'' ([/gene/DDB_G0277879 ugpB]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12060658 Bishop et al. 2002)]. mRNAs from ''uppA'' and ''ugpB'' accumulate coordinately between 6 and 18 hours of development ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25887420 Rosengarten et al. 2015)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 24-MAY-2016 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0272150.summary: Williams and colleagues ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24006265  Robery et al. 2013]) identified a G-protein-coupled receptor mutant, grlJ-, by screening a mutant library for resistance to a commonly used bitter standard, phenylthiourea. grlJ- cells showed a significantly increased tolerance to phenylthiourea in growth, survival and movement. Analysis of the cell-signalling pathway involved in the detection of phenylthiourea showed dependence upon heterotrimeric G protein and phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase activity, suggesting that this signalling pathway is responsible for the cellular effects of phenylthiourea. This is further supported by a phenylthiourea-dependent block in the transient cAMP-induced production of phosphatidylinositol (3,4,5)-trisphosphate (PIP3) in wild-type but not grlJ- cells.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 22-JAN-2014 RD; annotation contributions: PMID:24006265 Robin Williams

Actobindins are small proteins with two actin-binding WH2 (Wiskott Aldrich syndrome homology region 2) domains. ''Dictyostelium'' has three genes encoding actobindin, [/gene/DDB_G0270884 abnA], [/gene/DDB_G0269518 abnB], and [/gene/DDB_G0269520 abnC]. While proteins are identical for ''abnB'' and ''abnC'', both are 72% identical to ''abnA''. All three ''Dictyostelium'' actobindins are 50 to 51% identical to the ''Acanthamoeba'' protein.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 06-APR-2005 PF

DDB_G0288061.summary:
Using an apoaequorin expressing strain, Ludlow ''et al.'' showed that ''Dictyostelium'' posseses P2X receptors that facilitate rapid Ca2+ influx in response to extracellular ATP and ADP. Deleting [/gene/DDB_G0272004 p2xA] or [/gene/DDB_G0288061 p2xE] did not influence this behavior, suggesting these genes are not involved. However, this study proposes possible roles for [/gene/DDB_G0275293 p2xB], [/gene/DDB_G0275191 p2xC], or [/gene/DDB_G0288335 p2xD] [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18486207 (Ludlow et al. 2008)].
Most recently, Ludlow ''et al.'' showed that p2xB and p2xE, as well as p2xA, have ATP-gated channel activity when expressed in ''Xenopus'' oocytes. However, Na+ rather inhibited this activity to various degrees in these P2x channels, but K+, and NH4+ ions elicited a large response. Interestingly, p2xA and p2xB, but not p2xE are permeable to Cl- ions. No such ATP-gated channel activity was found for p2xC and p2xD. All ''Dictyostelium'' P2x proteins localize to the [/ontology/go/0031164/annotation/page/1 contractile vacuolar membrane], and not to the plasma membrane like P2X receptors from other organisms. By using a protease protection assay on tagged receptors the authors demonstrated that the transmembrane loop region containing the agonist (ATP) binding site lies within the lumen of the vacuole. A quintuple p2xA/B/C/D/E null mutant in wild type background AX2 shows a reduced response to the calmodulin inhibitor calmidazolium, suggesting a role of the ''Dictyostelium'' proteins in the [/ontology/go/0050848/annotation/page/1 regulation of calcium-mediated signaling]. The quintuple null mutant also shows a slight delay in its [/ontology/go/0006971/annotation/page/1 hypotonic response] when placed in water, however, single mutants in a AX2 background do not show any osmoregulatory defect. Taken together, this study suggests that it is still unclear which molecules are responsible for the extracellular purinergic response in ''Dictyostelium'' and it raises the possibility that the P2x receptors may play a role in the release of intracellular Ca 2+ stores in response to an ATP stimulus from within the contractile vacuole [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19833731 (Ludlow et al. 2009)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 11-MAR-2010 PF

DDB_G0278737.summary:
The ''rckA'' gene, identified by [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12686622 Sun and Firtel (2003)], encodes a protein that contains anRGS (regulator of G protein signaling) domain and a protein kinase domain ([/ontology/go/0004672/annotation/page/1 protein kinase activity]) that is similar to bothserine/threonine and tyrosine kinases. The ''rckA'' transcript is expressed at very low levels in vegetative cells, has a sharpincrease at 4 h and a sharp decline immediately after that point. A myc-tagged RckA resides in the cytoplasm ([/ontology/go/0005737/annotation/page/1 cytoplasm]),however, in response to a cAMP gradient, the protein translocates to the cell cortex ([/ontology/go/0005938/annotation/page/1 cell cortex]).
Disruption of the ''rckA'' gene results in precocious aggregation, however, slug formation is delayed. Conversely, cellsoverexpressing ''rckA'' have delayed aggregation. Expression of the cAMP receptor [/gene/DDB_G0273397 carA-1] is not affected in mutantcells, however, expression of the cell-type-specific markers [/gene/DDB_G0277141 cotC], [/gene/DDB_G0289075 spiA], [/gene/DDB_G0277853 ecmA], and[/gene/DDB_G0269132 ecmB] is delayed. Expression of RckA bearing key point mutations in the RGS and kinase domains results in aphenotype similar to ''rckA-'' cells. Interestingly, expression of RckA-E510G (a single mutation in the RGS domain) in ''rckA-'' cells functions to complement the null phenotype. This suggests that RckA-E510G has a low level of activity compared towild-type RckA. In addition to developmental defects, ''rckA-'' cells exhibit an increased rate of chemotaxis toward a cAMPgradient, while ''rckA'' overexpressors have a reduced rate.
In an attempt to elucidate the underlying signaling pathway in which RckA works, [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12686622 Sun and Firtel (2003)] investigated interaction with several signaling molecules. The phosphatidylinositol pathway does not appear to berelated as shown with experiments involving [/gene/DDB_G0278727 pikA], [/gene/DDB_G0283081 pikB], and [/gene/DDB_G0268620 pkbA]. RckA does in factinteract genetically with G protein alpha subunits ([/ontology/go/0007189/annotation/page/1 G-protein signaling, adenylate cyclase activating pathway]). In [/gene/DDB_G0276267 gpaB] (Gα2) null cells, the RckA proteindoes not translocate to the membrane, nor does it retain kinase activity. In contrast, translocation and kinase activity areunchanged in [/gene/DDB_G0286185 gpaE] (Gα5) null cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12686622 Sun and Firtel 2003]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 03-DEC-2004 KP

DDB_G0272618.summary:
The superpathway of oxidative and non-oxidative branches of the pentose phosphate pathway serves as an alternative way to oxidize glucose. This pathway couples NADP in its oxidative reactions, thereby synthesizing NADPH. The net reaction for this superpathway is 3 glucose 6-P + 6 NADP+ + H2O <=> 6 NADPH + 6 H+ + 3 CO2 + glyceraldehyde 3-P + 2 beta-D-fructose-6-P. Enzymes involved in the pentose phosphate pathway are: glucose 6-phosphate-1-dehydrogenase ([/gene/DDB_G0273131 g6pd-1]); 6-phosphogluconolactonase ([/gene/DDB_G0292898 pgl]); 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase ([/gene/DDB_G0277885 gnd]); ribose-5-phosphate isomerase ([/gene/DDB_G0276711 rpiA]); ribulose phosphate 3-epimerase ([/gene/DDB_G0278275 rpe]); transketolase ([/gene/DDB_G0272618 tkt-1]); and transaldolase ([/gene/DDB_G0280909 tal]).
The autophagy-related protein kinase Atg1 ([/gene/DDB_G0292390 atg1]) was shown to interact with Tkt in a yeast two-hybrid assay. In addition, ''atg1'' null mutants reduced transketolase activity, suggesting the presence of a regulatory pathway between autophagy and the pentose phosphate pathway in ''Dictyostelium''. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26246495 Mesquita et al. 2015)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 02-MAR-2017 RD

DDB_G0289193.summary:
Histones form the nucleosomal core ([/ontology/go/0000786/annotation/page/1 nucleosome]) ([/ontology/go/0006334/annotation/page/1 nucleosome assembly]) that is fundamental to chromatin structure (). The histone octamer is composed of an H3-H4 tetramer (two H3-H4 dimers) coupled with an H2A-H2Btetramer (two H2A-H2B dimers). The histone H1 linker protein plays a role in packaging nucleosomes into the 30 nmfiber found in chromatin ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9177486 Bukenberger et al. 1992]).
In ''Dictyostelium discoideum'' and ''Saccharomyces cerevisiae'', only one copy of histone [/gene/DDB_G0285319 H1] appears to be present, in comparison to other eukaryotes which have multiple copies and subtypes([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7867938 Hauser et al. 1995], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9046096 Ushinsky et al.1997]). Two putative H2A family members, [/gene/DDB_G0279667 H2AX] and [/gene/DDB_G0286747 H2AZ], and three H2Adomain-containing proteins, [/gene/DDB_G0289187 H2Av1], [/gene/DDB_G0289193 H2Av2], [/gene/DDB_G0289197 H2Av3], are present in ''Dictyostelium''. Two H2B domain-containing proteins also exist inthe ''Dicty'' genome: [/gene/DDB_G0293758 H2Bv1] and [/gene/DDB_G0276273 H2Bv2]. There are three histone H3proteins, [/gene/DDB_G0267402 H3a] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9177486 Bukenberger et al. 1992]), [/gene/DDB_G0270838 H3b], and [/gene/DDB_G0271092 H3c], and two H3 domain-containing proteins, [/gene/DDB_G0291185 H3v1] and [/gene/DDB_G0277979 H3v2]. We have also identified two histone H4proteins, [/gene/DDB_G0277183 H4a] and [/gene/DDB_G0276863 H4b], which have identical protein sequences but non-identical nucleotide sequences.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 13-APR-2004 KP

DDB_G0286335.summary:
The oxidative decarboxylation of alpha-keto acids in the catabolism of the branched-chain amino acids (isoleucine, leucine, and valine), is catalyzed by the branched-chain alpha-keto acid dehydrogenase complex. This mitochondrial enzyme contains 3 catalytic components, E1, E2, and E3. E1 is a heterotetrameric alpha2 ([/gene/DDB_G0286335 bkdA]), beta2 ([/gene/DDB_G0268020 bkdB]) enzyme, with 3-methyl-2-oxobutanoate dehydrogenase activity ().
E2 is a homo-24-meric dihydrolipoyl transacylase ([/gene/DDB_G0281797 bkdC]) that forms the core of the multienzyme and binds to both E1 and E3 ([/ontology/go/5515/annotation/page/1 protein binding]). The lipoyl group of E2 is reductively 2-methylpropanoylated by E1, and then passes this 2-methylpropanoyl to coenzyme A ([/ontology/go/8415/annotation/page/1 acyltransferase activity]). In addition to the 2-methylpropanoyl group, formed when E1 acts on the oxoacid that corresponds with valine, this enzyme also transfers the 3-methylbutanoyl and S-2-methylbutanoyl groups when E1 acts on the oxoacids corresponding with leucine and isoleucine, respectively.
The E3 enzyme ([/gene/DDB_G0291648 lpd]) is adihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase ([/ontology/go/4148/annotation/page/1 dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase activity]) that is shared by three 2-oxo acid dehydrogenase multienzyme complexes. These include the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, the 2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenase complex, the glycine cleavage system, and the branched-chain 2-oxo acid dehydrogenase complex.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 02-DEC-2004 PF

DDB_G0283909.summary: Spc97 ([/gene/DDB_G0285849 spc97]) and Spc98 form a complex with gamma-tubulin ([/gene/DDB_G0271738 tubC]) that initiates microtubule polymerization in the spindle pole body of yeast. The ''Dictyostelium'' homologs are encoded by ''spc97'' and ''spc98'', respectively. Throughout the cell cycle they are found in the centrosome which functions as the main microtubule-organizing center (MTOC) [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12018385  (Daunderer and Graf, 2002)]. Under high salt conditions Spc98 co-immunoprecipitates with gamma-tubulin but Spc97 fails to co-immunoprecipitate. In other organisms all 3 proteins are strongly held in a complex. In contrast to mammalian cells, there is no dramatic increase in microtubule nucleation during mitosis of ''Dictyostelium''. At prometaphase the gamma-tubulin/Spc98 complex rapidly redistributes from the centrosomal corona to the inner surfaces of the two outer layers of the centrosome allowing the microtubule spindle to drive the two spindle poles apart [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9880333  (Ueda et al. 1999)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12018385  (Daunderer and Graf, 2002)]. Functional microtubule-nucleating units may be formed when Spc97 associates with the gamma-tubulin/Spc98 complex. About 100 different proteins contribute to centrosomal functions including the products of ''tubC'', ([/gene/DDB_G0285849 spc97]), ''spc98'', ([/gene/DDB_G0288427 cenA]), ([/gene/DDB_G0288375 lis1]), ([/gene/DDB_G0270814 nek2]), ([/gene/DDB_G0283607 eb1]), ([/gene/DDB_G0268616 cepJ]) and ([/gene/DDB_G0278809 cepG]). [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15548420  (Graf et al. 2004)]. Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 30-NOV-2017 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0290267.summary: ''gefO'' encodes a Ras guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF, RasGEF). rasGEFs are key components of signaling networks in which they activate Ras family small GTPases by promoting the exchange of GDP for GTP. Expression of ''gefO'' during growth and development is hardly detectable with the highest, but still weak, level of ''gefO'' expression at 12 hours of development. Phylogenetic analysis reveals that ''gefO'', ''gefF'' ([/gene/DDB_G0293006 gefF]), and ''gefH'' ([/gene/DDB_G0276963 gefH]) are the least similar to other RasGEFs in ''Dictyostelium'' and other organisms ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16086850 Wilkins et al. 2005)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 30-APR-2021 RD

DDB_G0280545.summary:
There are 29 genes encoding actin in ''Dictyostelium'' with amino acid identity greater than 83%, ''act1''-''act29''. Seventeen of these genes encode identical proteins: [/gene/DDB_G0289553 act1], [/gene/DDB_G0274133 act2], [/gene/DDB_G0289005 act4], [/gene/DDB_G0289663 act5], [/gene/DDB_G0274135 act6], [/gene/DDB_G0280545 act7], [/gene/DDB_G0269234 act8], [/gene/DDB_G0274601 act9], [/gene/DDB_G0288879 act11], [/gene/DDB_G0274129 act12], [/gene/DDB_G0274599 act13], [/gene/DDB_G0274137 act14], [/gene/DDB_G0272520 act15], [/gene/DDB_G0272248 act16], [/gene/DDB_G0274727 act19], [/gene/DDB_G0274285 act20], and [/gene/DDB_G0274561 act21], while [/gene/DDB_G0289811 act10], [/gene/DDB_G0275023 act22], and [/gene/DDB_G0289487 act3] respectively have 1, 4 and 11 amino acid differences compared to the 17 identical genes. The proteins encoded by [/gene/DDB_G0274131 act17], [/gene/DDB_G0289489 act18], [/gene/DDB_G0268744 act23] and [/gene/DDB_G0289505 act24]are more divergent.
Actin is a major [/ontology/go/0005200/annotation/page/1 structural constituent of cytoskeleton]. Actin is one of the most abundant proteins in ''Dictyostelium'', constituting approximately 8% of the total protein in vegetative cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/561722 Alton and Lodish et al. 1977]).Actin synthesis is developmentally regulated, peaking shortly after starvation (reviewed by [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6894564 Firtel] in 1981). The different actin genes differ in their levels of expression, with [/gene/DDB_G0274135 act6], [/gene/DDB_G0269234 act8] and [/gene/DDB_G0274129 act12] being highly expressed both during growth and development compared to [/gene/DDB_G0289005 act4], [/gene/DDB_G0289663 act5], [/gene/DDB_G0280545 act7] and [/gene/DDB_G0272248 act16] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6286214 McKeown and Firtel 1981]). DDB_G0270658.summary: Acyl-CoA Binding protein is a small, highly conserved facilitator of intracellular lipid trafficking that is encoded by ''acbA''. It is also the precursor of an intercellular peptide signal that is referred to as DBI (Diazepam Binding Inhibitor) in humans and SDF-2 (spore differentiation factor) in ''Dictyostelium'' ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15897458 Anjard and Loomis, 2005)]. SDF-2 binds to the receptor histidine kinase DhkA ([/gene/DDB_G0280961 dhkA]) and converts it to a protein phosphatase. During culmination, GABA secreted by prespore cells triggers release of AcbA from other prespore cells. The protein has to diffuse to prestalk cells near the top of the rising stalk to be processed by the extracellular protease TagC ([/gene/DDB_G0286121 tagC]) and generate the 34 amino acid peptide that is SDF-2 ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9473320 Anjard et al. 1998)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15897458 Anjard and Loomis, 2005)]. When SDF-2 binds DhkA on prespore cells, the response regulator region of the cAMP phosphodiesterase RegA ([/gene/DDB_G0284331 regA]) is dephosphorylated leading to reduced enzymatic activity. The resulting accumulation of cAMP stimulates PKA ([/gene/DDB_G0283907 pkaC], [/gene/DDB_G0279413 pkaR]) activity leading to rapid sporulation. The SDF-2 cascade is initiated by a steroid binding to the G protein-coupled-receptor GrlA ([/gene/DDB_G0271684 grlA]) that signals GABA release and AcbA secretion and processing ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19176583 Anjard et al. 2009)]. AcbA lacks the N-terminal signal sequence necessary for classical secretion and is dependent on the membrane-associated protein GRASP ([/gene/DDB_G0293248 grpA]) for unconventional secretion ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17655921 Kinseth et al. 2007)]. Autophagy is involved in the unconventional secretion of AcbA in the pathway leading to SDF-2 signaling. AcbA is found in vesicles just beneath the plasma membrane until it is released to the intercellular space in response to GABA ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20472692 Cabral et al. 2010)]. Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 05-JAN-2017 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0269238.summary:
''rab11A'' encodes a guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G protein) of the Rab family of small GTPases. G proteins are key components of signal transduction networks in which they function as molecular signaling switches, binding to GDP in the off state while binding GTP in the on state. Guanine nucleotide-exchange factors (GEFs) promote the exchange of GDP for GTP on Rab GTPases thus activating them, while GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) inactivate Rab GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP. CnrF ([/gene/DDB_G0276119 cnrF]) displays GAP activity toward rab11A ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24335649 Parkinson, et al. 2013]). Disgorgin ([/gene/DDB_G0280955 dsgg]) exhibits weak GAP activity toward Rab11A. Drainin ([/gene/DDB_G0269130 phgA]) interacts with Rab11A in a GTP-dependent manner and serves as an effector of Rab11A. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18636095 Du et al. 2008]). ''rab11A'' is expressed at constant levels throughout growth and development and is associated with contractile vacuole complex membranes ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11686306 Harris et al. 2001]). Proteomic analysis reveals that Rab11A is also located in phagocytic vesicles ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16926386 Gotthardt, et al. 2006]), the Legionella-containing vacuole ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24373249 Hoffmann et al. 2013]), [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28183814 (Schmolders et al. 2017)], and ''M. marinum''-containing vacuoles (PMID:33531393; Hanna, ''et al.'' 2021).
''rab11A'' is involved in signaling networks that regulate contractile vacuole function. Dominant-negative Rab11A cells have altered contractile vacuole morphology and defective contractile vacuole function. Mutant cells are rounded with enlarged, swollen contractile vacuoles with some lysis of cells. There is also an enhanced rate of phagocytosis in Rab11A dominant-negative cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11686306 Harris et al. 2001]). Rab11A is activated in response to hypo-osmotic stress and recruits Drainin to the contractile vacuole membrane. Rab8A ([/gene/DDB_G0280043 rab8A]) and its Rab GAP disgorgin function downstream of drainin and rab11A to mediate contractile vacuole-plasma membrane fusion which is then followed by the discharge of water out of the cell ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18636095 Du, et al. 2008]). Rab11A is found in a complex with the ion channel receptor P2XA ([/gene/DDB_G0272004 p2xA]) and the calcium-regulated Rab GAP cnrF ([/gene/DDB_G0276119 cnrF]). Rab11A overexpressing cells display a phenotype similar to those of both ''p2xA'' and ''cnrF'' null cells: severe defects in hypo-osmotic response and large numbers of small vacuoles that fail to fuse with the plasma membrane. Both ''p2xA'' and ''cnrF'' null cells also contain higher levels of activated Rab11A, suggesting that P2XA inhibits Rab11A activity through the Rab GAP CnrF. These results suggest a model in which P2XA activation results in vacuolar calcium release, which triggers activation of CnrF Rab GAP activity and subsequent downregulation of Rab11a to allow vacuole fusion and contractile vacuole discharge ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24335649 Parkinson, et al. 2013]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 08-FEB-2021 RD

DDB_G0287855.summary:
PirA (PIR121) is a member of the Scar/WAVE complex, consisting of (Scar) ([/gene/DDB_G0285253 scrA]), PirA, ([/gene/DDB_G0279175 hspc300]), ([/gene/DDB_G0267956 abiA]), and ([/gene/DDB_G0274519 napA]). In migrating cells, the Scar/WAVE complex regulates the production of lamellipods and pseudopods through Arp2/3 complex activation. The Scar/WAVE complex localizes to the front of pseudopods and the tips of filopods, cell-cell contact zones, and the cell leading edge ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22891261 Veltman et al. 2012]). PirA interacts with Rac GTPase ([/gene/DDB_G0277869 rac1A]), ([/gene/DDB_G0268622 rac1B]), ([/gene/DDB_G0282365 rac1C]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30393033 Schaks et al. 2018]) and polarity regulator Leep1 ([/gene/DDB_G0293920 leep1]) (Yang, et al 2021, PMID:33978708). PirA and NapA also interact to form an independent heterodimeric subcomplex prior to formation of the mature Scar/WAVE complex ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21701600 Linkner et al. 2011]).
In ''pirA'' null mutants in an AX3 background, Scar is almost undetectable by Western blotting. ''pirA'' null mutant cells are abnormally large, have a high F-actin content, and extend pseudopods at more than three times the rate of wild type cells but have a decreased overall cell speed. Double ''pirA''/''scrA'' null mutants show none of the phenotypes exhibited by ''pirA'' single mutants, and instead appear to have a simple ''scrA'' null phenotype ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12956949 Blagg et al. 2003]). Disruption of ''pirA'' in an NC4A2 background however produces opposing phenotypes: ''pirA'' knockouts are smaller, rounder and make almost no discernible pseudopods, but they can chemotax efficiently ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16822579 Pollitt et al. 2006]). In ''pirA'' null mutants in an AX2 background (''pirA''/AX2 null) Scar, AbiA, and Hspc300 levels are severely decreased. ''pirA''/AX2 null cells largely lacked macropinocytic cups, filopods and pseudopods, but formed many bleb-like protrusions at the cell front. ''pirA''/AX2 null cells also have defects in cytokinesis and cell motility ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28889942 Litschko et al. 2017]).
GTP-bound Rac1 interacts with PirA, and PirA mutants in which the Rac1 binding site is deleted reveal that Rac1 binding with PirA is required for Scar/WAVE complex activation ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30393033 Schaks et al. 2018]). Leep1 interacts with both ScrA and PirA, and the similarity in phenotypes between overexpression of Leep1 and disruption of Scar suggests that Leep1 acts as a negative regulator of the Scar/WAVE complex. (Yang, et al 2021, PMID:33978708).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 18-JAN-2022 RD

DDB_G0273059.summary:
Members of the casein kinase I (CK1) family ([/ontology/go/0004681/annotation/page/1 casein kinase I activity]) of serine/threonine kinases have been implicated in manycellular processes. Casein kinases have been shown to phosphorylate the 14-3-3 ([/gene/DDB_G0269138 fttB]) protein inmammals, play a role in Wnt signaling in ''Xenopus laevis'' and ''Caenorhabditis elegans'', and maintaincircadian rhythms in ''Drosophila melanogaster''. Additionally, CK1 plays a role in DNA repair ([/ontology/go/0006281/annotation/page/1 DNA repair])in ''Saccharomyces cerevisiae'' and ''Schizosaccharomyces pombe'' ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10880352 Moreno-Bueno et al. 2000]).
Two casein kinase I family members have been identified in ''Dictyostelium discoideum'', ''cak1'' and [/gene/DDB_G0292354 DDB_G0292354]. Cak1 is highly similar to CK1s in yeast and in metazoans. DDB0216336 is a putative caseinkinase I that is highly similar to the CK1 subfamily tau-tubulin kinase (TTBK) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12471243 Manninget al. 2002]). The Cak1 protein has been shown to phosphorylate casein when it is expressed in''E. coli'' cells, and localizes to both the cytoplasm ([/ontology/go/0005737/annotation/page/1 cytoplasm]) and the nucleus ([/ontology/go/0005634/annotation/page/1 nucleus]) inimmunofluorescence assays. Null mutations and overexpression of a dominant-negative form of Cak1 fail to produce viable cells, indicating that this protein may be essential for growth.Overexpression of wild-type Cak1 results in decreased sensitivity to the DNA-damaging agent hydroxyurea; this suggests a role for Cak1 in DNA repair ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10880352 Moreno-Bueno et al. 2000]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 05-MAY-2004 KP

DDB_G0287587.summary: Starved Dictyostelium cells aggregate into groups of roughly 10(5) cells. Cells in which the ''smlA'' gene is disrupted form small aggregates. The ''smlA'' mRNA is expressed in vegetative and early developing cells, and decreases at about 10 hours of development. The sequence of the cDNA and the derived amino acid sequence of the SmlA protein show no significant similarity to any known sequence. Immunofluorescence and staining of Western blots of cell fractions indicates that SmlA is a 35x10(3) Mr cytosolic protein present in all vegetative and developing cells and is absent from ''smlA''- cells. The absence of SmlA does not affect the growth rate, cell cycle, differentiation, or developmental speed of cells. Synergy experiments indicate that mixing 5% smlA cells with wild-type cells will cause the wild-type cells to form smaller fruiting bodies and aggregates. SmlA appears to regulate the secretion or processing of a secreted factor that regulates aggregate size, counting factor (CF) [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8787732 (Brock et al.1996)]. Compared with wild-type or [/gene/DDB_G0274597 ctnA] countin cells, ''smlA''- cells have large cAMP pulses and small cGMP pulses [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11371560 (Tang et al.2001)]. ''smlA'' null cells have decreased adhesion, increased motility, increased amounts of polymerized actin and the ABP-120 actin-crosslinking protein, as well as increased phosphorylation and redistribution of myosin ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11090633 Roisin-Bouffay et al.2002], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11818526 Tang et al.2002]). The presence of adenosine rescued the ''smlA'' null decreased aggregate size phenotype and induced formation of larger aggregates ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22269093 Jaiswal et al. 2012)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 23-OCT-2003 PG

DDB_G0272110.summary:
The ''gskA'' gene encodes the ''Dictyostelium'' homologue of glycogen synthase kinase 3 (GSK3), a highly conserved serine/threonine kinase. It is required for the cAMP induced formation of prespore cells and inhibition of stalk cells. Disruption of ''gskA'' creates a mutant that aggregates but forms few spores and an abnormally high number of stalk cells [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7813009 (Harwood et al. 1995)]. Extracellular cAMP activates GskA through the cAMP receptor cAR3 ([/gene/DDB_G0277829 carC]) [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9847246 (Plyte et al. 1999)] and the tyrosine kinase ZAK1 ([/gene/DDB_G0276025 zakA]) [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10571182 (Kim et al. 1999)], stimulating prespore differentiation. A second receptor, cAR4 ([/gene/DDB_G0277831 carD]), appears to negatively regulate GskA [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9284050 (Ginsburg and Kimmel, 1997)], to promote prestalk formation. GskA itself was shown to phosphorylate STATa ([/gene/DDB_G0281381 dstA]) and enhance its nuclear export [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11032815 (Ginger et al. 2000)]. There is also evidence that GskA phosphorylation activates the beta-catenin homologue aardvark ([/gene/DDB_G0288877 aarA]) [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11130075 (Crimson et al. 2000)].
It has been proposed that cAMP receptor-mediated pathways converge at GskA suggesting that the anterior (prestalk) / posterior (prespore) axis of ''Dictyostelium'' is regulated by an ancient mechanism that is shared by the Wnt/Fz circuits for dorsoventral patterning during early ''Xenopus'' development, and establishing ''Drosophila'' segment polarity [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9284050 (Ginsburg and Kimmel, 1997)]. In ''Dictyostelium'' it has been suggested that a single ligand, cAMP, activating receptors cAR3 and cAR4 with distinct affinities, alternatively either activates or inhibits, respectively, GskA-specific activity [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10980428 (Kim and Kimmel, 2000)].
While the original ''gskA''-null mutant was created in the uracil auxotroph DH1 strain, Schilde ''et al.'' deleted the gene in AX2. This had the advantage of creating a mutant with a milder phenotype, where a significant number of cells progress through development with relatively normal spore/stalk cell proportions. In this AX2/''gskA''-null strain, early development is accelerated but slug migration is impaired. Consistent with the accelerated early development, cell-specific markers [/gene/DDB_G0277853 ecmA], [/gene/DDB_G0269132 ecmB], and [/gene/DDB_G0267412 pspA] are precociously expressed. ''ecmB'' expression in wildtype is restricted to the slug tip, just as they commit themselves to stalk cell differentiation. In the AX2/''gskA''-null mutant, however, ''ecmB'' is expressed throughout the prestalk region of the slug, suggesting that ''gskA'' is involved in a repressive signalling pathway preventing premature stalk cell commitment. Microarray analysis identified the large gene C2 family ([/gene/DDB_G0280847 2C]) that requires ''gskA'' for optimal expression, suggesting that ''gskA'' may also play an activator role [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15342480 (Schilde et al. 2004)].
''gskA'' null mutants have aberrant aggregation and defective chemotaxis toward both cAMP and folate. In addition, ''gskA'' was shown to be required for both phosphatidylinositol 3,4,5-trisphosphate (PIP3) and target of rapamycin complex 2 (TORC2)-mediated signalling. Furthermore, ''gskA'' null mutant cells do not generate cAMP pulses during aggregation, demonstrating that GskA plays a major role in the regulation of chemotaxis and early ''Dictyostelium'' development [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20534815 (Teo et al. 2010)]. Using phosphoproteomics ([/gene/DDB_G0274383 pdeD]), ([/gene/DDB_G0283767 dct]) and ([/gene/DDB_G0293044 sogA]) were identified as substrates which are phosphorylated by GskA. Knockout mutants of all 3 genes are defective in chemotaxis. The carboxylesterase D2 ([/gene/DDB_G0276969 D2B]) is a downstream effector of GskA [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29626371 (Baumgardner et al. 2018)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 29-MAY-2007 PF

DDB_G0273533.summary:
A family of four highly related G-protein coupled receptors, CAR1, CAR2, CAR3, and CAR4 (genes ''[/gene/DDB_G0273397 carA-1]'' ''[/gene/DDB_G0288179 carB]'', ''[/gene/DDB_G0277829 carC]'', ''[/gene/DDB_G0277831 carD]'', respectively), mediate developmental responses to cAMP [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2049880 (Saxe et al., 1991]; [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7496377 Ginsburg et al., 1995)]. CAR1 and CAR3 have 56% amino acid identity and show approximately equal affinity to cAMP in vitro [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1537842 (Johnson et al., 1992)]. Both are coupled to trimeric G proteins with the Galpha2 subunit (gene ''[/gene/DDB_G0276267 gpaB]''). CAR1 is expressed immediately after the initiation of development. Single-molecule imaging using TIRF microscopy showed that CAR1 is uniformly distributed and diffuses rapidly in the plane of the membrane. The rate constant for dissociation of cAMP from CAR1 was found to be about 1 second [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11679673 (Ueda et al., 2001)]. CAR1 is phosphorylated upon persistent stimulation with cAMP resulting in internalization on a timescale of 5 min followed by degradation after 13 min [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21541374 (Serge et al. 2013)]. cAMP induces the cAR1-mediated dissociation of G protein subunits to a similar extent in both undifferentiated and differentiated cells. Dissociation is stimulated by caffeine and requires the microtubule network [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29698704 (Islam et al. 2018)].
Cells lacking CAR1 fail to aggregate or express developmentally regulated genes that are induced by pulses of cAMP [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1692327 (Sun et al., 1990)]. Stimulation of cAMP and cGMP accumulation in response to addition of cAMP is lost in these cells. However, they can still respond to high concentrations of cAMP by using the CAR3 receptor [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9578623 (Kim et al., 1998)]. A double ''carA/carC'' mutant lacking both receptors shows no response to cAMP and an abolished synthesis of cGMP [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7949426 (Insall et al., 1994)]. Using a non-phosphorylatable carA mutant, Brzostowski and colleagues demonstrated that receptor phosphorylation is required to regulate adenylyl cyclase adaptation, long-range oscillatory cAMP wave production and cytoskeletal actin responses [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23902692 (Brzostowski et al. 2013) ]. Sites critical for cAMP binding, coupling to G proteins and regulated phosphorylation were delineated by PCR-mediated random mutagenesis [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8999903 (Kim et al., 1997]; [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8999904 Milne et al., 1997)].
Binding of cAMP to CAR1 results in the transient activation of TorC2 and the adenylyl cyclase ACA through a Ras pathway [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20660630 (Cai et al., 2010]; [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23657816 Liao et al., 2013)]. An incoherent feedforward loop in which ligand bound CAR1 activates both a Ras-GEF and a Ras-GAP can result in perfect adaptation of activated Ras about 20 seconds after addition of cAMP in a spatially uniform manner [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22215733 (Takeda et al., 2012)]. The LEGI model points out that membrane localization of the activator (GEF) and free diffusion of the inhibitor (GAP) can generate a spatial gradient of activated Ras within the cells in response to an external gradient of cAMP [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10221901 (Parent and Devreotes, 1999)]. Ultrasensitivity resulting from the opposing activities of GEF and GAP can dramatically amplify the signal and ensure that cells only respond to constant or rising concentrations of cAMP and that they do not respond to the decreasing concentrations of cAMP in the back of a wave [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25249632 (Skoge et al., 2014)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated 08-DEC-2015 PF; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0271502.summary:
Seven BEACH domain-containing proteins have been identified in the ''Dictyostelium'' genome: [/gene/DDB_G0269150 lvsA], [/gene/DDB_G0271504 lvsB], [/gene/DDB_G0280971 lvsC], [/gene/DDB_G0271502 lvsD], [/gene/DDB_G0282925 lvsE], [/gene/DDB_G0284333 lvsF], and [/gene/DDB_G0268088 lvsG].
Disruption mutants were created in ''lvsA-F''. Phenotypic analyses of these mutants indicate LvsC-F proteins are not required for cytokinesis, osmoregulation (contrary to [/gene/DDB_G0269150 lvsA]), lysosomal traffic (unlike [/gene/DDB_G0271504 lvsB]) or other processes such as growth and development ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3308452 Wang et al. 2002]). Howver, data from highthroughput analysis of mutants indicates that inertions in the ''lvsD'' gene causes aberrant cAMP wave formation, aberrant culmination, and aberrant vegetative growth ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17659086 Sawai et al. 2007])
A double mutant in [/gene/DDB_G0280955 DDB_G0280955] and ''lvsD'' enhances the large contractile vacuole phenotype of disgorgin-; whereas overexpression of GFP-lvsD suppresses it, suggesting ''lvsD'' is involved in the organization of the contractile vacuole. Since LvsD is cytosolic, it is possible that it interacts with [/gene/DDB_G0269150 lvsA] to inhibit its role in contractile vacuole organization([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18636095 Du et al. 2008]). Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 21-NOV-2008 PG

DDB_G0269240.summary:
''racH'' encodes a guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G protein) of the Rho family of small GTPases. G proteins are key components of signal transduction networks in which they function as molecular signaling switches, binding to GDP in the off state while binding GTP in the on state. Guanine nucleotide-exchange factors (GEFs) promote the exchange of GDP for GTP on Ras GTPases thus activating them, while GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) inactivate Ras GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP. Possible GEFs for RacH include RGBARG ([/gene/DDB_G0269934 rgbA]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/32531280 Buckley et al. 2020]), GxcC ([/gene/DDB_G0284845 gxcC]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23363311 Plak et al. 2013]) and gxcDD ([/gene/DDB_G0279733 gxcDD]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17584488 Mondal et al. 2007]).
RacH is a key mediator in signaling pathways that regulate vesicle trafficking ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26940518 Rivero et al. 2016]). ''racH'' mRNA is expressed as two transcripts, both of which are undetectable at the vegetative stage, but expression increases at the onset of development. ''racH'' expression reaches a maxium level during the aggregation stage followed by continued, but decreased expression during later stages of development. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11201251 Okuwa et al. 2001]), ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11222756 Rivero et al. 2001]). RacH localizes predominantly to membranes of the endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus and nuclear envelope. ''racH'' null mutants have defects in pinocytosis, exocytosis, the acidification of early endosomes and the secretion of acid phosphatase from the lysosome. In addition, the distribution of the post-lysosomal marker vacuolin ([/gene/DDB_G0289485 vacA]) is altered in ''racH'' null mutants, but growth, cytokinesis, cell motility and chemotaxis are normal. In a cell-free system, RacH stimulates actin polymerization, suggesting that RacH is involved in actin-based trafficking of vesicular compartments ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17004322 Somesh et al. 2006]). ''racH'' also plays a role in host-pathogen interactions. ''racH'' null mutant cells are more susceptible to infection by ''Mycobacterium marinum'' ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17587329 Hagedorn et al. 2007]) and ''Legionella pneumophila'' ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21655438 Balest et al. 2011]). RacH is also involved in the release of bacteria from the infected cell. ''racH'' mutant cells are deficient in intercellular spreading of mycobacteria and lack an F-actin based structure termed the ejectosome that is responsible for the nonlytic release of cytosolic mycobacteria ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19325115 Hagedorn et al. 2009]). ''atg1'' ([/gene/DDB_G0292390 atg1]) null mutants are also defective in intercellular transmission of mycobacteria, indicating that a functioning autophagy pathway is required for the ejection of mycobacterium from ''Dictyostelium discoideum'' ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25646440 Gerstenmaier et al. 2015]). ''Yersinia pestis'' YopE blocks the effects of overexpressing RacH, suggesting that RacH could be a target of YopE ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19602247 Vlahou et al. 2009]). Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 17-JUN-2020 RD

DDB_G0276829.summary:
[/gene/DDB_G0272837 ifkA] and ''ifkB'' encode homologs of a kinase that phosphorylate the translation initiation factor eIF2alpha ([/ontology/go/0004686/annotation/page/1 elongation factor-2 kinase activity]), responsible for [/ontology/go/0006446/annotation/page/1 regulation of translational initiation]. The two Ifk proteins possess all of the hallmarks of typical GCN2 proteins, including the characteristic kinase domain and the HisRS domain. IfkB is unique among GCN2-like proteins in that it does not possess the amino terminal pseudokinase domain. ''ifkB'' expression is constant during growth and development ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12697064 Fang et al. 2003]).
In ''Dictyostelium'', two members of the GCN2 (also known as PEK, pancreatic eukaryotic translation initiation factor kinase) family of protein kinases have been identified: [/gene/DDB_G0272837 ifkA] and[/gene/DDB_G0276829 ifkB]. Putative proteins belonging to the GCN2 family are: [/gene/DDB_G0276043 ifkC], [/gene/DDB_G0283065 DDB_G0283065], [/gene/DDB_G0268642 DDB_G0268642], [/gene/DDB_G0292734 DDB_G0292734], and [/gene/DDB_G0292734 DDB_G0292734].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 14-NOV-2003 PG

DDB_G0278907.summary:
Mob1 was originally identified in ''Saccharomyces cerevisiae'' as a binder of [/gene/DDB_G0280995 mps1], a kinase involved in mitotic regulation ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9436989 Luca and Winey 1998]). Mob1 serves as a substrate for Mps1 and functions to regulate the NDR kinases (nuclear Dbf2-related, [/gene/DDB_G0278457 ndrA], [/gene/DDB_G0288753 ndrB], [/gene/DDB_G0284839 ndrC], and [/gene/DDB_G0289543 ndrD]) in mammals, which are involved in cell proliferation ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15067004 Devroe et al.2004]). The Mob1 family of proteins are highly conserved but have no characterized function. In ''Dictyostelium'', three Mob1-like proteins exist: [/gene/DDB_G0278907 mobA], [/gene/DDB_G0292758 mobB], and [/gene/DDB_G0293706 mobC]. A fourth protein, [/gene/DDB_G0283625 DDB_G0283625], contains a Mob1-like motif, however, it does not cluster with Mob1 proteins from other species.
MobA has been shown to bind to [/gene/DDB_G0278457 ndrA] [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21134080 (Kastner et al. 2011)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 15-JUN-2012 PF

DDB_G0290079.summary: A branched heteropolysaccharide, which consists of galactose and N-acetylgalactosamine, is a primary constituent of the Dictyostelium spore coat. [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18996984  West et al. 2009] found that disruption of either ''pgtB'' or ''pgtC'' reduced synthase-like activity and blocked heteropolysaccharide formation. Spore coats from an ''pgtB'' ''pgtC'' double null mutant expressed reduced levels of crystalline cellulose, and also contained elevated levels of selected coat proteins. Mutant spores were unusually susceptible to hypertonic collapse and damage by detergent or hypertonic stress. These results suggest that the heteropolysaccharide is essential for spore integrity, which can be explained by a role in the formation of crystalline cellulose and regulation of the protein content of the coat.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 09-OCT-2014 RD

DDB_G0269214.summary: The ABC superfamily of genes is one of the largest in the genomes of both bacteria and eukaryotes. The proteins encoded by these genes all carry a characteristic 200- to 250-amino-acid ATP-binding cassette that gives them their family name ([/ontology/go/0042626/annotation/page/1 ATPase activity, coupled to transmembrane movement of substances]). In bacteria they are mostly involved in nutrient import, while in eukaryotes many are involved in export ([/ontology/go/0006810/annotation/page/1 transport]). Seven different families have been defined in eukaryotes based on sequence homology, domain topology, and function. Sequences from the well-advanced ''Dictyostelium'' genome project have allowed to recognize 71 members of this superfamily (including one on the chromosome 2 duplication). The ABCG family is characterized by the ABC domain preceding the transmembrane domain ([/ontology/go/0016021/annotation/page/1 integral to membrane]). All of the members of this family in animals are half-transporters while all of the fungal members are full transporters with two ABC-transmembrane units. No members of this family are found in bacteria. ''Dictyostelium'' and ''Arabidopsis'' have members of both types ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12456012 Anjard and Loomis 2002]). Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 18-OCT-2004 PG

DDB_G0273977.summary: Nascent proteins that contain a signal peptide, and are therefore secreted, are recognized by the[/ontology/go/0005786/annotation/page/1 signal recognition particle, endoplasmic reticulum targeting] (SRP), which is composed of 7S RNA plus [/gene/DDB_G0267622 srp9], [/gene/DDB_G0272590 srp14-1],[/gene/DDB_G0275211 srp19], [/gene/DDB_G0275455 srp54], [/gene/DDB_G0285821 srp68], and [/gene/DDB_G0291412 srp72]. The SRPcontains two domains: the Alu domain (SRP9/14) functions to arrest translational elongation and the Sdomain (SRP54, SRP19, and SRP68/72) plays a role in ribosome-nascent chain (RNC) recognition and SRP receptorbinding. After the RNC is bound, the SRP binds via SRP54 to the SRP receptor, an alpha/beta heterodimermade up of [/gene/DDB_G0277377 srpR] and [/gene/DDB_G0278543 srpRB] in the [/ontology/go/0005783/annotation/page/1 endoplasmic reticulum] (reviewed in [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15718142 Halic and Beckmann 2005] and [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16092520 Pool2005]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 17-NOV-2005 KP

DDB_G0273067.summary:
The lectin Discoidin I binds N-acetylgalactosamine and galactose [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/4517669 (Rosen et al. 1973)]. Discoidin I subunits associate to form a tetramer [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/4858710 (Simpson et al. 1974)] and are expressed from a family of 3 different genes: ''dscA'' ([/gene/DDB_G0273063 dscA-1]) ([/gene/DDB_G0273919 dscA-2]), ''dscC'' ([/gene/DDB_G0273065 dscC-1]) ([/gene/DDB_G0273885 dscC-2]) and ''dscD''. [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6279874 (Poole et al. 1981)]. Monomeric discoidin I is located mainly in the cytosol, while the tetrameric form of discoidin I is detected in multilamellar bodies and is externalized during aggregation [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2581974 (Barondes et al. 1985)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8416797 (Fukuzawa et al. 1993)]. Discoidin I gene expression is induced by prestarvation factor (PSF) and conditioned medium factor, ([/gene/DDB_G0275007 cmfA]) but is down-regulated by cAMP [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7641976 (Blusch et al. 1995)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2049883 (Rathi et al. 1991)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1663029 (Gomer et al. 1991)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2196444 (Vauti et al. 1990)]. Mutants defective in discoidin I fail to stream during aggregation, implicating discoidin I in cell-substrate adhesion [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6509552 (Springer et al. 1984)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/4075402 (Crowley et al. 1985)]. In addition, discoidin I is thought to play an intracellular role, as mutants in which discoidin genes are not expressed also have an abnormally centered microtubule organizing center and more rounded cell morphology, suggesting a role for discoidins in cytoskeleton organization during aggregation [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1334012 (Alexander et al. 1992)].
''Dictyostelium discoideum'' strains that carry bacteria secrete approx. 80 times higher levels of DscA and DscC than non-carriers. Secreted DscA binds to ''Klebsiella pneumoniae''. DscA binding protects bacteria from extracellular killing, promotes their internalization and prolongs their retention in both ''Dictyostelium discoideum'' and mammalian cells. Plant lectins induce the same response, suggesting that modified uptake and persistence of lectin-coated bacteria in eukaryotic cells is a general phenomenon, termed lectin-induced modified bacterial internalization [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30049880 (Dinh et al. 2018)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 24-AUG-2018 RD
