DDB_G0293834.summary:
The WASP/SCAR family of adaptor proteins regulates actin polymerization by coupling Rho-family GTPases to the activation of the Arp2/3 complex [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15506982 (Blagg and Insall, 2004)]. The homolog of WASP (Wiscott-Aldrich syndrome protein) in ''Dictyostelium'' is encoded by ''wasA''. Cells expressing reduced levels of ''wasA'' showed reduced F-actin levels and significant defects in organizing polarized F-actin assembly, resulting in an inability to establish axial polarity during chemotaxis. WASP preferentially localizes at the leading edge and uropod of chemotaxing cells [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15728724 (Myers et al. 2005)]. In wild type cells, WASP is involved in vesicle trafficking from the Golgi to the surface membrane [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19409937 (Lee et al. 2009)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20573979 (Veltman and Insall, 2010)]. WASP has been seen at clathrin-coated pits rather than associated with pseudopods. However, in SCAR-depleted mutants ([/gene/DDB_G0285253 scrA]), WASP replaces the functions of SCAR and localizes to pseudopods where it stimulates the Arp2/3 complex to initiate dendritic growth of F-actin. [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22891261 (Veltman et al. 2012)]. Cells lacking both SCAR and WASP are unable to grow, make pseudopods or migrate using blebs, however actin polymerization is normal. Pseudopods are replaced in double SCAR/WASP mutants by aberrant filopods, induced by the formin dDia2 ([/gene/DDB_G0285589 forH]). Further disruption of dDia2 in SCAR/WASP cells restored the ability to generate blebs, allowing them to migrate. However the triple knockout cells still contain near-normal F-actin levels revealing that SCAR, WASP and dDia2 compete for actin [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29191847 (Davidson et al. 2017)].
WASP both regulates, and is regulated by, activated Rac GTPases RacC ([/gene/DDB_G0293526 racC]) and Rac1A ([/gene/DDB_G0277869 rac1A]). WASP interacts with activated Rac via its CRIB motif, and this interaction is required for WASP to generate pseudopods in the absence of SCAR/WAVE. However this interaction also provides a means for WASP to remove activated Rac from the membrane via endocytosis. Thus WASP contributes to front-rear cell polarity by controlling localization and cellular levels of activated Rac. [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31786060 (Amato et al. 2019)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 08-APR-2020 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis annotation contributions: PMID 22891261 Robert Insall.

DDB_G0287125.summary: Profilins are small, well-conserved, actin-binding proteins that also bind other proteins as well as phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2). Dictyostelium has three genes encoding profilin, ''proA'', ([/gene/DDB_G0286187 proB]) and ([/gene/DDB_G0271142 proC]) [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1725525  (Haugwitz et al. 1991)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17467078  (Arasada et al. 2007)]. ''proA'' is expressed during early development giving a peak of mRNA abundance at T=11 hrs [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25887420  (Rosengarten et al. 2015)]. ''In vitro'', profilin I raises the critical concentration of G-actin necessary for F-actin formation and delays the onset of elongation of F-actin [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1725525  (Haugwitz et al. 1991)]. When profilin I binds G-actin it stimulates the exchange of ADP by ATP in G-actin which allows it to polymerize. Single mutants in which ''proA'' is inactivated show no significant defects, but double mutants with null mutations in both ''proA'' and ''proB'' have growth and developmental defects. The cells do not grow in suspension and become multinucleated when grown on solid supports. Aggregation proceeds well but mounds do not culminate and spores are not formed by the double mutants. F-actin is 60% more abundant in the double mutants than in wild type cells [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7954798  (Haugwitz et al. 1994)]. In addition, profilin double mutants are defective in macropinocytosis, fluid phase efflux, and secretion of lysosomal enzymes, but are more efficient in phagocytosis than wt cells. Disruption of the ''lmpA'' ([/gene/DDB_G0267406 lmpA]) gene in the profilin double null background suppressed the endocytic defects and phagocytic increases, suggesting that LmpA may act as a negative regulator of profilin [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10848626  (Temesvari et al. 2000)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11683394  (Seastone et al. 2001)]. Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 17-DEC-2019 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0292266.summary:
''amdA'' encodes AMP deaminase which functions in the interconversion of purines ([/ontology/go/0003876/annotation/page/1 AMP deaminase activity]), ([/ontology/go/0009167/annotation/page/1 purine ribonucleoside monophosphate metabolic process]). ''amdA'' is contitutively expressed in ''Dictyostelium''. Disruption of the ''amdA'' gene results in short, thick stalks and glassy sori with less than 5% the normal number of spores, indicating a defect in [/ontology/go/0030435/annotation/page/1 sporulation]. These cell also have a significantly increased proportion of prestalk cells of the pstA type. This alteration in cell-type proportioning is a cell-autonomous consequence of the loss of AMP deaminase ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11784104 Chae et al. 2002]).
A recently characterized ''Dictyostelium'' cell type, the aspidocyte, is highly resistant to detergents and develops in the presence of a number of toxic chemicals, including heavy metals, inhibitors of sterol, protein or RNA synthesis and of mitosis. ''amdA''- cells form aspidocyte more readily than wild type cells. Since ''amdA''- cells have higher AMP levels compared to wild type cells, this could be a signal for aspidocyte differentiation ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17259634 Serafimidis et al. 2007]). Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 30-NOV-2004 PG

DDB_G0272248.summary:
There are 29 genes encoding actin in ''Dictyostelium'' with amino acid identity greater than 83%, ''act1''-''act29''. Seventeen of these genes encode identical proteins: [/gene/DDB_G0289553 act1], [/gene/DDB_G0274133 act2], [/gene/DDB_G0289005 act4], [/gene/DDB_G0289663 act5], [/gene/DDB_G0274135 act6], [/gene/DDB_G0280545 act7], [/gene/DDB_G0269234 act8], [/gene/DDB_G0274601 act9], [/gene/DDB_G0288879 act11], [/gene/DDB_G0274129 act12], [/gene/DDB_G0274599 act13], [/gene/DDB_G0274137 act14], [/gene/DDB_G0272520 act15], [/gene/DDB_G0272248 act16], [/gene/DDB_G0274727 act19], [/gene/DDB_G0274285 act20], and [/gene/DDB_G0274561 act21], while [/gene/DDB_G0289811 act10], [/gene/DDB_G0275023 act22], and [/gene/DDB_G0289487 act3] respectively have 1, 4 and 11 amino acid differences compared to the 17 identical genes. The proteins encoded by [/gene/DDB_G0274131 act17], [/gene/DDB_G0289489 act18], [/gene/DDB_G0268744 act23] and [/gene/DDB_G0289505 act24]are more divergent.
Actin is a major [/ontology/go/0005200/annotation/page/1 structural constituent of cytoskeleton]. Actin is one of the most abundant proteins in ''Dictyostelium'', constituting approximately 8% of the total protein in vegetative cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/561722 Alton and Lodish et al. 1977]).Actin synthesis is developmentally regulated, peaking shortly after starvation (reviewed by [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6894564 Firtel] in 1981). The different actin genes differ in their levels of expression, with [/gene/DDB_G0274135 act6], [/gene/DDB_G0269234 act8] and [/gene/DDB_G0274129 act12] being highly expressed both during growth and development compared to [/gene/DDB_G0289005 act4], [/gene/DDB_G0289663 act5], [/gene/DDB_G0280545 act7] and [/gene/DDB_G0272248 act16] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6286214 McKeown and Firtel 1981]). Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 19-SEP-2003 PG

DDB_G0278661.summary: TSET is the latest addition to trafficking proteins, which is ancient but frequently lost or reduced in evolution. The TSET complex is a heterohexamer and was named for the protein subunits in the complex, TSPOON (sigma-like), TPLATE (beta-like), TCUP (mu-like), TSAUCER (alpha, beta, gamma, delta, epsilon, zeta-like), TTRAY1, and TTRAY2. This ancient adaptor complex (AP) was identified in organisms such as Dictyostelids and land plants, such as ''Arabidopsis''. Only the TCUP subunit has been retained in fungi and animals, in mammals it has evolved into the cargo adaptor muniscin. A TSPOON-GFP fusion (gene tstD) has been shown to physically bind the 5 other TSET subunits. The TTRAY subunits are beta-propeller / alpha-solenoid proteins and form the scaffold for the TSPOON, TPLATE, TCUP, TSAUCER, heterotetramer. TIRF microscopy showed a punctate temporary localization of the complex to the plasma membran [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24867644  (Hirst et al. 2014)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated,, 11-DEC-2018 PF

DDB_G0276101.summary: Members of the structural maintentance of chromosomes (SMC) family are involved in manybiological processes, including sister chromatid cohesion ([/ontology/go/0007064/annotation/page/1 mitotic sister chromatid cohesion]), chromosome condensation([/ontology/go/0007076/annotation/page/1 mitotic chromosome condensation]), and DNA repair ([/ontology/go/0006281/annotation/page/1 DNA repair]). In ''Dictyostelium'', as in all eukaryotes, six members of thisconserved family exist: [/gene/DDB_G0291752 smc1], [/gene/DDB_G0284499 smc2], [/gene/DDB_G0276101 smc3], [/gene/DDB_G0286403 smc4], [/gene/DDB_G0290919 smc5], and [/gene/DDB_G0288993 smc6]. These proteins contain globulardomains at either end, separated by a hinge domain. The SMC proteins are capable of formingthree different types of heterodimers: Smc1-Smc3, Smc2-Smc4, and Smc5-Smc6 (reviewed in[http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12360193 Jessberger 2002]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 17-DEC-2004 KP

DDB_G0267426.summary:
Citrate synthase catalyzes the condensation of acetyl-CoA and oxaloacetate to citrate. is present throughout ''Dictyostelium'' development ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15225305 Porter and Wright 1977]).CshA is an active citrate synthase localized in the [/ontology/go/0005777/annotation/page/1 peroxisome].The non-mitochondrial form of this enzyme catalyses citrate synthesis in the [/ontology/go/0006097/annotation/page/1 glyoxylate cycle]. ''cshA'' is expressed maximally during vegetative growth.
''cshA'' null mutants has defects in [/ontology/go/0006909/annotation/page/1 phagocytosis] and fluid-phase [/ontology/go/0006897/annotation/page/1 endocytosis], which result in poor growth both on bacterial lawns and in axenic suspension. ''cshA'' null cells display aberrant developmental morphology on bacterial lawns, but development is normal on buffered agar. ''cshA'' disruption results in a 50% reduction in enzyme activity. The remaining activity could be due to the citrate synthase encoded by the [/gene/DDB_G0276965 gltA] or the [/gene/DDB_G0287281 DDB_G0287281] genes ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15225305 Huang et al. 2004]). There is a fourth gene citrate synthase gene in the genome, [/gene/DDB_G0275311 DDB_G0275311], that is predicted to be localized to the mitochondrion. Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 30-AUG-2004 PG

DDB_G0274599.summary:
There are 29 genes encoding actin in ''Dictyostelium'' with amino acid identity greater than 83%, ''act1''-''act29''. Seventeen of these genes encode identical proteins: [/gene/DDB_G0289553 act1], [/gene/DDB_G0274133 act2], [/gene/DDB_G0289005 act4], [/gene/DDB_G0289663 act5], [/gene/DDB_G0274135 act6], [/gene/DDB_G0280545 act7], [/gene/DDB_G0269234 act8], [/gene/DDB_G0274601 act9], [/gene/DDB_G0288879 act11], [/gene/DDB_G0274129 act12], [/gene/DDB_G0274599 act13], [/gene/DDB_G0274137 act14], [/gene/DDB_G0272520 act15], [/gene/DDB_G0272248 act16], [/gene/DDB_G0274727 act19], [/gene/DDB_G0274285 act20], and [/gene/DDB_G0274561 act21], while [/gene/DDB_G0289811 act10], [/gene/DDB_G0275023 act22], and [/gene/DDB_G0289487 act3] respectively have 1, 4 and 11 amino acid differences compared to the 17 identical genes. The proteins encoded by [/gene/DDB_G0274131 act17], [/gene/DDB_G0289489 act18], [/gene/DDB_G0268744 act23] and [/gene/DDB_G0289505 act24]are more divergent.
Actin is a major [/ontology/go/0005200/annotation/page/1 structural constituent of cytoskeleton]. Actin is one of the most abundant proteins in ''Dictyostelium'', constituting approximately 8% of the total protein in vegetative cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/561722 Alton and Lodish et al. 1977]).Actin synthesis is developmentally regulated, peaking shortly after starvation (reviewed by [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6894564 Firtel] in 1981). The different actin genes differ in their levels of expression, with [/gene/DDB_G0274135 act6], [/gene/DDB_G0269234 act8] and [/gene/DDB_G0274129 act12] being highly expressed both during growth and development compared to [/gene/DDB_G0289005 act4], [/gene/DDB_G0289663 act5], [/gene/DDB_G0280545 act7] and [/gene/DDB_G0272248 act16] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6286214 McKeown and Firtel 1981]). Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 19-SEP-2003 PG

DDB_G0283761.summary:
Cytoplasmic fucosyltransferase activity specific for the addition of fucose to the Skp1 protein ([/gene/DDB_G0269230 fpaA]/[/gene/DDB_G0273251 fpaB-1]) was first identified by [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1577798 Gonzalez-Yanes and colleagues (1992)]. This alpha(1,2)-fucosyltransferase activity was later attributed to the [/gene/DDB_G0283761 pgtA] gene; null cells for ''pgtA'' exhibit increased cell size in phase contrast microscopy and oxygen requirement that is very similar to that of [/gene/DDB_G0275699 gnt1] null cells, but rescues the defective fruiting body morphology ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11423539 van der Wel et al. 2001]). The PgtA protein (also known as FT85) was later determined to be a bifunctional diglycosyltransferasealso that also possesses glycoprotein-N-acetylgalactosamine 3-beta-galactosyltransferase activity. Thus this protein adds a fucose and galactose modification to Skp1 ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15123660 Ketcham et al. 2004]).
Glycosylation of Skp1 has been extensively studied in ''Dictyostelium''. The initial step in Skp1 glycosylation involves the hydroxylation of Pro143 by a proline hydroxylase ([/gene/DDB_G0277759 phyA], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9660787 Teng-umnuay et al. 1998]). HyPro143 is then modified by the glycosyltransferase [/gene/DDB_G0275699 gnt1], which transfers a GlcNAc (N-acetylglucosamine) to the Skp1 protein ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10593934 Teng-umnuay et al. 1999]). Then the Skp1-GlcNAc is extended PgtA, which processively adds galactose and fucose ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11423539 van der Wel et al. 2001], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12244067 van der Wel et al. 2002]). Subsequently two additional galactose residues are added by [/gene/DDB_G0283005 agtA] to yield the Skp1 pentasaccharide (GGFGGnOSkp1; [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16495217 Ercan et al. 2006], reviewed in [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31128470 West and Kim 2019]).
Skp1 is the only detectable protein modified by purified PgtA added to pgtA-null extracts ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19687007 Wang et al. 2009]).Further investigations showed that full SKP1 glycosylation is required for optimal oxygen sensing during development, for example [/gene/DDB_G0283005 agtA] knockout and overexpression mutants require an elevated oxygen level to culminate, similar to the phenotype of the [/gene/DDB_G0277759 phyA] mutant ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19687007 Wang et al. 2009], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22128189 Zhang et al. 2011], reviewed in [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25988702 West and Blader 2015]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 19-MAR-2020 PF
DDB_G0283761.note: The coding sequence from the Sequencing Center has a 3 nt insertion in a highly repetitive region compared to GenBank record AF279134, resulting in 1 amino acid insertion at position 413, with respect to the protein predicted by the Sequencing Center.

DDB_G0289541.summary:
VasP is an actin polymerase that belongs to a conserved family of actin regulatory proteins. VasP is directly involved in accelerating filament elongation by delivering monomeric actin to the growing barbed end [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18923426 (Breitsprecher et al. 2008)]. ''vasP'' transcripts are expressed in vegetatively growing cells and expression increases upon starvation, peaking at 8 hr., and then remains high until fruiting body formation [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12388544 (Han et al. 2002)]. VasP localizes to the leading edge in migrating cells and to the tips of filopodia [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12388544 (Han et al. 2002)]. In addition, VasP localizes to macropinosomes, and in a narrow band at the advancing rim of the phagocytic cup (Korber, et al 2022, PMID:35101769).VasP interacts with Formin H ([/gene/DDB_G0285589 forH]) [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16675552 (Schirenbeck et al. 2006)], Profilin III ([/gene/DDB_G0271142 proC]) [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17467078 (Arasada et al. 2007)], and Scar/WAVE regulatory complex component AbiA ([/gene/DDB_G0267956 abiA]) [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28889942 (Litschko et al. 2017)]. In ''abiA'' null cells, VasP does not translocate to the leading edge, revealing that the recruitment of VasP to leading edge depends on AbiA [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28889942 (Litschko et al. 2017)]. VasP is phosphorylated in response to hyperosmotic stress and cAMP stimulation. VASP phosphorylation abolishes its interaction with WASP ([/gene/DDB_G0293834 wasA]) while phosphorylation contributes to its binding to WIPa ([/gene/DDB_G0270430 wipA]) with higher affinity. [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20191567 (Lin et al. 2010)].
VasP plays a role in controlling the actin cytoskeleton during chemotaxis, filopodium formation, macropinocytosis, and phagocytosis. ''vasP'' null mutants are unable to form filopodia and have aberrant actin filament formation with F-actin concentrated in a few small regions around the cell periphery. They also have defects adhering to the substratum and suppressing lateral pseudopod extension, resulting in a defect in chemotaxis to cAMP [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12388544 (Han et al. 2002)]. Myosin-I heavy chain MyoI ([/gene/DDB_G0274455 myoI]) fails to target efficiently to the cell cortex in ''vasP'' null cells. VasP produces a cortical actin network at the leading-edge cortex that activates MyoI, and together, VasP and MyoI drive filopodia initiation by further bundling and polymerizing actin. (Arthur, et al 2021, PMID: 34042588). Deletion of VasP results in substantial defects in both the macropinocytosis of bulk fluid and phagocytosis of yeast particles. There is a significant delay in the closure of the phagocytic cup during phagocytosis in ''vasP'' null cells. After cup closure, VASP localizes to the distal side of internalized phagosomes and initiates localized de-novo actin assembly to propel the phagosome deeper into the cell (Korber, et al 2022, PMID:35101769).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 10-FEB-2022 RD

DDB_G0268020.summary:
The oxidative decarboxylation of alpha-keto acids in the catabolism of the branched-chain amino acids (isoleucine, leucine, and valine), is catalyzed by the branched-chain alpha-keto acid dehydrogenase complex. This mitochondrial enzyme contains 3 catalytic components, E1, E2, and E3. E1 is a heterotetrameric alpha2 ([/gene/DDB_G0286335 bkdA]), beta2 ([/gene/DDB_G0268020 bkdB]) enzyme, with 3-methyl-2-oxobutanoate dehydrogenase activity ().
E2 is a homo-24-meric dihydrolipoyl transacylase ([/gene/DDB_G0281797 bkdC]) that forms the core of the multienzyme and binds to both E1 and E3 ([/ontology/go/5515/annotation/page/1 protein binding]). The lipoyl group of E2 is reductively 2-methylpropanoylated by E1, and then passes this 2-methylpropanoyl to coenzyme A ([/ontology/go/8415/annotation/page/1 acyltransferase activity]). In addition to the 2-methylpropanoyl group, formed when E1 acts on the oxoacid that corresponds with valine, this enzyme also transfers the 3-methylbutanoyl and S-2-methylbutanoyl groups when E1 acts on the oxoacids corresponding with leucine and isoleucine, respectively.
The E3 enzyme ([/gene/DDB_G0291648 lpd]) is adihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase ([/ontology/go/4148/annotation/page/1 dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase activity]) that is shared by three 2-oxo acid dehydrogenase multienzyme complexes. These include the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, the 2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenase complex, the glycine cleavage system, and the branched-chain 2-oxo acid dehydrogenase complex.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 02-DEC-2004 PF

There are 29 genes encoding actin in ''Dictyostelium'' with amino acid identity greater than 83%, ''act1''-''act29''. Seventeen of these genes encode identical proteins: [/gene/DDB_G0289553 act1], [/gene/DDB_G0274133 act2], [/gene/DDB_G0289005 act4], [/gene/DDB_G0289663 act5], [/gene/DDB_G0274135 act6], [/gene/DDB_G0280545 act7], [/gene/DDB_G0269234 act8], [/gene/DDB_G0274601 act9], [/gene/DDB_G0288879 act11], [/gene/DDB_G0274129 act12], [/gene/DDB_G0274599 act13], [/gene/DDB_G0274137 act14], [/gene/DDB_G0272520 act15], [/gene/DDB_G0272248 act16], [/gene/DDB_G0274727 act19], [/gene/DDB_G0274285 act20], and [/gene/DDB_G0274561 act21], while [/gene/DDB_G0289811 act10], [/gene/DDB_G0275023 act22], and [/gene/DDB_G0289487 act3] respectively have 1, 4 and 11 amino acid differences compared to the 17 identical genes. The proteins encoded by [/gene/DDB_G0274131 act17], [/gene/DDB_G0289489 act18], [/gene/DDB_G0268744 act23] and [/gene/DDB_G0289505 act24]are more divergent.
Actin is a major [/ontology/go/0005200/annotation/page/1 structural constituent of cytoskeleton]. Actin is one of the most abundant proteins in ''Dictyostelium'', constituting approximately 8% of the total protein in vegetative cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/561722 Alton and Lodish et al. 1977]).Actin synthesis is developmentally regulated, peaking shortly after starvation (reviewed by [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6894564 Firtel] in 1981). The different actin genes differ in their levels of expression, with [/gene/DDB_G0274135 act6], [/gene/DDB_G0269234 act8] and [/gene/DDB_G0274129 act12] being highly expressed both during growth and development compared to [/gene/DDB_G0289005 act4], [/gene/DDB_G0289663 act5], [/gene/DDB_G0280545 act7] and [/gene/DDB_G0272248 act16] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6286214 McKeown and Firtel 1981]). Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 19-SEP-2003 PG

DDB_G0293438.summary: The ABC superfamily of genes is one of the largest in the genomes of both bacteria and eukaryotes. The proteins encoded by these genes all carry a characteristic 200- to 250-amino-acid ATP-binding cassette that gives them their family name ([/ontology/go/0042626/annotation/page/1 ATPase activity, coupled to transmembrane movement of substances]). In bacteria they are mostly involved in nutrient import, while in eukaryotes many are involved in export([/ontology/go/0006810/annotation/page/1 transport]), ([/ontology/go/0016021/annotation/page/1 integral to membrane]). Seven different families (A to G) have been defined in eukaryotes based on sequence homology, domain topology, and function. ''Dictyostelium'' has 71 ABC transporters (including one on the chromosome 2 duplication) and 11 ABCB family members: [/gene/DDB_G0293416 abcB1], [/gene/DDB_G0293438 abcB2], [/gene/DDB_G0291714 abcB3], [/gene/DDB_G0279915 abcB4],[/gene/DDB_G0292554 abcB5], [/gene/DDB_G0282931 abcB6], [/gene/DDB_G0269720 abcB7], [/gene/DDB_G0293002 tagA], [/gene/DDB_G0286119 tagB], [/gene/DDB_G0286121 tagC], and [/gene/DDB_G0286123 tagD]. The B family includes three main subtypes: full transporters involved in multiple drug resistance (MDR), half-transporters targeted to mitochondria, and half-transporters involved in peptide transport [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12456012 (Anjard and Loomis 2002)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 16-JUN-2003 PG

DDB_G0279413.summary: ''pkaR'' encodes the regulatory subunit of the cAMP dependent protein kinase PKA ([/gene/DDB_G0283907 pkaC], [/gene/DDB_G0279413 pkaR]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3467359 Mutzel et al. 1987], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1312226 Simon et al. 1992)]. cAMP functions as a second messenger within cells by activating PKA when it binds to the regulatory subunit PkaR. The regulatory subunit can reassociate with the catalytic subunit and inhibit it when the phosphodiesterase RegA ([/gene/DDB_G0284331 regA]) hydrolyses cAMP bound to PkaR ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9435289 Shaulsky et al. 1998], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20923972 Moorthy et al. 2011)]. PKA plays multiple roles throughout development ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1728597 Harwood et al. 1992], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9126295 Mann et al. 1997], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9729606 Loomis et al. 1998], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25872182 Loomis et al. 2015)]. Strains with constitutive PKA activity as the result of null mutations in ''pkaR'' develop precociously ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1312226 Simon et al. 1992], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7937993 Mann et al. 1994], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7713325 Hopper et al. 1995)]. These mutant cells are also impaired in chemotaxis as the result of being unable to suppress lateral pseudopods in the front of natural cAMP waves ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12582123 Zhang et al. 2003)]. PKA ([/gene/DDB_G0283907 pkaC], [/gene/DDB_G0279413 pkaR]) also mediates the response of several xenobiotic compounds, including valproic acid, a treatment for bipolar disorder, [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16759735  (Boeckeler et al. 2006)] and curcumin [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29135990  (Swatson et al. 2017)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 27-SEP-2018 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis
DDB_G0279413.note: The sequences from the Sequencing Center and GenBank record M15081 are identical.

DDB_G0288251.summary:
''roco4'' encodes a large, multi-domain protein of the Roco family. Roco4 contains an amino terminal leucine-rich repeat (LRR) region, a Roc small GTPase domain, a COR (C-terminal of Roc) domain, a protein kinase domain and a WD40 repeat domain in the C-terminal region. ''roco4'' is an ortholog of human LRRK2, mutations in which are associated with Parkinson disease. Eleven ''Dictyostelium'' proteins belong to the Roco family: ([/gene/DDB_G0291079 gbpC]), ([/gene/DDB_G0273259 qkgA-1]), ([/gene/DDB_G0269250 pats1]), Roco4, ([/gene/DDB_G0294533 roco5]), ([/gene/DDB_G0279417 roco6]), ([/gene/DDB_G0267472 roco7]), ([/gene/DDB_G0286127 roco8]), ([/gene/DDB_G0288183 roco9]), ([/gene/DDB_G0291710 roco10]) and ([/gene/DDB_G0268636 roco11]).
''roco4'' is expressed during both growth and development with the highest level of expression during the slug stage of development. Roco4 showed a uniform cytosolic distribution and ''roco4'' expression is highly enriched in the prestalk region of the slug. Slug development is delayed in ''roco4'' null mutants, and stalks in ''roco4'' mutants have severely reduced cellulose levels, leading to unstable stalks that are unable to properly lift the spore head above the surface ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20348387 van Egmond and van Haastert 2010]). The 3D structure of Roco4 has been solved. Roco4 mutants lacking serine 1187 and serine 1189 lack kinase activity and are unable to rescue ''roco4'' null developmental defects, whereas Roco4 with a G1179S mutation (Roco4(G1179S)) displays an increase in kinase activity. Mutations in the corresponding residue in human LRRK2 are associated with late-onset Parkinson disease ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22689969 Gilsbach, et al. 2013]). Roco4(G1179S) mutants also display similar developmental defects as ''roco4'' null mutants. Both the ''roco4'' null mutant and the Roco4(G1179S) mutant have defects in phototaxis, and additional phenotypes which are characteristic of mitochondrial impairment. In ''roco4'' null cells, there is an increased level of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and a significant increase in basal mitochondrial respiration, ATP synthesis rate, and complex I activity compared with wild type cells, while the Roco4(G1179S) mutant displays lower mitochondrial activity. Taken together, these results indicate that ''Dictyostelium discoideum'' Roco4 and human LRRK2 have a conserved role in the regulation of mitochondrial activity (Rosenbusch, et al. 2021, PMID:34568343).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 13-OCT-2021 RD

DDB_G0283065.summary:
Initiation of protein translation in eukaryotes is regulated by phosphorylation of the alpha subunit of eukaryotictranslation initiation factor 2 (eIF2alpha). During periods of amino acid starvation, eIF2alpha is inactivated viaphosphorylation by the serine/threonine kinase ([/ontology/go/0004674/annotation/page/1 protein serine/threonine kinase activity]) GCN2 (general control nonderepressible), also known asPEK (pancreatic eukaryotic translation initiation factor kinase). The PEK family of protein kinases is highly conservedfrom yeast to humans, however, the effect on translation in metazoans is global whereas GCN2 in yeast acts to inhibittranslation of specific species of mRNA ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7855893 reviewed in Wek 1994]).
In ''Dictyostelium'', two members of the PEK family of protein kinases have been identified: [/gene/DDB_G0272837 ifkA] and[/gene/DDB_G0276829 ifkB]. Putative proteins belonging to the PEK family are: [/gene/DDB_G0276043 ifkC], [/gene/DDB_G0283065 DDB_G0283065], [/gene/DDB_G0268642 DDB_G0268642], [/gene/DDB_G0292734 DDB_G0292734], and [/gene/DDB_G0292734 DDB_G0292734].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 17-SEP-2004 KP

DNA-dependent RNA polymerase catalyzes the transcription of DNA into RNA using the four ribonucleoside triphosphates as substrates ([/ontology/go/0003899/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase activity]). RNA polymerase II is composed of 12 subunits: [/gene/DDB_G0279193 rpb1], [/gene/DDB_G0288257 rpb2], [/gene/DDB_G0292244 rpb3], [/gene/DDB_G0282739 rpb4], [/gene/DDB_G0291636 rpb5], [/gene/DDB_G0291037 rpb6], [/gene/DDB_G0284891 rpb7], [/gene/DDB_G0278039 rpb8], [/gene/DDB_G0268306 rpb9], [/gene/DDB_G0272036 rpb10], [/gene/DDB_G0277677 rpb11], and[/gene/DDB_G0283365 rpb12]. Subunits 5, 6, 8, 10, and 12 are common to all threeRNA polymerases (reviewed by [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9618449 Hampsey] in 1998).

DDB_G0278809.summary: The centrosomal protein CP148 is encoded by ''cepG'' [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19466752  (Schulz et al. 2009)]. During metaphase CP148 is in the cytoplasm but during telophase it re-enters the expanding centrosomal corona where it remains until prophase when it returns to the cytopasm as the corona dissociates. CP148 is found in an intermediate position between outer coronal proteins and the central core centrosomal proteins. Cells with reduced levels of CP148 as the result of RNAi inhibition of ''cepG'' have cytosolic centrosomes lacking a corona and their interphase microtubules are disorganized. However, formation of the mitotic spindle and astral microtubules are unaffected in the ''cepG'' knock-down strain [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22223109  (Kuhnert et al. 2012)]. CP148 interacts with CP161 ([/gene/DDB_G0282851 cepL]) and protein localization studies in ''cepL'' and ''cepG'' depletion strains reveal that both are scaffolding proteins cooperating in the organization of the centrosomal corona [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29690637  (Pitzen et al., 2018)]. About 100 different proteins contribute to centrosomal functions including the products of ([/gene/DDB_G0271738 tubC]), ([/gene/DDB_G0285849 spc97]), ([/gene/DDB_G0283909 spc98]), ([/gene/DDB_G0288427 cenA]), ([/gene/DDB_G0288375 lis1]), ([/gene/DDB_G0270814 nek2]), ([/gene/DDB_G0283607 eb1]), ([/gene/DDB_G0268616 cepJ]) and ''cepG''.[http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15548420  (Graf et al. 2004)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 02-FEB-2019 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0267446.summary: The regulatory subunit of calcineurin is encoded by ''cnbA''. The primary sequence of this calcium/calmodulin dependent protein phosphatase is very similar to the sequences of calcineurin B in mammals that all have two calcium binding EF hands [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11352578  (Aichem and Mutzell, et al. 2001)]. In the absence of calcium, calcineurin A ([/gene/DDB_G0276883 canA]) and calcneurin B form inactive heterodimers that are converted to active heterotetramers when they bind Ca++/calmodulin [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25518940  (Sugden et al. 2014)]. RNA-seq studies have shown that canA and cnbA are coordinately expressed during early aggregation and reach a peak at 11 hrs of development [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25887420  (Rosengarten et al. 2015)]. Inhibition of calcineurin activity with the polyphenolic aldehyde, gossypol, reduces the rate of growth and the number of aggregates formed after 24 hrs of development [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15621416  (Weissenmayer et al. 2005)]. cAMP relay is inhibited within 10 minutes of addition of 10 microM gossypol. Gossypol also stimulates nuclear translocation of the prestalk transcription factor DimB ([/gene/DDB_G0291372 dimB]) within a few minutes and blocks nuclear translocation of the transcription factor TacA ([/gene/DDB_G0291342 tacA]) in response to calcium indicating that calcineurin mediates these responses [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22944283  (Thewes et al. 2012)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25518940  (Sugden et al. 2014)]. Cells lacking calcineurin as the result of expression of RNAi for either canA or cnbA form a reduced number of fruiting bodies with short stalks [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16512895  (Boeckeler et al. 2006)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23686520  (Thewes et al. 2013)] These mutant strains are also hypersensitive to high levels of cations showing that calcineurin is responsible for stress responses as in other organisms.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 16-APR-2018 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0289881.summary: The ''atg5'' gene was isolated among several members of the autophagy family of genes, conserved from yeast to man. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12626495 Otto et al. 2003)]. Macroautophagy is used by eukaryotic cells to recycle non-essential cellular components during starvation and development. ''atg5'' null mutants grow normally, but survival during nitrogen starvation is reduced and development of the mutant is severely impaired. On bacterial lawns ''atg5'' mutant cells do not aggregate, but form multi-tipped aggregates on filters ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12626495 Otto et al. 2003)]. The multi-tipped phenotype of ''atg5'' mutants is similar to that of mutants in other autophagy genes ''atg6'', ([/gene/DDB_G0269244 atg6A]) ''atg7'', ([/gene/DDB_G0271096 atg7]) ''atg101'', ([/gene/DDB_G0288287 atg101]) ''tipC'', ([/gene/DDB_G0267422 tipC]) and ''tipD'' ([/gene/DDB_G0275323 tipD]). Experiments with GFP-labelled autophagy proteins indicate that the atg5-atg12 ([/gene/DDB_G0282929 atg12]) conjugation system that has been described in yeast, is conserved in ''Dictyostelium'' [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12626495  (Otto et al., 2003)]. Axenically grown ''atg5'' null cells plated on filters form aberrant fruiting bodies which do not produce viable, detergent-resistent spores. Wild-type cells in a chimaera do not rescue the developmental defects, showing that the ''atg5'' mutation is autonomous ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12626495 Otto et al. 2003)]. Mutants lacking ''atg5'', ''atg7'' and ''atg9'' ([/gene/DDB_G0285323 atg9]) are impaired in cAMP induction of prespore gene expression, indicating that autophagy is required for this process ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31051160 Yamada et al. 2019)]. ''atg5'' single, ''atg5''/''atg12'' double, and ''atg5''/''atg12''/''tipD'' triple knockout mutants revealed similar defects in the conjugation of ATG8 to phosphatidylethanolamine, development, and cell viability indicating that Atg5, Atg12, and TipD act as a functional unit in canonical autophagy. However, distinct and sometimes opposite phenotypes in growth, macropinocytosis, phagocytosis, and proteasomal activity in these mutants reveal autophagy-independent functions for these genes, while providing further support that the ubiquitin proteasome system is dependent on intact autophagy for full activity. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/32397394 Karow et al. 2020)]Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 08-DEC-2020 RD

phenotypes: aberrant cellular response to nitrogen starvation

DDB_G0271086.summary: ''gip1'' encodes a 35 kDa protein containing a pleckstrin homology domain at the amino terminus. Gip1 was identified using a tandem affinity purification of Gbeta ([/gene/DDB_G0277143 gpbA]) and was shown to bind the heterotrimeric G-protein complex mainly through the beta/gamma subunit. ''gip1'' null mutants have severe defects in gradient sensing and display aberrant chemotaxis to cAMP, exhibiting normal chemotaxis at low cAMP concentrations, but defects at higher concentrations. Gip1 binds and sequesters G proteins in the cytosol. cAMP receptor ([/gene/DDB_G0273397 carA-1], [/gene/DDB_G0273533 carA-2]) activation induced G-protein translocation from the cytosol to the plasma membrane is dependent on Gip1 as shown by reduced membrane translocation of Galpha2 ([/gene/DDB_G0276267 gpaB]) in ''gip1'' null cells. These findings suggest that Gip1 regulates G protein translocation to the plasma membrane along chemical gradients at high chemo-attractant concentrations, offering an explanation for the ability of chemotactic cells to recognize chemical gradients over a wide range of concentrations. [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/27044073  (Kamimura et al. 2016)]. Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 28-NOV-2018 RD

DDB_G0293850.summary:
The size of ''Dictyostelium'' fruiting bodies is controlled at least in part by a secreted counting factor (CF), a multisubunit complex. The role of CF in size regulation has not yet been elucidated, although a negative effect on cytosolic glucose levels has been observed.
NADPH-coupled aldehyde reductase reduces a wide variety of aldehydes to the corresponding alcohols, including converting glucose to sorbitol ([/ontology/go/0042593/annotation/page/1 glucose homeostasis]). The levels of this enzyme appears to be regulated by CF. Cells in which the ''alrA'' gene, encoding aldehyde reductase ([/ontology/go/0004032/annotation/page/1 aldehyde reductase activity]), has been disrupted, form aggregates much larger than wild type cells ([/ontology/go/0031158/annotation/page/1 negative regulation of aggregate size involved in sorocarp development]). ''alrA''- cells have reduced [/ontology/go/0006928/annotation/page/1 cell motion]. ''alrA''- cells secrete reduced levels of [/gene/DDB_G0274597 ctnA] and [/gene/DDB_G0273175 cf50-1], two components of CF. This could explain why ''alrA''- cells form large groups ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14551196 Ehrenman et al. 2004]).
''alrA'' is highly upregulated by glutathione (GSH) depletion. The enzyme glutamate-cysteine ligase, encoded by [/gene/DDB_G0284651 gcsA], catalyzes the the first and limiting step in GSH biosynthesis. Null mutants in ''gcsA'' have an absolute requirement for exogenous GSH. ''alrA'' overexpression protects [/gene/DDB_G0284651 gcsA] null mutants from GSH depletion, while underexpression makes the cells more sensitive. ''alrA'' also protects from the toxic by-product of glycolysis methylglyoxal, by breaking it down to non-toxic lactic acid using GSH as a co-factor ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18990192 Choi et al. 2008]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 22-JAN-2009 PG

DDB_G0277155.summary: Following the endosymbiosis of bacteria to create mitochondria, eukaryotes adapted to translation of mitochondrial proteins in the cytoplasm by synthesizing translocase proteins. This group of proteins form the mitochondrial outer membrane translocase (TOM) complex and function to import nuclear-encoded gene products into the mitochondria. Two components of this complex were identified in ''Dictyostelium'': a major channel protein, [/gene/DDB_G0277155 tom40], contains a putative transmembrane beta-barrel, and associates with [/gene/DDB_G0282897 tom7] in other species. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15155803 Macasev et al. 2004]). Additional bioinformatic analysis identified two additional subunits of the Dictyostelium TOM complex, [/gene/DDB_G0283573 tom20] and [/gene/DDB_G0275389 tom70] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26074248 Wojtkowska et al. 2015]). Tom40 localizes to the mitochondrion and has been identified as a component of the mitochondrial outer membrane TOB/SAM complex ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31714697 Mazur et al. 2019])Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 18-NOV-2019 RD

DDB_G0279149.summary: ''pip5k3'' encodes a phosphoinositide kinase that plays a role in early phagosome maturation. In ''pip5k3'' null cells delivery of vacuolar ATPase components ([/gene/DDB_G0291858 vatM]) and ([/gene/DDB_G0277401 vatB]) and the protease cathepsin D ([/gene/DDB_G0279411 ctsD]) to phagosomes is inhibited, reducing the ability of cells to acidify newly formed phagosomes. As a consequence, ''pip5k3'' null cells are unable to generate an effective antimicrobial environment and kill captured bacteria. ''pip5k3'' null cells are also more susceptible to infection by the intracellular pathogen ''Legionella pneumophila'' ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30730983 Buckley et al. 2019]). ''pip5k3'' was identified in a REMI mutant screen as a clone with an abnormal fruiting body morphology, and ''pip5k3'' null mutants created by homologous recombination had enlarged lower stalks with maturing spores becoming increasingly vacuolated. ''pip5k3'' null mutants initially have normal pre-spore differentiation; however, at low cell density, a proportion of the pre-spore cells at the base of the structure then transdifferentiate into stalk-like cells with a single large vacuole and cellulose wall; at high cell density, the majority of pre-spore cells transdifferentiate into stalk-like cells. (Yamada et al. 2021, PMID:34490246).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 14-DEC-2021 RD

DDB_G0278409.summary:
The protein encoded by [/gene/DDB_G0283267 shkA] contains a C-terminal SH2 (Src homology 2) domain that shares sequencesimilarity with the mammalian PI3K adaptor protein p55 and has been shown to possess [/ontology/go/0004713/annotation/page/1 protein-tyrosine kinase activity] in addition to [/ontology/go/0004674/annotation/page/1 protein serine/threonine kinase activity]. Cells carrying a null mutation for''shkA'' exhibit severe developmental phenotypes and have defective [/ontology/go/0030036/annotation/page/1 actin cytoskeleton organization and biogenesis],[/ontology/go/0006935/annotation/page/1 chemotaxis], and [/ontology/go/0006909/annotation/page/1 phagocytosis]. Biochemical analysis shows that protein kinase B([/gene/DDB_G0268620 pkbA]) activation is significantly higher than wild-type. In addition, the rate of translocationof PH (pleckstrin homology) domain-containing proteins [/gene/DDB_G0285161 dagA], [/gene/DDB_G0268620 pkbA], and [/gene/DDB_G0285845 phdA] is reduced. The ShkA protein localizes to the [/ontology/go/0005938/annotation/page/1 cell cortex]; this localization isdependent upon its SH2 domain ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11274054 Moniakis 2001]).
Four additional uncharacterized genes exist in the ''Dictyostelium'' genome that are highly similar to shkA in domainarchitecture: [/gene/DDB_G0288617 shkB], [/gene/DDB_G0290451 shkE], [/gene/DDB_G0278409 shkC], and [/gene/DDB_G0281343 shkD].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 06-JAN-2005 KP

DDB_G0291752.summary: Members of the structural maintentance of chromosomes (SMC) family are involved in manybiological processes, including sister chromatid cohesion ([/ontology/go/0007064/annotation/page/1 mitotic sister chromatid cohesion]), chromosome condensation([/ontology/go/0007076/annotation/page/1 mitotic chromosome condensation]), and DNA repair ([/ontology/go/0006281/annotation/page/1 DNA repair]). In ''Dictyostelium'', as in all eukaryotes, six members of thisconserved family exist: [/gene/DDB_G0291752 smc1], [/gene/DDB_G0284499 smc2], [/gene/DDB_G0276101 smc3], [/gene/DDB_G0286403 smc4], [/gene/DDB_G0290919 smc5], and [/gene/DDB_G0288993 smc6]. These proteins contain globulardomains at either end, separated by a hinge domain. The SMC proteins are capable of formingthree different types of heterodimers: Smc1-Smc3, Smc2-Smc4, and Smc5-Smc6 (reviewed in[http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12360193 Jessberger 2002]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 17-DEC-2004 KP

DDB_G0288569.summary: Strumpellin is a member a five protein assembly, the WASH complex, whose core members are WASH ([/gene/DDB_G0292878 wshA]), SWIP ([/gene/DDB_G0283355 swip]), FAM21 ([/gene/DDB_G0276221 fam21]), ([/gene/DDB_G0267948 ccdc53]) and Strumpellin. The WASH complex is highly conserved [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23993425  (Insall et al. 2013)] and plays an essential role in the endosomal system and is responsible for recycling of the V-ATPase from post-lysosomes prior to exocytosis. Mutations in either one of the five members results in a complete block in exocytosis [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21606208  (Carnell et al. 2011)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23369714  (Park et al. 2013)]. ''washc5'' null cells display defects in cell growth, phagocytosis, exocytosis, and lysosome function which are rescued by expression of Strumpellin. An N471D point mutation in the human ortholog of Strumpelin (WASHC5) is associated with the neurodegenerative disorder Heriditary Spastic paraplegia 8. A mutant with a point mutation in the corresponding residue in Dictyostelium ''washc5'' has defects in lysosome function and exocytosis [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30061306  (Song et al. 2018)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 05-SEP-2018 RD

DDB_G0284293.summary:
The homeodomain is a sequence-specific DNA binding motif that consists of a helix-turn-helix. Homeobox-containing proteins have transcription factor activity. They have beenidentified in most if not all phyla of eukaryotes. Inmetazoans, homeobox-containing proteins are known to be involvedin regulating the anterior-posterior body plan and in thespecification of certain cell types and anterior-posteriorcompartments (see [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9486804 Han and Firtel 1998] and references therein). There are 14 predicted proteins that contain homeobox domains in ''Dictyostelium'':[/gene/DDB_G0275173 hbx2], [/gene/DDB_G0291075 warA], [/gene/DDB_G0291197 hbx3], [/gene/DDB_G0272967 hbx4], [/gene/DDB_G0273127 hbx5-1] (on the chromosome 2 duplication: [/gene/DDB_G0273645 hbx5-2]), [/gene/DDB_G0277505 hbx6], [/gene/DDB_G0278225 hbx7], [/gene/DDB_G0279257 hbx8], [/gene/DDB_G0280473 hbx9], [/gene/DDB_G0284293 hbx10], [/gene/DDB_G0295787 hbx11], [/gene/DDB_G0286733 hbx12], [/gene/DDB_G0288975 hbx13], and [/gene/DDB_G0289677 hbx14].
[http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25963254 Mishra and Saran 2015] performed a genome-wide classification and comparative genomic analysis of the 14 homeobox genes present in D. discoideum, and found that they could be classified into 3 groups: TALE, OTHER and NOVEL classes, ''hbx10'' belonging to the OTHER class.
A peptide with cell penetrating abilities has been isolated, which is 16 amino acids long and contained in the Hbx10 protein, residues 343 to 358. The peptide, its kind often called penetratin, has been named Cupid. A Cupid-GFP fusion protein has been tested on mammalian, whole plant cells, plant leaf protoplast and fungal cell cultures. When observed using confocal microscopy, GFP fluorescence has been detected within the cell cytosol in 60 minutes, demonstrating Cupid-GFP has permeated the cells and folded correctly. These data suggest that Cupid can act as a molecular vehicle, delivering proteins, such as GFP, into the cytosol of a variety of cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/32792509 Fenton et al. 2020]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 24-AUG-2020 PF

DDB_G0270666.summary:
The GDT (growth-development transition) family of proteins are related by their involvement in the progression into developmentand by their sequence similarity. All members contain a putative transmembrane domain ([/ontology/go/0016021/annotation/page/1 integral to membrane]), and with the exception of [/gene/DDB_G0285895 gdt5] and [/gene/DDB_G0292314 gdt7], contain a putative protein kinase domain ([/ontology/go/0004672/annotation/page/1 protein kinase activity]) that is similar to the MLK (mixed-lineagekinase) family. Both [/gene/DDB_G0278723 gdt1] and [/gene/DDB_G0270666 gdt2] have been previously characterized, however, [/gene/DDB_G0278723 gdt1] lacks a conserved catalytic residue and therefore may not function as a kinase. Similarly, the [/gene/DDB_G0270544 gdt6]protein lacks this essential residue found in [/gene/DDB_G0270666 gdt2], [/gene/DDB_G0285891 gdt3], [/gene/DDB_G0270550 gdt4], and [/gene/DDB_G0270668 gdt8] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15236669 Chibalina et al. 2004]).
In a search for mutants resistant to a phospholipase D (PLD) inhibitor, [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15236669 Chibalina et al.2004] identified ''gdt2''. Similar to the [/gene/DDB_G0278723 gdt1] mutant, ''gdt2'' null cells express high levels of discoidinand aggregate prematurely. However, unlike Gdt1, Gdt2 does not appear to be in the PKA pathway; treatment of ''gdt2-''cells with a PKA inhibitor represses discoidin expression, bypassing the discoidin overexpression phenotype. Also in contrastto ''gdt1'' is the ''gdt2'' expression profile: the ''gdt2'' transcript can be detected at constant levels at all stages of development([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15236669 Chibalina et al. 2004]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 10-SEP-2004 KP

DDB_G0284651.summary:
The enzyme encoded by [/gene/DDB_G0284651 gcsA] is a gamma-glutamylcysteine synthetase (GCS) that catalyzes the first step in glutathione biosynthesis .[http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15993406 Kim et al. (2005)] created a gcsA null strain that is inviable in the absence of glutathione (GSH). Mutant cells cultured with GSH predominantly arrest at the mound stage, while those that go on to produce defective fruiting bodies contain sori with inviable spores. This phenotype is cell autonomous as ''gcsA'' null cells sort to stalk regions in cell mixing experiments with wild-type cells. Further supporting a role for the GCS protein in sporulation is the absence of prespore and spore markers [/gene/DDB_G0277141 cotC], [/gene/DDB_G0267412 pspA], and [/gene/DDB_G0289075 spiA] in ''gscA'' null cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15993406 Kim et al. 2005]).
[http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24373846 Kim et al. (2013)] showed that aggregation was inhibitied in gcsA disrupted cells, and that this developmental defect was rescued by exogenous GSH. In addition, there was no detectable expression of genes required for early development: [/gene/DDB_G0273397 carA-1],[/gene/DDB_G0281545 acaA], and [/gene/DDB_G0283907 pkaC]. However, constitutive expression of [/gene/DDB_G0283605 yakA] in gcsA- cells rescued the defects in developmental initiation and the expression of early developmental genes, suggesting that glutathione initiates ''Dictyostelium'' development through the regulation of YakA. Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 07-MAY-2014 RD

DDB_G0283917.summary: ''sir2A'' was found to be expressed during both growth and development with maximum expression during the loose aggregation stage. Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 25-JUL-2018 RD

DDB_G0271676.summary: The role of Nwk/Bzz1p-like protein (NLP) and Syndapin-like protein (SLP), in the regulation of the formation and trafficking of WASP-vesicles during chemotaxis was investigated by [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19409937  Lee et al. 2009]. Deletion mutants of either ''nlp'' or ''slp'' did not cause significant defects, but deletion of both genes causes the loss of polararized F-actin organization and significant defects in chemotaxis. WASP and NLP are colocalized on vesicles and interactions between the two are required for vesicle formation from Golgi. Microtubules are required for polarized trafficking of these vesicles as vesicles showing high directed mobility are absent in cells treated with nocodazole. Our results suggest that interaction of WASP with NLP/SLP is required for the formation and trafficking of vesicles from Golgi to the membrane, which might play a central role in the establishment of cell polarity during chemotaxis. Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 13-JAN-2015 RD

DDB_G0287707.summary:
DNA-dependent RNA polymerase catalyzes the transcription of DNA into RNA using the four ribonucleoside triphosphates as substrates ([/ontology/go/0003899/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase activity]). Three distinct zinc-containing RNA polymerases are found in eukaryotic nuclei: [/gene/DDB_G0275759 rpa1] for the ribosomal RNA precursor ([/ontology/go/0006360/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase I promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005736/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase I complex]), [/gene/DDB_G0279193 rpb1] for the mRNA precursor ([/ontology/go/0006366/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase II promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005665/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase II, core complex]), and [/gene/DDB_G0277199 rpc1] for 5S and tRNA genes ([/ontology/go/0006383/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase III promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005666/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase III complex]).
RNA polymerase III is a multisubunit complex. The subunits encoded by [/gene/DDB_G0277199 rpc1] (ortholog of ''S. cerevisiae RPO31''), [/gene/DDB_G0293560 rpa2] (''RPC2''), [/gene/DDB_G0268080 rpc3] (''RPC82''),[/gene/DDB_G0277671 rpc4] (''RPC53''), [/gene/DDB_G0271514 rpc5] (''RPC37''), [/gene/DDB_G0286521 rpc9] (''RPC17''), [/gene/DDB_G0272022 rpc34] (''RPC34''), [/gene/DDB_G0273425 rpc25-1] (''RPC25''), and [/gene/DDB_G0287707 rpc11] (''RPC11'') are unique to RNA polymerase III. Orthologs of ''RPC31'' and ''RPC17'' have not been identified in the ''Dictyostelium'' genome. Two subunits, [/gene/DDB_G0291362 rpc19] and [/gene/DDB_G0282339 rpa5] (''RPC19'' and ''RPC40'' in ''S. cerevisiae''), are common to RNA polymerase I and RNA polymerase III and correspond to subunits 3 and 11 of RNA polymerase II. Subunits [/gene/DDB_G0291636 rpb5], [/gene/DDB_G0291037 rpb6], [/gene/DDB_G0278039 rpb8], [/gene/DDB_G0272036 rpb10], and [/gene/DDB_G0283365 rpb12] are common to all three RNA polymerases ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12407181 Peyroche et al. 2002], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12381659 Schramm and Hernandez 2001]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 11-JUN-2009 PG

Gene ''tpp1F'' is a member of a ''Dictysotelium'' family of tripeptidyl-peptidase 1 encoding genes ([/gene/DDB_G0269914 tpp1], [/gene/DDB_G0290333 tpp1B], [/gene/DDB_G0275693 tpp1C], [/gene/DDB_G0287357 tpp1D], [/gene/DDB_G0283033 tpp1E]). The Tpp1 proteins are lysosomal serine proteases, which remove tripeptides from the N-terminus of proteins and is conserved from mammals to amoebae. Mutations in tripeptidyl peptidase 1 have been associated with infantile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (NCL), a neurodegenerative disease.
The ''Dictysotelium''Tpp1F protein was shown to have tripeptidyl-peptidase 1 activity. It also interacts with the Golgi pH regulator GPHR ( gene [/gene/DDB_G0283855 gpr89]) and localizes to the ER and to lysosomes. The single ''tpp1F'' knockout does not show any developmental or growth phenotype, possibly because of functional redundancy in the protein family [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28546289 (Stumpf et al. 2017)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 23-OCT-2017 PF

DDB_G0267688.summary: ''Dictyostelium cpnD'' belongs to the highly conserved copines, a family of ubiquitious Ca(2+)-dependent phospholipid-binding ([/ontology/go/0005544/annotation/page/1 calcium-dependent phospholipid binding]) proteins. In their N-terminal half, copines contain two Ca(2+)- and phospholipid-binding domains (C2 domains) present in such proteins as phospholipase C and protein kinase C. Much of the C-terminal half consists of a von Willebrand Factor type A domain (VWFA) typically found in the extracellular portions of membrane proteins like integrins. Thus copines represent a fusion of intracellular (C2) and extracellular (VWFA) domains. However, there are no signal sequence or hydrophobic transmembrane sequences in the predicted proteins suggesting copines are intracellular proteins. Copines are thought to be involved in membrane trafficking. It is of particular interest that copines, first found in the highly phagocytic protozoan ''Paramecium'' and then isolated from mammalian spleen and liver, seem to be abundant in cells and organs that are, or contain, phagocytes. In this context it comes as no surprise that phagocytic ''Dictyostelium'' has a total of six copine genes[http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16343335  (Damer et al. 2005)]. The widespread distribution of copines from protozoans to mammals and their high similarity suggest they play important role(s) in eukaryotic biology. Reviewed in [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12440769  (Tomsig and Creutz, 2001)]Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 05-APR-2004 PF

DDB_G0289145.summary: Pde7 has a signal sequence at the N-terminus for secretion across membranes followed by a catalytic domain very similar to that of the major extracellular cAMP phosphodiesterase PdsA ([/gene/DDB_G0285995 pdsA]), and is responsible for residual cAMP phosphodiestedrase activity on the surface of cells that lack PdsA. Pde7, like PdsA, is a dual specificity phosphodiesterase which hydrolyzes both cAMP and cGMP [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17040207  (Bader et al. 2007)]. '' pde7'' lies three genes downstream of ''pde4'' ([/gene/DDB_G0289121 pde4]) on chromosome 5 and, like ''pde4'', is expressed only between 6 and 16 hours of development. Both ''pde4'' and ''pde7'' encode secreted phosphodiesterases with similar affinities to cAMP but Pde7 accounts for less than 3% of the activity during slug stages [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17040207  (Bader et al. 2007)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 15-NOV-2018 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0270126.summary: ''rasY'' encodes a guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G protein) of the Ras family of small GTPases. G proteins are key components of signal transduction networks in which they function as molecular signaling switches, binding to GDP in the off state while binding GTP in the on state. Guanine nucleotide-exchange factors (GEFs, rasGEFs) promote the exchange of GDP for GTP on Ras GTPases thus activating them, while GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs, rasGAPs) inactivate Ras GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP. An analysis of ''Dictyostelium'' ras family genes reveals that ''rasU'' ([/gene/DDB_G0270138 rasU]), ''rasV'' ([/gene/DDB_G0270736 rasV]), ''rasW'' ([/gene/DDB_G0270122 rasW]), ''rasX'' ([/gene/DDB_G0270124 rasX]), ''rasY'', and ''rasZ'' ([/gene/DDB_G0270140 rasZ]) form a separate phylogenetic clade ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29614268 Park et al. 2018]). Expression of ''rasY'' is upregulated in response to intracellular ''Mycobacterium marinum'' and ''Legionella pneumophila'' infection ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31823727 Kjellin et al. 2019]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 26-MAR-2020 RD

DDB_G0285175.summary: Vmp1 is a transmembrane protein that, like Atg9, is essential for autophagy and may be involved in membrane trafficking. Highly similar proteins are present in lower eukaryotes and plants although a homolog is absent in the fungi lineage. Vmp1 contains a domain of unknown function (PF09335) which is also found in bacterial DedA proteins and other eukaryotes. Mutation of a strictly conserved glycine residue within this domain inactivates Vmp1 ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30785211 Tabara et al. 2019)]. Vmp1 is found on the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and is essential for the function of the contractile vacuole that protects cells from hypo-osmotic conditions and is also required for the initiation of development ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18641456 Calvo-Garrido et al. 2008)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20009561 Calvo-Garrido et al. 2010)]. Regions of the ER containing phosphatidylinositol-3-phosphate (PtdIns3P) that usually generate autophagosomes are non-functional in ''vmp1'' null mutants, demonstrating a role for ''vmp1'' in modulating PtdIns3P signaling ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25131297 Calvo-Garrido et al. 2014)]. Vmp1 null mutants also have defects in growth and macropinocytosis, and contain accumulations of large ubiquitin-positive protein aggregates similar to those found in some neurodegenerative human diseases.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 01-MAR-2019 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0272192.summary:
The neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses (NCLs), commonly known as Batten disease, belong to a group of neurological disorders causing blindness, seizures, loss of motor function and cognitive ability, and premature death. ''Dictyostelium'' Mfsd8 is a homolog of human MFSD8 (CLN7), identified as one of the mutated genes in the disease. Conserved key residues, protein domains and a structural model greatly overlap between both, the human and and ''Dictyostelium'' protein. Mfsd8 proteins contain multiple transmembrane domains.
GFP-fusions show that Mfsd8 localizes to endsomal compartments and acidic vesicles, including late endosomes. Mass spectrometry has been used to reveal the Mfsd8 interactive. Among the interacting proteins cathepsin D has been independently verified ([/gene/DDB_G0279411 ctsD]). Other interacting candidates are [/gene/DDB_G0285793 cadA] or [/gene/DDB_G0281605 cfaD]. The three proteins also interact with Cln5 ([/gene/DDB_G0275299 cln5]) suggesting a NCL protein network. The ''mfsd8'' null mutant is involved in protein secretion. During starvation, intracellular levels of CtsD and Cln5 are reduced compared to wild-type. Because expression levels are not affected by the mutation, conditioned starvation buffer has been tested for the proteins and elevated levels found. Thus Mfsd8 negatively regulates secretion of CtsD and Cln5 during starvation )[http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/32087303 Huber et al. 2020]). Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 21-JUL-2020 PF

DDB_G0288065.summary: CdcD is a member of the triple A ATPase family and is the ortholog of human VCP (p97), mutations in which cause autosomal-dominant IBMPFD (inclusion body myopathy with early onset Paget's disease of bone and frontotemporal dementia). Overexpression of wild type or mutant ''cdcD'' in both AX2 and ''atg9'' ([/gene/DDB_G0285323 atg9]) null cells results in defects in growth, phototaxis, development, proteasomal activity, and ubiquitinylated proteins, indicating misregulation of multiple essential cellular processes. Expression of wild type ''cdcD'' in ''atg9'' null cells results in aberrant fruiting body morphology, however the expression of ''cdcD''(R155C/E219K) in the ''atg9'' null strain rescued this defect ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23056506 Arhzaouy et al. 2012)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29912958 Arhzaouy et al. 2018)]. CdcD has ATPase activity which is abolished in a ''cdcD''(E219K) mutant. CdcD binds to the UBX domain-containing protein 9 (UBXD9) ([/gene/DDB_G0279285 DDB_G0279285]). CdcD is found in the cytoplasm and the nucleus, and the presence of UBXD9 causes an increased enrichment of CdcD in the nucleus ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/27132113 Rijal et al. 2016)]. CdcD expression is dependent on both the kinase and the RNase activities of IreA ([/gene/DDB_G0267650 ireA]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29632077 Ongay-Larios et al. 2018)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 08-JAN-2021 RD

DDB_G0279307.summary:
''Dictyostelium discoideum'' contains three highly similar vacuolin genes: ([/gene/DDB_G0289485 vacA]), ([/gene/DDB_G0279191 vacB]) and ''vacC''. They share a domain structure similar to metazoan flotillins, with a central PHB-like domain and a C-terminal coiled-coil region. Expression of ''vacC'' is upregulated in response to intracellular ''Mycobacterium marinum'' infection ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31823727 Kjellin et al. 2019]). All three vacuolins are tightly associated with membranes, and are recruited very early to phagosomes and steadily accumulate on post-lysososomes until exocytosis [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9276759 (Rauchenberger et al. 1997]), [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16445684 (Peracino, et al. 2006]), ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/32482795 Bosmani, et al. 2020]).
''vacC'' null mutants have a severe defect in phagocytosis, and a ''vacA''/''vacB''/''vacC'' triple null mutant revealed that the phagocytic defect results from impaired particle recognition. ''vacA''/''vacB''/''vacC'' mutants also have defects in plasma membrane protein recycling, decreased cell surface adhesion, and a more rapid phagosome maturation. In addition, ([/gene/DDB_G0274455 myoI]) (MyoVII) and ([/gene/DDB_G0290481 talA]) gene expression and protein levels are reduced in ''vacA''/''vacB''/''vacC'' mutants, and MyoVII expression rescues the adhesion, particle uptake and surface protein recycling phenotypes in these mutants. These results suggest that the absence of MyoVII and TalA are responsible for the uptake defects observed in vacuolin knockout mutants, and lead to the proposal that vacuolins stabilize the MyoVII/TalA complex formed at specific areas of the phagocytic cup and early endocytic compartments ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/32482795 Bosmani, et al. 2020]). Gene has been comprehensively annotated 03-NOV-2020 RD

DDB_G0283441.summary: During analysis of a ''Dictyostelium'' mutant defective in chemotactic responses, [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25609090  Lin et al. 2015] identified a novel actin-binding protein serving to modulate cell migration. AbpG is enriched in cortical/lamellipodial regions and colocalizes with F-actin.The 501-550 residue region of AbpG is essential for AbpG to localize to lamellipodia and is sufficient for binding to F-actin, and represents a novel actin-binding protein domain. In addition ''abpG'' null cells have significantly higher F-actin levels compared with wild-type cells. DDB_G0289197.summary:
Histones form the nucleosomal core ([/ontology/go/0000786/annotation/page/1 nucleosome]) ([/ontology/go/0006334/annotation/page/1 nucleosome assembly]) that is fundamental to chromatin structure (). The histone octamer is composed of an H3-H4 tetramer (two H3-H4 dimers) coupled with an H2A-H2Btetramer (two H2A-H2B dimers). The histone H1 linker protein plays a role in packaging nucleosomes into the 30 nmfiber found in chromatin ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9177486 Bukenberger et al. 1992]).
In ''Dictyostelium discoideum'' and ''Saccharomyces cerevisiae'', only one copy of histone [/gene/DDB_G0285319 H1] appears to be present, in comparison to other eukaryotes which have multiple copies and subtypes([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7867938 Hauser et al. 1995], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9046096 Ushinsky et al.1997]). Two putative H2A family members, [/gene/DDB_G0279667 H2AX] and [/gene/DDB_G0286747 H2AZ], and three H2Adomain-containing proteins, [/gene/DDB_G0289187 H2Av1], [/gene/DDB_G0289193 H2Av2], [/gene/DDB_G0289197 H2Av3], are present in ''Dictyostelium''. Two H2B domain-containing proteins also exist inthe ''Dicty'' genome: [/gene/DDB_G0293758 H2Bv1] and [/gene/DDB_G0276273 H2Bv2]. There are three histone H3proteins, [/gene/DDB_G0267402 H3a] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9177486 Bukenberger et al. 1992]), [/gene/DDB_G0270838 H3b], and [/gene/DDB_G0271092 H3c], and two H3 domain-containing proteins, [/gene/DDB_G0291185 H3v1] and [/gene/DDB_G0277979 H3v2]. We have also identified two histone H4proteins, [/gene/DDB_G0277183 H4a] and [/gene/DDB_G0276863 H4b], which have identical protein sequences but non-identical nucleotide sequences.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 13-APR-2004 KP

DDB_G0269154.summary: N-linked high mannose oligosaccharides on glycoproteins are trimmed by alpha-glucosidase. A strain lacking alpha-glucosidase II was found to be missing a post-translational modification common to many lysosomal enzymes and the mutation was subsequently mapped to the ''modA'' locus on chromosome 1 [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/57116  (Dimond and Loomis, 1976)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/96112  (Free et al. 1978)]. The activity of several lysosomal acid hydrolases is reduced in ''modA''- mutant strains. Failure to remove two alpha-1,3-linked glucose residues from the N-linked oligosaccharides delays intracellular transport of the hydrolases from the rough endoplasmic reticulum to the Golgi complex and secretion from lysosomal compartments [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2505671  (Ebert et al. 1989)]. Loss of the enzyme also results in a block to addition of fucose to neutral N-glycans and a major reduction in addition of bisecting N-acetylglucosamine residues [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24574058  (Hykollari et al. 2014)]. The ''modA'' gene was cloned from a REMI mutant that makes short, thick stalks and was found to be highly similar to mammalian and yeast alpha-glucosidase II genes [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9397534  (Freeze et al. 1997)]. The original nitrosoguanidine induced mutation was the result of conversion of a G to an A in the codon at position 644 replacing glycine with aspartate.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 24-JAN-2019 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0277879.summary: ''ugpB'' is responsible for most of the uridine diphosphate glucose pyrophosphorylase activity (UDP-glucose pyrophosphorylase) during development ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12060658 Bishop et al. 2002)]. Biochemical assays found a 10 fold increase in UDP-glucose pyrophosphorylase activity between 10 and 20 hours of development ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6067273 Ashworth and Sussman, 1967)]. Mutant strains lacking this enzyme activity develop well until culmination but then arrest as gnarled fingers with reduced levels of polysaccharides ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/944665 Dimond et al. 1976)]. Disruption of ''ugpB'' results in reduced levels of glycogen and development ending with small, gnarled fruiting bodies ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12060658 Bishop et al. 2002)]. There is a second gene encoding UDP-glucose pyrophosphorylase, ''uppA'' ([/gene/DDB_G0289875 uppA]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3035502 Ragheb et al.1987)]. Disruption of ''uppA'' results in cells that develop normally and have only slightly reduced UDP-glucose pyrophosphorylase activity ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12060658 Bishop et al. 2002)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 24-MAY-2016 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0278225.summary:
The homeodomain is a sequence-specific DNA binding motif that consists of a helix-turn-helix. Homeobox-containing proteins have transcription factor activity. They have beenidentified in most if not all phyla of eukaryotes. Inmetazoans, homeobox-containing proteins are known to be involvedin regulating the anterior-posterior body plan and in thespecification of certain cell types and anterior-posteriorcompartments (see [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9486804 Han and Firtel 1998] and references therein). There are 14 predicted proteins that contain homeobox domains in ''Dictyostelium'':[/gene/DDB_G0275173 hbx2], [/gene/DDB_G0291075 warA], [/gene/DDB_G0291197 hbx3], [/gene/DDB_G0272967 hbx4], [/gene/DDB_G0273127 hbx5-1] (on the chromosome 2 duplication: [/gene/DDB_G0273645 hbx5-2]), [/gene/DDB_G0277505 hbx6], [/gene/DDB_G0278225 hbx7], [/gene/DDB_G0279257 hbx8], [/gene/DDB_G0280473 hbx9], [/gene/DDB_G0284293 hbx10], [/gene/DDB_G0295787 hbx11], [/gene/DDB_G0286733 hbx12], [/gene/DDB_G0288975 hbx13], and [/gene/DDB_G0289677 hbx14].
[http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25963254 Mishra and Saran 2015] performed a genome-wide classification and comparative genomic analysis of the 14 homeobox genes present in D. discoideum, and found that they could be classified into 3 groups: TALE, OTHER and NOVEL classes, ''hbx7'' belonging to the NOVEL class.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 07-JUL-2015 RD

DDB_G0292816.summary: ''racL'' encodes a guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G protein) of the Rho family of small GTPases. G proteins are key components of signal transduction networks in which they function as molecular signaling switches, binding to GDP in the off state while binding GTP in the on state. Guanine nucleotide-exchange factors (GEFs) promote the exchange of GDP for GTP on Ras GTPases thus activating them, while GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) inactivate Ras GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP. GxcC ([/gene/DDB_G0284845 gxcC]) is a possible GEF for RacL ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23363311 Plak et al. 2013]). ''racL'' is expressed only at low levels and exclusively after 12 hours of starvation ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11222756 Rivero et al. 2001]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 03-JUN-2020 RD

DDB_G0271504.summary:
Seven BEACH domain-containing proteins have been identified in the ''Dictyostelium'' genome: [/gene/DDB_G0269150 lvsA], ''lvsB'', [/gene/DDB_G0280971 lvsC], [/gene/DDB_G0271502 lvsD], [/gene/DDB_G0282925 lvsE], [/gene/DDB_G0284333 lvsF], and [/gene/DDB_G0268088 lvsG]. LvsB is the closest ''Dictyostelium'' homolog of the mammalian Lyst protein (LYSosomal Trafficking regulator) that causes Chediak-Higashi syndrome (CHS), characterized by impaired lysosomal transport and resulting in partial albinism, immunodeficiency and neurological problems.
''lvsB'' null mutants have defects in lysosome organization and biogenesis, and exhibit enhanced regulated secretion of lysosomal enzymes, a phenotype reminiscent of the Chediak-Higashi syndrome ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11865029 Cornillon et al. 2002]). They also appear to have enlarged acidic lysosomes, probably due to an increase in fusion rates and suggesting that LvsB acts as a negative regulator of fusion ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11854420 Harris et al. 2002]). Consistent with its requirement for proper lysosome organization, LvsB is localized to the lysosome and phagocytic vesicle ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17488289 Kypri et al. 2007]).
LvsB contributes to lysosome function by antagonizing the function of Rab14 ([/gene/DDB_G0281337 rab14]), a protein that promotes homotypic fusion among lysosomes. Expression of activated Rab14 phenocopies the loss of LvsB, causing inappropriate heterotypic fusion between lysosomes and post-lysosomes while expression of inactivated Rab14 suppresses the phenotype of LvsB null cells and restores their lysosomal size and segregation from post-lysosomes. These results suggest that LvsB binds to late lysosomes and promotes the inactivation of DdRab14, which then allows the lysosomes to mature into post-lysosomes for eventual secretion ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23387437 Kypri et al. 2013]). Comparison of the phenotypes of ''lvsB'' null cells with those of two mutants known to be defective in lysosomal fission, ''apm3'' null ([/gene/DDB_G0277901 apm3]) and WASH null ([/gene/DDB_G0292878 wshA]), revealed differences in the temporal localization of the post-lysosomal marker vacuolin, vesicle acidity, and vesicle fusion dynamics, further supporting a role for ''lvsB'' as a negative regulator of vesicle fusion ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25086066 Falkenstein et al. 2014]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 29-JUL-2020 RD

DDB_G0276943.summary: The Plasmodium falciparum chloroquine resistance transporter (PfCRT) carries a point mutation (K76T)that is found in chloroquine-resistant strains of malaria, posing a major health risk. Threehomologs of PfCRT exist in ''Dictyostelium discoideum'': [/gene/DDB_G0276943 crtp1], [/gene/DDB_G0277321 crtp2], and [/gene/DDB_G0270204 crtp3] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11343215 Nomura et al.2001], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15883156 Naude et al. 2005]), all of whichcontain ten predicted transmembrane domains ([/ontology/go/0016021/annotation/page/1 integral to membrane]). The CRTp1 protein is localized to the[/ontology/go/0012506/annotation/page/1 vesicle membrane], and a fusion of the N-terminus of ''Dictyostelium'' CRTp1 with PfCRT localizes tothe endosomes. Transformation of ''Dictyostelium'' cells with mutant PfCRT allows the cells toexpel chloroquine, making it an ideal system in which to study malaria drug resistance ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15883156 Naude et al. 2005]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 20-OCT-2005 KP

In a search for novel receptors similar to the cAR (cAMP receptor) proteins ([/ontology/go/0001646/annotation/page/1 cAMP receptor activity]), [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14732403 Raisley et al. (2004)] identified three crl (cAMP receptor-like) genes: [/gene/DDB_G0280983 crlA], ''crlB'', and [/gene/DDB_G0283619 crlC]. DDB_G0274569.summary: ''acgA'' encodes one of the three adenylyl cyclases in ''Dictyostelium''. AgcA forms a homodimer and was characterized as the first intramolecular osmosensor in eukaryotes [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14718564  (Saran and Schaap 2004)]. The SDF-1 pathway acts through AcgA and PKA to prepare prespore and prestalk cells for terminal differentiation [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21602484  (Anjard et al. 2011)]. The only other CHASE domain in a ''Dictyostelium'' protein is the binding site for SDF-2 in the receptor histidine kinase, DhkA ([/gene/DDB_G0280961 dhkA]).Basic annotations have been added to this gene, 22-JUN-2015 PF; summary contribution: Bill Loomis
