DDB_G0282835.summary:
The MADS-box (for the initials of the first identified members: MCM1, ARG80 from yeast, Deficient from Arabidopsis and SRF from humans) is a in a highly conserved60 amino-acid region that contain a dimerization and a DNA-binding domain ([/ontology/go/0003700/annotation/page/1 transcription factor activity]), ([/ontology/go/0006355/annotation/page/1 regulation of transcription, DNA-dependent]). The serum response factor (SRF) is a DNA-binding proteininvolved in the transcriptional activation ofgenes in response to serum in cultured mammalian cells (see [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9729488 Escalante and Sastre 1998] and references therein).There are 4 predicted proteins that contain a MADS box in the ''Dictyostelium'' genome: [/gene/DDB_G0281387 srfA], [/gene/DDB_G0282835 srfB], [/gene/DDB_G0268920 srfC], and [/gene/DDB_G0283483 srfD].
''srfB'' is expressed in vegetative cells as well as during late aggregation (6-12h). Its promoter has three different transcription start sites active in different cell types. Null mutants of ''srfB'' have a number of different phenotypes: accelerated aggregation, abolished streaming, decreased growth rate, aberrant cytokinesis, and increased pinocytosis. The developmental defects can be rescued by providing cAMP pulses, indicating that at last some of the defects observed are due to aberrant cAMP signaling ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18339368 Galardi-Castilla et al. 2008]). Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 23-MAY-2008 PG

DDB_G0292554.summary: The ABC superfamily of genes is one of the largest in the genomes of both bacteria and eukaryotes. The proteins encoded by these genes all carry a characteristic 200- to 250-amino-acid ATP-binding cassette that gives them their family name ([/ontology/go/0042626/annotation/page/1 ATPase activity, coupled to transmembrane movement of substances]). In bacteria they are mostly involved in nutrient import, while in eukaryotes many are involved in export([/ontology/go/0006810/annotation/page/1 transport]), ([/ontology/go/0016021/annotation/page/1 integral to membrane]). Seven different families (A to G) have been defined in eukaryotes based on sequence homology, domain topology, and function. ''Dictyostelium'' has 71 ABC transporters (including one on the chromosome 2 duplication) and 11 ABCB family members: [/gene/DDB_G0293416 abcB1], [/gene/DDB_G0293438 abcB2], [/gene/DDB_G0291714 abcB3], [/gene/DDB_G0279915 abcB4],[/gene/DDB_G0292554 abcB5], [/gene/DDB_G0282931 abcB6], [/gene/DDB_G0269720 abcB7], [/gene/DDB_G0293002 tagA], [/gene/DDB_G0286119 tagB], [/gene/DDB_G0286121 tagC], and [/gene/DDB_G0286123 tagD]. The B family includes three main subtypes: full transporters involved in multiple drug resistance (MDR), half-transporters targeted to mitochondria, and half-transporters involved in peptide transport [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12456012 (Anjard and Loomis 2002)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 16-JUN-2003 PG

DDB_G0292758.summary:
Mob1 was originally identified in ''Saccharomyces cerevisiae'' as a binder of [/gene/DDB_G0280995 mps1], a kinase involved in mitotic regulation ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9436989 Luca and Winey 1998]). Mob1 serves as a substrate for Mps1 and functions to regulate the NDR kinases (nuclear Dbf2-related, [/gene/DDB_G0278457 ndrA], [/gene/DDB_G0288753 ndrB], [/gene/DDB_G0284839 ndrC], and [/gene/DDB_G0289543 ndrD]) in mammals, which are involved in cell proliferation ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15067004 Devroe et al.2004]). The Mob1 family of proteins are highly conserved but have no characterized function. In ''Dictyostelium'', three Mob1-like proteins exist: [/gene/DDB_G0278907 mobA], [/gene/DDB_G0292758 mobB], and [/gene/DDB_G0293706 mobC]. A fourth protein, [/gene/DDB_G0283625 DDB_G0283625], contains a Mob1-like motif, however, it does not cluster with Mob1 proteins from other species.
MobA has been shown to bind to [/gene/DDB_G0278457 ndrA] [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21134080 (Kastner et al. 2011)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 15-JUN-2012 PF

DDB_G0272562.summary: Three closely related genes, gene ''[/gene/DDB_G0272833 csbA]'', gene ''[/gene/DDB_G0272562 csbB]'' and gene ''[/gene/DDB_G0272756 csbC]'', encode 12 kDa proteins that form contact site B which functions in cell-cell adhesion during early development [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8626027  (Xu et al., 1996)]. Early adhesion can be blocked by 10 mM EDTA and is mediated by contact site B [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/5002049  (Gerisch, 1968]; [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/4993098  Beug, et al.1970)]. Early adhesion can also be blocked by antibodies to a glycoprotein, gp24, encoded by gene ''[/gene/DDB_G0285793 cadA]''cadA [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3569662  (Knecht et al., 1987]; [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8663243  Wong et al., 1996)]. Antibodies to gp24 recognize the fusion protein generated by a lamda gt11 expression construct carrying a portion of the ''csbA'' cDNA [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3149564  (Loomis, 1988)]. Deletion of all 3 ''csb'' genes delayed the appearance of EDTA-resistant adhesion by 6 hours [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8626027  (Xu et al., 1996)]. Expression of ''csbA'' and ''csbB'' is stimulated about 3 fold by cAMP during early development, increases to about 24-fold during aggregation and slowly falls after the slug stage to 3-fold at full culmination compared to vegetative cells [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25887420  (Rosengarten et al., 2015)]. DDB_G0267428.summary: The ABC superfamily of genes is one of the largest in the genomes of both bacteria and eukaryotes. The proteins encoded by these genes all carry a characteristic 200- to 250-amino-acid ATP-binding cassette ([/ontology/go/0042626/annotation/page/1 ATPase activity, coupled to transmembrane movement of substances]) that gives them their family name. In bacteria they are mostly involved in nutrient import, while in eukaryotes many are involved in export([/ontology/go/0006810/annotation/page/1 transport]). Seven different families (A to G) have been defined in eukaryotes based on sequence homology, domain topology, and function. ''Dictyostelium'' has 71 ABC transporters (including one on the chromosome 2 duplication). The ABCH family includes members that do not fit into the seven eukaryotic families and are not necessarily related to each other. ''Dictyostelium'' has five genes that compose this group: [/gene/DDB_G0292384 abcH1], [/gene/DDB_G0267428 abcH2], [/gene/DDB_G0275697 abcH3], [/gene/DDB_G0283479 abcH4], and[/gene/DDB_G0293528 arsA]. The ''Dictyostelium'' [/gene/DDB_G0292384 abcH1] and [/gene/DDB_G0267428 abcH2] genes have a single ABC domain and no TM domain. They cluster with ABC transporters involved in the uptake of polar amino acids[http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12456012  (Anjard and Loomis 2002)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 16-JUN-2003 PG

DDB_G0268920.summary:
The MADS-box (for the initials of the first identified members: MCM1, ARG80 from yeast, Deficient from Arabidopsis and SRF from humans) is a in a highly conserved 60 amino-acid region that contain a dimerization and a DNA-binding domain. There are 4 proteins that contain a MADS box in the ''Dictyostelium'' genome: [/gene/DDB_G0281387 srfA], [/gene/DDB_G0282835 srfB], [/gene/DDB_G0268920 mef2A], and [/gene/DDB_G0283483 srfD] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9729488 Escalante and Sastre 1998]).
Mef2A has been found to be more similar to animal Mef-2 proteins than to SRF proteins. Mef2A mutant strains show reduced growth when feeding on bacteria and are able to develop, but spore production is significantly decreased. Prespore cell differentiation is greatly reduced and prestalk differentiation is slightly abnormal, especially in the tip organizer. A comparison of the genes transcribed by mutant and wild-type strains during development indicates that prestalk gene expression is enhanced, while prespore gene expression is decreased [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23577638 (Galardi-Castilla et al. 2013)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 25-NOV-2013 PF
DDB_G0268920.note: Note, the curated model was created from information in PMID 23577638 where it was determined that this gene contains two exons (and one intron) in the 5' UTR. The last nucleotide in the 2nd UTR exon provides the A for the start codon, which is completed with the TG in the next exon  (representing the CDS). However, database constraints did not allow for a single nucleotide exon at the 5' end and 3 upstream nucleotides (AAA) needed to be added to create an in-frame sequence. This currently results in an extra amino acid (K) preceding the actual N-terminal M residue. The correct protein sequence starts with a Methionine and is 1,048 aa long; UniProt record Q55F37 contains the correct sequence. 21-NOV -2013 PF

DDB_G0277759.summary:
The [/gene/DDB_G0277759 phyA] gene encodes a prolyl 4-hydroxylase (P4H1) that catalyzes hydroxylation of Skp1 ([/gene/DDB_G0269230 fpaA]/[/gene/DDB_G0273251 fpaB-1]) protein at Proline 143. HyPro143 is subsequently glycosylated by a series of reactions; this post-translational modification is necessary for nuclear enrichment of Skp1 in wild-type ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8287496 Sassi et al. 2001]). The ''Dictyostelium'' P4H1 protein is predicted to be related to the mammalian hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF)-1alpha-type prolyl 4-hydroxylase (P4H). This similarity is further evidenced by common properties, such as enzyme kinetics and cofactors, shared by both the Dd P4H1 and P4H ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/PUB4889 van der Wel et al. 2005]).
Glycosylation of Skp1 has been extensively studied in ''Dictyostelium''. The initial step in Skp1 glycosylation involves the hydroxylation of Pro143 by P4H1, [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9660787 Teng-umnuay et al. 1998]). HyPro143 is then modified by the glycosyltransferase [/gene/DDB_G0275699 gnt1], which transfers a GlcNAc (N-acetylglucosamine) to the Skp1 protein ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10593934 Teng-umnuay et al. 1999]). The Skp1-GlcNAc is extended by a bifunctional diglycosyltransferase, [/gene/DDB_G0283761 pgtA], which processively adds galactose and fucose ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11423539 van der Wel et al. 2001], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12244067 van der Wel et al. 2002]). Subsequently two additional galactose residues are added by [/gene/DDB_G0283005 agtA] to yield the Skp1 pentasaccharide (GGFGGnOSkp1; [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16495217 Ercan et al. 2006], reviewed in [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31128470 West and Kim 2019]).
A ''phyA'' null mutant lacks Skp1 hydroxylation ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/PUB4889 van der Wel et al. 2005]) and is unable to culminate under normal conditions; this defect is rescued at highly elevated oxygen levels (40-70%). ''in situ'' staining with an antibody raised against P4H1 shows that it is constitutively expressed in tipped mounds and slugs. Interestingly, the Skp1 hydroxylation and development defects of the ''phyA'' null mutant can be rescued by expressing ''phyA'' either in prespore or prestalk cells. Active P4H1 was required for complementation, as a mutant with no activity, R276A, failed to culminate ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17699611 West et al. 2007]). Further mutant analyses showed not only is Skp1 a substrate for P4H1, it is also a functional mediator of P4H1 activity in cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20969846 Wang et al. 2011]). Additional investigations showed that full SKP1 glycosylation is required for optimal oxygen sensing during development, for example [/gene/DDB_G0283005 agtA] knockout or overexpression mutants require elevated oxygen levels to culminate ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19687007 Wang et al. 2009], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22128189 Zhang et al. 2011], reviewed in [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25988702 West and Blader 2015]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 12-MAR-2020 PF

DDB_G0270814.summary:
The NIMA (never in mitosis) family of serine/threnonine protein kinases ([/ontology/go/0004674/annotation/page/1 protein serine/threonine kinase activity]) wereoriginally identified in mitotic mutants of the fungus ''Aspergillus nidulans''. NIMA-related kinases havebeen cloned in several vertebrates, however, ''nek2'' represents the first identified non-vertebrate Nek2 kinase [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11956323 (Graf 2002)].
[http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11956323 Graf (2002)] demostrates that ''Dictyostelium'' Nek2 localizes to the microtubule-organizing centers (MTOCs) ([/ontology/go/0005813/annotation/page/1 centrosome]), although acytoplasmic ([/ontology/go/0005737/annotation/page/1 cytoplasm]) pool of Nek2 also exists, similar to its vertebrate counterpart. Overexpression of a ''GFP:nek2'' fusion constructresults in abnormal nuclear morphology and supernumerary MTOCs ([/ontology/go/0007098/annotation/page/1 centrosome cycle]). Overexpression of a series ofdeletion constructs results in a supernumerary MTOC phenotype only when the C-terminal domain is expressed and not when thecatalytic kinase domain alone is expressed. This implies a centrosome nucleation function for the C-terminal domain([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11956323 Graf 2002]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 07-APR-2004 KP
phenotypes: increased number of microtubule organizing center

DDB_G0291352.summary: ''Dictyostelium'' contains orthologs of the core components of the presenilin/gamma-secretase complex: presenilin A ([/gene/DDB_G0291352 psenA]), presenilin B ([/gene/DDB_G0292310 psenB]), Aph-1 ([/gene/DDB_G0267976 aph1]) and nicastrin ([/gene/DDB_G0287801 ncstn]) which are capable of amyloidogenic processing of ectopically expressed human amyloid precursor protein (APP) to generate amyloid-beta peptides. Gamma-secretase activity is required for phagocytosis in Dictyostelium, and gamma-secretase mutants have primary defects in pre-spore/spore differentiation [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20699477  (McMains et al. 2010)]. A double null mutant lacking both presenilin A and presenilin B genes is blocked at the aggregation stage prior to morphogenesis. Either PsenB or human Psen1 can rescue the developmental phenotype of this mutant. In addition, presenilin loss in Dictyostelium results in elevated cAMP levels and enhanced stimulation-induced calcium release, suggesting that presenilins regulate these intracellular signalling pathways. [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24463814  (Ludtmann et al. 2014)]. ''Dictyostelium'' orthologs of the gamma-secretase complex PsenA, PsenB, Aph-1, and Nicastrin are necessary for macropinocytosis, phagocytosis, and autophagy, indicating roles in a general defect in lysosomal trafficking and degradation. In addition, loss of psenA/psenB and Aph-1 leads to an accumulation of ubiquitinated proteins, suggesting impaired protein degradation in these mutants. All of the endocytic defects in PSEN ortholog mutants can be fully restored by proteolytically inactive ''Dictyostelium'' PsenB and human PSEN1, demonstrating an evolutionarily conserved non-proteolytic role for presenilin in lysosomal trafficking and autophagy. [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30806144  (Sharma et al. 2019)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 23-JUL-2019 RD; annotation contributions: PMID:24463814 Grant Otto

DDB_G0290009.summary:
Sepiapterin reductase (SR, EC: 1.1.1.153) participates in the biosynthesis of L-erythro-tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4), a co-factor for aromatic aminoacid hydroxylation, nitric oxide synthesis, and glyceryl-etherhydroxylation ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10727395 Thony et al. 2000]). The first reaction in BH4 biosynthesis is catalyzed by GTP cyclohydrolase I ([/gene/DDB_G0288481 gchA]), which converts GTP to dihydroneopterin triphosphate (H2-NTP), which is transformed to 6-pyruvoyltetrahydropterin (PPH4) by 6-pyruvoyltetrahydropterin synthase (PTPS) ([/gene/DDB_G0279095 ptsA]). The diketo compound is reduced further to BH4 by SR through two consecutive reductions.
Cells in which ''sr'' has been knocked out still produce a small amount of pteridine (L-erythro-biopterin and D-threo-biopterin), possibly through a different pathway involving aldehyde reductase ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21256841 Choi et al. 2005]). The mutant exhibits decreased growth rates, reduced spore viability, impaired mitochondrial function, and increased sensitivity to oxidative stress. The authors propose that tetrahydropterines have an antioxidant function in ''Dictyostelium'' ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17976377 Kim et al. 2007]). Basic annotations have been added to this gene, 19-AUG-2008 PG

DDB_G0293526.summary:
''racC'' encodes a guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G protein) of the Rho family of small GTPases. G proteins are key components of signal transduction networks in which they function as molecular signaling switches, binding to GDP in the off state while binding GTP in the on state. Guanine nucleotide-exchange factors (GEFs) promote the exchange of GDP for GTP on Ras GTPases thus activating them, while GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) inactivate Ras GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP. GxcT ([/gene/DDB_G0269610 gxcT]) binds RacC and is a likely GEF for RacC ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24248334 Wang et al. 2013]). The armadillo-like protein Darlin ([/gene/DDB_G0288771 darA]) binds RacC, but GEF activity has not been demonstrated ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9802899 Vithalani et al. 1998]). Additional possible GEFs for RacC include DockD ([/gene/DDB_G0284725 docD]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19037099 Para et al. 2009]), ZizB ([/gene/DDB_G0293084 zizB]), ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22366457 Pakes et al. 2012]), gxcDD ([/gene/DDB_G0279733 gxcDD]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17584488 Mondal et al. 2007]) and GxcC ([/gene/DDB_G0284845 gxcC]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23363311 Plak et al. 2013]). DRG ([/gene/DDB_G0291978 xacA]) contains both GAP and GEF domains, and DRG displays weak GAP activity for RacC ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9188459 Ludbrook et al. 1997]). Other possible GAPs for RacC include GAPA ([/gene/DDB_G0269140 gapA]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21085675 Mondal et al. 2010]) and DGAP1 ([/gene/DDB_G0287585 rgaA]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22302991 Filic et al. 2012]), ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26940518 Rivero et al. 2016]).
RacC has multiple binding partners that may function as downstream effectors. These include: the myosin heavy chain kinase PakB ([/gene/DDB_G0276459 pakB]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15509655 de la Roche et al. 2005]), PakC ([/gene/DDB_G0267450 pakC]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15470506 Park et al. 2004]), coronin A ([/gene/DDB_G0267382 corA]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24347642 Swaminathan et al. 2013]), WASP ([/gene/DDB_G0293834 wasA]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16968699 Han et al. 2006]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31786060 Amato et al. 2019)] and WASP-B ([/gene/DDB_G0272811 wasB]) [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23791739 (Chung et al. 2013)]. RacC also binds to the Rho GDP-dissociation inhibitor RhoGDI1 ([/gene/DDB_G0291077 rdiA]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12163018 Imai et al. 2002]).
''racC'' plays an important role in signaling networks that regulate F-actin assembly during ''Dictyostelium'' chemotaxis and other processes that depend on the organization of the actin cytoskeleton. ''racC'' is expressed during growth, but ''racC'' mRNA levels decrease significantly during aggregation before again increasing late during development ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8294042 Bush et al. 1993]). ''racC'' overexpression results in aberrant F-actin organization with cells displaying unusual dorsal and peripheral F-actin rich surface blebs. Overexpression of ''racC'' also results in increased rates of phagocytosis, but a decrease in macropinocytosis and exocytosis rates ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9763450 Seastone et al. 1998]). ''racC'' is activated at the leading edge of chemotaxing cells where it binds and activates WASP. ''racC'' null mutants have defects in both chemotaxis and cytokinesis, and in addition display decreased levels of F-actin polymerization and reduced PI3K ([/gene/DDB_G0278727 pikA], [/gene/DDB_G0283081 pikB]) activation and translocation to the membrane in response to cAMP stimulation ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16968699 Han et al. 2006]). RasC is aberrantly localized in ''wasB'' null cells, and these mutants also have higher levels of activated RacC, suggesting that WASP-B plays a role in the regulation of actin polymerization by modulating the activity and localization of RacC ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23791739 Chung et al. 2013]). ''racC'' null cells also have a streaming defect, forming smaller and more fragmented streams. The adenylate cyclase ACA ([/gene/DDB_G0281545 acaA]), which is normally enriched in the uropod at the back of chemotactically migrating cells, is mainly associated with intracellular vesicular structures in ''racC'' null cells, revealing an important role for RacC in the regulation of ACA localization ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26315268 Wang et al. 2015]). The cell proliferation repressor AprA ([/gene/DDB_G0281663 aprA]) requires RacC to induce chemo-repulsion revealing that ''racC'' also plays a role in chemo-repulsion signal transduction pathways ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30462573 Rijal et al. 2018]). Activated Rac1A ([/gene/DDB_G0277869 rac1A]) and RacC both regulate, and are regulated by, WASP. WASP interacts with activated Rac genes via its CRIB motif, and this interaction is required for WASP to generate pseudopods in the absence of SCAR/WAVE ([/gene/DDB_G0285253 scrA]). However, this interaction also provides a means for WASP to remove activated Racs from the membrane via endocytosis. Thus, WASP contributes to front-rear cell polarity by controlling localization and cellular levels of activated Rac. [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31786060 (Amato et al. 2019)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 06-MAY-2020 RD

Overexpression of [/gene/DDB_G0289815 cupB] antisense mRNA abolishes multicellular development; cells fail to aggregate completely. The sevencalcium up-regulated ''cup'' genes identified are: [/gene/DDB_G0267466 cupA], [/gene/DDB_G0289815 cupB], [/gene/DDB_G0289283 cupC], [/gene/DDB_G0293536 cupD], [/gene/DDB_G0294531 cupE], [/gene/DDB_G0289813 cupF], and [/gene/DDB_G0289883 cupG] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14871937 Coukell et al. 2004]). There are three other related genes, [/gene/DDB_G0290563 cupH], [/gene/DDB_G0272242 cupI], and [/gene/DDB_G0277959 cupJ]. Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 24-MAR-2008 PG

DDB_G0289331.summary: The ABC superfamily of genes is one of the largest in the genomes of both bacteria and eukaryotes. The proteins encoded by these genes all carry a characteristic 200- to 250-amino-acid ATP-binding cassette that gives them their family name ([/ontology/go/0042626/annotation/page/1 ATPase activity, coupled to transmembrane movement of substances]). In bacteria they are mostly involved in nutrient import, while in eukaryotes many are involved in export ([/ontology/go/0006810/annotation/page/1 transport]). Seven different families have been defined in eukaryotes based on sequence homology, domain topology, and function. Sequences from the well-advanced ''Dictyostelium'' genome project have allowed to recognize 71 members of this superfamily (including one on the chromosome 2 duplication). The ABCG family is characterized by the ABC domain preceding the transmembrane domain ([/ontology/go/0016021/annotation/page/1 integral to membrane]). All of the members of this family in animals are half-transporters while all of the fungal members are full transporters with two ABC-transmembrane units. No members of this family are found in bacteria. ''Dictyostelium'' and ''Arabidopsis'' have members of both types ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12456012 Anjard and Loomis 2002]). Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 18-OCT-2004 PG

DDB_G0291362.summary:
DNA-dependent RNA polymerase catalyzes the transcription of DNA into RNA using the four ribonucleoside triphosphates as substrates ([/ontology/go/0003899/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase activity]). Three distinct zinc-containing RNA polymerases are found in eukaryotic nuclei: [/gene/DDB_G0275759 rpa1] for the ribosomal RNA precursor ([/ontology/go/0006360/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase I promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005736/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase I complex]), [/gene/DDB_G0279193 rpb1] for the mRNA precursor ([/ontology/go/0006366/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase II promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005665/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase II, core complex]), and [/gene/DDB_G0277199 rpc1] for 5S and tRNA genes ([/ontology/go/0006383/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase III promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005666/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase III complex]).
RNA polymerase I is a multisubunit complex. The subunits encoded by [/gene/DDB_G0275759 rpa1] (ortholog of ''S. cerevisiae RPA190''), [/gene/DDB_G0288449 rpc2] (''RPA135''), [/gene/DDB_G0268198 rpa43] (''RPA43''), [/gene/DDB_G0290909 rpa49] (''RPA49''), and [/gene/DDB_G0278263 rpa12] (''RPA12'') are unique to RNA polymerase I. Two subunits, [/gene/DDB_G0291362 rpc19] and [/gene/DDB_G0282339 rpa5] (''RPC19'' and ''RPC40'' in ''S. cerevisiae''), are common to RNA polymerase I and RNA polymerase III and correspond to subunits 3 and 11 of RNA polymerase II. Subunits [/gene/DDB_G0291636 rpb5], [/gene/DDB_G0291037 rpb6], [/gene/DDB_G0278039 rpb8], [/gene/DDB_G0272036 rpb10], and [/gene/DDB_G0283365 rpb12] are common to all three RNA polymerases. Yeast has two additional subunits, ''RPA34'' and ''RPA14'', that do not have clear orthologs in other species, including in ''Dictyostelium'' ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12407181 Peyroche et al. 2002], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12381659 Schramm and Hernandez 2001]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 11-JUN-2009 PG

DDB_G0292560.summary: ''racJ'' encodes a guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G protein) of the Rho family of small GTPases. G proteins are key components of signal transduction networks in which they function as molecular signaling switches, binding to GDP in the off state while binding GTP in the on state. Guanine nucleotide-exchange factors (GEFs) promote the exchange of GDP for GTP on Ras GTPases thus activating them, while GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) inactivate Ras GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP. ''racI'' mRNA is not expressed during the vegetative stage, but is weakly expressed at all stages of development with maximum expression levels after 12 h of starvation, corresponding to the first finger stage ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11201251 Okuwa et al. 2001]), ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11222756 Rivero et al. 2001]). mRNA levels of ''racJ'' increase during sexual development, suggesting that ''racJ'' may function in sexual development ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16573737 Muramoto et al. 2006]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 01-JUN-2020 RD
DDB_G0292560.note: The sequences from the Sequencing Center and GenBank record AF310896 are identical.

DDB_G0267424.summary: Ammonia signaling is essential to the developmental program of ''Dictyostelium''. It is involved in regulatingchemotaxis, the choice between slug migration and culmination, and cell-type specification via differential geneexpression. Ammonia concentrations are regulated in part by environmental factors, however, cellular processes such astransport ([/ontology/go/0008519/annotation/page/1 ammonium transmembrane transporter activity]) and metabolism can alter intracellular concentrations. In the ''Dictyostelium'' proteome,three putative ammonium transporters exist: [/gene/DDB_G0277503 amtA], [/gene/DDB_G0277889 amtB], and [/gene/DDB_G0267424 amtC]. The transcriptlevels of the three ''amt'' genes are constant throughout development, however, their spatial expression patterns, asdetermined by ''in situ'' hybridization, are both distinct and complementary. The ''amtA'' gene is generallyexpressed in the prestalk regions, although it is also found in the upper and lower cups of the sorus and in regionscontacting the substratum. The ''amtB'' transcript is observed primarily in prepore regions and in the spore region ofthe sorus, but is absent from the upper and lower cups. Expression of ''amtC'' is similar to that of ''amtB'', however, it appears transiently in the anterior tip during the first finger stage. Disruption of the ''amtC'' gene results in larger multicelluar structures and developmental arrest at the slug stage, although a smallpercentage of slugs are able to fruit after 40+ hours of starvation ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14686953 Follstaedt et al.2003]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 19-AUG-2008 PG

DDB_G0267430.summary: The ABC superfamily of genes is one of the largest in the genomes of both bacteria and eukaryotes. The proteins encoded by these genes all carry a characteristic 200- to 250-amino-acid ATP-binding cassette that gives them their family name ([/ontology/go/0042626/annotation/page/1 ATPase activity, coupled to transmembrane movement of substances]). In bacteria they are mostly involved in nutrient import, while in eukaryotes many are involved in export ([/ontology/go/0006810/annotation/page/1 transport]). Seven different families have been defined in eukaryotes based on sequence homology, domain topology, and function. Sequences from the well-advanced ''Dictyostelium'' genome project have allowed to recognize 71 members of this superfamily (including one on the chromosome 2 duplication). The ABCG family is characterized by the ABC domain preceding the transmembrane domain ([/ontology/go/0016021/annotation/page/1 integral to membrane]). All of the members of this family in animals are half-transporters while all of the fungal members are full transporters with two ABC-transmembrane units. No members of this family are found in bacteria. ''Dictyostelium'' and ''Arabidopsis'' have members of both types ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12456012 Anjard and Loomis 2002]). Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 18-OCT-2004 PG

DDB_G0275267.summary: The WRKY family proteins contain one or two WRKY domains, which consists of the heptapeptide WRKYGQK as well as a zinc-finger ([/ontology/go/0008270/annotation/page/1 zinc ion binding]). WRKY proteins have specific [/ontology/go/0003677/annotation/page/1 DNA binding] activity towards the W-box, TTGAC(C/T). In plants, WRKY transcription factors control the expression of genes involved in many varied processes: responses to stress, including infection by pathogenic organisms,heat shock and cold shock, as well as many normal processes, such as growth and metabolism ([/ontology/go/0006355/annotation/page/1 regulation of transcription, DNA-dependent]). Outside the kingdom of plants, WRKY transcription factors have only been identified in ''Giardia lamblia'', a primitive eukaryote, and in ''Dictyostelium''. The implications of this observation have been analyzed by [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15629062 Zhang and Wang] in 2004. The authors conclude that WRKY proteins originated in early eukaryotes and have greatly expanded in plants. Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 11-FEB-2005 PG

There are 29 genes encoding actin in ''Dictyostelium'' with amino acid identity greater than 83%, ''act1''-''act29''. Seventeen of these genes encode identical proteins: [/gene/DDB_G0289553 act1], [/gene/DDB_G0274133 act2], [/gene/DDB_G0289005 act4], [/gene/DDB_G0289663 act5], [/gene/DDB_G0274135 act6], [/gene/DDB_G0280545 act7], [/gene/DDB_G0269234 act8], [/gene/DDB_G0274601 act9], [/gene/DDB_G0288879 act11], [/gene/DDB_G0274129 act12], [/gene/DDB_G0274599 act13], [/gene/DDB_G0274137 act14], [/gene/DDB_G0272520 act15], [/gene/DDB_G0272248 act16], [/gene/DDB_G0274727 act19], [/gene/DDB_G0274285 act20], and [/gene/DDB_G0274561 act21], while [/gene/DDB_G0289811 act10], [/gene/DDB_G0275023 act22], and [/gene/DDB_G0289487 act3] respectively have 1, 4 and 11 amino acid differences compared to the 17 identical genes. The proteins encoded by [/gene/DDB_G0274131 act17], [/gene/DDB_G0289489 act18], [/gene/DDB_G0268744 act23] and [/gene/DDB_G0289505 act24]are more divergent.
Actin is a major [/ontology/go/0005200/annotation/page/1 structural constituent of cytoskeleton]. Actin is one of the most abundant proteins in ''Dictyostelium'', constituting approximately 8% of the total protein in vegetative cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/561722 Alton and Lodish et al. 1977]).Actin synthesis is developmentally regulated, peaking shortly after starvation (reviewed by [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6894564 Firtel] in 1981). The different actin genes differ in their levels of expression, with [/gene/DDB_G0274135 act6], [/gene/DDB_G0269234 act8] and [/gene/DDB_G0274129 act12] being highly expressed both during growth and development compared to [/gene/DDB_G0289005 act4], [/gene/DDB_G0289663 act5], [/gene/DDB_G0280545 act7] and [/gene/DDB_G0272248 act16] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6286214 McKeown and Firtel 1981]). DDB_G0287295.summary:
ForC is a formin that lacks a typical FH1 domain but contains FH2 and FH3 domains; it also contains an N-terminal GBD domain. ForC null mutants were able to aggregate but unable to form slugs or develop into full fruiting bodies. Depending on the substratum, aberrant fruiting bodies or tipped mounds were formed. ForC was found to localize to macropinocytotic crowns and cell contact sites colocalizing with the actin cytoskeleton. These results suggested that forC is involved in cell-cell adhesion during later development ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12538772 (Kitayama and Uyeda 2003)]). Further localization studies showed that both the GBD and FH3 domains are required for ForC targeting to cell-cell contacts and early phagocytic cups and macropinosomes ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21846933 (Dames et al. 2011)])
Faix and colleagues found that ForC binds F-actin and crosslinked actin filaments into loose bundles of mixed polarity. The ForC protein is expressed at the onset of early aggregation and peaks around the culmination stage. Accordingly, ForC null cells were markedly impaired in chemotaxis, showing a weaker response to cAMP and a strongly impaired migration speed and development beyond the strongly delayed aggregation stage was very compromised. Spore formation was drastically reduced. When beta-galctosidase was expressed in wild type under the control of the forC promoter, staining was limited to the prespore region and absent from prestalk cells. Furthermore the contact site A gene [/gene/DDB_G0289073 csaA] was expressed 4 hours later in the forC null mutant than in wild type ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23906540 (Junemann et al. 2013)])Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 24-JAN-2014 PF

DDB_G0269114.summary:
Nucleomorphin is a calmodulin binding protein. The numA1 isoform was identified in an expression library screen for calmodulin binding proteins. This protein contains nuclear localization signals (NLS), a Calcium-Calmodulin binding domain (CaMBD), and a glu/asp rich repeat (DEED). A GFP-numA1 fusion protein localized to patches in the nucleoplasm. Cells expressing GFP-NumA1 lacking the acidic DEED repeat showed an increased number of nuclei, which suggests numA1 regulates mitosis [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11919178 (Myre & O'Day 2002)]. A longer isoform, numA2, contains an additional BRCT (Breast Cancer C-Terminal) domain found predominantly in proteins involved in cell cycle checkpoint functions responsive to DNA damage. While the shorter transcript is uniformly expressed throughout development, the larger transcript is expressed at low levels during vegetative growth, increasing by 4 h to remain high throughout development [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15535983 (Myre & O'Day 2004a)]. A two-hybrid screen using numA1 as a bait identified [/gene/DDB_G0283153 cbpD1], a calcium binding protein, to bind numA1, and this interaction required presence of the DEED domain [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15325281 (Myre & O'Day 2004b)]. It has also been shown that the NLS, not the CaMBD, is sufficient for nuclear translocation of numA1, and that the nuclear localization is crucial for its ability to regulate the nuclear number [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15896312 (Myre & O'Day 2005)].
In normal development, numA1 is highly expressed in vegetative cells and expression decreases 80% over the first 4 hours starvation. Differentiation inducing factor 1 (DIF-1) completely blocked the starvation-induced decrease in numA1. Conversely, treatment of vegetative cells with cAMP or ammonia, decreased numA1 expresssion. These results show that numA1 expression is regulated by developmental morphogens [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19000924 (O'Day et al. 2008)].
In 2011, mumA1 has been found to localize to nucleoli and to a lesser degree to the nucleoplasm in interphase. During mitosis, numA1 relocalizes to the centrosome and nuclear envelope. Nuclear or nucleolar localization signals ((NLS/NoLSs) have been mapped [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21327858 (Catalano & O'Day 2011)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 23-OCT-2012 PF

DDB_G0287823.summary:
An ''lrrB'' disruptant strain grows and develops normally until the tipped mound phase, but subsequent development is delayed by several hours and results in misshapen fruiting bodies. Gene expression in ''lrrB'' null cells is aberrant during growth, including multiple genes that are either under, or over-expressed. In addition, LrrB was determined to interact with 3 proteins: FttB, CldA, and CldB. The additional finding that 3 LrrB-regulated genes are similarly misregulated in a ''cldA'' disruptant strain suggests that LrrB and CldA interact to control gene expression during growth and early development. [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20457612 (Sugden et al. 2010)]
Further research by [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21396932 Sugden et al. 2011] characterized the role of ''lrrB'' in multicellular development. Slug formation in ''lrrB'' null mutants is delayed, and the slugs are highly defective in both phototaxis and thermotaxis. ''LrrB'' also develops differently in the darkness than in the light; in the dark, mutants arrest development as an elongated mound, a process termed dark stalling by the authors. LrrB null slugs are defective in pstO prestalk cell differentiation and display aberrant gene expression patterns, including reduced expression of the ecmB gene. In addition, ''LrrB'' null culminants have aberrant morphology, lacking a basal disc and sometimes containing multiple stalk fragments. These results suggest that LrrB is an adaptor protein which is active in diverse developmental signaling pathways. Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 12-NOV-2014 RD

DDB_G0271750.summary: ''nfaA'' encodes a Ras GTPase-activating protein (GAP, rasGAP). RasGAPs are key components of signal transduction networks in which they inactivate Ras GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP. ''nfaA'' null mutants are defective in chemotaxis to cAMP, and display reduced speed and directionality compared with wild-type (wt) cells. ''nfaA'' null mutants also display elevated basal levels as well as extended kinetics of cAMP-induced Ras activation compared to those of wt cells. The kinetics of activation of the Ras small GTPases RasG ([/gene/DDB_G0293434 rasG]) and RasB ([/gene/DDB_G0292998 rasB]) are delayed and extended in ''nfaA'' null mutants, indicating that NfaA has GAP activity towards both RasB and RasG. In chemotaxing ''nfaA'' null cells, Ras activity is also spatially mis-regulated resulting in multiple lamellipod-like extensions and no defined leading edge. Both phosphatidylinositol-3,4,5-triphosphate production and PKB ([/gene/DDB_G0268620 pkbA]) activation are delayed and prolonged in ''nfaA'' null cells. In addition, ''nfaA'' null cells also display random cell motility and cytokinesis defects, and F-actin polymerization is elevated in the mutants. Taken together, these results indicate that ''nfaA'' is involved in the regulation of chemotaxis to cAMP, PI3K signaling, and cytokinesis through the regulation of RasB and RasG activity ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18948008 Zhang et al. 2008]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 15-MAR-2022 RD

DDB_G0290165.summary:
The eukaryotic basic-leucine zipper (bZIP) transcription factors are proteins that dimerize through their leucine repeats to form a coiled coil with two flanking alpha-helices that constitute the basic region that binds DNA ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11017199 Fujii et al. 2000]). There are 19 putative bZIP transcription factors in the ''Dictyostelium'' genome: [/gene/DDB_G0278971 dimA], [/gene/DDB_G0291372 dimB], [/gene/DDB_G0279439 bzpC], [/gene/DDB_G0278379 bzpD], [/gene/DDB_G0269338 bzpE], [/gene/DDB_G0279529 bzpF], [/gene/DDB_G0282749 bzpG], [/gene/DDB_G0277681 bzpH], [/gene/DDB_G0290173 bzpI], [/gene/DDB_G0274993 bzpJ], [/gene/DDB_G0282049 bzpK], [/gene/DDB_G0284023 bzpL], [/gene/DDB_G0282047 bzpM], [/gene/DDB_G0286411 bzpN], [/gene/DDB_G0290169 bzpO], [/gene/DDB_G0290303 bzpP], [/gene/DDB_G0288705 bzpQ], [/gene/DDB_G0290165 bzpR], and [/gene/DDB_G0290171 bzpS]
[http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22403666 (Singleton et al. 2012)] determined that ''bzpR'' null mutants had reduced spore viability and stalk defects, developmental defects similar to those of an eIF2alpha mutant that cannot be phosphorylated. Additional findings indicate that BzpR regulates aspects of development in Dictyostelium, serving as a downstream effector of eIF2a phosphorylation. BzpR production is translationally regulated during development by eIF2alpha phosphorylation by IfkA and IfkB, and through the use of upstream ORFs within the bzpR 5' UTR.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 02-Nov-2017 RD

DDB_G0275029.summary:
The 2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenase complex catalyzes the overall conversion of 2-oxoglutarate to succinyl-CoA and CO2. It contains multiple copies of 3 enzymatic components: E1, E2, and E3. E1 ([/gene/DDB_G0280353 odhA]) has 2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenase activity (). Multiple copies of E1 are bound to a core of dihydrolipoamide succinyltransferase (E2), which also binds multiple copies of lipoamide dehydrogenase (E3). The lipoyl group of E2 ([/gene/DDB_G0275029 odhB]) is reductively succinylated by E1, and then passes this succinyl group to coenzyme A ([/ontology/go/4149/annotation/page/1 dihydrolipoyllysine-residue succinyltransferase activity]).
The E3 enzyme ([/gene/DDB_G0291648 lpd]) is adihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase ([/ontology/go/4148/annotation/page/1 dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase activity]) that is shared by three 2-oxo acid dehydrogenase multienzyme complexes. These include the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, the 2-oxoglutarate dehydrogenase complex, the glycine cleavage system, and the branched-chain 2-oxo acid dehydrogenase complex.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 03-DEC-2004 PF

DDB_G0277859.summary:
The ''mlcE'' gene codes for the essential myosin light chain (ELC) of myosin II. Antisense or mlcE-null mutants resemble [/gene/DDB_G0286355 mhcA] mutants. They grow poorly in suspension and become large and multinucleate. Despite the cytokinesis ([/ontology/go/0000910/annotation/page/1 cytokinesis]) defect myosin localizaion in the cells was shown to be normal. While mlcE- cells are able to respond to chemoattractant with proper directionality, their rate of movement is reduced ([/ontology/go/0006928/annotation/page/1 cell motility]). Aggregation is delayed, and only 50 % of the aggregates progress further to form shorter fruiting bodies with thicker stalks ([/ontology/go/0030587/annotation/page/1 sorocarp development]). Studies using lacZ reporter constructs expressed from cell type specific promoters showed the localization of prespore cells is more susceptible to the loss of ELC ([/ontology/go/0016477/annotation/page/1 cell migration]) than prestalk cells. In myosin purified from the mlcE- cells the actin-activated ATPase activity ([/ontology/go/0030898/annotation/page/1 actin-dependent ATPase activity]) was greatly reduced. This result and the proper localization of myosin in mlcE- cells suggest that its phenotypic defects primarily arise from defective contractile function of myosin rather than its mislocalization [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1535025 (Pollenz et al. 1992)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7593282 (Chen et al. 1995)].
Deletion mutations showed that both the amino and carboxyl termini of the ELC are required for binding to the myosin heavy chain (MHC). When these mutants were analyzed for their ability to complement the cytokinesis defect displayed by mlcE- cells, a correlation to the level of ELC carried by the MHC was observed, indicating that a stoichiometric ELC-MHC association is necessary for normal myosin function in vivo [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7499275 (Ho et al. 1995)]. The ELC wraps around an alpha-helix that extends from the myosin head, where it is believed to play a structural support role. However, substitution mutations of charged residues in loops I, II, III, and helix G of the ELC lead to reduced actin-activated ATPase activity despite stoichiometric binding to the heavy chain. This result suggests that the ELC contributes to myosin's enzymatic activity in addition to providing structural support for the alpha-helical neck region of MHC [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9020178 (Ho et al. 1997)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 19-SEP-2003 PF

RNA polymerase II is composed of 12 subunits: [/gene/DDB_G0279193 rpb1], [/gene/DDB_G0288257 rpb2], [/gene/DDB_G0292244 rpb3], [/gene/DDB_G0282739 rpb4], [/gene/DDB_G0291636 rpb5], [/gene/DDB_G0291037 rpb6], [/gene/DDB_G0284891 rpb7], [/gene/DDB_G0278039 rpb8], [/gene/DDB_G0268306 rpb9], [/gene/DDB_G0272036 rpb10], [/gene/DDB_G0277677 rpb11], and[/gene/DDB_G0283365 rpb12]. Subunits 5, 6, 8, 10, and 12 are common to all threeRNA polymerases (reviewed by [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9618449 Hampsey] in 1998).

DDB_G0289489.summary:
There are 29 genes encoding actin in ''Dictyostelium'' with amino acid identity greater than 83%, ''act1''-''act29''. Seventeen of these genes encode identical proteins: [/gene/DDB_G0289553 act1], [/gene/DDB_G0274133 act2], [/gene/DDB_G0289005 act4], [/gene/DDB_G0289663 act5], [/gene/DDB_G0274135 act6], [/gene/DDB_G0280545 act7], [/gene/DDB_G0269234 act8], [/gene/DDB_G0274601 act9], [/gene/DDB_G0288879 act11], [/gene/DDB_G0274129 act12], [/gene/DDB_G0274599 act13], [/gene/DDB_G0274137 act14], [/gene/DDB_G0272520 act15], [/gene/DDB_G0272248 act16], [/gene/DDB_G0274727 act19], [/gene/DDB_G0274285 act20], and [/gene/DDB_G0274561 act21], while [/gene/DDB_G0289811 act10], [/gene/DDB_G0275023 act22], and [/gene/DDB_G0289487 act3] respectively have 1, 4 and 11 amino acid differences compared to the 17 identical genes. The proteins encoded by [/gene/DDB_G0274131 act17], [/gene/DDB_G0289489 act18], [/gene/DDB_G0268744 act23] and [/gene/DDB_G0289505 act24]are more divergent.
Actin is a major [/ontology/go/0005200/annotation/page/1 structural constituent of cytoskeleton]. Actin is one of the most abundant proteins in ''Dictyostelium'', constituting approximately 8% of the total protein in vegetative cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/561722 Alton and Lodish et al. 1977]).Actin synthesis is developmentally regulated, peaking shortly after starvation (reviewed by [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6894564 Firtel] in 1981). The different actin genes differ in their levels of expression, with [/gene/DDB_G0274135 act6], [/gene/DDB_G0269234 act8] and [/gene/DDB_G0274129 act12] being highly expressed both during growth and development compared to [/gene/DDB_G0289005 act4], [/gene/DDB_G0289663 act5], [/gene/DDB_G0280545 act7] and [/gene/DDB_G0272248 act16] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6286214 McKeown and Firtel 1981]). Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 19-SEP-2003 PG

DDB_G0278727.summary:
Disruption of ''pikA'' had no effect on growth or development; however strains in which both ''pikA'' and ([/gene/DDB_G0283081 pikB]) were disrupted showed both growth and developmental defects. [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7565716 (Zhou et al. 1995)]
To investigate the minimal requirements for chemotaxis, [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22081140 Kortholt et al. 2011] obtained quantitative data on Ras activation and chemotaxis in cAMP and folic acid gradients using a variety of Dictyostelium mutant cell lines from the four signaling pathways that contribute to chemotaxis: PI3K, TorC2, PLA2, and sGC. Their results demonstrate that Ras is activated at the leading edge, through a pathway consisting of G-alpha/beta/gamma, which does not depend on either of the four pathways. The authors measured chemotaxis of mutant cells exposed to cAMP gradients with different steepness and found that many mutants will chemotax in shallow gradients, despite a reduced sensitivity. Expression of multiple pathways increases sensitivity, with some combinations of pathways exhibiting weak amplification while others produce good chemotaxis with strong signal amplification. The results of cluster analysis revealed that one cluster of signaling pathways, including PI3K + TorC2 + sGC, is involved in inducing orientation of the cell towards the gradient, while a second cluster consists of cGMP + PLA2 and functions as a memory of current direction. Thus one individual pathway does not contribute strongly to chemotaxis, but it can synergize with other pathways, which together increases the sensitivity about 150-fold. These results suggest a conceptual model of chemotaxis in which a basal signaling module consisting of heterotrimeric and monomeric G proteins provides activation of Ras at the leading edge, which is sufficient for chemotaxis.Basic annotations have been added to this gene, 13-MAR-2018 RD

The ''Dictyostelium'' [/gene/DDB_G0270836 fbp] and [/gene/DDB_G0291648 lpd] protein sequences have been used in a phylogenetic analysisthat studied gene transfer between parasitic organisms and their hosts [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15003488 (Huang et al. 2004)]. LSM10 and LSM11 associate with the U7snRNA, whereas LSM12 is hypothesized to be involved in RNA methylation ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11574479 Pillai et al. 2001], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15225602 Albrecht and Lengauer 2004]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 13-MAR-2006 KP

DDB_G0277867.summary: ''rab1B'' encodes a guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G protein) of the Rab family of small GTPases. G proteins are key components of signal transduction networks in which they function as molecular signaling switches, binding to GDP in the off state while binding GTP in the on state. Guanine nucleotide-exchange factors (GEFs) promote the exchange of GDP for GTP on Rab GTPases thus activating them, while GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) inactivate Rab GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP. ''rab1B'' is expressed at detectable levels in growing cells and expression remains constant at approximately the same level during development ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8294041 Bush et al. 1993]). ''rab1B'' is highly similar to ''rab1A'' ([/gene/DDB_G0283757 rab1A]), and to human Rab1A and Rab1B, which are key regulators of intracellular membrane trafficking. ''Yersinia pestis'' survives and replicates intracellularly within ''D. discoideum'' within structures visually analogous to ''Yersinia''-containing vacuoles observed in infected mammalian macrophages. In macrophages, ''Y. pestis'' recruits host Rab1B protein to the phagosome, resulting in inhibition of phagosome acidification and disruption of the remaining phagolysosomal metabolic pathway, and suggesting a possible related role for ''rab1B'' in ''Dictyostelium'' ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29350155 Markman et al. 2018]). Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 26-AUG-2020 RD

DDB_G0293872.summary:
IdhB is the ''Dictyostelium'' protein that is most similar to the beta subunit of mitochondrial ([/ontology/go/5739/annotation/page/1 mitochondrion]) NAD+-dependent isocitrate dehydrogenase (), which catalyzes the oxidative decarboxylation of isocitrate into alpha-ketoglutarate, the third step in the [/ontology/go/6099/annotation/page/1 tricarboxylic acid cycle].
While the the metazoan enzyme complex is a heterooligomer of subunits alpha, beta, and gamma in the apparent ratio of 2:1:1, the fungal enzyme is a heterodimer of subunits 1 and 2 in equal proportions. In ''Dictyostelium'' one alpha ([/gene/DDB_G0271344 idhA])and one putative beta subunit have been identified.
The ''Dictyostelium'' cytosolic and mitochondrial NADP+-dependent isocitrate dehydrogenases ([/gene/DDB_G0272208 idhC], [/gene/DDB_G0272210 idhM]) have also been identified.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 17-JAN-2005 PF

DDB_G0284471.summary: ''kif8'' encodes a large protein (209 kDa) that belongs to a family of kinesins with multiple functions [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14641909  (Kollmar and Glockner 2003)]. The highly conserved motor domain is at the N- terminus. There are 7 WD-40 repeats at the C-terminus that make a seven-bladed beta propeller implicated in protein-protein interactions that could hold specific cargo to the molecular motor. Null mutants lacking Kif8 grow and develop normally. However, knocking out ''kif8'' suppresses the disruption of the interphase microtubule network and the formation of rockets that result from expression of a dominant-negative 380-kDa form of dynein ([/gene/DDB_G0276355 dhcA]). It appears that dynein and Kif8 cooperate in organizing the interphase microtubule distribution [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18430243  (Nag et al. 2008)]. ''kif8'' influences microtubule architecture. ''kif8'' null mutants have a less radial, more disorganized microtubule array and an increased average distance of the centrosome from the cell center. Kif9 localizes to the cytoplasm with no enrichment seen at microtubule tips [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31067156  (Odell et al. 2019)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 27-MAY-2019 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0280459.summary: The ABC superfamily of genes is one of the largest in the genomes of both bacteria and eukaryotes. The proteins encoded by these genes all carry a characteristic 200- to 250-amino-acid ATP-binding cassette that gives them their family name ([/ontology/go/0042626/annotation/page/1 ATPase activity, coupled to transmembrane movement of substances]). In bacteria they are mostly involved in nutrient import, while in eukaryotes many are involved in export([/ontology/go/0006810/annotation/page/1 transport]), ([/ontology/go/0016021/annotation/page/1 integral to membrane]). Seven different families (A to G) have been defined in eukaryotes based on sequence homology, domain topology, and function. ''Dictyostelium'' has 71 ABC transporters (including one on the chromosome 2 duplication) and 13 ABCC family members: [/gene/DDB_G0280541 abcC1], [/gene/DDB_G0280055 abcC2], [/gene/DDB_G0287691 abcC3], [/gene/DDB_G0286559 abcC5], [/gene/DDB_G0287593 abcC6], [/gene/DDB_G0291243 abcC7], [/gene/DDB_G0284867 abcC8], [/gene/DDB_G0285165 abcC9], [/gene/DDB_G0280977 abcC10], [/gene/DDB_G0280973 abcC12], [/gene/DDB_G0280539 abcC13], [/gene/DDB_G0287589 abcC14], and [/gene/DDB_G0280459 abcC15]. Transporters of the C family have been shown to transport glutathione conjugants as well as to export cadmium ions. They are always found as full transporters with two copies of the transmembrane-ABC unit. Many of the genes of this family in humans and other animals have an additional transmembrane domain at the N terminus [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12456012 (Anjard and Loomis 2002)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 17-MAY-2004 PG

DDB_G0284601.summary:
CK2 (casein kinase II), a ubiquitous serine/threonine kinase, is one of the most highly conserved proteins in eukaryotic cells. The protein kinase usually forms a tetramer, comprised of two catalytic alpha or alpha' subunits, and two regulatory beta subunits. The ''Dictyostelium'' [/gene/DDB_G0276885 casK] gene encodes a previously cloned CK2 alpha chain [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1448100 (Kikkawa et al., 1992)]. In addition, the ''Dictyostelium'' genome contains another putative alpha chain [/gene/DDB_G0286481 DDB_G0286481], and a single ortholog of the CK2 beta chain, ''csnk2b''.
The CK2 alpha chain encoded by [/gene/DDB_G0276885 casK] has been identified by PCR, based on similarity. Northern blot analysis of [/gene/DDB_G0276885 casK] during development, as well as CK2 activity ([/ontology/go/0004682/annotation/page/1 protein kinase CK2 activity]) throughout development both show a constitutive expression and presence of CK2 during the ''Dictyostelium'' life cycle. Attempts to delete the ''casK'' gene failed, indicating that it is an essential gene [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1448100 (Kikkawa et al., 1992)]. However, in yeast, which has two CK2 genes, only (haploid) cells carrying disruptions in both CK2 alpha chains are inviable [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2196445 (Padmanabha et al., 1990)].
Protein kinase CK2 represents a family of closely related kinases with broad specifity. There are hundreds of target molecules, implicating CK2 in many signalling pathways ([/ontology/go/0007165/annotation/page/1 signal transduction]), including such involved in cell survival. For recent reviews see [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12396231 (Litchfield, 2003)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12631575 (Meggio & Pinnal, 2003)], and [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12062170 (Ahmed et al., 2002)].
The presence of a second putative CK2 alpha- and one putative CK2 beta chain in ''Dictyostelium'' suggests that the tetrameric holoenzyme in this organism consists of two different alpha chains and two identical beta chains. However, currently there is no eperimental evidence that these putative genes are expressed and further investigation is necessary.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 10-MAY-2004 PF

DDB_G0273523.summary:
DNA-dependent RNA polymerase catalyzes the transcription of DNA into RNA using the four ribonucleoside triphosphates as substrates ([/ontology/go/0003899/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase activity]). Three distinct zinc-containing RNA polymerases are found in eukaryotic nuclei: [/gene/DDB_G0275759 rpa1] for the ribosomal RNA precursor ([/ontology/go/0006360/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase I promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005736/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase I complex]), [/gene/DDB_G0279193 rpb1] for the mRNA precursor ([/ontology/go/0006366/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase II promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005665/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase II, core complex]), and [/gene/DDB_G0277199 rpc1] for 5S and tRNA genes ([/ontology/go/0006383/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase III promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005666/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase III complex]).
RNA polymerase III is a multisubunit complex. The subunits encoded by [/gene/DDB_G0277199 rpc1] (ortholog of ''S. cerevisiae RPO31''), [/gene/DDB_G0293560 rpa2] (''RPC2''), [/gene/DDB_G0268080 rpc3] (''RPC82''),[/gene/DDB_G0277671 rpc4] (''RPC53''), [/gene/DDB_G0271514 rpc5] (''RPC37''), [/gene/DDB_G0286521 rpc9] (''RPC17''), [/gene/DDB_G0272022 rpc34] (''RPC34''), [/gene/DDB_G0273425 rpc25-1] (''RPC25''), and [/gene/DDB_G0287707 rpc11] (''RPC11'') are unique to RNA polymerase III. Orthologs of ''RPC31'' and ''RPC17'' have not been identified in the ''Dictyostelium'' genome. Two subunits, [/gene/DDB_G0291362 rpc19] and [/gene/DDB_G0282339 rpa5] (''RPC19'' and ''RPC40'' in ''S. cerevisiae''), are common to RNA polymerase I and RNA polymerase III and correspond to subunits 3 and 11 of RNA polymerase II. Subunits [/gene/DDB_G0291636 rpb5], [/gene/DDB_G0291037 rpb6], [/gene/DDB_G0278039 rpb8], [/gene/DDB_G0272036 rpb10], and [/gene/DDB_G0283365 rpb12] are common to all three RNA polymerases ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12407181 Peyroche et al. 2002], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12381659 Schramm and Hernandez 2001]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 11-JUN-2009 PG

DDB_G0289667.summary: ''gefD'' encodes a Ras guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF, RasGEF). rasGEFs are key components of signaling networks in which they activate Ras family small GTPases by promoting the exchange of GDP for GTP. ''gefD'' has both Ras GEF and Rho GAP (GTPase activating protein) domains. ''gefD'' is expressed throughout growth and development in AX3 cells, with maximal expression between 8 to 12 hours after starvation ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16086850 Wilkins et al. 2005)]. cAMP-stimulated RasC ([/gene/DDB_G0281385 rasC]) and RasG ([/gene/DDB_G0293434 rasG]) activation was normal in ''gefD'' null strains, indicating that GefD was not involved in the activation of either RasC or RasG during early development ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17380187 Kae et al. 2007]). ''gefD'' null cells exhibit normal growth, morphology, phototaxis and development ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16086850 Wilkins et al. 2005)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17380187 Kae et al. 2007]). However, the confinement of Ras activation to the membrane region at the source of cAMP stimulus is abolished in both ''gefD'' and ''gefE'' ([/gene/DDB_G0269252 gefE]) null mutants, suggesting that ''gefD'' and ''gefE'' contribute to restrict activation of Ras to the front of chemotaxing cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23886948 Kortholt et al. 2013]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 25-MAR-2021 RD

DDB_G0293198.summary: ''kif10'' encodes a member of a family of kinesins with multiple functions [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14641909  (Kollmar and Glockner 2003)]. Cells lacking Kif10 grow normally and there are no obvious morphological defects in mitotic microtubule arrays but the microtubule-organizing center (MTOC) appears slightly aberrant [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18430243  (Nag et al. 2008)]. Knocking out ''kif10'' suppresses the disruption of the interphase microtubule network and the formation of rockets that result from expression of a dominant-negative 380-kDa form of dynein ([/gene/DDB_G0276355 dhcA]). It appears that dynein and Kif10 cooperate in organizing the interphase microtubule distribution [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18430243  (Nag et al. 2008)]. mRNA levels for ''kif10'' are low during early development but then increase to relatively high levels between 12 and 18 hrs of development before returning to very low levels [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25887420  (Rosengarten et al. 2015)]. This is the same pattern seen for the mRNAs encoding mitotic motor kinesins suggesting that Kif10 might also have a subtle role in mitosis.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 04-JUL-2017 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0293008.summary:
''Dictyostelium cpnA'' belongs to the highly conserved copines, a family of ubiquitious Ca(2+)-dependent phospholipid-binding proteins. In their N-terminal half, copines contain two Ca(2+)- and phospholipid-binding domains (C2 domains) present in such proteins as phospholipase C and protein kinase C. Much of the C-terminal half consists of a von Willebrand Factor type A domain (VWFA) typically found in the extracellular portions of membrane proteins like integrins. Thus copines represent a fusion of intracellular (C2) and extracellular (VWFA) domains. However, there are no signal sequence or hydrophobic transmembrane sequences in the predicted proteins suggesting copines are intracellular proteins. Copines are thought to be involved in membrane trafficking. It is of particular interest that copines, first found in the highly phagocytic protozoan ''Paramecium'' and then isolated from mammalian spleen and liver, seem to be abundant in cells and organs that are, or contain, phagocytes. In this context it comes as no surprise that phagocytic ''Dictyostelium'' has a total of six copine genes. The widespread distribution of copines from protozoans to mammals and their high similarity suggest they play important role(s) in eukaryotic biology. Reviewed in [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12440769 (Tomsig and Creutz, 2001)].
CpnA has been shown to be expressed throughout the life cycle and to bind ''Dictyostelium'' membranes in a calcium-dependent manner. A GFP-CpnA fusion construct showed CpnA to localize to the cytosol, and transiently, in a calcium-dependent manner, to the plasma membrane, the contractile vacuolar membrane, the phagocytic vesicle membrane, and to membranes of the endolysosomal pathway [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16343335 (Damer et al. 2005)].
Smith and colleagues found that CpnA is involved in the regulation of aggregation, slug size, and culmination during ''Dictyostelium'' development. In addition, CpnA seems to be involved in the function and differentiation of prestalk cells and plays a role in a calcium-regulated signaling pathway critical to triggering the initiation of culmination [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20525180 (Smith et al. 2010)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 21-AUG-2012 PF

DDB_G0282575.summary: ''tbcrA'' encodes a Rab GTPase-activating protein (GAP, rabGAP). RabGAPs are key components of signal transduction networks in which they inactivate Rab GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP. TbcrA contains an an N-terminal Regulator of chromosome condensation (RCC1) domain and a C-terminal Rab-GTPase-TBC domain. TbcrA was identified as an interactor of PripA ([/gene/DDB_G0275795 pripA]) during a screen for proteins that localize to the macropinosome during the macropinosome maturation process. TbcrA localizes to both macropinosomes and phagosomes, and colocalizes with PripA on macropinosomes. TbcrA also interacts with and has GAP activity towards the Rab GTPase Rab5A ([/gene/DDB_G0271984 rab5A]). In both ''pripA'' and ''tbcrA'' null cells, there is decreased inactivation of Rab5A, suggesting that PripA and TbcrA function in a complex. In addition, both ''tbcrA'' and ''pripA'' null cells have delayed macropinocytic and phagocytic cargo degradation. Taken together, these results support a role for the PripA-TbcrA complex in regulating macropinosome maturation by linking early and late macropinocytic compartments and promoting the fusion of Rab5 ([/gene/DDB_G0271984 rab5A])-marked early macropinosomes to Rab7 ([/gene/DDB_G0269236 rab7A])-marked late macropinosomes (Tu, et al 2022, PMID:35379834).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 20-APR-2022 RD

DDB_G0277889.summary: Ammonia signaling is essential to the developmental program of ''Dictyostelium''. It is involved in regulatingchemotaxis, the choice between slug migration and culmination, and cell-type specification via differential geneexpression. Ammonia concentrations are regulated in part by environmental factors, however, cellular processes such astransport ([/ontology/go/0008519/annotation/page/1 ammonium transmembrane transporter activity]) and metabolism can alter intracellular concentrations. In the ''Dictyostelium'' proteome,three putative ammonium transporters exist: [/gene/DDB_G0277503 amtA], [/gene/DDB_G0277889 amtB], and [/gene/DDB_G0267424 amtC]. The transcriptlevels of the three ''amt'' genes are constant throughout development, however, their spatial expression patterns, asdetermined by ''in situ'' hybridization, are both distinct and complementary. The ''amtA'' gene is generallyexpressed in the prestalk regions, although it is also found in the upper and lower cups of the sorus and in regionscontacting the substratum. The ''amtB'' transcript is observed primarily in prepore regions and in the spore region ofthe sorus, but is absent from the upper and lower cups. Expression of ''amtC'' is similar to that of ''amtB'', however, it appears transiently in the anterior tip during the first finger stage. Disruption of the ''amtC'' gene results in larger multicelluar structures and developmental arrest at the slug stage, although a smallpercentage of slugs are able to fruit after 40+ hours of starvation ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14686953 Follstaedt et al.2003]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 19-AUG-2008 PG

DDB_G0289117.summary:
Besides ''mhcA'' ([/gene/DDB_G0286355 mhcA]) that encodes the classical myosin heavy chain, ''Dictyostelium'' carries genes for 12 unconventional myosins. ''myoB'' encodes myosin IB which has an N-terminal 45 kDa motor domain with an actin-activated ATPase and a carboxy terminal domain that is rich in glycine, proline and alanine and can bind to filamentous actin [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2762320 (Jung et al. 1989)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2519618 (Titus et al. 1989)]. A basic region in the tail is predicted to bind to acidic phospholipids in the plasma membrane [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24747353 (Brzeska et al. 2014)]. MyoB associates with a 8-kDa light chain encoded by ''mlcB'' ([/gene/DDB_G0290077 mlcB]) that has about 30% sequence identity with calmodulin [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16415352 (Crawley et al. 2006)]. ''myoB'' mRNA is abundant during the first two hours of development, decreases to a minimum at T=6 hrs and then reaccumulates to a peak at T=11 hrs. ''mlcB'' is coordinately expressed.[http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25887420 (Rosengarten et al. 2015)].
MyoB is non-filamentous and concentrates in F-actin structures of anterior pseudopods of polarized cells where it may move actin filaments relative to the membrane [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2797149 (Fukui et al. 1989)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2519618 (Titus et al. 1989)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22367211 (Brzeska et al. 2012)]. Phosphorylation of serine 322 in response to the chemoattractant cAMP increases movement of MyoB on F-actin [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11084033 (Gliksman et al. 2001)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18089562 (Tsiavaliaris et al. 2008)]. MyoB may also be involved in recycling of plasma membrane components from endosomes back to the cell surface [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10973992 (Neuhaus and Soldati, 2000)].
Cells lacking MyoB turn twice as frequently as wild type cells and have reduced efficiency of chemotaxis [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1666340 (Wessels et al. 1991)]. Fluid phase dextran uptake by pinocytosis is normal in cells lacking MyoA ([/gene/DDB_G0280039 myoA]) MyoB or MyoC ([/gene/DDB_G0276617 myoC]), but is impaired in cells lacking both MyoA and MyoB or both MyoB and MyoC suggesting that myosin I isoforms function cooperatively [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8522584 (Novak et al. 1995)]. The double null mutants ''myoA''/''myoB'' and ''myoB''/''myoC'' are covered in spikey filopodia suggesting that these myosin Is may have a role in limiting the extension of processes. MyoB and MyoC have been found in a complex containing p116, ([/gene/DDB_G0292386 carmil]), capping protein ([/gene/DDB_G0267374 acpA]), ([/gene/DDB_G0272104 acpB]) and the Arp2/3 nucleating complex indicating that these myosin Is may be involved in recruiting the machinery responsible for F-actin nucleation and elongation [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11425877 (Jung et al. 2001)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12753645 (Soldati, 2003)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 13-AUG-2019 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0280473.summary:
The homeodomain is a sequence-specific DNA binding motif that consists of a helix-turn-helix. Homeobox-containing proteins have transcription factor activity. They have been identified in most if not all phyla of eukaryotes. Inmetazoans, homeobox-containing proteins are known to be involvedin regulating the anterior-posterior body plan and in the specification of certain cell types and anterior-posterior compartments (see [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9486804 Han and Firtel 1998] and references therein). There are 14 predicted proteins that contain homeobox domains in ''Dictyostelium'':[/gene/DDB_G0275173 hbx2], [/gene/DDB_G0291075 warA], [/gene/DDB_G0291197 hbx3], [/gene/DDB_G0272967 hbx4], [/gene/DDB_G0273127 hbx5-1] (on the chromosome 2 duplication: [/gene/DDB_G0273645 hbx5-2]), [/gene/DDB_G0277505 hbx6], [/gene/DDB_G0278225 hbx7], [/gene/DDB_G0279257 hbx8], [/gene/DDB_G0280473 hbx9], [/gene/DDB_G0284293 hbx10], [/gene/DDB_G0295787 hbx11], [/gene/DDB_G0286733 hbx12], [/gene/DDB_G0288975 hbx13], and [/gene/DDB_G0289677 hbx14].
A genome-wide classification and comparative genomic analysis of the 14 homeobox genes present in D. discoideum found that they could be classified into 3 groups: TALE, OTHER and NOVEL classes, ''hbx9'' belonging to the TALE class ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25963254 Mishra and Saran 2015)]. ''hbx9'' is expressed in the anterior portion of prestalk cells. ''hbx9'' null cells display several phenotypes: decreased cell proliferation, cell-cell adhesion, chemotaxis to cAMP and a delay in the onset of aggregation. In ''hbx9'' null cells proportioning and patterning is altered in favor of the pstA cell type. In addition, ''hbx9'' null cells have reduced expression of genes involved in cAMP signaling, including yakA ([/gene/DDB_G0283605 yakA]), acaA ([/gene/DDB_G0281545 acaA]), carA ([/gene/DDB_G0273397 carA-1], [/gene/DDB_G0273533 carA-2]) and others suggesting that Hbx9 controls cell proportioning of prestalk cells by modulating cAMP signalling during the growth-to-development transition ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28027501 Mishra et al. 2016)].'''Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 23-FEB-2017 RD'''

DNA-dependent RNA polymerase catalyzes the transcription of DNA into RNA using the four ribonucleoside triphosphates as substrates ([/ontology/go/0003899/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase activity]). RNA polymerase II is composed of 12 subunits: [/gene/DDB_G0279193 rpb1], [/gene/DDB_G0288257 rpb2], [/gene/DDB_G0292244 rpb3], [/gene/DDB_G0282739 rpb4], [/gene/DDB_G0291636 rpb5], [/gene/DDB_G0291037 rpb6], [/gene/DDB_G0284891 rpb7], [/gene/DDB_G0278039 rpb8], [/gene/DDB_G0268306 rpb9], [/gene/DDB_G0272036 rpb10], [/gene/DDB_G0277677 rpb11], and[/gene/DDB_G0283365 rpb12]. Subunits 5, 6, 8, 10, and 12 are common to all threeRNA polymerases (reviewed by [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9618449 Hampsey] in 1998).

DDB_G0274115.summary: The ABC superfamily of genes is one of the largest in the genomes of both bacteria and eukaryotes. The proteins encoded by these genes all carry a characteristic 200- to 250-amino-acid ATP-binding cassette that gives them their family name ([/ontology/go/0042626/annotation/page/1 ATPase activity, coupled to transmembrane movement of substances]). In bacteria they are mostly involved in nutrient import, while in eukaryotes many are involved in export ([/ontology/go/0006810/annotation/page/1 transport]). Seven different families have been defined in eukaryotes based on sequence homology, domain topology, and function. Sequences from the well-advanced ''Dictyostelium'' genome project have allowed to recognize 71 members of this superfamily (including one on the chromosome 2 duplication). The ABCG family is characterized by the ABC domain preceding the transmembrane domain ([/ontology/go/0016021/annotation/page/1 integral to membrane]). All of the members of this family in animals are half-transporters while all of the fungal members are full transporters with two ABC-transmembrane units. No members of this family are found in bacteria. ''Dictyostelium'' and ''Arabidopsis'' have members of both types ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12456012 Anjard and Loomis 2002]). Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 18-OCT-2004 PG

DDB_G0275453.summary: The ABC superfamily of genes is one of the largest in the genomes of both bacteria and eukaryotes. The proteins encoded by these genes all carry a characteristic 200- to 250-amino-acid ATP-binding cassette that gives them their family name ([/ontology/go/0042626/annotation/page/1 ATPase activity, coupled to transmembrane movement of substances]). In bacteria they are mostly involved in nutrient import, while in eukaryotes many are involved in export ([/ontology/go/0006810/annotation/page/1 transport]), ([/ontology/go/0016021/annotation/page/1 integral to membrane]). Seven different families (A to G) have been defined in eukaryotes based on sequence homology, domain topology, and function. ''Dictyostelium'' has 71 ABC transporters (including one on the chromosome 2 duplication) and 11 ABCA family members: [/gene/DDB_G0291994 abcA1], [/gene/DDB_G0267438 abcA2], [/gene/DDB_G0293436 abcA3], [/gene/DDB_G0274121 abcA4], [/gene/DDB_G0274119 abcA5], [/gene/DDB_G0291245 abcA6], [/gene/DDB_G0271140 abcA7], [/gene/DDB_G0271138 abcA8],[/gene/DDB_G0291980 abcA9], [/gene/DDB_G0283387 abcA10], and [/gene/DDB_G0275453 abcA11],One of the defining characteristics of the A family is the presence of a regulatory domain with multiple sites for phosphorylation by various protein kinases in the region after the first ABC domain [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12456012 (Anjard and Loomis 2002)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 16-JUN-2003 PG

Both CpiA and CpiB are capable of inhibiting cysteine proteases in vitro ([/ontology/go/0004869/annotation/page/1 cysteine protease inhibitor activity]),([/ontology/go/0006508/annotation/page/1 proteolysis]). A third cysteine protease inhibitor, [/gene/DDB_G0277001 cpiC] (cystatin A3), exists in the ''Dictyostelium''genome, however, it has yet to be characterized ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15255188 El-Halawany et al. 2004]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 23-SEP-2004 KP

DDB_G0280705.summary: The CHD (chromodomain-helicase-DNA binding) protein family is one of the major ATP-dependent, chromatin remodeling factors that regulate nucleosome positioning and access of transcription factors and RNA polymerase to the eukaryotic genome.
