DDB_G0285995.summary: The major extracellular cAMP phosphodiesterase is encoded by ''pdsA'' ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3023365 Lacombe et al. 1986)]. A signal sequence for secretion is cleaved from the N-terminus along with 49 amino acids. Transcription of ''pdsA'' is initiated at promotors 1.9 kb and 3 kb upstream of the translational start site during growth and early development, respectively ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2157967 Faure et al. 1990)]. After 10 hours of development, ''pdsA'' is transcribed only in prestalk cells starting from a third promotor that is positioned close to the coding sequence. The phosphodiesterase secreted by prestalk cells is necessary for slug and fruiting body formation but not for aggregation ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7851634 Wu et al. 1995)]. Null mutations in ''pdsA'' result in non-cell autonomous defects in aggregation ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9405107 Sucgang et al. 1997)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19477920 Garcia et al. 2009)]. PdsA is part of the circuit that generates 6 minute oscillations in cAMP during aggregation ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9843585 Laub et al. 1998)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15131307 Maeda et al. 2004)]. It acts in the extracellular environment to reduce cAMP in the back of the wave and resets the oscillator ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23473502 Masaki et al. 2013)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 15-APR-2016 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0285323.summary: ''atg9'' was isolated together with several other members of the autophagy family of genes, conserved from yeast to man ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12626495 Otto et al. 2003)]. Macroautophagy is used to recycle cellular components during starvation and development. ATG9 has 6 transmembrane domains and is found on small vesicles where it may be involved in membrane trafficking to autophagosomes ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20603609 Calvo-Garrido et al. 2010)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20070309 Tung et al. 2010)]. ''atg9'' is rapidly induced during early development and is necessary for normal morphogenesis. Growth is somewhat impaired in mutant cells lacking ATG9. Aggregates of cells lacking ATG9 have multiple tips and generate long, thin slugs that often break up and make only a few small misshapen fruiting bodies ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20070309 Tung et al. 2010)]. The multi-tipped phenotype of ''atg9'' mutants is similar to that of mutants in other autophagy genes ''atg6'', ([/gene/DDB_G0269244 atg6A]) ''atg7'', ([/gene/DDB_G0271096 atg7]) ''atg101'', ([/gene/DDB_G0288287 atg101]) ''tipC'', ([/gene/DDB_G0267422 tipC]) and ''tipD'' ([/gene/DDB_G0275323 tipD]). The rate of phagocytosis of bacteria and yeast is also reduced in ''atg9''- mutant cells. A similar reduction is also seen in the atg16 mutant, ([/gene/DDB_G0275323 tipD]), suggesting that autophagy might be involved in the efficient degradation of bacteria ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25878144 Xiong et al. 2015)]. Although uptake of the intercellular pathogen ''Legionella pneumophila'' is reduced 8 fold, those bacteria that get into the ''atg9''- mutant cells are more successful in establishing a replicative niche and replicating ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20070309 Tung et al. 2010)]. Transcripts of ''atg9'', ''atg8'' and ''tipD'' accumulate following infection with Legionella suggesting a protective role for autophagy in ''D. discoideum'' ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16469056 Farbrother et al. 2006)]. Mutants lacking ''atg9'', ''atg5'' ([/gene/DDB_G0289881 atg5]) and ''atg7'' ([/gene/DDB_G0271096 atg7]) are impaired in cAMP induction of prespore gene expression, indicating that autophagy is required for this process ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31051160 Yamada et al. 2019)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 10-DEC-2019 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis and Ricardo Escalante

DDB_G0291243.summary: The ABC superfamily of genes is one of the largest in the genomes of both bacteria and eukaryotes. The proteins encoded by these genes all carry a characteristic 200- to 250-amino-acid ATP-binding cassette that gives them their family name ([/ontology/go/0042626/annotation/page/1 ATPase activity, coupled to transmembrane movement of substances]). In bacteria they are mostly involved in nutrient import, while in eukaryotes many are involved in export([/ontology/go/0006810/annotation/page/1 transport]), ([/ontology/go/0016021/annotation/page/1 integral to membrane]). Seven different families (A to G) have been defined in eukaryotes based on sequence homology, domain topology, and function. ''Dictyostelium'' has 71 ABC transporters (including one on the chromosome 2 duplication) and 13 ABCC family members: [/gene/DDB_G0280541 abcC1], [/gene/DDB_G0280055 abcC2], [/gene/DDB_G0287691 abcC3], [/gene/DDB_G0286559 abcC5], [/gene/DDB_G0287593 abcC6], [/gene/DDB_G0291243 abcC7], [/gene/DDB_G0284867 abcC8], [/gene/DDB_G0285165 abcC9], [/gene/DDB_G0280977 abcC10], [/gene/DDB_G0280973 abcC12], [/gene/DDB_G0280539 abcC13], [/gene/DDB_G0287589 abcC14], and [/gene/DDB_G0280459 abcC15]. Transporters of the C family have been shown to transport glutathione conjugants as well as to export cadmium ions. They are always found as full transporters with two copies of the transmembrane-ABC unit. Many of the genes of this family in humans and other animals have an additional transmembrane domain at the N terminus [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12456012 (Anjard and Loomis 2002)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 16-JUN-2003 PG

DDB_G0274051.summary: ''Dictyostelium cpnB'' belongs to the highly conserved copines, a family of ubiquitious Ca(2+)-dependent phospholipid-binding ([/ontology/go/0005544/annotation/page/1 calcium-dependent phospholipid binding]) proteins. In their N-terminal half, copines contain two Ca(2+)- and phospholipid-binding domains (C2 domains) present in such proteins as phospholipase C and protein kinase C. Much of the C-terminal half consists of a von Willebrand Factor type A domain (VWFA) typically found in the extracellular portions of membrane proteins like integrins. Thus copines represent a fusion of intracellular (C2) and extracellular (VWFA) domains. However, there are no signal sequence or hydrophobic transmembrane sequences in the predicted proteins suggesting copines are intracellular proteins. Copines are thought to be involved in membrane trafficking. It is of particular interest that copines, first found in the highly phagocytic protozoan ''Paramecium'' and then isolated from mammalian spleen and liver, seem to be abundant in cells and organs that are, or contain, phagocytes. In this context it comes as no surprise that phagocytic ''Dictyostelium'' has a total of six copine genes[http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16343335  (Damer et al. 2005)]. The widespread distribution of copines from protozoans to mammals and their high similarity suggest they play important role(s) in eukaryotic biology. Reviewed in [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12440769  (Tomsig and Creutz, 2001)]Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 05-APR-2004 PF

DDB_G0287687.summary: A family of nearly identical small proteins, GerA, GerB, and GerC, ([/gene/DDB_G0287293 gerA]), ([/gene/DDB_G0287583 gerC]) are coordinately synthesized during late culmination and again following the initiation of germination of spores [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2926809  (Giorda et al. 1989)]. Each of the proteins is 127 amino acids long and has a cannonical signal sequence at the N-terminus that could direct co-translational transport across membranes. No conserved domains are present that could give an indication of possible functions. The nucleotide sequences of the respective genes, ''gerA'', ''gerB'', and ''gerC'', are all very similar and are free of introns. These genes may result from recent duplications.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 10-OCT-2018 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0278581.summary: The discoidin-inducing complex (DIC) was isolated from conditioned medium for its ability to induce theexpression of discoidin ([/gene/DDB_G0273063 dscA-1]), an early development gene ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15947191 Kolbinger et al. 2005]). The DIC constituents were determined to be [/gene/DDB_G0285995 pdsA], the novel proteins [/gene/DDB_G0278581 psiF] and [/gene/DDB_G0267470 dicB], and an unknown protein. Both PdsA and DicB are dispensable for discoidin expression, whereas the DicA1 protein isa strong activator of discoidin transcription. DicA1 contains a PA14 (anthrax protective antigen) domain known to be involved in [/ontology/go/0030246/annotation/page/1 carbohydrate binding] and several '' Dictyostelium'' (CTDC) repeats, which exist in several proteins found in the [/ontology/go/0005576/annotation/page/1 extracellular region]. The DicB protein, however, contains no conserved functional domains([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15947191 Kolbinger et al. 2005]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 14-NOV-2005 KP

DDB_G0294531.summary: In a search for genes up-regulated by intracellular calcium ([/ontology/go/0043157/annotation/page/1 response to cation stress]), [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14871937 Coukellet al. (2004)] identified [/gene/DDB_G0277861 patA], a homolog of the yeast vacuolar ATPase PMC1, andseven ''cup'' genes, which encode highly conserved proteins that contain ricin B lectin domains involved incarbohydrate binding. During the developmental program, ''cup transcripts'' are detected at low levels at earlyand late stages and at higher levels during the slug stage. Immunoflourescent staining shows Cup proteinsthroughout the cell in vegetative cells ([/ontology/go/0005737/annotation/page/1 cytoplasm] and [/ontology/go/0005634/annotation/page/1 nucleus]), however, aggregating cells and cellsstressed with 50 mM calcium chloride show increased staining in the [/ontology/go/0005938/annotation/page/1 cell cortex]. Overexpression of [/gene/DDB_G0289815 cupB] antisense mRNA abolishes multicellular development; cells fail to aggregate completely. The sevencalcium up-regulated ''cup'' genes identified are: [/gene/DDB_G0267466 cupA], [/gene/DDB_G0289815 cupB], [/gene/DDB_G0289283 cupC], [/gene/DDB_G0293536 cupD], [/gene/DDB_G0294531 cupE], [/gene/DDB_G0289813 cupF], and [/gene/DDB_G0289883 cupG] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14871937 Coukell et al. 2004]). There are three other related genes, [/gene/DDB_G0290563 cupH], [/gene/DDB_G0272242 cupI], and [/gene/DDB_G0277959 cupJ]. Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 14-FEB-2005 KP

DDB_G0292004.summary: ''docC'' encodes a putative Rho guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF, RhoGEF). RhoGEFs are key components of signaling networks in which they activate Rho family GTPases by promoting the exchange of GDP for GTP. The adaptor protein ElmoE ([/gene/DDB_G0279657 elmoE]) associates with the Rho GTPase RacB ([/gene/DDB_G0279605 racB]) as well as with both DocC and ZizA ([/gene/DDB_G0275035 zizA]) suggesting that ElmoE, DocC, and ZizA may form an evolutionarily conserved Elmo/Dock complex to serve as a GEF for RacB ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22264729 Yan et al. 2012]). DocC localizes to mitochondria (MacWilliams and Hermann, unpublished observations). ''docC'' is threefold overexpressed in a strain lacking the retinoblastoma-like gene ''rblA'' ([/gene/DDB_G0290551 rblA]). ''docC'' is also strongly cell-cycle regulated, expressed in late G2 along with most DNA replication and mitotic genes. Taken together, these results suggest that ''docC'' may play a role in the cell cycle, possibly in cytokinesis (MacWilliams, unpublished observations).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 07-JUN-2021 RD

DDB_G0280039.summary: Besides ''mhcA'' ([/gene/DDB_G0286355 mhcA]) that encodes the classical myosin heavy chain, ''Dictyostelium'' carries genes for 12 unconventional myosins. ''myoA'' encodes a short myosin I with a conserved head region and a tail region that is not predicted to form an alpha-helical structure or have coiled-coil interactions [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2519618  (Titus et al. 1989)]. It associates with calmodulin ([/gene/DDB_G0279407 calA]) which provides calcium control [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21671662  (Crawley et al. 2011)]. The abundance of ''myoA'' mRNA is relatively low and decreases an hour after the initiation of development [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25887420  (Rosengarten et al. 2015)]. Cells lacking MyoA make turns twice as frequently as wild type cells, have increased lateral pseudopod formation, and have reduced efficiency of chemotaxis [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8382977  (Titus et al. 1993)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8824735  (Wessels et al. 1996)]. Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 25-JUL-2019 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0279915.summary:
The ABC superfamily of genes is one of the largest in the genomes of both bacteria and eukaryotes. The proteins encoded by these genes all carry a characteristic 200- to 250-amino-acid ATP-binding cassette that gives them their family name. In bacteria they are mostly involved in nutrient import, while in eukaryotes many are involved in export. Seven different families (A to G) have been defined in eukaryotes based on sequence homology, domain topology, and function. ''Dictyostelium'' has 71 ABC transporters (including one on the chromosome 2 duplication) and 11 ABCB family members: [/gene/DDB_G0293416 abcB1], [/gene/DDB_G0293438 abcB2], [/gene/DDB_G0291714 abcB3], [/gene/DDB_G0279915 abcB4],[/gene/DDB_G0292554 abcB5], [/gene/DDB_G0282931 abcB6], [/gene/DDB_G0269720 abcB7], [/gene/DDB_G0293002 tagA], [/gene/DDB_G0286119 tagB], [/gene/DDB_G0286121 tagC], and [/gene/DDB_G0286123 tagD].
The B family includes three main subtypes: full transporters involved in multiple drug resistance (MDR), half-transporters targeted to mitochondria, and half-transporters involved in peptide transport [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12456012 (Anjard and Loomis 2002)]
The AbcB4 transporter has been shown to anchor the cell-cell adhesion molecule [/gene/DDB_G0285793 cadA] to the plasma membrane [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24426151 (Yang et al. 2013)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 23-JAN-2014 PF

In ''Dictyostelium'', clear orthologs of the Lsm proteins exist:[/gene/DDB_G0279837 lsm1], [/gene/DDB_G0281779 lsm2], [/gene/DDB_G0277107 lsm3], [/gene/DDB_G0287053 lsm4], [/gene/DDB_G0268716 lsm5],[/gene/DDB_G0275719 lsm6], [/gene/DDB_G0289499 lsm7], and [/gene/DDB_G0288479 lsm8]. DDB_G0267588.summary: PIP5 kinase, PikI, produces PI(4,5)P2 and is essential for efficient chemotaxis of Dictyostelium [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24485835  (Fets et al. 2014)]. Without PikI, PI(4,5)P2 levels are reduced by 90%, and while ''pikI'' null cells move at normal speeds, they are highly disorientated in cAMP gradients. Following chemotactic stimulation, Ras is efficiently activated in ''pikI'' null cells, yet Ras-dependent responses (including activation of PKB) are severely impaired. PikI is phosphorylated by PKB, and in vitro studies of a phosphomimic mutant suggest that this phosphorylation increases PikI activity. These results suggest that adequate PI(4,5)P2 levels are required to couple activated Ras to its downstream effectors and that these levels are regulated by PikI, making it a crucial player in gradient sensing.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 05-FEB-2015 RD

DDB_G0273725.summary: Dictyostelium Snf12 is an ortholog of yeast SNF12 and of human BAF60a. Both Dictyostelium Snf12 and human BAF60a possess a SWIB domain and a conserved COG domain. Snf12 localizes predominantly to the nucleoplasm and redistributes to the cytoplasm during mitosis. Under stress by addition of the antibiotic actinomycin D, Snf12 relocalizes to the nucleoli where it is also visible in nucleolar regions atypically protruding from the nucleus. Snf12 contains three putative nuclear localization signals (NLSs), of which NLS-3 has been shown to be necessary and sufficient for nuclear localization [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/22623154 (Catalano & O'Day 2012)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 24-OCT-2012 PF

DDB_G0282459.summary: Cells sense the chemorepellent AprA ([/gene/DDB_G0281663 aprA]) through the G-protein-coupled receptor GrlH. ''grlH'' null mutants are insensitive to the chemorepellent AprA and display phenotypes of rapid proliferation, insensitivity to AprA-induced proliferation inhibition and chemorepulsion, and reduced binding to AprA. AprA binds to the G-protein coupled receptor GrlH, and requires GrlH and the G protein Gbeta ([/gene/DDB_G0277143 gpbA]) to inhibit proliferation and induce chemorepulsion, and also uses the G protein Galpah8 ([/gene/DDB_G0284469 gpaH]) to inhibit proliferation. AprA requires GrlH to activate Ras proteins ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29440579 Tang et al. 2018]), ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30462573 Rijal et al. 2018]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 10-DEC-2018 RD

DDB_G0284065.summary: ''rapgap9'' encodes a putative Rap GTPase-activating protein (GAP, rapGAP). RapGAPs are key components of signal transduction networks in which they inactivate Rap GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP. ''rapgap9'' was identified in a bioinformatic search for Rap GAP domain proteins in ''Dictyostelium'' and RapGAP9 is an ortholog of human Rap1 GTPase-activating protein RAP1GAP2. Upon chemoattractant stimulation, RapGAP9 transiently and rapidly translocates to the cortex. ''rapgap9'' null cells are flatter and more spread out than wild type (wt) cells and are multinucleated, indicating a defect in cytokinesis. ''rapgap9'' null cells exhibit an aberrant F-actin polymerization profile with a slightly elevated basal level of F-actin and a proportionally elevated second peak compared with wild type cells which exhibit a sharp intial peak and a second lower, broader peak. ''rapgap9'' null cells display increased cell-substrate adhesion, extend an increased number of filopodia compared with wt cells, and also have a defect in chemotaxis to cAMP, displaying decreased speed and reduced directional movement compared with wt cells. In addition, ''rapgap9'' null cells have spores that are 40% smaller than wt cells. Taken together, these results suggest that RapGAP9 is involved in the regulation of cytokinesis, morphogenesis and development through controlling the reorganization of the cytoskeleton ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24513283 Mun et al. 2014]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 22-MAR-2021 RD; annotation contributions: PMID:24513283, Taeck Jeon
DDB_G0284065.note: Two different introns exist in the 5'UTR of this gene, as evidenced by ESTs.

DDB_G0287801.summary: ''Dictyostelium'' contains orthologs of the core components of the presenilin/gamma-secretase complex: presenilin A ([/gene/DDB_G0291352 psenA]), presenilin B ([/gene/DDB_G0292310 psenB]), Aph-1 ([/gene/DDB_G0267976 aph1]) and nicastrin ([/gene/DDB_G0287801 ncstn]) which are capable of amyloidogenic processing of ectopically expressed human amyloid precursor protein (APP) to generate amyloid-beta peptides. Gamma-secretase activity is required for phagocytosis in Dictyostelium, and gamma-secretase mutants have primary defects in pre-spore/spore differentiation [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20699477  (McMains et al. 2010)]. ''Dictyostelium'' orthologs of the gamma-secretase complex PsenA, PsenB, Aph-1, and Nicastrin are necessary for macropinocytosis, phagocytosis, and autophagy, indicating roles in a general defect in lysosomal trafficking and degradation. In addition, loss of psenA/psenB and Aph-1 leads to an accumulation of ubiquitinated proteins, suggesting impaired protein degradation in these mutants. All of the endocytic defects in PSEN ortholog mutants can be fully restored by proteolytically inactive ''Dictyostelium'' PsenB and human PSEN1, demonstrating an evolutionarily conserved non-proteolytic role for presenilin in lysosomal trafficking and autophagy. [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30806144  (Sharma et al. 2019)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 23-JUL-2019 RD

DDB_G0278009.summary: ''racN'' encodes a guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G protein) of the Rho family of small GTPases. G proteins are key components of signal transduction networks in which they function as molecular signaling switches, binding to GDP in the off state while binding GTP in the on state. Guanine nucleotide-exchange factors (GEFs) promote the exchange of GDP for GTP on Ras GTPases thus activating them, while GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) inactivate Ras GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP. A phylogenetic analysis reveals that RacI ([/gene/DDB_G0277897 racI]), RacM ([/gene/DDB_G0289103 racM]), RacN and RacO ([/gene/DDB_G0277791 racO]) cluster significantly together, suggesting that they might also function in the same processes ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16762450 Vlahou et al. 2006]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 09-JUN-2020 RD

DDB_G0291970.summary:
''Dictyostelium'' cofilin was identified through a search for actin monomer binding proteins ([/ontology/go/0003785/annotation/page/1 actin monomer binding]) in whole cell lysates. A 15 kDa protein was isolated and purified, which was shown to depolimerize actin filaments ([/ontology/go/0030042/annotation/page/1 actin filament depolymerization]) in a dose-dependent manner and to decrease the viscosity of actin filaments. This activity was inhibited by phosphatidylinositides. Cloning the cofilin gene resulted in the identification of 2 identical genes, [/gene/DDB_G0277833 cofA] and ''cofB'' that differed only in their intron and promoter sequence. When promoter activities were tested, only ''cofA'' was found to be expressed, predominantly in vegetative cells. No promoter activity was detected for ''cofB'', suggesting that ''cofB'' might be a pseudogene. This data is in conflict with the fact that several ESTs have been detected for this gene. Attempts to delete the ''cofA'' gene failed, while deletion of ''cofB'' yielded mutants with no detectable phenotype. This confirmed that ''cofB'' is not expressed and suggested that ''cofA'' is an essential gene [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7738034 (Aizawa et al., 1995) ].
Overexpression of ''cofA'' was shown to stimulate bundling of actin filaments ([/ontology/go/0051017/annotation/page/1 actin filament bundle formation]) in alpha-actinin ([/gene/DDB_G0268632 abpA]) -induced actin latticeworks, probably by severing the filaments [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8636212 (Aizawa et al., 1996) ]. In overexpressing cells also showed that cofilin, together with the actin-interacting protein [/gene/DDB_G0278733 DAip1], plays a pivotal role in reorganizing the actin bundles in response to hyperosmotic stress ([/ontology/go/0006972/annotation/page/1 hyperosmotic response]) [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10421841 (Aizawa et al., 1999) ]. To investigate the actin depolimerization activity of cofilin further, Ichetovkin ''et al.'' showed, by two independent methods, that both native and recombinant cofilin sever actin filaments ([/ontology/go/0006972/annotation/page/1 hyperosmotic response]), but to different extents [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10744862 (Ichetovkin et al., 2000) ].
Recently, cofilin was found to be dependent on the MADS box transcription factor [/gene/DDB_G0281387 srfA]. The authors found an expression profile of cofilin that differed from that published for ''cofA''. While ''cofA'' expression was originally tested by promoter activity and later confirmed by western blot, this analysis was done by Northern blot. As a consequence of the discrepancy the authors referred in their paper not to cofilin A ([/gene/DDB_G0277833 cofA]), but to the identical cofilin B [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15075287 (Escalante et al., 2004) ].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 21-MAY-2004 PF

DDB_G0286119.summary: The ''tagB'' gene was recovered from a REMI mutant that was blocked at the tipped aggregate stage ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7744252 Shaulsky et al. 1995)]. TagB is a composite protein with an amino-terminal serine protease section and a carboxy-terminal ABC transporter section. TagB processes the secreted precursor of Spore Differentiation Factor 1 (SDF-1) to generate the active phosphopeptide signal that prepares prespore and prestalk cells for terminal differentiation ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21602484 Anjard et al. 2011)]. Expression of ''tagB'' starts at 4 hours of development and is restricted to prestalk cells in slugs. Development of ''tagB'' null mutants is blocked at the tipped aggregate stage and neither spores nor stalk cells are made. The mutant phenotype is non-cell autonomous as shown by rescue of spore and stalk formation in the mutant cells by co-developing wild type cells. The wild type cells would be expected to generate SDF-1 in the extracellular space that could signal nearby ''tagB'' null mutant cells. Tandem duplications on chromosome 4 generated ''tagB'', ([/gene/DDB_G0286121 tagC]), and ([/gene/DDB_G0286123 tagD]) which all encode membrane-embedded proteases ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12456012 Anjard and Loomis, 2002)]. The amino acid sequences of TagB and TagC are highly similar but they process different proteins into different signals.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 17-MAY-2016 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0289655.summary: The ABC superfamily of genes is one of the largest in the genomes of both bacteria and eukaryotes. The proteins encoded by these genes all carry a characteristic 200- to 250-amino-acid ATP-binding cassette that gives them their family name ([/ontology/go/0042626/annotation/page/1 ATPase activity, coupled to transmembrane movement of substances]). In bacteria they are mostly involved in nutrient import, while in eukaryotes many are involved in export ([/ontology/go/0006810/annotation/page/1 transport]). Seven different families have been defined in eukaryotes based on sequence homology, domain topology, and function. Sequences from the well-advanced ''Dictyostelium'' genome project have allowed to recognize 71 members of this superfamily (including one on the chromosome 2 duplication). The ABCG family is characterized by the ABC domain preceding the transmembrane domain ([/ontology/go/0016021/annotation/page/1 integral to membrane]). All of the members of this family in animals are half-transporters while all of the fungal members are full transporters with two ABC-transmembrane units. No members of this family are found in bacteria. ''Dictyostelium'' and ''Arabidopsis'' have members of both types ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12456012 Anjard and Loomis 2002]). Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 18-OCT-2004 PG

DDB_G0267650.summary: During endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress, unfolded proteins accumulate in the ER lumen. A highly regulated pathway known as the unfolded protein response (UPR) has evolved to restore ER homeostasis. The putative serine/threonine protein kinase ''ireA'' is orthologous to the highly conserved IRE1 gene which is involved in the regulation of the UPR. IreA was found to localize to the ER, and ''ireA'' null cells fail to cope with ER stress, displaying lysed cells with poor growth and collapsed ER cisternae. In addition, IreA participates in an ER stress-induced transcriptional response which modulates the levels of a diverse set of transcripts. In control cells, ER stress triggers autophagy and autophagy is also induced in ''ireA'' null cells, demonstrating that ''ireA'' is not required for autophagy induction. However in ''ireA'' cells, autophagosomes are persistent, abnormal and trapped at the ER, suggesting that they are unable to degrade autophagic cargoes and that IreA-mediated recovery of ER homeostasis is required to achieve a fully functional autophagy-dependent degradation ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29632077 Ongay-Larios et al. 2018]), ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29890774 Dominguez-Martin et al. 2018]). Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 24-OCT-2019 RD

DDB_G0279925.summary:
The ''mlkA'' gene encodes the myosin light chain kinase (MLCK-A). The MLCK-A was purified, and found to phosphorylate ([/ontology/go/0004672/annotation/page/1 protein kinase activity]) the ''Dictyostelium'' RMLC (myosin regulatory light chain, [/gene/DDB_G0276077 mlcR]) with high specificity [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3032987 (Griffith et al., 1987)]. RMLC phosphorylation occurs only on serine residues ([/ontology/go/0004674/annotation/page/1 protein serine/threonine kinase activity]) [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3029131 (Berlot et al., 1987)] and S13 has been identified as the phosphorylation site [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7806572 (Ostrow et al., 1994)].
Despite the high sequence similarity of ''mlkA'' with calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinases, including myosin light chain kinases from higher eukaryotes, it was shown that there is neither a calmodulin binding domain ([/ontology/go/0005516/annotation/page/1 calmodulin binding])in the ''mlkA'' sequence, nor calcium/camodulin-dependent activation ([/ontology/go/0004685/annotation/page/1 calcium- and calmodulin-dependent protein kinase activity]) of the kinase [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1651931 (Tan & Spudich, 1991)]. In fact, in ''Dictyostelium'' whole cell lysates as well as in ammonium sulfate fractions, no calcium/calmodulin-regulated MLCK-A activity was detected [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2380188 (Tan & Spudich, 1990)]. However, two activation mechanisms of the MLCK-A have been identified: autophosphorylation at T289 ([/ontology/go/0046777/annotation/page/1 protein amino acid autophosphorylation]) in the C-terminal autoinhibitory domain, and phosphorylation in the activation loop at T166 by a yet unidentified kinase [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8947030 (Smith et al., 1996a)]. Although the Dictyostelium MLCK kinase has not been identified, rat calcium-calmodulin-dependent protein kinase kinase can be used as a surrogate activator of MLCK-A, phosphorylating it on Thr-166 [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14570871 (Tokumitsu et al., 2004)]. Residues 283-288 function as an autoinhibitory sequence, and although autoinhibition is fully relieved by T166 phosphorylation, removal of the autoinhibitory domain alone does not generate maximum enzymatic activity. Thus phosphorylation of T166 by an upstream kinase releases autoinhibition and increases the catalytic activity of the MLCK-A.
Early studies found that cAMP stimulation ([/ontology/go/0019933/annotation/page/1 cAMP-mediated signaling]) increases RMLC phosphorylation due to a transient activitation of the MLCK-A [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/3029131 (Berlot et al., 1987)]. Liu and Newell reported that the MLCK-A in cGMP-deficient mutant strains failed to phosphorylate the RMLC in response to cAMP, implicating cGMP in the regulation of MLCK-A activity [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7983143 (Liu & Newell, 1996)]. More recently it was shown that MLCK-A activation through T166 phosphorylation is indirectly activated by cGMP ([/ontology/go/0019934/annotation/page/1 cGMP-mediated signaling]) [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9789030 (Silveira et al., 1998)].
A ''mlkA''-null mutant was generated, and, grown in suspension, showed a slight cytokinesis defect ([/ontology/go/0000910/annotation/page/1 cytokinesis]). The defect became more severe when cells were grown with heat-killed bacteria. However, the cytokinesis inefficiency is mild in comparison to [/gene/DDB_G0276077 mlcR] and [/gene/DDB_G0286355 mhcA] mutants. Also, different from those mutants, ''mlkA''-null cells were able to complete development. Because there is still phosphorylated RMLC present in ''mlkA''-null mutants, it has been suggested that there is at least one more kinase that phosphorylates the RMLC [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8901579 (Smith et al., 1996b)]. However, it has been shown that MLCK-A is the only kinase that is responsible for RMLC phosphorylation during chemotaxis ([/ontology/go/0050920/annotation/page/1 regulation of chemotaxis]), and that this process is activated by cGMP and [/gene/DDB_G0291079 gbpC] [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16546177 (Goldberg et al., 2006)].
MLCK-A is in the CAMK group of the protein kinase superfamily. It is 48-51% identical to four other putative ''Dictyostelium'' CAM kinases ([/gene/DDB_G0275057 DDB_G0275057], [/gene/DDB_G0271550 DDB_G0271550], [/gene/DDB_G0282429 DDB_G0282429], [/gene/DDB_G0292624 DDB_G0292624]). However, it is not known whether one or more of these kinases represents other MLCK(s), or if the other ''Dictyostelium'' MLCK enzyme(s) are more distantly related.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 09-FEB-2006 PF

DDB_G0289967.summary: Sirtuins are evolutionarily conserved NAD-dependent protein deacetylases which play important roles in various biological processes. ''Dictyostelium'' Sir2D localizes to the nucleus and was found to be expressed throughout growth and development. Deletion of ''sir2D'' revealed a variety of defects in growth, development and autophagy. ''sir2D'' null cells have smaller aggregates, multi-tipped mounds, and display defects in both prestalk and prespore cell differentiation. Sir2D regulates the expression of several autophagy-related genes and ''sir2D'' null cells shows reduced autophagic flux. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/27528044 Lohia et al. 2016)]. RNAi-mediated knockdown ''sirD'' cells have a delayed development phenotype and interact with the transcription factor MybB ([/gene/DDB_G0275445 mybB]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/31016257 Taniura et al. 2019)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 01-MAY-2019 RD

DDB_G0277539.summary:
The wee1 family of tyrosine kinases ([/ontology/go/0004713/annotation/page/1 protein-tyrosine kinase activity]) were originally identified in a screen formutants that undergo mitosis at a reduced cell size in the fission yeast ''Schizosaccharomycespombe'' ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7262540 Nurse and Thuriaux 1980]). Since then, members ofthe wee1 family have been shown to play an essential role in cell cycle regulation ([/ontology/go/0000074/annotation/page/1 regulation of progression through cell cycle]) in several other organisms, including thebudding yeast ''Saccharomyces cerevisiae'', the African clawed frog ''Xenopus laevis'', andseveral metazoans ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14625382 reviewed in Kellogg 2003]).
Wee1 phosphorylates a specific tyrosine residue on the mitosis promoting protein Cdk1/Cdc2/Cdc28 ([/gene/DDB_G0272813 cdk1] in ''Dictyostelium''). Phosphorylation of this residue by Wee1 inhibits Cdk1/Cdc2/Cdc28,thereby delaying entry into mitosis from G2. Cdk1/Cdc2/Cdc28 is inactivated by dephosphorylation of thetyrosine residue by the phosphatase Cdc25/Mih1 ([/gene/DDB_G0283617 cdc25] in ''Dictyostelium''), allowingentry into mitosis ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14625382 reviewed in Kellogg 2003]).
Three uncharacterized putative wee1 family members exist in the ''Dictyostelium'' genome: [/gene/DDB_G0291842 DDB_G0291842], [/gene/DDB_G0277539 DDB_G0277539], and [/gene/DDB_G0291133 DDB_G0291133]. Interestingly, ''Schizosaccharomyces pombe'' and animals also have three wee1 family kinases: wee1, mik1, and myt1.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 21-MAY-2004 KP

DDB_G0269248.summary:
Developing ''Dictyostelium'' cells aggregate to form fruiting bodies containing typically 2 x 10(4) cells. To prevent the formation of an excessively large fruiting body, streams of aggregating cells break up into groups if there are too many cells. The breakup is regulated by a secreted complex of polypeptides called counting factor (CF) . CF is composed of 4 polypeptides, including Countin (encoded by the [/gene/DDB_G0274597 ctnA] gene), cf50, [/gene/DDB_G0269248 cf45-1] and [/gene/DDB_G0284363 cf60]. The amino acid sequence of CF45-1 has some similarity to lysozymes, but recombinant CF45-1 has no detectable lysozyme activity. Disrupting the cf45-1 gene results in the formation of large groups when cells are grown with bacteria on agar plates and then starve. However, unlike ''ctnA-'' and ''cf50-'' cells, ''cf45-1-'' cells sometimes form smaller groups than wild-type cells when the cells are starved on filter pads. In the exudates from starved cells, CF45-1 is present in an about 450-kDa fraction that also contains countin and CF50, suggesting that it is part of a complex. Recombinant CF45-1 decreases group size in colonies of ''cf45-1-'' cells, as well as in colonies of wild-type and ''cf50-'' cells. Like ''ctnA-'' and ''cf50-'' cells, ''cf45-1-'' cells have high levels of cytosolic glucose, high cell-cell adhesion, and low cell motility. Together, the data suggest that CF45-1 participates in group size regulation [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12912898 (Brock et al. 2003)]. CF and group size have also been mathematically modeled [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16371424 (Dallon et al. 2006)], which together with experimental evidence has been reviewed in [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18426773 Jang and Gomer 2008].
Recent studies classified all lysozymes in ''Dictyostelium''. CF50 and CF45-1 have been assigned to belong to the Entamoeba-type lysozyme family that contain a GH25 domain. Like the other family members ([/gene/DDB_G0274181 lyEh1], [/gene/DDB_G0293492 lyEh2], [/gene/DDB_G0293566 lyEh3], [/gene/DDB_G0276439 lyEh4]), CF50 and CF45-1 have the three conserved Asp and Glu residues, though these counting factor proteins have shown only little, if any lysozyme activity [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/32061941 (Lamrabet et al. 2020)]Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 13-APR-2020 PF

DDB_G0271734.summary:
''rapgap1'' encodes a Rap GTPase-activating protein (GAP, rapGAP). RapGAPs are key components of signal transduction networks in which they inactivate Rap GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP. RapGAP1 belongs to the Rap/Ran-GAP superfamily. ''rapgap1'' is expressed at all stages of development. Upon uniform cAMP stimulation, cytosolic RapGAP1 translocates to the cell cortex, and in chemotaxing cells RapGAP1 preferentially localizes to the leading edge. RapGAP1 binds to cortexillin ctxA ([/gene/DDB_G0289483 ctxA]), and CtxA negatively regulates the cortical localization of RapGAP1. ''rapgap1'' null cells show extended kinetics of chemoattractant-mediated Rap1 ([/gene/DDB_G0291237 rapA]) activation and exhibit a moderate increase in the level of Rap1-GTP, indicating that RapGAP1 has specific GAP activity for RapA.
''rapgap1'' null cells are more flattened and spread that wild type (wt) cells and have a significant increase in cell-substrate attachment, while cells overexpressing RapGAP1 have a defect in cell-substrate attachment. In addition, ''rapgap1'' null cells have decreased myosin II assembly and aberrant F-actin levels. ''rapgap1'' null cells move slower than wt cells in a cAMP chemoattractant gradient; whereas mutant cells overexpressing RapGAP1 move at a higher speed, indicating a defect in chemotaxis to cAMP. These results indicate that ''rapgap1'' is involved in the regulation of cell adhesion, chemotaxis and myoII assembly through the mediation of RapA activation ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18039932 Jeon et al. 2007]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 28-MAR-2022 RD

DDB_G0282373.summary: ''gbpD'' (''gefU'') encodes a 144 kDa protein that has a conserved RasGEF domain near the N-terminus followed by a cyclic nucleotide binding domain that has lost affinity to cyclic nucleotides [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12011437  (Goldberg et al. 2002)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12952076  (Bosgraaf et al. 2002)]. The domain arrangement is similar to that in the second half of GbpC ([/gene/DDB_G0291079 gbpC]). ''gbpD'' is expressed throughout growth and development, with highest levels of expression between 8 and 12 hours of development ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16086850 Wilkins et al. 2005)]. The phenotype of mutants that have lost GbpD is almost opposite that of mutants that have lost GbpC; ''gbpD'' null mutants are hyperpolarized, make few lateral pseudopods and have improved chemotaxis. Overexpression of ''gbpD'' results in cells that are unable to polarize, extend many lateral pseudopodia and are greatly impaired in chemotaxis to cAMP, much like gbpC null mutants, suggesting that overexpressed GbpD might block the function of GbpC [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15827084  (Bosgraaf et al. 2005)]. Consistent with this interaction, the phenotype of double mutants lacking both GbpC and GbpD is indistinguishable from that of cells lacking only GbpC [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12952076  (Bosgraaf et al. 2002)]. Moreover, GbpD is an exchange factor for the small GTPase Rap1 ([/gene/DDB_G0291237 rapA]) which binds to the Ras-binding domain of PI3K ([/gene/DDB_G0278727 pikA], [/gene/DDB_G0283081 pikB], and [/gene/DDB_G0275011 pikC]) and stimulates its activity [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16769729  (Kortholt et al. 2006)], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20089846  (Kortholt et al. 2010)]. Rap1-GTP is found preferentially at the leading edge of cells migrating chemotactically. Cells overexpressing GbpD have high levels of PIP3 in the membrane resulting in the formation of multiple lateral pseudopods and increased cell-substratum adhesion. However, overexpression of GbpD in pikA/pikB null cells does not induce the cell-substratum adhesion or multiple lateral pseudopods phenotypes, indicating that a GbpD/RapA/PI3K pathway helps control pseudopod formation and cell polarity. [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20089846  (Kortholt et al. 2010)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 08-JUN-2021 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0285051.summary: ''rab32D'' encodes a guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G protein) of the Rab family of small GTPases. G proteins are key components of signal transduction networks in which they function as molecular signaling switches, binding to GDP in the off state while binding GTP in the on state. Guanine nucleotide-exchange factors (GEFs) promote the exchange of GDP for GTP on Rab GTPases thus activating them, while GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) inactivate Rab GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP. DDB_G0279151.summary: ''cenB'' encodes a centrin which is 51% identical to CenA but is not localized to the centrosome. CenB is found throughout the nucleus in interphase cells but disappears as the cells enter mitosis even though the nuclear envelop does not fully breakdown during mitosis [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/20539780  (Mana-Capelli et al. 2010)]. Cells lacking CenB have enlarged nuclei with protrusions of the envelop and abnormal centrosome-nucleus anchoring. There are also supernumerary centrosomes and defects in the organization of the microtubule-organizing center (MTOC) in the mutant cells. CenB appears to be required to maintain nuclear architecture during interphase and to be part of the machinery that regulates centrosome duplication. [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19465563  (Mana-Capelli et al. 2009)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 18-DEC-2017 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0287679.summary: TSET is the latest addition to trafficking proteins, which is ancient but frequently lost or reduced in evolution. The TSET complex is a heterohexamer and was named for the protein subunits in the complex, TSPOON (sigma-like), TPLATE (beta-like), TCUP (mu-like), TSAUCER (alpha, beta, gamma, delta, epsilon, zeta-like), TTRAY1, and TTRAY2. This ancient adaptor complex (AP) was identified in organisms such as Dictyostelids and land plants, such as ''Arabidopsis''. Only the TCUP subunit has been retained in fungi and animals, in mammals it has evolved into the cargo adaptor muniscin. A TSPOON-GFP fusion (gene tstD) has been shown to physically bind the 5 other TSET subunits. The TTRAY subunits are beta-propeller / alpha-solenoid proteins and form the scaffold for the TSPOON, TPLATE, TCUP, TSAUCER, heterotetramer. TIRF microscopy showed a punctate temporary localization of the complex to the plasma membran [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24867644  (Hirst et al. 2014)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated,, 11-DEC-2018 PF

DDB_G0280495.summary: Fumarate hydratase is an enzyme of the [/ontology/go/0006099/annotation/page/1 tricarboxylic acid cycle] that hydrates fumarate into malate ([/ontology/go/0004333/annotation/page/1 fumarate hydratase activity]). The holoenzyme consists of a homotetramer. While bacteria have 3 different fumarases there is one in ''Dictyostelium'' and animals, which belong to the class-II fumarase family and are found in the [/ontology/go/0005739/annotation/page/1 mitochondrion] and in the [/ontology/go/0005737/annotation/page/1 cytoplasm]. In rat it has been shown that the mitochondrial and cytosolic fumarases are synthesized from the same mRNA by alternative translational initiation [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1633825  (Suzuki et al., 1992)]. ESTs support that there are two isoforms in ''Dictyostelium''. The longer isoform contains a putative mitochondrial targeting sequence that is absent in the cytosolic isoform, which is 19 amino acids shorter at the N-terminus.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 01-FEB-2005 PF

DDB_G0270838.summary:
Histones form the nucleosomal core ([/ontology/go/0000786/annotation/page/1 nucleosome]) ([/ontology/go/0006334/annotation/page/1 nucleosome assembly]) that is fundamental to chromatin structure (). The histone octamer is composed of an H3-H4 tetramer (two H3-H4 dimers) coupled with an H2A-H2Btetramer (two H2A-H2B dimers). The histone H1 linker protein plays a role in packaging nucleosomes into the 30 nmfiber found in chromatin ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9177486 Bukenberger et al. 1992]).
In ''Dictyostelium discoideum'' and ''Saccharomyces cerevisiae'', only one copy of histone [/gene/DDB_G0285319 H1] appears to be present, in comparison to other eukaryotes which have multiple copies and subtypes([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7867938 Hauser et al. 1995], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9046096 Ushinsky et al.1997]). Two putative H2A family members, [/gene/DDB_G0279667 H2AX] and [/gene/DDB_G0286747 H2AZ], and three H2Adomain-containing proteins, [/gene/DDB_G0289187 H2Av1], [/gene/DDB_G0289193 H2Av2], [/gene/DDB_G0289197 H2Av3], are present in ''Dictyostelium''. Two H2B domain-containing proteins also exist inthe ''Dicty'' genome: [/gene/DDB_G0293758 H2Bv1] and [/gene/DDB_G0276273 H2Bv2]. There are three histone H3proteins, [/gene/DDB_G0267402 H3a] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9177486 Bukenberger et al. 1992]), [/gene/DDB_G0270838 H3b], and [/gene/DDB_G0271092 H3c], and two H3 domain-containing proteins, [/gene/DDB_G0291185 H3v1] and [/gene/DDB_G0277979 H3v2]. We have also identified two histone H4proteins, [/gene/DDB_G0277183 H4a] and [/gene/DDB_G0276863 H4b], which have identical protein sequences but non-identical nucleotide sequences.
The three H3 histones present in the ''Dictyostelium'' genome are highly similar to H3 histones in othereukaryotes, including mammalian sequences. [/gene/DDB_G0270838 H3b] and [/gene/DDB_G0271092 H3c] encode proteins 136 amino acids in length, theconserved length for H3, whereas [/gene/DDB_G0267402 H3a] has a 3 amino acid insert compared to other sequences ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9177486 Bukenberger et al. 1992]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 13-APR-2004 KP

DDB_G0283603.summary: ''rab32A'' (''rabE'') encodes a guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G protein) of the Rab family of small GTPases. G proteins are key components of signal transduction networks in which they function as molecular signaling switches, binding to GDP in the off state while binding GTP in the on state. Guanine nucleotide-exchange factors (GEFs) promote the exchange of GDP for GTP on Rab GTPases thus activating them, while GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) inactivate Rab GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP. Rab32A is similar to human RAB32 and human RAB38 which are involved in the regulation of phagosome maturation. Rab32A is also similar to ([/gene/DDB_G0269416 rab32B]) and ([/gene/DDB_G0275675 rab32C]). ''rab32A'' is expressed at very low levels during growth, but expression increases significantly after 8 hours of development, suggesting a role for ''rab32'' during development [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10025509  (Norian et al. 1999)]. Proteomic analysis reveals that Rab32A is localized to phagocytic vesicles ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16926386 Gotthardt, et al. 2006]) lipid droplets ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24036346 Du, et al. 2013]) and also to the Legionella-containing vacuole [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28183814  (Schmolders et al. 2017)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 02-OCT-2020 RD

''gefB'' encodes a Ras guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF, RasGEF). rasGEFs are key components of signaling networks in which they activate Ras family small GTPases by promoting the exchange of GDP for GTP. ''gefB'' is expressed throughout growth and development in AX3 cells, with maximal expression after 8 hours of starvation ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11102804 Wilkins et al. 2000)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16086850 Wilkins et al. 2005)]. ''gefB'' expression also increases during sexual development ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15740584 Ishida et al. 2005)]. The similarity in phenotypes of ''gefB'' and ''rasS'' ([/gene/DDB_G0283537 rasS]) null mutants, and the observation that the phenotypes of ''gefB''/''rasS'' double null cells are no more severe than either parent suggests that RasS is activated by GefB ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11102804 Wilkins et al. 2000)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12854977 King and Insall et al. 2003)].
''gefB'' is involved in signaling pathways regulating motility and macropinocytosis. ''Dictyostelium'' cells in which the ''gefB'' gene is disrupted move unusually rapidly but are unable to perform macropinocytosis and therefore to grow in liquid medium. Phagocytosis is also significantly decreased in ''gefB'' null cells. ''gefB'' null cells are strikingly more flattened, elongate, polarized and dominated by a single large lamella in which F-actin is concentrated. Aggregation is delayed in ''gefB'' null cells and the mutants do not form aggregation streams. Mutant cells form few, small but normally proportioned fruiting bodies ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11102804 Wilkins et al. 2000]). ''gefB'' null cells extend blebs more frequently than wt cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26317626 Sugiyama et al. 2015]). In ''gefB'' null cells generated in an AX2 background, there is no macropinocytosis defect compared with ''gefB'' null cells generated in an AX3 background ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30967009 Williams et al. 2019]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 23-MAR-2021 RD

DDB_G0292804.summary: ''arcC'' encodes the 21 kDa subunit of the Arp2/3 complex [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11807934  (Insall et al. 2001)]. The seven subunits of this 200 kDa complex are encoded by ([/gene/DDB_G0277825 arcA]), ([/gene/DDB_G0282813 arcB]), ''arcC'', ([/gene/DDB_G0269102 arcD]), ([/gene/DDB_G0288319 arcE]), ([/gene/DDB_G0272106 arpB]) and ([/gene/DDB_G0283755 arpC]). The subunits of mammalian Arp2/3 are very similar to ''Dictyostelium'' homologs. Arp2/3 binds to the side of F-actin filaments and initiates polymerization of a new F-actin chain at an angle of 70 degrees leading to a branched actin network that can alter the shape of cells. The ability to nucleate new actin filaments is greatly stimulated by direct interactions with members of the WASP/SCAR family [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11807934  (Insall et al. 2001)]. The Arp2/3 complex largely mediates the actin polymerization response to chemotactic stimulation and contributes to cell motility, pseudopod extension and adhesion in Dictyostelium chemotaxis. The complete Arp2/3 complex is essential for growth; partial loss of activity of either ArcB or ArpB impairs growth and chemotaxis [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/17553489  (Langridge and Kay, 2007)]. mRNA from each of the genes encoding Arp2/3 subunits accumulates coordinately to reach a peak at 3 hours of development and gradually decreases thereafter [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25887420  (Rosengarten et al. 2015)]. The Arp2/3 complex interacts with the protein CARMIL, which serves as a scaffold for the assembly of a larger complex of proteins involved in the nucleation and termination of actin filament assembly. The complex consists of CARMIL ([/gene/DDB_G0292386 carmil]), AcpA, ([/gene/DDB_G0267374 acpA]) AcpB, ([/gene/DDB_G0272104 acpB]) the Arp2/3 complex, and type I myosins MyoB ([/gene/DDB_G0289117 myoB]) and MyoC ([/gene/DDB_G0276617 myoC]) [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11425877  (Jung et al. 2001)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 23-MAY-2019 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0284891.summary:
DNA-dependent RNA polymerase catalyzes the transcription of DNA into RNA using the four ribonucleoside triphosphates as substrates ([/ontology/go/0003899/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase activity]). Three distinct zinc-containing RNA polymerases are found in eukaryotic nuclei: [/gene/DDB_G0275759 rpa1] for the ribosomal RNA precursor ([/ontology/go/0006360/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase I promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005736/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase I complex]), [/gene/DDB_G0279193 rpb1] for the mRNA precursor ([/ontology/go/0006366/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase II promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005665/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase II, core complex]), and [/gene/DDB_G0277199 rpc1] for 5S and tRNA genes ([/ontology/go/0006383/annotation/page/1 transcription from RNA polymerase III promoter]), ([/ontology/go/0005666/annotation/page/1 DNA-directed RNA polymerase III complex]).
RNA polymerase II is composed of 12 subunits: [/gene/DDB_G0279193 rpb1], [/gene/DDB_G0288257 rpb2], [/gene/DDB_G0292244 rpb3], [/gene/DDB_G0282739 rpb4], [/gene/DDB_G0291636 rpb5], [/gene/DDB_G0291037 rpb6], [/gene/DDB_G0284891 rpb7], [/gene/DDB_G0278039 rpb8], [/gene/DDB_G0268306 rpb9], [/gene/DDB_G0272036 rpb10], [/gene/DDB_G0277677 rpb11], and[/gene/DDB_G0283365 rpb12]. Subunits 5, 6, 8, 10, and 12 are common to all threeRNA polymerases (reviewed by [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9618449 Hampsey] in 1998).
The ''Dictyostelium rpb7'' gene has been shown to be a functional homologue of ''Saccharomyces cerevisiae RPB7'' by its ability to rescue the defects of a null mutant in the ''RPB4'' gene ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/14704357 Singh et al. 2004]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 09-APR-2004 PG

DDB_G0268744.summary:
There are 29 genes encoding actin in ''Dictyostelium'' with amino acid identity greater than 83%, ''act1''-''act29''. Seventeen of these genes encode identical proteins: [/gene/DDB_G0289553 act1], [/gene/DDB_G0274133 act2], [/gene/DDB_G0289005 act4], [/gene/DDB_G0289663 act5], [/gene/DDB_G0274135 act6], [/gene/DDB_G0280545 act7], [/gene/DDB_G0269234 act8], [/gene/DDB_G0274601 act9], [/gene/DDB_G0288879 act11], [/gene/DDB_G0274129 act12], [/gene/DDB_G0274599 act13], [/gene/DDB_G0274137 act14], [/gene/DDB_G0272520 act15], [/gene/DDB_G0272248 act16], [/gene/DDB_G0274727 act19], [/gene/DDB_G0274285 act20], and [/gene/DDB_G0274561 act21], while [/gene/DDB_G0289811 act10], [/gene/DDB_G0275023 act22], and [/gene/DDB_G0289487 act3] respectively have 1, 4 and 11 amino acid differences compared to the 17 identical genes. The proteins encoded by [/gene/DDB_G0274131 act17], [/gene/DDB_G0289489 act18], [/gene/DDB_G0268744 act23] and [/gene/DDB_G0289505 act24]are more divergent.
Actin is a major [/ontology/go/0005200/annotation/page/1 structural constituent of cytoskeleton]. Actin is one of the most abundant proteins in ''Dictyostelium'', constituting approximately 8% of the total protein in vegetative cells ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/561722 Alton and Lodish et al. 1977]).Actin synthesis is developmentally regulated, peaking shortly after starvation (reviewed by [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6894564 Firtel] in 1981). The different actin genes differ in their levels of expression, with [/gene/DDB_G0274135 act6], [/gene/DDB_G0269234 act8] and [/gene/DDB_G0274129 act12] being highly expressed both during growth and development compared to [/gene/DDB_G0289005 act4], [/gene/DDB_G0289663 act5], [/gene/DDB_G0280545 act7] and [/gene/DDB_G0272248 act16] ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/6286214 McKeown and Firtel 1981]). Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 19-SEP-2003 PG

The DIC constituents were determined to be [/gene/DDB_G0285995 pdsA], the novel proteins [/gene/DDB_G0278581 psiF] and [/gene/DDB_G0267470 dicB], and an unknown protein. Both PdsA and DicB are dispensable for discoidin expression, whereas the DicA1 protein isa strong activator of discoidin transcription. DicA1 contains a PA14 (anthrax protective antigen) domain known to be involved in [/ontology/go/0030246/annotation/page/1 carbohydrate binding] and several '' Dictyostelium'' (CTDC) repeats, which exist in several proteins found in the [/ontology/go/0005576/annotation/page/1 extracellular region]. The DicB protein, however, contains no conserved functional domains([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15947191 Kolbinger et al. 2005]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 14-NOV-2005 KP

The [/gene/DDB_G0285211 fadA] gene was originally identified by [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10504413 Saito and Ochiai (1999)] in a search for ESTs containing the conserved histidine-box domain found in proteins capable of unsaturated fatty acid metabolic processes.. Overexpression of the FadA protein and subsequent analysis by mass spectrometry revealed that thisprotein is specific for 5-Delta desaturation of C16 and C18 fatty acids. A second desaturase,[/gene/DDB_G0282147 fadB], was later identified by [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10712614 Saito and colleagues (2000)].Similar experiments with the FadB protein show a specificity for the 5 position in C18 fatty acids.
Null mutants of ''fadB'' show no detectable phenotype, whereas ''fadA-'' cells have an increased toleranceto higher temperatures during development compared to wild type. This is indicative of the importance of membrane fluidity, which is regulated byfatty acid modification of desaturases such as FadA and FadB ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15632431 Saito et al.2005]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 07-JUN-2021 PF

DDB_G0291235.summary: ''ranA'' belongs to the Ras superfamily of small GTPases but is only distantly related to other Ras proteins within this superfamily. Ran family GTPases are GTP-binding proteins which regulate receptor-mediated transport between the nucleus and cytoplasm. They are required for the import of proteins into the nucleus and export of RNA from the nucleus. ''ranA'' is an ortholog of human RAN which encodes GTP-binding nuclear protein Ran and which is involved in nucleocytoplasmic transport. RanBP ([/gene/DDB_G0287391 ranbp1]) is an ortholog of human RANBP1 and likely serves as an effector protein contributing to the activation of RanA. Northern analysis indicates that ''ranA'' is expressed at relatively high levels during growth phase, but at significantly reduced levels late in development ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8479927 Bush and Cardelli, 1993]). Tandem affinity purification identified an interaction between ranA and CP224 (cepJ) ([/gene/DDB_G0268616 cepJ]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15548420 Graf et al. 2004]) and proteomic analysis identified RanA as a component of the centrosome ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16512674 Reinders et al. 2006]), suggesting that RanA may play a role in cytokinesis. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25496424 Hilbi et al. 2014]). Proteomic analysis revealed that RanA is found in Legionella-containing vacuoles ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/19482547 Shevchuk et al. 2009]), ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/18980612 Urwyler et al. 2009]), ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24373249 Hoffmann et al. 2013]) and ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/28183814 Schmolders et al. 2017]). Studies using human RAN in ''Dictyostelium'' cells reveal that RAN is activated by the ''Legionella pneumophila'' Icm/Dot substrate LegG1. Ran activation by LegG1 leads to microtubule stabilization and promotes intracellular pathogen vacuole motility and bacterial growth ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25496424 Hilbi et al. 2014]). Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 28-APR-2021 RD

DDB_G0282905.summary: A comprehensive study classified all lysozymes in ''Dictyostelium''. In addition to the 5 known amoeba type lysozymes ([/gene/DDB_G0275123 alyA], [/gene/DDB_G0275119 alyB], [/gene/DDB_G0275121 alyC], [/gene/DDB_G0273197 alyD-1] and [/gene/DDB_G0286229 alyL] ), two new related lysozymes in this family have been identified, [/gene/DDB_G0282905 alyE] and [/gene/DDB_G0282893 alyF]. These genes are next to each other and almost identical, thus possibly a more recent gene duplication. In the past, gene models for these two new lysozymes gave rise to proteins with one or two transmembrane domains. Thus they first have been named alyTM1 and alyTM2, respectively. However, new sequence analyses resulted in updated gene models coding for proteins containing a signal peptide like the other 5 aly family members. Alignment of the 7 proteins allowed the identification of one conserved Asp and one Glu residue in the C- terminal portion of each protein, which might represent the amoeba lysozyme active site [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/32061941 (Lamrabet et al. 2020)].Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 22-APR-2020 PF
DDB_G0282905.note: This gene model was previously extended at the 5 prime end and contained 1 transmembrane domain, and the gene has originally been named alyTM1 (PMID:32061941); in accordance with authors the gene model has been updated and is now fully supported by sequence resources and similarity. 22-APR-2020 PF

DDB_G0271344.summary:
IdhA is the ''Dictyostelium'' ortholog of the alpha subunit of mitochondrial ([/ontology/go/5739/annotation/page/1 mitochondrion]) NAD(+-dependent isocitrate dehydrogenase (), which catalyzes the oxidative decarboxylation of isocitrate into alpha-ketoglutarate, the third step in the [/ontology/go/6099/annotation/page/1 tricarboxylic acid cycle].
While the the metazoan enzyme complex is a heterooligomer of subunits alpha, beta, and gamma in the apparent ratio of 2:1:1, the fungal enzyme is a heterodimer of subunits 1 and 2 in equal proportions. In ''Dictyostelium'' one alpha and one beta subunit ([/gene/DDB_G0293872 idhB]) have been identified.
The ''Dictyostelium'' cytosolic and mitochondrial NADP+-dependent isocitrate dehydrogenases ([/gene/DDB_G0272208 idhC], [/gene/DDB_G0272210 idhM]) have also been identified.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 17-JAN-2005 PF

DDB_G0286121.summary: TagC is a composite protein in which a serine protease is attached to an ABC transporter ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7744252 Shaulsky et al. 1995)]. It processes acyl coA-binding protein (AcbA) [/gene/DDB_G0270658 acbA] to generate the 34 amino acid peptide signal Spore Differentiation Factor 2 (SDF-2) that induces rapid sporulation ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9473320 Anjard et al. 1998)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15897458 Anjard and Loomis, 2005)]. The protease domain of TagC is exposed to the external environment when gamma-Aminobutyric acid (GABA) signals through the surface G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR), GrlE ([/gene/DDB_G0291356 grlE]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16672332 Anjard et al. 2006)]. Since secretion of AcbA is also induced by GABA, the two events are coordinated. Expression of ''tagC'' starts at 4 hours of development and is restricted to prestalk cells in slugs. Development of ''tagC'' null mutants is blocked at the tipped aggregate stage and neither spores nor stalk cells are made. The mutant phenotype is non-cell autonomous as shown by rescue of spore and stalk formation in the mutant cells by co-developing wild type cells. The wild type cells would be expected to generate SDF-2 that could signal nearby ''tagC'' null mutant cells. Tandem duplications on chromosome 4 generated ([/gene/DDB_G0286119 tagB]), ''tagC'', and ([/gene/DDB_G0286123 tagD]) which all encode membrane-embedded proteases ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12456012 Anjard and Loomis, 2002)]. The amino acid sequences of TagB and TagC are highly similar but they process different proteins into different signals.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 18-MAY-2016 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0289001.summary:
Single and double knock-out mutants of ''phg2'' and ''pyk3'' generated by [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/24587195 Vu et. al 2014] displayed aberrant transcriptional regulation of STATc and STATc-dependent genes. The absence of Pyk3 and/or Phg2 resulted in diminished or completely abolished increased transcription of STATc-dependent genes in response to sorbitol. In addition, there was reduced STATc phosphorylation and a significant delay in nuclear translocation of STATc in ''phg2'' and ''pyk3'' null cells. These results establish a role for ''pyk3'' in the activation of STATc in response to hyperosmotic conditions.
Extending these results, [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25143406 Araki et. al 2014] show that two tyrosine kinase like enzymes: Pyk2 (SplB) and Pyk3 are involved in the hyper osmotic-induced activation of STATc. A double mutant of ''splB'' and ''pyk3'' is completely unresponsive to hyperosmotic stress-induced activation of STATc. Both Pyk3 and SplB undergo increased autocatalytic phosphorylation when cells are stressed. Pyk3 and STATc were shown to interact. In addition, under stress Pyk3 and SplB accumulate in different parts of the cell: Pyk3 moves from the cytosol to the cortex, whereas SplB accumulates in cytosolic granules that colocalize with PTP3.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 09-APR-2015 RD

DDB_G0288755.summary:
The transcription factor GBF ([/ontology/go/0003700/annotation/page/1 transcription factor activity]), ([/ontology/go/0006357/annotation/page/1 regulation of transcription from RNA polymerase II promoter]) was purified by virtue of its binding to a regulatory element called G-box ([/ontology/go/0003677/annotation/page/1 DNA binding]) [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8125261 (Schnitzler et al. 1994)]. GBF is highly basic and contains two putative zinc fingers. However, ''in vivo'' GBF function requires only one intact zinc finger[http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11397018 (Brown and Firtel 2001)]. Upon starvation, GBF is activated by high cAMP concentration via a G-protein-independent pathway involving [/gene/DDB_G0273397 carA-1], the high-affinity cAMP receptor that regulates aggregation [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7774015 (Schnitzler et al. 1995)].
G boxes are found in the promoters of several postaggregative and cell-type-specific genes, including [/gene/DDB_G0277829 carC], [/gene/DDB_G0276761 cotB], [/gene/DDB_G0277141 cotC], [/gene/DDB_G0290957 cprA], [/gene/DDB_G0279799 cprB], and [/gene/DDB_G0269132 ecmB]([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1321061 Ceccarelli et al. 1992], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2897942 Datta and Firtel 1988], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8482418 Fosnaugh and Loomis 1993], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/9126295 Gollop and Kimmel 1997],[http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2163344 Haberstroh and Firtel 1990], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/1668278 Haberstroh et al. 1991], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2545528 Hjorth et al. 1989], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2159939 1990], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/2843819 Pears and Williams 1988], [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8065317 Powell-Coffman et al. 1994]).Consistent with these data, analysis of the ''gbfA''-null cell line provided additional evidence that GBF is a key component of the development switch between aggregation and multicellular differentiation as a general inducer of postaggregative and cell-type-specific gene expression ([/ontology/go/0007275/annotation/page/1 multicellular organismal development]). The ''gbfA''-null cells aggregate and express pulse-induced genes normally, but as cells reach the loose mound stage, the postaggregative signaling machinery is not induced, and subsequent morphogenesis is not initiated (reviewed by [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10611970 Aubry and Firtel] in 1999). Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 28-MAY-2004 PG

DDB_G0276967.summary:
''racF2'' encodes a guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G protein) of the Rho family of small GTPases. G proteins are key components of signal transduction networks in which they function as molecular signaling switches, binding to GDP in the off state while binding GTP in the on state. Guanine nucleotide-exchange factors (GEFs) promote the exchange of GDP for GTP on Ras GTPases thus activating them, while GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) inactivate Ras GTPases by binding to them and promoting their intrinsic GTPase activity to hydrolyze bound GTP to GDP. GAPA ([/gene/DDB_G0269140 gapA]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/21085675 Mondal et al. 2010]) interacts with and is a possible GAP for RacF2.
RacF2 shares 94 percent sequence identity with another ''Dictyostelium'' Rho GTPase, RacF1 ([/gene/DDB_G0269176 racF1]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10198067 Rivero et al. 1999)]. ''racF2'' mRNA is expressed throughout the life cycle but is most highly expressed during sexual maturation with an almost 100-fold higher level of expression than during asexual development. Analysis of ''racF2'' null and overexpression mutants suggest that the gene affects sexual cell fusion and asexual development through the regulation of EDTA-sensitive cell-cell adhesion. RacF1 and RacF2 are likely to have redundant roles in sexual cell fusion ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16573737 Muramoto et al. 2006]), ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/26940518 Rivero et al. 2016]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 20-MAY-2020 RD

DDB_G0284545.summary: Sphingosine kinase phosphorylates sphingosine to form sphingosine 1-phosphate (S1P), a lipid signaling molecule involved in many varied cellular and physiological processes ([/ontology/go/0017050/annotation/page/1 D-erythro-sphingosine kinase activity], [/ontology/go/0006648/annotation/page/1 dihydrosphingosine-1-P pathway]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15059942 Saba and Hla, 2004]). ''Dictyostelium'', as human, yeast, and other eukaryotes, have two genes coding for sphingosine kinase, [/gene/DDB_G0272522 sgkA] and [/gene/DDB_G0284545 sgkB]. Biochemical properties of the SgkA and SgkB proteins demonstrate that they correspond to the human Sphk1 and Sphk2, respectively. SgkA is localized to the [/ontology/go/0005829/annotation/page/1 cytosol], the [/ontology/go/0005634/annotation/page/1 nucleus], and in some pseudopodia ([/ontology/go/0031143/annotation/page/1 pseudopodium]). Single and double knock outs showed that sphingosine kinase is involved in [/ontology/go/0008284/annotation/page/1 positive regulation of cell proliferation] and in resistance to the chemotherapeutic drug cisplatin ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15643073 Min et al., 2004]). Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 11-FEB-2005 PG

DDB_G0275211.summary: Nascent proteins that contain a signal peptide, and are therefore secreted, are recognized by the[/ontology/go/0005786/annotation/page/1 signal recognition particle, endoplasmic reticulum targeting] (SRP), which is composed of 7S RNA plus [/gene/DDB_G0267622 srp9], [/gene/DDB_G0272590 srp14-1],[/gene/DDB_G0275211 srp19], [/gene/DDB_G0275455 srp54], [/gene/DDB_G0285821 srp68], and [/gene/DDB_G0291412 srp72]. The SRPcontains two domains: the Alu domain (SRP9/14) functions to arrest translational elongation and the Sdomain (SRP54, SRP19, and SRP68/72) plays a role in ribosome-nascent chain (RNC) recognition and SRP receptorbinding. After the RNC is bound, the SRP binds via SRP54 to the SRP receptor, an alpha/beta heterodimermade up of [/gene/DDB_G0277377 srpR] and [/gene/DDB_G0278543 srpRB] in the [/ontology/go/0005783/annotation/page/1 endoplasmic reticulum] (reviewed in [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15718142 Halic and Beckmann 2005] and [http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16092520 Pool2005]).Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 17-NOV-2005 KP

DDB_G0286647.summary: ''ecmD'' encodes a protein, EcmD, that has almost exactly the same size and amino acid sequence as EcmC ([/gene/DDB_G0286663 ecmC]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/7729573 Ti et al. 1995)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11488929 Wang et al. 2001)]. Both of these proteins associate with cellulose in the extracellular matrix (ECM) deposited on the substratum by migrating slugs. However, ''ecmD'' mRNA starts to accumulate at 11 hours of development, 5 hours earlier than ''ecmC'' mRNA ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/25887420 Rosengarten et al. 2015)]. Therefore, it could be an essential component of the sheath formed at the mound stage. ''ecmD'' is a prestalk-specific gene.Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 15-JUL-2016 RD; summary contribution: Bill Loomis

DDB_G0283537.summary:
''rasS'' encodes a guanine nucleotide-binding protein (G protein) of the Ras family of small GTPases. G proteins are key components of signal transduction networks in which they function as molecular signaling switches, binding to GDP in the off state while binding GTP in the on state. Guanine nucleotide-exchange factors (GEFs, rasGEFs) promote the exchange of GDP for GTP on Ras GTPases thus activating them, while GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs, rasGAPs) inactivate Ras GTPases. The similarity in phenotypes of ''rasS'' and RasGEF B ([/gene/DDB_G0269222 gefB]) null mutants suggests that RasS is activated by RasGEF B ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/11102804 Wilkins et al. 2000)], ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/12854977 King and Insall et al. 2003)]. RasS interacts with the protein kinase Phg2 ([/gene/DDB_G0283699 phg2]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/15194808 Gebbie et al. 2004)] and the phosphatidylinositol 3-kinases pikA, ([/gene/DDB_G0278727 pikA]), pikB ([/gene/DDB_G0283081 pikB]) and pikF ([/gene/DDB_G0268548 pikF]) ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23843627 Hoeller et al. 2013)] suggesting that these kinases may be downstream effectors of RasS.
''rasS'' is expressed during vegetative growth ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10652263 Chubb et al. 2000)] with maximum levels detected during aggregation ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/8290260 Daniel et al. 1994)]. ''rasS'' null mutants from a DH1 background are highly polarized and display altered F-actin cytoskeleton organization. They also have severe defects in growth and macropinocytosis, a reduced rate of phagocytosis, and a higher rate of cell motility during growth ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/10652263 Chubb et al. 2000)]. However, ''rasS'' null cells from an AX2 background have opposite phenotypes-decreased cell motility and cell polarity ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/16822579 Pollitt et al. 2006)], no defect in the rate of macropinocytosis but decreased macropinosome formation ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30967009 Williams et al. 2019)]. ''rasS'' null strains created in a non-axenic Ddb strain background have modestly increased cell motility and decreased macropinocytosis ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29847546 Paschke et al. 2018)]. Expression of constitutively active mutants of both RasS and RasG ([/gene/DDB_G0293434 rasG]) in a non-axenic Ddb background causes fluid uptake to more than double ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30967009 Williams et al. 2019)]. In addition, fluid uptake is more strongly reduced in ''rasG''/''rasS'' double null mutants than in ''rasG'' single null mutants, suggesting that RasS and RasG ([/gene/DDB_G0293434 rasG]) are the key Ras proteins involved in macropinocytosis ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/30967009 Williams et al. 2019)]. Taken together, these results suggest that RasS is a positive effector of macropinocytosis and a negative effector of cell movement. ([http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/29847546 Paschke et al. 2018)]. Gene has been comprehensively annotated, 13-MAR-2020 RD
